Chan Master Wuyun Wu of Lin’an Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Chang of Jingci, was a native of the Tiexi region. He ascended the hall and said: "The old fellow Yuetang said: 'To act...'"
When walking, one does not see walking—what is this? When sitting, one does not see sitting—what is this? When putting on clothes, one does not see putting on clothes—what is this?
When eating, one does not see eating—what is this? Although this mountain monk sleeps in the same bed as them, we nevertheless each have our own dreams.
Why is this? Because when walking, one sees walking; when sitting, one sees sitting; when putting on...
When he puts on his robes, one sees him putting on his robes; when he eats his meal, one sees him eating his meal.
There is no principle that is not seen, nor is there anything that can be identified as "what is this? Everyone, tell me: is it the old man’s [view], or is it Wuyun’s?
[He] takes up his staff, strikes once, and says: "Apricots are red, peaches are white, and roses are purple; Yet when asked about the spring breeze, none know it at all."

Chan Master Yuanmiao Chichan of Zhongzhu in Lin’an Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Lingyin Guang. He was the son of the Wang family of Wuzhou. A monk asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off the flow of all streams?
The Master said, "Even Buddhas and Patriarchs have no opening through which to speak. The monk asked, "What is the phrase that covers like a casket? [The Master replied: "..."
The "Heaven and Earth" phrase. The Master said, "It encompasses the earth and fills the heavens. [The monk] asked, "What is the 'phrase of following the waves and riding the currents'?
The Master said, "Sometimes entering the wild weeds; sometimes ascending the solitary peak. Ascending the hall, he said: "At dusk the rooster announces dawn;
At midnight the sun shines bright. Startling the snow-lion, It opens its crimson eyes wide. Ascending the hall, he said: "The plum blossoms of last year..."
The willow of the year; its color and fragrance. [He] lets out a shout. After a long while, he says: "If one does not receive this shout, it is almost as if one were still speaking of the old ways.
Now tell me, after having spoken thus, what then? His eyes bulge out.
Chan Master Lingyan Yuanri of Fuzhou, successor to Chan Master Yuantong Tan, ascended the hall and said: "There is nothing that is not realized; there is nothing that is not attained.
For nine years he faced the wall in vain labor; a three-legged donkey leaps up into the sky; a clay ox enters the sea leaving no trace. Thus it was.
It is truly like this. "Nine times nine is eighty-one" is a leap of the fingers.

Regarding the question asked by a monk of the Dharma successor of Chan Master Haichan of Yuelu, concerning the Master Si Da of Yuyuan in Jingmen Commandery: "What is the single seal that seals the void? The Master said:

"The myriad phenomena are gathered back into the ancient mirror. [The student] asked, "What is 'one seal stamping the water'? The Master said, "The reflection of the autumn moon falls upon a thousand rivers.
[The student] asked, "What is 'one seal stamping the mud'? The Master said, "Observe closely before the patterns have yet arisen."

Chan Master Ji’an Shen of Guangxiao Temple in Wenzhou, a successor in the sixteenth generation under the lineage of Chan Master Miaozhu of Nanyue, was a native of his own prefecture. He ascended the hall and said: "Dragons beget dragons; phoenixes beget phoenixes."
The rat raises its young along the wall. Master Bodhidharma did not understand Zen. Traveling through Wei and visiting Liang, he made nothing but a hollow clamor.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "One-nine, two-nine; meeting, they do not extend their hands. Three-nines make twenty-seven; at the fence-top they blow the *bīlù* flute.
Suddenly I recall Little Śākyamuni, with his twin sons embracing their knees. Do you know? Do you not know? Is it real? Is it not real? Ma!"
[The Master] ascended the hall to deliver a discourse on the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Vimalakīrti remained silent; Samantabhadra spoke at length.
The sages of successive generations have alternately displayed their strengths and weaknesses. Do you not see? In the third month, when the flowers fall, the cuckoo cries out;

every single cry is a drop of blood. [The Master] ascended the hall: The wind whistles, the leaves flutter, the clouds drift in fragments, and the waters stretch boundlessly. Standing alone upon the riverbank...
To whom does he speak as he stands? A flight of two or three wild geese soaring beyond the heavens.
*Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume Thirty-Six;
*Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume Thirty-Seven.
Compiled by the Abbot of Seikan Zen-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (Your Servant) Chōei;
reviewed by the Abbot of Kokaigan-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (Your Servant) Chōkei; presented for imperial inspection.
Dharma heir of Chan Master Shishuang Yuan of the Linji school,
the eleventh generation under Mount Heng.

Chan Master Huanglong Huinan of Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of Xingzhou. He relied upon Ledu Tan-cheng and served as his successor, receiving disciples and spreading the Dharma;
his reputation resounded throughout all quarters. Once, while traveling with Yunfeng Yue through the Western Hills, they conversed at night regarding the Dharma-way of Yunmen.
Feng said, "Although Master Cheng is a successor of Yunmen, his dharma path is different.
The Master questioned him as to why they were different. Feng replied, "Yunmen was like nine-refined cinnabar; it could point iron into gold. Master Cheng was like quicksilver;

it may be admired for its luster, but when placed in the furnace, it flows away. The Master grew angry and threw his pillow at him. The next day, Feng apologized for his transgression and spoke again: "Yunmen..."
The Master’s bearing was like that of a king. "To speak of death is to speak of the lowly," he said. "Master Cheng has a Dharma to bestow upon others; that is the language of death.
Can the language of death truly bring people to life? He then turned and walked away. The Master pulled him back, saying, "If you think so, then who can satisfy your mind?
Feng replied, "Shishuang Yuan’s skillful means surpass those of all other quarters. You ought to go see him; do not let it be too late. The Master [nodded].
He reflected silently to himself: "Master Yue appreciates Cuiyan; this has led me to see Shishuang. What does this have to do with Master Yue? He immediately set out for Shishuang.

On the way, he heard that Ciming was not attending to his duties and had neglected the monastic community. Consequently, he ascended Mount Heng and paid his respects to Xian of Fuyan. Xian appointed him as the Secretary.
Shortly thereafter, Xian passed away, and the Prefectural Governor appointed Ciming to fill the vacancy. Upon arriving there, [Ciming] looked at him...
He disparaged and rejected various points one by one, labeling them as heterodox interpretations. The Master was disheartened by this and went to his quarters.
The next day, Yunmen said, "When you, Secretary, travel with your disciples, even if you have doubts, you may sit and discuss them.

The Master’s entreaty became even more earnest. Yunmen said, "You study Yunmen Chan; you must surely be well-versed in its essential meaning. For instance, regarding the saying, 'I bestow three blows upon Dongshan.'"
"Staff! There is a portion for receiving the staff; there is no portion for receiving the staff. The Master said, "There is a portion for receiving the staff.

Mingse Zhuang said, "From morning until evening, the crows' cawing and the ravens' crying—all these should receive the staff. Ming then sat upright and received the staff while offering incense and performing a prostration.
Ming asked again: "Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman of Mount Tai—I have thoroughly investigated her for you. And yet—"

"That was the place where he passed the old woman's test. The Master broke into a sweat and could not provide an answer. The next day he went to visit again, but Ming continued to revile him incessantly.
The Master said, "Is reviling the compassionate bestowal of the Dharma? Ming asked, "Do you take that as reviling?
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: "Standing out from the forest is Zhaozhou; The old woman’s test..."
Regarding the origins of his defeat and disappearance: now the four seas are as clear as a mirror. Let travelers not treat the road as their enemy.

[He] presented this to Ciming, who nodded in approval. Later, he opened a Dharma hall at Tong’an. On the day he first accepted the invitation, a monk was sent by Letan to examine the Master’s proclamations.
Among them were these words: "The ocean of wisdom has no inherent nature; it arises because of the awakening to delusion. As for the awakening to delusion, its source is fundamentally void."
To see the Buddha within the ordinary mind—this is simply to rest as it is.

One might think that Tongan lacks a point of resolution, yet he allows you to follow your own deluded desires, saying, "Seven in the Southern Dipper, eight in the Northern Dipper. When a monk returned and reported this to Cheng, Cheng was displeased;
from then on, his former friendship with Letan was severed. A monk asked: "My house has its own 'same wind' (tongfeng) matter. What is this 'same wind'?"
[The Master] remained silent for a long time. The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall take my leave of the Master. The Master said, "A person of such keen intelligence is hard to find.
The monk bowed. Addressing the assembly, [the Master] said: "In the land south of the Yangtze, spring is cold and autumn is hot. Lately, however—"
"Drops of water, drops of ice. A monk asked, "What is it like when there are drops of water, drops of ice? The Master said, "This is not yet a matter for the rank of a patch-robed monk.
The monk asked, "What is a matter for the rank of a patch-robed monk? The Master said, "Drops of water, drops of ice. Question:
When Niu-tou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds carry flowers to offer him? The Master said, "A mulberry tree with its roots firmly planted."

[A monk] asked about the "broad-horned water buffalo. [The Master] said: "Having seen it, why does it not bite the flower? The Master said: "The trousers have no crotch; the pants have no opening. [Another monk] asked:
"Even for one who is non-active and without affairs, there is still the difficulty of the golden chain. I wonder where the fault lies?"
The Master said, "When a single character enters an official gate, even nine oxen cannot pull the cart out. The student said, "I do not yet understand; I beg the Master for an expedient means.
The Master said, "At the head of Dayu Ridge, laughter turns into weeping. A questioner asked, "One does not go; two do not stay. Please, Master, speak.
The Master said, "Before the Hall of the High Ancestor, Fan Kuai was enraged. The student said, "If that is so, then today I have met with harmony."
"Furthermore," the Master said, "Looking up at the sky, one does not see the sky. [The monk] asked about the staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji:
"From the present day until now, few have picked this up. I ask the Master to pick it up. The Master said, "A crossbow of a thousand *jin* does not fire its trigger for the sake of a field mouse.
[The monk] said, "A master of the school is present today. The Master then shouted; the monk bowed, and the Master [departed].
He said: "Monks from the Five Lakes, practitioners with a single staff—before you have even reached Tongan, you must not fail to harbor doubt. Entering the hall, he said:
"Swallowing the vast ocean horizontally and overturning Mount Sumeru upside down—even before the eyes of a patch-robed monk, these are but ordinary tea and rice.
A traveler on the path must sit within the great Dharma-hall amidst a forest of thorns; in the midst of mixing mud and water, one must recognize one's own original nature."
As for this very face before you, how can it be seen? He then took up his staff and said, "Even if you were to see it, you would still not escape my staff.
Ascending the hall, he said: "When the states of both sage and ordinary person are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed. He then raised his whisk and said:
The whisk [leapt] up to the Thirty-three Heavens; it seized and tore out the nostrils of Śakra. Donkey-lipped Xiansheng clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying:
"Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one searches for a person who can discern good from evil, yet not even one in ten thousand is found."
Striking the meditation seat and descending from it, ascending the hall to speak of the wondrous and discuss the profound—this is the treacherous villain of a time of great peace.
Administering blows and shouts—these are the heroes of a chaotic age. Heroes and villains, blows and shouts, the wondrous and the profound—all are but superfluous things.
"In Huangbo’s school, nothing at all is employed. But tell me, what is it that is constantly used in Huangbo’s school?
[He] lets out a shout. Ascending the hall: When the bell is struck, the bell rings; when the drum is beaten, the drum resounds. The assembly respectfully bows in inquiry.
Tongan stood upright with palms joined. "This is worldly dharma; that is Buddha-dharma. *Tu!*" He ascended the hall and said:
"There is one person who studies the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in the morning and contemplates the Prajñāpāramitā in the evening, diligent day and night without a moment's rest.
There is another person who does not practice Chan and does not discuss doctrine, but simply takes his broken mat and sleeps in the sun. Thus, these two people are the same."
Arriving at Huanglong, [he asked]: "One person acts; one person does not act. Which of these two is the true resting place? After a long silence, he said:
"The Goddess of Merit and the Lady of Darkness—a wise master accepts neither. Ascending the hall, he said:
"When the mind-king does not move falsely, the six realms are simultaneously penetrated. Lay aside the three-foot sword; cease playing with the bow. He struck the meditation seat.
The Seat below the Platform. Entering the Hall: "How far away is the Way? It is true in every encounter. How distant are the sages? They are divine as soon as one realizes them.
He then held up his staff and said, "The Way and the sages are both entirely upon the tip of this Guizong staff.
Why do you all fail to recognize this? If you could recognize it, the lands of the ten directions would be reached without traveling there. Hundred... [text continues]

The three thousand samādhis are accomplished through non-action. If you do not yet understand this, there are cold and heat that shorten your lifespan, and there are ghosts and spirits that envy your blessings.
Ascending the hall: At midnight, the black hen is hurried; it startles the Brahma King from his sleep.
A Vairambha wind suddenly arises, blowing down Mount Sumeru. On the official road, no one travels; private wine is drunk by many. At this moment—
At such a time, Linji and Deshan could open their mouths and spread their eyes; they had their staffs and shouts, yet they were of no use.
You all must each seek out the deed of inheritance for your ancestral estate; do not mistake the bridge on a donkey’s saddle for your father’s chin.
Ascending the hall, he cited Master Dazhu, who said: "When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world."
When body, speech, and mind are impure, this is called the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. What a fine message!
This was an expedient means employed by the ancients to provide you all with a point of entry. Once you have gained an entrance, you must also gain an exit.
To climb a mountain, one must reach its summit; to enter the sea, one must reach its bottom. If you climb a mountain but do not reach the summit, you will not know the vastness of the universe.
If you enter the sea but do not reach the bottom, you will not know the depth of the blue ocean.
Once you know its vastness and know its depth, with a single step you overturn the four great oceans, and with a single blow you topple Mount Sumeru; then, with hands relaxed, you arrive home.

People do not recognize it. A magpie shrieks and a crow caws among the cypress trees. Entering the hall, he said: "A thousand ways of speaking, ten thousand metaphors—only to teach you to return home early.
Where do you go? After a long silence, he said: "The wind has risen tonight; fragrance fills the courtyard, blowing down three or five peach trees.
Because a fundraising master had returned, he entered the hall and said: "In this world there are five things that are not easy."
First, it is not easy to transform one thing into another. Second, it is not easy to give. Third, it is not easy to transform the raw into the cooked.

Fourth, it is not easy to sit upright while eating. There is yet another kind of "not easy. Who is this person? After a long silence, he said, "Hmm? and then descended from his seat. (At that time, Cuiyan Zhen was the head seat.
The Librarian asked, "Just now the Master spoke of a fifth 'not easy. Who is this person? Zhen replied, "One who has a beard on the back of their head—do not associate with such a person.")
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Held horizontally or used upside down, it pierces through Maitreya’s eyes;
where light departs and darkness arrives, it knocks off the patriarchs’ nostrils. At such a time, Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra would swallow their breath and silence their voices;
Linji and Deshan would laugh out loud. But tell me, what are they laughing at? *Du!* (A shout). The Master constantly asked this within his quarters."
The monk said, "Everyone has their own karmic conditions for birth; where is the Venerable’s own birth-condition?
Just as they were exchanging blows in this dialogue, [Linji] reached out his hand and said, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?

He then asked about what the masters from all quarters had attained through their studies, but he then lowered his feet and said, "How are my feet like a donkey’s feet? For over thirty years, he demonstrated these three things.

Question: Among the students, none were able to grasp its essential meaning. Even when someone offered a response, the Master never accepted or rejected it. The monastic communities designated these as "The Three Barriers of Huanglong.
The Master himself composed verses on them, beginning with: "Regarding the conditions of birth, everyone recognizes the words; But how could the water jelly ever leave the shrimp?
One sees only the sun rising in the east— Who can still drink Zhaozhou’s tea? My hand..."

The Buddha’s hand is raised all at once; let the Chan practitioner take this up directly. Without moving a blade or brandishing a weapon, the Way is revealed; right where one stands, one transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs.
My feet and the donkey’s feet walk side by side; at every step, one treads upon the unborn. If you can realize this, the clouds will clear and the sun will emerge.
Only then will you know that this Way extends both vertically and horizontally. The general verse says: "Where the conditions for birth are severed, the donkey’s hoof is extended;
When the donkey’s hoof is extended, the Buddha’s hand opens. To report to the students who travel the Five Lakes: Pass through each of the three barriers one by one.

On the sixteenth day of the third month in the Jiyou year of the Xining era of Emperor Shenzong of the Song dynasty, the letter of succession from the Fourth Patriarch, Yuanwu Keqin, arrived. He ascended the hall and said:

This mountain monk is of slight talent and meager virtue; how could he be fit to serve as a teacher to others? It is simply that I do not obscure my original mind and do not deceive the various sages.

Where once I had not yet escaped birth and death, now I have escaped birth and death; where once I had not yet left saṃsāra, now I have left saṃsāra; where once I had not yet attained liberation, now I have attained liberation;
where once I had not yet attained mastery, now I have attained mastery. Therefore, when the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One was with Dīpaṃkara...
"In the Buddha's presence, not a single dharma can be obtained. What, then, was transmitted at midnight at Huangmei by the Sixth Patriarch? He spoke this verse:
"Obtained or not obtained, Transmitted or not transmitted— When one returns to the root and attains the essential meaning, what more is there to say?
I recall Shoushan’s former disclosure: 'The daughter-in-law rides the donkey, while the mother-in-law leads it. The next day at noon, he sat upright and entered parinirvāṇa. His body was cremated.
He obtained five-colored śarīra relics, which were enshrined in a stupa on the mountain in front. His secular age was sixty-eight and his monastic seniority fifty years.
In the Gengyin year of the Daguang era of Emperor Huizong, he was posthumously granted the imperial title of Chan Master Pujue.
Chan Master Huanglong Zuixin Baojue of Longxing Prefecture,
the twelfth-generation descendant of Nanyue and dharma heir of Chan Master Huanglong Nan, was a native of the Wu clan from Nanxiong. He studied under Yunfeng Yue.
After three years, having gained nothing, he took his leave. Xue said, "You must go south to rely on Huangbo. The Master went to Huangbo, but for four years he did not achieve great enlightenment.
He took his leave again and went up to Yunfeng; however, as Xue had passed away, he stayed at Shishuang.
While reading the *Lamp Records*, he came to the passage where a monk asked Duofu, "What is the single cluster of bamboo of Duofu? Duofu replied, "One stalk."

When the two stalks were leaning, [Nanquan] said, "I do not understand. Fokuang said, "Three stalks, four stalks, all bent. At this, the Master attained enlightenment and thoroughly perceived the application of the two masters' methods.
He returned directly to Huangbo; as soon as he spread out his sitting cloth, Nanquan said, "You have already entered my chamber."
The Master leaped for joy and said, "The Great Matter has always been like this. Why did the Abbot teach people to 'examine the phrase' and search for it by every possible means?

Nan said, "If I had not taught you to investigate and seek in this manner until you reached the point where the mind has no application, and you saw and affirmed it for yourself, I would have buried you.
After he took up residence there, a monk asked, "What was the meaning behind Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall?"
"How is it? the Master asked. [The monk] said, "My body is poor and lacks a covering. [The Master] asked, "Are you not failing the former sages?
The monk replied, "How would you say it, Master, regarding your own point of view? The monk drew a circle. The Master said, "The swallow does not leave its nest."

The monks prostrated. The Master said, "It is still tolerable when it is deep in the night; it is only after midday that people begin to feel distressed. A monk asked, "How was it before you ascended this seat?
The Master said, "There was not a single thing at all. The monk asked, "And how is it after ascending? The Master said, "Looking up at the sky, one does not see the sky.
He ascended the hall and said, "The fool eliminates external objects but does not forget the mind; the wise man forgets the mind but does not eliminate external objects."
Regarding the objective realm: not knowing that the essence of mind and objects is fundamentally suchness (tathatā), one encounters obstacles at every turn when meeting conditions.
He then raised his whisk and said, "Look! This whisk traveled to the Western Heaven and has now returned to the land of Silla. Those who understand me say I am dragging through mud and water;
those who do not understand me say I have won a scene of strange eccentricity. Ascending the hall, he struck the meditation seat and said, "One..."
As soon as a speck of dust is raised, the entire earth is fully encompassed. For all of you, your ears are contained within a single sound; that single sound pervades the ears of all of you.
If you are a soaring falcon reaching for the clouds, you ought to seize the moment; a fish exhausted in a shallow pool merely toils in vain, splashing the waves.
To "not be a companion to the myriad dharmas" is precisely the Samādhi of Non-contention. Even if you proceed in this manner, what can be done?
If the strings are too tight, the sound is abrupt. If one could scatter pearls within a purple silk curtain, it would not necessarily mean that a good cause brings about an evil result.
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is a phrase, there is no phrase—like a vine leaning against a tree. For now, let everyone nod their heads as they please."
When the tree has fallen and the vines withered, there is no scheme above to pierce the heavens, nor any plot below to enter the earth.
O sharp-witted fellows, if you can fix a single eye here, you will see them moving freely in every direction—seven ways and eight ways. Holding up his whisk, he said:
"Look! The sun overflows the eyes; ten thousand miles are not hung with a single cloud. But as for those beneath an overturned basin, how can one blame old [Shakyamuni]?"
The Monk ascended the hall and said: "If one clarifies only the self but does not awaken to what is before one's eyes, this person has eyes but no feet.
If one awakens to what is before one's eyes but does not clarify the self, this person has feet but no eyes.

According to these two types of people, throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is always something harbored within their chests. Since that thing resides in the chest, the state of unease is ever-present."
If you are currently [here], then being currently here causes you to become stuck at every turn. How can you attain a state of evenness and stability?

Did not the Patriarch say: "To grasp it is to lose the proper measure; one will surely enter a deviant path. To let go naturally, its essence has neither going nor staying"? [He] ascended the hall and said:
Before a master craftsman has appeared, jade and stone cannot be distinguished; before a skilled smelter is present, gold and sand are mixed together.
Is there anyone here who has attained self-awakening without a teacher? Come forth and discern it! He then raised his whisk and said: "Tell me, is this gold or is it sand?"
After a long silence, he said: "If you see it and do not take it, thinking of it will be a thousand miles away. He then ascended the hall and said:

"Sometimes I open the door to wait for a true friend (jñānin), yet the true friend does not come to pass by. Sometimes I take his hand and climb the high mountain, yet the man on the high mountain pays no heed.
At times I act as a defeated general, surrendering with folded hands into the hands of the *kalyāṇamitra*. At other times I become the wrathful Nīladaṇḍa, striking..."
"Bone crushing the marrow. At this very moment, is there anyone whose voices resonate together and whose natures seek one another?
If there is, then take a step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole; if not, you shall become a source of laughter before the peak of Shaoshi.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the state of empty space is realized, there is nothing..."
This is neither dharma nor non-dharma; thus, one simply lets it rest. Lowering the oars and securing the mooring ropes, one may for now moor the boat within the bay.
Yet, according to the gate of the patch-robed monks (*śramaṇera*), this is worlds apart. But tell me: what excellence is there within the gate of the patch-robed monks?
"Carrying the knotted staff across my shoulder, heedless of others, I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. [Ascending the hall: "One does not turn toward; two..."

He did not open [the door]. Turning his thoughts back to Nanyue and Tiantai, he said with a laugh: "How laughable! The white clouds have no fixed abode; blown away by the wind, they are blown back again.
Ascending the hall, he said: "It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. A man of clear eyes cannot be deceived for even a single moment.
You who are wise, your own mind is moving—calm and steady now! Where do you see the Patriarch? Thereupon, he threw [his staff].
The Master struck the whisk and said, "Look! He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the past have already passed away; the Buddhas of the future have not yet been born.
Right now, in the Dharma of the present, it is entrusted to Huanglong. If you let it go, it is hazy and indistinct, yet within it there is something.
If you hold it fast, it is profound and obscure, yet within it there is an essence. Now tell me: is it letting go that is it, or is it holding fast?"
This is it: "The thread on the tip of the bamboo pole is for you to play with; not violating the clear waves, its meaning is naturally distinct. Entering the hall, he said:
"A tiger’s head sprouting horns—people find it difficult to handle. Like sparks from flint and flashes of lightning, they must be met everywhere. Even a man of heroic resolve would find it hard."

Mongdina was able to skillfully manipulate things: he could hold the sun and moon in his hands and carry Mount Sumeru on his back, casting them toward other directions, yet the sentient beings therein were neither aware nor cognizant of it.
Even if those sentient beings were to ride a donkey into the eyes of others, those people would likewise be neither aware nor cognizant of it.
Do you understand? To offer this very body and mind to every dust mote and land is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Master En ascends the hall: Before a single bubble has arisen, before the ancient sail has set forth, the wind-signal has not come, and no one is rowing the oars.
At this very moment, how can the currents of the water be discerned? Do you not see where the old master Yunmen extended his hand?
Vast and clear, the waves leave no path for penetration. Again, one sees not the Elder of Huating leaking his celestial mechanism; at night’s deep, he returns empty-handed, carrying the bright moon.
Do not wonder that we meet yet do not recognize one another; let the ten thousand ages remain vast and dark. [Ascending the hall.]
When Mazu ascended the hall, Baizhang rolled up his mat. Later generations, unable to grasp the origins of this wind, all say that he left no trace behind.
Little do they realize that within the peach-blossom waves, it is precisely the right time to unfurl the sails; at the head of the Qili Rapids, it is even more fitting to cast one’s line for fish.
Surely there must be some man here who can distinguish between floating and sinking and discerns the depths—step forward and try to determine the currents! It is like this:
None. For now, I shall take up the fisherman’s flute and idly blow it by the seashore. Ascending the hall, he said: “The wind whistles and the tree leaves fly;
the wild geese do not come, and news is scarce. No one sings the song of returning home; it leaves me clapping my hands in vain hesitation. Ascending the hall, he said:
“Regarding the image in a mirror, some say it exists, yet one cannot grasp it even with both hands. Regarding the image in a mirror, some say it does not exist.”

[The Master] left a footprint. The Master said, "Go ahead and drag through the mud and carry the water. [A monk] asked, "What if one goes in this very way? The Master said, "As expected. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The Tathāgatas of the past do not need to be examined again. The Bodhisattvas of the present cannot simply let things pass.
Those who practice and study in the future must not be deceived by even a single point. Therefore, it is said in the scriptures: If..."
If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate that the nature of the dharma-realm is entirely created by mind alone.
Nevertheless, under the gate of Yunju, this is precisely like gold dust falling into the eyes. [Ascending the hall: "The view of the ordinary and the view of the sage."
Spring clouds flash with lightning; true words and false words alike are like flowers in the sky or the moon reflected in water.

I am reminded of Changzi seeing Shitou, who could say: "A single speck of snow upon a red furnace. [He] struck the meditation seat and ascended the hall, saying: "Take tortoise hair for arrows and hare horns for a bow."
Nachi, in a fit of wrath, shot an arrow that pierced through space; space collapsed, causing mountains to crumble and valleys to overflow.
Walls, tiles, and rubble emitted radiance as they took refuge in the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. Striking the meditation seat, he ascended the hall and said:
"The moonlight blends with the clouds into white; The sound of pines carries the chill of dew. What a truly excellent message— Rely on you gentlemen to examine it closely. Master Huanglong.
He collapsed his body onto the floor. "Is there anyone who can still lift him up? If the patriarchs and ancestors have not settled their affairs, the calamity will reach their descendants.
He struck the meditation seat. Entering the hall, he said: "All sounds are the voice of the Buddha. With his whisk, he struck the meditation seat and said:
"The Brahma-sound is profound and far-reaching; it causes people to delight in hearing it. He then said: "All forms are the form of the Buddha," and he picked up the whisk.

Now the Buddha emits a radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Those who have already attained it should receive it upon their heads and practice accordingly;
those who have not yet attained it should know it thus and believe it thus. [He struck the meditation seat and descended from it.

On the night of the seventh day of the seventh month in the year of Ren-shen during the Yuan-you era of Emperor Zhezong of the Song dynasty, at the hour of Zi, he said to the assembly: "Holding the position as abbot in three places, I have not transmitted a single [dharma]."
"Regarding the Dharma: fire and wind gather and disperse; this is the constant nature of physical phenomena. After my passing, you must not follow worldly sentiments.
You should instead cremate me according to the Dharma and return my bones to the stupa. He then spoke a verse: "This year I am sixty-six; the conditions for the three places are fulfilled.
At midnight the mountain burns with fire; I leap into the flames to bathe. Having finished speaking, he entered nirvana. Upon cremation, relics of five colors were obtained.
Śāriputra, the stupa is at Yunju.
Chan Master Daomai Huixiu of Tanzhou was the son of the Ying family of Yingzhou. A monk asked:

"In the past, the water-buffalo of Daomai’s mountain—since it was let loose, its tracks have vanished. Today, fortunately, we encounter the Master ascending the seat; I wonder, what of the people of this age?"
“Where should one seek it? The Master said, “One must not trample upon the crops. [The monk] said, “In that case, the horns are already clearly visible.
The Master said, “You are merely clutching a metal whip given by a mountain boy.”
Chan Master Weisheng Zhenjue of Huangbo in Ruizhou was the son of the Luo family of Tongchuan. While he was residing at a lecture hall, his fan happened to strike the window lattice with a sound.
Suddenly, he recalled a passage from the teachings: "When drums are struck in all ten directions, they are heard simultaneously in all ten places. Thereupon, he attained great enlightenment.
He informed his lecture master, who instructed him to seek out a teacher through formal inquiry. The Master went directly to Huanglong. Later, because of Ruizhou...

The Prefectural Governor commissioned Longlin to select a master for Huangbo. Longlin assembled the community and uttered a turning phrase: "Reciting hymns on the bell tower; planting vegetables beneath the bed.
He said, "If anyone can explain this, they shall go to serve as the abbot. The Master stepped forward and replied, "A fierce tiger sits blocking the road.

Longlin was greatly pleased and sent the Master there. Consequently, he came to be revered by all quarters. *Note: The term "Long" (龍) refers to the monk Longlin (龍藺). The "Master" (師) is Xuefeng Yicun (雪峯義存).*
The hall [of Linji], Linji’s shout, and Deshan’s staff are left for Zen practitioners as models.

Guizong’s whetstone and Xuefeng’s ball—this is the style of that lineage for receiving those of superior capacity. If it were Huangbo, however, it would be otherwise: there would be neither shout nor staff.
It is neither ground nor polished, nor is it rolled like a ball. Before you is the front mountain; behind you is the main mountain.
It blocks your eyes and presses against the gate of your face. If you can see into this, you will attain the stage of non-retrogression and, until the end of the future, seek nothing from another.
If you do not attain even this, the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) turns instead into poison. [The Master] ascended the hall.
"Silent and desolate; the bright moon descends into the empty valley. Vast and expansive; the brilliant sunlight flows across the four seas.
On the road to Caoxi, the passage of people is utterly cut off; before the Many-Sons Stupa, the crowds are as dense as at a marketplace.
Even if you can realize this here with such distinct clarity, it is not yet the livelihood of a patch-robed monk. A man of great capacity must be...
Into the dark hells they are driven, their shackles and chains struck and broken; amidst the ranks of hungry ghosts, fire is set and drink is snatched away.

The Tower of Maitreya is toppled, and the Palace of the Empty King is demolished; the auspicious sprouts and rare grasses are uprooted by the roots, leaving thorns to grow everywhere across the earth.
Chan Master Yousheng Fazhu of Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Zheng family of Chaoyang. In his later years, he met Huanglong, under whom he received profound certification of his realization.
He ascended the hall and said: "This matter is like a physician’s prescription for diagnosing an illness. Furthermore, when one's belly is filled with a mixture of poisons, it is not easy to treat;

it requires medicine that causes dizziness and nausea before it can be cured. Even if one were to administer such medicine according to one's own whims, it would only serve to further delude and confuse them."
To aggravate his chronic ailment while seeking its cure—is this not perverse? The grass before the Dharma Hall grows deep, yet he feels no shame in his heart.
Chan Master Subhūti (Zi Qi) of Kaiyuan Temple in Qizhou was the son of the Xu family of Quanzhou; he relied upon Kaiyuan Ne and passed the scriptural examination.
Du [Fahui] specialized in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*. He went to visit Cuiyan Zhen and asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Zhen spat on the ground and said, "Where does this single drop fall? The Master rubbed his chest and said, "Today my spleen aches. Zhen smiled.
After taking leave, he studied under Jicui for over a year and fully mastered his Way. While attending Cuiyan during an interval, they discussed the past and present. Just then—
During a great snowfall, Cui said, "Can this not be swept away with a single broom? The Master replied, "It cannot.
Cui asked, "Then when the sky clears and the sun rises, and the clouds and vapors disperse and dissolve—would they still exist? The Master said, "One who knows this is like one who splits bamboo:
even with a hundred nodes, every section shall be severed at the first touch of the blade. How could there be any room for sound or for deliberation? One day...
Cui sent a monk to ask him in advance, "What are the old master’s three barriers? The Master replied with a stern voice, "How can you concern yourself with matters of the distant past?

Upon hearing this, Cui marveled at him even more. Thereupon, his reputation became renowned throughout the monastic community. After Cui passed away, Fourth Patriarch Yuan appointed him to share the seat.
In his quarters, he gave this turning word: "A person has a mouth, yet cannot speak it; what is their name?"
"For whom? Later, the lineage was transmitted to Donglin Zong, who sighed and said, "The Head Seat Qi is like an iron mountain ten thousand fathoms high;
it will be difficult indeed to engage his verbal pulse. Not long after, Kaiyuan was established as a Chan monastery, and the Master was invited to serve as the First Patriarch.
He ascended the hall and said: "Space has no interior or exterior; phenomena and principle have their long and short. To follow them is to realize Bodhi; to oppose them is to..."
The afflictions are vexed; the lanterns are constantly dozing; even the pillar is distressed. The Great Way is right before one’s eyes—where else could one seek it?
(With the whisk, he strikes the meditation seat. Entering the hall: On four sides there are no doors; in the ten directions there are no walls.
Hair is disheveled, ears are prominent. Every man is a great hero; how can one be without a rope and yet be self-bound?
"Bound! Now tell me: how do you express the single phrase that transcends and liberates? After a long silence, he said: "Treading through grass shoes, walking barefoot. A monk asked:
"I do not ask about Mount Sumeru containing a mustard seed; but what of when the Great Dharma Wheel is turned within a mote of dust?
The Master said: "One step forward, one step further. The monk said: "If so, then arriving in India in the morning and returning to Tang in the evening."

[The monk] arrived at the monastery grounds. The Master said, "Being a guest is not as good as returning home. [The monk] replied, "I have long admired your reputation for the Way; I request that you grant me an audience.
The Master said, "The clouds and moon are the same, yet the streams and mountains are each different."
Chan Master Xingwei of Yangshan in Yuanzhou was a native of Hexi. He received full ordination at Dafu Temple in the Eastern Capital and studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuánjué).
Having developed some slight doubts, he took up his traveling bag to wander the lands, seeking exclusively to penetrate the meaning of the Patriarchs.

Upon arriving at Huanglong, six years passed. One day, he requested instruction; he was immediately struck with a shout and driven out. As his foot was about to cross the threshold, he suddenly realized the original intent. Thereafter, he emerged into the world [to teach].

Yangshan’s reputation for the Way was widely renowned. He ascended the hall and said, "Does the great assembly understand? The events of past and present cannot be concealed; the affairs of daily life cannot be hidden.
Since they cannot be hidden or concealed, they manifest before us in our daily activities. Now I ask you all: what is this manifest reality? [He paused for] contemplation.
He ascended the hall again and said, "Does the great assembly see? When the eyes are opened, one universally contemplates the ten directions."
When the eyes are closed, they encompass all existence. Neither open nor closed—what is its appearance? Do you see its appearance?
Those of long-standing practice and high virtue understand it the moment it is raised. For beginners and those new to the path, recognize this appearance;
do not merely indulge in sleep. When you sleep, what do your eyes see? If you say you see nothing, how are you any different from a dead person? Even if you were to take cinnabar...
Master Qing: On the tip of your brush you paint green mountains and blue waters, bamboo-clad trees and peach blossoms; these are merely semblances.
Even if a stonecutter were to use his chisel to carve out herds of sheep and wild beasts, they too would be nothing but semblances.
If it were the true form, then even you, Master Qing, or a stonecutter, would have no place to apply your hand. You all must—
"See! You must truly open your eyes to perceive it. After a long silence, he said: "Broad, it is but a single thread;
narrow, it is but an inch and a half. He struck the meditation seat with his whisk. Ascending the hall, as soon as the drum rolled and the assembly gathered like clouds, he said:
"Everyone looks up at me; I, the mountain monk, look down at you. What is it that you look up at? What is it that I look down at? After a long silence, he said:
Facing one another yet not knowing each other. Entering the hall for the discourse: The Way does not reside in sound or form, yet it is not separate from sound and form.
Every word and every phrase, every movement and every stillness—whether hidden or manifest, whether expansive or vertical—it is nothing other than the Buddha-work.

It is present in daily life; it has remained thus through all time. How could the principle ever be at variance? The Master inscribed his own portrait, saying: "My true likeness is difficult to capture; it is variegated and manifold."

"Bo-bo! If you wish to arrange it, the moment you set pen to paper, you have already erred. The Master maintained a most rigorous demeanor. He sat in *zuowang* (sitting in oblivion), forgetting both night and day.
Whenever someone came to visit him who possessed faults, he would vacate his own seat to invite them in, rising personally with palms joined in reverence.

When Nan heard of this, he considered it too extreme in its aloofness from others, arguing that it did not accord with the principle of "harmonizing light with dust. He cautioned the Master against such behavior. The Master replied, "My cultivation of the Way is not yet complete; [I must remain thus for another] year..."
Time flows like a river. Even those of great capacity, such as Yunmen and Zhaozhou, still remarked, "I only have two meals a day;
this is a distracted use of mind. How much more so for those of superior capacity whose daily progress multiplies over kalpas?

On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the Gengshen year of Emperor Shenzong’s Yuanfeng era, he preached a verse and passed away. Upon cremation, five-colored śarīras were obtained, along with bone-relics.
Bound together by ropes and hooks, the stupa was erected to the east of the monastery. His secular age was sixty-three; his years of ordination were thirty-three.
Chan Master Cigan of Fuyan on Mount Nanyue, a native of the Du clan from Tongchuan, ascended the hall and said: "The mind of the ancient Buddha is right here now.
If you do not understand, you will suffer in deep reflection. The autumn rain falls lightly; the autumn wind whistles. Now here, now there. If...
In response: "The reeds and flowers on the sandy shore are intermingled in green and yellow; upon what does the Chan practitioner rely? After a long silence, he said: "Zha!
Chan Master Shouzhi of Yungai in Tanzhou was the son of the Chen family of Jianzhou. While traveling, he arrived at Dajian in Yuzhang.
At that time, Fachang was staying at Weicao on Mount Xi. Hearing that he had thoroughly completed his training, the Master went to visit him.
Fachang asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Daning. Fachang said, "Last night the main gate collapsed; did you know it? The Master was startled and said, "I did not know.
Fachang said, "In Wuzhong, there is a stone Buddha that many people have never even seen. The Master was bewildered and immediately prostrated himself in worship.
Chang sent an envoy to pay his respects to Zhen of Cuiyan; for a long time, he had no realization, yet he did not waste a single moment of his time.
When he finally visited Huanglong at Jicui, he was able to resolve all his doubts. Later, he led the assembly at Shishuang and subsequently established the Dharma lineage at Dagui.
He later moved to Yungai, where a monk asked: "There is a stringless lute that is not made of worldly wood; today I have carried it here, and I ask the Master to play it."
[He plays] one tune. The Master pats his knee once. The monk says, "The golden wind rustles in harmony with the pure melody; I pray the Master will use skillful means to grant us another sound.
The Master says, "In Shanfu, they water the iron ox. Ascending the hall, [the Master says]: "Tightly lacing my water-proof boots, I tread upon the moon of Lake Xiang.
Grasping an iron caltrop in hand, I break through the dragon and tiger’s lair. Turning my body and climbing up the tree—only then do I see it."
"Without birth or extinction," he laughed at old Gautama. "A snap of the fingers surpasses Maitreya. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Yesterday, I watched for fish on a high mountain;
walking, I lost my horse while riding it. Someone picked up a camel and walked off; though a thousand pieces of gold were offered as a reward, not even one was found.
"If you can realize this point here, I will not charge you for the price of your straw sandals. Ascending the hall, he raised an example:
Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk said, "I am going to pick tea. Zhaozhou said, "Idle. The Master said:
"To speak of it or not to speak of it—where can one search for it? Scales on the dragon’s back behind; donkey's feet before the face. A somersaulting flip;
solitary clouds and wild cranes. A-he-he! Addressing the assembly: "Without leaving this very place, it is ever profound and still. If you seek it, I know you will not find it."
It is visible. Although the former sages spoke thus, they merely fashioned a mold to cast it. If you cannot emerge from it, you will only be clutching the ancients' legacy;
if you can emerge from it, only then will there be some slight correspondence. Yun-gai, however, was not like this:
riding a fine steed around Mount Sumeru, he went over the mountains seeking the tracks of ants—how many people could possibly know this? Master.
He resided in the East Hall of the monastery. In the *Xinhao* year of Emperor Huizong’s Zhenghe era, Siji (Sixin) retired from his duties.
Huanglong entered the mountains from Hunan to pay his respects; it was already evening. An attendant monk announced his arrival, and the Master, trailing his sandals, spoke as he walked:
"Bring a candle so we may look at him; what does his face look like that his fame has caused such clamor throughout the universe? Siji also—
He cried out in astonishment. "Bring him closer! I wish to examine him. Is he the true senior uncle, or is he a false one?
The Master then struck him a blow right in the chest. Sishin said, "Indeed, it is truly so," and then prostrated himself. Host and guest found great harmony, their joy being profound.
When Sishi died, Fuhui again took charge of Huanglong. Upon receiving the news of his passing while he was residing at Kaifu, the Master ascended the hall and said:
"A misfortune for the Dharma-gate; the Dharma-banner has collapsed. Within the mountain of the five aggregates, all has been turned to ash. Last night, the earthen ox passed through a single thread."
Huanglong entered saṃsāra from this point on. On the seventh day of the third month in the year of Yiwu (1115) of the Zhenghe era, the Master ascended the seat and spoke this verse:
"Before entering the world, my head was like a horse’s scoop; After entering the world, my mouth was like a donkey’s snout.
In a hundred years, it must ultimately decay of its own accord; Let the whole world speculate as it pleases. He returned to his quarters, sat upright, and passed away. He was ninety-one years old.
In his sixty-sixth year, Chan Master Heshan Hedong Wenming Huizhi of Fuzhou was asked by a monk, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Private paths allow for the passage of carriages and horses.
The monk took a step forward, and the Master said, "The official highway does not admit even a needle."
Chan Master Zhaokong of Jianlong Monastery in Yangzhou was a native of the Lin family of Jinjiang, Quanzhou.
He left the household life at Kaiyuan Monastery and went to study under Huanglong. Huanglong showed him the "Three Barriers" (sanguan yu); after a long time, he fully realized the Way.

He subsequently resided at Qianming Monastery in Gaoyou and Huiji Monastery in Wujiang, and later took up residence at Jianlong. On ascending the hall, he said: "The new year has just begun; in an instant, it is already [past]."
This was the first day of the second month; the weather was mild and harmonious.

I intended to bring up a seasonal circumstance to deliberate upon with everyone, but Śakra and Brahmā appeared, poking their heads out from among the willow catkins outside the gate, and first spoke this verse:
"Fluttering, light tufts of silk are carried here and there by the wind; Next, balls of cotton roll along—do not say that I am not here."
"Chatter. At that moment, he encountered an asura who seized him and said, "No matter how much you chatter, when suddenly met by the west wind, the leaves fall from the Wei River and fill Chang’an.
How do you speak this one phrase? Thereupon, Śakra shrank his head and entered the eye of a willow.
After a long while, he said, "Study! On the sixteenth day of the eighth month of the Jisi year of the Yuanyou era during the Song Emperor Zhezong’s reign, the Master [passed away].
He preached in verse to transform others. His stupa was erected during the Jianlong era.
Chan Master Baoben Huiyuan of Anji Prefecture was the son of the Ni family of Chuzhou. At nineteen, he became a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*).

He traveled extensively through various monastic assemblies and attained awakening under Huanglong’s "Three Barriers" teaching. After he took up residence [at his monastery], a monk asked: "The Buddhas do not appear..."
"World, Bodhidharma did not come from the West. At such a time as this, I do not know whether he came or not. The Master said, "He has struck right through your nostrils.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The white clouds disperse; the red sun rises in the east.
Look up at the heavens; look down at the earth. East, west, south, north—let you freely observe the sights. The eyes of Bodhidharma cannot be measured even by a bushel. Yanjue...
When have you ever recognized a shadow? If Sudhana had not gone south, the nostrils of the patch-robed monk would pierce the heavens;
reaching this point, they are all pierced at once. A monk came forward, bowed, and said, "I, your student, have a question. Will the Master answer it? The Master said, "I answered you yesterday.
The monk asked, "How about today? The Master said, "Come tomorrow. [The Master] ascended the hall for the discourse. A monk...
Question: "Is it true that all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas are various skillful means? The Master said, "Yes.

[The monk] asked, "If so, why is it that the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words? The Master said, "Do not misunderstand this. The monk made a single stroke with his sitting cloth.
The Master shouted, saying, "The mark of the quiescence of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. Those who study now..."
The Path of Seeing cannot be proclaimed in words; thus, one intends to sever deliberation and forget objective conditions, blocking off sight and hearing.
Such a view as this has not yet attained a portion of mastery. Do you all wish to understand the mark of quiescence? When you step out the door, you do not see so much as a single hair;
before your eyes are white clouds and green peaks. The Master sat rather than lay down for over thirty years during the Song dynasty.
On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month in the *Xinwei* year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong (1091), he ascended the seat and spoke this verse:

"Fifty-five years of a dream-like and illusory body; Who among east, west, south, and north is truly kin? When white clouds have dispersed beyond the green mountains, A fresh crescent moon hangs in the autumn sky ten thousand miles wide.
Having finished speaking, he passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Mount Hyeon. Thirty years later...

In that year, he was posthumously granted the title of Chan Master Zhengwu, and his stupa was named Dingying. An imperial decree was issued to establish Xianhua Temple and to ordain monks annually to maintain the incense and lamps.
Chan Master Qingxian of Renshan Longqing Monastery in Jizhou was the son of the Zhuo family of Fuzhou.

His mother dreamed that a Western monk gave her a bright pearl, which she swallowed; thereafter she conceived. Upon his birth, white light illuminated the room. From childhood, he did not approach wine or meat.

At the age of eleven, he left secular life; at seventeen, he received full ordination; and at twenty, he traveled extensively to visit various masters. Later, he visited Huanglong at Huangbo. Huanglong...
The Master asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Baizhang. The Master asked, "When did you leave there? The Master replied, "On the thirteenth day of the first month.
Longtan said, "Your heels must ache terribly; I shall give you thirty blows! The Master said, "Not merely thirty blows.
Longtan shouted, "After traveling on pilgrimage for so long, you have not a breath of spirit left! The Master said, "Even hundreds of thousands of Buddhas are just like this. Longtan said, "You..."
"Coming in such a manner, how could there ever have been so much as a hair’s breadth that reached the realm of the Buddhas?
The Master said, "The Buddhas may not necessarily reach the realm of Qingxian. Long asked, "What is your place of origin? The Master said, "In the morning, I ate white congee."
Now he felt hungry again and asked, "What is my hand like? Is it a Buddha’s hand? The Master said, "Playing the lute under the moon.
He asked, "What is my foot like? Is it a donkey’s foot? The Master said, "A heron standing in the snow is not of the same color [as the snow].
Long sighed and looked at him, saying, "You have shaved off your hair and beard; for what purpose do you do this? The Master said, "I simply wish to be without affairs. Long said, "If that is so..."
"A few sounds of the clear chime are beyond right and wrong; there is but one idle man in the world. The Master said, "What words are these?
Long said, "A quick-witted monk! The Master said, "That is unnecessary. Long said, "There is an Elder Bian here; you must be on your guard.
The Master said, "What longings does he have? Long said, "He will strike your back twice. Furthermore—
"How is it? the Master asked. "What are you doing? [Yunmen] replied. "He spread out both hands," [Yunmen] said.

"Where did he learn this deception? the Master asked. Yunmen laughed loudly. The Master then spread out both hands himself, and Yunmen shouted at him. He asked again, "Loose and relaxed, 'two people share one bowl'—how do you understand this?
The Master said, "In pieces. "The entire earth is this Mount Sumeru," [Yunmen] said.
"Mountains, gathered in the palm of my hand—how do you understand this? The Master said, "A double case.

[The Master] said, "Here, you may speak as you please in barbarian tongues or Chinese; but when you reach Tong’an, how will you pass through? (At that time, Ying of Shǎowǔ was serving as the Head Seat at Tong’an, and the Master wished to go see him.
The Master said, "He too must reach such a state before it is possible. [The Master] said, "What if he suddenly points to fire?"
Luzu said, "This is a black-lacquered brazier; that is a black-lacquered incense table. Where is there a place it does not reach?
The Master said, "Right before Qingxian. Let us speak this way for now; if it were anyone else, they would laugh at you, Master.
