Another monk entered next, and the Master again said, "You do not understand; go out. The monk also left. Yet another monk entered, and the Master said, "The two who came before..."
"Senior monk, one person knows how to gather but not how to release; another knows how to release but not how to gather.
Can you still distinguish between them? The monk said, "I accept this as my own record. The Master said, "After accepting it as your own record, what further good news is there?
The monk clapped his hands once and departed. The Master said, "In thirty years, he will attain realization. As soon as the Master saw the monk...
As he entered, the Master said, "Śākyamuni has come! The monk stepped forward, and the Master said, "So, it was not you after all," and struck him.
Next, another monk entered; the Master likewise said, "Śākyamuni has come! The monk offered a formal greeting right before him and then departed.
The Master said, "It seems as if it were real. He asked an attendant, "Of all those who have entered the room, how many could speak it?
How many failed to reach it? The attendant replied, "I simply watched. The Master extended his hand and said, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
The attendant said, "The weather is cold; please roll up your sleeves, Master," and he departed. The Master followed after him.
[The Master] struck the bamboo whisk and said, "Tell me, is this a reward for you or a punishment? [He asked:
"In the Teachings it is said that 'every particle speaks, every world-system speaks, without ceasing. I wonder, what serves as their tongue?

The Master struck the right corner of the meditation seat once and said, "The World-Honored One spoke where there was no speaking; Kāśyapa heard where there was no hearing. [He then] struck the left corner of the meditation seat once.
[The monk] said, "I know that today’s command shall not be issued in vain. The Master said, "What do you recognize as good and what as evil?

On the anniversary of Yuanwu’s death, [Wuzu] offered incense and said: "This venerable one was by nature stubborn and headstrong; he displayed an over-the-top recklessness and employed an extraordinary bluntness.
He claimed, 'I will trade my wooden prayer beads for the eyes of all people in the world. Little did he realize that he was himself deceived."
"A filial son will cut the tethering rope and pierce his own nostrils. Since the end of the rope is already in the hands of Jingshan, if he wishes to bring him to life, it is Jingshan who does so;
if he wishes to bring him to death, it is also Jingshan who does so. But tell me, by what shall this be verified?
He then burned incense and said, "This shall be the verification. In the master’s quarters, he frequently questioned the monks, calling them "bamboo."

If you call it a "bamboo rake," you miss the mark; if you do not call it a bamboo rake, you turn your back on it. You must not speak, nor must you remain silent. You must not deliberate, nor must you hesitate.
You must not engage in intellectual calculation within the faculty of thought, nor must you attempt to take hold of it at the very moment it is raised.
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! When the monk attempted to offer a word, the Master struck him out. At that time, there were few who could master such a pivot.
There was an elder named Zhufeng who said, "When I contemplate this story, it is like having already confiscated a person's entire property and wealth, yet still demanding that they pay more.
The Master said, "Your analogy is extremely clever. I truly do want you to pay me back;
since you have nowhere to escape from, you must seek out a path to death—either by throwing yourself into a river or leaping into a fire."
Only when one has regained their life do they begin to die; having died, they then slowly rise up once more.
If you call them a Bodhisattva, they rejoice; if you call them a thief, they flare up in anger. Yet, fundamentally, they remain the same person as before.
Therefore, the ancients said: "Letting go at the precipice, one takes it up of one's own accord; after death, one revives again—this cannot deceive you.
Only upon reaching this point does one finally realize the meaning of the bamboo stick story. The Master, having grown old, requested to retire from his post.

In the spring of the Xinsi year, he received imperial permission to withdraw and reside in the Moonlight Hall. In the night of the Guiwei year of the Longxing era, a star fell upon the temple, its light shining brilliantly toward the west.
However, he was subsequently shown to be slightly ill. On the ninth day of the eighth month, when his disciples came to inquire after his health, the Master exhorted them to propagate the Way.
He then said slowly, "I shall set out tomorrow. At the fifth watch of the night, he personally wrote a final memorial to the throne, and further composed a letter of farewell to Layman Ziyuan.
The attendant Liaoxian requested a verse. [Dongshan] again wrote in large characters: "Living is just like this; dying is just like this.
Whether there is a verse or no verse—what a fuss! He threw down his brush and passed away peacefully.

At dawn, a snake about one chi long with a white waist and head was seen prostrating itself upon the railing of the Dragon King Well, appearing as if dressed in mourning. This was the manifestation of the Dragon King.
He passed away. The fourfold assembly wailed in grief, and when the Emperor heard of it, he sighed deeply. He composed an imperial eulogy for the Master’s portrait, which read:
"Birth and death are not extinction; permanence is not abiding. Perfect enlightenment is empty and luminous, manifesting wherever objects appear.

The Chancellor and others followed in succession to offer sacrifices, arriving in great numbers. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa beside the Bright Moon Hall. He was seventy-five years of age.
In the fifty-eighth year of the Xia [era], an imperial decree designated the Mingyue Hall as Miaoxi Hermitage; he was posthumously titled Pujue, and his stupa was named Baoguang.
At the beginning of the Chunxi era, his complete recorded teachings in eighty fascicles were bestowed upon him and circulated alongside the Tripitaka.
Chan Master Fozhi Duanqiao of Yuyang Mountain in Qingyuan Prefecture was the son of the Qian clan of the Shaoxing era. He was a descendant of the Kings of Wuyue.
His sixth-generation ancestor had governed Kuaiji and consequently settled there. From birth, the Master was precocious; his features were profound and elegant.
At fourteen, he drove away crows at Dasan Temple; at eighteen, he received the tonsure and the full precepts. He then went to rely upon Master Yi of Jingci. Not long after...
Ji heard the monks strike a pillar and say, "Why do you not speak of Chan? At that moment, he suddenly attained realization.
He went to visit Longmen Yuan, Ganlu Zhuo, and Letan Xiang, all of whom esteemed him for his exceptional brilliance. Later, he met Yuanwu at Zhongfu.
Wu asked, "Who knew that the Eye of the True Dharma would be extinguished at the hands of this blind donkey? Is it extinguished right now, or not?
The Master replied, "I ask you, Reverend, to simply shut your mouth. Wu said, "This is still within the realm of ordinary sentiment. As the Master was about to respond, [Wu struck him].
Wu struck him, and the Master immediately cast off all that had been obstructing him. He served as an attendant at Tianning Temple, where he was appointed to oversee the secretarial office.

Soon thereafter, he shared the teaching seat, and his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. The Regional Inspector of Jingxi invited him to open a Dharma hall at Danxia; subsequently, he moved to Huqiu and then retired from Mount Jingshan.

In response to the requests of the clergy and laity of Pingjiang, he established a hermitage at Xihua, where he remained for several years. Later, by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Baoning Temple in Jiankang. Afterward...
He moved to Wanshou in Suzhou, followed by Xiansha at Mount Shou in Min Province and Xiuchan. He was subsequently summoned by imperial decree to fill the position at Lingyin.
When Empress Dowager Cining of the Song dynasty visited the residence of Prince Wei, she invited the Master to expound the Dharma and bestowed upon him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*.

He requested leave to return to his former retreat at Xihu. In the autumn of the Wuchen year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong, he accepted the summons from Yuwang Monastery and ascended the hall to preach.
When Deshan entered the gate, he would strike with his staff; most people bury their traces within their leather bags. When Linji entered the gate, he would shout;
they all appear and disappear within the realm of sound. If you are a truly heroic monk, you must have the wind blowing beneath your feet, transcending the tracks of past and present.
[The Master] takes up his staff, strikes once, and lets out a shout, saying: "What is this like?"
If you call it "the staff and the shout," you are still drowsy and have not yet awakened. If you do not call it "the staff and the shout," you do not yet recognize Deshan or Linji.
After all, how is it? Then he struck once and said: "Do not touch it at all. He ascended the hall and said:
"The entire earth is the eye of the śramaṇa; throughout the ten directions is one's own light. Why is it that when the drum is beaten in Pūrvavideha in the east..."
In Aparagoyānī they do not hear it; in Jambudvīpa lamps are lit; in Uttarakuru they sit in darkness.

Even if one were to speak with complete mastery within this very point, it would still be a livelihood within the realm of light and shadow. [The Master] struck his whisk and said, "It is all shattered into a hundred fragments.
What is the path for emerging? [He] threw down the whisk and said, 'Study! He then ascended the hall."
Movement brings forth shadows; awakening gives rise to ice. Even if one remains unmoving and unawakened, it is still like the rattle of a cartwheel from the Qin era.

Reaching this point, one must immediately manifest a thousand distinctions; with secret illumination, ten thousand doors open simultaneously, and the pivot of the wheel is turned upon the tip of a hair.
The life-vein does not sink into the sea of poison. At times awakening is like still water; at times movement is like stars flying;
at times both movement and awakening are forgotten; at times illumination and function are sovereign. But tell me: at such a time as this, is it movement? Is it awakening?
This is illumination; this is function. Is there anyone who can distinguish between them? An iron ox blocks the ancient road; when touched, one’s very bones and hair turn cold.

Ascending the hall, he said: "When walking, there is no trace of walking; when speaking, there is no mark of speaking. If walking and speaking reach their destination, you will find yourself struck by the arrow.
If walking and speaking are not yet clear, the divine blade cuts through everything. Even if your speech is without leakage, as for your walking..."
One is no longer confused about the directions, yet one still remains stuck within the shell and leaks from the husk.

If one were a great garuḍa with golden wings, flapping with vigor, or a divine colt with a hundred thousand *yojanas* and ten shadows, galloping across the four quarters and eight extremities, one would not take food haphazardly nor bury oneself wherever one happens to be.
Furthermore, if one does not rely on anything at all, is there still a portion for practice? At every moment and in every particle of dust lies the essential ford. Entering the Hall:
It is easy to fill the vast valleys of the great ocean, yet difficult to fill a leaking cup. If one possesses firm mastery, there is neither difficulty nor ease.
If one sets aside the entire earth, there is ample room; if one lets out even a single hair’s breadth, there is no way through. Suddenly, if one neither sets it aside nor...
"Let go! Where do you tread? Sharing sincerity and common joys and sorrows—even drinking water, one must be nourished.
A monk asked, "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "You are a tenant farmer. [The monk] asked, "What is the host within the guest?"
The Master said, "Meeting one another is still muddled. [A monk] asked, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "The sword’s radiance pierces the clouds of sorrow.
[The monk] asked, "What is the host within the host? The Master said, "Beating the bones and striking the marrow. Whenever the Master presided over the assembly, his countenance was invariably stern.

He never ate or slept apart from the community, and he never grew weary in proclaiming the Way. In the tenth month of the seventh year of the Xiangxing era (1130), he manifested the subtle [signs of departure].
He fell ill. On the eighteenth day, the head seat Fachuán requested his final instructions. The Master said, "Exhaust this mind and intention;

support one another with the Way. Having spoken these words, he passed away. After the cremation, his eyes, teeth, and tongue remained unburnt, and the ground emitted light throughout the entire night.
Those who obtained śarīras were beyond counting; they did not cease for over a month. Huang Guan Luo Zhao had regularly sought the Way from the Master.

Once, having returned from outside, he alone had obtained nothing. His aspiration for the Way was earnest and intense; just as he was eating with a guest, while chewing his food, there was something in his mouth.
When he spat it out, it was a śarīra, about the size of a bean and the color of amber. A seeker of such things took it away.
He then prostrated twice at the site of the cremation. Hearing a sound from within the incense casket, he opened it immediately; what was obtained was as before, yet somewhat more lustrous and red.
His disciples took the remains and divided them to enshrine in pagodas on Mount Mao and at Xihu. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dawu.
Chan Master Fóxìng Fǎtài of Dàméi in Tánzhōu was a native of the Lí family in Hànzhōu. A monk asked, "Principle changes according to phenomena, encompassing all existence as a single, tranquil void;
phenomena follow along with principle, equalizing all differences as they all return to the ultimate reality.
What is the realm of principle? The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. The monk asked, "What is the realm of phenomena?"

The Master said, “The myriad phenomena are densely arrayed. [A monk] asked, “What is the dharma-realm where principle and phenomena are without obstruction? The Master said, “East, west, south, and north.
[The monk] asked, “What is the dharma-realm where phenomena and phenomena are without obstruction? The Master said, “Above, below, and the four intermediate directions.

[He] ascended the hall and said: “If one pushes back toward the Real, the Real has no marks; if one exhausts the delusive, the delusive has no form. Since both the Real and the delusive are non-existent, all is vast and open.”
Yet the eyes are exposed. Since the eyes are exposed, what do you see? "The morning sun melts the snow at the crags;
the northern wind blows open the plum blossoms of winter. Entering the hall, he said: "When one seizes the precious sword, one uses it immediately; how could there be any hesitation?"
Raising his eyebrows, he immediately departs; there is no further hesitation or evasion. In every place, he manifests brilliantly throughout the present and illuminates the past;

in every place, he cuts through all nets and cages. He does not strike against the sharp edge [of the sword], nor does he look into the mirror. Setting aside for a moment the fact that he alone transcends the mundane world, what is it like when the myriad functions have been utterly exhausted?
"In the autumn of the eighth month, where is it hot? Ascending the hall, he said: "Nirvana has no alternative path."
The gates of skillful means are manifold. Lifting up his staff, he said: "Look, look! This staff of mine has swallowed the waters of the West River in a single gulp.
The carp of the Eastern Sea leaps and bounds up to the Thirty-three Heavens. Indra, filled with wrath, strikes Mount Sumeru with a blow that crushes it to powder.
The Earth Goddess, Sthāvarā, joins her palms in praise and says: 'Behold clearly the Dharma King!'"
The Dharma. Such is the way of the Dharma King. [The Master] struck the meditation seat with his staff and descended from the seat.

To understand the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena is not yet to be called the ancestral style of the Buddhas. To realize the total functioning and total illumination is likewise not the essential subtlety of the patch-robed monks.
One must directly break through the sturdy barrier and recognize the single aperture above. What is this single aperture above?
The spring chill is biting. It freezes the young to death. [The Master] ascends the hall: "Today is already the middle of the first month.

Everywhere the lanterns flicker and swirl; throughout the city, silks and brocades are crowded together. People come and go in turns, wandering and playing. Mañjuśrī has run into the midst of the bustling crowd;
Samantabhadra sits upright atop a high tower watching. But tell me, where is Avalokiteśvara? With a *zhentian* (a great wooden mallet) he strikes.
The painted drum resounds, its music blaring through the earth as the lutes and songs are played. Ascending the hall, it is vast and boundless, encompassing the ten directions.
It is level and expansive, transcending form and beyond appearance. The eyes wish to look, yet the pupils wither; the mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail.
Even Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra possess no skillful means here; Linji and Deshan need not hesitate to proclaim it. A tortoise swallows the iron ox of Shanhfu.
A snake bit the Great Image of Jiazhou, startling the carp of the Eastern Sea until this very day its belly remains swollen.
[The Master] laughs and ascends the hall. "The fire-clouds scorch the field crops; the spring sources have ceased their flow. Where is the Great Dragon King Pāyāga? He does not know where he is!
Striking the meditation seat with his staff, he says: "Look! Look! Clouds rise on the Southern Mountain; on the Northern Mountain—"
It was raining. The old monk then produced the sound of a thunderclap to augment his majestic radiance and cause it to spread afar.
He then spoke in a loud voice: "Hō-nō! Hō-nō! Ascending the hall, he said: "Sometimes speaking is wrong; sometimes speaking is right.
Whether coarse words or subtle speech, all return to the primary meaning. When Śākyamuni’s bowl rang out, it was a ringing sound; when Bodhidharma came from the West, it was the stench of excrement."
“Qi! There is only the water buffalo before the mountain, its body emitting rays of light that illuminate heaven and earth.

Ascending the hall, he said: “To gain mindfulness or lose mindfulness—there is nothing that is not liberation. What kind of talk is this? To establish dharmas or destroy dharmas—all are called nirvana.
[If you] try to deliberate or speculate, there is no connection. Wisdom and folly are both universally termed prajñā. Blank-minded buddha-nature—whether bodhisattvas or non-Buddhists [are all one].”
The dharmas that are accomplished are all bodhi; yet they are still but a mere trifle. Nevertheless, even so, it is like Emperor Yang losing his camel.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is right here in this very sound of speech. *Psh!* Great Master Fu!"
Failing to distinguish between good and evil, he used his "brightly shining" and "spiritually lucid" state to corrupt the men and women of households.
When Master Zhigong gave him a shout, the Great Being (Bodhisattva) said, "Do not speak thus; try saying something else. The Great Being then spoke another verse:
"Holding a hoe in empty hands, Walking while riding a water buffalo. A person passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. Master Zhigong rebuked him.
He laughed loudly and said: "The beginning was still somewhat tolerable; the end is even more distressing. Ascending the hall, he said:
"I recall in days past when I traveled abroad, I obtained two things: one was a vajra-hammer, and the other was the bone of a thousand sages.
Carrying them through the universe, my spirit and bearing were loftily prominent. For thirty years like this, I have used them as my standard. And yet, this year..."
I am old now; what thing could I possibly know? I cast down the vajra-hammer and shatter the bones of a thousand sages.
I fling them onto the crossroads; I can no longer cherish them. I pass through this floating life as I please:
taking south for north, calling a tortoise a turtle, and calling beans millet. Let those with clear eyes laugh at me for lacking any guiding line or rule.
Chan Master Cihu Guo Huoguan Jingyuan of Taizhou was the son of the Zhang family of Nanxi in Yongjia.
At the age of eighteen, he received full ordination under Xigong at Mount Ling. Later, he studied the Tiantai teachings for three years before departing to pay his respects to Yuanwu at Zhongfu.
The Master read from the recorded sayings of Sīxīn’s informal sermons, saying: "Since one is deluded, one must attain awakening;

since one has awakened, one must recognize delusion within awakening and awakening within delusion. When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, one establishes all dharmas from the place where there is neither delusion nor awakening."
Upon hearing this, the Master was filled with doubt and immediately hurried to the Buddha Hall. Pushing open the door panels with his hands, he attained a sudden and vast enlightenment.
Thereafter, as Yuan served him, his wit and eloquence burst forth with extraordinary brilliance. Yuanwu dubbed him "The Stubborn Attendant Yuan" and subsequently inscribed his own portrait.
He entrusted it with these words: "Throughout my life, I have spoken only of 'head-banging' Chan (niutou chan). When one encounters such a head-banger, it is like hitting an iron wall.
To strip away the cage and cut through the heels—bringing the entire great earth together, it is as pitch-black as ink.

In my later years, I have become even more 'knife-less' (uncompromising), brandishing the Vajra mallet to shatter all nests and lairs. If you wish to recognize the face of Yuanwu at some future time, I shall present it all to you at once. Yuan.
Wu returned to Shu, while the Master returned to Zhedong. He shrouded his brilliance and concealed his radiance, seeking neither fame nor high office.

When Governor Geng Yanxi of Kuacang—who had once sought instruction from Yuanwu—read the Master’s recorded sayings, he gained insight into the Master's character upon reaching the inscription for his portrait.
Consequently, when the Master began teaching at Nanyue Mountain, the governor dispatched messengers to search for him; they eventually found him among the assembly at Ba’en Temple in Tai.

The abbot’s quarters were cramped, and as he was being pressed to accept the appointment, the former head monk (fangzhang), an eminent disciple of Lingyuan, heard of his teaching and was likewise deeply struck by its extraordinary nature.
A monk asked, "Regarding the meaning of Sansheng’s statement: 'Whenever I meet a person, I come forth; yet when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others'?

The Master said, "An eighty-year-old old man chewing raw iron. The monk asked, "What about Xinghua’s statement: 'Whenever I meet a person, I do not come forth'? The Master said, "An eight-foot-tall man carrying a water jar on his head."

[The monk] said, "He comes out. As soon as he comes out, he becomes a human being. [The Master asked,] "Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, "Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, waves overturn the void;
heaven cannot cover it, and earth cannot support it. What thing is this? The Master said, "A holeless iron hammer.

[The monk] said, "All classes of beings, including devas and humans, all receive the power of this grace. The Master said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization. [The monk] asked about the three periods of time.
"The Buddhas have not exhausted the ultimate meaning of their words; I beg the Master to speak quickly. The Master said: "Blinking one's eyebrows. [The student] asked:
"In years past, the site of Sanping was restored. On this day, Yuanwu held high the ancestral seal, beginning its transmission from the Master.
What is the Linji school? The Master said: "To kill or to give life without blinking an eye. [The student] said: "Drawing back the mirror before one’s eyes."
"Those who truly comprehend it are rare. What is the Yunmen school? The Master said, "The three eyes atop the head illuminate heaven and earth.
[The student] asked, "Before anything is raised, one already knows; before anything is spoken, one already sees. What is the Guiyang school? The Master said, "Pushed forward, they do not go ahead;

held back, they do not retreat. [The student] asked, "The triple world is mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. What is the Fayen school? The Master said, "The staff points directly at the person."
The Master said, "The tips of arrows meet point-to-point; there is no room for yielding. [The student] asked, "In establishing transformation, how does one avoid deviating onto the 'Bird Path'?
When returning to the source, how does one again manifest the wondrous family style? What is the Cao-Dong school? The Master said, "Holding a night-bright talisman in hand, how many know the dawn?
[The student] asked, "Is there still a path above this? The Master said, "There is. [The student] asked, "What is the path above?"
The Master said, "A vast expanse of blackness. A monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "By coveting that one grain of millet, he has lost his provisions for half a year.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, this group of fellows was off by seven or eight;
after King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, this group of fellows was off by two or three. Now, this group of fellows stands and sits with solemn dignity."
Tell me: is this being off by seven or eight, or falling short by two or three? Can you still determine the correct answer? [The Master] raises his whisk and says: "Hūṃ! Hūṃ!
On the occasion of the Buddha-Bath Ceremony, he ascends the hall and says: This Old Śākyamuni, as soon as he was born, acted as a source of laughter;
pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, he declared, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored. Later...
Master Yunmen said: "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs, just to ensure peace in the world.
Yet there are still those who refuse to let it go, instead saying, "Only Yunmen could truly praise the Patriarch.
But tell me, where is he praising him? Is it at the point where he says, "I would have struck him dead with a single blow"? Consider this.
Ximeng was lost in the midst of the encounter. Today, at Nanming, having just assumed the position of abbot, I can only let it pass.
If I did not let it pass, every person throughout the entire world would have to beg for their lives. Now, as there is no other way, I shall simply join the assembly.
[The Master] proceeded toward the Buddha Hall. He gave each person one ladleful [of soup]. "Why is this? Have you not heard it said:
'It is better to violate a rule than to overstep a precedent'? Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The jackal howls; the lion roars.
Eyes wide open, mouth agape, he moves the Southern Star and stumbles past the Northern Dipper. Assembly, do you know where this falls?"
Crouching beneath the Vajra steps, a divine tortoise runs through the fire. Master [Zhaozhou] retired to live on Western Mountain.

Geng Longxue invited him to ascend the seat at Jingguang Temple. Lingfeng Gu raised the case of Baiyun seeing Yangqi, where Yangqi instructed him to recite the verse on awakening to the Way by Chaling, and requested the Master’s critique.
The Master then said: "All you Zen practitioners, Yangqi laughed loudly; his eyes watched..."
The southeast; the mind is set on the northwest. Baiyun has departed in realization, yet his hearing of the matter is not true.
To call a bell a jar—when examined closely, even the old fellow Yangqi is all upon the rack. Taking the wrong for the right:
if it were Nanming, it would not be so. "I have a bright pearl; take care not to let it slip past you head-on. Although it is face-to-face, [do not miss it].

[The Master] presented [the matter]. "It must also be broken with a single blow. Raising his whisk, he said, "Do you understand? When a chess player meets an opponent of equal skill, there is no room for concealment;

when a poem reaches the point of being recited repeatedly, only then does one see its craftsmanship. The Master manifested illness. He requested West Hall Master Ying’an Hua to serve as the Seat-Head (Zuoyuan) and entrusted him with the affairs of the monastery.
He gave instructions as was his custom. Suddenly, he clenched his fist and passed away. Upon cremation, five-colored relics were obtained.
His teeth and tongue were intact, and his right fist remained unimpaired. He was enshrined in a stupa before Liu-Ruan Cave to the east of the monastery. His age was fifty-three.
Chan Master Xiansha Zhaosheng of Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "There is no Maitreya above in heaven; there is no Maitreya below the earth."
"Tell me, where is Maitreya? After a long silence, he said: "When walking at night, do not step on white;
it is either water or stone.
Chan Master Yunbian of Nanfeng in Pingjiang Prefecture was a native of that region. He received the full precepts under Master Zhang of Ruifeng in Min.

He returned home and visited Qiónglóng Yuán. Suddenly, he attained realization and subsequently shared his insights with him. Yuán said, "Although you have gained entry, you have not yet reached the proper mark. You must truly spur yourself on.
Thereupon, he took his leave and sought out various seats of learning before attending Yuanwu Keqin.
Upon entering the room and just as he stepped through the door, Yuanwu said, "Look beneath your feet! The Master struck the pillar once. Yuanwu asked, "Why do you not speak directly?"
[The Master] took up a phrase. The Master said, "If the teacher shakes his head, the disciple wags his tail.

Wuzhuo said, "Try wagging your tail for me. The Master performed a somersault and left. Wuzhuo laughed heartily. From this, [Wuzhuo] became known by his name. Later, while residing there, a monk asked, "What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'?
The Master said, "The hegemon arrives at the Wu River. [The monk] asked, "What is 'taking away the environment but not..."
"Seizing both man and the environment," the Master said. "When building an altar to enshrine a general, how is it that both man and the environment are seized?
The Master said, "Ten thousand miles of mountains and rivers attain great peace. "How is it that both man and the environment are not seized?

The Master said, "The dragon roars and mist rises; the tiger roars and wind is born. "Is there still something beyond this 'same upward direction'? The Master said, "Right before one's face, you have missed it. The student asked:
Truly a master of the art! The Master said: "A ghost deludes people in broad daylight. One day, while walking through the city with monastics and laypeople, they reached Shilang Lane.
Someone asked, "The lane is right here; where is Shilang? The Master raised his arm and said, "Follow me!"
Chan Master Huiyuan of Xiatang at Lingyin Temple in Lin’an, known as Fohai, was born into the Peng family of Meishan.

At the age of thirteen, he became a monk under Zongbian of Yaoshi Monastery. He went to Daci Temple to study the scriptures, but later left to rely on Huizhong of Lingyan, where he attained a slight realization.

The World-Honored One said, “So it is, so it is. Nowadays, those in the monastic forests believe this to mean—
"Past and gone is Wide-Forehead; he was a Buddha who manifested as a butcher by means of skillful means. To see Wide-Forehead in this way—how fortunate that there is no connection!
Again it is said: Wide-Forehead was a man who killed people without blinking an eye; he cast down his butcher’s knife and became a Buddha on the spot.
How fortunate that there is no connection! It is also said: Wide-Forehead cast down his butcher’s knife and declared, 'I am one of the thousand Buddhas.'"
One number. This Buddha is quite distinct and clear; fortunately, there is no connection to be made. Do you wish to recognize Guang'e?
After the wind and rain have passed over the peach blossoms by the roadside, where can horse hooves avoid the remaining petals?
Chan Master Jue of Tianfeng in Taizhou ascended the hall and said: "Within the realm of non-arising, there is no place for settled dwelling;
atop a precipice ten thousand fathoms high, how can one pause? For now, look into the void, let go of everything, and turn yourself over directly—how do you speak this single phrase?"
When a person encounters good fortune, their spirit becomes refreshed; when entering fire, their true golden color becomes even more brilliant.
When the Head Seat Daozu of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Monastery first met Yuanwu, he attained enlightenment under the phrase "Mind itself is Buddha.

After some time, Yuanwu appointed him to share the seat [with the abbot]. One day, while leading the assembly into the inner quarters for private instruction, there were about twenty people remaining. The Master...
Suddenly he asked, "When birth and death arrive, how can one avoid them? The monk had no reply. The Master threw down his whisk and passed away peacefully.
The assembly was all struck with astonishment. They immediately informed Wuzhuo, who came and called out, "Head Seat Zuzhao!
The Master opened his eyes and looked at him. Wuzhuo said, "Rouse your spirit and pass through the barrier. The Master nodded his head and finally entered nirvana.
The head seat Yunju Zongzhen of Nankang Commandery was a native of Danqiu.

While attending Yuanwu at Yunju, one day as he gazed up at the bell tower, he suddenly attained realization. When someone questioned him about this, the Head Seat responded with three verses, the last of which says:
I have a single pivot upon which I directly point it out to you: a thunderclap in the blue sky, as swift as a flash of lightning.
To Deshan and Linji, the staff and the shout were merely expedients; how could this untransmitted wondrous essence ever be lacking for you? Upon awakening to this, he was greatly delighted.

Ultimately, he maintained his integrity with high resolve, and his reputation for the Way grew ever more profound. He once wrote on a wall: "Dwelling atop the highest peak among a thousand crags, my years approach..."
With ears so supple they receive all things with ease, he avoids having his name mentioned by others. He would rather be a monk of a hundred clumsy skills this very day.

By Xu Fu (style name Shichuan), Layman Donghu, Confidential Secretary. Whenever he attended his late father, the Dragon Diagram Official, to visit Fachang and Lingyuan, they would discuss the Dharma all day long;
yet when the official heard of it, he treated it with disdain. When Fachang passed away, [Xu] was laughing.

During their conversation, the Duke was struck by his extraordinary nature and began to place deep faith in this Way. Later, following the death of his father, he reflected that there was no way to repay his boundless debt of gratitude.
He commanded Lingyuan to return to the site of the ancestral tomb to preach the Dharma. When Lingyuan ascended the seat and finished the exchange of questions and answers, he said:

"O virtuous ones, consider the Dragon Diagram (the Duke). In his daily life, he has read ten thousand scrolls of books; like water being passed from one vessel to another, not a single drop has been lost. Now tell me, where does he seek [his reward]?"
"Where have you always been attached? Now that you have cast off consciousness, where will this one who has read ten thousand scrolls of books be attached?
Upon hearing this, the Official was suddenly enlightened and said, "I have no regrets.
Yuan descended from his seat and asked, "Scholar, what did you just see that led you to speak thus? The Official replied, "If there were anything seen..."
"Then you have simply set the Master aside," Yuan said. Gong replied, "In that case, the old monk is not as good as you.
Yuan laughed heartily. During the Jingkang era of Emperor Qinzong of the Song dynasty, [Wang] Gong served as a Ministerial Secretary (Shangshu Waibulang).
Together with several fellow officials who shared his aspiration, he hung his alms bowl in Zemo Hall at Tianning Temple and applied himself diligently to the study of Yuanwu. Yuanwu—
He also admired his [Wu’s] transcendent insight. One day, he went to the Secretary’s Office and, pointing to Wu’s crown, said, "This old fellow has not yet even touched the ground with his heels.
Wu turned his face away and said, "How could a turtle ever escape from inside a jar?
The official said, "I am glad that this old fellow has finally touched the ground with his heels. Wu said, "Do not slander him. The official then withdrew.
The Prince of the Commandery, Zhao Lingjin, styled Biao zhi, was known as the Layman Chaoran. While serving as the governor of Nankang, his administration was successful and his affairs were few;

he frequently associated with Chan monks. He occasionally converted the public hall into a "room of Māgha" (a hermitage). It happened that Yuanwu was residing at Mount Ou; the Prince joyfully sought instruction from him under his guidance.
Yuanwu did not grant him any concessions, but when the Prince pressed his request firmly, Yuanwu said: "In this matter, one must..."
"It must be so; one must simply die once before it can be attained. The Master (Gong) understood this in his heart and once recorded it in a brief note, which said in part:

"My family was poor and suffered a robbery; who knew that nothing remained? The house was empty and unoccupied; how many times have thieves come and ransacked it? Now I have awakened to the vision [of reality].

I entrust you with this; please grant me your protection. In the winter of the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty, the Master was together with the Imperial Secretary Wang Zao.
Chancellor Li Bing and Vice Minister Zeng Kai went to Mount Jing to visit Dahui. When Dahui heard of their arrival, he ordered the drum to be beaten for them to enter his room.
The two gentlemen were delighted; they tucked incense in their sleeves and hurried toward him. Dahui said, "Regarding the story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl, how do you gentlemen understand it?
Li Bing replied, "What kind of bowl are you looking for? He then brushed his sleeves and walked out. Dahui rose, grabbed him by the collar, and said, "The ancients..."
"Others have attained enlightenment here; for what reason do you not? As the official was about to respond, Huairang struck him and said:
"What bowl are you looking for? The Master said, "Only by returning this old man [to his true nature] will it suffice.
Li Mison, a Minister of the Court and known as Layman Puxian, had studied while young, reading five lines at once.

At the age of eighteen, he passed the provincial examination and attained the jinshi degree in the capital; he subsequently rose through the ranks of high office until, at twenty-eight, he became a Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
This man frequently entered Yuanwu’s quarters. One day at dawn, as he was returning from Tianjin Bridge on horseback, he suddenly attained realization;

sweat poured from his entire body. He went straight to Tianning Monastery, where it happened that Yuanwu was stepping out the door. Seeing him from afar, Yuanwu called out, "Layman, congratulations! Your great matter is now finished.
The man replied in a stern voice, "Why are you blinding me with your eyes, Master? Yuanwu then gave a shout. The man—

He also shouted. Thus, his spiritual sharpness was swift and incisive; whenever he engaged in dialogue regarding awakening, he never yielded when the moment was right. Later, the Master was transferred to the Ministry of Personnel (*Li-bu*).

He requested a stipend from the state’s sacrificial offices and returned to Lianjiang in Min Province, where he built a hermitage to enjoy himself. One day, suddenly manifesting slight illness, he immediately requested hot water to bathe.
Upon finishing his bath, he sat cross-legged and composed a verse, saying: "In vain have they spoken of Muxiu and Huhou since of old; today, I shall divide..."
It was clearly revealed: the void toppled Mount Sumeru; what need is there to speak of the "path above"? He then cast aside his brush and passed away.
The practitioner Jue’an, surnamed Zu, was the niece of You Chayuan of Jian’ning. From her youth she had no desire to marry and devoted herself to the ancestral Way.
Upon hearing the words of Yuanwu’s public address, she attained clear and thorough understanding. Yuanwu said, “You must still cast this away as well.”
Upon seeing this, he finally attained freedom. The Patriarch answered with a verse: “The pillar protrudes its horizontal bone; Space brandishes its claws and fangs.
Even if you were to understand it fundamentally, It would still be grit in your eye.”

Renrenbenming (Renrenbenming) was titled "The Hall of Illumination. Having attained perfect enlightenment through his own internal resonance, he traveled extensively to consult renowned masters and received their seals of approval from all.

On the full moon of the second month in the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty, he personally wrote three verses and sent them to Cudang Qing, subtly revealing his intention to depart this world.
At the end of that month, he bid farewell to his relatives and passed away. Cudang appended a colophon to the back of those verses:
Published. Mahamati also once spoke to elucidate this, his verse saying: "To not recognize afflictions as bodhi is folly; If one follows after afflictions, that is delusion.
At the moment of their arising and ceasing, one must realize them: A hawk flies over Silla, yet people do not know it.
To not recognize afflictions as bodhi— Pure flowers grow from the mud. When someone comes to ask me what to do," he said.
Having eaten rice gruel and rice, wash the alms bowl. Do not concern yourself with it; do not concern yourself with it. All day long, you are a simpleton playing with sea-sand.
If you wish to recognize your original true face, it is precisely the Great Liberation of the Patriarchs.
Those who cannot speak it die beneath the axe; those who can speak it also die beneath the axe. After all, what is it? Night travel is forbidden; at first light, you must depart.
Upon arriving at Chengdu, he met Lord Fan, who had been a widow for many years and habitually sat rather than lay down.

Having heard that Yuanwu was residing at Zhaojue Temple, he went there to pay his respects and requested instruction on the causes and conditions for entering the Way. Yuanwu directed him to contemplate the phrase: "It is not mind; it is not Buddha."
"It is not a thing. What is it? For a long time, Fan had no realization. He wept and said to Wù, "Master, what skillful means do you have that might allow me to understand more easily?
Wù replied, "I do have a skillful means. He then instructed him to simply look into: "What is this?
Later, Fan attained a realization and said, "So, it has always been this near!"
Chan Master Wenshu Xindao of Changde Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Taiping Qin.
He was a native of the Xu family in Meizhou. At the age of thirteen, he received full ordination.

He went to Chengdu to study the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only), believing that he had reached the ultimate understanding. A fellow student challenged him, saying: "The three realms are mind-only; all phenomena..."

"Only consciousness! Now that the myriad phenomena before our eyes are so vividly manifest, where does the mind-consciousness reside? The Master was at a loss for an answer and departed the mountain pass.
He wandered throughout the Yangtze and Huai regions until he reached Taiping in Shu. There, he heard the Night Session teaching of Foguan, who raised the koan of Zhaozhou’s "Cypress Tree.
Upon reaching the point where Jue Tiezui said, "The former master did not say such words; do not slander the former master," [the Master] thereupon...

Great doubt arose within him. After a long period of sustained mindfulness, one night he attained sudden enlightenment. He immediately hurried to the master’s quarters, intending to recount his realization.
Upon seeing him arrive, Master Jian closed the door. The Master said, "Master, do not deceive me. Jian replied, "The ten directions have no walls;
why do you not enter through the door? The Master punched a hole in the window paper. Jian immediately opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak!"
The Master held up a mirror with both hands, blew upon it with his mouth, and departed. He then presented this verse: "Zhaozhou has the 'Pine Tree' koan;
Zen practitioners have transmitted it throughout the world. Most merely pluck the leaves and seek the branches, Unable to directly realize the source.
Jue says there are no such words— This is truly reviling one right to their face. Zen students...
If one possesses the all-pervading eye, one should skillfully discern the true from the false within this. Jiañ (Jiàn) deeply agreed with this and praised it whenever he encountered guests.
Later, he was ordered to share the seat [with the Master]. When Xiang (Xiáng) took charge of the monastery, he invited the Master to open the Dharma at Tianning.
Before long, he was promoted to the position of Wen-shu on Mount Dabie. "The lion yawns; the elephant king roars. Yunmen hides his body inside the Big Dipper. Baiyun...
For what reason is it called "hand"? The Buddhas of the three periods cannot know; yet the wildcat and the white ox know that it exists.
But tell me, what is this matter of their knowing it? Rain beats upon the pear blossoms as butterflies fly; the wind blows the willow catkins as they roll away.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and pointed directly upward, saying: "At such a time, [it] pierces through arrogance."
Śakra, with his heel, struck once and said: "At such a time, he shatters the skull of King Yama. Then, pointing to the east, he said:
"At such a time, he pierces the eyes of the carp in the Eastern Sea. Pointing to the west, he said:
"At such a time, he blocks the nostrils of the Queen Mother of the West. But tell me: how is it when it is not like this at all? This year's rain.

There is much moisture; each [item] should be dried frequently in the sun. In the Jihai year of the Xuanhua era of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, an edict was issued to change the name of monks to "Virtuous Practitioners" (Deshi).

He ascended the hall and said: "The matter of the Patriarch’s intent coming from the West is, this morning, exceptionally new. Formerly he had the appearance of a Bhikṣu; now he takes the form of the Old Lord (Laojun).
He wears a silver-brown robe over a crane-feather cloak, and his head is wrapped in a banana-leaf turban. A guest of leisure in the forests and springs—" Two [lines missing].
To receive the sovereign's grace is what is meant by the Way. Thus it is said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must observe the conditions of time and season.
Now tell me, what is the present season? Vairocana wears a jeweled crown to manifest the conventional within the ultimate;
Mañjuśrī, appearing as an old man, dons a crane-feather cloak to conform to the exigencies of the times. If one person acts thus, so shall all.

It is the same for human beings. When great masters establish monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*), they rejoice at the gathering of the immortals, where together they sip the wine of the Immortal of Confusion and sing the *Bùxū* verses in unison.
Sometimes they read the *Língbǎo Dúrénjīng*; sometimes they discuss the elixirs of longevity and immortality.
Under the moon, they play the zither, their fingertips emitting the sounds of antiquity; before the pavilion, they arrange their chess pieces, their subtle moves revealing divine mechanisms.
Stepping forward, one reaches the Great Brahma Heaven; stepping back, one enters the city of the Nine Obscurities.

As for the phrase "neither advancing nor retreating," how would you express it? Even if one were to transcend to the path of the Three Clarities, it remains ultimately but a single illusory body within saṃsāra.
In the ninth month of the Gengzi year, [the Master] resumed the monastic robes and ascended the hall. He did not don the field-robes (of a layperson), but wore those of a monk.
The feathered robe suits the physical appearance of the Old Lord quite well. For over a year and a half, I have reflected idly upon this: in general, rise and fall each have their own time.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, foretold in advance that the Dharma would encounter difficulties; this is clearly recorded in the scriptures, and there is no one who does not know it in detail.
Comparing the dates, the present moment is precisely that time. The Māras have gained the opportunity to delude and disrupt the True Teaching, and the monks have changed into laymen.

They altered the physical form [of the scriptures] and changed the Buddha’s names; they gave rise to false interpretations and excised passages from the sutras. They silenced the sound of the gongs and cymbals and added feet to the begging bowls.

Through many such deceptions, they sought to deceive the Sagely Sovereign. Fortunately, it was due to the sagely virtue and sagely brilliance of our Emperor that he did not forget the sacred entrustment.
The Imperial Calligraphy was specially bestowed and promulgated throughout the realm, permitting monks and nuns to once again don their robes and shave their heads.

This is truly like cold ashes catching fire once more, or withered wood flourishing anew. Without leaving the form of a layperson, they assume the form of a monk; without departing the realm of Māra, they enter the realm of the Buddha.
The Dharma drum resounds once more, and the collapsing order is restored. Those who were lost in the wine of immortality are transformed into the sweet nectar of ambrosia. They walk forth...
Empty words. They are translated as "Songs for Returning Home. Setting down the silver wooden tablet, he picks up the *niṣīdana*.
Yesterday he bowed his head and joined his palms; today he greets with *vaṃdanā* and asks after one’s health. Only the old manner has changed, not the old person.
"I venture to ask the great assembly: Is the person of old one, or two? After a long silence, he said: "The autumn wind also knows how to resent the scattered mess;
it blows away the ashes of the Way from those years. In the spring of the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era of Emperor Gaozong, he addressed the assembly.
Regarding the account of Linji’s entry into extinction and his entrustment to Sansheng, [the text] says: "The treasury of the true Dharma eye is extinguished by a blind donkey.
Never did Linji speak such words; people of past and present have all spread this falsely. Do not believe it; simply wait and see after three months.
When the intercalary third month arrived, the rebel Zhong Xiang rose up in revolt. His followers wished to lead the Master southward into exile, but the Master said: "In the study of the Way..."
Having fully understood birth and death, what is there to avoid? When the bandits arrived, the Master said, "Kill me quickly to satisfy your hearts.
The Master was ultimately harmed; his blood all turned into white milk. The bandits were struck with terror and remorse; they drew their mats over him and departed.
Chan Master Zhibing of Nanhua in Shaoyou was a native of Yongkang in Shu.

Early in his travels, not long after he had left his hometown, he heard that his preceptor’s monastery had been reduced to ashes by fire. Upon receiving the letter, the Master threw it to the ground and said, "This merely disturbs people's minds.
He was stern and severe in character; those from all quarters called him "Iron-Face Bing. Once, ascending the hall, he said: "This matter is most rare."
How extraordinary! To speak directly without obstruction: the old farmer from the eastern neighbor’s field has received his share of the teaching.
It not only penetrates sound and form, but also accords with the times and seasons. If you ask what school this belongs to, the eight characters do not even touch the surface.

[He] struck the meditation seat and descended. Ascending the hall, he spoke day after day and brought it up at every moment: "The earth supporting the mountains—how much difference is there? [He then said: "The parrot of Longxi..."
The mynah bird wins people’s pity; it is mostly because it can talk. Cease your reflections and keep its company.
A wise person, upon hearing this, should immediately seize it. There is yet another thing that is truly marvelous: the cat is uniquely adept at catching mice.
Ascending the hall, he stirred the air with his staff and said: "He stirs the long river into butter and milk; even the shrimp and crabs still have eyes."
He spat out some eye-secretion, struck the ground once, and said: "The great earth is transformed into gold, yet the pauper remains as before, bare-boned and naked.
Is it because he has no share in it himself? Or is it because he refuses to take responsibility? Among them, there may be a man capable of bearing this burden and putting it into practice."
"How many people have lost their wealth and incurred calamity? He struck the meditation platform once more and said, "Do you understand?

When you reach the Jewel Mountain, you must open your eyes; do not let yourself return in haste with empty hands. Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring light is radiant and flowers vie to bloom; The nightingale cries as the moon sets behind the western mountains.
Gavāmpati sticks out his tongue in long astonishment— To whom can this clear matter be explained?"
*Sha.* Ascending the hall, he said: "Delusion does not delude itself; it is established in opposition to awakening. Awakening does not awaken itself; it is spoken of because of delusion.

Therefore, awakening is the substance of delusion, and delusion is the function of awakening. Both delusion and awakening are non-existent. From within this, there is neither distinction nor commonality.
When neither distinction nor commonality can be shifted, the Patriarchs could not bring them here. The nostrils weigh a thousand catties."

Chan Master Longya Zhicai of Tanzhou was the son of the Shi family in Shuzhou. He served diligently under Fojian, never declining difficult tasks, and his reputation had already spread throughout the monastic community.
While traveling, he arrived at Huanglong at dusk; it happened that Sishin was at the triple gates.
When asked where he had come from, he stated his name, and it was immediately known that he was Cai, the steward of Taiping in Shuzhou.
The next day, he entered the room. Sīxin asked, "If you understand the first phrase, you understand the final phrase;
if you understand the final phrase, you understand the first phrase. Setting aside both the first and the final, how do you understand Baizhang’s story of the wild fox?
The Master said, "I already knew where he was coming from upon entering the door; why must you further bring up his views?"
Zhongni said, "New Elder, you are dead in the hands of the Senior Monk. The Master said, "Though the words differ, the ultimate principle is without discrepancy.
Zhongni asked, "What is this matter that is without discrepancy? The Master said, "If one does not strike the horn of Huanglong, how can one know the pearl beneath its chin?
Zhongni then struck him. When he first resided at Yuelu, on the day he opened the hall for teachings, a monk asked:
"Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout—today I request the Master to comment upon them. The Master said, "Suru suru. [The monk] said, "Suru suru.
Is there still the meaning of the West [coming from India] or not? The Master said, "Suru suru.

For this reason, the monastic community called him "Cai Suru" (Suru Suru). Later, he moved to Longya. Because Emperor Qinzhong of the Song dynasty ascended the throne, various officials requested [his presence].
Having finished the formal address for the Emperor upon ascending the hall, he took his seat and held up his staff. Tapping it once, he said: "The Preface to the Imperial Edict states:
'The originally profound realm, the wondrous field of all Buddhas. Just now, this staff has already explained this for you all.

If you awaken to it here and now, there will be no principle that is not revealed and no phenomenon that is not encompassed. If this is not yet the case, I cannot help but provide another way of entry."
News: The sun of the Sage shines with renewed brilliance; the four seas are clear and full. Heaven’s harmony brings joy and peace, extending auspicious blessings.
Grasping the staff, joy arises; casting it to the ground, the cry of "Ten Thousand Years! resounds like a mountain call. [He casts down the staff. He descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he snaps his fingers once and says: "A single snap of the fingers perfects the eighty thousand gates; in an instant, the three great kalpas are extinguished. If you see this...
When you are able to practice, practice; when you are weary, rest. If you do not understand this, it is like two mandarin ducks carrying a turtle on their backs.
Ascending the hall, he cited the words of Sīxīn: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a family that has three sons. The first son is intelligent and wise;
he filially supports his parents, receives guests who come and go, and manages the family estate. The second son..."
The eldest son was fierce, stubborn, and cunning; he was greedy, lustful, and addicted to wine, lying drunk in the streets and alleys and ruining the family estate.
The third son was blind, deaf, and mute; unable to distinguish beans from wheat, he was incapable of any task other than eating his meals.
Among these three, Huanglong wished to select one for a purpose. Furthermore, there were four lines: "In death there is life; in life there is death; in death there is permanence."
"Death. Living within life, always living. Use these four lines to test the monks of the world. The Master said, "What do you call these 'four lines'?
What are the surnames and names of the three men? If you can recognize them, you will walk hand-in-hand with Huanglong, without the slightest interval between you.
If this is not yet so, I cannot help but offer flowers upon the water. The three men together—
The essence and function are not function; the four propositions are identical in sound—emptiness and non-emptiness. If you wish to recognize the three men and the four propositions:
when the golden crow first rises, it is a mass of red. The Master resided at Longya for thirteen years, governing the assembly with austerity and frugality;
the monks revered him. Grand Marshal Xi Gong Zhen moved him to Yunxi, where he stayed for four years. This was the year Wu-wu of the Shaoxing era under Emperor Gaozong.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, he suddenly assembled the community and entrusted them with the affairs of the temple. He then wrote a verse, saying: "On this Mid-Autumn day of the Wumwu year, my life as a renunciant and my tenure as abbot have come to an end.
Even upon departing, there is not even a 'self' to be found; how could there be any empty space to be sought? His final instructions were as usual.
On the twenty-third day, he again assembled the community and addressed them, asking: "Nirvana and birth-and-death are both entirely like flowers in the sky."

"Buddha" and "sentient beings" are both merely metaphorical designations (*adhivacana*). "How shall you all proceed? he asked. When the assembly all offered their responses, none were in accord with his intent.
The Master shouted, "Suffering! Suffering! and then said, "White clouds surge from the earth; the bright moon hangs in the sky. Having spoken, he passed away with a smile.
Upon cremation, five-colored *śarīra* relics and sacred bone fragments were obtained, which were enshrined in a stupa at the northwest corner of the monastery.

Chan Master Penglaiqing of Mingzhou ascended the hall and said: "A phrase exists, yet no phrase exists; it is like a vine leaning against a tree. Let the various quarters nod their heads as they will.
But when the tree falls and the vine withers, there is no plan to soar toward the heavens above, nor any scheme to enter the earth below.
O sharp-witted ones! If you can fix a single eye here, you will see [the Dharma] moving freely in all directions—seven ways, eight ways. He raised his whisk.
He said: "Look, look! One song, two songs—no one understands them. After the rain has passed, the autumn waters in the night pond are deep.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Within the cry of the cuckoo, the spring light fades; fallen flowers cover the ground, unable to remain.
Upon the crystal palace, no traces of passage remain—who can understand how to plant a rootless tree? Raising his staff, he said: "This is the rootless one. Now tell me—"
He untied the flower and said nothing. After a long silence, he remarked: "It is simply because of the rain all night that another spring has passed.
Ascending the hall, he cited Fayan’s saying: "If you recognize the bench, there is more than enough room around it. Yunmen said: "If you recognize the bench..."
Heaven and earth are vastly different. The Master said: "These two old men—one stands atop the highest mountain peak;
the other walks upon the deepest ocean floor. Even so, one is not 'is,' and two are not 'are. Amidst falling blossoms and flowing water, a parrot cries;
the rain has ceased at the quiet pavilion, the night is already half spent, and a sliver of moon rises once more from the bottom of the sea."
Chan Master Shouxun Foding of Heshan in Anji County was the son of the Shi family of that prefecture. He visited Guangjian Ying, but did not find resonance there.
He then went to Taiping, where he joined the assembly to seek instruction; however, he made no progress whatsoever. Thereupon, he sealed his bedding and declared:

"If I do not attain thorough penetration in this life, I vow never to open this again. From then on, he sat during the day and stood through the night, as if mourning for a deceased parent. After more than...
After seven weeks, Fojian suddenly ascended the hall and said, "The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by a single Dharma. Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
He went to see Fojian, who said, "What a pity that this bright pearl was picked up by such a madman!"
He then questioned him, saying: "Lingyun said, 'Since the moment I first saw the peach blossoms, until now I have had no further doubts.
What is it that he does not doubt? The Master said: "Do not say that Lingyun has no doubts; even now, if you try to find a place where there is doubt, it is utterly unobtainable.
Yuanjian said: "Xuansha said, 'How perfectly true! How perfectly true! I truly can guarantee for you, elder brother..."
"He has not yet penetrated through. "Where is it that he has not yet penetrated? The Master said, "I know well that you, Venerable Sir, are earnest in your compassionate concern for others.

Jueyan agreed with this. As the Master rose from his prostrations, he presented a verse: "All day long I gaze at the sky without lifting my head; Only when the peach blossoms are in full bloom do I raise my eyes.
Even if you possess a net that covers the heavens, If you can penetrate the secure barrier, then simply rest. Jueyan then commanded him [to speak further].

Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua of Tiantong in Mingzhou was the son of the Jiang family of Qizhou. From birth, he was extraordinary and outstanding.

Chan Master Lan’an Dingxu of Xichan Monastery in Fuzhou was the son of the Lin family of that same prefecture. As a youth, he was renowned for his success in the civil service examinations.

At the age of twenty-five, while reading the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teachings), he suddenly exclaimed, "How nearly have I been misled by the scholar’s cap! He then desired to leave the household life.

His mother found this difficult to accept, as the marriage ceremony was scheduled for that very year. The Master then cut her off, saying: "The peach and apricot trees entrust their blossoms all at once to the spring breeze;
from now on, the green bamboo and yellow flowers shall be my eternal companions. He eventually followed Baoshou, joyfully becoming a bhikṣu.

Carrying his single staff, he traveled through Huxiang, visiting renowned masters everywhere. Finding no difference in the flavor of the Dharma, he returned to his hometown and built a hermitage on Qiang Peak.
He remained at the summit for three years without descending. Foceng Cai entreated him to emerge and lead the assembly at Dacheng.
Once, while inquiring with students about the karmic conditions regarding "the mind itself is Buddha," Miguang—a friend of the Master—wrote to him from Miaoxi Hermitage on Yangyu Island, saying:

He then went to Mount Yunju, where he stayed for two years. He subsequently visited Mount Dongting and Mount Jiufeng. In the spring of the year of the Dog (1158), he returned to Mount Xuefeng. In the summer of that same year, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jiuhua. In the autumn, he was appointed Abbot of Mount Tiantong. In the winter, he was summoned to the capital to serve as State Preceptor. In the spring of the following year, he was again appointed Abbot of Mount Tiantong. In the summer, he was granted the title "Great Master of Universal Wisdom. In the autumn, he retired to Mount Xuefeng. In the winter, he passed away on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month. He was sixty-nine years old. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Xuefeng. His posthumous title was "National Teacher Wuxin. His dharma heirs included Xuedou Chongxian, Xuedou Zhixian, and others. His recorded sayings and correspondence fill ten volumes. The Master’s name was Hongzhi, and his style name was Wuxin. He was a native of Fuzhou. His ancestors were of the Zhang clan. His father, Zhang Wenji, served as a district magistrate. The Master was born in the year of the Monkey (1091). At age eighteen, he left home to study under Master Daokai of Mount Shishuang. At twenty-one, he received full ordination. He then traveled to various places to seek instruction, eventually meeting Dahui at Mount Yunju. After his enlightenment, he traveled extensively throughout the realm, visiting famous mountains and monasteries. He finally settled at Mount Xuefeng, where he taught for many years. His assembly numbered over a thousand monks. His teaching style was simple and direct, emphasizing the immediate realization of one's own nature. He composed numerous gathas and verses, which are widely circulated and highly regarded by practitioners of the Way. His legacy continues to inspire students of Chan to this day.
