Yantou’s eyes looked toward the southeast, yet his intent lay in the northwest. What a fine squeeze! One’s very life has fallen into the hands of another.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To speak where one cannot practice is to gouge a sore upon good flesh. To practice where one cannot speak is to lean on a fence and grope for a wall.
To reach both practice and speech is like a stone sprout putting forth branches. To reach neither practice nor speech is to carry snow to fill a well. Departing.
The four propositions are cut off and the hundred negations are transcended, so [the Master] does not ask. Everyone, tell me: Mañjuśrī asked about the Dharma-gate of Nonduality;
for what reason did Vimalakīrti remain silent? He gave a shout and said: "To covet another's single grain of millet, one loses half a year’s worth of provisions.
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still transgression? Yunmen replied:
The monk said, "Mount Sumeru. The Master said, "Great or small, Yunmen does not even recognize the head of the matter.
A monk asked, "What is the matter of the void's dissolution? The Master said, "The offense shall not be punished with a heavy sentence. In his later years, the Master retired to Tiantong.

Through his guidance and instruction with the tongs and hammer of discipline, students gathered like clouds. Later, he passed away while sitting peacefully without illness. His disciples erected a stupa for him on the central peak of the mountain.
Chan Master Baizhuo Shandeng of Kuangxiao Temple in Quzhou was the son of the Min clan from Wujiang, Huizhou. A monk asked: "The world..."
"What was the intent of the Venerable One’s initial thought? The Master said, "One person transmits what is false; ten thousand people transmit what is true.
[The monk] said, "When there is spirit, one adds more spirit; where there is no elegance, one is elegant nonetheless. The Master said, "Praise indeed—praise is insufficient.
[The monk] said, "It is just as the Great Master Yunmen said: 'If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to the dogs.'"
"Eat, my son! I only hope for peace throughout the world. But ultimately, what eye do you possess? The Master said, "Seek it behind the crown of your head.
Ascending the hall, he said: "By day there is bustling clamor; by night there is profound stillness. One runs hither and thither along the long corridors, yet at every step, nothing is lacking.
Yet failing to recognize the master of the house, one enters the wild weeds with one's whole body. There, one stumbles upon Fu Dashi, who asks:"
I inquire after the Elder Vimalakīrti, who lies ill in the city of Vaiśālī. How many know the dawn of heaven? If one is a person of transcendent capacity, they do not seek it "over there.
Why is this so? He lets out a shout and says: "Running downhill, one does not stop; such a swift opportunity is hard to encounter."
Nan Shuji was a native of Fuzhou. Having long relied upon Ying’an, he attained sudden enlightenment through the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature.
He composed a verse which says: “The dog has no Buddha-nature; Rāhu’s star enters his destiny.
It is not that he kills people himself; He is surely killed by others. Ying’an praised him for his carefree liberation. At the end of the Shaoxing era, he passed away at Guizong.
The Layman Li Hao, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, styled De-yuan, was known by the sobriquet Zheng-xin.

In his youth, he read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as if visiting an old homeland; he took it to heart and never forgot it. Later, he went to Mingguo Monastery and entered the room to pay his respects to the Master.

Ying’an struck him on the chest and asked, "Minister, after death, where will you go? Startled, the official broke into a cold sweat. Ying’an shouted at him to leave. The official withdrew to engage in private study. Not long after...
Within ten days, he had completely ascended to the inner sanctum of the teaching hall. He sent a verse to his fellow practitioner Yan Chao-kang, saying:
"The gate has a shop of Sun Bin; The home harbors the wife of Gan Zhi. Sleeping at night and rising early— Who awakens, and who is deluded?

In the hermitage, there was one known as Shanyou who sold rouge; he too had long studied under Ying’an and was quite self-important. The Master presented him with this verse: "Without applying [the rouge],"...
The rouge naturally possesses elegance. Often, practitioners of Zen stop here. Having passed through the snares of past and present, they come here to receive a blow of the fist.

The teacher Yan Chao Kang was a layman from Changxing in Huzhou. He once sought the Way from Xuedang at Jianfu Monastery and later met Ying’an at Ba’en Monastery, where he attained the essential meaning.
He composed a verse which says: “Zhaozhou said the dog has no Buddha-nature;
I say the dog does have Buddha-nature. Suddenly, beneath these words, I knew my own home; From now on, I will not believe Zhaozhou’s mouth.”
"Exerting one's spirit, shake yourself free. Following behind others, there are no skillful hands. Riding a cow while seeking the cow—this makes people laugh to death.
Only now do I realize my former errors. At that time, Da-hui was in Mei-yang; Yan presented this verse to him, and Da-hui’s reply in a letter stated briefly:
"Following behind others, there are no skillful hands"—these eighty-four thousand [teachings] are all your public path of life.
Chan Master Zhong’an Huikong of Fashi Monastery in Quanzhou, a dharma heir of Chan Master Jiaozhongguang, was a native of the Cai family of Ganzhou.

On the first day of spring, he ascended the hall, took up his staff, struck it once, and said, “First, strike the head of the spring ox. He struck it again and said, “Afterward, strike the body of the spring ox.”
The tail startles him up into the void; he enters the pore of a lotus fiber. Śākyamuni has no way to hide his tracks; Maitreya flees a thousand miles in haste.
Mañjuśrī, however, knows where it lands, clapping his hands and laughing with joy. But tell me, what is there to be joyful about? "Last night the spring breeze entered the gate;
immediately one sees a thousand flowers blooming on the tip of the pestle. [He] ascended the hall. [At] a thousand households...
Pavilions and towers. In a flash of autumn wind, one only notices a coolness arising in the sleeves; one does not realize the leaves are falling from the gardens.
If you can realize this here and now, then everywhere is the manifestation of the Absolute Truth. If it is not yet so, then for now, let us meet with formal greetings of "how are you?
Ascending the hall, he cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, saying: "The Buddha told Subhūti: 'In all those lands, there are as many sentient beings as there are...'"

The various states of mind—the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are. Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all minds are "not-mind"; it is precisely for this reason that they are called "mind.
Do you understand the essential point? "With the spring breeze, his horse’s hooves fly swift; in a single day, he views the flowers of Chang’an in their entirety.

A monk asked, "The Buddhas of the past established these precedents: the observance of the *śīla* and the summer retreat (*varṣā*). What is the fundamental principle behind this? The Master said, "Lapis lazuli."
[The Master] spread out Mount Sumeru inside his bowl. The monk then shouted; the Master then struck him.
Chan Master Tanmi Hunyuan of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Lu family of Tiantai. He left home under Dao-rong of Zifu Monastery.
At sixteen, he received full ordination and studied the teachings of the Tiantai school. Finding them to be overly subtle and restrictive, he eventually abandoned them to go and attend upon Dahui.
At Jingshan, he visited Xuechao Yici and Yuan of Ciana once more. Upon entering Min, he stayed at Dongxi Chan Monastery but had no realization. He then went to Quannan to study under Jiaozhong Guang.

Guang appointed him as the attendant for the assembly, but he resigned from his post and returned to his former quarters. One day, while reflecting on the karmic incident of Xiangyan striking the bamboo, he attained sudden enlightenment.
He composed a verse and presented it to Guang; however, Guang challenged him with the words of Xuansha regarding "not yet having reached the ultimate."

[The Master] was unhindered. Zhong said, "You may now go see Miaoxi. He immediately took his leave and went to Mei Yang. After serving diligently for four years, he ascended the hall following [Miaoxi's] departure.

Regarding the "Small Private Session" (xiaocan) of Deshan where no answer was given—a matter that has become a subject of talk in the monastic community for a thousand ages—it is said that those who ask questions receive thirty blows.
They are accustomed to speaking of "criticism" (he) and "floundering" (hang). At that time, a monk stepped forward—one truly capable of breaking through. Deshan...
He struck him. Elegant and refined. Before you had even asked a question, a cangue was placed upon your head and shackles were fastened upon your feet.
"Where are you from? "Once we meet, it breaks the spirit. "A man from Silla. He took his hand and smiled joyfully.
Had he not yet stepped onto the boat’s railing, I would have given him thirty blows. Yunmen, as before, continues to deceive and confuse others.

To pass such a judgment today based on his emotional state—well, I would give him thirty blows too. Now tell me: is this a reward or a punishment? Those who possess the eye of a true student of the Way [should know].
Let us examine this: [The Master] ascends the hall. He cites the kōan concerning Yunmen’s question to a monk regarding "Luminous, tranquil illumination pervading the sands of the Ganges.
The Master says: "Sifting for fish and shrimp on level ground; shooting a soaring osprey across the vast heavens. The lame-legged old Yunmen—thousand errors and ten thousand errors.
Later, he passed away and was interred in a stupa at his home mountain.
Chan Master Xinan Wuyin of Qingyuan in Jizhou was the son of the Li family from Changle in Fu prefecture.
At the age of eleven, he left Min province and became a novice under Guang Chan-yue of Xujiang. It was only after five years that he finally received the monastic robes.
One day, Guang gave the "Verses on the Fifty-three Teachers of the Buddha-land" to the *vina* (chant leader), while the Master attended by his side.

Upon hearing the phrase, "When dwelling in the forest, there is a time one must see the Buddhas of the ten directions; observe this single mind in leisure and without affairs," he immediately grasped the essential point.
He was exceptionally gifted with sharp faculties, and was subsequently sent back to Min to visit the masters Gushan Foxin Cai, Dongchan Yue’an Guo, and Xichan Lan’an Xu.
At that time, Hui was residing at Guishan; the Master went there to seek him out, and [Hui] gave him a single...

At midnight, while feeling about for his clean towel, he experienced a sudden and great awakening. At dawn, he hurried to the abbot’s quarters to communicate what he had realized, presenting a verse that said:
"The karmic consciousness was vast and boundless, originally having no basis. Last night at the third watch, I turned my head and took a look."
A single flash of spiritual radiance, originally and uniquely manifest. Anan nodded in approval. He then left the mountain and went to Jianfu Temple, where he met Yan Wanan.
Upon entering the room for instruction, his responses were swift and agile. Yan raised his voice sternly and said, "This fellow from Fuzhou has been corrupted by others.
The entire assembly was struck with astonishment. Not long after, he traveled again to Mei Yang to see Dahui. Dahui asked, "What is it?"
The Master said, "Meeting face-to-face, there is no other dharma. Dahui asked, "How does one maintain this?
The Master replied, "When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. Subsequently, he followed Dahui back to the north.
One day Dahui asked, "Among so many people who have entered the room, how many have spoken to the point, and how many have not? The Master replied, "I, Zhen, simply..."
Huike looked on. Suddenly, he extended his hand and said, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? The Master replied, "The weather is cold; please, Master, let me fold up your sleeves.

Huike suddenly struck him with a bamboo staff and said, "Tell me now, was that a reward for you or a punishment? The Master then offered this verse: The hand of the Buddha is my hand, My hand is the hand of the Buddha. If you wish to know where they differ, Look at the tip of the staff.
He presented ten or so kōans concerning the patriarchs and Buddhas for the sake of Hui. Regarding the World-Honored One’s first birth, he said: "To thrust one's head out at once is already a mistake;
how much more so to open one's mouth and claim supremacy? Had he known how to deeply conceal his tongue at that time, he would have spared his descendants the burden of idle worries.
Hui struck his palm in rhythmic approval (kijik). Later, he propagated the Dharma at Tiantai Zhenru and subsequently moved to Baoen.
A monk from Shanglan in Yuzhang and Qingyuan in Jizhou asked: "The Third Sage said, 'Whenever I meet someone, I come forth;
when I come forth, I do not act for others. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "When the flower is moved, the butterflies arrive with it.
The monk asked, "Xinghua said, 'Whenever I meet someone, I do not come forth; when I come forth, I immediately act for others. How is this? The Master said, "Buying a stone, one obtains clouds."
Rao ascended the hall. He raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? Yunmen said, "The golden wind reveals its essence.
The Master said, "Yunmen strikes at the collar from within his sleeves and cuts the lapel from beneath his armpits;

he is indeed a skilled hand. Yet, if one examines him closely, he cannot avoid being caught by threads and strings. If someone were to ask Baen, 'What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? he would simply—"
He said to him: "Next year there will be new branches; the spring wind’s vexation shall not cease until the end. Ascending the hall, he took up his staff and said:
"Within the lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma. He pointed to his staff and said, "This is the staff of Hengquan;
which one is the One Vehicle Dharma? He struck the ground once and said: "The momentum of a thousand peaks ceases at the edge of the mountain range; the myriad..."
The sound is sent back to vanish upon the sea. On the nineteenth day of the fifth month of the Renzi year of the Shaohui era of the Song dynasty, the Guangzong Emperor passed away.
He inscribed a verse, saying: "The final phrase is entrusted face-to-face; if one hesitates or deliberates, it becomes mere worldly convention."
He then passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Luo Hu Ying Zhongwen composed a biography of his conduct.

Chan Master Duan’an Zu Zhu of Gong’an in Jingnan Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yan of Donglin. He was a native of Nanping. Once, he ascended the hall and said: "It is not mind. It is not...

This is the Buddha; it is not a thing. Having dried up the drool of the wild foxes and overturned the lair of the mountain ghosts, within the level fields and shallow grasses, the tawny-tailed tiger reveals itself;
amidst the vast emptiness of the great void, the majestic hawk of the high heavens is released. Hehehe!
Revealing its very bone and marrow, he casually brings it forth before the assembly. After all, what exactly is this clearly manifest thing?

*Du, du!* He ascends the hall and says: "Jade dew hangs from the green grass; the golden wind stirs the white water-plantain. A single cry of the cold wild goose awakens those who have not yet awakened."
Chan Master Fayuan of Ba’en in Tingzhou was a native of Guozhou. On ascending the hall, he cited the karmic conditions concerning Juzhi’s raising of a finger and spoke in verse:
The beautiful lady rises from sleep, too lazy to comb her hair; She takes up her golden hairpin and, having inserted it, leaves it at that.
In the main, it is better for her natural form to remain as it is; Without applying rouge or powder, she is nonetheless elegant and refined.
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Sheng family of Yuqian.
In his youth, he relied upon Master Yikan of Mingtang Temple as his teacher. He first studied under various elders, including Dayu Hongzhi, Zhengtang Dayuan, and others.

Later, hearing Donglin say to the assembly, “In this place of mine there is nothing else that is profound or marvelous; there is only soup made of wood shavings and rice made of iron nails,” [he took up residence there].

"Chew on this! The Master secretly rejoiced at these words and went directly to pay his respects. He presented his insights to Linji, who said, "According to your way of seeing, you are sitting right within the mirror-like awareness.
The Master’s doubts did not cease; he cast away everything he had previously attained all at once.
One day, he heard a monk cite Nanquan’s saying: "When people see this single stalk of flower, it is like being in a dream. At this, he suddenly attained silent realization.
Suojue said, "Striking the grass is only intended to startle the snake. The next day, he entered the room, and Lin asked, "Where was it that Yantou secretly revealed his meaning?
The Master replied, "Today I have caught this old thief red-handed. Lin said, "The life of the Great Master Bodhidharma rests in your hands.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, he was suddenly struck a fist to the chest; at that moment, he attained great enlightenment. Directly—
He broke into a sweat that soaked his back. Nodding his head, he said to himself, "Was Linji’s statement, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this,' not a hollow word?
He then presented a verse, saying: "To act for others, one must act thoroughly; to kill a man, one must see blood. Deshan and Yantou—ten thousand miles, a single line of iron.
After Linran had taken up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One did not speak..."
He said, "Kāśyapa hears what he has not heard. He planted his staff upright and said, "Where do the flowing waters and yellow leaves come from?
An ox with cold crows passes through the distant village. Ascending the hall, he cited Xuefeng’s instruction to the assembly:

"The entire earth is this gate of liberation. Why, when one takes it by the hand, can one not be dragged in? The Master said, "Great Xuefeng indeed split the talk into two pieces. Since it is the whole..."
"The great earth—this is a gate of liberation. What is the use of dragging it about? Ascending the hall, he said:
"If you go on like this all the time, the grass before the Dharma Hall will be ten feet deep. If you come back like this all the time, the mud under your feet will be three feet deep.
Tell me, what then? Every third year there is an intercalary month; the rooster cries at the fifth watch. Ascending the hall, he raised up the case of Wanzan Xian.
The Master said: "To sit upon the Buddha’s throne and chop off the Buddha’s feet—to show no respect for Confucius of the Eastern House and instead go to a foreign land to practice ritual and music.
The Master added: "It is not that entering the mud and the water is not the way of the former masters; yet, alas, the cicada clings to the withered wood."
Weeping until tears run dry, he does not turn his head back. Zhenzhuo held up his staff and said, "Truly, there are those who do not turn their heads back.

Jingci [Yuanwu] bowed three times toward Shengzi. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Buddhas of the three periods speak of existence within non-existence—like picking up a flower-needle from a vast plain.
The Patriarchs of the six generations seek non-existence within existence—like a monkey reaching for the moon reflected in water. To depart from these two paths is like..."
What talk could there be? My house has no concern for matters of rise and fall; all day long it occupies the clouds over Lake Dongting.
Yuan’an accepted the invitation of Zhìzhě and led the assembly, saying: "On South Mountain there is an old Demon King. His piercing eyes emit flashes of lightning;
his mouth is like a blood-basin as he scolds the Buddhas and Patriarchs; his teeth are like sword-trees as he reviles the various quarters. Several times the winds of karma have blown upon him."
Immovable. Blowing it so that the yellow mountains tremble; together with Śikhin and Fu Dashi, they break down the door with a single fire.
Still the same Meng Bala, deceiving countless foolish men and women, who open their eyes wide and enter the boiling cauldron with a grand air.
Suddenly, a monk came forward and said, "If you are indeed a *kalyāṇamitra*, why do you deceive people by leading them into the boiling cauldron?
He replied to him, "This is not within your sphere. Later, he entered nirvana and was interred in a stupa at the southern hermitage of the monastery.

Chan Master Zhizhe Yu’an Zhenci of Wuzhou was the son of the Li family from Tongzhou. Initially, he relied upon Chengdu Zhengfa Monastery, where he left the household life and received full ordination.
Later, while traveling among lecture halls, he listened to a discourse on the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*. Upon reaching the passage, "The four elements are each separate;
where does this illusory body now reside? Ultimately it has no substance and is truly like a phantom," he attained realization and composed a verse.
He said, "A single bright pearl is here with me; whenever it is moved or stirred, it emits light that shakes the earth.
He returned to present this to his teacher, who tested him with the kōan regarding the dog having no Buddha-nature.

The student replied, "Even hundreds of thousands of millions of kōans do not go beyond this verse. The teacher considered this insolence and dismissed him. Thereupon, the student traveled south, arriving at—
While staying at Lushan Yuan Tong, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Preceptor. When he entered the room for the assembly, he raised the following case:
A monk asked Yunmen, “When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then? Yunmen said, “The Buddha is also dust.

Wan’an let out a shout immediately upon these words, pointed to his own chest, and said, “The Buddha is also dust. He then composed a verse: Brushing away the dust to see the Buddha— The Buddha is also dust.

Question finished, answer finished. Turn yourself around right here and now. "I urge you to drink one more cup of wine; once you have passed out of the Yang Pass to the west, there will be no old friends left.
Furthermore, he offered a verse on the Samādhi of Every Dust-Mote: "Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket. A discerning jewel-seeker sits at the bottom of the abyss.
Upon every single dust-mote, Mount Sumeru walks. The clear-eyed Persian smiles and snaps his fingers. He smiles and snaps his fingers—Śāla."
"A pure breeze rises from the branches of the *hú* tree. Wan’an deeply approved of this.
Zen Master Shao Yuan of Zhaojue Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture ascended the hall and said: "Melting bottles, plates, hairpins, and bracelets into a single gold;
stirring butter, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor. Thus, when host and guest are in accord, the internal and external are at peace. The five ranks of the ruler..."
Your servant Qi has penetrated through it all. These four kinds of discernment form a single thread. If one lets go, there is a fine drizzle and the autumn wind whistles;
if one holds fast, it is utterly empty—dare anyone even cast a direct glance upon it? Tell me, is it better to let go for the sake of others?

Holding fast to the way of being human is excellent. At ease, it is just like the arrival of the autumn wind; without intending to cool others, people cool themselves. Entering the hall, he raised the following case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall? Yunmen said, "The golden wind reveals its essence."
The Master said: "To clarify the mechanism of falling into the tiger's trap, one must be a monk of true substance. Great Master Yunmen possessed a samādhi that transcends the common herd;

striking the joints and knocking at the gates, he extended a single hand from within a flash of lightning to untangle adhesions and remove bonds for others, to pull out wedges and extract nails—truly an adept indeed. Yet, if we examine it closely, it is much like..."
[The Master] crossed the ladder with the bandits. Zhaojue, however, was not like this. Suddenly, someone asked: "What is it like when the tree withers and the leaves fall?
He simply said to him: "Setting sun and solitary wild goose fly together; autumn waters and the vast sky are one color.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Zhaozhou’s first meeting with Nanquan. Zhaozhou asked: "What is the Way? Nanquan said: "The ordinary mind is the Way."

Zhaozhou said, "Is it not that you are still merely moving toward it? Wuzu Quan said, "The moment you intend to move toward it, you have already deviated. Zhaozhou said, "If you do not intend to move toward it, how can you know what is the Way?
Quan said, "The Way does not belong to knowing, nor does it belong to not-knowing. To 'know' is deluded cognition; to 'not know' is indeterminate ignorance (*avyākṛta*).
If one truly penetrates the Way that is free from doubt, it is vast and open like the great void—how could one forcibly impose distinctions of right and wrong?"
The Master said: "How extraordinary, all you Zen practitioners! Although this śrāmaṇera has only recently entered the Way, he turned [the teaching] around with a single stroke;
is he not a clever person? Nanquan was like a skilled archer—every arrow he shot hit the red center.
Had it not been for Zhaozhou, it would have been difficult indeed to uphold [the transmission]. Thus, at the very point where 'ordinary mind is the Way' is spoken, he struck the pivot."

Cast out the things within your breast; lose the kōan before your eyes. When it is clear in every head and manifest in every object, you will be able to walk with confidence and speak with confidence.
At ease, you bring forth [the truth], and in every instance there is a path for your own emergence. But tell me, by what do you verify this?
Have you not seen how, when a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? the answer was: "The cypress tree in the courtyard"?
Shuzi asked, "When the myriad dharmas return to the One, where does the One return? He replied, "I am in Qingzhou making a cotton shirt that weighs seven *jin*.
He asked, "What is Zhaozhou? He replied, "The east gate, the west gate, the south gate, and the north gate.
[Zhaozhou] untangles the sticky and removes the bonds for others; he extracts the nails and pulls out the wedges, cutting off the tongues of all people under heaven and piercing through them.
The nostrils of all people in the world—this is surely not the pivot for the teaching that "ordinary mind is the Way.
It is certainly not a concocted phrase nor a superimposed set of verses that pushes people into stagnant water. This is precisely the model for a śrāmaṇera;
you should study it. If you wish to travel a thousand li, the first step is the beginning. Under the bright sun and clear sky...
"Quickly put on your fine shirt.
Chan Master Jian of Huizhou went to visit Dahui at Mount Jing. At that time, Wan’an was serving as the Head Seat (Shouzuo).
One day, while leading the assembly into the private interview room, he asked the Master: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven—no clear-eyed monk can count them out."
"Try counting them for me," the Master said. The Teacher then gave a shout. The Hermit said, "Seven, six, five, four, three, two, one.
What will you do now? As the Teacher was about to respond, the Hermit struck him and said, "Do not speak recklessly! At these words, the Teacher attained realization.
He suddenly spoke a verse, saying: "Do not speak recklessly! Your hair stands on end with cold; You know only that the plum has ripened, Yet you do not realize your nose is aching.
In his verse on the "Puppy Has No Buddha-Nature" koan, he said: "The old man Zhaozhou is utterly without face;
To speak thus is to deviate from the source, Causing gods and ghosts to wail."
Chan Master Chuliang Su’eng of Zifu Temple in Kunshan, Pingjiang, was the son of the Liu family from Shanyin.
At the age of thirteen, he began his travels to seek teachers. Initially, he served as an attendant to Miaoxi; later, he followed Wannian Yan as his master and served as his secretary (*shuji*).

He was highly proficient in literary composition, and everyone referred to him as Secretary Liang. He once resided at Faxi Monastery in Xiuzhou, where he offered incense to designate himself as a successor to Wannian. [He did so] for a second time.
During the Shaoxing era, he resided at Mount Lu on the coast of Kuaiji. Later, when You served as the Prefect of Linhai, he was invited to take charge of Zigaoseng Temple;

subsequently, he led the monasteries of Jianfu and Zifu on Mount Kunshan. On the day of Wuyin, the sixth month of the Dingwei year of the Chunxi era under Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty, he passed away due to illness.
His final instructions were that his remains be interred at Zhilin Temple on Mount Lu, a temple which he and Yan’an had built together.
Chan Master Mukan An-yong of Gushan, Fuzhou, was a dharma heir of Chan Master Xun of Xichan. He was the son of the Wu family of Min County.

Having become a monk at the age of twenty, he visited Lanan at Yunmen before long. One day, upon entering the inner quarters for instruction, Lanan said: "I do not ask about words; I do not ask about no-words."

The Master said, "World-Honored One. After a long silence, he could not find a way to meet the World-Honored One in that state of stillness. He then followed him and let out a shout. Suddenly, he attained realization.

He prostrated and said, "Had it not been for today’s question, how could I have lost this opportune moment before my eyes? Yun'an granted him permission. Later, while presiding over the assembly in the Dharma hall, he said:
"If you wish to clarify this matter, you must possess the skillful means of the spark struck from stone and the flash of lightning. Only then...

To be able to cast off one’s entire body upon the head of a steep and precipitous cliff, and to attain great stability within the depths of white clouds—this is like searching the ground for a golden needle;
at this very moment, the crown of the skull must burst asunder. Reaching this point, even if one were to adapt according to the situation, it would be of no avail.

One does not meet with its sharp edge; the whole body is liberated alone. It is like wading through mud and water. As for this one phrase of the fundamental function being fully brought forth—how do you speak of it?
He struck his whisk and said: "Tempered and drawn forth, the seven-star light shines brilliantly; once you understand how to wield it, you may roam freely anywhere under heaven.
He ascended the hall and, citing Muzhou’s instruction to the assembly, said: "If you people have not yet attained a point of entry, you must..."
“If you have attained an entrance, once you have attained an entrance, you must not forget this old monk. The Master said, “To speak in such a manner—how thick is your face?
Muan said, “I am not like that. As long as you have not attained an entrance, you must attain an entrance.
Once you have attained an entrance, you must cast that entrance away before you can succeed. [He] ascended the hall and took up [the whisk].

Holding up his staff, he said, "Linji’s little page has never yet spoken directly to the point. Today, putting on a total display of feigned innocence, I want everyone to know that there is something here.
He threw down the staff and descended from the seat. A monk asked, "What is it like when one turns over and stands upside down atop the peak of Mount Sumeru?
The Master said, "I have never seen the hair-tip star appear. The monk said, "In that case, it must be a torrential flood."
"The mountain peaks are overturned! The Master said, "Do not act recklessly. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "The thunder is immense, yet there is not a drop of rain.
Chan Master Nanya of Baitang at Longxiang in Wenzhou ascended the hall and said: "Upon the summit of Rui Peak, beside the Phoenix Pavilion."

Sharing a bowl of thin gruel, they sit in meditation with their heads shrouded by a hundred-patch robe. When the Second Patriarch prostrated three times and stood in his place, it was already too much;
that old barbarian Bodhidharma had exhausted every bit of marrow and skin, leaving a scene of utter chaos.
As for the rest of such types, what is there to say? Did Pota speak this way to escape the censure of the various quarters? *Claps hands.*

The Ropes Bed said: "It would have been fitting to let the prisoner remain so that his wisdom might grow. Ascending the hall, he said: "The great capacity values directness; the great function values sudden manifestation.
Even if there were a 'biting the arrowhead' capacity, it must be struck down with a single blow. Why? Within the treasury of our King, there is no such blade. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Purple ferns stretch out their fists as bamboo shoots break through the tips; willow flowers fall away as green shadows interlace. *Fen* (分) [This appears to be a fragmentary line].
This clarifies the single-line transmission of the Western Patriarch. When the yellow oriole calls, it speaks its nest-language;

if you can see this here and believe it with deep conviction, then according to the standards of other quarters, you would certainly be settled beneath a bright window. But under the gate of Longxiang, one is simply struck down by a single blow.
Why? It is not that I find it difficult to dwell together with others; rather, for the most part, the distinction between the ordained and the laity must be made clear.
Chan Master Tianwang Zhiqing of Fuzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his whisk, he said: "This very thing cannot be covered by heaven, nor can it be supported by earth.
It pervades the world and fills space; it forms into spheres and lumps. Reaching this point, where can the Buddhas of the three periods of time go to search for it?
Where can the patriarchs of the six generations go to grasp it? All you patch-robed monks under heaven..."
Monk, where can one find the term "remote"? Unless one attains realization for oneself, one must practice both "striking" and "singing" together.
Even so, this is not yet the place where a patch-robed monk walks. What, then, is the place where a patch-robed monk walks?
He plunges his body crosswise into a sea of right and wrong; he strides freely through a thicket of jackals and tigers.
The Master of the Anfen Hermitage at Jianmen in Nanjian Prefecture had studied under Mukan in his youth at Anguo Monastery.

Later, he relied upon Lan’an, yet had not yet attained profound realization. He took his leave to visit Dahuai at Jingshan; while traveling along the riverbank, he gazed up in admiration at the imperial palaces.

Hearing the Street Official shout, "The Minister is coming! he was suddenly and completely enlightened. He composed a verse, saying: "For many years this matter has hung upon my breast; I have questioned all quarters, yet my eyes remained unopened.
Now, at this moment, liver and gall are both rent asunder— A single cry: 'The Minister comes upon the river!
He then went straight back to Xichan, where Lan’an conferred upon him the *kāṣāya*. From that time on, he no longer regulated his dwelling place. Later...
He lived in seclusion at Jianmen, where his transformative influence spread throughout the regions south of the Ling Mountains. Students followed him;

the gāthās and verses he composed were produced with a swift hand, totaling more than a thousand pieces that circulated widely in the world. He addressed the assembly, saying: "This entire field of land—do you all [understand it]?"
Tell me, before heaven and earth were yet divided, where did it abide? To penetrate directly to the bottom is already to have failed the Venerable One;
there is no small amount of neglect here. If you further hesitate or engage in deliberation, it will be more than ten thousand miles of white clouds.
Suddenly seizing his staff, he struck them and dispersed the assembly, saying: "From the Buddhas above down to the sentient beings below, their very lives and natures are all contained herein."
When I, this mountain monk, examine what is in my own hands, there is immeasurable transgression.
Is there anyone who can find fault with it? [He strikes the meditation staff once. "The wrongdoer has a head; the debt has an owner. Then, looking left and right, he said:
"Since coming out of the cave, I have had no rival; where one may show leniency, one should show leniency. Addressing the assembly: "As for the fifteenth day..."
"Previously, all the stars in the heavens bowed toward the North; after the fifteenth day, there is no water in the human world that does not flow toward the East.
Having cast away both what came before and what followed, the local dialects differ everywhere. Then, counting on his fingers, he said:
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen. Brothers, now..."
"What is the date? After a long silence, he said: "In our shop, every cent is settled at once; there is no credit.
Chan Master Zongdai of Gushan in Fuzhou, a successor of Chan Master Yue of Dongchan, ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One said: 'One should know thus; one should see thus.'"
Understanding it thus, he did not give rise to the notion of dharmas. He then shouted, saying: "Jade is originally without flaw, yet it possesses flaws.
Chan Master Shiban Zhishi of Gushan in Fuzhou thanked Li Shenqing and Chen Zhongling. He ascended the hall and said:
"In the days when I was at East Creek, when flowers bloomed and leaves fell, I often intended to cast gold to fashion a Zichu. (From the *Gujin*).
When people speak in this manner, it is much like a charred *tong* lute hanging on a wall, rarely meeting a true connoisseur.

Today, Baiyun is fortunate that these two gentlemen have arrived; it is precisely when the six directions are clear and all the myriad sounds are stilled. Unable to resist, I shall once again tune the vermilion strings.
He tried playing a single melody. Holding his staff crosswise, he asked, "Do you all hear it? To hear it is not non-existent; yet tell me, what tune is this?
He struck the ground with his staff and said: "The infinite meaning of the rare sound of primordial antiquity—who knows it after the one who knows?
He ascended the hall for formal instruction. "Speech is slander; silence is deception. Neither speaking nor remaining silent only increases falsehood. He gave a shout.
With one shout, he said: "The spring breeze blows down the peach and plum blossoms; light mist and sparse rain enshroud the green peaks.
Chan Master Deqin of the Yuan-an Cloister at Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a native of Xinghua. When he first arrived at Mount Jing, he reached the mountain gate.
With a snap of his fingers, he entered.
Chan Master Dun’an Zongying of Qianyuan Monastery in Fuzhou, a successor of Chan Master Jing of Xichan, ascended the hall and, striking his staff, said: "This impatient fellow! Only—
With a single stroke. Leaning on his staff, he said, "A person of keen intelligence does not need to have it raised again. Is there anyone here now who is of such keen intelligence?
After a long silence, he said, "When one attempts to capture the mythical *qilin*, even the rabbit does not appear."
Chan Master Biefeng Yun of Huayan Monastery in Xinghua Prefecture first resided at Zhitu in Fuzhou, and later moved to Huayan in Fuquan.
He ascended the hall and said: "A thousand kinds of words and ten thousand modes of explanation are intended only to ensure that you remain forever unconfused.

But tell me, what is it that you do not confuse? To call it a bamboo cane is to strike against it; not to call it a bamboo cane is to turn your back on it. He ascended the hall again and said: "Maitreya..."
"Mahāsattva Le, you entered the monastery in the morning and attained perfect enlightenment by evening. You are entirely like a dull-witted fellow; what use is there in that?
Even if you could see Mount Zhiti and the Twin Peaks from across the mountains, you should still turn back immediately—I would give you thirty blows right under your heels!
Upon ascending the hall, he cited the words of Zhenjing: "There is no Chan, there is no Dao, there is no original source, and there is no..."

"Exquisite! To be truly at ease, one must clarify that single aperture. The Master said, "Since there is neither Chan nor the Way, and neither the primal nor the subtle, where could one find that single aperture?
If there were a single aperture to be clarified, how could one attain true ease? Do you all wish to attain ease right now?
He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Tathāgatas of the past have already perfected this gate."
This is truly extraordinary talk! The Bodhisattvas of the present are each now entering perfect clarity.
As for the crime of slandering others, those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma; do not neglect it.
Alas, in this vast and boundless universe there are countless people—how many among them are true men?
Chan Master Zhongji Wushan Licai of Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "I cite Xuedou’s words: 'Three parts of one's life have already passed;
that single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished. Greedily pursuing the days as they pass in trivial toil—when called back, it does not turn around;
what can be done? Old man Xuedou was coarse and crude, blunt and uncouth. You must further investigate for thirty more years."

"Even after many years, one has still not realized Zen. Nevertheless, though it is so, the land is vast and the people are few; let me try to provide this footnote: 'The three eyes of Maheśvara are blinded;
north, south, east, and west, the paths cannot be distinguished. Ascending the hall, he raised the story of Zhaozhou’s "Go drink tea.
The Master said: "Zhaozhou meets everyone and offers them tea; who would have known that such a matter arises from within the household? To turn over one's hand..."
He creates clouds and rain; with the wind, he scatters earth and sand, drawing forth Dongshan’s lack of clever intellect so that even when asked about the Buddha, he says, "Three catties of hemp.
Reading this verse from Chan’an’s *Yulu*: The Persian from the South Sea holds secret mantras;
Of thousands of words and myriad phrases, few people know them. A spring breeze comes from nowhere; It blows down three or four branches of peach blossoms.

The Daoist Ruo Shisan of Mount Xianzhou in Jianning Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Kai Shan Qian, had frequently used his own spiritual matters to question various Chan elders, yet he attained no entry into realization.
When Kai Shan returned and settled in a thatched hut to the left of the mountain, Ruo Shisan went there to serve him and seek instruction. During the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty...
On the eighth night of the third month in the year of Gengshen, I attained sudden and clear enlightenment. I composed a verse and presented it to Master Shan, saying:
"Originally there was no seam or fissure; Upon touching it, it immediately shone with brilliance. Since it is a treasure worth a thousand pieces of gold, Why need one use it to shoot at a sparrow?

Master Shan replied: "When it snaps with a *chui* sound, true joy and liberation arise; Birth and death, ordinary and sage, all sink into stillness. Under the mountain of Xianzhou, I laugh aloud, hehe!"
He did not fail the mutual expectations of their long-standing hearts.

Chan Master Miaofeng Zhi of Lingyin Monastery in Lin’an, a successor of Chan Master Guang of King Aśoka Monastery, was a native of the Liu clan of Huzhou. His family had resided in Pengcheng for generations.

In previous generations, all [members of his clan] attained high office. The Master was by nature lofty and pure; at the age of thirteen, he left home to receive instruction at the Qizheng Yuan of Deqing.
Whenever he encountered a scripture or treatise, he immediately grasped its essential meaning. He then went to Mount Mao to study under Fozhao.

Having attained realization through the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner, Zhaoyin composed a verse, saying: "Today I have opened a single thread for you; with bolts severed and iron cut, my school shall arise.
He then entered Mount Kuanglu, where he planted his staff beneath Miaogao Peak for ten years. Later, he went to reside at Huíyīn in Tāizhōu, and finally settled at Línghǐn.
As Línghǐn was close to the imperial palace, it was crowded with the constant traffic of carriages and horses; the Master, however, kept his door shut.
He neither welcomed nor saw anyone off. Even when high officials or nobles came to see him, he would merely exchange greetings regarding the weather.

At that time, as the Heavenly Child (Tiantong) monastery had its seat vacant, Zheng Qingzhi, who was then holding the helm of state, submitted a formal petition urging the Master to accept the invitation. The Master said, "I am already past my nineties;
do I still travel by night without rest? He declined and did not go. Entering the hall for the sermon, he said: "Responding to things and manifesting form..."
The moon in the water—picked up at the snap of a finger, revealed all at once. [The Master] strikes the left side of the meditation seat with his whisk and says:
"This is the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of burning coals. He strikes the right side and says: "This is the sword-trees and the knife-mountains.
"In front are Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta; behind are Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. As for this one move in the center, do you know where it lands?"
"Ma! He struck once more and said, "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago; even until now, he has not attained the Sublime. Entering the hall, he said:
"Long-standing practitioners of high caliber have eyes that look out over the four seas and nostrils that reach to the heavens; they see with a vision that is intimate and direct."
To speak, one speaks intimately; to act, one acts intimately; to employ, one employs intimately. Yet, you simply do not recognize this old monk’s staff. Why? He said to the assembly:
"When the mountain is about to reach nine fathoms high, one does not add even a single basketful of earth.
Fenyang said, "If you recognize the staff, your journey as a pilgrim is finished—this is a mistake. Sanjiao said, "Recognize it..."
"The staff enters hell as fast as a whistling arrow. The old monk, however, says otherwise: "Recognizing the staff is a mistake;
at Wondrous Peak, three people made mistakes. This is not medicine for those who are ill. Pang Jushi sells a colander; Qingping Daoshi speaks of a wooden ladle.
When the Master was about to pass away, he bathed his body, sat in the lotus position, and wrote this verse: "Coming is thus; going is thus."

Coming and going were as one; a pure breeze swept across ten thousand li. Having finished his writing, he passed away on the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of the Year of Yiwei in the Duanping era of Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty.
He was eighty-four years of age and seventy-one years since his ordination.
His body was cremated, and countless śarīras were obtained, which were interred on the western ridge of Lingyin Monastery.

Chan Master Beijian Ju Jian of Jingci Temple in Lin’an was the son of the Long family of Tongchuan. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations. He received the full precepts at Guangfu Monastery in his home district.
He studied under Biefeng Tudu, investigating the teachings in silent contemplation. One day, while reading the records of Wan’an, he attained a profound realization.
He then went to study further under Fozhao, with whom his spiritual faculties were in accord. From that time on, he remained within Fozhao’s circle for fifteen years.
He traveled to Jiangxi to visit Zhongwen at Luhu. When he engaged in discussion with the Master, Zhongwen was greatly amazed by him.
He subsequently bestowed upon him the "Great Wisdom" bamboo rattle. He emerged into the world to preside over Baon Guangxiao Temple in Tai.

When Grand Councilor Zhen Xishan served as the Imperial Commissioner for Jiangdong, he used his influence to urge him to accept the post, but he could not be persuaded. He then withdrew into seclusion at Beijian on Feilai Peak.
For ten years he resided at Beijian. He subsequently served at Tiefo in Xiayu, Zhejiang; Xianqing and Biyun in Changzhou; Huiri in Suzhou; and Daochang on Lake Tai.
Later, by imperial decree, he moved to Jingci Temple. Entering the hall, he said: "To realize the One, all matters are finished.
A monk who has settled his affairs does not recognize a single character. Even if you are thus, it still does not qualify as the full manifestation."
"Where the power of Yu did not reach, the sound of the river flows toward the west. [The Master] ascends the hall and cites the case of Elder Master Mi and Dongshan while they were at a bakery.
Elder Mi drew a circle on the ground and said to Dongshan, "Take this with you. Dongshan said:
Holding it up, Baoning Yong said, "Not only could those two elders not lift it; no one in the entire world could lift it either.
The Master said, "Beijian dares to say that Baoning’s resources were exhausted and his strength spent. Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Zhaozhou entering the monks' hall, saying, "Thief!
Thief! Upon seeing a monk, he seized him and said, "The thief is right here! The monk said:
"It is not I," Zhaozhou said, pushing him away. "It is indeed so," [the monk] replied, yet he was unwilling to take responsibility for it. The Master said, "Zhaozhou’s gathering-in was too lax;
his letting-go was too urgent. Jingci, however, is not like this: "A house-thief is difficult to guard against; the family wealth will surely be lost."
Holding up his staff, he said: "One may only err in seizing; one must not err in releasing. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Taking great perfect enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equality. Drinking the official wine, lying on the official street—dying right where one is, buried right where one is.
Originally there is no rank or position; why use forceful arrangement? Ascending the hall, [he said]: "Yunyan’s twenty..."
Nian was at Yaoshan, clarifying only this matter: "The clear pool does not permit the blue dragon to coil. For forty years, Zhaozhou did not allow his mind to be distracted;
except for the two times of rice gruel and meals, these were considered distractions of the mind. How could a rabbit ever leave its burrow?

In the spring of the *Chunyu* cycle of the *Pingwu* year during the Chunyou era of Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty, he manifested illness. He requested a brush and wrote a verse, further inscribing at the bottom of the paper:
He said, "On the first day of the fourth month, take care. When that time arrived, he passed away while dozing. He was eighty-three years old;
his dharma age was sixty-two. His entire body was interred beside the Chang Pagoda at Yuet Tang, in accordance with his final instructions.
His *Beijian ji* (Collected Works of Beijian) in nineteen volumes remains in circulation.
Chan Master Rushan Ruoyan of Jingshan, Lin’an Prefecture, was the son of the Zhou family of Taizhou.
Entering the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Jiangshan calls this a 'staff'; you all also call this a 'staff.
Is there any distinction between them or not? Though we lean on the same railing, we view the mountain colors differently. [Quotation from] *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
The eulogy says: At Vaiśālī, he manifested illness and displayed his folly, adding nothing but suspicion to the bellies of the people of the age.
Had it not been for Mañjuśrī’s personal examination and exposure, who would have known of these underlying ailments?
Chan Master Xian, known as Puguang of Shangfang in Huzhou, possessed a naturally extraordinary and refined character. His eloquence was vast and unimpeded.
Entering the hall for discourse, he cited a monk who asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, "No. The Master said:
"The dog has no Buddha-nature; this is due to that great man. Though right and wrong enter his ears, a gourd hangs upon the wall. (This concludes the eulogy.)
The image-polisher said: "Once a word has left the mouth, it is as difficult to pursue as a team of four horses. Fortunately, the Sovereign has granted him pardon.
At the heart of the Yangtze River, a boat breaks a reed; how can the danger of the wave-head compare to the peril of this question?"
Chan Master Xingkong of Dongchan Monastery in Fuzhou ascended the hall for formal instruction. He cited a case where a monk asked Yanguan, "What is the original body of Vairocana?
Yanguan said, "Bring me the pure water pitcher. When the monk brought the pitcher to him, Yanguan said:

[The Master] returned it to its original place. The monk asked the official again, "The ancient Buddha passed away long ago. The Master said, "It is difficult to show patterns and colors to the blind;
it is difficult to provide sounds to the deaf. Since this monk could not appreciate the present opportunity, Yanquan’s [effort] was rendered in vain.
Yunmen said, "There are no traces," but he could not support Yanquan's position. [He] used his whisk.
The Master drew a single line and said, "The preceding entanglements are all cut off at once. Now tell me, after all, what is the Dharmakāya Vairocana?
He threw down his whisk and descended from the seat.
Chan Master Guyun Quan of Yuwang Monastery in Qingyuan Prefecture ascended the hall and said: He cited a monk asking Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is cold spring water in an ancient ravine?
Xuefeng replied, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom. The monk asked, "And for those who drink from it? Xuefeng said, "It does not enter through the mouth.

He further cited Zhaozhou being asked, "What is it like when there is cold spring water in an ancient ravine? Zhaozhou said, "Bitter. The monk asked, "And for those who drink from it? [Zhaozhou said,] "Even more bitter."
Zhaozhou said, "Dead. The Master said, "One person follows the waves; another cuts off the flow of all streams. Examining them both, they are equally lacking in understanding.

Today, if someone asks Yuyang, 'What of the cold spring in the ancient ravine? you should simply answer him: 'One must personally see Xuefeng. As for those who drink from it, ask Zhaozhou. [There was a verse:
The cold spring in the ancient ravine— How many people have drunk from it? If you wish to know its flavor, You must first see Xuefeng. [End of Verse] There was one who sent [this].
The verse for the monk’s return to Fengshan reads: A phoenix chick beneath Mount Fenghuang— Its patterns just revealed, its wings are now complete.

When deluded, one is separated by a thousand miles; when awakened, it is right at the edge of the mouth. Therefore, when a monk asked Shishuang, ‘What is Chan? Shishuang replied, ‘Brick. A monk also asked Muzhou.”
"What is Chan? Zhaozhou said, "A fierce fire frying oil. Again, a monk asked Shoushan, "What is Chan?
Shoushan said, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind. "O Great Assembly, there is no cross-path on the Way; where one stands is solitary and precarious.
These three great elders traveled upon a living path before sound and employed a numinous mechanism outside of time. If you were to examine this with the true eye of a patch-robed monk..."
To speak of them as they are, there are indeed differences in their excellence. One is like Zhang Liang entering the fray; another is like Xiang Yu employing his troops;
another is like Kongming gauging the enemy. If one can discern these clearly, one may stand shoulder to shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Nevertheless, if a monk were suddenly to come forth and say, "Venerable sir, you have split your words into two separate pieces," [the previous discussion]—just now...
The Way. The Way has no crossroads; it is without faction and without partiality. Yet now, you have again divided it into so many categories of superior and inferior.
How will you respond? Do you understand? "Holding hands while climbing the mountain, we all exert our strength together; the breath escaping from the throat is known only by oneself.

In the autumn of the Gengzi year of the Chunxi era of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty, he manifested a slight illness. He wrote a verse, sat in the lotus position, and passed away. [Funeral rites were held. Tea.
His teeth and tongue remained uncorrupted, and he obtained countless relics of five colors, which were interred in the stupa at Hengshan.
His bones were divided and returned for burial to the left of Wannian Temple.

A monk asked Chan Master Daoci of Jinshan in Runzhou, a successor of Chan Master Zhongfeng Ying of Mount Jing: "Xuefeng said, 'At the Wangzhou Pavilion, I have already seen you. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Half a pound in the left eye. The monk asked, "And at Wushan Ridge, I have already seen you. The Master said, "Half a pound in the right eye."
[The student] asked, "When you have already understood, what then? The Master said, "Eight *liang* in the right eye.
[The student] asked, "You have already met me before the Sangha Hall; how about that? The Master said, "The nostrils point downward with the large end first.
[The student] asked, "As for Gehu suddenly entering the abbot’s quarters and Baofu entering the Sangha Hall—what was the meaning of this? The Master said, "Water flows along the edge of the rock..."
Cold flows out; the wind comes from within the flowers, bringing fragrance. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "This great matter is all-pervading; there is nowhere it does not reach.
Even before I, Xiu of Jiaoshan, left Dongxia, I had already met you all. But tell me, what is this matter of meeting?
How many with their heads and horns have become dragons, while the shrimp and crabs continue as before to glare with their eyes?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Supreme Way is rooted in the one mind; the dharma of the mind is rooted in non-abiding.

The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous awareness that does not relish objects; its nature and characteristics are profoundly still. Therefore it is said: 'When I beat the drum, the four great continents participate together.
When the staff is held horizontally, it spans the heavens and the earth; when the alms bowl is spread out, it covers the sands of the Ganges. Arriving...
Here, where the Elephant King roams, foxes and rabbits leave no trace. When the moon appears in the water, the wind and clouds are naturally distinct.
Neither past nor present can contain it; throughout kalpas its name remains unknown. A thousand sages fall before its wind; who would dare to speak against its head?
*Tu!* Within my king’s treasury, there is no such blade.
At Penglou Hermitage on Mount Jinshan in Zhenjiang Prefecture, it was heard that Chan Master Yongcong was the son of the Xu family of Xuanzhou in Hangzhou.
In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Dongzifu Temple in his native district. At fifteen, he traveled with his father to Mount Jing;

there, he admired the sharp and incisive eloquence of Biefeng and petitioned his father, vowing to study under him. Biefeng took a liking to him. Subsequently, he served under Dayu, Tiantong, Dangchushan, Anmishan, and Quan.

During his prime, the Master traveled back and forth between the two lords for over ten years. Later, he journeyed through Min, Yue, the regions east and west of the Yangtze River, and north and south of Lake Dongting.
Whenever he encountered men of renown, he would engage them in extensive and concise discourse until, with dignified composure, he had fully exhausted the depths of his treasury of knowledge.

He entered the monastic order at Jinghui Temple in Taizhou, moved to Baoning and Jiangshan in Jinling, and finally passed away at Mount Jinshan. He was sixty-five years old and had been a monk for five years.

The Master said, "No merit at all. The Emperor asked, "Then who is it that does not possess merit? The Master said, "It is you, Your Majesty. Raising the first mallet of Mount Sumeru, the jade pass and golden lock are difficult to strike open. To strike again from behind and tread upon the void is but wasted effort;
one should regret having traveled so far across ten thousand miles.

Shangtang of Master Sanfeng Yin of Wuzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Yong of Shuanglin, cited the story of the Wild Fox and offered this verse: "Not falling, not being obscured—this is the crime of slandering others.
Not obscured, not falling—this is binding oneself without a rope. Pitiful, the willow catkins follow the spring wind; sometimes..."
Returning from the West to the East,
Chan Master Meng’an Yuancong of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Guifeng Guang;
he was the son of the Zhu family of Fuzhou and served within the assembly of Huia Chan Master.

He attained the essential heart of the Dharma. Among his many disciples, he was the preeminent senior student. In the Ding-si year of the Qinyuan era, having come from Xuefeng in Fuzhou, he received an imperial decree to move to Mount Jing.
Ascending the hall, he cited the karmic conditions regarding Yaoshan’s initial visit to Shitou and his subsequent realization upon studying under Mazu, saying:
"When I was with Shitou, it was like a mosquito trying to bite an iron ox. He then offered this verse: "Emptying my belly and pouring out my guts, I speak..."
Facing him, one does not know for what reason he still hesitates. Right now, you should seize it with fierce determination;
do not wait until dawn and lose the rooster. Ascending the hall, the Master raised this case: One day, while Zhaozhou was on the latrine, he saw Wenyuan passing by.
He suddenly called out, "Wenyuan! Wenyuan responded, "Yes? Zhaozhou said, "I cannot speak the Buddha-dharma to you while on the latrine. The verse says:
Clearly and brightly, the Way cannot be spoken; by whom can this principle be known? A spring breeze arrives, and flowers lie scattered across the ground.
A verse requested by a parting traveler for a monk says: Before the mountains the wheat ripens and the rain has just cleared; Mulberry and poplar trees are lush green, joined by fresh willow hues.
Without a hair’s breadth remaining, the wind-bone is revealed; Every single thing is, in its entirety, the body of a bhikṣu.
Chan Master Zijuān of Deshan, a native of Tongchuan and a dharma successor of Chan Master Xing of Dayue, addressed the assembly from the high seat: "When seeing the seeing, that seeing is not seeing;
seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. He let out a shout and said: "The whale swallows the ocean until it is empty, revealing..."
A coral branch emerges. Suddenly, a monk from among the assembly comes forward and says, "Elder, stop your drowsy talk!
I would grant that he possesses a single eye. Ascending the hall, [the Master] held his staff across his chest and said:
"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven; seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Counting them thus in both forward and reverse order, when one counts until the future, there is none."
Throughout the day, because of seeing the seven, one sees the one; having seen the one, one forgets the seven. One treads through empty space until the iron ox breaks into a sweat;
breath ceases and no trace remains. Throwing down his staff, he said: "You must let go of even this before your study of the Way is complete.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Sometimes one takes away the person but does not take away the environment. This staff has been let loose seven times."
The Eight Sudden Deaths. Sometimes the object is seized but the person is not; at such times, this mountain monk is sevenfold topsy-turvy and eightfold upside down.
Sometimes both person and object are seized; the staff and I both vanish their traces and swallow our voices. Sometimes neither person nor object is seized;
[the Master] plants his staff and says: "Accompany me for a thousand miles; taking you across ten thousand mountains. Suddenly, one bumps into Linji.
Furthermore, how is it so? He gave a shout and said: "If one has not yet clarified the seal of the mind-ground, it is difficult to pass through the barrier of the Patriarch.
Chan Master Yue-lin Shiguan of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou, a successor of Chan Master Dahong Zheng, was a native of the Huang family of Hougan, Fuzhou. A monk asked him:
"Third, the Holy Path: when meeting people, it emerges; once emerged, it does not act for people. What do you think? The Master said, "Wrong.
[The monk] asked, "Xinghua said: 'When meeting people, it does not emerge; once emerged, it immediately acts for people. What about that? The Master said, "Wrong."
Xinghua said, "The banner and spear have fallen; Sansheng has bared his very liver and gall. The Master said, "He cannot lead [the way].
Xinghua said, "As for today, how do you, O Monk, act for the sake of others? The Master said, "One blow, one scar. [The Master] cited the story of Xuansha’s Three Kinds of Illness.
The verse says: Blind, deaf, mute—caught and defeated! If you ask further, "How about this? It is blind.
Deaf, mute, and speech-impaired.

Chan Master Wansong Huana Dalian, a successor of Chan Master Yunju Hui, offered this eulogy for a portrait of Śākyamuni Emerging from the Mountains: "Practice fulfilled and merit perfected, he penetrates [to the source]."
The bones are worn to the extreme; unable to endure such emaciation, the hair hangs in disarray. My transgressions now number beyond measure.

The Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, Volume 48.
Compiled by the monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital;
reviewed by the monk (Chao Kui), Abbot of Gu Huayan Temple in the Capital. Presented for Imperial Review.
Presented as belonging to the Eighteenth Generation below Nanyue in the Linji School.
Chan Master Pō’ān Zuǎn of Wōlóng Mountain in Kuīzhōu was a successor of Chan Master Tiāntóng Jié.
He was a native of the Wáng family of Guǎng’ān in Shǔ. Having heard that the elder master Yuán was residing at Zhāojié, he went there to inquire about the Dharma;
their words were in accord, and he was instructed to serve as the attendant for Huánnwù’s incense offerings. One day, following [Huánnwù] from the abbot’s quarters...
Previously, when Yuan asked, "Is there anyone in the hut? the Master replied, "There is no one. Yuan struck him a blow across the chest with his fist and said, "What about you?
At that moment, the Master suddenly attained realization. He left the gorges to rely on Deshan Yuan for the tonsure, and soon thereafter received full ordination.

While staying at Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou, he sat through a snowy night and thought to himself, "I have been traveling as a pilgrim for several years, yet I still cannot reach the ultimate penetration. While he was in a state of deep frustration, suddenly—
Hearing the bell toll, he hurried to the rear gallery. Looking up, he saw the two characters "Zhao Tang" (Illuminating Hall), and his doubts were instantly resolved.
Shortly thereafter, he visited Shui'an Yiyu at Shuanglin. Shui asked, "Setting aside for a moment the Elder Siṃha being beheaded by the King of Kaśmīra—"
"You say: Why does the bearded man of Western Heaven have no beard? The Master said, "It is not until the Twin Trees that this story is brought up.
Shui said, "Today I have run into a true adept. The Master said, "The heart does not betray the person;
the face shows no shame. Shui then stepped back. The Master said, "I have seen through you. When Shui retired from his duties at the monastery, he went to visit Miam.
Wuguo invited the Master to serve as the guest prefect. One day, while in his quarters, Wuguo was discussing with a monk by his side the famous koan:
"It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. Upon hearing this, the Master attained a sudden and great enlightenment.

The following day, Wuguo encountered the Master in front of the dormitory and said to him, "Under no circumstances may you employ any clever artifice. Try to reveal some sign of your realization. The Master replied instantly, "The Abbot’s quarters."
Inside [the hall], there was a guest. Wumen laughed heartily. When Wumen moved to Jiangshan, the Master attended him, serving him for five years in total.
Upon taking his leave to return to Sichuan, Wumen sent him off with a verse: "Coming ten thousand miles from the south, like a raft crossing the stream;

Rushing through the flowing water, he strikes the primordial gate. He blinds the Vajra-eye at the crown of the head; Going and staying are as a pearl rolling across a tray. Upon reaching Kuimen, Shang...
I write this to Master Yang Gongfu. You were invited by Wolong to leave the secular life, but before long you took your leave and traveled extensively throughout the Wu region.
At Huazang you were the successor to Dun’an Yan; at Jinnshan to Tui’an Qi; at Lingyin to Xiaohan Wu;

and at Jingshan to Meng’an Cong—all of whom appointed you as the First Seat and charged you with preaching the Dharma. Subsequently, you resided successively at Jianfu in Changzhou, Lingyan in Zhenzhou, and Xiu... in Pingjiang.
Fengqiong resided at Zifu Monastery in Huzhou. Finally, he was invited by Zhang Gongyai to serve as the founding abbot of Guangshou Huiyun.
He presided over six monasteries in total, all of which were requested by princes and high-ranking officials; it is a pity that his complete records have been lost.
What remains here is but a single slice from a great cauldron. Ascending the hall, [Yangqi said]: "When I first settled at Yangqi, the walls of my hut were thin;
the bed was covered all over with snow and pearls. I shrank my neck and sighed in secret. I recall instead the ancients dwelling beneath the trees.
Yangqi competes for victory, not for inferiority; Xiupeng competes for inferiority, not for victory. When Xiupeng first settled, there was no distinction between kin and stranger. A person.
Every individual possesses the pearl of the Canghu Sea; one can gaze upon the lakes and mountains until one’s eyes can no longer take it in.
"Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants"—this was the opening of the hall address. He cited Master Mimian: "When asked about matters of winter, he said: 'The mountain-great-yellow of the capital.
For the sake of a single grain of rice, he lost six months' worth of provisions. Xiufeng did not do so; when asked about matters of winter, he said: "The capital..."
The Master brought out the "Great Yellow" (rhubarb root). He sought but a single grain of rice, yet obtained a century’s worth of provisions.
Should a steward say, "Venerable Sir, Venerable Sir, do not speak of a century’s provisions; even half a year’s supply would suffice," he should simply reply to him:
"If you possess the resolve, you shall certainly not be deceived. Ascending the hall, he cited Dongshan: "What is Chan? It is the Jambū tree."
It is on the southern edge of Hainan. Near at hand, it is not separate from the square inch of the mind;
far away, it is a hundred thousand eight thousand *li*. After all, how is this "Chan, Chan"? The Master said: "Even the vaulting heavens have a place where they reach.

What is Chan? The Jambu tree is on the southern edge of Hainan; it props up the heavens and supports the earth. Supporting the earth and propping up the heavens—it cannot be skillfully described; it requires only transmission of the mind. After all...
"How is Zen? How is Zen? [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "Before the fifteenth day, it is as clear as a mirror;
after the fifteenth day, it is as black as lacquer. But what about on the fifteenth day itself? A yellow warbler perches in the lofty trees, singing repeatedly;
butterflies dote on the fragrant clusters, flying in pairs. The Master retired from Zifu and proceeded to Jingshan, where Meng’an entrusted him with the establishment of the monastic community.

There was a Venerable Bao who possessed great knowledge and insight. Whenever he encountered a teacher opening the hall for instruction, he would invariably respond with sudden, swift wit, seizing the initiative to claim victory.
One day, when the Master opened his room for teaching, Bao arrived. The Master delivered this statement:

"Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a treasure hidden within the mountain of form. Before he had finished speaking, Bao prepared to open his mouth; the Master struck him immediately.
He went out. After Master Baoyu had finished raising the story, he proceeded to speak; when he was halfway through his speech, he too was struck and sent out.

Thinking that the Master was intentionally breaking him down, he returned to his single-layered robe, removed it, and left. After the cremation, the local people collected the *śarīra* relics and presented them to the Master.
The Master picked them up and said, "Venerable Baoyu, even if you have eight *hu* and four *dou* of *śarīra*, set them against one wall and give them back to me."
Before he was born, there was a turning word that came forth; he threw it to the ground, and there was seen only pus and blood.
A man of the Way asked, "What is it like when one cannot catch hold of the monkey? The Master said, "Why use catching? It is like wind blowing across water; patterns form naturally.
He showed this to the Seat-Master with a verse: "Even seeing is already apart from seeing; it is not true seeing. When the eight returns are exhausted, there is nothing left to return to."
The trees have fallen, the autumn sky reveals the bare bones of the mountains; who knows who can recognize this old Gautama?

In his later years, while residing at Mount Jing, as he was about to pass away, he wrote a letter bidding farewell to those close to him. He further composed a verse, saying: "The final word has already become a source of distress;
to write it out before others is a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away with serene composure. (The Song Dynasty, Ningzong’s Jiading era)
It was the ninth day of the sixth month in the year of Xinwei. His final instructions were that his bones be scattered among the trees;
however, the Abbot of Shiqiao collected the remains and erected a stupa on a separate peak to the right of the existing one. He was seventy-six years of age and forty-nine years since his ordination.
Chan Master Songyuan Chongyue of Lingyin in Lin’an was a native of the Wu clan of Longquan in Chuzhou.
From his youth, he was outstanding and extraordinary. At an early age, he aspired to the supramundane Dharma. At twenty-three, he left home.
He first visited Miaoxian at Lingshi, and subsequently met Dahui Zonggao at Mount Jing. When Dahui ascended the hall, he praised Ying’an of Jiangshan for being direct in character.

Jie heard of this and set out before dawn. Upon his arrival, he entered the room and sought instruction morning and evening. One day, Dayuan asked, "The World-Honored One had a secret word; Kāśyapa did not conceal it. What do you say to this? The Master replied, "I have left the Master at a loss. Dayuan gave a loud shout, and the Master attained realization.

Dayuan was greatly pleased and, regarding him as a vessel of the Dharma, spoke a verse to encourage him: The Dharma is not hidden; it is right here before you. If you can see it clearly, you will know its source. If you do not see it, you will wander in confusion.

If you wish to understand, look back at your own face. Do not seek it elsewhere; it is not far away. It is like the moon reflected in water, appearing yet not real. If you grasp at it, you lose it; if you let go, you find it. This is the true transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Do not doubt it for a moment. The Master was further inspired by this.
Having shaved his head, he received full ordination at White Lotus Monastery in Lin’an during the early Longxing era of the Song dynasty.
From then on, he traveled extensively to consult various great masters, yet few could satisfy his mind. He subsequently entered Min Province to see Muguan Yong.

When Yong posed the question, "The phrase 'having a phrase' and 'having no phrase' is like a vine leaning against a tree," the Master replied, "Torn asunder. Yong asked, "Langye said, 'What a pile of rotten firewood! What do you say to that? The Master...
[The Master] said, "It is like adding a point to an arrow. Yong said, "Observing your words, I cannot surpass you, Elder; yet it is as if you have not yet reached the mark.
In the future, when the fly-whisk handle is in your hands, you will be unable to guide others, nor will you be able to test them.

The Master said, "To guide others—causing an ordinary person of common ground to leap directly into the realm of the sages—is indeed difficult. As for testing people, one strikes them as they pass right before one's face."
Without even waiting for him to open his mouth, he already knew the very marrow of the man’s bones; what difficulty could there be? Yong raised his hand and said, "I have told you clearly:
when the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue. You shall know this for yourself later. Over a year passed before he met Miam at Xishan in Quzhou.
As soon as [Yong] asked a question, Miam answered immediately, and Miam merely smiled. The Master was so intent on reaching the ultimate that he forgot everything else.
Whether sleeping or eating, Mian moved from Jiangshan to Huayan and then to Jingshan, and the Master followed him in all instances.

One day, while Mian was hanging up the notice for the evening session to enter the room with the assembly, he asked a monk, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. The Master was standing by his side at that time.
He attained a sudden and great awakening, whereupon he said, "Only today do I finally understand Master Mudan’s saying: 'The opening of the mouth does not depend on the tongue.

A sudden turn of the pivot toward the ultimate. Throughout billions of years, there is but one Buddha."
The Snowy Mountains have never separated the Dragon Tower.
Chan Master Yunchao Yan of Ruiyan in Taizhou composed an eight-character verse on the title of the scripture, saying: "The character 'yi' (以) is not formed;

Chan Master Wua-zang Wu-ai Jue-tong ascends the hall for the Green Sprout Assembly: "Breaking open a single mote of dust, the Great Sutra emerges;
