This is "treading through the straw sandals. Time and age drift away; they cannot be toyed with.
You must exhaustively investigate until the place of departure is clear, so that it corresponds with the account of the entrance previously mentioned—only then will it be right. It is further said:
"If you simply rest in this manner, where would all these complications I have just described be placed? Even if you were all to [attain realization] at once..."
It cannot be swept clean by mere effort. I, this mountain monk, however, have an ancient saying to present to you all.
Remember how Changqing addressed the assembly: "Once it has been swept clean, you must come forward and seek it from me.
If I strike you with a blow, you should feel shame; but if I do not strike you with a blow, what then? Xuedou said: "Clean..."
Jie has tidied everything up; yet he must come forward and seek me out. If there were a single blow to reach you, then you would be at fault;
if not a single blow reached you, then it was settled between us as equals. Those two great elders—what fine blows they gave!
Yet they could not help but engage in calculations of gain and loss. Tianfeng is otherwise: having tidied everything up, one must still come forward and seek me out.
"Seeking! There is one blow that reaches you; this is like adding embroidery to brocade. There is no blow that reaches you; this is like adding frost to snow. Now tell me:
does the former instance benefit others, or does the latter instance benefit others? If you can discern this clearly, then come forward and speak when the plaque is hung next time."
Chan Master Xutang Zhiyu of Jingshan in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Daochangyan. A native of Siming, he appeared in the world at Xingsheng Monastery in Jiahe,
then moved to Guangxiao, Xianxiao in Mingzhou, Yanfu, Ruiyan, Baolin in Wuzhou, and finally to Yuyang and Boye in Siming.
Jingci Temple in Hangzhou. At the end of the Song dynasty, during the reign of Emperor Yanchun, he was appointed by imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.

He successively presided over ten monasteries. Within his quarters, he would pose these critical remarks: "Why is it that those whose own eyes are not yet clear take empty space and wear it as trousers?
Why is it that they draw lines on the ground to create a prison and cannot pass beyond them? Why is it that those who enter the sea to count its sands [remain stuck] upon the tip of a needle?"
**Standing on One Foot** A monk asked, "The single phrase prior to sound does not fall into the trap of permanence. When shifting positions to accord with function, how do you meet it?
The Master said, "When greeting, one does not reach out the hand. The monk asked, "But tell me, what about 'Ten Thousand Years for the Son of Heaven'?
The Master said, "Auspicious grass grows in a fortunate era; numinous flowers bloom in early spring. The monk said, "It truly causes the nine provinces and four seas to resonate like thunder."
The wind blows. The Master said, "When leaving the gate, one only fears not being the first to arrive. Ascending the hall, he said: "Spring wind is like a blade; spring rain is like rich fat.
Under the gate of the patch-robed monk, what use is there for such idle chatter? Ascending the hall, he said: "If words are sufficient, one speaks all day long and exhausts the Way.
If words are insufficient, one speaks all day long and exhausts phenomena. Now tell me, are the Way and phenomena one or two?"
Second: If you say the Way is one, why is the guest mountain high and the host mountain low?

If you say it is two, why does [the Zhuangzi] say that "heaven and earth are a single finger" and "all things are a single horse"? If you can distinguish the black from the white within this, I shall return to you the price of your straw sandals.
If it were otherwise, I would simply wish for the silkworms and wheat to ripen next year. To Rāhula’s son, I give one coin. Ascending the hall for the summer retreat:
There was once a man who consumed ten thousand taels of gold daily; he followed this same sacred regulation, yet no one recognized him.
If anyone could recognize him, I would grant that person the allowance of consuming ten thousand taels of gold daily. Ascending the hall at Baolin.
From the beginning there are no gates or doors. To draw near to others, one must not place them in a realm of nothingness;
one simply requires that all people be like iron entering the earth, transforming together with the soil. Only then can they transcend. As for those who carry in dung, I am at my wits' end for them.
[The Master] ascended the hall and cited how Songyuan, when on the verge of passing away, addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who have long practiced..."
"Brothers, there are those who walk upon the true path, yet they cannot employ the 'Black Bean' method. The Way of Linji is on the verge of being extinguished and unheard of—how tragic!
The Master said, "The Elder of Vulture Peak is much like one leaning on a staff while riding a horse; although he avoids the peril of falling, he cannot escape the disapproval of bystanders.
Later in life, the Master resided at Jingci. On the day of his entry into the monastery, he [conducted] the formal inspection.
While they were engaged in a sequence of questions and answers, suddenly a celestial messenger delivered an imperial decree, asking: "Why did Zhaozhou travel on pilgrimage for eighty years?
Why did Xutang reside in the mountains for eighty years? The Master then cited the story of Zhaozhou’s pilgrimage to Linji and offered this verse:
Zhaozhou traveled on pilgrimage only at eighty; Xutang returned to the mountains at eighty. There is another pivot that expands the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Within the nine-layered palace, he moved the imperial countenance. The celestial messenger returned with this eulogy, and the Emperor was greatly pleased;
he specially bestowed five hundred *shí* of rice and one hundred bolts of silk. Later, while residing at Yewang and Jingshan, he was likewise granted abundant rewards and gifts.
He once cited the public address of Dongsi: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. The sword has long since departed, yet you are merely marking the boat."
The verse says: Yesterday, passing by the western bamboo grove, A neighbor’s young child cried out across the stream.
The mountains were cold and the waters solemn as half the leaves turned yellow and fell; Countless crows returned to perch upon the trees. Daci ascended the hall and said:

"This mountain monk does not understand how to answer questions; I only know how to recognize the illness. At that time, a monk stepped forward, and Daci immediately returned to his quarters. The verse says: Light as...
A mere hair-tip becomes as heavy as a mountain. From the earth’s edge to the ends of the world, he departs and returns again and again.

When the yellow leaves fall, the mountain’s bones are revealed; by the waterside, the stones still bear their ancient patterns. On the eighth day of the tenth month in the Guihai year of the Zhizhen era, he passed away.

His stupa was enshrined below Zhiling on Mount Jing. The Kingdom of Goryeo had previously invited the Master to receive offerings for eight years. He was a disciple who inquired after the Dharma and followed him constantly.
Regarding Qianzhi: during the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty, the King dispatched a Dharma heir to the mountain to sweep the pagoda.
There, Chan Master Shifan Yan of Tiantong in Mingzhou raised the question posed by Grand Master Lu Xun to Nanquan: "What is your surname?"
Jianquan said, "My surname is Wang. The Master asked, "Do you have any attendants? Jianquan said, "The four ministers are not obscure.
The Master asked, "In what position does the King reside? Jianquan said, "Moss grows upon the jade palace. The Master asked, "What is it like when moss grows upon the jade palace?

Jianquan said, "It is a matter that does not abide in the central throne. The verse says: The golden duck’s incense has faded; the night watch is deep. Silent and profound, the jade palace is covered in purple moss. The high void...
The moon shines through a thousand gates; on the Great Way, there is no one—only walking alone. Regarding the incident of Dadian raising his staff and expelling the Head Seat, the verse says:
A single string of mani-jewels, confronting the situation face-to-face. He deceived the Head Seat to death and left Moliya Chanru in doubt.
Having exhausted all these wretched tricks, In spring and autumn, he has never known them from the start.
Chan Master Shixi Xin Yue of Mount Jing in Hangzhou, successor to Chan Master Jinshan Kai, was a native of Meizhou in Western Sichuan. He ascended the hall and, citing a case, said:
A monk asked Jiufeng, "What is the student's own self? Jiufeng replied, "Ask someone else. The monk said, "I will accept it just like this."
"How was it at that time? Feng said, "Mount Sumeru must once again bear Mount Sumeru. He spoke in verse: "One knows one's own cold and warmth for oneself;
Who else can be asked about the Patriarch’s intent from the West? To take it all upon oneself is to be the whole;
Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, one bears Mount Sumeru. [Huitang] raised this story because Huang Shan-gu asked him, "I beg the Master to point out the shortcut."
The Master said, "As for Confucius saying, 'Disciples, do you think I am hiding anything from you? I hide nothing from you,' how would you explain this, Taishi?
Gu was about to respond when the Master said, "Not so, not so. Gu remained in a state of confusion and distress.
One day, while attending the Master on a mountain walk, the osmanthus trees were in full bloom. The Master said, "Taishi, have you heard of the sound of wood?"

Zhixiang Magu said, "I have heard it. Yangshan said, "I have nothing hidden from you. Magu was relieved and immediately prostrated, saying, "The Master’s heart is so earnestly like that of an old woman.
Yangshan smiled and said, "It is simply that I wish for you to reach home. He then offered this verse: "The dwelling of that man is in the White Cloud Village;
North, south, east, and west, the roads stretch far and wide. How many times he wished to return, yet could not; Now, at last, he has arrived."
Suddenly hearing the secluded fragrance sent by the cliff-orchids, he cites Master Pang’s saying: “Having sons, I do not marry them off;
having daughters, I do not give them away. He offers this verse: Gathering the sentiments of mountain clouds and ocean moon, The circle is complete, the nose straight, the eyes and brows horizontal.
With a whisk of tortoise hair and a staff of rabbit horns, He beats the void until it rings out *baobao*. He then cites the story of Master Pang visiting Dading Ti.
The Kōshi (Strainer) Incident. [The Master] took it up, saying: "Pujie held it fast, yet was struck by Pang Gong’s painful needle.
He was driven to turn left and lean right, following one after another.

When the strainer was lifted and they called out to dance together—if you say this is merely painting a cat from a model, you would surely have to cast Ziqi out of pure gold. A monk asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said:
The Dwarf Watching the Play A verse for sending off a monk returning to Shuanglin: Before reaching Shuanglin, I see my old acquaintance:
Eyebrows arch like the new moon; eyes hold the autumn air. Before exchanging words of greeting, you should first ask: Why is it that the bridge flows while the water does not?
On the ninth day of the sixth month, [the Master] passed away.

Zen Master Bei Shan Long of Shenguang Monastery in Fuzhou, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Chong of Mount Jing, addressed the assembly: "This very mind is Buddha. Where there is water and bamboo, there is a house."
It is well. Neither mind nor Buddha; without socks and without cap, the body is free. Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.
Leaning idly against the balustrade at the clear dawn: red banana leaves draw in the azure morning glory. The Verse for Paying Homage to the Stupa of Jingqing:
"Accustomed to asking, 'What is that sound before the gate? The pond frog laughs at you as it croaks of its own accord. In recent years, [it has been] neglected...
At Que Tianhua Temple, while the formal instruction was only halfway through, Chan Master Ying of Gaotai on this mountain ascended the hall.
He cited the story of a turtle by the side of Dasui’s hermitage. A monk asked, "All sentient beings have skin wrapped around their bones;
why is it that this particular sentient being has bones wrapped around its skin? Dasui picked up a straw sandal and covered [the turtle] with it.
[The Master] said, "On the back of a tortoise. The monk was speechless. The Master offered this verse: "Do not insist on forcibly dividing the skin and bones;
when the six viscera are obtained, let them remain as six viscera. With a single shoe, everything is completely covered; this monk has nothing left to contemplate."
Chan Master Jianweng Jing of Tiantong in Mingzhou ascended the hall and cited the story of Damei regarding "The mind itself is Buddha.
He offered this verse: "The husband’s heart is as thin as a leaf, the wife is as pure as ice. The husband speaks of gold; the wife does not respond.

Even if they should happen to share a single smile, Who would believe for half a lifetime that she keeps the solitary lamp? He then cited the passage where Mañjuśrī asked Āmrapālī: "What is it that gives birth to all dharmas?"
What is discourse on the meaning? The verse says: The question is clear; the answer is direct. Meeting face-to-face according to the occasion, there is no deception.
Birth and death, life and death, have originally no bounds. The moon rises over the green mountains—a single sphere of jade.

[The Master] cited Yunmen’s address to the assembly: “Awaken to the Way by hearing sound; clarify the mind by seeing form. He then raised his hand and said: “Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, take this money...”

He bought some steamed buns (*húbǐng*). Setting them down, he said, "So, it was all just talk about *mántóu* (steamed buns). He then offered this verse: Who is it that plays this tune before the wind?

Its melody is so lofty, who would deign to let it fall into these present times? Seeing no one who understands the meaning within the song, He once again takes up his cloud-flute and blows it out of the blue.

Chan Master Nantang Bian of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou, successor to Chan Master Yunchao Yan, ascended the hall and said: "When the Old Śākyamuni was born in the royal palace, what a fine newborn child he was!
He certainly left people with doubts. Yet when he said, 'In the heavens above and the earth below, there is only I alone...'"

"Uniquely Honored One. The failure has already occurred. Later, in cold silence, there was shame and remorse. Throughout forty-nine years and over three hundred assemblies, he attempted to save and rescue them;
yet when his saving and rescuing could not reach them, he gathered everything together; yet even that gathering could not suffice.
O virtuous ones, do you wish to see the point of Śākyamuni’s failure? "Much speaking leads only to contention; affliction arises from forcing oneself to speak."
Tou ascends the hall: "You are here; I am also here. Where humans and devas meet, both are able to see one another.
In these clear times, there is no need to sing songs of great peace. For one *guan*, you can buy three pecks and a half of rice;
for two *guan* five hundred cash, you can buy a large bolt of fine silk. O Zen practitioners, although this is so, there is still leftover rice in the kitchen.
"There is a hungry person on the road. [The Master] ascends the hall. He cites a monk who asked an ancient worthy, "When the myriad objects come to invade you, what then?
The worthy said, "Sit and be annoyed by them. That ancient worthy possessed the skillful means to block the surging waves, yet he could not avoid laboring his mind and expending effort.
If someone were to ask me, Jinshan, "When the myriad objects come to invade you, what then? I would simply say to him: "Since I..."
Having no mind toward the myriad things, how could they ever fail to constantly surround one? [Ascending the hall:
"If I were to break it open and explain it to you, you would surely revile me later. If I do not break it open and explain it to you, I fear you will remain complacent and miss the mark.
Suppose a man were to come forth and say, 'The Elder has fallen into a verbal trap. To him, I would simply say: 'Old monk...'"
Regarding the transgression, the verse lamenting Yunchao says: "Others say the Master has been dead for long; I alone linger on, undecided in my doubt.
Since the nest is empty and the clouds have dispersed, Yet in the depths of spring, the cuckoo still cries.
The verse sent to Tiebian says: "I contemplated the four lines and sent them to Chengtian; They came together as a whole, yet one side was missing. Even so, they do not form a complete verse."
It is not a poem. How could it be brought forth before others? A verse sent to Wuzu says: "The turtle and the ape cannot be parted;
the elder brother calls and the younger responds as if forgetting all cares. But when it comes to the point of paradox, once again, one's heart and liver are not brought along."
Chan Master Yixi of Qingxi at Mount Huqiu in Suzhou sent this verse to a departing monk: Ten thousand folds of Tai Mountain enter the brow, green;

Traveling together on the road, each hastens toward his own destination. At the clear dawn, the rooster cries in the moonlight of the thatched inn— Who is it that rises first to call out, "Elder Brother?"

Eulogy on the Portrait of the First Patriarch by Chan Master Gaofeng Yue of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou, Successor of Chan Master Daoci of Jingci: Unfurling his banner and arraying his ranks, he entered the land of Liang;

before even beholding the Emperor’s countenance, he had already surrendered. Though he possessed supernatural powers, they could not be fully displayed; with a single reed boat, he crossed over lightly.
Changjiang. Chan Master Longyuan Jieqing of Daochang Monastery in Huzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wuyue Zhaodeng.
He was a native of the Wang family of Changxi in Fuzhou and received full ordination there.

Yixing Fazang of the Qi dynasty went to Yuwang Temple to pay his respects to Jichuangzhao. Upon entering the inner chamber, he attained realization of the essential meaning and served as the attendant-in-chief, later taking charge of the temple keys.
He emerged from seclusion at Shouguo Temple in Siming and subsequently moved to the Kaishou Daochang. Ascending the hall, he said: "The three months of spring have drawn to a close;
the foliage is deep green and the blossoms are sparse. Movement turns one toward external objects; stillness leads one astray regarding the Dharma. Do not be obscured by form, nor by sound."
Riding [upon the wind], I idly listen before the breeze as the cuckoo cries. Ascending the hall: All day long one is in a state of bustling activity;
yet that matter remains unimpeded. It is manifest yet not revealed; it is hidden yet not concealed. O assembly, tell me:
what is the principle of being hidden yet not concealed? The jade plum forms fruit upon the green tree; the stone sprout sends forth shoots up against the green window.
The Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, Volume Forty-nine;
The Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, Volume Fifty.
Compiled by the Abbot (Subject) Monk Chao Yong of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital.
Verified and presented by the Abbot (Subject Monk) Chaokei of the Ancient Kegon-ji Temple in Kyoto;
Rinzai School.
Chan Master Gaofeng Yuanmiao of West Tianmu Peak in Hangzhou,
a descendant of the twenty-first generation under Nanyue and a successor of Chan Master Yangshan Qin, was the son of the Xu family of Wujiang. His mother dreamed of a monk riding...
While traveling by boat, she conceived. On the twenty-third day of the third month in the *wuxu* year of the Jiaxi era of the Song dynasty’s Lizong reign (1258), at the hour of Shen, she was born.

As soon as she left her swaddling clothes, she delighted in sitting in the full-lotus posture. Whenever she encountered a monk entering the door, she would immediately feel a deep affection for him and wish to follow him.
At the age of fifteen, she earnestly requested her parents to allow her to enter Miaoyin Temple in Jiahe to take Fazu as her teacher. At sixteen, she shaved her head.

At seventeen, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). At eighteen, he studied the teachings of Tiantai. At twenty, he changed his robes and entered Jingci Monastery, vowing to remain there for three years until death.
At twenty-two, he requested further instruction from Duanqiao Lun, who directed him to investigate the koan: "From where does life come? To where does death go?
Thereupon, he did not let his side touch the mat, forgetting both body and mind. While Xueyan Qin was staying at Beijian, the Master [Yunmen Wenye] carried incense and went to visit him.
He went to pay his respects; as soon as he had offered his greetings, he was struck and driven out, and the door was closed.
He went again, and only then was he permitted to approach. He was instructed to contemplate Zhaozhou’s “Mu” (No). From then on, he investigated and questioned [his teacher] every day without fail.

Later, whenever anyone entered the gate, Qin would immediately ask, "Who is it that has dragged this corpse here? Before the sound of his voice had even faded, he would strike them. This happened countless times. Afterwards—

While Qin was traveling to Nanming, the Master ascended Mount Shuangjing. Less than half a month had passed since he began attending the hall when, suddenly in a dream, he recalled the dialogue raised by Duanqiao in his room:
"All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return? A state of intense doubt immediately arose, and for three days and nights his eyes did not close.
On the anniversary of Shaolin’s founder, while joining the assembly at the Three Pagodas to chant sutras, he suddenly looked up.
Upon beholding the true eulogy of the Fifth Patriarch, he said: "In a hundred years, there are thirty-six thousand mornings; turning it over and back, it is originally this very man.
Suddenly, he broke through the doubt regarding the "dragging corpse," at which time he was twenty-four years old. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, he went to Nanming.
As soon as Xiqin saw him, he asked, "Who brought this corpse here for you? The Master then gave a shout. Xiqin raised his staff;
the Master seized it and said, "You may not strike me today. Xiqin asked, "Why may I not strike you?"
The Master shook out his sleeves and departed. The following day, Yunquan asked, "When the myriad dharmas return to the One, where does the One return?

The Master replied, "A dog licking a hot oil pan. Yunquan said, "Where did you learn such empty talk? The Master said, "I specifically want the Master to have doubts about this. Yunquan then desisted and left.
From then on, their intellectual sharpness was such that neither would yield. The following year, he spent the summer retreat at Jiangxin and visited Xuedou.
He met Master Xi-sou Tan, who was staying at the Dan-guo hall. Tan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master threw down his meditation cushion.
Tan said, "The dog has no Buddha-nature; what do you say to that, Upadhyaya? The Master replied, "I cast it out for everyone to see. Tan then personally escorted him back to the hall.
Later, when Tan hung up his plaque at the Daochang and began teaching at Tian-ning, the Master attended him in all matters. One day, Tan asked:

"During the vast expanse of the daytime, are you still able to be the master? The Master replied, "I am able to be the master. Yunquan asked, "In the midst of sleep and dreams, are you able to be the master?
The Master replied, "I am able to be the master. Yunquan asked, "When one is fast asleep—without dreams, without thoughts, without seeing, and without hearing—where is the master?
The Master was speechless. Yunquan instructed him, saying, "From this day forward, it shall also not..."
I do not require you to study the Buddhas or the Dharma, nor do I require you to pore over antiquity or modernity. Rather, simply eat when hungry and sleep when weary.
As soon as you wake from sleep, rouse your spirit and recognize: "This master of mine who has just awakened."
"Ultimately, where shall I find a place to settle my body and establish my life? The Master then resolved to enter Longxu, vowing to himself:
"I shall risk this one lifetime to become a simpleton; I must by all means clarify this one crucial point. After five years had passed...

Because he was staying with a fellow monk, the latter pushed his pillow off the bed, and as it hit the floor with a sound, [Dongshan] attained great enlightenment. He said to himself: "It is like the Great Sage appearing at Sizhou;
it is like a traveler returning to his hometown. Originally, it is just that same person from before; one has not changed one's former way of walking.
He lived at Longxu for nine years, binding together wood to make a hut. Wind pierced it and the sun scorched it; through both winter and summer he wore but a single robe and did not use a fan.
He did not maintain a hearth; he merely sustained his life by pounding pine needles daily and mixing them with congee. In the *jiashu* year of the Xianchun era, he moved to Shuangji Peak in Wukang.

In the spring of the *bingzi* year of the Deyou era, when the great army arrived, the Master sat upright behind closed doors as if nothing were amiss. Once the situation had settled, visitors arrived in crowds at his door;
the Master packed his belongings in a cloth bag and fled under the cover of night, heading straight for Shiziran on Western Tiantai Mountain. The cliff rose a thousand *zhang* from the earth.
Cliffside rocks stood like a forest. The Master immediately constructed a small cell about one *zhang* square within a cave and inscribed it with the name "Gate of Death.

He completely discarded all attendants and fine clothing; using a broken jar as a cauldron, he took but a single meal every other day. To reach the cave, one had to climb a mountain path by means of a ladder, so that even his disciples rarely saw him.
Together they built the Shizi Monastery and requested the Master to open the hall for formal teaching. It happened that Xueyan was at Dayang, where he sent the Master a bamboo staff.
The *bì* (comb) and *fúzi* (whisk). In the *Dīnghài* year of the *Zhìyuán* era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty, he took the incense from his breast and brought it forth.

He ascended the hall. A monk asked: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination.
When Layman Pang spoke thus, was there still a way in which he benefited others? The Master said: "There is. The monk asked: [What is it? The Master said: [He]... (text fragmentary).
"Ultimately, it lies in that one phrase. The Master said, "Ask from the beginning. [The monk] asked, "What is 'the assembly where the ten directions gather together'?
The Master said, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages mingle. [The monk] asked, "What is 'every single person studying non-action'?
The Master said, "Mouth swallowing Buddhas and patriarchs; eyes overshadowing heaven and earth. [The monk] asked, "What is 'the field for selecting Buddhas'? The Master said:
[Ten thousand *li*] from east to west, eight thousand from south to north. [The monk asked: "What is it like to 'return home as a top graduate with an empty mind'?

The Master said, "Moving one's countenance, one reveals the ancient path; one does not fall into the trap of silent stillness. [The monk asked: "If that is so, then every word reveals the ultimate truth, and every sentence points toward the source.
The Master said, "Where do you see this? The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "That too is like swinging a club to strike at the moon. [The monk asked: "This..."
"Let us set this matter aside for now. As for today at Xifeng, where the ten directions have gathered and the Field for Selecting Buddhas has opened—what auspicious signs are there ultimately?
The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the forested universe—sentient and insentient alike—all fully become Buddhas.

[The monk] asked, "If all have already become Buddhas, why is it that I, a student, do not become a Buddha? The Master said, "If you were to become a Buddha, how [could you even ask such a question]?"
He instructed the great assembly on attaining Buddhahood, saying: "Where exactly does the fault of a student lie? The Master said: "South of Xiang and north of Tan. The monk asked:
"Do you permit this student to repent? The Master said: "Prostrate yourself.
The monk then prostrated. The Master said: "A lion bites; a donkey from Han chases after clods of earth. He then continued: "The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and the successive patriarchs..."
The Master, continuing until he addressed the elder monks throughout the land, struck the meditation seat once with his whisk and said, "Everyone here has fallen into a pit or a ditch;
is there anyone who can leap out? He struck it again and said, "Three lifetimes are sixty kalpas.
Ascending the hall, [he said]: "The realms of boundless lands are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip; ten ages of past and present..."
From beginning to end, one never departs from the present moment. It is just like this old monk, who every day dwells within Zhanggong Cave;
whether lying down horizontally or upright, whether singing or chanting—do you all know this? Every day you dwell within the field for selecting Buddhas.
Going east or going west, whether in anger or in joy—does the mountain monk still know this?
If both parties know it, one cannot avoid being split into many bodies to be pounded in a mortar, or having one’s tongue pulled out to be plowed with a plow.

If neither knows it, take it for granted that Śākyamuni will fold his hands and the Monkey King (Hanuman) will take refuge. Why is it so? Have you not heard it said: "The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all calamities"?
Ascending the hall: "The myriad dharmas return to the One. To what place does the One return? He then looked to his left and right and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall: "The entire world of the ten directions is a single alms bowl. You all eat porridge and rice within it; you defecate and urinate within it;
you walk, stand, sit, and lie down, even down to every movement and stillness, within it."
It is all contained within. If you can recognize it, Master Bodhidharma would have served as nothing more than your foot-washing slave.
If you do not recognize it, with what will you eat your morning and evening porridge? *Chan*! [The assembly] concludes the retreat; the abbot ascends the hall for the formal address.
The great limit is ninety days; the small limit is seven days. Within the coarse there is the subtle; within the subtle there is the dense.

Dense upon dense, without interval, not even a speck of dust can stand. At this very moment, it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall: advancing, there is no gate; retreating, one loses [the way].
It is like falling into a ten-thousand-fathom deep pit, with precipitous cliffs and thorny brambles on all four sides.
One must absolutely be a fierce and heroic person who turns directly beneath and leaps out. If there is even a single moment of hesitation, even the Buddha cannot save you.
This is the supreme primordial gate; I exhort everyone to exert their strength. Although this mountain monk does not concern himself with it, I shall break precedent to join those who do.
A person passes through this message: [○@(│*│*│)] [○@(─/─/─)] [○@∴]. Addressing the assembly: "The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs;
The stone tiger before the cliff cradles its cub as it sleeps. The iron snake drills into the Vajra-eye; Kunlun rides the elephant while the egret leads.
Within these four lines, there is one phrase that can both grant and take away, and can both kill and give life. If anyone can discern and identify it, [they shall attain liberation].
"The matter of a lifetime of study is finished. [This was] the incense offering for the anniversary of Master Xueyan’s death. "In years past, you blinded my eyes; today, you pierce my nose.
When grievances are requited one after another, there is no end to it. It would be better to overcome oneself and return to ritual propriety.

Having spoken thus, he inserted the incense, covered his face with his sleeve, and made the sound of weeping. Then, placing his sitting mat over his left shoulder, he performed a prostration in the manner of a woman.
He said: "It is not only by blending with the light and becoming one with the dust that one avoids mutual stagnation. The Master once gave this instruction in his room:

"A person of ultimate penetration is fundamentally free from birth and death; why then is their life-root (*mūla*) not severed? The public cases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are but a single principle;
why then is there clarity and lack of clarity? A great practitioner of the Way should follow the conduct of the Buddha."
Why do you not observe the *vinaya*? The brilliant sun is in the sky; there is nowhere it does not illuminate. Why is it obscured by a single fragment of cloud?
Every person has a shadow; it never leaves them for even a single step. Why do you fail to tread upon it? The entire earth is a pit of fire.
What samādhi have you attained that you are not burned up? If your response does not accord with the truth, I shall close my door and refuse to receive you. [The Master] himself—

Unless one possesses the eye that penetrates the barrier, few do not turn back in dismay at the precipice. In the year Xinmao, Qu, the Prefect of Heisha, came to the mountain to pay his respects and offered a vast estate to support the assembly.
The Master firmly declined and would not accept it. Qu then petitioned the authorities, whereupon a separate Chan monastery was established on Lotus Peak called Dajue.
It was decided that its annual revenue should be used to provide for the permanent endowment, and he requested [the Master] to appoint a successor to the Dharma.
In the winter of the Yǒngzhēn *yǐwèi* year of Emperor Chéngzōng’s reign (1295), the Master suffered from a stomach ailment. It happened that Zǔyōng came to visit him;
the Master entrusted him with his final affairs. At dawn on the first day of the twelfth month, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
For thirty years at Xifeng, I have spoken falsely of Prajñā; my offenses fill the heavens.

At the very end, there is one phrase that I dare not burden you all with—I take it upon myself alone. Is there anyone among the assembly who knows its ultimate destination? After a long silence, he said:
"A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth lie between. Between the hours of Chen and Si, he spoke another verse: "Coming, I do not enter death;"
Guankou. He did not depart from the Deadman’s Recess (Siguan). An iron snake burrows into the sea; it topples Mount Sumeru. All is suddenly still and silent.
His final instruction was to enshrine his entire body in a stupa at the Deadman’s Recess. He was fifty-eight years old and forty-three years since his ordination.
Chan Master Chiding of Iron Ox at Lingyun in Hengzhou was a native of the Wang family from Boxi in Taituo.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of the late Song Dynasty Minister Zhi. From childhood, he was austere, upright, and possessed aspirations beyond the mundane world.

At the age of thirty, he visited Xifeng Ken’an to have his hair shaved and there heard the essential teachings of the separate transmission. Subsequently, he went to rely upon Xueyan Qin, residing at Cao...
The Master practiced the ascetic dhūta-precepts. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"Brothers, when you are practicing the Way, if for seven days and nights you maintain an uninterrupted state of mindfulness yet find no point of entry, then cut off my head and make it into a ladle for excrement.
The Master understood this silently and exerted himself with vigorous diligence. Because he suffered from dysentery, he prohibited all medicine, food, and drink, maintaining only right mindfulness.
He did not close his eyes for seven days. At midnight, he suddenly perceived that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were entirely like snow;
his own person was majestic and vast, such that heaven and earth could not contain it. After a short while, he heard the sound of wood being struck, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment.

Sweat poured from his entire body, and his illness was cured. At dawn, he went to the abbot’s quarters to relate this experience. Yunmen questioned him repeatedly, and finally commanded him [to remain].
While serving as a monk, one day he attended Master Qin’s formal lecture. Master Qin raised the question: "When a deceased monk has died and been cremated, where has he gone?

He himself provided the following response on behalf of the deceased: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth—these fully manifest the body of the Dharma King. Upon hearing these words, the Master’s doubts were completely washed away.

He immediately stepped out from the assembly, prostrated, and said, "Just now, when the Master expounded upon Prajñā, the stone lion before the Dharma Hall was so startled that it danced with laughter without ceasing.
Yunqin said, "Try to say something about it. The Master replied, "When spring returns beyond the kalpas, all things are withered."
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there is not a single speck of dust. How can one speak of the Dharmakāya’s transcendence?
It makes the blue-eyed barbarian of the Western Heaven laugh to death. Qin struck the table and said, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—there is not a single speck of dust.
What is this? The Master made a gesture as if overturning it. Qin laughed and said, "One win, two wins. One day, while entering the room for instruction, Qin said, "The point of intimacy..."
"Bring me a phrase of the Way," he said. The Master replied, "I will not speak. Yunqin asked, "Why do you not speak?

The Master picked up the incense box and said, "This is not worth half a coin. Yunqin said, "A talkative fellow. Later, while Yunqin was inspecting the hall, the Master lay down to sleep, wrapping himself in a paper quilt.
Yunqin summoned him to the abbot’s quarters and said in a stern voice, "I am inspecting the hall, and you are fast asleep!"
"If you can speak, I shall let you pass; if you cannot speak, I shall drive you down the mountain. The Master replied spontaneously:
"The iron ox has no strength and is too lazy to plow the fields; With its rope and plow, it sleeps amidst the snow. The great earth, a mass of white silver, covers all;
Deshan has nowhere to lay his golden whip. Qin said, "What a fine iron ox! Thereupon, he was given that as his title, and it became widely circulated at once.

There were none among his peers who did not respect and submit to him. In the fifth year of the Zhizhi era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty (the Wuzi year), he reached Taoyuan Mountain in Xing County;
finding its seclusion and depth pleasing, he conceived the intention to dwell there in retirement.

Before long, Magistrate Chen and his subordinates entered the mountain to seek the Way, and they all followed him, performing the rites of disciples. Thus, he greatly propagated the school of Xueyan. This continued until the Dade era of Emperor Chengzong.
On the fifteenth day of the first month of the Gui-mao year, he passed away. He was sixty-four years old; his dharma-age was twenty-six.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Shatan, thirty *li* north of the monastery. His disciple Bie-liu-jing traveled to Zhejiang to visit the Duke of Wenjing, Yu Ji, requesting an inscription for his master’s stupa.
Yu asked, "Which came first: the iron ox, or the ox-driver? Jing replied, "The Master..."
Upon seeing Yangshan approach, Yushan said with a smile, "I shall try to sketch a portrait of you for you.
Chan Master Xubai Xugul of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was the son of the He family of Yiwu in Wuzhou.
At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head at Zishou Monastery in Dongyang and received full ordination; he then went to visit Xuzhou Yuan at Shuanglin.
Lin also relied upon Dong-sou Ying at Jingci Temple, where he served as the internal secretary (*neiji*).

When Shilin took over his position, the Master served as the attendant (*shizhe*). One day, he went to visit Xueyan Qin at Beijian. Qin raised the karmic connection concerning Huanglong’s meeting with Ciming to question him;
he praised the Master as being sharp and capable. Later, when Qin moved to Dayang, he sent a letter summoning the Master, who then occupied the position of the First Seat (*dizhuozuo*). One day...
Qin asked, "When Linji was at Huangbo, he received sixty blows of the staff three times. Why did he then punch Daoyu in the ribs?
The Master said, "It was enough to leave people feeling utterly frustrated. Qin struck him immediately. The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
In the *Wuyou* year of the Zhiyuan era of Emperor Shizu (1286), as Qin was about to pass away, he patted the Master’s shoulder and said, "I entrust this burden to you. The Master said, "..."
He would never allow one to be buried alive here. Not long after, Qinhua passed away, and the assembly invited the Master to succeed him on the seat.
He once offered three statements to test those who came to study. He said: "Set aside the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings;
bring forth a single phrase from within the mouth of a toad. When the dog heard the sound of the vomit, why did it bite through the ground in front of the treasury hall?
"Zhu Ruo swallowed Jiyun Peak at Jingqiao Bridge—what kind of function (ji) was this? Few have been able to respond correctly. For thirty summers he sat in meditation;
his regulations were stern and rigorous, allowing no concessions whatsoever. When Tieguansu was traveling on pilgrimage, he once called upon this master.
On the occasion of a small *sīmān* (winter solstice) discourse, the Master raised the kōan concerning Yunmen’s “millet cake. Shu presented four verses as an offering.
The Master asked, "Who are you? Shu replied, "I am Upāsaka Shu. The Master said, "Where have you come from? Shu replied, "From Yunmen.
The Master said, "Are you mad? Are you crazy? Shu replied, "Where are your eyes, Master? The Master then gave a shout; Shu also shouted. The Master struck him.
With a single punch, Yunmen’s disciple Zhishu stepped forward to intercept him, saying, "Setting aside the blow for a moment, what is the meaning of the 'Yunmen bun'?
" The Master flung his hand and snatched away Zhishu’s robe, saying, "Wrong! He followed this by throwing several more punches, saying, "The fist has no eyes;
you will be scrutinized by others hereafter. Without a second thought, the Master seized Zhishu’s seven-strip cassock, tripped him to the ground, and kicked him across the waist nine times.
The staff said, "I shall let you know my skill. He replied, "This skill of yours is superior to that of Linji and Deshan.
The Master called for the steward and ordered him to place the staff's hands in irons and send him to the storehouse, where he was not released until nightfall.

The next day, when the Master ascended the hall, he instructed an attendant to say to the staff, "Today the Master ascended the hall to interrogate and examine you before this assembly of humans and devas. The staff replied, "Attendant..."
"Go and deliver my message to the Master. In a short while, before the assembly of gods and men, he will bring up various ancient *gong'an* one by one;
I shall answer each one in turn. After a brief moment, the drum sounded. Shu waited for a long time, but the attendant did not arrive.
During a year of famine, the Master always shared his food with the community. One day, he was conversing with a guest until past midnight, and he became hungry.

He could not overcome his own [desire]. His attendant requested that he take a spoonful of grain to make a meal. The Master said, "It must not be so. How can the permanent property of the monastery be used privately by its abbot?
In the *Bingchen* year of the Renzong *Yanyou* era, the Provincial Administration submitted a petition for imperial decree to invite the Master to preside over Mount Jing. A monk asked:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. What does this mean?
The Master said, "Relatives do not give gifts to one another. When the Master was young, he once dreamed of traveling to the Hall of Arhats at Jingci Temple.

Reaching the southeast corner, he suddenly saw a venerable elder pointing toward the space between the lintel and the beam, where there was a poem that read: "A single chamber vast and empty opens at the summit;
Several peaks like paintings, their green surpassing moss. Casually turning over the *pātra* leaves, The hundred-seam *kāṣāya* robe is cut and tailored by itself.
The Master initially did not understand it. Only after he moved from Mount Yang to Shuangjing did he finally realize that Mount Yang had possessed [this insight].
The *Pātra-leaf Sūtra* [was preserved]; at Mount Jing, there was the robe of Yangqi. The master’s destiny had already been predetermined.

Previously, when the Emperor Shizu summoned him for an audience and he preached the Dharma to his satisfaction, the Emperor bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Fojian. During the Dade era, he was further granted the title Dayuan.
Upon taking charge of Mount Jing, he was additionally conferred the title Huizhao. On the twelfth day of the fourth month of the Renxu year of the Zhi-zhi era of Emperor Yingzong—

On that day, he wrote by hand to entrust his protection to his lay patrons and exhorted his disciples. He spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly and passed away in the Budōken (Hall of Immovability).

His entire body was interred in a field of calamus. He was posthumously titled Daben (Great Discernment), and his stupa was named Hōge (Precious Flower). He was seventy-six years of age and fifty-seven years since his ordination.
His *Pakkan-shū* (Collected Works on Waterfalls and Rocks) and his *goroku* (Recorded Sayings) were circulated in the world.
Chan Master Tianyin Muzhan Yuanzhi of Nengren Monastery in Jianchang Prefecture was the son of the Yao family of Gaoyang. Both his father and elder brother were former advanced scholars (jinshi).
The Master aspired to the school of emptiness; at the age of nineteen, he went forth under Huilang to shave his hair and don the robes.

After serving him diligently for several years, he received the same transmission and seal of approval from Yangshan as did Fohuang Fenggan. During the Yuanzhen era of Emperor Chengzong of the Yuan dynasty, he emerged into the world to lead Nengren Monastery.
In his collected works, *Mushen ji*, there is a preface to the "Sending Off Master Miaozhi to Xi. Its summary states:
"In the past, when Master Yue of Long’an was already leading the assembly at Dongshan, he still considered his own realization of the Way to be incomplete.

He therefore concealed his name and went into seclusion, seeking [the truth] amidst the common activities of eating, drinking, laughing, and talking. Upon hearing a single extraordinary word from Master Su, he emptied himself [of his preconceptions]."
He humbled himself and approached with the decorum of an inquirer, showing no resentment for being treated as an inferior.
Ultimately, within the span of a brief conversation, he was able to secure what he had desired for his entire life.

Not only did this ensure that the Way of Yun’an would not fall into decline, but had it not been for Su Gong’s reliance on Yue to bring him into the world, the world would likely never have known what kind of person he was. Indeed, fame—
This is the outward manifestation of the Way. In antiquity, when people possessed its manifestation, they sought its substance to respond to it.
But now, the scholars of today allow the manifestation to harm the substance; once they occupy a certain name, they assume an air of lofty superiority that cannot be bent.
Even if they inwardly measure themselves and find it unsatisfactory, how would they ever deign to humble their minds to seek what they have not yet attained?
"Alas! This is why the present differs from the past; this is why the Way has declined," and so forth. In the Great Virtue year of Wuxu, he passed away at Mount Lu.
He was forty-two years of age and had twenty-three years of seniority as a monk.
When Chan Master Xian of Andongshan and An’an first established himself at Xifeng in Jianyang, Shiwu Hongguo went to pay him a visit.
The Master asked, "Where are you from? Guo replied, "Tianmu. The Master asked, "What instruction did you receive there? Guo said, "All dharmas return to the One."
The Master asked, "How do you understand this? Guo was speechless. The Master said, "This is a dead word.
What kind of person afflicted by a feverish illness would teach you to be like this? Guo bowed and requested a direct pointing-out.

The Master said, "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, run past quickly. When Guo replied, his answer did not accord with the meaning. The Master said, "This, too, is a dead word."

Upon hearing this phrase, Xiong was overcome with a sudden outpouring of sweat. Later, when he entered the room for private instruction, the Master again brought up the previous conversation to interrogate him.

Xiong replied, "When one mounts a horse, one sees the road. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Having been here for six years, you still harbor such a view! Xiong, driven by indignation, abandoned his studies and departed.

While on the road, he suddenly looked up and saw a pavilion in the wind; at that moment, he attained a sudden and profound realization. Returning to the Master, he said, "Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell."
"This too is a dead word. 'To hurry past where there is no Buddha'—this too is a dead word. Today I have understood the living word.
The Master asked, "How do you understand it? He replied, "On the Qingming festival, when the rain has just cleared, the yellow oriole sings clearly upon the branch.
The Master nodded his head in approval.

Chan Master Zhuyu Jian, a successor of Chan Master Lün of Jingci, citing the karmic conditions regarding Elder Fu’s “Sacred Arrow,” offers this verse: “Double reins of green silk, a jade steed neighs;
A pale white spring robe, girdled with a green sash. Returning at midnight, he passes beneath the flowers; The golden whip strikes down [the blossoms].”
Scattered red petals fly. It is also said: "Within the nine-layered city, it is not at all remote; though arrows pierce through layer after layer, they are but doubled in abundance.
Suddenly encountering the place where the three armies encircle, there is clearly a path leading straight to the heavens.

He cites the public case of Linji visiting Pingtian and offers this verse: "The road before one's eyes is as level as a grindstone; why do you not stride forth with dignity? To provoke [the encounter]..."
When the ox-nature of his wife arises, he is pitiable as he stands naked, enduring the blows of the staff.
Chan Master Juexiangjian addressed the assembly, citing the time when Dongshan was unwell and sent a novice monk to deliver a message to Yunju.
He instructed him, saying: "If he asks whether the Master is at ease, you should simply say: 'The road to Yunyan is nearly finished.'"
"It is finished! You have spoken these words; you must step back and stand at a distance, for I fear he will strike you. The śrāmaṇera took his instructions and departed.
Before the sound of his voice had even faded, Yunju struck him with a blow of the staff. The verse says: "The path to Dongshan leads through Yunyan."
To pass through the place of utter severance and reach it is difficult; only when one opens the living eye at the tip of the staff does one know that there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation.
Addressing the assembly, he raised the case: Touzi asked a monk, "It has rained well for several days. Tell me, from where does the rain come?"

The monk had no reply. Later, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he attained awakening. He composed a verse: Travelers on the crossroads compete to gather fragrant blossoms, Unaware that spring’s light passes before their eyes.
Last night, a sudden rain showered down the falling petals; In all one hundred and ten cities, the flowing waters are fragrant.
One day, Chan Master Bao of Fangshan at Ruiyan in Taizhou hung up the sign for the evening private interview with the assembly.
He posed a koan, saying: "When Nanquan cut off the cat, what was it like? The assembly offered various responses, but none were in accord with the truth.
At that moment, a servant standing nearby said, "The rat has grown too large. The Master laughed and said, "What an excellent turn of phrase! It is only that it should not have come from your mouth."
Emerging from within, he reveals the verse on "Non-seeing," saying: "The man of the Way has attained his way and come forth from the mountains;
He lays bare his entire heart and mind before me. Level and even like the surface of a mirror, Translucent and profound, utterly free of a speck of dust.

Suddenly, having found the phrase for turning back, He rolls up his patched robe like cold clouds and departs. Upon the Eighty-thousand-fathom Flower-Crest Peak, A single laugh shatters [all barriers]."
Open the iron mask; once you have reached your home mountain, all conceptual thought ceases. Breaking off withered vines, lean against the bamboo gate.
Within the heap of dung fire, the news is good: the fragrance of the taro is the very fragrance of the Way.
Master Yongzongben ascended the hall and, citing the *gong'an* of Jia Shan’s visit to Shipin, offered this verse: “In laughter, he abandoned Zhulin Temple;
I thought there was so much more at Huating. His very life was lost beneath the oar; Look closely, and you will see that victory and defeat were his own doing.”
Chan Master Dongyan Jingri of Tiantong in Ningbo was a dharma successor of Chan Master Xiyuan Hui.
He was the son of the Liao family from Duchang in Nankang. From childhood, he abstained from meat and pungent roots.
At fifteen, he received the tonsure at Xianglin on Mount Lu. He first visited Changyang and Shishuang, and subsequently traveled to Zhejiang to seek out Chishi.
He was utterly unyielding and did not conform to others. He ascended Mount Jing and met Wuzhun Shanfeng, who held him in high esteem. Later, he visited Xiyuan Hui at Tiantong;
the latter’s instructions were entirely consistent with those of Shanfeng, and he thus attained a profound realization of their intent. Shanfeng appointed him as the Keeper of the Canon.

Subsequently, he served as the First Seat under Kaixian Wuwen Can, whereby his reputation grew increasingly prominent. During the Jingding era of the Song dynasty’s Lizong reign, he went forth to preside over [a monastery].
Yuántōng succeeded him as abbot of Dōnglín. In the *Renchén* year of the Zhìyuán era of the Yúan dynasty, he moved to Yùwáng. Not long after, he retired to live in seclusion at Xuědòu.

In the *Gēngzǐ* year of the Dàdé era, he became the head of Tiāntóng. The Master was born in the *Xīnyí* year of the Jiādì era of the Sòng dynasty and passed away in the *Wùshēn* year of the Zhìdà era of the Yúan dynasty.
As he was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he wrote a verse, saying: "Heaven is the canopy and Earth is the casket; what need have I for a stūpa?"

At the hermitage, he said, "My bones shall become ash amidst the mountains and rivers; my words have been spoken as an arrow—do not engrave them. Two days later, having bathed and sat upright, he passed away.
Upon cremation, his jawbone remained unbroken. He was interred at Cheongungu (Clear Wind Valley) on the western cliff. He was eighty-eight years old.
The seventeenth day of the twelfth month, the seventy-first [anniversary].
Zen Master Yueting Zhong of Jinling Jiangshan, a successor of Zen Master Wuxue Yuan, cited a monk’s question: "Baoyun, the old year has already passed; the new year..."

[The Master] arrived. [A monk asked: "What is the meaning of 'non-transmigration'? Yun said, "The eyebrows are above the eyes. He then offered this verse: Having finished fishing, he returns and does not moor his boat;
In the river village, the moon has fallen, and it is just right for sleep. Even if a night wind should blow him away, He remains by the shallow waters amidst the reeds.
Falling leaves have already followed the flowing stream; The spring breeze has not yet released the hundred flowers. Green...
The face of the mountain remains as it was; all day long it lies spread out facing the setting sun.

[This refers to] the story of Mañjuśrī spending the summer retreats in three places and Kāśyapa striking the gavel with the intent to expel him. The verse says: "The young lord in brocade robes is accustomed to wandering through spring;

The beautiful lady with white hair harbors much resentment and vexation. Though he is wealthy, he still complains that his mouth is too small; Being poor himself, there is nothing he can do about his own body."
Citing the story of Ciming hanging up the notice for the assembly on a winter day, the verse says: Painted above, painted below; painted short, painted long.
Clearly revealed, broadly deliberated upon—how does this compare to the "Great Yellow" (rhubarb) produced in the capital?

Chan Master Zhuyuan Miaodao of Jianyan in Kunshan, Suzhou, was a successor of Chan Master Yuwang Hong. He was the son of the Chen family of Ninghai. As a youth, he suffered from a disease in his right eye.
His mother took him to pray before an image of Avalokiteśvara. As the Master looked up at the image, he saw that there was a small spider’s web over its right eye. Thereupon—

He removed it for him, and the master’s eye ailment was subsequently cured. His parents, believing that he had a karmic affinity with the Buddha, sent him to Zhengyan at the Six Harmonies Monastery in Hangzhou to receive ordination.
Yan ordered him to study the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, but the master said, "If I do not study even a single dharma, how can I study a hundred dharmas?
He then went to visit Hengchuan Gong of the Yuyang Monastery. One day, upon hearing the master raise the koan of "dry dung," he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.

He immediately presented a verse, saying: "Yunmen’s dried-up shit-stick; its radiance illuminates the ten directions. As soon as Maofeng sets foot [upon the path], on the fifth day he arrives at Qiantang.
Guo was struck with wonder and, looking at the assembly, said: "This youth is one who has returned for a second birth.

In the year Yichou of the Zhizhi era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty, he went forth to preside over Ciyuan in the district, and later moved to Jianyan in Kunshan. One evening, while with the assembly...
Tea ceremony. [The Master] cited the story of Layman东坡 (Dongpo) visiting the spring at Mount Jiangshan. The mountain master asked, "What is the noble surname of this great Confucian?
The Layman replied, "My surname is 'Scale'. The mountain master asked, "What kind of scale is that? The Layman said, "It is the scale used to weigh the elders of the world.

The mountain master then gave a shout and said, "Now tell me, how much does this one shout weigh? The Layman was speechless. The Master then commanded the assembly to provide a response on his behalf. At that time, another [monk] stepped forward.
Yuan Yuan. He suddenly rose and trimmed the candle. Liao Tang coughed once and cleared his throat. The Master smiled and said, "Attendant Yuan Yuan trims the candle;
one attendant clears his throat. A monk requests that the Master provide a substitute for him. The Master said, "It does not exceed this.
On another evening, Xin Gufan came to the abbot’s quarters and requested instruction on Zhaozhou’s "Mu" (No) kōan. The Master spoke in a stern voice: "Night!"
He went down deep. Gufan returned to the hall. Efa said, "If you would not speak to me, that was that; why must you show such anger? Someone reported this to the Master.
The Master said, "He will realize it for himself later. Upon hearing this, Gufan attained immediate and total clarity.

The Renzong Emperor summoned him to reside at Hongfu Temple on Mount Huangyan and bestowed upon him the title Dinghui Yuanming (Circumspect Wisdom, Perfect Clarity). In the year of Bingchen, during the Yanyou era.
The two monasteries of Jingci and Lingyin both vied to invite him there, yet he declined them both.
Having passed the age of seventy, longing for the secluded seclusion of Mount Zhituo, he went there to spend the remainder of his life.
At the age of thirteen, Chan Master Gulin Qingmao of Baoning in Jinling became a full monk.

Upon hearing an elder monk cite the words of Gaofeng Yuanmiao exhorting the monastics, he could not help but shed tears profusely; he then realized there existed a single point that transcends birth and death and surpasses both sages and ordinary people.

He resolved to seek instruction with fervor, traveling extensively to visit various masters. When Hengchuan resided at Yuyang Monastery, the Master went there to call upon him and was struck by his hammer-like teaching.
As he brushed it away, he first realized that touch is pure. After attaining the Dharma, he went forth in Kaiyuan of Wu, moved to Yongfu in Poyang, and later presided over Baoning in Jinling.
While ascending the hall, a monk asked: "A hair swallows the vast ocean; a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru."
"This is a matter within the scope of a patch-robed monk; this is not a matter within the scope of a patch-robed monk. The Master said, "Remove that great mountain at the gate.
[The monk] said, "When the whale swallows the ocean water to its end, the coral branches are revealed. The Master said, "An iron caltrop behind the head of the Vajra.
[The monk] said, "As for what is said in the teachings: 'I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention, being foremost among men.'"
“What is the samādhi of non-contention? The Master said, “I give you thirty blows. [The monk] said, “Benevolence and righteousness are both severed in poverty;
worldly sentiment tends toward those with wealth. The Master said, “Those who recognize kindness are few; those who betray it are many. [The monk] asked:
“I recall that in the past, when Shouzhuang arrived at Langye, Langye asked him, ‘Where have you recently departed from? Shouzhuang replied, ‘From the Two Zhe regions.’”
Langye said, "Does it come by boat or by land? Huangbo said, "By boat. Langye asked, "Where is the boat? Huangbo said, "At the wharf. "What is the meaning of this? the Master asked.
[Huangbo] said, "To open one's mouth is to reveal one's heart. [The Master] asked, "Langye said, 'A phrase that does not involve the journey'—how do you speak such a phrase?
What is the phrase that does not involve the journey? The Master said, "It does not reach the village in front; behind—"
A guest monk asked, "What about when Master Ju, brandishing his sitting mat, said, 'Old fellows who make things up are as numerous as hemp and millet'? How do you explain that?
The Master said, "A burnt brick strikes a frozen patch right down to the bottom. The monk asked, "Later, Langye asked an attendant, 'Who was this person?
The attendant replied, 'It was Master Ju. Why did Langye then go in person to the guest quarters? The Master said, "He went to see him off."
The questioner asked, "Is this not Master Ju? Please do not take offense for having inadvertently provoked you just now.
The Master said, "There is a thorn in the soft mud. Ju shouted, "When did you, Elder, arrive at Fenyang? I have long heard your name in Zhejiang;
seeing that your understanding is such as this, how can it be said that your fame 'resounds through the universe'? Langye then prostrated himself and said, "I, [Name],..."
[The student] said, "That was a fault. Wherein lay his fault? The Master said, "If one does not ascend the tower to look out, how can one know the depth of the vast ocean?
[The student] said, "Later, Dahui said: 'When these two great elders met, it was like the sun and moon shining in the sky;
dragons and elephants trampling over them. I wonder, was this truly so or not? The Master said, "To add mud upon mud—this is yet another layer. [The student] said, "Langye..."
Later, he encountered Ciming and brought up this story. Ciming said, "To raise [the case] is merely enough for one’s own understanding;
yet you have fallen into error—how can you act as a teacher? Do you approve of him, or do you not? The Master said, "A single drop of ink forms two dragons.
Ciming said, "One may truly say: 'When the dragon meets the water, its spirit increases; when the tiger encounters the mountain scenery, its fierce majesty grows. The Master said, "..."
In a deserted place, he rubbed his forehead and gazed at you, asking, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Nailing with nails and gluing with glue.
He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Ants do not eat iron. He asked, "What is 'the partial within the absolute'?
The Master said, "The grass fills the Dharma Hall. He asked, "What is 'the absolute within the partial'? The Master said, "Moss seals the ancient [gate]."
The Emperor asked, "What is 'coming from the center'? The Master said, "A monkey wearing a scholar's cap.

The Emperor asked, "What is 'arriving through the synthesis'? The Master said, "The sun rising and the moon setting. The Emperor asked, "What is 'reaching through the synthesis'? The Master said, "Cutting off the water to stop the wheel.
The Emperor said, "I have received your instructions on the five ranks of ruler and subject; what about matters beyond the 'curtain of night-brightness'? The Master said, "Seize the dawn."
He did not return home. At twilight, while awaiting the rising sun, he ascended the hall and said:

"If I speak of the Buddha-dharma to provide for the assembly, my beard and eyebrows will inevitably fall out. If I speak of worldly dharmas to provide for the assembly, I shall enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Setting aside these two paths, what exactly shall I say? My three-inch tongue has no place to use it; my pair of empty hands have nothing to offer."
Not forming a fist. A small-scale sermon. [The Master] raised the case: A monk asked Lingyun, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Lingyun said, "Standing at the edge of a poisoned mortar, planting crabapples at the bottom of a well. The monk said, "I do not understand. Lingyun said, "This year’s peaches and plums are precious;
each one is worth a thousand pieces of gold. Dahui said, "As for this koan, from antiquity until now, no one has ever brought it up."
[The Master] said: "Come forth! This mountain monk will not spare his verbal karma; I shall further annotate and break it down for you all. 'Facing the chopping block, facing the chopping block.

Planting crabapples at the bottom of the well. This year’s peaches and plums are precious; each one is worth a thousand pieces of gold. The Master said: "Great assembly, consider this dialogue where Lingyun answered the monk.
Now tell me, how does this compare to when Linji was with Huangbo and asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times?"
"Having been struck with sixty blows of the staff, are they the same or different? If you say they are the same, there is no such thing as a 'sameness' in the Dharma.
If you say they are different, how could the Buddha-dharma have two distinct varieties? I always admire what Daie said: "In my place, we speak of the 'clam-son Chan.
As soon as one opens their mouth, the heart, liver, and five viscera are revealed—this very thing is it. Nevertheless, even so, it is largely the same.
A Small Lecture: "The Man Who Scoops Horse Dung in the City. An ancient said: "For ninety days, the feet are restrained—fish swim within a net;
for three months, they dwell in seclusion—birds enter a cage. When life and death are exhausted, the silkworm makes its cocoon. How can one penetrate these three layers?"
Holding up his staff, he said: "When the mountain is nearly nine *ren* high, one fails to add even a single basket of earth.

At Kaiyuan Temple, during a small-scale *chan* (sermon), he raised the case of Xuefeng asking Deshan: "By what dharma do the sages of all ages instruct people? Deshan replied: [The sound of the staff striking the floor].
"In my school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma taught to others.
Later, a monk asked Xuefeng, "When you saw Deshan, what did you obtain that you then ceased [speaking]? Xuefeng said, "At that time, I went empty-handed and returned empty-handed."
The Fifth Patriarch picked up the case and said: "To speak now to those who have not yet penetrated it: there were two men coming from Dongjing who asked him, 'Where have you recently departed from?
He replied, 'Suzhou. They then asked, 'How are things in Suzhou?
He said, 'Everything is as usual. Although this was so, they could not deceive the mountain monk. Why? It was simply because their dialects were different. Ultimately, it is like this."
"What? asked Suzhou Master Ling of Shao Bo. "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure; that which flows from oneself is no different from rubble.
Old Dongshan followed the mold to cast his bricks, yet he failed to realize that these two great elders were simply suffering from overeating.

Nevertheless, since you have come from Dongjing, why do you speak with a Suzhou accent? *Note: This passage is a Zen dialogue concerning the nature of enlightenment and the distinction between inherited tradition and innate realization.*
The Master said: "In the Hall. Once, while eating sweetmeats during a winter night, Dongshan asked Head Seat Tai, 'There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth, black as lacquer;
it is always present within activity, yet cannot be contained within activity.
Where does its fault lie? Tai replied, 'Its fault lies within activity. Dongshan then called for an attendant to remove the table of sweetmeats. The Master [said]: "..."
It is said: "These words, in the various quarters today, are never failed to be brought forth during winter nights for a commentary to be added.
Yet, regarding the main text, not a single word has been spoken. Some say: 'Dongshan saw only the sharpness of the chisel's tip, but did not see the squareness of the chisel's handle;
why does he suppress and distort people? Others say: 'The Head Seat Tai did not get it.'"
"Eating sweets? For now, let it be said that no one on this great earth may eat them; those who succeed are few, while those who fail are many.
Little do they realize that Dongshan possesses the skillful means of 'partiality and correctness' and 'mutual interplay' that avoids transgression.
Even if Head Seat Tai were to say, 'It does not reside within active function,' he still could not avoid eating from his nest. After a long silence, he said: "The water flows..."
From where do the yellow leaves come? A cow, trailing crows of winter, passes through a distant village.

New Year’s Eve Small Lecture: Tonight, the year ends, the month ends, and the day ends. Yet worldly affairs drift on and on—when will they ever end? Tomorrow, the year is new, the month is new, and the day is new;
amidst a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, all is seen anew. Therefore it is said: "When exhausted, there is change; with change, there is penetration. [He] lowers the hook.
Throughout the four seas, one merely hooks the fierce dragon; regarding the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices, everyone certainly does not know them.

If you can achieve harmony between sound and resonance, each guarding the ancestral fields and gardens, and knowing that rice is made from grain, you will avoid the blind donkey who extinguishes our school.
(He plants his staff and says: "No one has recognized the sweat of horses in battle from the past; it only requires..."
A Further Discourse on Meritorious Deeds Throughout the Ages: Yongfu’s Small Lecture upon Entering the Monastery.

In the bustling marketplace of red dust, at the crossroads of the city streets, at the tips of the hundred grasses, or atop the solitary peak—if you attempt to deliberate upon this as "Buddha-dharma," you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow.
Directly, the myriad functions cease and all sages are left behind. Before sound there is no sound; after form there is no form.
To examine this closely, it is precisely the deluded thoughts prior to the skull.

Even if one were to smash the skull, strip away the brain-casing, kick over Mount Sumeru, and trample the great ocean underfoot—only to have the matter resolved at the base of one's heels—it would still be a case of falling into the seventh or eighth rank.
A man of broad learning and superior character, an eminent figure who transcends conventional bounds, must act for himself; throughout his life, he shall never abide within another’s nest.

To the assembly gathered here: I hope you will examine this well. That I, a mountain monk, have traveled two thousand li through the hardships of land and water to join you here is not for any other purpose than this:
the reconstruction of the Hall of Rest on the Winter Solstice. Opening wide the doors and windows, I begin anew.
In its ancient scale, who is it that faces the window? Having cut off the tracks of both sages and ordinary folk, the blue-eyed barbarian monk is at a loss.
Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his slaves; the lanterns and the pillars raise their brows. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra serve as his messengers.
It cannot be drawn, it cannot be painted. When it falls, it is not another thing—flowers in clusters, brocade in clusters. Even so...
Transversely, it is not dust; seize it and go. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—tread upon them and they provoke anger. The body of the Dharma King is fully revealed.
From antiquity to the present, those who speak of the "original" or the "wondrous," yet fail to distinguish between the monastic and the lay, are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.

Regarding principle and regarding phenomena, how many are there who can transform and transcend the conventional? A clever fellow, free from fixed patterns, knows that such matters are as they are and simply lets them be.
But tell me, what is it that he knows? Cold comes and heat goes; when yin reaches its extreme, yang is born. The jade tree in the courtyard blooms early;
this too surpasses the waters flowing uphill at Dongshan. (He plants his staff and gives a shout.)
"Ho! [The Master] ascends the hall. He cites the Night Session of King Yuhua, which says: "Shaoshi has no gates or doors; how can one attain penetration?
Standing patiently through the deep night, listen as I speak of east and west. The Master calls to the assembly, saying: "There is the provisional, there is the real;
there is illumination, there is function. It simply must not be understood in such a way. Be careful! [This is for] the New Year’s Eve."
"Consider this: of the three hundred and sixty days in a year, tonight marks the very end.

You all must likewise recognize that there is a time when one reaches the end regarding the matter of one's own nature. If you have not yet reached that end, you must press forward with resolute discernment.
Have you not seen how Daishu attended more than seventy virtuous teachers who possessed the great eye of wisdom?"
There are only one or two such people. Furthermore, what is it to possess the great eye? On the sea, the Fifth Patriarch sought out dozens of venerable masters;
yet when he reached the assembly of Yuanjian of Fushan, he truly could not open his mouth.
Later, upon arriving at Baiyun, he bit through a single iron sour dumpling and only then did he come to possess all flavors. He then said: "The flowers bloom."
The cocks' crests flatter the early autumn; who can dye their purple silk-threads? Sometimes stirred by the wind, they lean against one another, as if fighting incessantly before the steps.
He gave a shout and said: "If the cultivation of the mind has not yet reached the groundless state, ten thousand kinds and a thousand variations will flow away with the current.
In a small assembly (xiaocan), he raised the example of Sīxīn showing the community: "A high-ranking traveler-monk knows how to open his alms bowl."
Bag. Cast off the pack and hat; set aside all medicinal taboos. Where one person is, you must go; where half a person is, you must go;
where no person is, you must go there in person. The Master said: "Such talk is like black rock honey—sweet from the center to the edge.
Nevertheless, were it not for the wild geese arriving at night, how could one see the autumn at the sea-gate? (New Year’s Eve)
Small Assembly Sermon: Tonight the year ends, yet how could it ever truly end? Tomorrow the new year arrives, yet in truth it does not come.

Thirty-six hundred breaths revolve like the hub of a wheel; how many times the tide has ebbed and flowed again. Where the pivot of the mechanism turns, even a flash of lightning leaves one bewildered.

When the Great Function manifests before you, who can discern its true mark? Erase the dust of deluded emotions before they arise; forget the ultimate principle beyond words and explanations. Every person...

The nostrils point toward heaven; every one of you dwells in peace and prosperity. When Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra give rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma, they are banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains.
When the lanterns and the pillars suddenly manifest the adamantine eye, they burst into great laughter.

"Three pounds of flax," "a dried piece of excrement"—if you all attempt to deliberate upon these as matters of Buddhist Dharma, you will enter hell as swiftly as a shot arrow. Upon reaching [this point], [the master] said: [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "到" (to/arrive at). The translation reflects the available portion.]
In this state, the path of thought is severed and the sphere of mental activity ceases. There is a single, level equanimity, wherein all things are naturally exhausted in stillness.
At such a time as this, how is it? "Last night the east wind melted the remaining snow; on the branches of the withered tree, flowers bloom once more.
The Small Sermon for the Retreat Opening: Tomorrow the summer retreat begins. If you merely pass the days in indolence, then when the drum is beaten and you ascend [the seat], what will you do?
The Hall. It is simply that one cannot escape through deliberation. When all of you crowd together and come forward, you cannot help but take south for north.
