Before the Seven Buddhas, there was never such a message; after the Seven Buddhas, although such a message exists, in the end it is impossible to fully awaken to the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Tathāgata, nor can one enter the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment. Body.
The mind abides in the wisdom of equanimity. Consequently, for ninety days, people concerned themselves only with their mouths and bodies rather than with cultivation;

they turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the dust of the senses, idly prolonging the passage of time and years. The Fifth Patriarch said: "Master Bodhidharma came with his feet following his faith and spoke with his mouth following his faith.
Yet the descendants of later generations have turned this into mere calculation. If one succeeds through calculation, then heaven will be clear and earth will be peaceful."
Yunmen’s fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra.

A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a single blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. A chicken from Chu is no phoenix from Mount Dan; it merely loves to crow atop the *wutong* tree.
The Master once gave this instruction: "There is still more above; let the lion’s claws and fangs be revealed."
Within this, there was further deliberation; yet, one cannot avoid the image of someone brandishing a sword at the very gate. Who would dare to confront this numinous blade?
The Master’s verbal prowess was sharp and piercing, and his insight and skill were extraordinary. Since the time of Ying’an, he was likely the foremost person.
He once compiled the *Zongmen Tongyao* (Essentials of the Patriarchal School). Later, he passed away at Baoning.
Chan Master Jue’en of Tianyi Duanjiang in Yuezhou was the son of the Gu family of Cixi. His physical stature was tall and slender, and his pure integrity was firmly established.
In his youth, he relied upon Yunmen Guangxiao to receive the tonsure. Later, at Yanqing Monastery in Mingzhou, he heard the *Sijiaoyi* (The Rituals of the Four Teachings);

in seven days, he mastered it thoroughly. Master Wen was astonished and marveled at his extraordinary talent. He then went to attend upon Hengchuan at Yuyang Monastery, where he attained spiritual resonance within the master’s quarters.
Internally, he possessed a profound memory; his virtuous deeds became increasingly manifest day by day. At that time, all the worthy scholars and gentlemen delighted in associating with him.
He emerged from the world at T'ien-p'ing in Su-chou, later moving to K'ai-yüan, then to Pao-fu in Ming-chou, and finally to T'ien-i in Yüeh-chou.

One day, while the assembly was standing in attendance within his quarters, he suddenly leaned on his staff and said: "This old monk stands amidst the void, leaning upon his rustic staff—clearly [so it is]."
He drew a portrait of Subhūti, looked left and right, and said, "Do you understand? After a long silence, he cast down his staff, leaned against his meditation cushion, and passed away.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Gong of Jingci.
Chan Master Dehai of Dongyu in Lingyin, Hangzhou, was the son of the Chen family of Linhai, Taizhou.
At the age of fourteen, he left home to become a monk under the Sichuanese monk Anshi. He went to study with Gang of Shilin at Chengtian Temple. Gang asked, "What is your own self?
As the Master hesitated, Gang pushed him out of the room. The Master immediately became filled with doubt. One day, while entering the inner quarters, Gang asked:
"The entire earth is the adamantine true body. Where would you place yourself, Master? As the Master was about to respond, Gong struck him. From this moment on, he attained thorough realization.

Later, when Gong moved to Jingci Monastery, he appointed the Master to serve in the *shisī* (attendant's office). One day, in the meditation hall, Gong raised the story of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant.
The Master said, "It is not that the cat is lost; it must be that the dog is lost. Gong said, "That is so."
"To betray? That is not betraying. The Master said, "Deceiving others and deceiving yourself. Gong struck him with a bamboo staff and said, "It is you, Hai-zi, who will carry on our lineage.
In the *Gengyin* year of the *Zhizhi* era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty, he appeared in the world at Hanyan on Mount Tiantai.
In the *Yisi* year of the *Dade* era, he moved to Hanshan in Gusu. In the *Jiyou* year of the *Zhida* era, he moved again to Dongchan in Kunshan. In the *Xinhai* year...

He was granted a golden-embroidered Dharma robe by imperial decree. In the Gui-chou year of Huangqing, he moved again to Zhongzhu. In the Yi-mao year of Yanyou, an edict appointed him as the abbot of Jingci Monastery.
Upon arriving at the mountain gate, he said: "The Pure Gate of Compassion; a single lake of autumn water.

Entering or not entering? A tiger bites a tiger; a snake swallows a turtle's snout! With a roar, he shouted once. His assembly numbered over ten thousand. Within his quarters, he offered this pith instruction:
"Holding a sharp-edged sword in hand—why does the monkey not die? Biting through the iron ball—why are there hungry people on the road?
The Persian removes his hat; the sugarcane is bitten at its sweet tip. Fish take water as their life—why do they die within it?

None of those present could provide an answer that accorded with the truth. In the year of Yichou (1325) of the Taiding era, he moved again to Lingyin Monastery. In the ninth month of Dingmao (1327)...

Manifesting a slight illness, he summoned his disciples and, having completed his final instructions, passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He was seventy-two years old and fifty-eight years since his ordination.
He was posthumously granted the title Chan Master Mingzong Huiren. His recorded sayings from six assemblies remain in circulation.
His stupa is located at the foot of the rear mountain of Yuwang Monastery.

Chan Master Zhuyun Jingtan of Tiantong Monastery in Jiaxing was the son of the Yan family of Putian. Having long relied upon Shilin, he later resided at Zhiping in Wuzhou, Beichen in Suzhou, and Tiantong in Huzhou. Ascending the hall, he said: "The golden crow rises in the east; the jade hare sinks in the west. Clever monks search here and there. Suddenly, they smash through empty space. [He remained silent.
The kalpa exists only in this very moment. (He planted his staff upright. He descended from his seat. A monk asked, "The Three Worthies have not yet attained it;
the Ten Sages find it difficult to know. What is this school? The Master said, "A holeless flute and felt clappers.
The monk asked, "What is the mind of nirvana? The Master said, "Mount Sumeru. The monk asked, "What is discriminating wisdom? The Master said, "The four great oceans."
Chan Master Shouyong of Dongzhou at Tiger Hill in Suzhou sent this verse to a departing monk: "In movement and stillness, how could one ever be entangled?
Why need one further penetrate that which exists before birth? The ancestral garden lies a thousand miles away; now you return home. On land there is the journey; on water there is the boat.
He spoke these words for Layman Zhang Yi of Juezhai upon his entry into the Way, and offered this verse: "A single blow, and the sound of the bell reaches [the ear]."
The faculty of hearing: the ocean of three thousand worlds is simultaneously darkened. The thief departs from the side of the lump of flesh; tomorrow, it remains as it was, not leaving the gate.
[Disciple of] Chan Master Dushan of Jing Mountain.

Chan Master Jingfu of Huya Peak at Mount Jingshan in Hangzhou was a native of Huai'an. During the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, Emperor Shizu once summoned him for an audience, and he presented a verse to the Emperor.
Its gist was as follows: "All Tathāgatas of the past dwell securely within the secret treasury;
the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present have realized the Way and turned the wheel of Dharma; all sentient beings are the World-Honored Ones of the future. By means of this...

Through deluded thoughts and attachments, one is bound by the fetters of afflictions and entangled in obscurations; thus, one becomes lost in the bodies of the six realms and pointlessly undergoes the sufferings of the three miserable paths.

One only thinks of the Buddhas of the past and present, yet fails to revere the Honored Ones of the future. Thus, one forms enmity with the Buddhas, perhaps even slaughtering and killing living beings.

Failing to realize that the characteristics of sentient beings are entirely the body of *dharmatā*, one remains ignorant. In the past, there was the monk Never-Disparaging (*Sadāparibhūta*), who prostrated to all and said:

"I do not slight you; you shall all become Buddhas. If you can maintain mindfulness that both yourself and others are equally future Buddhas, your blessings and lifespan will increase in this present life, and in birth after birth, you shall be born in the Buddha-lands. Upon reading this, the Emperor was greatly delighted and asked, "Among the emperors since the time of God, have there been any who observed the precept against killing?
The Master replied, "In the past, Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty once said to his ministers: 'Last night I was hungry.'"

"It is so. I intended to sacrifice a sheep, but fearing the consequences for those who might follow, I have made this a constant practice. I would rather endure a momentary hunger than bear witness to endless slaughter.
The ministers all cried out "Ten-thousand-year reign! The Emperor praised and accepted his advice, and immediately received the precepts from the Imperial Preceptor.
A monk from Tiantong Zhuxi Tan Chan Temple in Mingzhou came for an audience. The Master asked, "From where have you come? He replied, "From Jinge.
The Master asked, "How high is the peak of Jinge Mountain? He replied, "Its summit cannot be seen. The Master rebuked him. One day, the Master ascended the seat.
Regarding the public case of the World-Honored One holding up a flower: the monk had an awakening upon hearing these words.
Chan Master Baoye Yuan of Dingshui Temple in Yuezhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yu of Mount Jing;
he was born into the Chen family of Mount Xiangshan. Having received full ordination and traveled to observe various quarters, he encountered a monk.
Liu Zhuyu, who had abandoned the Way for the sake of worldly things, saw his anxiety manifest in his countenance. Xu Tang refused to let him descend from the hall;
Liu Qian became enraged and imprisoned him to humiliate him. The Master served him with the utmost reverence; whenever he had doubts, he would ask, and they were resolved as soon as he questioned.

After a long time, he attained a state of vast clarity. One day, Xu Tang said, "Yuan! You have now reached the Great Peace. When Tang took charge of Mount Jing, [he appointed the Master to succeed him].
He was appointed as the head of the assembly. He went to serve as abbot at Jianyan in Pingjiang, then moved to the Water and Land (Shuilu) Assembly at Quanzhou, and subsequently moved to Dingshui.

There, he recounted the story of the World-Honored One and the Five-Supernormal-Power Seer, composing a verse which said: "If you ask me about that one supernormal power, the mouth is the gateway to disaster."

Invoking the cause while carrying the fruit: the Great Dharma King of Shame, Modesty, Compassion, and Mercy. *Pingding li ren bu shu huo* (The Fire element does not belong to the *ping* and *ding* trigrams nor to the *ren* branch).

Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited the case of the scholar Zhang Zhuo’s visit to Shishuang. Shishuang asked, "Scholar, what is your noble surname? Zhuo replied, "My surname is Zhang and my given name is Zhuo.
Shishuang said, "In this place, even 'cleverness' cannot be found; from where, then, does 'Zhuo' come? At these words, Zhuo attained great enlightenment.
The verse says: Advancing forward, there is a precipice three thousand *zhang* high; Retreating backward, there are cliffs ten thousand layers deep.
Precious is the Elder Zhang Zhuo of the Great Tang, Who dances in the spring breeze with an iron hammer that has no seams. Later, he resided at Yunjing (Cloud Peak).
He passed away during the *Xinchou* year of the Zhiyuan era of Emperor Yuan Shizu. His stupa was erected at Yunjing. He was seventy-five years of age at the time of his death.
Chan Master Xianji Yun of Suzhou Huqiu had long relied upon Master Xutang at Mount Jing, where he served as the First Seat.
One day, Baoyue Yuan requested instruction from Xutang regarding Deshan’s “last word”: "If one says it exists, how could Deshan have failed to understand?
If one says it does not exist, yet Yantou said that Deshan had not yet understood. I beg the Master’s compassion [to resolve this]."

Bi pointed this out to him. Daowang said, "I do not understand; you should go ask the Head Seat. Yuan went to the Master, who happened to be returning from a mountain excursion. He called for water to wash his feet;
Yuan hurriedly brought the water forward and then prostrated himself as the Master rubbed and massaged his body. Yuan then looked up and raised the previous conversation to question him.
The Master took the water and splashed it on him, saying, "What is that final phrase? Yuan did not attain realization.
He went up again to see Master Tang. Tang asked, "How did the Head Seat explain it to you? Yuan recounted the previous conversation. Tang said, "That fellow told me he understood.
At this, Yuan was relieved and grasped the meaning. [The Master] cites the anecdote of Xinghua’s "repaying the price" and offers this verse:
The treasure of the royal house is naturally difficult to repay; How could Xinghua ever have dared to borrow it?

Look! Since heaven and earth have no private covering or supporting, they remain until this day to stabilize the Central Plains. [The Master] cites the question posed by Grand Master Lu Xun to Nanquan: "In my home, there is a single stone that has served as both a seat and a bed. May it be fashioned into a Buddha? Sitting and reclining through many springs, half covered in moss and half shrouded in clouds. Without edges or seams, it is difficult to grasp;
one can only speak of one’s own liver and entrails to others.
Chan Master Nan-sou Mao, a successor of Chan Master Yue of Jing-shan, cited the story of the ferrywoman at Yan-ťou who threw her child overboard. He offered this verse:
"The destitute ghost-child by the ferry at E-zhu— His entire capacity failed him when he struck the boat’s side. How else might one utter a turning word To save him?"
The Seventh Son of the Old Lady cites the story of Jia Shan visiting Chuanzi. The verse says: "Without form and without flaw, he immediately turned his spear back;
It was only because he trusted lightly that the ascetic Zhi. Had he not reached the banks of Huating, What could even an iron boat-paddle have done to you?
Citing the story of Layman Pang falling while descending a bridge and being helped up by Lingxiao, the verse says: Filial...

Compliance with the treasury and defiance of filial piety; when one’s ugliness is exposed before others, it cannot be concealed. Those who are close kin in this life were bitter enemies in past lives.

Chan Master Dongsheng Deming of Mount Yuyang in Mingzhou—a Dharma heir of Chan Master Miyuan of Mount Yuyang—was born into the Liu family of Yongdong. At the age of sixteen, he relied upon [the Sangha].
The moon in Xixi Lake was clear; he shaved his head and received full ordination. He first visited Xisou Tan at Xuedou, and subsequently studied under Wanji Mi.
Mi raised the question: "Wenshu is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to emerge from the woman's samādhi?
Why was Wuming able to emerge? The Master replied: "In spring colors there is no high or low; the flower branches are simply long or short. Mi held him in high esteem.
He was appointed to hold the keys of the treasury. He succeeded the King of the World (the Emperor) and was granted the honorary title "Buddha-Sun Universal Radiance" (Fó rì pǔ guāng).

The Master composed a verse on the koan of the Boatman’s capsizing boat, which says: "In this vast and tranquil world, he occupies the vital ford; A single oar is his livelihood, yet it weighs as much as a thousand *qín*.

On the road by the Zhu River, passing travelers are few; The depths of his mind cannot be matched by the vast blue sea. Later, he passed away and was interred in the Dongyun Pagoda. His lifespan was... [years].
[He was] eighty-four [years old]. At sixty-eight [years of age], Yuan Yue, Scholar of the Hanlin Academy, composed this inscription.
*Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume 55; *Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume 51.
Compiled by the Abbot of Seigan Zen-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (臣) Chōei;
reviewed by the Abbot of Kokaigan-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (臣) Chōkei; presented for imperial inspection.
Dharma heir of Chan Master Gaofeng Miao, the twenty-second generation descendant of the Linji school under Mount Heng.

Chan Master Mingben of Zhongfeng in Tiantu, Hangzhou, was the son of the Sun family of Qiantang. His mother dreamed that the Wayman Wumen (Wumen Kaido) arrived at her home carrying a lantern, and she gave birth to him.
His divine appearance was exceptionally extraordinary; as soon as he left his swaddling clothes, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture and chanting Buddhist hymns.
Whenever he laughed or played, he invariably engaged in acts of devotion. At the age of nine, he lost his mother; at fifteen, he resolved to leave the household life.

At home, upon reaching the age of twenty, he read the *Transmission of the Lamp*. Arriving at the passage where the daughter Amalā asks Mañjuśrī, "If one clearly knows the principle that birth is non-birth, why is it that one is still driven by the cycle of birth and death?
he harbored a doubt. He went to study under Gaofeng Miao at the "Deadly Barrier" (Sīgǔan).
Gaofeng was solitary, lofty, stern, and cold, never lending a word or a hint of favor to others; yet, upon seeing the Master, he was filled with joy and wished to [accept him as a disciple].
He shaved his hair. One day, while reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage concerning "shouldering the Tathāgata" and attained a sudden, clear realization.

He was twenty-four years old at the time, during the *Cǐxū* year of the *Zhìyuán* era of Emperor Shizu. The following year, he then shaved his head and received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Not long after, he...
While observing a flowing spring, he had a realization. He immediately went to Miaoxiu to seek certification, but Miaoxiu drove him away with a blow.

Shortly thereafter, a rumor spread among the common people that the government was selecting young boys and girls. The Master asked, "If someone were to come and ask the Abbot for a young boy or girl, what would you do?
Miaoxiu said, "I would simply hand him a bamboo comb. At these words, the Master attained complete clarity, penetrating to the very source of the Dharma.
Zhaozhou Miào then wrote a true eulogy and gave it to his master, saying: "My appearance is inconceivable; even Buddhas and patriarchs cannot behold it.
Only I, this unworthy child, have been granted permission to catch a glimpse of half its nose. When asked about the relative merits of his various disciples, Miào said:
"As for Head Seat Yì, he is certainly a single stalk of old bamboo, yet it is bent seven ways and eight ways. As for Steward Běn, however—"
The new bamboo shoots on the fishing pole will one day form a forest; their future growth is not easily measured. When Miaoxian passed away, the Master took charge of the monastery affairs.

Finding the constant inquiries from kings and ministers to be a distraction, he resigned from his duties and traveled between rivers and lakes, sometimes by boat and sometimes dwelling in mountain huts.
He had no fixed residence and styled all his dwellings "Abiding in Illusion" (Huànzhù). When Emperor Rénzōng summoned him, he did not go.
The Emperor bestowed upon him a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya* and the title of Chan Master Fúcí Yuánzhào Guǎnghuì. Furthermore, by imperial decree, Shīzǐ Chányuàn was renamed Shīzǐ Zhèngzōng Chánsì.
At that time, the Xuānzhènyuàn left the positions at Língyǐn and Jìngshān vacant to await the Master, but he declined them both. Emperor Yīngzōng succeeded...

The Imperial favor and bounty were as they had been under the previous dynasty. Prince Wang Zhang, the Prince of Shen and Marquis of the Household (Fu-ma Tai-wei), submitted a memorial requesting that, by imperial decree, the Master be invited to ascend the seat and address the assembly:
"The Great Way is non-action; the Great Achievement does not preside over it. The Great Goodness leaves no trace; the Great Name is not dwelt upon.
In every place, the Sea-Seal emits its radiance; for ten thousand generations, the Golden Branches stand out in splendor. [He then] sought out Yuan-tong.
Within Chaoyindong Cave, the Great Being purchased stones and found an abundance of clouds; at Mingqing Temple, he cultivated the Ruyilun practice, and flowers arrived accompanied by butterflies.
Fragrant winds played the music of the Four Heavens, and the sound of the *brahman* resonated like thunder across the great earth.
For two thousand years he has already manifested as a king, and for five hundred kalpas he has constantly served as a lord of the world. The entire Great Canon of Teachings follows [his guidance].

The pivot of destiny turns; hundreds of thousands of virtuous deeds are manifested at will. May the Emperor live for ten thousand years within the nine-layered palace, and may the Three Han kingdoms be preserved by the Sovereign State.
These are the ordinary practices of the Grand Marshal, Prince of Shen, the Layman Hai-in.
Furthermore, as for a single phrase that accords with the Buddha-dharma, how shall it be pointed out? Auspicious clouds arise, encompassing heaven and earth—without beginning and without end.
Auspicious vapors rise on the anniversary of High Peak’s passing. The Master holds up incense and says:

"Within Suxin Hermitage, in the center of Lake Tai, we suddenly encounter the anniversary of his compassionate departure. Worldly appearances cannot yet be forgotten. Great Assembly, Old Monk High Peak has arrived!
Rain steams the green of sprouts and leaves; wind shakes the fragrance of rice flowers. He says: "The spring enters the cold cliffs beyond adding anything; the withered [branches]..."

Of the affairs of the year, already one month has passed. As for the meditation cushions and the Zen boards, do you still perceive them?

As for the lanterns and the pillars—do you still forget about subject and object? If you have not yet understood this, do you realize that the previous month has passed in such a void?
If you do not take the impermanence of birth and death as your own primary responsibility and apply yourself with diligent vigor, [you will continue to waste your time].
If one establishes a separate career for oneself, then even after a month, one will not yet have escaped further empty loss; it will merely result in several more bouts of drowsiness.
Throughout the twelve months, nothing more than this cycle of futile waste occurs. To shave the head and dye the robes is to transcend the mundane and go beyond the worldly.
What is it that you intend? Do you still know that life exists only as long as the breath remains? That this youthful vigor does not linger, but is like a galloping horse?
If you do not seize this moment while the breath has not yet ceased, and while this vigorous color is still fit for enjoyment, you must risk your very life.
Seize upon the critical phrase (*huatou*) and engage in dialogue with it to reach a clear understanding. As for that analogy of the crab falling into the boiling water, whom can you blame?
Have you not seen how Shigong was in Mazu’s assembly? While he was performing chores in the kitchen, Mazu asked him, "What are you doing here?
Shigong replied, "I am tending the ox. Mazu asked, "How do you tend the ox? Shigong said, "Each time it enters..."
He cleared away the grass and suddenly pulled the ox back by its nose. The Master said, "You truly know how to herd an ox. Look at our predecessors:

even during their daily labors, they never for a moment forgot this Way. How could they be like people today, who do not pick up a blade of grass when it lies across them nor step on one when it stands upright?

The Master frequently rebuked students for merely valuing intellectual comprehension while failing to seek genuine awakening. He addressed the assembly, saying:
"The reason why contemporary Zen practice lacks efficacy is, first, the absence of the sincere resolve of the ancients; second, [the failure] to..."

It lies in the failure to recognize the root of birth and death. Whenever I see a student, I invariably ask: "What do you call this?"
When people were caught in the cycle of birth and death, or were utterly bewildered and unable to respond, he would invariably encourage and instruct them.
He wrote in a letter to the Elder Dajue: "We parted on the sixth day; I did not have time to see you off, and my lingering thoughts for you remain constant, never for a moment forgotten."

I suspect this was because you feared that I might merely conform to worldly conventions. I and you have been close friends for sixteen years; our mutual intentions have been perfectly transparent and clear.
I never imagined that you would fail to understand my humble feelings and instead wish to involve me in such matters. Why is this so?

How can affairs be so subject to reversal? That the ancients were so deeply concerned with the lineage of dharma heirs and the direct transmission was because the source and course of the Great Dharma must not be misrepresented.
In these degenerate times, customs have grown thin; there are those who offer gold to request a whisk and exchange a temple for a succession.
I have often felt heartache over this. Although the Great Awakened One (Dajue) was the founder of this mountain by our late master, yet throughout the ten directions...
In the monastic forests, there are many venerable elders; yet you would set them aside and not choose them, while insisting that I preside over it—how narrow is your perspective!
It is not that I fear being the abbot, but rather that I truly fear succeeding to the Dharma from the founder.
Therefore, I have withdrawn and declined with all my might, proposing instead that you serve as the master. This is precisely because you yourself were a disciple of Master Yishan; how could you...

If one were to merely conform to worldly conventions and change the one whom they revere—speaking from this perspective, I would still not wish for those who have served under my late master to take turns presiding over the Great Enlightenment;
how much less, then, could I allow them to follow the branches and extend the vines to become my successors?
Upon hearing your command, I was struck with alarm. I am exclusively dedicated to going against the current. I have already informed the Abbot of this;

I hope you will directly bring forth [the Dharma] with the voice of the Jade Gorge. If you wish to conform to worldly custom and appoint a successor, I shall most certainly not associate with you for even a single day.

In the autumn of the *wuhai* year of the Zhizhi era (1323), he manifested illness. When someone came to inquire after him, the master said, "The Huanzhu Hermitage leaks above and is pierced on the sides;

He departed after the Mid-Autumn Festival. On the morning of the fourteenth day of the eighth month, he wrote a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying:

"I have one phrase to entrust to the great assembly. If you ask further how it is, there is no basis upon which to rely. Having set down his brush, he sat upright and passed away. On that day, a white rainbow pierced through the mountains.
He was sixty-one years of age; thirty-seven years since his ordination. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the stone cliff overlooking the Yangtze River to the west of the temple.
In the *Jihsi* year of the Tianli era, Emperor Wen bestowed the posthumous title Zhijue and named his stupa Fayun. In the *Jiaxu* year of the Yuantong era,
he was further granted the title Guoshi Puying, and thirty volumes of the Master’s writings were titled the *Guanglu* and granted entry into the Great Canon for circulation.
Chan Master Duanya Liaoyi of Xitianmu Mountain in Hangzhou was the son of Tang Deqing.
He first began to speak at the age of six, yet he remained ignorant of worldly affairs. At seventeen, a monk passed by his door reciting the words from High Peak Miaokong’s formal address:
"If you wish to exhaust the view for a thousand li, climb one more story higher. The Master suddenly said, "This is a great good friend."
"It is consciousness. I ought to go see him. His mother was struck with wonder and amazement at this. He immediately went up to Sigan (the "Dead Barrier") to serve as an attendant.
Miaole gave him the koan, "Where does one return? and thus conferred upon him the name Congyi (Following One).

On another day, while Miaole was raising the koan for the assembly, "The Ox Passing Through the Window Lattice," the Master heard it and felt doubt. Day and night he investigated it. Once, while passing by Potang (Bowl Pond), he saw snow falling from the tips of pine branches.

There was a monk named Xing who went to visit Miaoxian and presented a verse, saying: "Without asking of south, north, east, or west, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow.
Before his voice had even ceased, Miaoxian struck him with a painful blow and drove him back; unaware, Xing fell to the bottom of a cliff. People thought he must have died.
His fellow students felt their way through the creepers to rescue him, but he was uninjured. If the Master remained unaware, they renewed their vow to attain realization within seven days.
Before that period had even passed, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He rushed to see Miaodao and said, "Old Monk, today you shall not deceive me.
He presented another verse, saying: "The mountains and rivers of the great earth are a single expanse of snow; The sun shines upon them once, and they leave no trace."
From this point on, do not doubt the Buddhas and Patriarchs; there is no longer north, south, east, or west. Miaoguo then ascended the hall and said:
"I have spread a vast net across the heavens to strike phoenixes and snare dragons, yet I have never encountered so much as a single shrimp or crab.
Today, a tiny gnat has flown right into it. Thirty years from now, atop a solitary peak at the very summit, it will raise its voice and let out a great cry. Now tell me—"
"What are you crying out for? He raised his whisk and said, "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow. The Master then seized the whisk and proclaimed for the assembly:
"If there is even one person in the entire world who awakens to the true source and returns to it, they will know everything from beginning to end."
Miaoshan praised his brilliance and agility. Later, he returned to Deqing to visit his parents, and subsequently accompanied his mother to Wukang, where he built a thatched hut to dwell.
Seeing him mingling with the mundane world, people could not fathom his intent. After five years had passed, he returned to the mountains to see Miaoshan.
Miaoshan said, "Many people say you are dragging through mud and water. The Master replied, "Two eyes facing two eyes," and then requested ordination. Furthermore—
His name was Liaoyi. When the positions of the abbot and the vice-abbot fell vacant, the two masters Ben and Yong also passed away in succession.
The Master then exerted himself to comply with the assembly’s request to succeed them on the seat. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"If you wish to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, to be forever liberated from worldly toil, you must strip away the skin and replace the bones, severing the past to be reborn anew—like embers glowing from cold ashes, or withered wood flourishing once more. How could you possibly act otherwise?"
It is easy to understand. I have been with the Old Monk for many years; every time I was struck by his great staff until it pierced to my very marrow, I never once harbored a thought of leaving him.
It is only today that, upon touching a place of pain, I find myself involuntarily shedding tears.
"How can this be compared to you, who, filled with joy and exultation, bite into a bit of bitter flavor and then immediately shake your head and turn away?
You do not realize that this bitter flavor can eliminate a hundred ailments. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Set aside speech and silence, movement and stillness;

bring forth a single phrase! He further asked: "When the single breath does not return, where will you find a place to settle your body and establish your life? The Master’s preaching was thus responsive.

At the stupa. That evening, he conversed with the monks as usual. At midnight, he said, "I, the old monk, shall depart for Tiantai tomorrow. A monk said, "I wish to follow you there.
The Master replied, "Even if you were to gallop like a horse, you could not catch up with me. The following day at noon, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
He was seventy-two years of age and had forty-nine years of ordination. Initially, when Zhongfeng passed away, [Zhuhong] attended his funeral.
During a period of fasting, the Master smiled and said to the assembly, "Twelve years hence, there shall be another gathering for this old monk.
Twelve years passed, and at that time, his entire body was enshrined within Lion Rock. On the day of his passing, thunder crashed and rain lashed down, turning the bright day into darkness.

At the time of the burial, snowflakes fell in profusion, and the forest trees were draped in white mourning. Those who escorted the funeral numbered several thousand. In the year of Jiaxu of the Zhizhi era... (The text continues with the date: *zhìyuán bǐng*).

He once composed verses on the theme of "Mountain Dwelling" by Yongming, saying: "If I wish my mind to be extinguished, it shall be extinguished at once;
why need I seek a matchmaker further? At the crossroads of a thousand differences, I have closed them all; at the levers of ten thousand distinct functions, I have brought them all to rest."
He cut down trees and bound reeds to build a hut where he lived. Gathering thorny branches, he wove a fence and opened a path beside the stream.
It was because this Lazy Zan lacked spiritual efficacy that the Imperial Edict came for him three times. He also said: "In my ordinary, cold detachment, I know my own faults."
Withdrawing my steps, I leave no trace as I dwell amidst the emerald peaks. Sweeping away the hundred-year dream of honor and disgrace, I turn back to the fundamental mechanism of many kalpas.

There are those who, as soon as they apply some effort and feel their minds become light and at ease or perceive things before them as pure, immediately let go of everything.
They then compose verses and hymns with a quick tongue and fluent speech, imagining themselves to have achieved great realization. Thus they waste a lifetime;

Brothers, if you wish to transcend birth and death, you must practice with true resolve and attain realization through true awakening; only then will it be achieved.
Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhengyuan of Hangzhou Jingshan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Ling of Jingshan.

Kang was twenty-seven years old when he left home to shave his head and receive the full precepts. He traveled to various regions to seek instruction, first visiting Xugu Ling.

Chan Master Shaodai of Baolin in Wuzhou was the son of the Wu family of Wuyuan. His family had resided in Tongjiang for generations, and he took this as his title.

In his youth, he entered Fengshan Temple in his native village to leave the household life; there he shaved his head, received the dyed robes, and was fully ordained. He then went to study under Xugu.
At Mount Jing, he received the seal of the mind and traveled extensively throughout the rivers and lakes. Wherever there were renowned masters, he went to visit them all.
One day, he sighed with profound realization, saying, "From this day forward, I have come to know that the Dharma has no diverse flavors.
He then ceased formal inquiry and read through the Tripitaka three times by hand; he thoroughly mastered the principles of both Buddhist and non-Buddhist studies. Dongyu resided at Jingci Temple.
Please preserve this key to the treasury. In the *wenshen* year of the Zhishun era of Emperor Wen of the Yuan dynasty (1320), he appeared in the world at Wulong in the commandery.

Later, he moved to Baolin in Yunhuang, where his Dharma assemblies were renowned for their extreme prosperity. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he struck the drum to assemble the congregation to express his gratitude.
When the assembly requested a verse, the Master took up his brush, cast it to the ground, and said: "Even if I were to write until Maitreya’s descent into birth, how could I ever..."
Departing from this world, he passed away with effortless ease. His worldly age was seventy-four, and his monastic seniority fifty-eight.
Upon cremation, his *śarīra* were like deep blue pearls, and his teeth and jaw remained unbroken. He authored three collections of recorded sayings (*yùlù*).
Chan Master Shiwu Qinggong of Fuyuan, Huzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Daochang Xin.
He was the son of the Wen family in Changshu, Suzhou, and was born at the beginning of the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty.
In his youth, he relied upon Xingjiao Chongfu Temple to shave his head and receive full ordination. He first visited Master Gaofeng Miao for instruction.

He showed that the myriad dharmas all return to the One. "Where does the One return? he asked, instructing [Miaoxian] to investigate this. Miaoxian served him diligently for three years without achieving any realization.
He then took his leave. Miaoxian said, "There is a blind donkey in Wenzhou; there is Ji'an in Huai. You should go see them. Consequently, he went to Jianyang.

When Chan Master Zan arrived at Anxin’s monastery, Anxin interrogated him with rigorous scrutiny. The Master resolved to investigate deeply out of indignation, and he suddenly attained a thorough realization.
Consequently, he remained to serve under him for several more years before taking his leave. As Anxin saw him off at the gate, he said, "In days to come, we shall share the same coffin.

Not long after, Anxin moved to another monastic center, and the Master again relied upon him, serving as the keeper of the library and the keys. Later, when Yuetang Yin became the abbot of Lingyin Monastery, he invited the Master to reside there as the first seat.
After his second term as abbot ended, he established a hermitage on Mount Xawu by Lake. He personally performed all manual labor, such as gathering firewood and vegetables.

Delighting in poetry, he composed several verses on mountain life that circulated throughout the monastic community. In the fourth month of the *xīn-wèi* year of the Zhìshùn era of the Yuan Wénzōng reign (1331), he went forth to reside at Fúyuán in Dānghú.
Upon entering the monastery for the formal assembly, he ascended the hall; his grip was firm, and not a single sharp edge was revealed.
It is let loose. The ten directions intersect vertically and horizontally; meeting in the depths of water and clouds, one is instead atop a thousand peaks.

yesterday, by the side of Tianhu Hermitage, earth was tilled and smoke was cultivated. Therefore it is said: "The Dharma has no fixed form; it meets with conditions."
"The very essence of the school can thus be transmitted. The wind of true stillness reverently assists the transformation of non-action.
