Tell me: should I speak it now, or should I not? He struck his knee and said: "Whether you understand me or find fault with me, I have no words to offer."
Ascending the hall: Huangmei had Old Lu tread the pestle; Shitou criticized Yaoshan for not doing so.
There may be a fathom-long reed that can withstand winds from all eight directions, but without a three-foot whip, it is difficult to control a thousand-li horse.
In a garden of *eranda* (Ilan), sandalwood does not grow; on the head of a *himalaya* (Huangbo) tree, how could one seek honeyed fruit? Ascending the hall: Movement is like walking.
Clouds: stillness like the spirit of the valley; the salty taste within water; the glue and blue pigment within color. One cannot see the fine rain soaking one’s clothes;
one hears no sound when withered flowers fall to the ground. Entering the hall: that which is heard cannot be heard; that which is seen cannot be seen.
Last night at the fifth watch, the wind blew down the peach blossoms; crimson clouds arise upon the surface of the green moss. A hundred birds do not come, yet spring is in full bloom.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To eat food is to satisfy hunger; to drink water is to quench thirst; to wear clothes is to avoid the cold;
to return home is to arrive at one's destination. To study the Way is to reach that place where the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot open their mouths."
In practicing Zen, one must reach the place where the patriarchs of successive generations have never set foot.
If you do not do so, you will rely on their doorways, lean against their walls, follow others' instructions, and consume others' spittle; none of this makes one a true man. Fuyuan speaks thus:
"Good medicine is bitter to the taste; loyal words are harsh to the ear. Ascending the hall, he said: "Whether saint or ordinary person, upon entering the gate..."
Then you see the nostrils of the Persian; with eyes open, you see the heart and liver of the clam;
with mouth open, you see the two eyebrows of everyone hanging right there before your eyes. Why then do you fail to see him? "Before the clear-eyed person, three feet is darkness.
Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Dharma came to Shaolin and sat facing the wall for nine years. His ramparts were not secure; Shushan sold them."

The single robe is spread out; one sees people for a thousand miles. At the head of the road, paths are manifold and complex; here at Fuyuan, the walls and moats are firm and secure. The path is level and straight.
Everyone travels every day upon this correct road and dwells in a place of stability and security.

Yet, as for that single plot of land in the midst—why is it that you do not tread upon it? Ascending the hall, he said: "To establish knowledge within one's perceptions is the very root of ignorance."
To know seeing as non-seeing—this is *nirvāṇa*. The spring mountains are layered with chaotic greens; the spring waters ripple with empty blues.
Vast and silent between heaven and earth, standing alone, what limit can one’s gaze reach? [He] picks up his staff and says, "I let Śākyamuni Buddha pass.
[He] plants the staff and says, "I pierce Xuedou’s nostrils through. After a long silence, he says, "A sword leaves its precious scabbard because of injustice; medicine [is used] because of..."

"Rescuing the Sick" and "Bringing Out the Golden Pitcher," as well as the "Cottage Taboo. The Master held up the incense and said: "In this place where we meet without fortune, West Peak and Jianyang—how many matters of injustice are there?
They are all contained within this single burner of incense. The Small Retreat on the Eve of the Year-End. At Beichan’s New Year’s Celebration:
"The rites and music of the three dynasties are fully present; Old Wang burns paper money, and in one way, the cups and plates are left in disarray. — By Master Gong.
The Master sat firmly, adhering to pure poverty. Furthermore, encountering a year of famine, it was difficult to compete with others in wealth.
From the beginning of the year until its end, he lived as one household with everyone else, adjusting to abundance or scarcity as appropriate; he never once went away with a forced smile.

Rather than borrowing land to plant flowers and falsely posing as a "fine hero," he simply stayed within his own house, measuring the water and operating the pestle himself, so as to avoid seeking [from others].
People merely manage to get by with two meals a day; this is sufficient to fulfill the responsibilities of the abbot. An ancient said:
"Sometimes I gather wild vegetables and boil them with their roots; I chop fresh green firewood and burn it with its leaves.

It is not that the father’s poverty brings suffering to the son, but rather to prevent the child from becoming spoiled by family wealth. Ascending the hall: On the first day of the twelfth month, the water gives birth to the bones; they are empty and luminous.
Self-illumination requires no exertion of mind or strength. Amidst white egrets, cold geese, and reeds, there is nowhere to seek their traces.
When the sun grows warm and the ice melts, the waters broaden; as before they fly back, piercing through the azure luster of the lake.
Upon ascending the hall at Pingshan, [the Master said]: "‘This very mind is Buddha’—this is not it. ‘Neither mind nor Buddha’—this is also not it. Neither mind..."
"This Buddha is neither a thing nor not a thing. To say 'it is so' is not right; to say 'it is not so' is not right.
To say 'it is both so and not so' is altogether not right. Looking closely, he leaves you with no place to apply the mind—yet this is precisely where one should apply the mind.
Striking the meditation staff, he said: "The lotus pierces the level ground to become a leaf; the bamboo shoots pass over the neighbor's house to become a grove."

He resided there for seven years. Later, citing old age as his reason, he retired and returned to Tianhu. Emperor Shun bestowed upon him incense and silk, and the Empress granted him a golden-embroidered Dharma robe.
Among those who heard of the reputation of Tianhu, there were none whose hearts were not refreshed and spirits not filled with longing;

they considered him to have truly attained the legacy of the ancient masters of yore. On the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the *renchen* year of the Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. In the middle...
He gathered the assembly at night for a final farewell. When the assembly requested instructions on his final affairs, the Master sought out a brush and wrote a verse, saying:
"The green mountains do not harbor stinking corpses; Once dead, what need is there to dig into the earth to bury them? Look at me: I have no fire of samādhi;

A single pile of firewood, cutting off the past and ending the future. Having finished writing, he threw down the brush and passed away. His body was cremated, and five-colored śarīra relics were found. He was enshrined in a stupa at Tianhu.

The original [inscription] was paired with the stupa of Master An to demonstrate the intention of not forgetting their shared niche. He lived to the age of eighty-one and had been in the monastic order for fifty-four years.

The State Preceptor of Goryeo, Taego Yu, had formerly attended the Master and received his essential instructions. When the King heard of him, he held him in deep admiration and respect, and this was reported to the imperial court.

An edict was issued posthumously bestowing upon him the title of Zen Master Buddhist Compassion Wisdom Illumination (Bucihyeojō Seonsa). Furthermore, a formal letter was requested to be sent to Jiangzhe, requesting that he be invited to Jingci Monastery.
Ping entered Tianhu Mountain Forest to divide the master’s *śarīra* relics and returned to his country to offer them in worship.
Chan Master Pingzi Chulin of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was the son of Wang Shi, a member of the Renhe clan of that prefecture.
At birth, there were extraordinary signs. When he was twelve years old, his parents sent him to Guangyan Temple in the district to enter the monastic life. At seventeen, he received full ordination.

He took leave of his mother to travel in all directions. His mother prepared his traveling gear and sent him on his way; yet after several days, he returned again. His mother spoke to him through a wall, admonishing him:
"In general, when studying the Way, one must maintain a mind of non-retrogression. Why do you hesitate so much?
The Master then severely chastised himself and set out upstream along the Tuo River to visit Ji’ān Xìn at Jīnhuá. Upon seeing him, Xìn recognized his potential and invited him to stay.
As an attendant, one night Xìn rolled paper soaked in oil to serve as a candle. He held it up and showed it to the Master, saying, "When Longtan blew it out, what did you do?

Just as the Master was about to answer, Xìn suddenly covered his mouth with his hand; from this, he attained awakening. When Xìn moved to Daochang, he appointed [the Master] to keep the treasury keys.
Before long, he was charged with holding the whisk and ascending the seat to preach, his eloquence flowing like water from a jar, and the assembly all bowed in respect.
I humbly submit. Upon the passing of Master Xin, he went to rely upon Master Xugu at Mount Yang. One day, a monk holding a tea ladle requested a verse;
when Ling saw it, he was struck with wonder and sighed, "The Gate of the Patriarchs has a true successor. He appointed him to the position of Second Seat.

In the *guichou* year of the Yuan Renzong Huangqing era (1313), he took up residence at Daci Dinghui Temple. As for the incense offered in homage, he was the dharma heir of Jiwang. He subsequently resided at [the aforementioned temple].
He resided at Hufuyan. He moved again to Zhongzhu. In the *kuiwei* year of the Zhizheng era of Emperor Shundi (1363), the Director of the Xuanzheng Yuan requested that he reside at Jingci Temple.
He remained there for eighteen years, during which the halls, pavilions, bells, and drums were all renovated.
The Chancellor Dashier Temür requested that he move to Lingyin Temple; while he was planning to restore its ruins, Zhang and Wu entered Hangzhou from Suzhou, and the area was ravaged by war.
They arrived in succession, and the timber for the hall was completely consumed by fire. The Master said to the assembly, "My karmic conditions have come to an end.

He then returned to Jingci Monastery, changed his robes, bathed, gathered the assembly, and after reciting a verse, passed away on the first day of the fifth month of the Xin-chou year. He was eighty-three years of age.
His monastic seniority was sixty-six years. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Puhui Xingwu.
His stupa is located to the right of Jingju Hermitage. Chan Master Zhigang of Zhengjue Shimen in Luoshan, Wuzhou, was a native of the mountain foot.

Having received the Dharma from Jiwang Xin, he returned home after his travels. There, local elders recounted past events, and they constructed a monastery on that very site, inscribing the characters upon its lintel.
He said: "Perfect Enlightenment. On the day of the New Year’s Eve, he ascended the hall to express his gratitude to the Head Seat Dao De and Attendant Shun for their nursing of the sick.

The year’s affairs have ended and the cycle of the year is complete. Among all things, nothing is more honored than the Way; among all things, nothing is more precious than virtue. Enlightenment is the very cause of *prajñā*.
"Conformity is itself Bodhi-Buddha. You should know that planting beans does not produce hemp; cause and effect are naturally clear and distinct.
Nevertheless, tell me: how can this be seen? Among the eight fields of merit, nursing the sick is foremost. *Small Assembly Sermon*.
Trampling over the sea of birth and death, not a single drop remains; overturning the city of nirvāṇa, not a speck of dust stands.

This is achieved without expending further effort—like a mighty warrior brandishing his halberd, its sharp edge never meeting resistance; like a master archer, there is not even a hair’s breadth of error.

Thus, one naturally encounters the source everywhere; at every turn, one accords with the Way. Without relying on cultivation or realization, it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. To the end.
The great earth is the site of supreme and wondrous enlightenment; pervading the Dharma-realm is the true ground of suchness.

To awaken to this, every person has their share; to realize it, each individual lacks nothing. When not a single thought arises, one enters samādhi; when not a single speck of dust moves, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
Benefiting oneself and others, all shall ascend to the other shore. Relinquishing the whole body, one attains total freedom. Upon reaching this—
In this place, what need is there to speak of nirvana or birth-and-death, of true thusness or Buddha-nature? There is not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind;

one simply reaches the point where the ten directions are cut off at once. Today, as I proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā, it is specifically for the sake of commemorating the late Master Zu’ān of Shangfeng.
Without shifting his feet, he has transcended to the Land of Bliss; without a single thought being stirred, he has realized non-arising. [The Master] strikes the whisk and says: "See!"
Pervasive from the beginning, there is no concealment; the myriad cassia blossoms scatter their celestial fragrance. In his verse of parting for the assembly at the time of death, he said:
"Seventy-six years have passed; all is clearly vast and open. I have pressed through the void until Mount Sumeru stands overturned."
Chan Master Tianzhen Weize of Haimen, Hangzhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Kuanglu Yuan.
His courtesy name was Lao Ren Bingbo (The Elder of Ice and Gall). He was the son of the Fei family of Wuxing.
His mother dreamed that a strange monk came to her door for alms; upon waking, she became pregnant. When he was born, a wondrous fragrance permeated the air. From his childhood...
In his [seventeenth] year, he took refuge at Youfu Gaolin Monastery in Hangzhou and received ordination as a monk. At the age of sixteen, he received the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

At twenty-three, he traveled to various regions to pay respects to eighteen venerable elders, including Chushi, Qianyan, Wujian, and Wumen; however, the four conditions for spiritual resonance were not met.
Later, he went to Mount Lu and encountered Wuji Yuan, from whom he drew close and studied intensely, remaining silent all day long without speaking.
One day, while visiting Yuan (Xuedou Chongxian) as he was using the toilet, the Master hurried forward and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

Yuan seized him and said, "Speak! Speak! At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. Thereafter, he traveled through the rivers and lakes, eventually settling at Lingyin on Mount Ping, where he was appointed to the position of Librarian.
Later, because his preceptor had grown old and infirm, he returned to attend upon him. [He traveled] in all directions.

Students arrived in great numbers and earnestly requested that he open the Dharma hall. On the day of the opening of the hall, a monk asked, "What is the means by which the Buddhas and Patriarchs benefit sentient beings?
The Master said, "A dog licking a hot oil pan. The monk asked, "Today you have opened the hall, Master; do you have any means to benefit others?
The Master said, "A fierce tiger sits in the middle of the road. The monk asked, "Is there no skillful means? The Master let out a thunderous shout.
A monk asked, “What is the Buddha of the Sun’s Face? The Master said, “Clouds arise this very day.
The monk asked, “What is the Buddha of the Moon’s Face? The Master said, “Look again tonight. Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case of Mingguo, who said:
“Before the fifteenth day, one draws water and sets fire; after the fifteenth day, magpies screech and crows caw. On the fifteenth day itself, the wind is calm and the waves are still.”
"Peace! The country is prosperous and the people are at ease. If you have a single word that reaches [the mark], I will silence your mouth.

If you do not have a single word that reaches it, you will blind your own eyes. For three coins, one marries a dark-skinned old wife; she does not comb her hair nor wash her face—knowing whether she is a commoner or a sage.
The Master said, "Old man Ying’an is much like one who relies on wealth to bully the poor; he has not failed to show off his cleverness. Hǎi... [text fragment]
The gate is not so. Before the fifteenth day, light does not depart from darkness; after the fifteenth day, darkness does not depart from light.
On the fifteenth day itself, light and darkness are suddenly forgotten, transcending all conditions of past and present.
Where, then, do you all seek to investigate? Striking the whisk, he said: "In leisure, one finds no accord with the joy of forest and springs; sitting long, one hears only the wind."

The Sound of Rain: An Address on the Eighth Day of the Twelfth Month. Before the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda, when not even a single dharma or a single word was yet understood, one had already transcended the Buddhas and surpassed the patriarchs.
Why, then, did the Yellow-Faced Old Man only attain enlightenment on the night of the eighth day of the twelfth month?
This fellow who eats wine dregs confuses the world; when will he ever come to an end? Today, Haimen shall expose him for what he is.
"It is understood. You people, have you attained the Way even now? He struck his staff and said, "I thought the beard was red, but here is another red-bearded barbarian.
Ascending the hall, he looked around at those present and said, "Look at this; what a state of frantic urgency!"
"Even so, at this point, one must not let it pass. [He lets out a shout. He descends from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "To speak of fire is to be burned by fire; to speak of water is to be drowned by water; to understand Chan is to be bound by Chan.

Pointing to the left with his hand, he said: "Yet this monk has seen right through me. On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, he ascended the hall: "By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars. One boards the boat."
Doubt is like the shifting shore; by squeezing one's eyes, flowers appear before them. Old Gautama reached it in the past but did not point it out;
today you, Venerable One, point it out but do not reach it. Do you all wish to see the morning star? (He brandishes the whisk to form a circle and lets out a shout. Ascending the hall, he said:
"If I were to raise this matter from the highest perspective, it would be like shooting an arrow downward. Even if a Buddha or an Ancestor came..."
"Coming together in the midst [of this assembly], where would you all flee? If you possess such an eye, you are fit to be teachers of gods and men;
if not, you will not even be able to save yourselves. Should anyone ask me about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, I would simply say to them:
'Today I have lost by one turn of phrase. Is there anyone who can avoid this arrow? He struck the meditation desk.
Holding his staff, he ascended the hall. "I sit and you stand; who gains and who loses? Even so, even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to arrive, it would still be difficult to discern.
He drew a circle with his whisk and said, "Tsk! No monk in all the world can leap out of this! He then ascended the hall.
Matters of ascending; matters of descending. Cut off both ends and cease clinging. Suddenly let loose the turtle-nosed snake to bite you to death;

only then will you know it is difficult to evade. *Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ!* Today Haimen, unable to restrain his impatience, has overstepped the bounds to deliver this message for all of you. Do you all understand? (He strikes once with the whisk.)
Dian said: "Casually casting down the living elixir; a vast, clear wind stirs heaven and earth. Ascending the hall, he said:

"Chrysanthemums bloom by the eastern fence, their fragrance drifting; the sea and sky are vast and wide, the moonlight of autumn. Holding it forth in the light of day, I brandish the 'Blow-off-the-Hair' sword."
Annihilating all that is horizontal and vertical, beyond the six states of non-restraint—ascending the hall. The wind at the peak is sharp and urgent; the hairs on one's skin stand on end.
If you cannot endure this, you have no choice but to deliberate in a warm place. But tell me, what is it you are deliberating about?
They deliberate and say: "The Bodhisattva Guanyin uses money to buy a sesame cake; yet when she lets go of her hand, it turns out to be a steamed bun.
Everyone eats their fill, and having slept comfortably and warmly, they only feel their snoring breath as they wake. Suddenly, amidst cold ashes, there is a crackling fire."
Having pressed right up against the face, do not take offense at this dream-telling of Hai-men. *A shout.* Ascending the hall:
The cricket chirps in the courtyard at dawn; the hibiscus reflects in the autumn waters. Gazing afar, the sea and sky are clear; gulls and egrets fall like rain.
When sleepy, one sleeps; when hot, one seeks the cool; when cold, one turns toward the fire. Each moment is naturally true; each moment is luminously wondrous.
Why must you take steps forward to discuss Zen and discuss the Way? You mistake fish eyes for pearls and take orange peel for fire. Have you not heard it said:
The great capacity must penetrate thoroughly; the great function must be direct. Not recognizing the Sage Confucius of the Eastern House, one instead seeks ritual and music in a foreign land.

(He struck his staff. On the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the Jiaxu year of the Yuantong era of Emperor Yuan of the Yuan dynasty, he wrote a letter bidding farewell to his dharma companions, spoke a verse, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.
Upon cremation, white milk flowed like a stream, and *śarīra* relics coalesced and solidified.
His remains formed five-colored relics, which were interred to the west of his residence. He was posthumously titled Zhenguang (True Enlightenment), and his stupa was named Jiguang (Tranquil Light).
His age at death was seventy, and his years of ordination were fifty.
Chan Master Yuanzhan of Songyan in Mingzhou had long associated with eminent masters (nāgas and elephants). Later, he studied under Fangshan Bao and attained the essential meaning [of the Dharma].
Once, while traveling through Songyan in Mingzhou, he was so captivated by its purity and excellence that he could not bear to leave; he subsequently sat cross-legged upon a rock.
Suddenly, two tigers appeared, crouching at his side as if to guard him. The Master commanded them to lie down, and he rested his head upon their backs and fell into a deep sleep.

The local mountain folk marveled at this; they established a monastery at that very spot for him to dwell in. The Master did not involve himself in worldly affairs, remaining as tranquil as water beyond the giving of the Dharma.
When he was about to pass away, he took leave of the assembly and entered his coffin, where he spoke this verse: "Having bathed and put on my robes, I am born."
The funeral rites were completed. He sat in the lotus position and entered his stupa. "The iron tree blooms; the clay ox bellows. For a month, a long radiance shone throughout heaven and earth.
He further addressed the assembly, saying, "Fifteen years hence, this temple shall be consumed by fire. If you open my stupa, the fire may be extinguished."

When the appointed time arrived, it was indeed as expected. The assembly hurriedly opened the shrine, and the Master’s countenance and spirit were as if he were still alive; his nails and hair had both grown long.
Chan Master Ling Yiyuan of Fengshan in Hangzhou was a native of Ninghai.

He left the secular world under Yunfeng at Mount Jing and studied under Foshan Bao at Ruiyan, where he served as the Hall Superintendent. One day, during a private interview, he requested instruction on Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman.
The Master said, "Venerable Ba, try and offer a word. Ba said, "All the people in the great earth are at a loss as to what to do with this old woman.

Ba continued, "I, however, am not like that; all the people in the great earth are at a loss as to what to do with Zhaozhou. At these words, the Master was like one who has broken out in a sweat after an illness.
Later, while presiding over Fengshan, he ascended the hall and cited the occasion when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and Mañjuśrī [held his fly-whisk].
The Case of the Proclamation of the Gavel. The Master said: “The World-Honored One has already spoken erroneously; Mañjuśrī has already transmitted erroneously;
today at Xinfengshan, I have already raised it erroneously. Do you understand? When a written character is transcribed three times, ‘wu’ becomes ‘a’ and ‘yan’ becomes ‘ma.
One day, seeing a monk tossing a "Chart for Selecting Buddhas," he showed him a verse, saying: “As for the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and sentient beings, do not seek them within the chart.”
A forceful contest. Cast the Heart-Seal forth lightly before you; sit with dignified composure in the field of tranquil light. He spoke again: "The ancients had no leisure even to trim their nails.
You later generations, how can you bear to let your time pass in vain? For now, cast aside your diagrams and choose the Buddha."
When the moment of the ultimate convergence arrived, he cast forth a single seal and, filled with joy, exclaimed, "I have attained Buddhahood!
Little did he know that at all times and in all places, these are precisely the sites where you attain Buddhahood; yet you remain unaware of this.
The acupuncturist Ding Sheng had long relied upon Master Baoshan, hoping to clarify his fundamental nature. One day, while sharpening a glass needle, he attained a realization.
He composed a verse and presented it to Baoshan, saying: "Lift it up! Lift it up! Let it go! Let it go! This single point of radiance illuminates heaven and earth.
Baoshan was pleased by the purity and simplicity of his practice and granted him approval.
A verse by Chan Master Pingshi Di of Tiantong in Mingzhou, successor to Chan Master Rujing of Tiantong, sent to Librarian Yun to bid him farewell upon his visit to Yuansou at Jingshan:
"The old fellow on the mountain head is eighty-one; Such is this great Dharma city of the Southeast. His twin hair-tufts have grown white with the passing years."

A single word can cause the ancient style to become pure. In dealing with others, one need not employ the "tiger-slaying" technique; in raising a child, how could one forget the sentiment of licking its calf?
Sitting before the Hall of the Bright Moon in the deep night, a lingering radiance reaches even to Chang-geng.

National Teacher Mengchuang Zhiyao of Nanzen-ji in Japan was a dharma successor of Chan Master Gaofeng Rujing. His secular surname was Minamoto; he was originally a native of Kii Province and a ninth-generation descendant of Emperor Uda.
He entered the monastic order at the age of nine and received full ordination at eighteen. He frequently dreamed of traveling to China.

At the two monasteries of Guoshu Mountain and Shitou, an old monk presented him with an image of Bodhidharma; consequently, he was named Shushi (Sparse-Stone). He then resolved to travel to study under various masters.
First, he visited Yishan Ning and fully expressed his sincerity in seeking the Dharma.

Ning said, "In my school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. The Master asked, "Is there not some expedient means? Ning replied, "From the very beginning, it is vast and empty."

However, this was a great skillful means. The Master remained in a state of doubt and frustration, never ceasing his efforts. He visited Gao Feng Ri again. Ri asked, "What instructions did Yishan give you?
The Master recounted his previous words. Ri shouted with a stern voice, "Why do you not say:

'The Master has leaked no small amount'? At these words, the Master had an awakening; he redoubled his self-exertion. One night, after sitting for a long time, he suddenly leaned against the wall and collapsed.

He attained sudden and great enlightenment and composed a verse containing the line: "Casually striking through the very bones of empty space. He presented it to Nyeon-ji, who granted his seal of approval (*inka*).
Thereupon, he brought forth the profound source of the Unstudied (Mugak) lineage to propagate it. Later, in his own country, he widely propagated the teachings and doctrines of Buddhism.
He was bestowed the title of National Preceptor Pujŏng. The Master’s will lay in the mists and clouds; leaving the world was not what he desired, yet wherever he was invited, he arrived.

He declined the offer with great earnestness. The ruler of that country raised an army and proceeded to the Southern Chan [monastery]. Upon entering for an audience, he invited the Master to sit and requested his departure.

The King said, "I have no other intention; I merely wish to inquire about the Way day and night. He further insisted that the Master enter the Heavenly Dragon [Monastery], where he bestowed upon him a title and a handwritten edict.
Later, he manifested his passing within the Inner Court of Tuṣita Heaven. His age was seventy-nine and his years of ordination sixty. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the court.
As for the nails and hair he had clipped during his lifetime and buried at Yunju, śarīras grew in clusters from within the hair.
Chan Master Kongshi Shuzhong Wuyun of Ruiyan in Taizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jianyan Dao. He was the son of the Chen family from Linhai in his native prefecture.
He received the tonsure under Jizhao at Mount Jing Mountain. After traveling to visit various masters, he first called upon Lingshi at Jingci Monastery, and later studied under Yiyuan Ling.

After more than a year, he returned for an audience with his master. Baizhao ordered him to reside in the Zhemu (Choosing the Tree) Hall. He then traveled again to Siming, where he visited Taibai and Dizang at Zhidi.
One day, accompanied by Mukan Cong and Dazong Xing, he went to Mount Zituo in Taizhou to pay his respects to Zhuyuan Dao.

As soon as he intended to open his mouth to ask about the "Mu" (No-thing) koan, he was struck with a shout by Dao. The Master attained a sudden, great enlightenment; it was as if his entire being had been penetrated.
Hànxià then presented this verse: "The dog has no Buddha-nature; Spring colors fill the imperial capital. Inside Zhaozhou’s East Courtyard, A gourd hangs upon the wall.
Dàoxiào said, "Even if you understand it thus, how can you attain it? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Moved by this, he spoke privately to his fellow practitioners, saying: "This matter is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
It certainly does not reside in words or written characters. Had we not encountered this old monk, we would have spent our entire lives buried in intellectual understanding.
Should we one day cover our heads with a thatched roof [attain enlightenment], we must not forget our origins. Later, Guding...
The patron Mingzhu invited the Master to return to Montang. There, he daily immersed himself in the profound mysteries and served as a model for his students.

Not long after, he returned to Siming to avoid the chaos of war and took no pleasure in leaving. He presided over two mountain monasteries, yet in each case he retired after barely three years had passed.
He first resided at Lingyan on Mount Xiang, and subsequently took charge of Ruiyan on Mount Huangyan. At that time, Mengtang E was residing there.
Ruilong: Master Xi was the successor of Jizhao. The Master said, "My original vow lies elsewhere; it cannot be diverted.

On the day he ascended the hall, he held up the incense and said, "When the ancients appeared in the world and offered incense, they did so to repay the milk of the Dharma. When people of today appear in the world and offer incense..."
This is to repay the kindness of the world. The Venerable Yuan (Mingyun) generally disagreed with this.
In years past, while traveling on pilgrimage, I went to Mount Zituo to visit an old monk in coarse cloth robes (*bunuo*). He had no dharma to bestow, and I had no dharma to receive.
It was precisely within this state of neither bestowing nor receiving that I produced [this offering] to present to the late Abbot Zhu Yuan Dao of Jianyan Chan Temple in Kunshan. Not...
To repay his virtue and requite his kindness, he simply wishes for everyone to understand this. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Ruiyan? The Master said, "The wind cannot enter.
The monk asked, "What is the person within the realm? The Master said, "Water cannot wet him. The monk asked, "I have already received your instruction on both the person and the realm;
as for the ultimate vehicle of the ancestral school, what is it like? The Master said, "The true does not conceal the false. The monk asked, [how about]...?
"The nature of all dharmas is quiescent extinction. [The student asked: "If so, why does the shore appear to move when a boat travels, or why does the moon seem to move when the clouds race?
The Master said, "A fine message, indeed; I only fear you will misunderstand it. [The student said: "That would be a double case. The Master said, "The waters of the sea do not freeze into ice.
[The student] asked, "What is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth? The Master said, "A live sparrow in the mouth of a fierce tiger. [The student asked: "What is..."
[The student asked about] the phrase "cutting off the myriad streams. The Master said, "The eight-sided staff in the hand of Vajrapāṇi.
[The student asked,] "What is the phrase 'following the waves and riding the currents'? The Master said, "Li Bai grasping the moon; Zhang Qian riding the raft.

[The student asked,] "Regarding the room of Vimalakīrti, it does not take the sun or moon as its illumination. What serves as the illumination in the Master’s room? The Master said, "When things see their master, the eye stands forth."

Zhushu asked, "When Mahākāśyapa closed his room at Rājagṛha and Vimalakīrti remained silent at Vaiśālī, how far apart were these two instances? The Master said, "They are buried together in a single pit.
Zhushu asked, "When Deshan entered the gate and immediately struck with his staff, and Linji entered the gate and immediately shouted—after all, what matter did they clarify?"

The Master said: "In the north of the pass, a thousand tents; in the south of the river, ten-thousand-hu ships. Small Assembly: Lingyan is steep and precipitous; those who arrive find it difficult to reach.
Those who have already arrived enjoy peace and security; those who have not yet arrived are solitary and exposed. As for those who are solitary and exposed—
Just as you are about to step forward to enjoy it, you must instead retreat and turn within yourself. Therefore it is said: "Matters do not have a single direction.
Sometimes one takes the head and makes it the tail; sometimes one takes the tail and makes it the head. In gathering and releasing, advancing and retreating, how could there be fixed tracks?
When Mahākāśyapa shut his room and Vimalakīrti remained silent, though these were called the full manifestation of the true command, they still had not reached the ultimate.
To reach the ultimate: This mountain monk, at the very beginning of entering this gate tonight and at the first gathering of our heads together, makes a threefold covenant with you all.
First, you must not give rise to the view of Buddha. Second, you must not give rise to the view of Dharma.
Third, you must not say that you do not give rise to the views of Buddha or Dharma. If you act in accordance with this, I guarantee that your eyebrows will become entangled. Suddenly—
He held up his staff and said, "A man of clear eyes has no fixed nest or trap. From the highest heights, one observes that there is nothing lacking;

from the lowest depths, one levels it and finds it more than sufficient. He struck the ground with the staff and said, "The iron ox does not eat the grass by the fence; he goes straight to sleep atop the summit of Mount Sumeru.
On the occasion of thanking the special messenger, he ascended the hall and said, "Master Bodhidharma traveled a hundred thousand miles from the West, wishing to become..."
He dispatched a letter to deliver his message to Han; yet when he stood face-to-face before King Liang, all his efforts could only yield the words, "I do not know.
He held up his staff and said: "There is guest and there is host; there is ritual and there is music. Hand and face are clearly distinguished as a white jade orb;
the golden bell is shaken at the crown of the head. Ascending the hall, he said: "The bright moon shines upon the high crags; the hanging waters resound on the front ridges. The ears and eyes..."
"How pure! In profound stillness, one understands the nature of mind. "Alas, Avalokiteśvara! Carrying snow, he comes to fill the well!
[The Master] ascended the hall. "The wind does not come, so the tree does not move; the mind does not arise, so objects do not reach it.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, "A dry piece of dung. A monk asked Yangqi, "What is the Buddha? Yangqi said, "A three-legged donkey."
"Playing with his hooves, he walks with grace. Great Assembly, I told you this was a dragon, yet you would not believe me. Indeed, he has won the silken prize and returned.

Upon entering the hall, the Zen practitioners said, "There is nothing we do not know; there is nothing we do not understand. Suddenly, if someone were to ask, "What is the matter of traveling on foot?
their mouths would hang like flat poles. Wherein lies the sickness? The sickness lies in having too much knowledge and too much learning.
"Understood. To study the Way in such a manner is not as good as being a farmer in a village of three households. Suppose someone were to ask, 'How are the crops this year?
One would explain every detail, pouring it out like water from a jar. This is because one has no intellectual understanding and no discrimination.
The autumn air is turning cold; each of you should return to your hall. Be careful. [He] ascended the hall and said: "Leaving behind kin and severing attachments, shaving the head..."
Dyeing your hair and wearing the robes, you have entered through this gate; for what purpose have you come? If you possess a sense of shame and a recognition of propriety, you are a true renunciant.
First, you leave the household of worldly dust and affectionate love; second, you leave the house on fire of the triple world; third, you leave the household of coarse delusions and afflictions;

fourth, you leave the household of subtle delusions and ignorance. Only when you have emerged from these four households can you truly be called a member of the monastic community. Now tell me: [what is it?]
"What is it like to be a patch-robed monk? To encounter an enemy and meet with foul-mouthed scoundrels. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"The mind is like a skilled performer; the intellect is like the conductor. The five consciousnesses are its companions, and delusive thoughts watch the performance.
Does the assembly yet recognize the Mind? If you recognize the Mind, you will recognize the Intellect. If you recognize the Intellect, you will recognize all phenomena."
Consciousness. To recognize consciousness is to recognize all cognitions; to recognize all cognitions is to recognize delusive thoughts. When delusive thoughts cease, all cognitions cease.

When all cognitions cease, the manas ceases. When the manas ceases, the citta ceases. When the citta ceases, everything ceases. Therefore it is said: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. [He lets out a shout and says: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth; sun, moon, and stars..."
On the day of Chén, [the Master] ascended the hall and said: "What fault is there? The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all atoms.
He held up his staff and said: "Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived! His three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores [are here]."
Each one emits great rays of light that penetrate through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Within them, whether they be sages or ordinary beings, sentient or insentient, all who are touched by this light will, without exception, realize Great Nirvana, attain Great Peace and Bliss, and achieve Great Enjoyment.
Leaning on his staff, he said: "If you do not investigate the root source at this very moment, you must wait until the future to question Maitreya."

Addressing the assembly: In this deep spring at the mountain temple, the grasses and trees are lush. Several times I have intentionally opened the wattle gate. The traveler remains ever beyond the green mountains;
the cuckoo calls out repeatedly, yet none returns. Ascending the hall:

Upon this ball of red flesh there is something—bright and clear, vivid and spiritual, hazy and elusive. It adapts and transforms according to circumstances, entirely without restraint. If you wish to know its origin...

[The Master] said: "It is clearly not apart from the lifting and setting down of one's feet. Nowadays, when one hears such talk in the monastic communities, people immediately dismiss it as 'old woman’s Zen.
Yet they do not realize that clouds emerge from mountain peaks without intention, and water flows after filling its pools;
it stops upon encountering high mountains and only comes to rest upon reaching the great ocean. [He] struck the meditation seat and descended. [He] ascended the hall. All...
The Buddha’s appearance in the world is the second head; the Patriarch’s coming from the West is the third.

Even if you were to establish a separate livelihood beyond the realm of Vipaśyin, or manifest the full power of killing and giving life at the tips of the hundred grasses, that old crow in the sack still does not know the single path for emerging.
But tell me, what is this path for emerging? (He raises his staff.)

It is said: "Upon the summit of Mount Zhuli, dewdrops fall upon ten-thousand-year-old pines. When offering incense on the anniversary of the founder's passing, before seeing Yantou, one’s mouth was like a foundation stone;
having seen Yantou, one’s eyes became like wooden buckets. This fundamental principle supports the earth and props up the heavens.
Why trouble yourself with questions, Master? Calling and summoning me back and forth, you still lack true alertness. Inserting incense, he said: "When meeting, one does not dismount;
each must hasten toward their own future. Ascending the hall for the memorial service, he said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it manifests through conditions.
Today is the anniversary of the Great Parinirvāṇa of the founding patriarch, Master Kōjō. This mountain monk will now..."
He spoke of making the unspeakably many worlds of the Ganges River into a single banquet;
taking ten billion Mount Sumerus as a single bowl of rice, and ten billion fragrant seas as a single bowl of soup, merely setting forth this offering. At such a time as this—
Now tell me: where shall this banquet be spread? If it is spread upon the world, the world itself has already become the banquet.
If it is spread within space, how can space be spread? Do not be vague or superficial; simply let it rest as it is.
Is there anyone among the assembly who can step forward and manage it? If so—
"No. I, this mountain monk, shall personally take it out myself. He raised his whisk and said:

"The worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the ten billion Mount Sumerus, and the ten billion fragrant seas—all these clusters of flowers and clusters of brocade are entirely upon the tip of this whisk.
Neither broad nor narrow, neither lacking nor superfluous. Tell me, assembly: will the Patriarch Kongzhao come to receive this offering?"
Nurturing is non-existent. Setting aside for a moment whether one receives it or not, tell me:
where does he dwell and establish his life right now? Striking the whisk, he said: "Before every door, the sun and moon blaze; in the Great Peace, there is no need for the majesty of a general.

Small Retreat *Chán* (Summer Retreat) General Introduction: At the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanjue*), everyone is fully endowed. In heaven, they share in heaven; on earth, they share in earth.
The Ground. From this point on, people overreached in their inquiries and were unable to grasp it.

Thus, Śākyamuni, the Tamer of Men, toiled to open the gate of skillful means, establishing periods and limits, like urging a living snake to transform into a dragon; he required you to personally realize and personally awaken to it.
Master Pang said: "The ten directions gather together as one; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas."
"The mind has passed the imperial examination and returned home. Good assembly! An arrow does not shoot in vain; when it is released, it must hit the mark. A word does not issue in vain;
when it is uttered, it must be entirely true. That the eye of a needle swallowed a fish from which a great elephant of Jiazhou was devoured—let us not speak of that for now.

But tell me: did the Great Master Ke truly obtain the marrow after his three prostrations? Or was it merely a matter of hearsay? (He strikes the meditation seat. "Another spring has passed; the platform..."

In the pavilion, the green shade is thick; entering the hall, they meet face to face yet do not bring it forth. As soon as the intention arises, one knows it exists. They have lost both eyes, yet they have kept a mouth.
On the summit of a solitary peak, they revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs; the aperture is pierced at the crown of the head.
At the crossroads of the city street, they act like madmen and lunatics; the talisman hangs from their elbows. Changsha’s tiger cub and wild dog—pick up this coarse thing!
Spicy millet. It is good for splitting the spine and pulling out the ribs. Please, attendant, announce the ascent to the hall. Zhaozhou and Wenyuan were competing in inferiority, not in victory.
These old fellows have no shame; they sit together and play the game. This causes those with clear eyes to have no way to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox.
Since the heterodox and the orthodox cannot be distinguished, it leads further on to the development of faults. Shuigan was incapable of a hundred things, yet he made use of them.
A scale without stars weighs up the great void; not a single grain or fraction is lacking or remaining.
Taking this as an auspicious omen, taking this as a pit or a trap, it cuts off the throats of the monks and continues the wisdom-life of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. [Ascending the hall.]
Those who sit within a deep well do not know the vastness of the great void; only those who forget their biased views can clearly perceive the perfect integration of ultimate principle.
To speak in such a manner is like taking the entire earth as a target for archery: wherever the bow is drawn, there is no point that is not hit.

Suddenly, someone from among the assembly might come forward and say, "To proclaim such a thing is something rarely heard in all antiquity. The mountain monk [replies]: [The target is the whole world.]

He called for his attendant and prepared a bowl of tea to offer him. Furthermore, when someone came forward and said, "To proclaim such a thing as this is not yet to bring forth the full realization," he again called for his attendant and prepared a bowl of tea to offer him. Now tell me: does he have a way of benefiting others?
"Snow may press it down, but it cannot crush the pine at the bottom of the ravine; The wind may blow, but it cannot move the moon in the heavens. Thus did the Master once say.
From within the hall, he uttered a turning word: "Sitting securely in the family shrine, why does the master of the house fail to recognize himself?
He overturns the great ocean and shatters Mount Sumeru; yet upon level ground, why can he not lift his foot? His eye-sight pierces through the four worlds."

His own eyebrows had fallen away entirely; why was it that they were not seen? His preceding and succeeding utterances were for the most part incongruent with conventional logic, and his spiritual pivot was so steep and towering that students could not even attempt to deliberate upon it.
The Master retired from his duties and entered Songyan (Pine Rock).

This rock was a place of profound seclusion by the Autumn River, situated atop ten thousand mountains where human tracks rarely reached. The Master sent away all his disciples and attendants, remaining alone in stark solitude. The assembly...

He wept and pleaded piteously, yet [the Emperor] resolutely refused and would not let him go. In the summer of the Jia-yin year of the Hongwu era of Emperor Taizu, the Kingdom of Japan sent an envoy to present tribute.
Having long admired the Master’s reputation for the Way, the envoy petitioned that the Master be sent to convert their country, offering a crystal rosary and a stone inkstone from Mount E as a gift.

The Emperor summoned the Master to the palace; however, the Master declined on the grounds of old age and illness. The Emperor took pity on him and did not dispatch him, instead allowing him to remain.

In the Heavenly Realm, the entire chamber was filled; the Master’s room extended for ten *zhang*. At that time, Song Gong Jingliao was serving in the Hanlin Academy; he visited the Master to engage in profound discussions on the subtleties of the Way.
Among the court officials of the day, there were none who did not hold him in deep reverence and admiration. That winter, he received an imperial decree to return east.

In the year Jiazi, his disciple Ju Ding resided at Cui Mountain in Yinzhou and welcomed the Master there to provide for his needs. Those from all quarters who came to pay their respects [were innumerable].
On the day of the *xū* (the 10th day of the lunar month), monks from Jincheng and Dali arrived at the capital. He specially received over fifty of them at Mount Cui;

they prostrated themselves before his seat and each requested a verse before departing. One day, he manifested slight illness and earnestly exhorted the assembly to hold fast to the ancestral Way with self-respect.
He took up his brush and wrote a verse, saying: "Seventy-eight years; there is no dharma that can be spoken.
This final phrase—how the pillar speaks! Ha! Having finished writing, he sat upright and passed away. It was the tenth day of the seventh month in the year of Bingyin during the Hongwu era.

He was seventy-eight years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination. His final instruction was to perform cremation, and the charred bones were to be scattered among the water and bamboo at Jingshan.
Not daring to follow [the original plan], he enshrined the remains at the site of Tangxia and buried them there. By nature, the Master was pure and sincere;

he treated his disciples like a compassionate mother. When encountering those within the Dharma who rebelled against the teachings or betrayed righteousness, he would invariably confront and rebuke them without the slightest leniency.
He served his master with the utmost reverence. He once attended Jizhao until the third watch of the night; unless commanded, he did not dare to withdraw.
His writings include the *Two Assemblies Record*, a re-evaluation of one hundred ancient cases from Xuedou’s *Niangu*, and a continuation of Dahui and Zhuan’an’s *Songgu* verses.
One hundred and ten entries. *Miscellaneous Records from a Mountain Hermitage*. *Verses on the Pure Land*. Compiled by Wu Sdao of Siming.
An Epigraph for [the Master’s] Deeds. Zen Master Liaotang Yi of Tiantong, Mingzhou: during the Renwu year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, he resided at Zhituo in Tai. Next...
He moved to Tianning and then Tiantong. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "In the past, when Baoshou opened the hall for teachings, Sansheng threw his whole body to assist him;
when Linji took up residence at a monastery, Puhua exerted all his strength to support him. Ultimately, what matter was being clarified? The Master said:

"Both ends are severed; a single sword leans against the cold heavens. The monk said, "If that is so, then the five ranks of ruler and subject are all arrayed together, and the trident of the three origins and the armor are withdrawn at once.
The Master said, "You have applied names and phrases incorrectly. The monk gave a shout.

The Master said, "Disciples of Chan who bring disorder to the lineage are as numerous as hemp and millet. He then said, "Take up a single blade of grass and make it the sixteen-foot golden body; take the sixteen-foot [body]..."
The Golden Body. [He] made it into a single blade of grass. Good assembly, those who have not endured bitter toil do not know this.
He then descended from his seat and ascended the hall. If you can directly grasp the first word and the final pivot, then the lanterns and pillars will shake the earth and radiate light.
If this is not yet so, Zhushan has lost ground today. Addressing the assembly: "The woodcutter’s song comes from the layered peaks."
The shadow of the sail falls upon the marsh isles. A monkey wearing a paper hat climbs straight to the tip of a tree branch.

The Seven-Star Sword and the Five-Cloud Tower. The ball strikes the person, and the person strikes the ball. Ten thousand matters are difficult to grasp and play with. The fish swallows the bubble on the water’s surface. Ascending the hall [he said]:
The *chángcǔ* bird does not perch in fragrant trees; Moshijia does not enter the vast ocean. Longquan and the *cáo* axe.
They are both iron, yet their sharpness and dullness differ vastly; a fine steed and a common hack share the same road, yet there is a difference in their speed.

With a whisk, he drew a line and said: "The flowers must bloom tonight; do not wait for the morning breeze. Small Assembly: The numinous light is never obscured; it is a magnificent legacy for all ages.
The mirror of wisdom is profoundly clear, responding universally throughout the ten directions. The time approaches the end of the year, and the season marks the beginning of the new month.
Yun: "The Dharma drum is struck and the great assembly gathers like clouds. Each one is authentically true; each one is luminously wondrous. What more is there to say?
If you speak of the existence of dharmas, you are again hindered by existence. If you speak of the non-existence of dharmas, you are again hindered by non-existence.
If you speak of neither existence nor non-existence, you are again hindered by neither existence nor non-existence. If you speak of neither not-existence nor not-non-existence..."
It cannot be grasped. Furthermore, it is neither non-existent nor non-non-obstructive. "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger.
"When the Sage acts, all things behold him. "The sun may grow cold; the moon may grow hot. No demons can destroy the True Teaching. With his whisk, he drew a line and said:
"On the head of the Huangbo tree hangs a honeyed fruit; the silent youth sings a folk song. He then asked:
"Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra—how is it that all phenomena share the same source? The Master said, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi.

[The student] said, "A single hair swallows the vast ocean; what more can be said therein? The Master said, "There is no need to hang up an ancient mirror; when dawn breaks, the rooster crows of itself.
[The student] asked, "In a place where right and wrong do not reach, is there still a phrase or not? The Master...
[The student] said, "I know full well that you are a pretender; your questions concern names and false dharmas. Since both person and dharma are empty, I ask the Master to point directly.
The Master said, "How many people have you questioned so far? [The student] said, "Where does one plant a rootless tree?

The Master said, "It is still tolerable at nightfall, but after noon, it brings distress to people. [The student] said, "It is right before our eyes. Why do you not answer me directly, time and again?"
[The Master] looked. The Master said: "A monastery may endure for a thousand years, but a monk exists for but a single morning.
Chan Master Dajue Zongxing of Mount Jing was a native of Taizhou.

He once traveled with Shuzhong and Muan as companions to visit various regions. After their travels, they stayed at Zituo; subsequently, he visited numerous famous monasteries before eventually moving to Mount Jing. As he approached his death, he suddenly sighed, saying: "Now, a man..."
[He was] thirty [years old]. His wife was six years old. Ultimately, they did not form a union.
She then passed away while sitting in meditation.
*Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume 511; *Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume 52.
Compiled by the Abbot of Seikan Zen-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (Subject) Chōei;
reviewed by the Abbot of Kokaigan-ji Temple in Kyoto, the Monk (Subject) Chōkei; presented for imperial inspection.
Dharma heir of Chan Master Baoning Miao of the twenty-second generation under Nanyue in the Linji lineage.
Chan Master Liaoyan Qingyu of the South Hall at Lingyan in Suzhou was a native of the Zhu family of Linhai in Taizhou.
He received the Dharma from Gulin. Initially, he appeared in the world at Kaifu in Zhongshan, subsequently moved to Benjue, and thrice presided over Lingyan.
On the day he ascended the hall, a monk asked: "The phoenix of the Cinnabar Mountain has nine-fold plumage; its station is so lofty it is separated from the five clouds."

"Seen but once in an age by all who gaze upon the four seas, I pray to hear the true song that answers Your Majesty. The Master said: "A thousand peaks look toward Mount Hua; ten thousand streams flow solemnly into the vast ocean. [The Emperor] said:
"When the Way prevails in the myriad regions, all return to the enlightened sovereign; in a single word free from partiality, all beings are benefited.

The Master said: "The Yellow River flows in nine bends; its waters originate from Kunlun. [The Emperor] said: "I have already received the Master’s instruction regarding my prayers and praises. As for [the matter of]..."
"What is the matter regarding the supreme vehicle? The Master said, "The eye does not see its own nose. "Caoshan’s stream is not stagnant water;
when a single drop suddenly arrives, a thousand waves compete to rise—what then? The Master said, "Step back! Step back! "I have never known how to hide another's virtues;
wherever I go, I meet people and speak of Xiangsi. The Master said, "Do not slander the mountain monk."
Question: "The heavens do not speak, yet the four seasons proceed; the earth does not speak, yet the myriad things grow. A student has doubts and wishes to hear your instruction. The Master said:
"Where ten thousand people look up in reverence, the red sun reaches the heart of heaven. [The student] said: "The rustic elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun;

he beats the drum with a thud-thud sound to sacrifice to the River God. The Master said: "To see with one's eyes and yet be as if blind; to speak with one's mouth and yet be as if mute. [The student] said: [As above].
"The road beneath Mount Hua has been so for a thousand ages; today it has added another who rides a donkey backward—P'an Lang.

The Master then gave a shout. [The student] asked: "The severe cold of midwinter is an annual occurrence. As for the shifting movement of the sun's course, what is its significance? The Master said: "Last night the sun’s orb shed osmanthus blossoms;
this morning in the moon’s cave, *zhicao* mushrooms have sprouted. [The student] asked: "Yangshan stepped forward with his hands crossed. What was the meaning of that?"
The Master said, "A servant seeing off a maidservant with excessive courtesy. Xiangyan joined his palms and stepped forward. The Master asked again, "And what then?

Xiangyan said, "Everyone is muddling along together. The Master said, "Setting aside these two paths, I ask you to speak otherwise. Xiangyan said, "In a place where there is no one, I shall look up at you with my hands cupped.

A monk asked, "The direct transmission of the single mind has already transcended the dualities of departure and subtlety; it cuts off all manifold distinctions. I pray that the Master will answer me."
[The student] spoke. The Master said, "A broken mirror does not reflect again; fallen flowers cannot climb back onto their branches. [The student] asked, "If one proceeds in this very way, what then?
The Master said, "A tortoise burrows through a ruined wall. [The student] asked, "What about when one clarifies the mind through form and manifests principle by relying on phenomena?"

The Master said, "A mangy horse tied to a withered post. [The student] said, "Three times nine is twenty-seven; the ox-head faces south, the horse-head faces north. What is the phrase that takes up the hand?
The Master said, "The partridge cries deep within the myriad flowers. [The student] asked, "What is it like when one does not stop until two are done?
The Master said, "Fishing for the moon at the bottom of the water. [The student] asked, "And what about taking a step back?"
The Master said: "Everyone they meet says, 'I have retired from office'; yet among those beneath the forest trees, not one has ever been seen.

A questioner asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "The mountain in front of you. The questioner said: "I do not ask about the Dharma; what is a monk? The Master said: [The mountain in front of you.]
"Three heads and two faces—this makes one loathed by others. The monk bowed. The Master then asked, "What is the Dharma?
He replied, "Next year there will be new branches; the spring wind that disturbs us shall never cease. The Master said, "It is because you did not ask the right question.
When yin reaches its limit and yang is born, I do not ask about that. What is the matter regarding the Gate of the Patriarchs? The Master said, "The stone笋 (shisun) sprouts forth."

The bamboo strip was twelve feet long. [The monk] asked, "Before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch, what was it like? The Master said, "A hundred-foot well before Mount Huayin. [The monk] asked, "After he saw him, what was it like? The Master said, "An eternal pine atop Mount Zhurong.

[The monk] asked, "Setting aside these two paths, I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma. The Master said, "Cease using the learning of the mundane to bury the mind of the Patriarchs. [The monk] asked: The bamboo strip was twelve feet long. "Before Niu-tou saw the Fourth Patriarch, what was it like? The Master said: "A hundred-foot well before Mount Huayin. "After he saw him, what was it like? The Master said: "An eternal pine atop Mount Zhurong.
"Setting aside these two paths, I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma. The Master said: "Cease using the learning of the mundane to bury the mind of the Patriarchs. Question:
If you raise one, you cannot raise two. When you let one point pass and fall into the second, how is it?
The Master said: "The ox in Huai Prefecture eats the grain; the horse in Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly. He said: "Yunmen’s fan leaps up to the thirty-third heaven, striking the nostrils of Śakra.
A sea bass in the Eastern Ocean receives a blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. How would you explain this further?
"What is it like? The Master said, "In Western Sichuan, painted images are cut down; in Shanfu, people's heads fall off. Question: "How was it before Niu-tou had seen the Fourth Patriarch?
The Master said, "At every place, green willows are fit to tie horses. Question: "How was it after he saw him?
