Chan Master Benyuan Shanda of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of the Chai family of Xianju. In his youth, he studied together with Jikan...
Xinxing was a wandering monk who vowed never to hold official monastic office. Initially, he met Xueyan at Yangshan; subsequently, he returned to Zhexi and studied under Yunfeng Hao of Mount Jing.

Upon entering the master’s room for instruction, he attained realization, and Hao granted him formal certification (*inka*). Coincidentally, the seat at Huiyun was vacant, and the master was appointed to fill it.
Later, he moved to Baoning, Jingci, and Mount Jing, where his achievements were all worthy of record. When the master resided in his quarters, he habitually did not set up [any formal seating].

He slept on a simple wooden bed. At night, he would burn incense and light candles, sitting upright until dawn; this was his constant practice. Furthermore, his physical constitution differed from that of others:
when encountering severe cold, he wore fine linen and ramie; when it was very hot, he wore silk and cotton wool. He once used his alms-bowl as a support.
He established Dayuan Monastery on a mountain halfway up the eastern road to receive traveling companions from all quarters.
One day, knowing that his time had come, he gathered the assembly and finished recounting the events of his lifelong journey as a wandering monk; he then sat upright and passed away.

The Chief Seat Dragon Rock Jin was repeatedly invited by monasteries in various regions, yet he remained lying high in bed and refused to rise. He once composed the "Song of Delighting in Leisure," a portion of which reads:
"The very mind is the Buddha; no-mind is the Way. All matters simply follow conditions; naturally, one’s body and mind are good.
I have never sought to dwell in a monastery; Even Buddhahood I would not aspire to achieve. I have never maintained the Vinaya, nor have I observed the precepts."
It has never been broken. Letting go or holding fast is entirely up to the person. To cling to the law while practicing is like a donkey pulling a millstone.
When you wish to walk, you walk; when you wish to sit, you sit. You are neither diligent nor lazy. A single volume of the *Three Character Classic* serves as your daily task.
At times you walk the bottom of the deep sea; at times you lie atop the high mountain peak. For how many lifetimes have you practiced?
One can become a person at leisure. Who would willingly allow themselves to be shackled by empty fame? I do not slight you; let others spit in my face as they please.
How much time can one obtain in a hundred years? Why must one insist on distinguishing between "mine" and "yours"? Even in poverty, there is no need for worry.
Enough with elaborate makeup; Yama, the King of Hell, invites all without distinction between kin and stranger. He consigns everyone to a single mass of red flames.
If you can maintain mastery over yourself, you will never let the wind blow your rudder off course. To patch what is torn and ward off the cold is enough;
pass your days with plain rice and coarse tea as circumstances allow. I compose songs of leisure and sing them myself, harmonizing my own tune. I am no idle man.
Willingly at leisure. How many people in this world can truly be called "leisurely"?
Master Ming of He Shan was a successor in the Dharma lineage of the State Preceptor Mingzhou Gong;
he maintained himself with integrity and purity, reciting the Lotus Sūtra daily. It happened that he heard Iron Mirror ascend the hall for a discourse.
He spoke, and thus attained the essential core of the mind. Once, while sitting in meditation at night, he composed a verse: "Exhausted is the single lamp by the mountain window;

The hearth-fire is gone, and all is cold and hushed. I leave this koan to be raised again tomorrow; The practitioner strikes the bell and ascends the tower once more. Because of this, Tiejing praised him highly upon ascending the hall.
At the end of his life, he passed away peacefully and without illness while sitting upright. During the cremation, his tongue remained unburnt.

Mingzhou, a successor in the twentieth generation under National Teacher Tiandong Jian of Nanyue, was the son of the Wang family of Changguo. He followed Master Meijian Fu.
Having received full ordination, he heard that Tiantong Zhihong was transforming others through the Way and went to visit him. Zhihong appointed him as his attendant.
One day, while in the master’s room, Zhihong raised the koan of Zhaozhou’s “The dog has no Buddha-nature,” and the Master attained a sudden and thorough realization.

Subsequently, he met Yuetang Yin at Lingyin Temple; Yuetang held him in high esteem and appointed him to oversee the office of the secretary. It happened that his preceptor, Zu Fangyan, was also there.
He traveled to Shanglan in Longxing, taking his teacher along as an attendant. While visiting Baiyang, he paid his respects to Huiji, who subsequently appointed him to share the teaching seat.
He left Shanglan and ascended to Xuedou in Mingzhou, where he remained for three years. When the seat at Dianshan in Songjiang became vacant, the community requested the Master to fill it.
Shortly thereafter, the temple was destroyed by fire. The Master rebuilt it. Later, he presided over Wanshou Temple. After serving for barely one year, he manifested a slight illness;
he changed his robes, wrote a verse, bid farewell to the assembly, and passed away. This was on the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month of the Yǒu year of the Zhìzhèng era (1365).
His body was cremated, and five-colored *śarīra* relics, as large as beans or grains, were beyond counting. He was sixty-six years of age and fifty years since his ordination.
Chan Master Simin of Dayu at Daofang in Huzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Xiangshan.

He brushed out his sleeves and departed. Thereupon, [Xuanzang] appointed him as the recorder. One day, Huizhang said to the Master, "You have now reached the field of great peace and bliss;
you should maintain it well. I possess the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa, which I shall secretly transmit to you so that they do not perish.
The Master covered his ears and left. After he began to propagate the Dharma, he served as abbot at Qingshou Temple twice.
The Great Ancestor (Shizu) treated him with the reverence due to a teacher.

There was a descendant of Confucius named Yuan Cuo who crossed the river to visit the Master and requested that the ancestral temple in Qufu be restored. The Master spoke on his behalf to Khuduhur, saying:

"Confucius taught people through the Way of Great Centrality and Ultimate Rectitude, the rites of the Three Bonds and Five Constants, and the fundamental principles of rectifying the mind and sincere intention. From Confucius to..."
Now, for fifty-one generations, he has inherited the title and maintained the ancestral sacrifices without ever failing.
When Huduhu (Hutuhu) subsequently memorialized the throne requesting that the hereditary rank be restored, the Master was fifty-six years old.

Suddenly afflicted with wind-paralysis, on the first day of the intercalary fourth month in the *ding-si* year of Renzong’s Yanyou era, he gathered the assembly, recited a verse, and then passed away peacefully. Upon cremation, śarīras were obtained.
His number of disciples was incalculable. He was posthumously titled Great Master Furu Yuanming.
He was the twenty-first generation descendant of Nanyue and a dharma heir of Chan Master Jingshan Ji.
Chan Master Kōngsǒu Xīnwù of Línghyìn in Hángzhōu was the son of the Niu family of Wúxiàn in Sū. At the age of nine, he entered Longxìng Monastery and received the tonsure under Báiyún Xián.
In the *wùxū* year of the Zhìzhèng era of the Yuán dynasty, he went to Jìngcí Monastery to consult Yú’ān Jì.
Yú’ān questioned him, saying, "What is the essential meaning of Yongmíng? The Master replied, "I am but a newcomer; I see only a single lake."
Shui approved this and subsequently permitted him to enter the inner quarters. On the day of Renshen (the 1st day of the 10th month), he was appointed to the second seat.
On the day of Guimao (the 2nd day of the 10th month), Lan’an of Zhongzhu requested that he share the teaching seat. The Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title Yuan-Ci-Zheng-Ji.

In the Gengxu year of the Hongwu era of Emperor Taizu of the Ming dynasty, he resided at Chongning in Zhejiang for eight years before moving to Zhongzhu. When the position at Lingyin became vacant, the Monastic Registrar [recommended him].
The Master’s name was [inserted]. He was selected and appointed to fill the vacancy. At that time, all the students packed their provisions and followed him.

Before long, due to past events concerning his former tenure as abbot, he reached the capital and passed away on the road. On his deathbed, he wrote a verse, saying: "At the age of fifty-five, I have attempted to patch up empty space;
I have trampled through the barrier of birth and death; at midnight, the sun stands at noon. His disciples, including Daojing and others, [recorded this].
He was cremated according to the Dharma; his tongue and his rosary remained unburnt. His remains were enshrined and returned to Lingyin, where they were interred on the eastern ridge.
Furthermore, a portion of his remaining bones was divided and buried at the site of Jiuqu in Xixi. This was on the third day of the fifth month of the Xinwei year of the Hongwu era.
There are three recorded collections of his sermons (*yulu*) that circulate in the world.

Chan Master Sidao Daoyan of Tiantong Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Yao family of Changzhou. His name was Guangxiao, and he styled himself the "Recluse Escaping Emptiness" (*Taoxuzi*).
At the age of fourteen, he left home to become a monk at Miaozhi Hermitage. During the military chaos at the end of the Yuan dynasty, he roamed the Yangtze River region.
Hulu was naturally reticent and concealed his brilliance. He studied under Yuanwu Keqin of Mount Jing and consulted him on the essentials of Chan, fully grasping its core essence.

He served as the head librarian for three years, after which he emerged from seclusion at Puqing Temple and was subsequently transferred to Tiantong Longquan Temple. He once inscribed his own portrait, saying:
"Having seen through the *bājiāo* and the staff, I casually reveal my refined elegance to the very bone; sometimes I brandish the tortoise-hair whisk, until it reaches its ultimate state."
The Sky Laughs and Nods its Head. During the Hongwu era, he was selected as a eminent monk and served Emperor Wen at the Yan residence.
During the Yongle era, due to his merit in assisting the founding of the dynasty, the Emperor wished to appoint him to an official post; however, he would not accept for a single day.

When the Emperor summoned him for an audience, he secretly had someone dress him in official robes and cap, and conferred upon him the rank of Imperial Tutor to the Crown Prince (Taizi Shaoshi). He was then urgently ordered to go forth and offer his thanks; having no other choice, he performed the prostrations. The Emperor then commanded: [text continues].

He never kept his hair long; his observance of the precepts was exceptionally strict. Once, when he was presented with two palace women, he would not accept them, and they were subsequently sent back.
He kept a single large rooster; as soon as it crowed, he would rise and recite the sutras with clear resonance. Even while attending to state affairs daily, he did not interrupt this practice.

Later, when his illness became critical, the Emperor visited his residence and bestowed upon him the utmost consolation and care. He presented him with a golden spittoon and asked what words he had to say.
He replied, "What more can one who has left the household life have to say? Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. His worldly age was eighty-five.

He was posthumously granted the title of Duke of Rongguo and the posthumous name Gongjing. Later, he was enshrined in the ancestral temple of the Great Zong, and his remains were transferred to Daxiongxing Temple for offerings.
There is a work titled *Daoyulu* (Record of the Way’s Remnants) in one fascicle that circulates in the world.
Chan Master Wenshi Wenxiu of Jingshan in Hangzhou, a dharma successor of Chan Master Wanshou Ren, was the son of the Li family of Kunshan; he left the household life under Shaolong.
At An Temple, he took Li Zhixing as his teacher. Later, Xingzhongren resided at Yunding; the Master went there to follow him, and they were in perfect accord, like a needle meeting its eye.
Initially, he resided at Pumen in Suzhou, then moved to Lingyan, and thirdly presided over Wanshou.

At the beginning of the Yongle era, an imperial edict was issued summoning those among the Confucians, Buddhists, and Daoists throughout the realm who were proficient in literary and doctrinal matters to compile the *Yongle Dadian*. The Master responded to this summons and composed [the required texts].

Having completed his formal leave-taking, he returned south to preside over the assembly at Jingshan. He ascended the hall and addressed the congregation. A monk asked, "The Dharma assembly has already commenced;

the Dharma drum has already sounded; the fourfold assembly has gathered like clouds. We pray that the Master will offer a blessing for the Emperor. The Master replied, "The sun and moon are the celestial eyes; Mount Sumeru is the mountain of longevity.
The monk asked, "When the World-Honored One appeared in the world, the heavens rained down the four flowers. When you, Reverend, appear in the world, what auspicious signs are there? The Master—

[The monk] said, "A single ox drinks water; five horses do not neigh. [The Master] said, "If that is so, then the meaning of joyful serenity shall be transmitted for a thousand ages, and the tradition of silent illumination shall spread in all four directions.
The Master said, "Better that good things never happen at all. He then said, "When the Tathāgata appeared in the world..."
These are dung-carriers. The Patriarch’s coming from the West was like a fortune-teller.
As for the rest—Deshan, Linji, Yunmen, Guishan, Xuefeng, Xuansha, Nanquan, and Zhaozhou—they each flaunted their mental acuity and alternately distinguished between illumination and function;
they were all nothing but smugglers of private salt. Here at New Pumen, I shall sweep them all away at once. Why? Because I have fortunately encountered Yao!
In the era of Shun, music was naturally harmonized through non-action. Again, [the Master] raised a monk’s question to Yangqi: "What is the Buddha?
Yangqi said, "A three-legged donkey prances about on its hooves. The monk asked, "Is it not just this very thing? Yangqi said, "Old man from Hunan. The Master remarked, "How great Yangqi was!
Yet, having been questioned by that monk, he could not avoid revealing both his hands and feet. He then ascended the hall and said: "Ten..."
There is no other path. Why then do some seek Tiantai in the south and others seek Wutai in the north? Before one’s eyes there is no different grass;
why then is the peach blossom red and the plum blossom white? After a long silence, he said: "Once the barrier of the Patriarchs is broken through, it is all one's own.
Lingyan ascended the hall and said: "The entire world is oneself. From where do the myriad phenomena arise?"
There are those who do not understand—thirty blows of the staff for them. There are also those who do understand—thirty blows of the staff for them as well.
Everywhere else, the assembly enters the hall after the morning gruel; here at Yunyan Monastery, they enter the hall for tea after the formal session.
Today is the first day of the seventh month; the golden wind rustles before the gate. We have deliberately beaten the drum and ascended the hall, yet not a single word has been spoken.
He went out. The pillar prostrated to Śākyamuni; the lantern inquired after the health of Jñānākara.
Only the monk of no affairs remains, as ever with eyes askance and nose straight. I dare ask the assembly: who is this monk of no affairs?
After a long silence, he said: "A beak three feet long. At Wanshou, upon thanking the head officers and praying for rain, he ascended the hall. "Clever monks turn the wheel."

Suddenly, he stood with his body turned sideways toward the guests, weaving together various conditions. He transformed charcoal into grain and listened as the rooster finished its crowing with a flutter of wings.
He watched as the tea ladle leaped from the ground. Striking his staff, he said: "Last night, the rain fell upon the river."
At the Hall for the Opening of the Summer Retreat (Xià) of the Ten-Thousand-Household Stream: "The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Yuánjué*) can give rise to all dharmas;
yet all dharmas have never been apart from the *Awakening of Mahāyāna*. Ants know of rain and seal their burrows; the *shíqū* insect responds to the seasons and raises its blossoms.
How many are there with hands and feet stuck? How many are there with the ten directions crisscrossed? At the Hall for the Closing of the Retreat (Jì): He raised [the following]:
At the end of summer, Cuiyan addressed the assembly, saying: "Throughout this summer, I have spoken here and there for you, my brothers.
Look and see: are Cuiyan’s eyebrows still there? The Master said: "He sells flour with the bran still on it. He then ascended the hall and cited an ancient worthy who said:

When the sun rises, the heart shines with light; when the heavens are overcast, the nature-ground is dark. Those who do not know heaven and earth are unaware that the Way of Firmness possesses both Qian and Kun.

Speaking thus, those who have attained thorough awakening throughout the ages are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; those who misunderstand are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.
With his whisk, he draws a line and says: "The Anavatapta Lake is forty *zhang* deep and forty *zhang* wide."
The Master gave a small evening discourse on New Year’s Eve: “Nāgārjuna filled his bowl with water; Kātyāyanīpūtra threw down a needle from her embroidery.
Deshan Yantou beckoned across the river; Gaoting strode off crosswise. Bells ring at dawn; drums beat at dusk. The wind moves and the dust rises.”
The magpies cawing and the crows crying—there is not a single place that is not this very moment. Now, on the thirtieth night of the twelfth month, I dare ask you all:
do you understand? Only when there are waves reaching the heavens can one accommodate a fish that swallows a boat.
There is a wind ninety thousand *li* thick; only with wings reaching to the heavens can one bear it.

When the Buddha was ascending the hall after his *nirvāṇa*, Śākyamuni the Old Man descended from Tuṣita Heaven and took birth in the womb of Mahāmāyā; even then, he was already infected by the grave illness of birth and death.
Upon his birth, he immediately pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth; it is evident that this was something that could not be artificially contrived.
When he beheld the appearance of the morning star, he suddenly awakened to the Way—this was precisely like a person with diseased eyes seeing floating flowers in the sky.
Throughout forty-nine years and more than three hundred assemblies, whether speaking extensively or briefly, directly or indirectly, openly or secretly, how could [it have been otherwise]?
He was not in a deep sleep nor did he speak deliriously; rather, as his end approached, he gently rubbed his chest and addressed the assembly, saying:
"You should all carefully contemplate my body, which is the color of purple-polished gold. Gaze upon it until you are fully satisfied, lest you later have cause for regret.

If you say that I have entered parinirvāṇa, you are not my disciples; if you say that I have not entered parinirvāṇa, you likewise are not my disciples. His illness had reached the point of being incurable.
No one is able to provide a cure. Not only do the physicians of this world fold their hands in helplessness, but even the divine physician Jīvaka must retreat three stations.
I, a distant descendant of the Northern Mountains, today intend to treat him. If I cannot effect a cure, future generations will forever lose their protector;
if I can effect a cure, then the body of purple-golden hue shall once again stand majestic.
Majestic and imposing! Brilliant and resplendent! Manifesting everywhere. Striking the whisk, he said: "The willow color is tender golden; the pear blossom is fragrant white snow.
Entering the hall, he said: "Only investigate the living word; do not investigate the dead word. It is manifest at every point."
To clarify each and every thing is a dead word. To take a step and tread upon the Southern Star, or turn one’s body and overturn the Northern Dipper, is a dead word.
What is the living word? "After the rain has passed through the streets of Suzhou, she puts on her embroidered shoes. When the assembly hesitated, he threw down his whisk and descended from the seat.
Ding Shan ascended the hall and said: "The myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images are all sealed by a single Dharma. The preceding...
The front is Bowel-Pot Peak; the rear is Reaching-the-Clouds Peak; in the middle is the Buddha Hall.
What do you call "one dharma"? After a long silence, he said: "The First Patriarch Guo-yi was originally a native of Kunshan. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Master Mazu said, 'Since the time of chaos, for thirty years there has been no lack of salt and sauce. Here there is not even two ounces of gold; it is common."
A man buys three *shēng* of wine and ascends the pagoda. There is no dharma before one’s eyes; the intent lies before one’s eyes, yet it is not the dharma of the present moment.
It is not something reached by the ears or the eyes. At the head of the inkstone-washing pool, the clouds drift slowly; atop the chicken-burying mound, the grass grows lushly.
The Master once gave this *chuíyǔ* (a vertical teaching) in his room: "The source of the Way is not far off—where is it? The Patriarch [went] to the West.
“Come! For what purpose? “Enlightenment has no tree; who established its name? A monk asked, “What is the guest within the guest?
The Master said, “Leaning on a staff, one stands by another’s gate. The monk asked, “What is the host within the guest? The Master said, “Leaning against a pillar in the hall.
The monk asked, “What is the guest within the host? The Master said, “One’s very life and destiny belong to another. The monk asked, “What is... [the text ends here].
He was the master among masters. The Master said: "Holding a vajra in his hand.
One day, seeing a monk passing through the courtyard, the Master called out in a stern voice, "The eaves of the roof are collapsing! The monk looked up; the Master said, "A hawk has flown to Silla.
As soon as the Master saw a monk enter the gate, he said, "You fellow who treads upon prefectures and counties—your heels deserve three blows with the staff."
"Ten blows! [The monk] said, "I have not even asked a question, yet I have already been granted these blows. The Master said, "Wait until you open your mouth; what would that be worth?
As the monk hesitated, the Master shouted and sent him out. Another monk entered for an audience and displayed his sitting cloth (*zuoju*).

The Master said, "In my place, there is no leftover soup or stale rice; there is no need to use up your worn-out cooking cloth. The monk said, "Out of compassion, O Monk. The Master said, "Ha! (laughter).
He overturned the blue stone pillar in front of the gate; throughout his life, the Master occupied the seat of enlightenment four times, each instance yielding observable achievements.
In his later years, he withdrew from public life and selected a site to the left of Jizhao Pagoda, where he built a thatched hut to dwell. At the age of over seventy, he passed away.
He authored the *Zengji Xuchuanteng* (Supplementary Collection of the Continued Lamp History) in four volumes, which remains in circulation today.
Chan Master Xibai Lijin of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jingshan Ming. He was the son of the Yao family of Suzhou.

In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Baoji Monastery. Upon meeting Guding Ming, [Ming] presented to him the kōan concerning Deshan’s encounter with Longtan. After a long time, [Lijin] attained realization.
Qi. In the *dingyou* year of the Yuan *zhizheng* era, he took up residence at Ruiwang Temple. Encountering the destruction of Tianning Monastery by fire, the Master rebuilt it from its ruins.

The Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title "Universal Salvation of Perfect Penetration" (*yuantong puzhi*). Because his mother was elderly and without support, the Master built a residence east of the city to provide for her care.

At the beginning of the Hongwu era under Emperor Gao of the Ming, he was transferred to Jingci Monastery. In the spring of the *xinhai* year, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Tianjie Monastery. In the winter of the *renzi* year—

An imperial edict was issued to convene an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*), and the Master was commanded to ascend the seat. The Emperor’s carriage arrived in person, and from the dukes and marquises downward, tens of thousands of listeners were present;
everyone attained a state of joy. One day, he suddenly said to his attendant monk, "I have a karmic debt from a previous life that remains unsettled;
I must repay it. He then manifested a slight illness, took leave of the assembly, and passed away. His stupa was erected to the west of the city of Jiaxing.
Chan Master Xiangyuan Renshu of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a native of Taizhou. One day, he hurried toward the gate and shouted loudly, "The slaughter has arrived!
The slaughter has arrived! How will you evade it? Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away.

Chan Master Jueyuan Huitan of Tianjie Monastery in Jinling was a dharma successor of Chan Master Longxiang Xun. He was the son of the Yang family of Tiantai. His mother dreamed that a bright moon fell into her lap and she swallowed it, after which she became pregnant.
When he was born, his physical appearance was striking and dignified. As he grew older, he did not associate with other children and relied upon [the teachings of] Yue.
Fagu Da-jun entered the monastic order at the age of sixteen and received full ordination from the Great Sangha.

Hearing that Xiaoyin Yan was the master in Central China, he went there to seek instruction and exhaustively expressed the intensity of his quest for the Way. Yan rebuked him, saying: "Those who enter through the gate..."
"This is not a household treasure; the Way resides within oneself. Why seek it from others? The Master withdrew and attained realization.
One day, upon hearing the story of Baizhang’s Wild Fox, he was suddenly and greatly enlightened, saying: "The Buddha-dharma has fallen into my hands.
It was only because it was so extremely clear that what was to be gained was delayed. Yun asked, "What principle have you seen? The Master spread out both his hands.
"It is not worth half a copper coin. Xun nodded his head in agreement. One day, as the Master entered the gate, Xun asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains. Xun said, "When you were traveling everywhere, crushing Luopo beneath your straw raincoat—how was that? The Master said:
Before entering the gate, he had already presented himself to the Master. Xian said, "Why do you not bring it forth right now?
As the Master hesitated, Xian gave a shout. From that moment on, the Master was completely liberated. On another day, Xian spread out both hands and showed them to the Master, saying:
"It has been laid open in eight characters; why then do you refuse to accept it? The Master said, "Do not come here to obstruct me.
Xing said, "Come closer and I will explain it for you. The Master covered his ears and went out. Later, when Xing presided over Longxiang, he had the Master share the seat with him.
In the *Renchen* year of the *Zhizheng* era of Emperor Shundi of the Yuan dynasty, he appeared at the Patriarchs’ Hall of Mount Niushou.
Three years later, he ascended the hall at Qingliang Guanghui. He said: "A single phrase—pitch black, yet without a handle; it has its own standard. After a long pause, he asked: "Do you understand?"

The pestle pounds toward the southeast; the millstone grinds toward the northwest. Entering the hall: "For the sutras there are masters of the sutras; for the treatises there are masters of the treatises.
Today, at Longhe, I shall let loose a single thread of the Way to divide the sections and arrange the segments. He raises his staff, strikes it once on the ground, and says:
Now tell me, what are these words? [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "This is a ready-made public case.

Among the assembly, there are many who have attained understanding, yet not a few who have misunderstood it. Consequently, gold and brass are not distinguished, and jade and stone are not differentiated.
Here at Longhe, we shall distinguish them directly: Layman Zhang and Layman Li—one has long arms, the other..."
"What a large eye! If everyone were like the Dharma-gate of Bodhidharma today, who would be able to shoulder it?
After a long silence, he let out a single sigh and descended from his seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The spring breeze blows vast and wide; the spring days linger on.

The yellow oriole sings upon the branches of the hundred flowers. Within this, there is boundless meaning—whom can we allow to know its message? Before he had finished speaking, a monk suddenly stepped forward and asked:
"How is it when the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be suppressed? The Master shouted fiercely, "Who is there to suppress?

He then said to the monk in the hall, "During the twelve periods of the day and night, you have no share for pecking and swallowing; you have no share for seeking and pursuing. Do you understand? The monk was at a loss.
The Master said, "If you do not yet understand three eights and nine, you will find it difficult to avoid brooding within yourself. The Imperial Preceptor bestowed [this teaching].

The Chan Master Jingjue Miaobian was his title. In the year of Yimwei, he moved to Baoning Temple. In the year of Bingshen, when Emperor Ming of the Gao family established Jianye as his capital, the Master went to visit him at the imperial camp.

Upon seeing him for the first time, the Emperor sighed and said, "A truly meritorious and virtuous monk. He ordered the Master to take charge of Jiangshan Temple. A year later, it was renamed Longxiang, which became the Great Tianjie Monastery;
by imperial decree, the Master was appointed to preside over it. The Emperor then established a grand memorial service and charged the Master with its conduct.

He ascended the seat to preach the Dharma when the imperial carriage visited him in person; the imperial favors bestowed upon him were most abundant. The Emperor inscribed the characters "The World’s Foremost Zen Forest" for him.

In the Wushen year of the Hongwu era, he was granted purple robes and a golden-embroidered square cassock, along with an imperial edict appointing him as the Great Zen Master Yanfan Shanshe Liguo Chongjiao, to serve as the abbot of the Great Tianjie Monastery and preside over the Buddhist affairs of all the mountains.

At that time, the selection process was orderly and the evaluation was most impartial. Those from the imperial house and the ancestral altars who were dedicated to their aspirations, as well as scholars dwelling in the mountains and forests who harbored the Way, rose up together like horses yoked side by side.
In the sixth month of the summer of the Gengxu year, the court deliberated upon the Western Regions, which had not yet submitted.

The Emperor, noting that those nations held the Buddha-vehicle in high esteem, issued a special edict for the Master to go there. Receiving this command, the Master set out on his journey that very day from Min.

Throughout the oceans, in every country and city he visited, there were none who did not hear of his reputation and come to seek refuge. In the seventh month of the autumn of the Xinhai year, he arrived at the kingdom of Coḷa.

There he proclaimed the majesty and virtue of the Son of Heaven and stayed at the Fo-shan Temple. Its king treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher, attending upon him from the second watch of the night until dawn;
the scholars and commoners of the entire nation all came to gaze upon him in reverence. In the ninth month, the Master manifested slight illness, and the king and his ministers all came to him.
They consoled one another. After a short while, he bathed and changed his robes, then said to those around him, "My illusory conditions have come to an end;
I cannot return to life. He sat upright in the full lotus posture. At the hour of midnight, the Master asked, "Is the sun about to rise? He replied, "Not yet.

The Master asked again, and after repeating the question several times, [the disciple] said, "The sun has risen. He passed away with a serene expression. His worldly age was sixty-eight. [He was a] monk.

Thereupon, the Master remained hidden among the assembly for fifteen years. In the *wǔwǔ* year of the Renzong Yuanzhao era (1318), he emerged from seclusion at Tiānbǎo Monastery in Fúmián.

The Imperial Preceptor bestowed upon him the monastery’s plaque and conferred upon him the title "Great Master Wondrous Enlightenment True Emptiness" (*Miaojue Zhenkong Dashi*). He subsequently moved to Pùxiān Monastery in Sōngxī.
Ascending the hall: A single phrase facing the assembly cuts off the very source. Holding fast and letting go, the entire mechanism is laid bare.
Seizing the crown of all sages, one pierces the eyes of the monks. Swiftly reflecting beyond the wind, rushing through the flowing tide and crossing the blade.

Directly attaining the leaping of the Wondrous Peak, the waves of the ocean of wisdom surge. At such a time as this, tell me: how do you speak that single phrase for the opening of the hall to offer blessings to the Emperor?
Striking the whisk, he said: "When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the entire body is revealed;

where the Elephant King walks, there is no trace of the fox. Small Assembly (Xiaocan): The Diamond Seal of Truth—throughout all lands, it is universally honored. It is the tongs and hammer of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Humans and devas are at a loss; no ladder stands before them; knowledge and understanding do not exist. Deshan’s staff penetrates from above to below;
Linji’s shout cuts off what came before and shines after. One being illumined, all are illumined; one moon, all functions.

Great Men wield the "blow-off" sword and hang the talisman behind their elbows. Releasing both and gathering both; killing completely and reviving completely. He picks up his staff and says: "The Crane."
There are nine gorges where wings have barely begun to lift; a horse that cannot travel a thousand *li* vainly pursues the wind. Ascending the hall on the Buddha’s Birthday:
Born in the Lumbinī Garden, endowed with eighty secondary marks, he walks with the gait of an elephant king and roars the roar of a lion.
Holding up his staff, he said, “Master Yunmen is coming! Then, striking it once, he said, “Father! Father! Ascending the hall.
Sansheng asked Xuefeng, “What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? Feng said, “Wait until it comes out of the net, and I will tell you.
Sansheng said, “Even the kōan of a teacher of fifteen hundred people, you do not recognize!
Feng said, “The old monk’s affairs as abbot are many. The Master said, “Sansheng was much like a venomous dragon stirring the sea; white waves surged and overflowed.”
Heaven! Had it not been for Xuefeng’s habitual entry into the surging waves, how could he have secured the dragon pearl in his grasp?
(He strikes the whisk and thanks the Hall Master. Entering the hall, he asks: "What is that which is within the Buddha Hall? *Sirili sulū; sulū sirili.*
The spring breeze of the River Kingdom cannot stir it; the partridge cries out amidst the deep flowers. [The Master] strikes the whisk and brings up the story of Xiangyan climbing the tree.
He offers this verse: Whether he has climbed the tree or not, an iron snake lies across the ancient road.
Face-to-face, he laughs heartily. Bitter gourds are bitter from root to tip. [The Master] brings up Linji’s “What is the Unranked True Person?”—it is a dried-up piece of dung!
The Verse says: "The True Man of No Rank is a dried-up dung-club; Linji was not yet a 'white-handed thief.

The stars and constellations fill the sky, and the moon’s disc stands alone. May people of this age cease their longing for a single pool of water; come aboard a light boat to drift across the Five Lakes.
Having resided there for three years, he took leave of his patrons and returned to Tianbao. There, he succeeded Shan-chou as the head of the monastery.

In the eighth month of the gengchen year of Emperor Shun’s Zhizheng era, he manifested a slight illness. He composed a handwritten letter inviting all those with whom he had traveled to enter the mountains. As it was said:

At noon, he bathed and sat upright, writing a verse that said: "Fundamentally there is no coming or going; a single phrase is fully presented. Crimson clouds pierce the azure void;

the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away. He was sixty-three years of age and forty-five years since his ordination. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Ruiyun.
At the monastery, Chan Master Cheng of Daci Zhiyan in Hangzhou was visited by Jiefeng. The Master said, "Where have you seen gods and ghosts come from?
Jiefeng replied, "I have caught the thief. The Master asked, "Where is the stolen property? Jiefeng gave a shout. The Master said:
"Neither opening the mouth nor closing the mouth is it. Bring forth a phrase that goes beyond this. Feng said, "Throughout the entire world, all is clearly manifest; nothing is concealed.
The Master raised his bamboo staff and said, "To call this a bamboo staff is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a bamboo staff is to turn one's back on it. What do you call it? Feng then overturned the meditation seat. The Master struck the bamboo staff three times and said, "Blind!"
Han: "I dare to come here and pluck the tiger's whiskers. Feng then prostrated himself and attended him for three years.

One day the Master said, "The ancients sought teachers and chose friends; one must not waste time in vain. Although you have attained the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, you have still not been able to turn yourself around toward the Ultimate.
Have you not heard how Fenyang saw Shoushan and said: 'Ten thousand ages, the blue abyss is empty'?"
Jieyue said, "Only after thrice stirring it up will you finally know. Feng was suddenly enlightened.
Zen Master Guzhou Ji was a successor of Chan Master Moshan Yi;
at that time, Zhong of Yueting resided at Jiangshan Monastery, and the Master served as the First Seat. Zhuyuan came to study with him.
Yuetting went to the Head Seat’s quarters. The Master asked Yuan, "Mongshan once said that the 'Pine-Planting Wayfarer' was born without the two conditions.
After Bodhidharma was buried at Xiongeri, he returned to the West with a single shoe.

Is this the wondrous function of spiritual powers, or is it simply the natural way of things? Yuan replied, "Body and spirit are both wondrous. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Not so. On another day..."
"You must realize this for yourself. Later, Yuan consulted Wuneng, who cited the Master's words. Neng said, "It is because you do not understand them.
Upon Yuan's explanation, he attained great enlightenment.
Chan Master Tieshan Qiong of Cihua in Yuanzhou left home at the age of eighteen. He first studied under Xueyan.
One day, while suffering from a headache and wishing to brew medicine, he was carrying a water jar in his hand when he encountered Jue Chibi, who said to him:

"You must be like Prince Nanda, who split his own bones to give them back to his father and split his flesh to give them back to his mother; only then will you be able to preach the Dharma for your parents. The Master—
He had a realization and composed a verse, saying: "A jade tower appears upon a single blade of grass; I have discerned the idle topics of past and present.
Lifting up the moon atop Mount Jiyun, I toss it before people like a ball of flowers. Not long after, Yankuan passed away. He visited Dongyan, but did not find accord there.
He then went to study under Mōngshān Yì, entering the inner quarters several times to present his understanding. Yì said, "It is simply that you are lacking one thing."

One day, when Rujing suddenly came upon the character "lack" (quàn), his body and mind were suddenly enlightened, penetrating to the very bone and marrow. He then leaped down from the meditation seat, seized Yiyuan, and asked, "What is it that I lack?
Yiyuan struck him three times with his palm. The Master bowed, and Yiyuan approved. During the winter solstice, he gave a small assembly lecture:
"At the beginning of the winter solstice month, sell the blanket to buy an ox; at the end of the winter solstice month, sell the ox to buy a blanket. He then struck the meditation desk.
Leaning on his staff, he said: "Here there is no tail and no head; at the midpoint, all is stilled. The eyes of sleep are wide open, and the five clouds manifest their auspiciousness.
Radiant breezes and clear moons pervade everywhere. A plum blossoms upon a withered branch by the ancient ferry;
before the wind, its dark fragrance occasionally drifts forth. Nevertheless, as for the single path leading upward—ten thousand miles to Yuzhou. How can this be seen? Relying on the staff."
He said, "Rest, rest. Later, he entered nirvana; his stupa was enshrined behind the Avalokiteśvara Pavilion.

Chan Master Yiyuan Yongning of Longchi Monastery in Yixing, Changzhou—a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Wankuan of Lake Tai—also styled himself Xuanhuazi (The Son of Illusion). He was a master of the Huaidong region.

He was the son of the Zhu family of the prefecture. For generations his clan had served as an official lineage. When he was six or seven years old, upon hearing the name of the Buddha, he would immediately prick up his ears and listen intently.
At nine, he earnestly requested to leave secular life, but his parents did not grant permission; the Master then refused to eat.

He studied under Master Yuan at Guanghui Temple, which was formerly the site where Fahai Zhaofa preached the Dharma. On the eve of this, the monks of the temple dreamed that they were welcoming Zhaofa. The following day, the Master...

When he arrived, those who understood him marveled at his distinction. At the age of twelve, the Prince of Henan enrolled him with the Monastic Registry (*Senglù*) and provided him with a certificate for his tonsure.

He soon received full ordination and traveled extensively through various regions. He visited Zhongfeng Haiyu at Wanshou Temple in Suzhou, and subsequently entered Qionglung to pay his respects to Ke’weng Shao.
Observing that the Master’s aspirations were extraordinary, Shao appointed him to oversee the library. At that time, he was only nineteen years old. Upon returning home to visit his parents...
In Piling, he again invited Mingji and Chang to Mount Jiaozzi to practice meditative concentration for five years. Chang said, "Master, your understanding is currently like this;
you should go quickly to see other teachers and not remain stagnant here. The Master nodded in agreement and subsequently traveled to Dahu in Huaixi to visit Wuyong Kuan.
Wuyong’s gate was strictly austere; as soon as the Master entered the door, [Kuan] shouted at him with a stern voice.
The Master performed a prostration outside the gate. After a long time, he was finally permitted to enter and see him. [Wumen] asked, "Where are you from? The Master replied, "Tongzhou.
[Wumen] asked, "How have things been lately in Huaihai—full or empty? The Master said, "The waters drench the sun and overflow the heavens;
not a single drop remains. Wumen immediately shouted and sent him out. The Master withdrew and did not sleep all night. One day, he heard Wumen cite Yunmen’s "Sumeru."

While they were conversing on the mountain, before the words had even ceased, the Master suddenly attained realization. He hurried forward, and Yuanwu struck him, saying, "What about Zhaozhou’s 'No-Character'?
The Master immediately replied, "Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; the myriad phenomena all beg for their lives. An empty basket holds dead snakes;
adding much or reducing little leaves nothing behind. Yuanwu sighed deeply. From then on, the Master attended him closely.

He attended [Wu]kuan for three years. Wu, having previously commissioned an image of himself based on the meaning of the "Severing Cliff" (Duanya) verse, personally inscribed it and presented it to the Master, saying:
"Your karmic conditions lie in the south. When you encounter a dragon, stay; when you meet a pond, dwell. The Master then accepted the command and returned south.
At that time, the venerable masters Xugu Ling, Yuansou Duan, Laiweng Qing, and Huanzhu Ben each occupied famous mountains. Great...

He manifested his transformative power through the spiritual capacities of others, striking them with his teaching such that all were brought into perfect accord. In the Gengshen year of the Yuan Dynasty (1320), he resided at Dàdòng in Guǎngdé.
To the left of the cave was Shíxiàng Temple, the site of the dharma-seat of Chénggōng, a disciple of Mázū. The Master restored this ruined site.
At that time, there was an elderly monk who had not fully realized the Way; he had fled to Shìxī, which lay facing the cave. People referred to this area as Guǎngdé.
The *Two Gates of Ambrosia* states: In the Guihai year of the Zhizhi era, the people of Longchi in Yixing respectfully invited the Master.

As his name corresponded to a prophetic record, he joyfully accepted the invitation. He named the site Yumen (Dragon Gate). Previously, there had been a pool at the summit of the mountain, its depth unfathomable;

whenever a dragon emerged, it would cause great floods, causing distress to the local residents. The Master conferred upon the dragon the Three Refuges precepts, whereupon it ceased to appear. He resided there for a long time.

He again went to a precipitous ridge to build a dwelling; the cliffs stood like they had been carved. He hewed wood to create a platform and settled upon wooden boards suspended in mid-air, his feet never crossing the boundary for three years.
The Imperial Preceptor, having long recognized the Master’s spiritual practice, conferred upon him the title Chan Master Hongjiao Pujie (Great Teaching, Universal Salvation).
In the year Tianding Yichou, he moved to Jiulisi; in Zhisun Gengwu, he moved again to Lishan; and in Yuantong Jiashu, [he went to] Zhejiang.

He served as the General Administrator of the Eastern Route of the West River and was the abbot of Tianning Wanshou Monastery in Changzhou. At the earnest invitation of the local governor, he accepted the post for eight years;
in recognition of his merits, he was bestowed the title "Wondrously Enlightened, Truly Pure" (Benjue Miaoming Zhenjing). In the year of Renwu of the Zhizheng era, he returned once more to Longchi.

Subsequently, he was summoned to the capital, where he was commanded to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma at Longguang Hall. The Emperor was greatly pleased and conferred upon him a golden-embroidered dharma robe. Furthermore...
He was titled Fohuixin (Awakened to the Buddha-mind). In the year Gengzi, he went forth to lead Shanquan Temple. In the year Jiaomao, Guangde suffered a severe drought;
when the Master arrived, a great rain poured down like a torrent. The assembly earnestly requested him to reside at Cihui Hermitage on Mount Macheng.

In the sixth month of summer during the Jiyou year of the Hongwu era of Emperor Taizu of Ming, he manifested slight illness. He instructed his disciples to cut paper and prepare inner and outer robes, saying, "I am about to depart."
He ordered the reliquary shrine to be moved to a remote precipice. Taking up his brush, he wrote a verse: "For seventy-eight years I have guarded my simplicity;
Clearly, it has all been one great failure. The clay ox turns over in the depths of the sea; In the midsummer heat, snow falls from the sky. Having finished writing, he passed away peacefully.

One month prior, the water in the pond had suddenly run dry; when the Master entered *parinirvāṇa*, it gushed forth more abundantly than ever before. Monks and laypeople alike were filled with longing.

Many came to admire him; some even burned their heads or scorched their arms as an act of offering. Upon his cremation, five-colored light manifested, and his teeth, jaw, and tongue remained unharmed.

His *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. His disciples divided the remaining bones and the indestructible remains among five locations—Longchi, Taiping, Qishan, Ziyun, and Mazhong—and constructed stupas to enshrine them. He was seventy-eight years old at the time of his death. [He was a] monk.
At sixty-five years of age, he had four recorded collections of his discourses (*yulu*) circulating in the world.

He was subsequently appointed to manage the storehouse keys; soon after, he was ordered to share the teaching seat. When Zhushu passed away, the Master succeeded him in leading the monastery's affairs. Not long thereafter, he left.
He arrived at Bai Zhang and ascended Mount Kāśyapa. Crossing the Yangtze River, he entered the Huai region to pay homage at the stupas of the various patriarchs.
From Jianye, he returned to Zhejiang, and subsequently went back to Ba’en Temple in Yongjia. He was later appointed as the abbot of Jiangxin Temple and further established Guiyuan Temple in Pingyang.
The imperial court bestowed upon him the temple plaque and a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*, conferring upon him the title Chan Master Foxing Yuanbian. The Chancellor Yan Zhibuhua...

He governed the region of Min and was invited to reside at Dongchan and Xuefeng. At the beginning of the Hongwu era of Emperor Ming, an edict was issued summoning ten eminent monks of realized virtue to assemble at Mount Zhongshan.
The Master responded to this imperial summons and ascended the seat to preach the Dharma; the Emperor visited in person and bestowed upon him the utmost consolation and honor.
Upon returning south, he was appointed as the abbot of Jingci. In the sixth year, he was again summoned to the capital. Shortly thereafter, he manifested a slight illness and bathed.
He spoke these verses and passed away while seated.
Chan Master Bifeng Baolin of Lingjiu Peak at Mount Wutai in Taiyuan was a successor of Chan Master Zhen of Jinyun; he was the son of the Shi family of Yongshou in Qianzhou.
He was named Zhou of Yiping. His parents were devoted to the good. A śramaṇa bestowed upon them an image of Avalokiteśvara. Not long after, the Master was born.

At the time of his birth, a white light filled the room, which his parents found extraordinary. When he was just six years old, they sent him forth to leave the household life. After he had undergone the tonsure and received the precepts—
Having traveled extensively among the lecture halls, he suddenly sighed and said, "The study of the Tripiṭaka is merely pointing at the finger that indicates the moon.

He then changed his robes and went to visit Zhina Ruhai at Jin-yun. There, he applied himself with diligent effort day and night; once, while carrying a basket to gather vegetables, he suddenly sat motionless in meditative concentration.
After three periods [of time], he finally awoke. Zhen asked, "Did you enter meditative absorption? The Master replied, "Yes. Zhen asked, "What did you see?
The Master said, "I have attained an awakening. Zhen asked, "How is this awakening? The Master held up his basket to show him. Zhen said, "Not so.
The Master set the basket on the ground and stood with his hands clasped before him. Zhen said again, "Not so. The Master then let out a shout. Zhen grabbed him by the chest and held him fast.
[The Master] said, "Speak! Speak! The Teacher clenched his fist and struck him. Zhen said, "Not yet. This was merely a temporary cessation of worldly toil.

You must cause the path of the mind to be cut off and penetrate the Patriarchal Barrier; only then can the Great Dharma be clarified. From that time on, the Teacher did not let his side touch the mat for three years.
One day, hearing the sound of wood being felled, his sweat fell like rain, and he said, "The ancients said, 'A great awakening occurs in one..."
"Eighteen times over. Small awakenings have been countless. How could I deceive you? Only today do I finally know what occurred before birth.
Hurry to see Zhen and seek certification. Zhen did not grant his consent. The Master overturned the meditation seat and left. The following day he saw Zhen again;
Zhen drew thirty circular diagrams, and the Master answered each one in detail. Zhen laughed loudly and said, "In this world, how many who study under a teacher have attained awakening?"

"There are none. Those capable of manifesting the great function of the spiritual capacity—how many such people could there possibly be? He then conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) and commanded him to go to the north, where the Way would be widely propagated.
Previously, while in meditative absorption, the Master had seen a mountain of exquisite beauty, with multi-storied pavilions and magnificent halls shimmering in gold and green.
Bodhisattvas were practicing the Way therein, and one of them beckoned to the Master, saying, "This is Secret Demon Rock (*Bimbara-giri*)."
"You are cultivating the Way therein; why have you so hastily forgotten it?

Later, while the Master was traveling to Mount Tai, he encountered a woman with disheveled hair, wearing tattered garments of five colors and walking barefoot at a slow pace, followed by a black mastiff.

The Master asked where she was going. She replied, "Into the mountains. The Master asked, "For what purpose do you enter the mountains? She replied, "I do not do anything at all. Having spoken, she vanished. [The Master] struck [the ground].

His companions could not see him at all; some said he was a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Mañjuśrī. Consequently, the Master established the Lingjiu Hermitage on the mountain to await those who would come from afar.
Monastics and laypeople, hearing of his reputation, flocked there from a thousand *li* away, often numbering as many as ten thousand.

In the winter of the Wuzi year of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era, he was summoned into the inner court. It happened that it was a great snowfall, and at night, a red light issued directly from the Master’s chamber.
It pierced the Milky Way. The Emperor above was struck with wonder and bestowed upon him a golden brocade *kāṣāya*. The following year, his prayers for rain were immediately answered;

by imperial decree, he was granted the title "Great Zen Master of Silent Illumination and Perfect Clarity" (*Jigao Yuanming Dacanshi*), and an edict ordered him to reside at Haerin Temple. During the early Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, the Emperor Gaozu summoned the Master to the capital, where he resided at Tianjie Temple.
His exposition of the Dharma met with the Emperor's approval. In the *Xinhai* year, he established the Pujihui (Universal Salvation Assembly) on Mount Zhong, and the Emperor commanded—

The Master presided over these affairs. He was granted *īśvara-phala* (vegetarian) offerings, and the Emperor personally visited him, bestowing a poem written with his own imperial brush; the honors and gifts were most generous.
In the sixth month of the Renzi year, he bathed, changed his robes, assembled the congregation to bid them farewell, and when his disciples requested a verse, the Master said:
"The Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures are still but old paper; what purpose would my words serve? He then sat upright and closed his eyes. His worldly age was sixty.
15. With fifty years of monastic seniority (*saṃgha-rakṣā*), his *dhātu* (relics) formed five colors upon cremation; his teeth and tongue remained uncorrupted.

This was Chan Master Zufang Dao of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, a successor to Chan Master Jianyan Yizhao. He was the son of the Lu family of Ning County in Siming. At the age of fourteen, he paid homage to...

Kunshan Jianyan invited Yue Tang Yan to receive ordination. He observed the precepts at Wutai in Ningbo and subsequently returned to serve as an attendant to Wuxian Xi at Jianyan, where he attained significant spiritual realization.
In the *bingchen* year of the Ming Hongwu era, he served under Fuxin while the latter resided at Linggu Monastery.
Tiantai Tan invited him to serve as the head of the secretariat (*jishi*). Mu’an Kang, Shuzhong Yun, and Muguan Cong all became his friends beyond their age differences.
Later, he resided at Guangxiao in Tiantai, then moved to Zituo, Mayu, Jingshan, Putuo in Mingzhou, and Nengren in Yuezhou. At the end of his life, he presided over Jingci Monastery.
In the year of Renshen, when Jingci was afflicted by the planet Mars (Venus), the Master renovated it entirely. The Prince of Shu bestowed upon him a patched robe and an alms bowl.
In the year of Bingxu during the Yongle era, the imperial court summoned the Master to serve as the General Director of the Buddhist Teachings; subsequently, he returned home.
He built a dwelling by the lakeshore and named it "Lotus Flower Abode" (Ōuhua Ju). In the year Dinghai, he traveled to the capital at the imperial summons for official business.

The Emperor ordered him to reside at Yuguo Temple on Mount Wutai. Not long after, he ascended the throne [of the hall] and suddenly said to his attendants, "My worldly karmic ties have likely come to an end.

Three days later, he bathed, changed his robes, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. This was on the third day of the seventh month in the year Jichou. He was returned to the Lotus Flower Abode for burial.

He lived in the shade of Huaju Monastery. His worldly lifespan was sixty-four years, and his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-vatsara*) was fifty. He left behind a collection of *yìyù* (unrestrained utterances) that circulates in the world.

Chan Master Wumeng Si'cong of Xiangyan in Ruzhou, a native of Lushan, was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Cihua Qiong. When he first visited Dufeng, [the master] ordered him to contemplate: "Not a single thing..."
Regarding the phrase "This mind is not Buddha, it is not a thing," Yunfeng, Yueshan, and five others established a covenant to investigate it together to its ultimate conclusion.
Subsequently, they visited Huaixi Wuneng, who instructed them to investigate the "Mu" (No) kōan.
One day, while conversing with his fellow practitioner, the Venerable Jing, Jing asked, "Over these six or seven years, what realization have you attained? The Master replied, "Every day..."
"Right now, there is not a single thing. Jing said, "Where does this whole bundle of yours come from? The Master was at a loss.
He then asked, "Ultimately, how should one clarify this great matter? Jing said, "Have you not heard it said:
'If you wish to know the essential meaning, look southward at the Big Dipper'? Having said this, he departed. Pressed by these words, the Master was completely at a loss for what to do.
For seven days, while walking and sitting in meditation, he happened to visit the bath attendant’s quarters. His state of doubt remained unresolved.
After a short meal-time interval, he suddenly felt a lightness and clarity within his chest; all people and things before him vanished from view, and sweat poured from his entire body.
He then encountered Jing, who held up a fan and said, “Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master immediately replied, “It is manifest when raised—how wondrous! A pure breeze pervades everywhere.”
It permeated his heart completely. "The message within this is not much," he thought, until he attained a state of total joy throughout his entire being.
From then on, when he spoke or composed verses, he encountered no obstacles whatsoever. Yet, even so, he could not find a sense of ease in his daily activities.
Consequently, he went to Mount Xiangyan to spend the summer retreat and again visited Wufang Pu. Pu asked him, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return?"
The Master said, "The nose stands upright and the eyes are slanted. Baizhang Pu said, "That is something learned. The Master said, "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree;
when the duck is cold, it enters the water. Baizhang Pu said, "I do not ask about that. What is your original face before your parents were born?"
The Master raised his fist and said, "Look! Fupin said, "A good thirty blows for you. The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
It happened that at that time Tieshan had returned from Goryeo and arrived at Shishuang. The Master went to see him. Tieshan asked, "Where is your native place?
The Master replied, "Ruzhou. Tieshan asked, "What is the countenance of Fengxue like? The Master then explained the twenty years of his diligent practice.
Yibian held him by the throat and asked, "What is the word 'Mu'? The Master said, "I have recently come from Tanzhou;
I have not received news from Hubei. Yishan said, "That is not it; speak further. The Master said, "When did you leave Goryeo, Preceptor?"

Mount [Shan] said, "You have not yet reached it; speak further. The Master then gave a shout and, shaking his sleeves, departed. Mount Shan said, "This brother is excellent in every way, yet he has one great ailment: he claims that he has attained realization.
Hearing this, the Master was moved by a sense of urgency and returned to the mountains of Guangzhou.

Only after seventeen years did he achieve complete liberation. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma has no fixed characteristics; when it encounters conditions, it becomes the source. He held fast to this principle.
The Vajra-sword swallows the thorns of the jujube bush and cuts off the tongues of the monks. It sits upon the crown of Vairocana’s head.
Taking a single blade of grass, it makes it the sixteen-foot golden body; taking the sixteen-foot golden body, it makes it a single blade of grass.
It leaves not even a thread of silk hanging, like the cold moon in the autumn sky, where cold ashes burst into flame. Arriving at this point, to call it "Buddha-dharma" is to enter the earth.
"Entering hell is like being struck by an arrow. It is not called 'Buddha-dharma. Entering hell is like being struck by an arrow. "Venerable ones, how will you ultimately understand this?
Have you not seen what the Boatman said: 'Where one hides the body, there is no trace; where there is no trace, do not hide the body'?
"Nevertheless, when viewed with the True Eye, all of these are merely idle furnishings. As for the portion belonging to a patch-robed monk..."
This was beyond the reach of ordinary discourse.
Chan Master Jizhao Wujie Dao of Yufeng in Yixing, Changzhou, was the son of Zhao of Wuxing.
At the time of his birth, a white light filled the room for three nights. It coincided with the descent of the Yuan army into the south; his mother, Lady Ji, was captured by the roaming troops.
He departed to seek his mother. Holding the name of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) most earnestly, he searched everywhere for more than ten years until he found her in Hejian.
Thereupon, they traveled together to pay homage at Putuo, where they received the tonsure from Tieshan Qiong.
Next, he visited Ji’an Xin at Daochang and Wuyin Yuan at Jingci. While boating on the lake, he heard a fisherman’s song and attained a sudden realization. He presented this to Yuan, who—
He said, "There is no place for you to settle here. The Master shook out his robes and departed. He subsequently built a hermitage on the southern slope of Mount Bian.
After his mother passed away and he had completed her burial, one night a person dressed in white appeared in the air and said, "Your karmic affinity lies in Yixing.

Thereupon, he obtained Mount Yufeng and established the Jizhao Chan Monastery. The people of the district followed him with great devotion. During the *wenzong* era of the Yuan dynasty, in the *Renshun* cycle year...
On the sixth day of the first month of the year Shen, he passed away while sitting cross-legged without illness. His secular age was sixty-five, and his monastic seniority was thirty years.
Following cremation, countless relics were recovered and enshrined in two pagodas at Jizhao and Zhongyin;
Zhongyin is located to the northeast of the county seat and was also founded by the Master himself.
Chan Master Lichong Cheng of Puming Monastery in Hangzhou, a descendant of the twenty-third generation under Nanyue and a dharma heir of Chan Master Fanglian,
was born into the Sun family of Qiantang. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order at Ciguang Monastery.
When Ruoshan left the household life, he first visited Zufa. In the meditation hall, Zufa raised the koan regarding the story of the mountain being burned by fire in the twelfth lunar month.
Ruoshan presented a verse, saying: "The white clouds obscure my former tracks; In the twelfth month, the mountain-fire burns bright red. Suddenly, the breeze of compassion fans it forth;
Where it was cold and freezing, it becomes warm and glowing. Zufa praised him. Later, Ruoshan established Puming Temple in Beiguo.
To welcome those yet to come, Ming Emperor Yingzong ascended the hall on the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the *Xinyou* year of the *Zhengtong* era.
At eighty-one years of age, he said: "Old age and illness follow conditions as I pass my days; this year I shall record the matters of next year, and next year I shall record the events of today.
On the *Guiyou* year, exactly as predicted, he passed away while seated. He was eighty-three years old. His remains were cremated, and no *śarīra* relics were found.
Calculating [the dates], he constructed a stupa at Puming.
Chan Master Zha’ān Zongjing of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was styled the Elder Tianxuan. He was the son of the Gao family of the prefecture.

Having tonsured himself at his home mountain from childhood, he happened upon the time when Zu Fanglian was presiding over the affairs of the monastery; the Master relied upon him and, after a long period, attained the essential meaning. Subsequently...

The Key to the Imperial Collection. In the *Xinmao* year of the Yongle era of the Ming Chengzu, he was selected by imperial decree to serve as the protector of the state. He subsequently moved to Xuedou.
In the *Yichou* year of the Zhengtong era of the Ming Yingzong, the Director of the Sangha Registry (Senglü) nominated him to fill the vacant seat at Jingci Temple.

In the *Dingmao* year, the imperial court bestowed upon him a copy of the Tripitaka; the Master went to the palace to express his gratitude and stayed at Mita Temple, where he manifested slight illness and addressed the Left...
The Master said, "My karmic conditions have come to an end. He bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away in stillness.
His secular age was seventy-six, and his monastic seniority was sixty. He was interred at the ancestral mound of Ouhua, where his *Recorded Sayings* from three assemblies remain in circulation.
Zen Master Taichu Qiyuan of Hulong, Ruian, Wenzhou, was a Dharma heir of Zen Master Wushi Yuchan. He was the son of the Japanese imperial clan, the Genji; his father was a high-ranking official.
At the age of nine, he was sent to Kennin-ji Temple to enter the monastic life. At eighteen, he requested an imperial edict to travel south for study, and spent three years on this journey.
He arrived in Fuzhou during the second month of the丙午 (bingwu) year of the Yuan Zhizheng era. He proceeded to the capital to present tribute and was introduced to the Emperor.

The Emperor was pleased and issued an imperial decree for him to meet with Jitan Le, instructing him to travel extensively to seek instruction from various masters. Later, he visited Wushi Jiefeng Yu. One day—

Yuyuan ascended the hall and said, "Snow covers the thousand mountains; why then is the solitary peak not white? A monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "The thunder rumbles, yet there are no raindrops at all.
Yuyuan said, "A thatched hut is roofed with lapis lazuli tiles; within a stone chamber is hidden an agate vase.
The monk said, "A tiger has mounted upon a tiger from the South Mountain. Yuyuan said, "A tiger gives birth to seven cubs; which one is it?"
"The one without a tail. The Master said, "The seventh one. Yuyi said, "I grant you thirty blows. From this, he was permitted to enter the inner chamber.
Later, he took his leave and went out of the mountain, where he thatched a hut on Mount Lu. He subsequently moved to Shilong and entered the world at Guangdu.
He moved to Sanfeng in Luoyang and later moved again to Hulong, where he once uttered the "Three Barriers" (Sanguan yu). The first says:
"The Śūnyatā-deva—why does he drag through mud and water upon level ground? The second says:
"The Golden-Winged Bird King splits the sea to seize and swallow dragons—why is he swallowed by a loach? The third says: "The Buddhas of the three periods cannot speak it."

"What does the *māhā* recite, you cat and white ox? On the first day of the third month in the *dinghai* year of the Yongle era of the Ming Emperor Chengzu, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:
"In life, it is an iron mask; in death, it is an iron mask. With a single blow, all is shattered into a hundred fragments.
He then said, "The sun circles Mount Sumeru," threw down his brush, and passed away while sitting. His stupa was erected at Nanyuan.
Chan Master Daoyong of Linggu Monastery in Jinling, whose style name was Feihuan Wuya, was the son of the Wu family of Xian’an in Quzhou.
His father dreamed that Mingguo arrived at his door before he was born. He entered the monastic order under Yufeng Yu of Wushi Mountain. Yu asked him, "Where have you come from?"
The Master responded at once, saying, "Empty space has no front or back. The boy pointed to a bell and showed it to the Master. The Master spontaneously composed a verse:
"Rolled out from within the hundred-fold smelting furnace, Empty space itself is never stained by dust. Now it hangs upon the heads of men; When struck, its great sound pervades the nine realms.
At that time he was only twelve years old. The boy was greatly amazed by this and immediately offered him congratulations.

Fahai served in his subordinate position for a long time; as his diligent devotion accumulated, all doubts and obstructions were completely resolved, and he attained unimpeded eloquence. Yu (the Master) gave him his seal of approval.
During the Yongle era of the Ming Chengzu, he was promoted to Right Director of the Buddhist Registry (Senglü You Chanjiao) and was decreed to reside at Linggu Monastery.

At that time, the court established a great vegetarian assembly (*dazhaihui*), and the ritual officials overseeing the affairs were extremely strict. Yet the Master appeared as if he paid them no mind, which caused those around him to wonder and question him.
The Master said, "I have a matter of great importance that is most urgent; I have no leisure for anything else. He bathed, changed his robes, sat in the lotus position, and wrote this verse:
"Life and death drift on, severed from worldly ties; Having received this grace, I rejoice forever in years of peace.

This time, casting off my hands, I return to emptiness; The snow has cleared, the clouds have vanished, and the moon is full. Having set down his brush, he passed away. When the Emperor heard of this, he dispatched an envoy...
The authorities performed the sacrificial rites. His *śarīra* were cremated, and the relics were distributed like rain. His disciples erected a stupa in the western valley of this temple.
He was the twenty-fifth generation descendant of Nanyue.
Chan Master Puan of Cihua in Yuanzhou, Jiangxi, was a dharma heir of Chan Master Mudian Qian.
Having received Mudian’s seal of transmission and instruction, he preached the Dharma in response to the capacities of his audience, much like Yanxiang or Hualin.
Having attained mastery over the Dharma, his transcendent and unrestrained brilliance was peerless; yet, people of the world often regarded him as a spirit.

Tong-seng identified him as such, yet he did not know that the Master was an ancient sage who had arisen through the power of his vows, manifesting in the human world to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddha and to guide and transform all beings;
he was truly an emissary of the Tathāgata. Even those who recently continued the transmission of the lamp regarded the Master as a divine monk (shénsēng), yet they omitted him from their records.
Now, having verified these facts, he has been included here, appended alongside Lùluó Dùn’ǒu Jì.

Verses for Paying Homage at the Stupa: The Master, riding upon the power of compassionate vows, arose as a lamp and banner for the world. Through divine transport, he responded to the resonance of sentient capacities;

his spiritual penetration manifested the Dharma. As the sound of the bell fades into the stillness of the evening, the aged cypress sheds its cold fragrance. Flowers fall like rain upon the stūpa; one should know that his protective embrace endures long.
