To the assembly: "The Old Man Śākyamuni could not push him open; Master Bodhidharma could not drive him out.

He drew in three snakes and nine rats from the field of Huizhi. Everyone says it is easy to call a snake, but difficult to send one away. [He] patted his knee and said: "What difficulty is there? It is within the home."
There is the *Baize-tu* (Diagram of Baize), which states that such monsters and spirits certainly do not exist. [The Master] showed this to the assembly.
Regarding the methods for managing a household and making a living when a daughter is about to be married off, she must request instruction from her parents for every detail.

However, as for bearing children and raising them, one is naturally capable of this without needing instruction. Therefore, the Confucian classics state: "There has never been anyone who learned how to raise children before they were married. This is indeed true.
Alas! The monastics of the Chan school in recent times are not so. They first study the preaching of the Dharma, and only then do they study how to become Buddhas.

It would be better for them not to be able to become Buddhas than not to understand how to preach the Dharma. How strange! Although the Master did not take charge of administrative affairs at the monastery, he constantly provided guidance according to the needs of others.
The Provincial Chancellor and other high officials all bowed their heads in prostration, performing the rites of disciples, and frequently rose up to serve him in the provinces of Jiang and Zhejiang.
Regarding various famous mountains, Jian refused to go to them and instead withdrew his traces to the Rongong area.

His disciples went to the region of Wu and constructed buildings on a site according to the regulations of a monastic forest (saṅghārāma), naming it Shizi Lin (Lion Grove). He resided there for thirteen years, and his reputation for the Way grew daily.

In the Jiamu year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, the Imperial Preceptor conferred upon him the title "Chan Master Foxin Pujie Wenhui Dabian" (Buddha-Mind Universal Salvation Wise-Wisdom Great Eloquence Chan Master), as well as—
He was granted a golden-embroidered Dharma robe. After his passing, he was interred in a stupa at Suiseigen.
Zen Master Kosen Ingen of Japan’s Kennin-ji Temple was the son of the Fujiwara clan of Sagami Province in his native land. The Fujiwara were the nobility of the nation.
At birth, the Master exhibited extraordinary signs; at the age of thirteen, his parents suddenly relinquished him to the monastic life, whereupon he received the tonsure and the precepts.

After receiving full ordination, he was filled with resolute determination and sailed south. Upon his first audience with Wujian at Tiantai, Wujian directed him to go to Tianmu to study under Zhongfeng Ben.

The Master served as his attendant. On several occasions, the Master presented his own insights, but Zhongfeng Ben rebuked him, saying, "If you do not sever the connection between the faculties and their objects, how can you be free from entanglement?
The Master withdrew and wept bitterly; he neglected both eating and sleeping. Moved by his sincerity, Zhongfeng Ben...
He said to him: "This mind encompasses all phenomena. In delusion, it is birth and death; in awakening, it is nirvana.
The delusion of birth and death is indeed not easily cast off, yet the awakening of nirvana is still but a speck of gold dust before the eye. Always know that Prajñā is like a great mass of fire:
to draw near it is to scorch one's head and sear one's brow. One must maintain only the single thought of non-retrogression. Thus he was born.
"Born together with me, you shall die together with me; naturally, you shall accord with the Way.

He further said, "Should you fail to awaken at this juncture, even if ten thousand Śākyamunis and a thousand Maitreyas were to pour out the waters of the four great oceans into your faculty of hearing, it would all be nothing but empty, delusive toil—none of it ultimate.
Upon hearing this, the Master was suddenly struck with awe, and sweat broke out from him. One day, he attained realization and hurried to inform his teacher.
Yin said, "You have already crashed into the silver mountains and iron walls. Wuben asked, "Since you have entered the silver mountains and iron walls, why have you come here?
The Master attained clear realization. Wuben then instructed him, saying, "Guard and uphold this well yourself.

He subsequently studied under various masters, including Xugu Ling, Gulin Mao, Dongyu Hai, and Yuejiang Yin; all these elders referred to him as a "lion cub. It was during this time that he met [the Master].
Seigen Chūshin returned to his native country, bringing the Master back with him; those both far and near revered them.
Initially, he presided over Eirin-ji in Kōshū, subsequently serving in eight different temples, before finally residing at Kenjō-ji in Sōshū. One day, manifesting illness, he said to his attendant:
"The time has come; you may bring your brush and inkstone. He then said, "My stupa is finished, but its plaque has not yet been inscribed.

He then boldly wrote the two characters "Xinyin" (Mind-Seal) and passed away while sitting upright. Initially, his disciples wished to paint a portrait of the Master and requested a eulogy in advance.
The Master drew a perfect circle and inscribed above it: "The wondrous form is perfectly luminous; suchness is unmoving. It meets one everywhere."
What kind of person was he? He lived to the age of eighty and had sixty-seven years of monastic seniority.
Master Nian’an Yuánhù of Yún’ān Cāngshān was a native of Dàlǐ. He attained realization through reading the *Zhèngdào gē* (Song of Realizing the Way).
The Du family bestowed upon him the title Master Hongbian. He studied under Zhongfeng Ben; the Master’s original name was Wunian (No-Thought).

Ben questioned him regarding the principles of "no-thought" and "non-arising" as expounded by Kumārajīva when he held the bowl and by Yongjia Xuanjue. The Master said: "My 'no-thought' differs from what they have heard.
The fault of Master Kumārajīva lay in the cessation of thought so that it does not arise; the fault of Yongjia lay in allowing thought to arise of its own accord."
Both of these involve mindfulness. As for my "no-mindfulness" (wunian): the essence of the mind is numinous, profoundly still, and unmoving.

It is like a mirror reflecting images, or like a lamp illuminating objects; it has never concealed even a hair’s breadth [of reality]. Only those who have thoroughly penetrated the source of the Dharma can fathom this;

it is not easy to discuss with those whose emotions are entangled and whose consciousness is bound. Originally, Shenken agreed with this and composed the "Exposition of the Words on No-Mindfulness. Hereafter...

Having received the seal of certification, he returned; the records widely refer to him as the Guardian Master (Huzangzhu). The Master dreamed that a deity bestowed upon him the methods of calligraphy.
Whenever he wrote characters, his right wrist appeared transparent like crystal, leading people to style him the "Jade-Wrist Chan Master" (Yuwanzhanshi).
Among his writings, the *Mirror-Polishing Method* (*Mojingfa*) and his own handwritten *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) have circulated in the world.
Anning Taihua Wuzhao Xuanjian was the first to serve as the head seat (*śāstrin*). He was skilled in expounding the sutras and śāstras, and his fame spread throughout all quarters.
Having traveled extensively across the land, he had deeply immersed himself in the gates of both Buddhist traditions and attained profound realization. He subsequently studied under Fenggong Miaoyan.
He served as the head seat (*śrīlābha*). After Miaoshiji passed away, he again met Zhongfeng Ben and once more became the first seat. Ben remarked:
"The Dharma Master Jian from Yunnan traveled eighteen thousand *li* to come to the two provinces of Zhejiang. From the time we first met until our parting, exactly three years have passed.
One day, he sought me out while I was traveling, and we conversed late into the night amidst the lakes and mountains. We then raised several passages from the Chan school."
This was a case of rotten, entangling vines. Unaware, he bit off his own thumb. As they were about to part in haste, the Master did not wish to investigate his offense;
he let him go with one stroke of leniency. With this, the dust of kalpas of accumulated toil was suddenly blown away by the lines: "The wind at the Black Dragon Pool in the fifth watch.
The Master returned to Yunnan, where he was held in high esteem by the Prince of Liang. He opened the Taihua Mountains and greatly propagated the ancestral Way. His disciples...

He had several hundred disciples, five of whom attained the Master’s mind-seal (*citta-mudrā*). Upon his passing, the King personally visited the burial site and enshrined his entire body in a stupa at the original mountain.
When Benwen (Wumen) received the news of the Master’s death, he personally composed a memorial inscription and dispatched an attendant to offer sacrifices. The text read in brief:
"I have observed many people, yet they are like those without a mirror; not only are such rare today, but they were also scarce in antiquity."
I do not grieve for the loss of that which lacks illumination; rather, I grieve that the ancestral Way has already fallen.

From this day forward, who will support the tottering and sustain the precarious? As I face the incense burner this evening, I share with the mountains, rivers, plants, and trees a sorrow for this world that is severed from the Way.
Chan Master Chongzhao of Panlong Lianfeng in Jining was the son of the Duang family of that prefecture. At the age of eighteen, he paid his respects to Yunfeng to receive the tonsure.
Yunfeng instructed him with the koan regarding the dog having Buddha-nature; for seven days, he severed all discursive thought to contemplate it.
One day, hearing the sound of wood being felled, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He subsequently traveled to the great monasteries and met ten masters, including Kong’an.

He had eight virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Finally, he met Tianmu Benyin, who granted him formal approval (*inka*). He returned to Yunnan and established Panlong Temple, where he resided.
On the full moon of the eighth month in the *Renwu* year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, he was summoned by the assembly to write a verse;

then, sitting in the lotus posture, he passed away. His body remained warm and supple, as if alive, for seven days. A rainbow pierced the sky for three days. To this day, his physical body remains present. So it is said.
He established six Brahma-purī monasteries, which were most magnificent and beautiful.

Chan Master Guimei Zhengyou of Gaoyang Mountain in Jianning Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Chengyan of Prajñā; he was the son of the Ding family of Guixi and relied upon Mount Moshan.
He originally received his training under Master Ye. Later, he studied under Master Juexue Cheng, through whom he clarified the fundamental tenets of the school.

He wandered through the Jianghuai region for nearly thirty years, seeking out beautiful mountains and waters where he might build a thatched hut to retire in seclusion. Admiring the secluded excellence of Wuyi, he eventually entered Min.
Initially, he presided over Tianxin in Nanpu. In the year of Jiǎzǐ during the Tiānbǎo era of the Yuán dynasty (1324), Jiǎng Dèmào, the Magistrate of Jiānyáng, along with the Elder...

Chen Yizong donated his garden to establish a hermitage and invited the Master to be its founding abbot. The imperial plaque bestowed upon it read "Dajue Miaozhi" (Great Enlightenment and Wondrous Wisdom).

Within his quarters, the Master constantly raised the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature to test and refine practitioners, never showing the slightest leniency. On the occasion of the opening of the retreat, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
Yangshan established the retreat. His ordinary livelihood was such that light shone from his eyes and his nostrils emitted breath. When hungry he ate; when weary he slept.

While others everywhere were scattering earth and raising dust, Yangshan’s mind was vast and empty, having attained the highest degree. Ascending the hall, he said: "The ninety-day period for restraining the feet has already passed its halfway mark.
If you have not yet clarified the ground of your own mind, it is like pulling a fire-drill—it will not produce fire. Do not let your time be spent in vain."
To resolve this idle case: on level ground, you have needlessly caught a thief. When the old monk comes forth to adjudicate for you, he says:
"The summer retreat—ascending the hall—is a deliberate error. The ninety-day restriction of the feet and the three-month *an-gu* (sitting in peace) are but self-binding without a rope."
The cloth bag is untied; heaven and earth are vast and empty. Letting go is like tortoise hair; gathering it back is like hanging a rabbit's horn.
Try hanging both eyes in the void; a gust of cool wind arises at the corner of the hall. Small Assembly: The moon has set behind the mountain peak, and all is bleak.
Clouds hang across the mouth of the valley, shrouding it in shadow. If you wish to clarify the matter of birth and death, you must see directly the person of original nature.

Is there anyone who can realize this person of original nature? After a long silence, he said: "When the night is still, there is no need to borrow the moon again; the jade hare dwells eternally within the great void.
The Master was born in the *yǐyou* year of the Zhìyuán era of Emperor Wǔzǔ of the Yuán dynasty and passed away in the *rénchén* year of the Zhìzhèng era of Emperor Shùndì.
He preached the Dharma for twenty-nine summers and remained in the world for sixty-eight autumns. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at his native mountain.
Zen Master Zhiyi Yizhen was the dharma successor of Zen Master Puren Deyin of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou; he was the son of the Zhao family of Lianxi in Wuzhou. At the age of ten, he...
He studied under Chautam at the Yanshuan Institute of Precious Stones. At fourteen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he began traveling to visit various masters.

At that time, Liao Ran was propagating the teachings of Dabian at Zhizhe Temple. The Master went there to pay his respects, whereupon their spiritual sparks ignited in mutual resonance. Liao Ran immediately appointed him as the attendant for the incense.

Later, when Dongyang presided over the monastic center, he invited the Master to serve as the recorder (*shuji*). Subsequently, he met Nanchu at Shuangjing Mountain, where he shared the teaching seat with him.
He preached the Dharma. In the year of Yiwu (1355) of the Zhizheng era, he appeared in the world at Xifeng Jingtusì.

In the year of Wuxu (1378), Emperor Taizu of the Ming personally led the Great Master to Wuzhou and visited Zhezhe Temple, issuing an imperial decree appointing the Master as its abbot. In the year of Jiachen (1384), he moved to Jingci Temple.
One day, manifesting a slight illness, he counted on his fingers and calculated, saying, "It is now the fifth month of summer. His attendants replied, "Indeed. The Master said, "The eighth month..."
"The eighth day is most auspicious; I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, he adjusted his robes, sat upright, and passed away.
His worldly age was sixty-four, and his years as a monk were fifty. He has three volumes of recorded sayings that circulate in the world.
Chan Master Zhizhan Dexiang of Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Jingci Lin.
He was a native of that province and, together with Tong’an, both were dharma heirs of Pingshan.

His virtuous conduct and refined character were highly esteemed by the worthies of his time. One day, as he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, the assembly requested him to speak a verse. The Master suddenly leaned back...
Zuo said, "This lot of wine-dregs swillers—what can I do against you? He then passed away into stillness.
During the Wumian year of the Hongwu era, Chan Master Tanyuan Yijian of Tong'an at Tianjie Monastery in Jinling became the abbot of Nanping Jingci.
Following the ravages of war, he renovated the halls, pagodas, bells, and drums, restoring them all. It is recorded that father and son succeeded one another on the seat.

A momentous occasion. In the twenty-fifth year [of his reign], by imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot of Dajianjie Monastery. Upon entering the monastery for the formal lecture on the high seat, he said:
"The Vairocana Buddha’s power of vow pervades the entire realm of sand-grains; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel.
As for this unsurpassed wheel—how does it turn? He struck the meditation staff and said, "It turns! It turns! Thereupon, he descended from the seat.
Chan Master Nanji Lanyun Zhian of Bailian on Mount Bian in Huzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Haimen Ze. He was the son of the Shen family of Jiaxing.

He left home at Jingmiao in Haining and visited Tianzhen, where he realized the essential meaning of the separate transmission. He concealed his brilliance and remained hidden from view, yet received invitations from various quarters.
He did not go. Later, he resided at White Lotus on Mount Bian and addressed the assembly: "The myriad dharmas return to the One. An unperforated iron hammer is hurled right before your face.
Where does the One return? It sweeps past the lands of India and Bingzhou.

A Linen Shirt from Qingzhou weighs seven catties. On the cold crags, ancient trees bloom with jade flowers in spring. O worthy ones, you ask earnestly for the ultimate point: the nostrils of one's mother-given self have been so from the beginning."
Zhi. Had he understood and known his place upon hearing these words, then "nine times nine" would have clarified "eighty-one. Later, he withdrew to return to the pure and wondrous.
He passed away, and his stupa was erected at Bian Mountain. Among his writings is the *Nanjie yuyao* (Essential Sayings of Nanjie).
Chan Master Bailing Zhidu of Fulin Monastery in Chuzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Huating Dushi. He was the son of the Wu family of Lishui.

At the age of fifteen, he received the tonsure from Chan Master Zhikong and practiced meditation at Lengqia Hermitage. After several summers had passed, he traveled to the region of Min, visiting various places throughout.
Traveling in various directions, he found no one whose views accorded with his own. He returned to his native village and built a dwelling there, naming it Folin (Blessed Forest).
Later, he visited Zhi of Lingshi at Jingci Monastery and called upon Yi of Duanya at Xifeng; in both cases, he did not find resonance.

Hearing that Wujian was preaching the Dharma at Mount Fahing, he went there to inquire of him, saying, "I do not yet understand the secret intent of the West—how is it? Wujian replied, "Wait for the *śāla* tree."
Feng nodded his head and said, "I shall tell you. As the Master was about to offer a word in response, Duan suddenly shouted.
The Master said, "At the summit of Mount Sola, white waves surge to the heavens; flowers bloom after芒種 (Mangzhong), and leaves fall before立秋 (Liqiu).

Duan said, "In my place, there is no leftover soup or stale rice. The Master said, "How could this not be leftover soup and stale rice? Duan nodded his head, and the Master thereafter served him with diligent devotion.
After several years, he took his leave. As he was departing, [Nanyue] looked at him and said: "In the past, Nanyue received the prediction and transmission from Dajian;
later, you received the mind-dharma from Mazu. It was like a needle meeting its eye—there was no need for many words. Do not wag your three-inch tongue to deceive others;
you must manifest true realization in your conduct, only then will you be able to repay the profound kindness of the Buddha. The Master took these words to heart and departed once more.
In Changsha, he visited Wufangpu; at Yunju, he called upon Xiaoyin. In the Jiamu year of the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, he returned to Folin.
He subsequently presided over Puci at Longquan, moved to Maoshan, and was later transferred to Wufeng.

In the Jiyou year of the Hongwu era under Emperor Taizu of the Ming, an imperial edict summoned eminent monks from throughout the land to hold a Dharma assembly at Jiangshan. The Master responded to the summons; as the proceedings were strictly regulated, he returned to Hangzhou.
He resided at Hupao. The following year, manifesting a slight illness, he returned to Folin. After bathing and changing his robes, he requested a brush and wrote a verse, saying:
"There is no world from which to take leave; there is no assembly with whom to part. Within the great void, what need is there to drive in stakes? He cast down the brush and passed away.
He was sixty-seven years of age and fifty-three years since his ordination. Upon cremation, relics of five colors were found, as were his teeth and rosary beads.
None were damaged. A pagoda was erected in the western courtyard.
The Chan Master Dameng Jingzhong Puzhuang of Hangzhou’s Jingshan Monastery, a dharma heir of the Chan Master Tiantong Yi, was the son of the Yuan family from Xianju, Tiantai. He relied upon...
Tiantong Zu’an left the monastic robes after a long time without attaining realization. He traveled abroad to visit Liaotang Yi at Tianning Monastery.
Yi asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Tiantong. Yi said, "Braving the rain and the cold, what such urgent business do you have?
The Master replied, "Precisely because the matter of birth and death is urgent. Yi asked, "What is this matter of birth and death? The Master made a striking gesture with his sitting cloth.
First: "Dare I come here to stroke the tiger's whiskers? [The Master] said, "Go to the hall. One day, while in the meditation hall, he raised the koan of the cypress tree in the courtyard.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, [the Master] struck him across the face with his palm. From this, he attained awakening.

Initially, he appeared in the world at Beichen in Fuzhou; later, he moved to Yunju. In the *Guiyou* year of the Ming Emperor Taizu’s Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned those of high conduct from throughout the land.
The śramaṇa Master accepted the imperial summons and responded with words that pleased the Emperor. That autumn, he was charged with the mission of offering sacrifices at Mount Lu;

when the rites were completed, the Emperor decreed that he should preside over Mount Jing. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Yunju? The Master replied, "The path turns and the stream winds back; the empty courtyard is still."

[The student] asked, "What is it like to be a person within the realm? The Master said, "In an era of great peace, one has a body of freedom. [The student] said, "I have already received your instruction regarding the person and the realm;
I wish to hear a single phrase for those at the beginning stage. The Master said, "A hairless hawk flies close to the sky.
[The student] asked, "When meeting a person who has attained the Way, if one does not respond with speech or silence, what then? The Master said, "One who has attained the Way."
[The monk] then realized [the truth]. He said, "How can you, Master, treat me with such hostility? The Master said, "Catching a thief is not as good as scaring one.
The monk said, "An eye of clarity cannot be deceived for even a single moment. The Master said, "I knew well that you did not have good intentions.
The Master once interrogated a monk, saying, "I have recently received an official document ordering me to 'settle' you, sir. The monk said, "I am no villain."
[The monk] said, "It is too subtle. The Master said, "One must still pass the examination before it is acceptable. [The monk] said, "Master, do not use your position to deceive people.

The Master extended his hand and said, "Bring forth your official document! As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm. Another monk said, "I have long heard that the Master possesses such a vital pivot of teaching.
The Master said, "This mountain monk has suffered a loss. A monk asked, "I have heard that the Master has the means to settle matters."
[The Master] asked, "Is it so? He gazed intently at him and said, "Have you come to confess? [The monk] replied, "This student has already overturned the meditation seat.
The Master asked, "Where are you from? [The monk] said, "Keep your eyes wide open! The Master said, "You are a spirit that clings to grass and perches on wood.
One day, the Master asked a newly arrived monk, "In this place of mine, tigers and wolves block the path, and thorns reach the heavens."
When the monk arrived, [the Master] asked, "What urgent business brings you here? The monk replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
The Master said, "I do not ask about the single phrase as you enter the gate; but as for the straw sandals beneath your feet, where did you get them? The monk hesitated, and the Master gave a shout.
He then asked, "Where did you leave from yesterday? The monk replied, "Mount Lu. The Master said, "There is no need for further examination. While the Master was weeding grass, a monk...
Question: "When will this patch of ground be cleared until it is perfectly clean? The Master raised his hoe and said, "I wonder, Senior Monk, what do you call this?
The monk was speechless. The Master threw down the hoe and said, "When will this patch of ground be cleared until it is perfectly clean?
Question: "Riding on the tiger's head and gathering up its tail—what about the matter in between? The Master said:
"He has attained freedom. [The student] asked: "It is just as the ancients said: 'I too cannot produce anything.

What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "Entering the water, one sees the tall man. [The student] asked: "Receiving the grace and bounty from the ninefold heavens above, you occupy the ancestral pass on the Five-Tufted Peak.
The Chan practitioners of the four seas all lean their ears; we pray to hear a single song of ten-thousand-year joy. I, your disciple, come forward."

"Come! Please, Master, offer a verse. The Master said, "Striking a golden bell atop the summit of Mount Sumeru. [The monk] said, "In that case, a person of transcendent measure clarifies matters of transcendent measure;
in times of great peace, one sings a song of great peace. The Master said, "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth.
[The monk] said, "The Master has traveled far from the capital and has recently arrived at Jingshan. What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said—
He said, "Wait until the Bowal Peak leaps; then I shall tell you. The other said, "I have just heard it said in the preface: 'A thousand-year-old withered tree meets spring;
a single generation’s *tánhuā* manifests as an auspicious omen. This may truly be called honest speech. The Master said, "Why do you employ so much consciousness and calculation?
The other said, "On this day when the feast for dragons and elephants is spread, one casually pulls out the brocade."
As he was about to depart, the Master said, "If you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, take care not to suffer the branding of the forehead. A monk requested further instruction.
The Master said, "In your own state, what is lacking that you come to request instruction? As the monk prepared to respond, the Master said, "You know only how to hurry along the journey;
you do not realize you have missed the way. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The alms bowl."

[The monk] turned his mouth toward the sky and said, "This is the property of the ancients. The Master said, "I, this old monk, use it most appropriately. [The monk] asked, "What is the extraordinary matter?
The Master said, "A field of a thousand years has eight hundred owners. [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It cannot be carried away even to this day;
it is left for the old farmer to plow. [Someone] asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The water falls from the cliff."
Shishu said: "It is just as the former masters have said: 'Upon the mountain there is a carp; at the bottom of the well there is dust.

What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "To see it and not seize it—to think of it for a thousand miles. He ascended the hall and cited Yunmen, who said: "On level ground there are countless dead people;
to emerge from the thicket of brambles is to be a masterful hand. At that time, a monk asked: "If that is so..."
"In that case, the head monk in the hall has a point of superiority. The Gatekeeper said, "Suru suru. The Master said, "Yunmen speaks thus; Yunju is not so.
On level ground there are countless people who can live; to enter the thorny forest is to be a true adept.
If someone were suddenly to come forth and speak of long and short, I would take up my staff and strike them across the spine. Why? Water."
"Moisture flows; fire seeks dryness. Calamity and fortune have no gate; it is only man who summons them himself. [The Master] addressed the assembly:

"Those who act as patriarchal masters have no choice but to provide instruction. A single word or half a phrase is nothing other than an attempt to pry out nails and extract wedges for students, to loosen adhesions and remove fetters.
It is like a skilled dancer with the Great Sword (Ta’a); naturally, they do not injure their own hands. Yet nowadays, those who occupy the seat of the master..."
They instruct their disciples merely to memorize characters and refine their speech for the sake of boasting to future generations, thereby increasing their evil habits;
they do not know the path by which they themselves emerged from birth. It is like one wearing tattered rags walking through a thicket of thorns, unable to move with ease.
The direct lineage of Shaolin has fallen to the ground here; this is truly a cause for lamentation. You who travel as itinerant monks must each carry your own eyes;
do not allow yourselves to fall into others' nets from which you cannot emerge. As the ancients said: "Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.
According to my own view, even if one were to suddenly forget all intellectual understanding, it would still be merely the gate.
"Foreign Han! Arriving here, you must distinguish between the black and the white before you may proceed. Take care! Ascending the hall, he said: "When every eye is met, one has never spoken;
when the feet move, how can one know the path? When the ancients spoke thus, it was much like laboring without merit.
As for my own view, I wish for all of you to know it together. He suddenly took up his staff, struck once, and said: "Only when the snow has melted away..."
Spontaneously spring has arrived; the Buddha is bathed and the assembly enters the hall. The true Buddha is formless—what is there to bathe?
In the Lumbinī Garden, one perceives empty flowers through delusion. If Yunmen’s command had not been put into practice, it would not have reached this day.
Suddenly grasping his staff, he calls to the assembly, saying: "How is the matter of today? One loses the sword in Kunming Lake, yet searches for it upon the banks of the Qujiang River."

Having received the saw, he set down his staff and descended from the seat. Entering the hall, he said: "When this old monk was clearing the wilderness, I unearthed a sharp axe from the site of the Dharma Hall.
For a long time I have kept it among you, brothers; if there is anyone who can make use of it, I shall entrust it to you with both hands.
But if you cannot bear its weight, I brought it here for no small reason of urgency—it would be better to cast it away."
"Stacked up in a heap; let it be scorched by the sun and blown away by the wind. Suddenly he picked up his staff, struck once, and said:
Whipping up the iron ox to plow the great earth—who can plant crabapples at the bottom of a well? Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Panshan showing the assembly:
"The mind-moon is solitary and full; its light swallows the ten thousand phenomena. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist.
When both light and objects are forgotten, what is it? Dongshan said, "If light and objects have not yet been forgotten, what is it? The Master said, "Two."

When the venerable elders play with objects whose names they do not know, I give each of them twenty blows of the staff. Has it not been said: "If one sees what is right and does not act upon it, what bravery is there?
On the first day of winter, he ascended the hall and spoke, citing the occasion when Dongshan was eating fruit with Chief Seat Tai during a winter night.
He asked: "There is a thing as bright as the sun and as black as lacquer; it is constantly present within activity. Activity...
"It cannot be gathered within the center. Where does the fault lie? Dazhu said, "The fault lies within movement and function.
Dongshan then ordered his attendant to remove the fruit table. The Master said, "To hesitate when one ought to sever leads, on the contrary, to invite chaos.
Had it been Jingshan, upon hearing him ask, 'Where does the fault lie? he would have immediately overturned the fruit table, thereby making Dongshan know that there is the [true] School."

He raised his staff and said, "If one does not shoot the stone tiger at Lan-tien, who would know him to be General Li?
He struck the staff and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "When one is deluded, all are deluded; when one awakens, all awaken. One...
All darkness is darkened; all light is illuminated. Thus it is said: "The dharmas of ordinary beings are fully present, yet ordinary beings do not know them;

if ordinary beings were to know them, they would be identical to sages. Reaching this point, worldly afflictions and *bodhi*-liberation are bound together as one.
A lump. Now tell me: in the Heaven of Neither Thought nor Non-Thought, how many people are currently cultivating the cause and realizing the fruit?
Holding up his staff, he said: "In a year there are three hundred and sixty days; every day begins from this very day. The staff also begins from this very day.
He struck the ground with the staff and said: "Shattering the gates of the Three Essentials and Three Mysteries, a pure breeze rises across the heavens and throughout the earth."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an instance: Once Xuan Sha drew a circle when Gushan arrived. Gushan said, "No one can get out of this.
Xuan Sha said, "I knew you would go about your business within the womb of a donkey or a horse.
Gushan asked, "How about you, Master? Xuan Sha said, "No one can get out of this. Gushan asked, "Why does the Master..."
"You can say it that way; I cannot say it that way. Xisha said, "I have attained it, but you have not.

Xuedou said: "Knowing only how to greedily gaze at the white waves, one does not realize that the hand-oar has been lost.

To fill the dust-motes and lands [of the universe]—this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

On the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the Guiwei year of the Yongle era of the founding emperor, he passed away at Budongxuan (The Immovable Studio). His secular age was fifty-eight; his monastic seniority was forty-five.
Wherever the smoke and flames of his cremation reached, śarīra relics appeared like strung beads. He was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Lingxiao Peak.

Chan Master Yuanming Yuanliang of Tiantong in Mingzhou was a dharma heir of Chan Master Shouchang Yuan. He was the son of the Zhou family of Ninghai. Initially he resided at Ruiyan, and later he moved to Tiantong.
He composed an inscription to accompany the stupa of Hongzhi, saying: "Alas! A mountain does not refuse the dust; thus it is able to achieve its [greatness]."
High indeed! Just as the ocean does not refuse the flowing streams, it is able to achieve its profound depth.

Were it not for the Master’s long-accumulated wheel of vows for the six perfections and ten thousand practices, how could he have established this great Dharma-work throughout antiquity and the present? When a Sage appears in the world, he acts as a teacher for a hundred generations;
such a once-in-a-thousand-year moment was attained only by the Master. Majestic is his stupa, which anchors this eastern valley. This is the first [inscription] of Dongshang.

The Patriarchate: As the true regulations begin to be restored, these humble words are proclaimed to be deeply engraved upon the cliffs and valleys. May the Master return once more to serve as a standard for the Dharma.
[Seal] of the Chan Master Tianjie, Dharma Heir.
Chan Master Juechu Hui’en of Jiangxin Temple in Wenzhou had long relied upon Fuxing. Fuxing resided by the Hulong River; the Master once shared the teaching seat with him to preach the Dharma.
Later, after Fuxing passed away, the Master emerged from seclusion at Shengquan in Jianye. He subsequently moved to Yashan in Yongjia.
Not long thereafter, the seat at Jiangxin became vacant, and the Prefectural Governor submitted a formal petition requesting the Master to preside over it. Whenever he was seen...
When someone knocked, he would call out loudly, "Rest! Cease! If anyone asked further, he would drive them away with his staff.
He has three volumes of recorded sayings (*yulu*) in which these teachings are preserved.

Chan Master Jianxin Laifu of Dingshui in Cixi, Yuezhou, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yue of Jingshan. He was a native of the Wang family of Fengcheng in Nanchang. From birth, he was exceptionally gifted;
from his youth, he harbored the aspiration to transcend the mundane world. In the Renwu year of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era, he received the tonsure at the western part of his home district.

He traveled to Fangsi Temple and proceeded to the Double Path (Shuangjing) to pay his respects to Nan Chu. After a long time, he attained realization and was appointed to oversee the internal records.
Not long after, he fled the military unrest to Kuaiji, where he eventually took charge of Dingshui Temple in Cixi. He brilliantly restored the ruined site.

Because the chaos of war prevented him from visiting his mother, he built a cottage east of a mountain stream and named it Puan, taking the meaning from the phrase used by the Venerable Master Chen. Later, he moved to Ningbo.
Tianning [Zhizhao] at Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou addressed the assembly. He cited the story of the old woman of the eastern city who did not wish to see the Buddha, and offered this verse:
The Buddha’s body radiates light like purple-polished gold; All the spirits of the great earth together revere it.
Having been born with two eyes, she never wished to see; The old woman truly possesses the heart of a man. He then cited the passage where Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti each spoke of non-duality.
Dharma Gate. The verse says: Having passed through the inquiry on illness in the realm of Abhirati, he discerned the old Vimalakīrti before a single word was spoken.

The place of seeing is merely ordinary; even if you could twist one’s nose until it bleeds, it would still be like a medicine bag behind a funeral bier.
When Shigong drew his bow to receive Sanping, the verse says: What did Shigong ever know of drawing a bow? To him belongs the power that achieves complete success.
He need not employ a golden arrowhead on the mugwort stalk; It pierces through the hundreds of thousands of layers of Mount Sumeru. A single bow.
Two arrows end a lifetime; before the trigger is pulled, the poison has already sprouted. To kill or to give life, one must personally strike the target; three taps on the string are but empty sound.
Quoting Lingyun’s seeing the peach blossoms, Xuansha said he had not yet reached the ultimate.
The verse says: All head toward Chang’an to tread the early spring; Purple steeds pursue fragrant dust wherever they go. Year after year, amidst the singing pipes in the eastern breeze.
"Who understands that there are but few who truly know peach blossoms? In the *wushen* year of the Hongwu era of the Ming Taizu, the Master was summoned as a renowned monk.

Upon arriving at the capital, he was granted a meal in the inner court and received lavish consolation and favor. It happened that a great assembly was being held at Mount Zhong; by imperial decree, the Master was ordered to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, the Prince of Shu, Zhu Chūn, was commanded to follow the Master and inquire about the Way. The Master then provided the Prince of Shu with an answer concerning the essential points of the method for practicing Chan.
It is said: The true lineage of the Chan school transmits mind through mind; it is presented directly and simply to reach those of the highest capacity.

It does not involve verbal explanations nor does it rely on conceptual understanding. It is like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning—seeing is immediate seeing, and realizing is immediate realization.
Once attained, it is forever attained; hearing it once brings a thousand awakenings, securing the Great Dhāraṇī. Its function is inexhaustible, yet its essence cannot be grasped.
It is exhausted. If one instead engages in discursive deliberation, grasping and rejecting, or making conceptual distinctions, all of this belongs to deviant dhyāna and deviant paths;
it is not the wisdom of Bodhi. When birth and death arrive, none of these will be of any use. Therefore, in investigation one must investigate truly, and in awakening one must awaken truly.

This is realized through self-verification and is not obtained by seeking from others. This is why Bodhidharma came from the West: he did not establish written words, but pointed directly to the person.

To see one's nature and achieve Buddhahood is called the "special transmission outside the teachings. When he met the Great Master Huik'e, the Second Patriarch, he merely pointed out the essence of the mind to enable him to awaken on his own.
When Huik'e was questioned regarding what he had attained, he said, "It is clearly and constantly known; words cannot reach it.
Only then did Bodhidharma grant him certification, saying, "This very thing is the intrinsically pure mind; do not harbor further doubts."
Furthermore, the word "knowing" (zhi) spoken by the Second Patriarch at that time precisely refers to the direct realization of the essence of mind (*cittatattva*).
For "mind" is the name, while "knowing" constitutes its essence. This knowing is the knowing of numinous awareness; it encompasses all wonders. Its nature is inherently spiritual and liberated;

it does not depend on conditions for its arising, nor does it originate from objects. It is not a knowing achieved through deliberate effort, mental activity, or discursive thought; it is simply true purity.

It is luminous and wondrous; empty, penetrating, and spiritually unimpeded. It responds universally and without end, knowing clearly and eternally. Sentient beings, due to their delusion regarding this knowing, give rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*).

If one realizes this knowing, one attains Buddhahood in a single instant. Generally speaking, throughout past and present, and encompassing both the ordinary and the sacred, there is no separate or distinct dharma;
it is solely this One Mind. This mind is itself the Dharma; outside the Dharma, there is no mind. This Dharma...
It is precisely the mind. There is no dharma apart from the mind. Have you not seen how Mañjuśrī addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying:
"Within the three realms, the mind is the sovereign. Those who can contemplate the mind attain ultimate liberation; those who cannot contemplate it remain ultimately submerged in saṃsāra.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also states: "Sentient beings are bewildered and distressed; turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses, they give rise to that dust."
Laborious, it possesses worldly characteristics. I, by means of my wondrous clarity that is neither born nor extinguished, unite with the Tathāgata-garbha;
yet the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, one becomes infinite and the infinite becomes one.

Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears. Without moving from the site of enlightenment, one pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing the ten [directions] within one's body.

Throughout the entirety of infinite empty space, upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests jewel-king lands; sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Thus it is known that to realize Bodhi is simply the mind itself.
Apart from the mind, there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha, there is no mind. To clearly recognize the mind is to wakefully behold the Buddha.
This is truly the wondrously luminous true awakening, perfectly illuminating and unimpeded; it is not something that can be grasped by ordinary intellect.

[This] can only be known through personal realization. Generally speaking, in the daily practice of study, if the essence of the mind is not clear, one will be swayed by external objects and give rise to delusions and inversions.
If the essence of the mind is clear, it is like seeing forms in broad daylight—distinct and free from doubt. Therefore, the former masters said:

"If the mind wanders and scatters, you must immediately collect it and cause it to abide in right mindfulness. As for this right mindfulness, you should know that it is simply the mind itself, and there is nothing else.
Regarding external objects, even this mind lacks self-characteristics, for it cannot be apprehended moment by moment. It is further said: "In delusion, the person pursues phenomena;

upon awakening, phenomena depend on the person. This means that in a state of delusion, one takes the mind to be the object and is thus robbed by the object, such that phenomena appear in a thousand variations.
In awakening, one realizes that the object is precisely the mind; every dust mote accords with the Way, and every phenomenon is complete in its entirety.

Truly so. Appearing and disappearing, unfolding and rolling up—all proceeds from me. Therefore, since the time of the ancient patriarchs, the Chan school has been transmitted through direct pointing and single-handedly holding up the essence, without any of this profusion of words or explanations.
One simply realizes that the mind is Buddha, immediately inherits the ancestral position, and sits upon the site of enlightenment.
It is like the kalaviṅka bird within its shell, whose cry already outshines all other birds; it is like the *hòujiān* tree emerging from the earth.
Yet it rises high above all other trees. Furthermore, for one who practices according to the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, if not a single thought arises, they are immediately called a Buddha.
How could they wait to accumulate merit over kalpas through gradual stages before attaining realization?
For the mind of all sentient beings is fundamentally the Buddha; it is only because deluded thoughts arise that they become sentient beings. If, for even a single moment—
If deluded thoughts do not arise, why would one not attain Buddhahood? Furthermore, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it.
If one is free from deluded thoughts, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will immediately manifest before one. This is what our Patriarch meant by:
To possess perfect understanding and perfect cultivation, entering directly and transcending all at once—how could such merit, which surpasses that accumulated over many kalpas, be a deceptive claim?
It is simply that people of the present day mostly lack sufficient faith, their vision is not intimate, and their practice does not reach the goal.

If one can truly believe, see intimately, and practice until reaching the goal, with the mind uninterrupted day and night and remaining as one whether awake or asleep, then by reflecting back upon the spiritual source, the direct nature will manifest.
There is no dharma that is not penetrated; there is no principle that is not harmonized. Spontaneous application is universally pervasive;

moving freely in all directions, one reaches this field where there is no need to worry about the Buddha or the inability to understand his language. Though remaining within birth and death, one constantly enters nirvana; though dwelling amidst the toil of worldly dust, [one remains ever free].
One shall dwell in a pure land; in every thought-moment, Śākyamuni appears in the world, and with every step, Maitreya descends to be born.

Awakening is spontaneously perfected without cultivation, and afflictions are naturally eliminated without severance. Subject and object both vanish, and conceptualization and perception are equally forgotten.

In its very essence, it is the truth; the single mind remains unmoving. Now, Your Highness, having long possessed right faith, the conditions for the Buddha-dharma have ripened, and your discernment has reached the vision.
Chao! The essence of the mind is already clear and possesses great power; there is no need to remain in a state of dull stagnation throughout the day or for years on end.

Rather, simply maintain perfect understanding and perfect cultivation in all activities—whether entering or leaving, rising or reclining, speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, and even when responding to affairs or interacting with others.

When issuing commands and giving orders, at all places and at all times, awaken as soon as a thought arises; remain constantly aware without obscuration. Clarify your reflections and forget worldly attachments;
after a long time, you will naturally attain realization. This is what the Third Patriarch meant by "empty clarity self-illuminating, without taxing the mind's power.
He also said: "Without leaving this very place, it is eternally serene; seek it and you know it cannot be seen. At this point, realize directly and immediately.
To attain such thorough penetration is to act without acting, to cultivate without cultivating, to gain without gaining, to achieve merit without merit,
and to realize realization without realizing— this is most appropriate and most essential. Long ago, when the King of Min invited Luoshan Xian to ascend the hall and expound the Dharma,
Luoshan took his seat, and as soon as he gathered up his *saṃghāṭī* robe, he said, "Take care," and immediately descended from the seat.
The King of Min stepped forward, took Master Shan’s hand, and said, "How is this assembly on Vulture Peak any different from today?
Observe how this master of Luoshan did not rely on words or speech; yet the King of Min possessed such divine discernment that he naturally transcended ordinary circumstances.
Later, Dongshan Cong remarked, "Luoshan could not restrain his impatience; he fully displayed his family style with a single roar. His writings fill a mountain of paper."

Do not exhaust yourself; you monks should cease seeking within conceptual meaning. This is where the ancients gave direct and straightforward instruction. When the eye of the school is clear, one differs from the masses.
It is precisely as it is said: "When meeting, do not bring it forth; when a thought arises, one immediately knows it exists.
How could this depend on raising eyebrows, blinking eyes, moving lips, or stirring the tongue? For me, a poor monk, to speak with such earnestness is already like painting a snake and adding a head.

Sufficient. I have presumed to trouble Your Majesty’s sagacious hearing. Nevertheless, having been granted this inquiry, I could not remain silent. I hope that during your leisure from state affairs, amidst your Great Perfect Illumination, you will deign to glance briefly over this;
it would also serve as proof that your long-cherished vows at Vulture Peak have not forgotten the ancestral Way, which would be no small fortune.
A further response to the Prince of Jin’s inquiry on the essentials of Chan: On the twentieth day of the second month, I respectfully received your decree. It was shown to me...
Admonition. Regarding the Dharma of the Buddha, which is to be realized within one’s own mind, how could I dare not reveal my humble thoughts and venture to present even a fraction of them?
Your Highness, as an emanation body of a Bodhisattva who has returned by virtue of your vows, you have extensively protected the Buddha-Dharma and benefited the world and all living beings.

In the intervals between attending to state affairs, you have constantly and earnestly investigated the "Great Matter" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; this is truly a testament to your not forgetting your origin.
This is due to the power of aspiration. However, in daily life, one should relinquish all external conditions and rest from myriad thoughts. As soon as a thought arises, one must be aware of it;

remain constantly aware without dullness. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; eating, drinking, or attending to daily activities; responding to affairs or interacting with others—observe whether you have mastery or lack mastery.
Do not allow yourself to be turned by external objects or follow after the sensory realms of others. For all the myriad events and principles of the world arise from...
The mind. When the mind is fully understood, there is no phenomenon that is not understood. Therefore it is said: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;

when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Thus one knows that the mind has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); dependent origination is itself emptiness. There is no need for elaborate effort.
This is the most concise and essential [teaching]. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Worldly speech and activities for sustaining life are all not in contradiction with the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Without destroying worldly appearances, one accomplishes the supramundane Dharma.
A former master said: "Do not deliberate at all upon any good or evil; naturally, you will enter the essence of the pure mind. This is...
The place where the Buddhas and Patriarchs directly point to people is this:

in your daily practice, regarding the things before you, do not concern yourself with whether they are good or evil, favorable or adverse, pure or defiled. It is like a precious mirror set upon its stand, clearly reflecting both the beautiful and the ugly;
as objects come, it responds; as objects go, it leaves nothing behind. Do not give rise to a single thought of discrimination or selection. Nor...
Do not ask whether it is during stillness or clamor, suffering or joy; simply exert yourself to the utmost and practice with sincerity.
When you reach a point where there is no principle by which to understand, that is indeed good news. Then, let everything be cast down at once.
Suddenly, when both knowledge and understanding are forgotten and both person and phenomena are extinguished, that is the moment of great rest, great sovereignty, and great bliss.
Long ago, there was a king who asked the Venerable Prajñātāra, "What is the Buddha? The Venerable replied, "To see one's nature is to be the Buddha.
The King asked, "Does the Master see your own nature? The Venerable replied, "I see the Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside?
The Venerable replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. The King asked, "When it is in operation, in how many places does it manifest? The Venerable...
He said, "When they manifest, there should be eight. The King said, "Please explain to me these eight manifestations. The Venerable One then replied: "In the womb, it is called the body;
dwelling in the world, it is called a person; in the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing;

at the nose, it is smelling fragrance; at the tongue, it is discourse; in the hand, it is grasping; in the foot, it is running. These manifestations appear everywhere, encompassing all things like the sands [of the Ganges]."
The realms are gathered and contained within a single minute atom. Those who recognize this call it Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*prāṇa*).

This is the very model for thoroughly investigating and clarifying one's own nature. Your Highness, having long possessed the seed-wisdom of *prajñā*, you will surely be able to perceive and understand this.
What need is there to wait for my humble words? Only within the Great Perfect Mirror, may mind seal mind; how fortunate would that be for all living beings! Thus is the Buddha-dharma.
It was fortunate that he did not fall into the later faction; however, he was subsequently arrested and subjected to punishment. At that time, he was over seventy years old.

Public opinion lamented his innocence. Alas! Was it thus that his karma was fixed? His works, the *Puan ji* (Collected Works of Puan) and the *Puan waiji* (Supplementary Collected Works of Puan), were circulated in the world.
Chan Master Xiuan of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, successor to Chan Master Ming of Lingyin, was born into the Li family of Linhai in Taizhou.

He attended Pujue at Lingyin. During a brief exchange of questions and answers, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. In the *bingxu* year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, he emerged from seclusion at Ansheng in Taizhou.
After five years, he was transferred to Long’en; another two years later, he filled the seat at Zhenru.
The following year, the Xuanzheng Yuan selected him to preside over Longhua. He occupied that seat for thirteen summer retreats. In the *guichou* year of the Ming Hongwu era, while in Hangzhou...

He summoned his attendants and said, "I am departing. The attendants brought forward inkstone and brush, but the Master waved them away, saying, "My school is fundamentally without words;
it is simply tranquil and still. He passed away at the age of sixty-nine, with fifty years of monastic seniority.

After cremation, his teeth and jawbone remained intact like strung pearls, and his *śarīra* were brilliant and lustrous, the color of refined gold. His disciples collected these remains along with his bones.

Half a year later, if one could have personally realized it at that moment, why would he not have struck with a fist right through the chest?

He possessed the true spirit of a *samgha* monk, and [the Master] consequently appointed him to the first seat. One day, when the Master ascended the high seat, he cited the saying:

He then established a hermitage at Mount Song on the Lanxi River, where he remained for nine years. The Master once sent him a verse, which began: "The yellow chrysanthemums grow lush..."
Autumn fills the eyes. Baiyun sat atop the azure peak; he lightly brought forth the phrase that knows neither guest nor host. With one shout, the waters of the thousand rivers flow backward.

A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Song? The Master said, "On all four sides, fine mountains support the sun and moon. One—

The lake’s autumn waters soak the azure sky. [A monk] asked, “What is it like to be a person within this realm? The Master said, “The three immortals could not paint it; I shall never transmit it to you.
[Another] asked, “What is the matter of the present moment? The Master said, “Eyebrows arching above the eyes.”
He asked, "Is there no place for you to settle yourself and establish your life? The Master said, "You have mistaken the weight of the scale.
Two monks came to visit; the Master asked, "Where have you come from? The monks replied, "Lung-hsi. The Master said, "I have heard that there are parrots in Lung-hsi."
"Is it so? The monk said, "Yes. The Master said, "Do you know how to compose poems and rhapsodies? The monk said, "I do. The Master said, "What kind of poem do you know how to compose?
Try saying one. The monk had no reply. The Master struck him and said, "You liar! You have not come from Longxi.

Today at Song Mountain, I raise it up once more: Flowers bloom on an iron tree—a spring unlike any other. I shall sleep beneath the shadowless tree and open wide the feast."
In the shop, he walks upon the back of empty space, extensively expounding the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). In every atom and every land, all is fully revealed;
in every object and every instance, all paths converge. He shatters the nest of the Demon King and cuts off the life-root of the monks.
He makes no strange deliberations and offers no interpretations of primordial mystery. Thus, even Vimalakīrti would be silenced, as they join in praising this era of peace. —Yantou.

Secretly revealing [the truth], he universally proclaims the ultimate transformation. At such a time as this, how do you express the single phrase for "praying for the Emperor and repaying his kindness"?
"A single piece of steady light illuminates the universe, directly causing the ten thousand nations to receive the sovereign's grace.
Ascending the hall, he extended both hands and said, "The gate of skillful means is wide open; enter here! Then, clenching his fists, he said, "The secure barrier is closed. He spoke.
This is private talk. Now tell me: how do you deal with the phrase "neither opening nor closing"? After a long silence, he gathered his saṃghāṭī robe and descended from the seat.

It is also said: "If you cannot bring it forth, you have failed; if you can bring it forth, all matters are concluded. If there is anyone who can say it, come forward and speak!
If there is none, I, Mount Song, shall reveal a message to you all. He spread his two hands and said: "When I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, his original radiance was such as this.
Later, while traveling to Dengwu in Gusu, he took pleasure in the way the mountains and waters coalesced there, and so he settled his staff [established his monastery].

Chan Master Wuyong Shougui of Tianlong Shui'an in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhen family of Wuzhou. At the age of eighteen...

He went to Kanghusan Mountain in Woutouli to shave his hair and dye his robes. During the Taiding era, he traveled to Western Zhejiang and happened upon Qianyan Chang, who was then residing at Longhua Temple.

Having cast down his brush, he passed away. The Imperial Chancellor of the Provincial Administration, Daśakīrti (達識鐵木爾), oversaw his funeral arrangements and constructed the Ciji Stūpa Courtyard.

The Heavenly Dragon (Tianlong) Temple at Xigang enshrined his entire remains in a burial vault. Throughout his life, the Master never kept any possessions beyond his immediate needs; he wore but a single robe through both cold and heat.
He was extremely strict in disciplining himself. Once, a tooth fell out, and his disciples placed it in a casket, where it produced five-colored śarīra relics.
His secular age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority was fifty-five.
Chan Master Weian Deran of Songyin in Huating, Songjiang Prefecture, was the son of the Zhang family of that locality.

In his youth, he followed Wuyong Gui to receive the tonsure and traveled extensively to consult various masters, yet he found no point of realization. Later, while in the assembly of Qianyan, he heard the words of a formal lecture and attained sudden enlightenment.
He once met Shiwu Gong, who said to the Master, "Your karmic affinity lies in Huating."

He inscribed the two characters "Songyin" (Pine Seclusion) and bestowed them upon him. Following this prophetic record, the Master returned to his native village and built a residence on the southern slope of Guohui, naming it Songyin.

For three years, he did not step beyond its threshold. He once drew blood to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which moved the heavens to manifest a wondrous response as celestial flowers filled the courtyard.

"The meaning of a thousand ages is clear. The Master said, "You have missed it by no small measure. [The monk] asked, "I have heard your words that 'the path beyond, not transmitted by the thousand sages'—is this truly so?

Now tell me: what do you say?

"The mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the grasses, trees, and the forests; the myriad phenomena of the cosmos, both sentient and insentient—from where do they come? After a long silence, he said:
"Do not use the intellectual learning of the common crowd to bury the mind of the Patriarch.

When asked about these two people, the Master said: "These two old fellows have been in and out of the same gate; they are karmic enemies from past lives.

When examined closely, both are equally deficient. I shall give each of them thirty blows of the staff. Now tell me, what was New Longfeng’s response to this?
"Uphold this! This is the reward; this is the punishment. [The Master] suddenly picked up his staff, struck it once on the ground, and said:
"In the heavens, every star bows toward the North; among men, no water flows but toward the East. Ascending the hall, he said: "The sun may grow cold, and the moon may grow hot.
No demons can destroy the True Teaching. It has its source, yet leaves no tracks. In the midst of the blazing heat of the sixth month, he scatters ice and snow. *Wen* (Recorded Sayings).
There is nowhere at all for him to settle his whole body; Samantabhadra has suddenly presented his own ugliness and clumsiness.

Whether this is a true statement or not a true statement—if there is no idle matter hanging upon the heart, it is simply a fine season in the human world. (A shout. The Abbot’s Hall discourse delivered by the Librarian and the Rector.

Sentient beings are those who do not understand the affairs within the Buddha-realm.

A single body is pure; many bodies are pure. A single world is pure; many worlds are pure. There is not a single speck of dust that is not the realm of True Suchness (Tathatā).

The stone lancet rouses the *gao-huang* [vital point], transforming the lamp oil. A single seed of radiance from the beginning of the kalpa is pressed forth through fierce effort and poured into the azure lapis lazuli.
The smiles of the three thousand Buddhas unfold—this is the *Zuochan Ming* (Inscription on Seated Meditation).

non-Buddhists and celestial Māras alike lose their souls. Those with iron brows and copper heads all grow pale; throughout the treasuries of past and present, no such treasure has existed.
Where in heaven or on earth could one find it? I earnestly report this to those who study the Source: seize this present life and you must—
Nǔlì (Effort) was summoned by Emperor Ming Taizu during the Hongwu era on account of his possession of the Way. Not long after, he returned home due to illness.
He once said, "Those who study the Dharma must not merely rely on their level of insight; what can a mere fragmentary understanding accomplish? It depends entirely upon how one practices.
On the fourteenth day of the fourth month in the Wuchèn year, he passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Songyin.
Chan Master Qingyin Lansi Dexing was a native of the Fang family from Yiwu in Wuzhou. At the age of twenty-four, he went to Fulong Temple to receive the tonsure and served there for several years.
Subsequently, he traveled extensively to visit various masters throughout the land. After a long time, he returned home to pay his respects, only to find that Qianyan had passed away.

In the *Renchen* year of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era (1352), he built a thatched hut west of the city and inscribed it with the name "Qingyin" (Pure Seclusion). Later, when the seat at Shengshou Monastery became vacant...
At the seat, the fourfold assembly requested the Master to preside over them. When Su Pingzhong once visited him, he did not utter a single word beyond the customary greetings of cold and warmth.
Su said, "When Master Qianyan receives guests, his speech flows like a hanging river, continuous and tireless. Why is it that you are now silent?
The Master replied, "The Way has neither concealment nor manifestation; how can there be speech or silence? Formerly, my late master never failed to..."
He said, "Yet I have never spoken. Now, though I have never spoken, it is as if I have never failed to speak. Su then struck his palms together in rhythmic approval and praised him.
On the fourteenth day of the eleventh month of the Renzi year of the Great Emperor Ming’s Hongwu era, he manifested slight illness.
