Chan Master Chang of Ming’ou at Huashan, whose secular surname was Jinhua, was a native of Pujiang in his own prefecture.

He thatched a hut on Mount Hua within his village and went to visit Qianyan, who showed him the essential points for entering the Way. Upon returning, he applied himself with diligence day and night without slackening. One—

One day, he suddenly took leave of the assembly and spoke a verse, saying: "Birth is fundamentally without birth; cessation is likewise without cessation. Casting off my hands, I go forth; a sliver of moon in the void.
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. This was the third day of the tenth month in the year of Bingchen during the Hongwu era of Emperor Ming Gaozong.
Chan Master Fashou of the Prajñā [Monastery] on Mount Tianwang in Jiangning once resided at Shengshou [Monastery] in Wuzhou as the First Seat.

At the end of the Dade era of the Yuan dynasty, he settled on this mountain. In the Jiamu year of the Zhi Zheng era, when the Ming Emperor Gao Di crossed the river, he entered the mountains alone on horseback and found his conversation with the Master to be in perfect accord.
The Emperor then dispatched General Miao to deliver offerings to him. After a long time, the Master traveled to Mount Lu.
The mountain was unknown; its location could not be found, and even the Buddha niche where he had resided no longer existed.

In the *dingmao* year of the Hongwu era, the Emperor recalled this matter and issued an edict to Huang Ligong, Vice Minister of Works, instructing him: "Since my crossing of the river, I once visited Chan Master Fashou and conversed with him;
he possessed remarkably profound insight. Now that he has passed away, you must select a monk who is dedicated to the Way."

On this old site, he established anew a single hermitage to manifest his imperial intent. Li Gong then recommended the monk Shao Yi, who was summoned for an audience and received his mandate before departing.
He erected the hermitage upon a lotus seed-cup on that mountain, which was granted the name "Prajñā Chan Monastery.
Zuo Chunfang’s Quji composed the "Record of Prajñā Chan Monastery," documenting these events in great detail.
Master Cizhou Ji of Jinshan on Mount Zishu in Runzhou, a successor of Chan Master Gumeng You, bowed to Xizhu and said, "I have caught the thief;
I request the Master to pass judgment. The Master asked, "Where is the stolen property? Xizhu struck the table once. The Master went toward him again.

He questioned him further, saying: "The Buddhas have not spoken it; the patriarchs have not transmitted it. Setting aside the flapping of lips and the stirring of tongues, and the blinking of eyes and the raising of eyebrows—bring me that one phrase of arriving home.
Zhuzhu remained silent. The Master said: "The time since the Sage has passed far away, yet there is still such a son as this.
Guard and uphold it well."
Chan Master Yifeng Ning presented his realization to Xizhu. The Master, in order to test him, showed him this verse: "Layer upon layer of green mountains, shrouded in misty rain;
The lion’s golden mane cannot be pierced through. I myself know that the time has not yet come;
Of ten times I draw the bow, nine times it is in vain."
Chan Master Konggu Jingle (1204–1298) of Zhengzhuan Yuan in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master An of Bian Mountain. He was the son of the Chen family on Yuan Mountain in Dongting, Gusu.
Initially, he met Lanyun An, who instructed him in the essentials of the Dharma. Later, at Huqiu, he paid respects to Shiban and received the tonsure.
When Huì’ān moved to Línghǐn, the Master followed him for seven years. While traveling to Tiānmù to pay respects at the ancestral pagoda of Gāopíng, he stayed there for over a year.
Suddenly, he attained a profound realization. He returned to Ān to seek verification; Ān expressed his joy for him.
Later, while the Master was residing at Bìyán, a monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "This question is most intimate. The monk said:
"How is it when one stands forth in full exposure? The Master said, "The journey has not yet reached the truth.
[The monk] said, "If a person from the South asks about snow, I would say it is willow catkins. The Master said, "How can you call a bell a water jar?
In his later years, at Xihu, he selected a site on Mount Xiujī to serve as his burial place. He built a dwelling there, naming it the Zhengzhuan Pagoda Temple. Furthermore, he himself...
The inscription for the stupa was composed. Its summary states: "Alas! Life and death are but a single dream; what need is there for a bone-stupa?

It is intended to manifest the fragrant flow of the Buddha-dharma and ensure that the traces of the numinous do not sever. By clarifying the true through the illusory, the vital pulse of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is secured, so that its source remains distant and its stream long.
Though the illusory body perishes, the Buddha-nature does not migrate. Those who come hereafter shall behold the towering stupa, with its peaks and ridges..."

Lush and verdant; birds sing in the lofty trees, and springs cascade from secluded crags. Without pursuing external objects, and without clinging to the internal mind, all likes and dislikes are utterly forgotten.
In this state of serene and harmonious contentment, one finally realizes that the Dharma-realm is the body, empty space is the mouth, and the myriad phenomena are the tongue.

He preached the Dharma day and night without ever ceasing. At this point, he attained clarity and achieved thorough penetration; like one suddenly sobering from intoxication, he experienced a vast and open awakening.
He then saw that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have never entered nirvana, and that this old monk has never passed into parinirvāṇa. Within the great perfect mirror, they face one another directly;
the intent of the Patriarch who came from the West is handed over with both hands throughout the myriad worlds of the great chiliocosm, encompassing self and others.
There is no separation even at the tip of a hair. Throughout ten thousand generations of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment of thought.
Master Lanyun was the preceptor of my own preceptor, Jinglong; as for the Dharma of my mind, I received his seal of approval from Lanyun.
This refers to Zen Master Nanji An, who attained the twenty-generation orthodox transmission of Linji. Tracing upward to the Heavenly Truth (Tianzhen), he reaches back to Wujie Yuan Xueyan Qin.

Regarding the succession of the Dharma, there is no fixed rule: for instance, Ānanda succeeded Kāśyapa as a successor to one who preceded him, while Xinghua succeeded Linji as a successor to one who followed him.
This principle penetrates past and present; arriving at the ultimate reality is what is most essential.

The Inscription reads: Vastly encompassing the Dharma-realm, it is empty and boundless. The ascent and descent of all spirits never cease. The Buddhas and Patriarchs manifest their responses as guides and teachers.
Having been graced by a subtle fortune in past lives, I encountered this transformative ritual. Unable to propagate the Way extensively, I acted according to what was appropriate for my strength.
I passed away in Wulin; my bones were interred on a mountain cliff. A stūpa was established in peace, its duration equal to that of the mountains. Through illusion...

Returning to illusion: conditioned and unconditioned, formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness—this Way is level and plain. Written in the spring of the Jiaoxin year (the 52nd year of Jinglong), by the Master at the age of fifty-two.
Among the Master’s writings are the *Konggu ji* (Collection from the Empty Valley) and the *Shangzhi Shangli bian* (Compilation on Upholding Rectitude and Upholding Principle).
Chan Master Jinling Tianjie Guzhuo Jun was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fulin Du.
A native of Songling in Gusu, he entered the monastic life at the age of thirteen at Rizhou Temple in Yuezhou.
At fifteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He first visited Shiwu Yonggong, and subsequently met...
Lanmu of Sanqu had attained proficiency in the practice of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration). He then went to call upon Gumei at Gao’ang;

as soon as he rose from his prostrations, he reported his realization exactly as it was. Gumei struck him and drove him out. This happened three times in succession, after which he returned home accompanied by a companion.

He established a boundary for himself to practice wall-contemplation for nine years. Every three years, he would burn one finger; after burning three fingers in succession, one day he suddenly attained sudden enlightenment (*diedi*).
He then went to visit Folin, with whom his Dharma combat was harmonious. Consequently, he remained there as the head of the assembly; at that time, he was twenty-eight years old.

When the community urged him to emerge from seclusion, the Master withdrew his traces and left the mountain, leaving behind a verse that said: "For half a year we relied on each other to sing the patriarch’s pivot."
"Several times we discussed the Way and received your august presence; upon leaving the mountains, you spoke of the path for returning. This was yet another addition of eyebrows above his eyes.

Having hidden his brilliance among crags and gullies for over thirty years, he possessed the lifelong favorite verse: "I love to nestle in the cliffs and valleys; for thirty years I have been too lazy to see off or welcome guests.
During the Hongwu era of Emperor Ming, he was commanded by imperial decree to ordain a thousand monks. Upon arriving—

Fanchang. At the request of the assembly, he ascended the hall for a general discourse at Mount Donglu. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The single character 'Chan' (Meditation) is also but a provisional name.
What is meant by 'investigating' (can)? It lies simply in faith. To deliberate is to deviate; to open one's mouth is to err.
If your resolve is not sincere and your will not sharp, you may spend the winter on this side and the summer on that side, yet today you have advanced."
After the sun had set, he searched for a long time but could not find it. He then said, "The Buddha-dharma has no efficacy," and turned instead toward external teachings.
He filled his belly with them and copied out entire volumes, like a stinking vat of fermented dregs. Such a one is nothing but a wild fox spirit;
even if Maitreya were to descend to be born in this world, what connection would there be? If a true seeker of the Way wishes to escape birth and death, they must penetrate through.
The Patriarchal Barrier. To penetrate the Patriarchal Barrier is to transcend birth and death; it is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then resting.
One must take the various patriarchs of the past as one's model. For what reason did Zhaozhou spend more than forty years without allowing his mind to be distracted?
For what reason did Changqing sit until seven cushions were worn through? For what reason did Xianglin take forty years before finally becoming a single, unified whole?
For what purpose? Even throughout successive generations, they have truly practiced, overcoming hardships and exerting their will—for what purpose?
Why do I, this mountain monk, today speak incessantly, citing the ancients to verify the present—for what purpose?

O Zen practitioners, since there exists the model of those from of old who did not spare their own lives, accumulating merit and virtue, and attaining wondrous realization through personal witness—why do you not [follow it]?
Exerting great courage and initiating great diligence, he made a profound and solemn vow before the Triple Gem:
"If I do not clarify the mystery of birth and death and penetrate the ancestral barrier, I swear never to descend from these mountains.

Having made this vow, he severed the paths of all manifold distinctions and refused to consort with the myriad dharmas. Before his seven-foot mat on the long meditation couch, he hung his alms-bowl bag high.
"Standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high," set a deadline for yourself and act with urgency. Spend this entire life practicing until you have reached total penetration.
If you resolve your mind in this way, you will certainly not be deceived. I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain.
In the Dinghai year of the Yongle era of Emperor Chengzu, he again received an imperial decree to reside at Tianjie Temple for the remainder of his life.
He was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Wanfeng Wei of the twenty-fifth generation under Nanyue.
Chan Master Baozang Puchi of Dengwu in Suzhou succeeded to the seat at Sheng’en as its second patriarch.
Wanfeng gave him a verse of entrustment, which says: "The fist strikes back where the ribs were pained by Dagu; The Three Essentials and Three Principles transcend both the orthodox and the biased.
A lion cub within the lair of Linji— Lamp after lamp, flame continues flame, transmitted through ancient and modern times. Later, he passed away and was interred in a stupa beside Wanfeng.
Chan Master Wusheng Xue of Jiupeng in Wuchang was the son of the Chen family of Yingshan in Suizhou. At the age of nine, he received his initial training from Wuji of Baolin Monastery.
He first visited Wumen, who presented him with the koan: "All dharmas return to One; where does the One return?
Thereupon, he entered Mount Song and applied himself to his studies with great diligence. One day, he attained a realization and composed a verse, which began: "For several years at Dongshan..."

The twilight mist was thick; leaning on the railing all day, he waited for a clear sky. At night, the moon suddenly rose in the frosty heavens, and the myriad phenomena were fully revealed within a single mirror.
Thereupon, he resolved to travel extensively to seek instruction. Later, he arrived at Gusu and met Dengwei Wei.

Under a sudden shout, he attained realization. Wei bestowed upon him a verse, which said: "The Linji school has been transmitted through five lineages; with one shout upon entering the gate, the whole is revealed."
Feng. With a "motherly heart" (lǎopó xīnqiè), he was able to act with ease; behold how a mud snake transforms into a dragon.
Later, returning to Baolin, his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. He subsequently resided at Jiufeng. During the *Renxu* year of the Hongwu era of Emperor Taizu, Empress Xiaoci passed away.

The Prince of Chu invited renowned monks from various mountains to assemble at Hongshan. Upon seeing the Master’s dignified appearance, they were struck with wonder and marveled at him, and he was specially retained there.
At his residence, [the Emperor] inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. Upon hearing of this, Emperor Gaozong summoned him to the private hall (biandian) and granted him a seat.

His responses were to the Emperor’s satisfaction, and he was treated with exceptional courtesy and generosity. The Emperor wished to retain him to preside over a monastery in the capital, but the Master resolutely declined. An imperial decree was issued for an official of the inner court to escort him back to Jiufeng.

On the day of Bingzi, the Emperor personally composed a scroll of poetry and prose titled "Mourning the Monk Wunian," and enclosed pine nuts and pine flowers within it, ordering an official of the inner court to deliver them.
He was escorted into the mountains, where he was consoled with words of profound sincerity. The Imperial Edict stated:

"Previously, the monk Wunian’s observance of the precepts was as pure as the bright moon, and his concentration and wisdom were as stable as a towering mountain. I came for a brief visit; since then, I have constantly held him in my thoughts.
As these feelings have not ceased, I have now specially dispatched an official to see you, bringing offerings of pine nuts and pine blossoms, along with poems and prose to honor you, Master."
He also offered these verses in response: "In the leisure between myriad affairs, you investigate the true source; At the tips of the hundred grasses lies the Chan of Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Within every pore, the lands of dust and worlds are fully contained; Upon the tip of a single hair, the sky of nature is revealed. Returning from meditative concentration, you sit watching clouds span the valley."
While enjoying the leisure of gazing upon the stone-spring, how can a monk beneath the forest trees repay [his debt]? May he pray for the Emperor’s longevity for ten thousand years.

The eunuch returned and reported this; the Emperor was greatly pleased. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month of the Jia-shen year of the Yongle era, Chengzu gathered the assembly and spoke a verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One lived seventy-nine; Wunian lived eighty. He has trampled over the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka)."

The sea remains as ever, its waters joining the sky; he passed away in serene stillness. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Sijian Rock. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Qingfu Guanghui.
An official was dispatched to present ceremonial silk, and a court scholar was commissioned to compose the inscription for the stupa.
Chan Master Haizhou Puci was a native of the Qian family in Changshu, Suzhou. He left home to become a monk at Mount Poshan as a youth and studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Upon reaching the passage, "Where there are only words and speech, there is no real meaning," he harbored a doubt. He went to visit Wanfeng and asked, "Regarding the statement that 'where there are only words and speech, there is no real meaning,' what is this real meaning?
Wanfeng struck him twice over the head and gave him a kick across the chest.
He said, "It is just this. The Master rose four times. [The monk] said, "This is indeed so, but it is too much trouble for the Master’s mind and energy.
Feng agreed with him and bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "The tortoise-hair is entrusted to the sons and grandsons;
The hare's horn is picked up to seek the ford. A single shout leaves the ears deaf for three days; Within this message, who may be intimate? The layman Shen Guan asked about the *Sūtra*.
The teaching is like a finger pointing at the moon. Once one has seen the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon. How is this principle to be understood?
The Master raised his hand and asked, "Is it the finger, or is it the moon? The student was at a loss. The Master struck the table once; the student was suddenly enlightened and attained realization.
When the head monk of Guolín came for an audience, the Master threw down his meditation cushion and said, "Try to say something about this.
The monk replied, "This very message is fundamentally beyond words; upon the broken meditation cushion, earth bursts forth and heaven cracks open.
The Master asked, "Tell me, what has cracked? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.

Chan Master Xizhu Benlai of Huanglong Shouchang in Jianchang was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jinshan Ji. Born into the Pei family of Chongren, he left home at the age of seven and, at thirteen, went to attend upon Yifeng Ning.
He served him for seven years, until one day he suddenly attained realization. His verse says: "For many years..."
Running outward, he lost his true soul. Meeting today, we are utterly different. Accompanying the golden-haired stone lion, he turns his head and swallows Mount Kunlun of iron.
Peak stillness. Running, he saw the Compassionate Boat at Jinshan. Rising from his prostrations, he immediately asked:
"Such-and-such has brought a thief here; we request the Master to pass judgment. Dayou asked, "Where is the stolen property? The Master struck the table once. Dayou then gave a shout.
Dayou further raised the story of Xiangyan climbing the tree, interrogating him repeatedly until he finally received certification of his realization.
Initially, he resided at Shousheng Monastery on Jian River. When the Ning Prince sent a letter inviting him, he declined three times and did not go, responding only with a letter concerning the Way.
[The Emperor] issued a decree bestowing upon him the title "Hui Guang Puzhao Dunwu Yuan Tong" (Wisdom Light Universally Illuminating Sudden Enlightenment and Perfect Penetration).

In the *Yongle* era of the Ming dynasty, the year *Yiyou*, at the request of the assembly, he ascended the hall at Shouchang to deliver a formal discourse: "The heavens and sun are bright and high, the summer heat gradually intensifies.

The pomegranate flowers burst forth like fire, shining within the courtyard. Within the eyes of the patch-robed monks, the true mechanism is revealed; the Unpositioned True Person is encountered face-to-face. Know the source directly."
Proposed to be separated by a thousand layers of clouds. To reach the matter of one’s own person, ascend the highest peak of Huanglong.
**Small Assembly (Xiaocan):** "Clear, clear, clear! A single expanse of sky, its light shining bright and white. Rest, rest, rest! The clouds fly high and the waters flow on their own.
With eyes opened wide and the whole body pervaded, there is no front or back; roam freely through the ten directions and the dust-mote worlds. Later, he resided at Shanguan in Min Province.
Reopening the Field of Merit. On the eighth day of the tenth month of the Renyin year, he suddenly asked for his brush and wrote this verse:
"This old beggar—when will his teaching ever end? Tumbling and turning, he merely follows the current; Whether he is a sage or an ordinary person, no one understands."
"Ha! Come, come; go, go! With the ocean deep and the sky clear, the wind pure and the moon bright, he finished writing. He sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
His secular age was sixty-eight, and his monastic seniority was fifty-five. His entire body was enshrined in the Dharma Hall for offerings.
Zen Master Dongpu Daolin Wujie Mingwu was a successor of Zen Master Tianjie Jun.
He was the son of the Mo family from Tongxian Town in Anyue, Shu.

"I have no Dharma to transmit; you have no mind to receive. With neither a mind to transmit nor a mind to receive, who would not achieve realization?"

[Zhaozhou] said, "If it is a treasure, you cannot possess it; if you possess it, it is no longer a treasure. Cuijun asked, "On what basis do you say this?

The Master stepped forward to offer his greetings, stood with his hands folded, and Cuijun said, "Bring me back that phrase from above. The Master then covered his ears and departed. He further presented a verse, saying:
"At midnight, pushing open the curtain, the moon is a single curve; Lightly treading upon the upper barrier, there is no need to look for it elsewhere."
Seeking outwardly from others—simply thus, with a joyful and smiling countenance. Jun acted as his assistant in celebrating this joy.

He crossed the ridge to Xingkeng, where he built a hermitage and did not venture beyond the mountains for twenty years. In the *Renzi* year of the Ming Xuanzong era, he accepted an invitation to Wulin at Hupao.
At the time of his death, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Literature and the Buddha-dharma are but empty forms; names, appearances, body, and mind are like mist upon a willow."
"Only birth and death are truly momentous matters; attend to them with diligence and do not delay. He asked the assembly, "How does one attend to them?
After a long silence, he said, "I have no leisure now to explain it for you; listen instead to the sound of the pines and the mountain stream. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of the hermitage. He was seventy years of age.
Chan Master Wunian Yuanxin of Founiu in Henan was the son of the Jin Tai Gao family.

Having left home and received full ordination, he first visited Wuji at Long’en, where he attained a realization. He returned to Mount Niu to live in a thatched hut for three years, after which he went again to Fanchang to study under Guzhu Jun.
Jun asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Mount Niu. Jun said, "The person is right here."
“Ox-ear,” [the Master] said. “Face-to-face, yet we do not recognize one another; the whole body is revealed, majestic and grand. Jùn said, “Even so, how can it be that his horns are not all present?
The Master said, “I am weary from walking in the mountains today. Jùn again picked up his bamboo staff and said, “To call it a bamboo staff is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a bamboo staff is to turn one’s back on it. How would you handle this, Upādhyāya? The Master said—
[The Master] said, "I have exerted my spirit and effort. Yunjun said, "That is not it; speak further. The Master then stepped forward, snatched the bamboo staff from him, and threw it to the ground.
Yunjun laughed heartily. The Master said, "I am at fault," and immediately prostrated himself. Yunjun then patted him and certified his realization.
The Master lived in seclusion in a hermitage for thirty years and then taught the Dharma at Mount Funiu. He addressed the assembly, and a monk asked: "What is the immediate [truth]?"
"The mind is itself Buddha. The Master said, "A wealthy child is easily spoiled. [The monk] said, "Neither mind nor Buddha. The Master asked, "Then how about this?
He said, "A deep pit is difficult to fill. The monk hesitated. The Master then said, "If you say 'the mind is itself Buddha,' it is much like gouging a sore on healthy flesh.
If you say 'neither mind nor Buddha,' what is different from applying moxa to a sore? Even if you were to say it is not the mind..."
"It is neither Buddha nor an object; this too is a trip on level ground. He asked, "Tell me, what is it ultimately like? After a long silence, he said:
"Sitting for a while, wipe the table and add incense to the burner; after the morning gruel, call the boy to wash the alms bowl."

The lay disciple He Mia'an’s dharma heir, Yangzhou’s Master Tian of Suanan, was a man of noted lineage from Jiangdu for generations. Having failed repeatedly in his attempts at the civil service examinations, he resolved to devote himself single-mindedly to the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
With fierce diligence, he engaged in intensive investigation. At that time, the Governor He Mia’an was propagating the Way in the southeast.

The Master (Shi) was a preeminent disciple who had entered the inner chamber [of the Dharma]. After he had been refined by the master’s hammering for a long time, the seal of mind (*cittamudrā*) was suddenly entrusted to him.

The Master then took up a bamboo rake in his hand to examine and test the monastics. Among those who came from all quarters to study under him, there were none who did not look up to Suanan as a living ancient Buddha.

Throughout the nation, he was called "Great Being Tian" (*Tian Dashishi*), and no one used his personal name. A monk asked: "By which gate does one exit upon the path to Potalaka? The Master said: "Up."
The Master said, "From which gate do you enter now? The monk said, "Why do you constrain people so? The Master said, "Watch where you step.
The monk raised his head and took three steps forward; the Master said, "Wrong. The monk then stepped back three paces; the Master said, "Now tell me—"
"It is your fault. It is my fault. The monk said, "Even before you raised it, I already knew it was wrong.
The layman said, "That is exactly why you deserve a blow with the staff. The monk was speechless. The layman said, "If you go to other places, explain this clearly to them.

Addressing the assembly, he said: "Lately, those who are earnestly devoted to Zen practice are few. As soon as they bring up a *huatou*, they are immediately ensnared by the two demons of dullness and agitation."
Little do they realize that dullness and distraction are precisely the antidotes to the state of doubt. When the power of faith is deep, the state of doubt will necessarily be profound;
when the state of doubt is profound, dullness and distraction will naturally vanish. Addressing the assembly: The great ocean does not harbor corpses;

empty space is not stained by the five colors; a mass of fire does not shelter mosquitoes or gnats. Within the Dharma of non-abiding, there is no establishment of delusion or enlightenment. Practice this now.
Chan. When the gate of light and shadow covers itself, one enters hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. To the assembly:
He cites the lay practitioner Zhang Jiu-cheng, who visited Chan Master Qing of Shanquan and asked: "This matter is inherently possessed by every person."
"Each and every one is perfectly accomplished. Is this so? Qing replied, "Yes. The Master said, "For what reason do I have no point of entry?

Qing took a string of white prayer beads from his sleeve and showed them to him. The Master looked up and down, unable to respond. Qing put the beads back into his sleeve and said, "These are yours; take them with you.
As soon as they involve discursive thought, they are no longer yours. The Master was struck with awe. One night, while using the toilet, he investigated [the matter].
Regarding the story of the cypress tree: suddenly hearing the sound of frogs, one attains immediate entry.

Today, as I bring forth this matter, you students of the Way must by no means seek understanding through discourses on the Ultimate or the Sublime; nor must you seek understanding through conceptualization or intellectual calculation.
When you reach that point where the time and the season coincide, you will naturally exert yourselves. But tell me: what is the phrase regarding "time and season"? Furthermore—
"How would you say it? A monk was reciting a sutra when a layman asked him, "What sutra are you reciting?
He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. The layman said, "The Lotus Sutra has sixty thousand characters; which of those characters has eyes? The monk was at a loss. The layman then struck him.
Another monk entered the gate and bowed. The layman shouted, "Go quickly! The monk bowed again. The layman said, "What kind of bowl are you looking for? The monk shouted. The layman then—
Master Zhang resided in a village of farming households within the city walls, using his own home as a hermitage. Scholars from all directions flocked to his presence by the day.
One day, while engaged in a tea conversation with the assembly of Zen practitioners, he suddenly threw down his cup, joined his palms, took leave of the group, and passed away.

Chan Master Da’an, a dharma successor of Chan Master Songyinran, was resolute in his vows and rigorous in his conduct, possessing the same spirit as his father. He frequently practiced the Prajñā Samādhi.

He passed away during the Bingshen year of the Ming Yongle era, leaving behind this verse: "I do not understand digging into the earth to seek heaven; yet I also know how to strike a stake into empty space."

Startled, he causes Mount Sumeru to topple and dance; the shrimp and frogs of the ocean's depths swallow the moon. He tramples over the great ocean of birth and death—what need is there to speak of the arising and ceasing of bubbles?
His worldly lifespan was seventy-seven years.
The Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, Volume Fifty-Eight and Volume Fifty-Nine.
Compiled by the monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital.
Verified and presented by the Abbot (Subject Monk) Chaokei of the Ancient Kegon-ji Temple in Kyoto;
Rinzai School.
Chan Master Xubai Huichan of Dongming, Hangzhou, the twenty-sixth generation descendant of Nanyue and successor to Chan Master Chishi of Dengwei,
was a native of the Wang family in Huguang. His father served as a tax collector in Danyang.

He served as a temple administrator and eventually made his home there. From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and did not resemble ordinary children. At the age of fourteen, he went to follow Miaojue Zhanran to receive instruction. One day, while assisting with the temple duties, Zhanran asked him, "What are you doing here? The Master replied, "I am slicing radishes. Zhanran said, "You only know how to slice radishes.

The Master replied, "I also know how to kill people. Zhanran extended his neck toward him, and the Master said: [The knife struck his throat. Zhanran said, "Ah! and fell to the ground. The Master called out to him, and Zhanran opened his eyes and spoke. The Master then composed a verse for him: "Thirty years of cultivation, All at once shattered by a single blow. The old man’s life has ended; The mountain gate is now closed. Zhanran passed away. The Master then returned to Mount Tiantai and lived in seclusion. Later, when the Emperor summoned him to the capital, he declined the invitation and remained in the mountains.

He passed away at the age of seventy-seven. His remains were interred on Mount Tiantai. The Emperor bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Great Master Zhixian" (Constantly True). His dharma heirs included Xingman, Daoyuan, and others. The Master’s character was simple and austere; he never sought fame or profit. He lived in the mountains for over thirty years, and those who came to seek him out were few. He was deeply learned in both Buddhist and secular classics, and his writings were numerous. He was particularly skilled at composing poetry and prose, which circulated widely throughout the world. His disciples numbered over a thousand. His teachings were transmitted through the generations, and his influence lasted for many centuries. His legacy remains a testament to his profound realization and his dedication to the path.

It is the custom not to execute surrendered generals; however, Yiran was an exceptional case. When Yiran was transferred to serve as the Prefect of Fuzhou at Shushan, the Master heard that Weian was propagating the Way at Songyin and intended to go see him.
Upon arriving at a small hermitage, he made a vow, saying: "If I do not achieve thorough realization on this journey, I shall certainly never return. He remained there for six days.
Suddenly, looking up and beholding the pines, he attained a sudden and profound awakening. Thereupon he returned, practicing with intense diligence day and night.

He sat as upright as an iron pillar; because of this, people everywhere called him "Chai the Iron-Backed. Later, he arrived at Dengwu in Gusu and visited Guolin, who instructed him to investigate Baozang Chi.
He related his realization in detail, to which Chi replied, "The Buddha-dharma is like the great ocean."
It turns deeper and deeper; where else could it rest but right here? One day, while standing in attendance in the room, Hui-chi asked, "Mind is not the Buddha, and wisdom is not the Way.
How do you understand this? The Master stepped forward to pay his respects and stood with his hands joined in *añjali*.
Hachi said, "After all this time you have been here, you still hold such a view. The Master then became indignant;
he neglected both sleep and food until the second night, when he suddenly attained thorough realization. He composed a verse, saying: "A single punch shatters the vast void;
The billions of Sumeru mountains leave no trace. I ask: who is the master within? The sun rises from the eastern sea."
Lunhong held him and said with a smile, "Even though it is so, you must still protect and maintain yourself well. When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself.
Having received these instructions, the Master took his leave and went to Pingsantang on Mount Tiangmu, where he gathered companions to undertake a three-hundred-day retreat.
When the period was complete, he went to Zhaokong Temple to receive full ordination. Later, he traveled to Gudaoshan in Anxi, where the peaks and ridges were exquisite.
Ba resolved to remain there for the rest of his life. He stayed for thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountain.

His reputation for the Way spread far and wide, and veteran monks vied with one another to seek instruction at his seat. He expanded the foundations and renovated the buildings until it became a great monastery.

In the year Yimao of the Xuande era of the Ming Xuanzong, an imperial plaque was bestowed naming it Dongming Chan Temple. Furthermore, he was commanded to ordain monks to maintain the sacred offerings. Alms and donations accumulated in abundance. The Master—
Furthermore, he donated his remaining assets to rebuild the Great Hall of Jingci Monastery.

On the first day of the sixth month in the *Xinyou* year of Emperor Yingzong’s *Zhengtong* era, he suddenly gathered the assembly, expressed his gratitude, and took his leave. When the assembly requested a verse, the Master said:
"The entire Tripitaka has no one to gaze upon it; what use are these few idle words? He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. Upon cremation, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
His stupa was erected at Dongwu on Mount Ben. His secular age was seventy, and his years of ordination were fifty-five.
Hu Gongyong, the Director of the Guozijian, composed the inscription for it.

Chan Master Huizhong Xuegu of Tianjie Monastery in Jianning Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shouchang Lai. During a formal assembly for the examination of practitioners (*tongcan*), the Master asked:
"From where have you come? He replied: "Pervading the void, there is no coming or going. The Master said: "Since there is no coming or going, who is it that drags [the body] along?"
The leather bag arrived here; [the Master] said, "Both inside and outside are empty; how can the leather bag exist?

The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied, "How could there be any 'meaning' in coming from the West? The Master said, "When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives..."
"Where do you establish yourself and find your livelihood? He replied, "With a step of faith, he overturns heaven and earth; alone, he is revealed. The Master then presented him with a verse:
"The true golden-haired lion has personally emerged from his cave; The wheel of Dharma is turned, and he enters the marketplace.
With one sudden roar across the vast void, The wild jackal hears it and its skull splits open."
Chan Master Shuchou Toudi Chushan Huan’ou Jingbi Shaoshi was the dharma heir of Chan Master Dongpu Wu. He was the son of the Lei family from Andang in Shu.
At the age of nine, he received his formal training under Master Xuanji Tong. He first visited Master Wujie Wu, and one day, upon hearing the sound of the wooden board, [he attained realization].
He had a realization. He then visited and questioned various masters, including Yuexi and Haizhou, all of whom praised him.

In the *Kaihai* year (*Guihai*, 1443) of the Zhengtong era of the Ming Emperor Yingzong, he again underwent examination under Wuzhun. Wuzhun asked, "In these past few years, where have you been staying?
The Master replied, "Vastly open and without fixed location. Wuzhun asked, "What have you attained? The Master replied, "Originally there was nothing lost; what is there to attain? Wuzhun said:
“This,” he said, “is something attained through study. The Master said, “Since not a single dharma exists, from where does study come?
Wuzhuo said, “Does this not fall into emptiness? The Master said, “I am not even I; who falls and what is empty? Wuzhuo said, “Ultimately, what is the matter?”
The Master said, "When the water falls, the rocks appear; when the rain clears, the clouds disperse. Wuzu said, "Do not speak so recklessly.
Even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to come, I would not permit you to swallow the ocean of the Tripitaka at will or manifest hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers;
even here, it is still not permitted. The Master said, "Although you, Master, hold fast at the vital ford, it is a pity that you exhaust yourself so much. Wuzu clapped his knee.

[The Master] gave a shout. Wuzhuo said, "One who can sustain the family must be one who can break the family; doing so to manage the household affairs will save you effort. The Master covered his ears and left.
That evening, Wuzhuo summoned him again and interrogated him, saying, "Bring forth all the stages of your previous realizations and speak them here.
The Master answered truthfully. Wuzhuo said, "Give me back the meaning of the word 'Mu' (No). The Master presented [his realization].
The verse says: Where the monk asked, the matters were manifold; When did Old Zhao ever involve himself in thought?
A single word spoken from the heart was fully revealed, Yet it turned out to be quite extraordinary, causing people to doubt. Wu said, "What is that place where you have no doubt?
The Master said, "Green mountains and blue waters, the warbling of swallows and the singing of orioles—everything is vividly clear; what more is there to doubt? Wu said, "Not yet."

While on the way to another monastery, the Master said: "The head touches the void; the feet tread upon solid ground. Upon awakening [to this], he struck the bell to assemble the assembly and conferred the seal of transmission upon him.
In the year of Renshen, he arrived at Jinling to visit Yuexi Haizhou, and subsequently went forth to reside at Tianzhu. A monk asked:
"What is the realm of Tianzhu? The Master said, "The ravine is wide and clouds return late; the mountain is high and the sun rises slow. "What is it like for one within this realm?
The Master said, "Below the forehead, the eyebrows cover the eyes; at the side of the cheek, the ear rests upon the brow. "What is the house style of Tianzhu?
The Master said, "A cloud-basin steamer cooks pine powder; an ice-cauldron boils moon-discs. [Question: "What about suchness?"
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "The Sea God has cast out a night-bright pearl.
[The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Mañjuśrī has lost his crystal cup. [The monk] asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "A raw-iron weight.
[The monk] asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "A stone and a clod of earth. [The monk] asked, "What is the Sangha? The Master said:
The Black Lacquered Staff. In the year Yihai of the Jingtai era, [Zhaozhou] moved to Touzi. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "Having left Mount Xuan far behind, you have come to occupy Touzi.

With the assembly gathered before you, we pray that the Master will offer a benediction for the Emperor. The Master said: "The eternal script within the cauldron; the ageless pine atop the peak. The monk said:
"I have already received the Master’s direct instruction regarding the benediction for the Emperor; as for the 'house style' of Touzi, what is it like? The Master—
[The student] asked: "A man carrying a water jar passes through the market; he is not the oil-seller. [The Master] said: "As for the Patriarch’s saying, 'I do not permit traveling at night;
you must arrive by dawn,' is this truly so? The Master said: "Even so, though there is sinew in the eye, how can one deny that the tongue has no bone?
[The student] asked: "Zhaozhou said, 'I am already as white as a monkey; he is even blacker than a monkey. What was his meaning?"

The Master said, "If it were not for the exhaustion of arrows and bows, he would not yet consent to raise the flag of surrender. A monk asked, "Venerable Sir, today you have ascended the seat to preach the Dharma;
I wonder what auspicious signs there were? The Master said, "The qilin strides beyond the crimson heavens; the *utpala* flower blooms amidst the fierce flames.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "When the snow melts, the mountain peak is revealed; the wind..."

The tree passed by, its head swaying. [A monk] asked, "How is it when the precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard? The Master said, "Gods cry out and ghosts wail. [The monk] asked, "How is it after it has emerged from the scabbard?
The Master said, "Buddhas and patriarchs swallow their voices. [The monk] asked, "How is it when it has emerged and when it has not yet emerged?
The Master said, "A hairless lock of chain sways at both ends. The monk lifted up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master then shouted. The monk hesitated; the Master—
He struck him and said: "To rub an itch on the head of a venomous snake or to throw one's body across the mouth of a fierce tiger—this must indeed be done by such a person as this.
That monk just now was much like a seasoned warrior who dared to come here to seize the drum and snatch the banner;
yet it is a pity he failed at the end, dying beneath the staff. Had he known how to turn his body toward a path of life, naturally—"
One must not encounter its sharp edge. Thus it is said: "To handle a snake, one must be a snake-handler; if you do not know how to handle a snake, the snake will bite you to death.
Again, on the day Fadelung opened the hall for his first sermon, after he had finished discussing the unresolved public case (kung-an) concerning the Elder Qingliang, the Master said:
"In general, when a patriarch appears in the world, he must first bring forth his own insight; only then can he establish [the teaching]."
Severing the past and present—observe the strategy of this Dharma-lamp. It is indeed beautiful, yet not yet fully resolved.
Today, I, the Old Hermit, shall also act for the sake of the Elder Sangu; there is a case that remains unresolved, so come forth and let me settle it for him.
"If someone asks, 'The Old Man of the Silkworm Bones—what unresolved koan does he have? you should immediately shout, with eyes fixed and alert, and strike them out with a succession of blows.
"Great assembly, when I, this mountain monk, uphold the Dharma in this manner, tell me: how does it compare to the application of means used by Faldeng?"
Furthermore, is there superiority or inferiority? If one can resolve this, I grant that they are a fellow student.

Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "This very thing is a source of confusion. How many monks have reached this point and been unable to open their mouths, unable to conceive of it through thought, and unable to bring it forth.
Now it has fallen into the hands of this mountain monk; whether I hold it horizontally or..."
"I! It is all up to me. To lift up or let go, to roll up or unroll, to kill or bring to life—all depends on me.

Holding his staff in the air, he pointed it with a single dot and said, "At this very moment, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old down to the elder monks of the world, upon reaching this point, they can do nothing but beg for their lives.
Is there anyone among you who can speak out on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Liang [responded].
After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said, "The blind Vajra-Eye has been overturned, and the precious throne of the Empty King has been cast down.
You all—what bowl are you looking for? He then descended from the seat. He ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, the Master adjusted his robes and took his seat.

After a long silence, he said, "Everyone, take this clearly to heart. He then descended from his seat and addressed the assembly: "The field for selecting Buddhas opens the pivotal mechanism of the Patriarchs.

To distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, one must employ the hammer and tongs. When the waves warm at the Dragon Gate and the wind and thunder stir, it is precisely the time for fish and dragons to undergo their transformation.
Is there anyone among you who can surge through the waves and dash against the billows? After a long silence, he struck a circle with his whisk.

The Master said, "A single move ahead of the occasion; presenting it fully face-to-face. He struck the meditation seat once and said, "A word beyond all phrases is revealed along with the sound itself.
No room for lingering thought or hesitation; no allowance for deliberation or analysis. By the time you blink an eye—"
The sword has long since departed. Even if Buddhas and Patriarchs were to arrive, they would have nothing but furrowed brows. Why?

Because it is not a path through which words can pass, nor is it something that can be fathomed by the mind or consciousness. If one were a truly outstanding monk, one should nod in agreement with a smile even before the word is raised;
this would still leave some room for excellence. In recent times, people’s hearts are not as they were of old, and those who study...
One must strive for true inquiry and genuine realization; yet these days, people merely echo sounds and inherit empty claims.

They take intellectual learning and superficial understanding as enlightenment, the forced interpretation of circumstantial conditions as investigation, the violation of monastic discipline as liberation, and the expedient seizing of positions as transcendence of the world.

Consequently, the ancestral style has declined and fallen into ruin, while demonic teachings blaze forth, obstructing the level path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and blinding the true eye of humanity.
Thus, the Way of our Patriarchs—the "special transmission outside the teachings"—is now cast to the ground.

The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, more than two thousand years ago, already recognized the mental afflictions of sentient beings and established numerous expedient means, graciously bestowing detailed regulations.

Therefore it is said: "Sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who hope to achieve the Way must not be allowed to seek awakening, lest they only increase their learning and grow in their self-view (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
It is further said: "For sentient beings who have not yet awakened, what skillful means can be employed to cause them all to attain enlightenment?

For this reason, the retreat (*kaṭhina*) and the summer rains retreat (*varṣā*) are established, so that one may realize the fruit within a fixed period. Once the three-month period has passed, one may go wherever one wishes without hindrance. Thus we know there is a method for untying the knots.
"It is the right time, O Great Virtues. During these ninety days, have you ever attained realization? As for those who have already realized it, let us set them aside for now.
If you have not yet realized it, then this entire period will again have been spent in vain.
If you are a true seeker of the Way, take the entire Dharma-realm as the site for the period of Perfect Enlightenment; regardless of whether it lasts a hundred days or a thousand, establish it."
Regarding the method for resolving doubts through the precepts: simply begin by raising the *huatou*. If you do not awaken after one year, practice for one year;
if you do not awaken after ten years, practice for ten years; even if it takes twenty or thirty years, or until the end of your life without awakening, remain resolutely unwavering in this resolve.
You must directly seek that which is thorough from beginning to end—the true, ultimate point—only then will you be at ease.
Sansheng said, "What is called 'one thought for ten thousand years'—is this not a hollow phrase? He raised his whisk and said, "Virtuous ones, do you know where it lands?
Today, I, the Delusive Old Man, shall not decline to be loquacious; I shall provide another commentary for you all:
A golden bullet forged in a fierce fire, when struck at the critical moment, is crushed yet remains perfectly round. Gains and losses are but casual."
"Cast both aside. The wind carries the sound of the tide out from the sea gate. When the Master came to the vegetable garden and saw a winter melon, he asked the gardener, "This one has no mouth;
why has it grown so large? The gardener said, "I have never been idle for even a single moment.
The Master said, "Does the master of the house provide you with some assistance as well? The gardener said, "I rely entirely upon him."

Quli said, "I request that you come and meet with this old monk. Linji bowed his head immediately. The Master said, "This is still merely a servant or a slave. Linji turned around and picked up a bamboo splint to bind some scaffolding. The Master then laughed heartily and looked back at his attendant, saying, "There are insects in the vegetable garden. Xingkong, the Head Seat, requested instruction on the Three Barriers of Mount Meng. The Master said: "The first barrier is: 'If you can pass through the Vulture Peak, you will see Mañjuśrī. Xingkong asked, "What is the meaning of 'If you can pass through the Vulture Peak, you will see Mañjuśrī'? The Master said, "It is like a person who has lost their way and asks for directions. Xingkong asked, "What is the meaning of 'If you cannot pass through the Vulture Peak, you will not see Mañjuśrī'? The Master said, "It is like a person who has found the road but does not ask for directions. Xingkong asked, "What is the meaning of 'Whether you can pass through the Vulture Peak or not, you will never see Mañjuśrī'? The Master said, "It is like a person who has neither lost their way nor found it, yet they do not ask for directions. Xingkong was greatly enlightened by these words. He then composed a verse: "The first barrier is like a person who has lost their way; The second barrier is like a person who has found the road; The third barrier is like a person who has neither lost nor found it. All three barriers are like a person who does not ask for directions. If one can understand this, one will see Mañjuśrī. The Master said, "If you can understand this, you will see Mañjuśrī. Xingkong said, "I have understood. The Master said, "If you have understood, then speak. Xingkong said, "I have understood. The Master said, "If you have understood, then speak.
