A bowl of white congee at dawn, a cup of clear tea in the afternoon—let no one bother with the tangled vines of old tales blooming in the cold. With both hands outstretched, he says:
"All you people, what dry wood or stubble are you seeking here? The Master has a poem on dwelling in the mountains which says: "Nothing to do."

The door of the mountain hut does not open; on the earthen steps, spring rains have caused green moss to grow. This mind was thought to be entrusted to no one—then, from where did the cry of a solitary bird come?
Later, he passed away at this same mountain site at the age of sixty-six. His collected works, titled the *Zhushiji* (Collected Works of the Bamboo Chamber), were circulated in the world.

Chan Master Ming Boluo of Dali’s Cangshan was the son of the Zhao family of his native district. Initially residing at the Hanging Rock of Cangshan, he venerated the Buddha in a cave to clarify the ground of his mind.
Later, he visited Dafang and had his mind-seal confirmed by Guting Jian. Upon returning, he continued his devotions to the Buddha.
One day, while walking in meditation upon the rock, he stood upright and passed away. For seven days he did not fall. The local people [prepared] incense and candles...
They performed the rites and offered prayers for him. His body was as light as a single leaf, and he was subsequently cremated.

Seven *śarīra* relics were obtained and enshrined within a stupa. Later generations named the cliff wall there "Pāra Rock. The mountain terrain is steep and perilous; those who ascend it are struck with awe.

When the wind blows through the grasses and trees, they all produce the sound of prostrating to the Buddha, a sound that continues without ceasing even to this day. Upon the stone where he prostrated, the imprints of his hands and feet remain vividly clear.
However, it was as if he had been born anew. He established a stupa at a hermitage on Mount Tang.
A lay practitioner from Ershui Daoan had long studied under Gu Tingjian, who showed him that "the myriad dharmas return to the One. He built a dwelling among the Nine Peaks of Shuimu;
upon hearing the sound of the water, he attained great enlightenment. When he saw Tingjian again, Tingjian looked at him and immediately said:
"Excellent! This time you, layman, shall sit securely within your own home. The layman replied, "I have never gone outside since I came here.
Yuanzhi asked, "How are matters at home? The layman said, "The four walls have been overturned. Yuanzhi approved of this. The layman bowed. Yuanzhi sent him a verse that read:
"The iron walls and silver mountains are all cast down; be careful and cherish this, do not harbor doubt. He sent it to him in the year [blank].
Seventy. At the time of his death, he spoke this verse: "I have long been accustomed to using tortoise hair; I have frequently grasped at rabbit horns.
Today it is clear: Zhaozhou’s bridge.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Da’gang Cheng.
Chan Master Tianshen Dufeng Benshan of Hangzhou was originally from the Wu family of Fengyang. His father, while serving in government office, traveled to Leyang in Guangdong where he was born.
At the age of seventeen, he left the household life. Initially, he met Yuanming, who presented him with the "Mu" (No) koan;
the Master was able to attain realization immediately. When he reported this to Yuanming, Yuanming said, "For twenty years I have been contemplating this 'Mu'. As it was, the Master...
"A mosquito trying to bite an iron ox. As soon as you begin to practice the Way, you will immediately develop many intellectual views.

He spoke again, saying, "Observing your spiritual capacity, it is distinct from that of others; do not let yourself be deceived by others into becoming an elder, for that would ruin your great matter."

Having received the Master’s instruction, he immediately made a vow and took an oath that in this life his goal would be awakening. Admiring the boundless style of Master Wuji, he entered the Sichuan region to seek out teachers.
Upon meeting Master Ji, who was summoned to the capital, he subsequently shut himself in retreat, forgoing even a bed or bedding, and kept only a small stool.
Feeling heavy and dull, he removed his bench. One day, hearing the sound of the temple bell, he attained realization and spoke this verse:

"Profoundly still and silent, all activity ceases; Touched upon, it roars like thunder without cause. With one sound that shakes the earth, all news is exhausted; The skull shatters and the dream finally returns.
He went again to visit [Master] Ji, but Ji had recently passed away. He then sought certification from Yuexi Cheng, who said:
The Buddha-dharma is not like fresh fish; one fears it will rot on that day. [Zhaozhou] merely struck east and west, secretly setting up examinations.
One day, while serving Cheng, they were sitting in the garden. Cheng asked, "What *huatou* have you been looking at lately?
The Master replied, "The word 'wu' (no). Cheng asked, "What is the word 'wu'? The Master said, "Looking at it now, it is just like a golden vajra in the mouth."

[Zhaozhou] presented the King’s precious sword. Cheng said, "What is the Vajra-King Precious Sword? The Master said, "Its cold radiance blazes forth, illuminating the past and soaring through the present.
Cheng said, "Give me back the sword! The Master said, "If you intend to move, you have already encountered its edge. Cheng said, [and remained silent].
Heng’an held his staff across the front of the hall and asked, "What about at such a time? The Master said, "If it were a Buddha, I would kill him;
if it were a Patriarch, I would kill him. Cheng said, "What about when the old monk comes? The Master said, "I will not spare you either. Cheng said, "What is it like after the killing?
The Master said, "Fortunately, all under heaven is at peace. Cheng said, "Ultimately, what is the meaning of the word 'wu' (no)? The Master said, "The evidence of the crime is clear. Cheng...
[Daowu] said, "Let us set aside the thief for a moment; return my stolen goods to me. The Master said, "Six times six is thirty-six. Lingzhao Cheng said, "That is not it yet; speak further.
The Master said, "The nights are short and sleep is insufficient; the days are long and hunger remains. Cheng said, "An ox passes through the lattice window."
"The head, the horns, and all four hooves have already passed through; for what reason does the tail not pass? The Master said, "There is not a single dharma that stands before the mind;
in a flash, the whole body is revealed in the open field. Deng asked, "Where do you now establish your dwelling and sustain your life?"

The Master said, "Where is there that does not honor [the Dharma]? Later, he took his leave of Fayan Cheng and traveled to the region of Zhejiang. He closed the gates at Wanfeng Hermitage on Mount Tianmu.

Fayan Cheng also received an imperial decree, graciously being granted permission to return to Dagaokou in Jinling; he sent a letter summoning the Master to receive his final instructions. At that time, the Master had gone elsewhere on business.
When Fayan Cheng approached the end of his life, he ordered that his robe and fly-whisk be sent to be bestowed upon him. The Master resided on the mountain for over forty years.
During the Tiānshùn era of the Míng Emperor Yīngzōng, he constructed the Three Pagodas of West Lake, as well as Zhāomíng on Mount Tiānmù, Bǎolián on Mount Wúshān, and Gānlù on the South Mountain.
At the beginning of the Chénghuà era of Emperor Xiànzōng, he shut himself away in Shíwū; later, he resided at Tiānzhēn.
A monk asked, "What is the master’s house style? The Master said, "In the front river, the tide is swift and the fish swim."
[The Master] said, "Astringent. Later, when birds were finding it difficult to alight upon the high peaks of the ridges, a monk requested further instruction, saying:
"Master Gaofeng said: 'The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs; the stone tiger before the cliff cradles its cub while sleeping.
An iron snake drills into the diamond eye; a wild goose leads an elephant on Mount Kunlun. Within these four lines, there is one line that can kill and can give life, can let go and can seize. If..."
"If a person can examine this thoroughly, the business of a lifetime of study is finished. [The student] asked, "I do not yet know which phrase that is.
The Master said, "Wait until you have attained awakening, and then I will tell you. [The student] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Have you not heard it said:
'If you have a staff, I give you a staff; if you have no staff, I take your staff away'? [This was spoken during a general discourse.]

The precious sword is fully wielded within daily life; with lofty brandishing and sweeping strokes, one acts with resolute composure. When withdrawn, souls and gallbladders lose their courage before the wind; when extended, skulls lie scattered across the earth.
Disregarding ten thousand deaths and ten thousand lives, a single spear and a single horse suffice to achieve victory.
Zhaozhou’s very life-force is manifest therein: the blood-stained blade reaches the heavens without revealing its edge. (He strikes with the whisk.)
With a single sweep of his whisk, he said: "The void is vast and transparent, with no news; ten thousand miles of cloudless sky, the Milky Way is azure.
Pressed so that Mount Sumeru enters a lotus fiber, Maitreya and Śākyamuni both cry out in distress. Riding an iron horse backward against the west wind, the startled earthen ox emerges from the sea.
O worthy ones, if you understand this as something extraordinary, you betray what is already revealed; if you do not take it as extraordinary..."
A special assembly. Embracing his stolen goods while crying out for injustice—how do you understand this? "To hide the world within the world;
only then will you see the horned sheep hanging from the treetops. In the year of Renyin, he passed away at Tianzhen; his stupa was erected at the original mountain.
Chan Master Pujie Guyue Jingcheng of Wutai Mountain in Taiyuan was the son of the Zhang family of Xihe.

He first studied under Yuexi Cheng, who instructed him to contemplate the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou. After two days, he attained a realization, which left Cheng deeply impressed. He subsequently entered Sichuan and lived in seclusion on Mount Feixue for three years.
One day, he went out to prepare rice; when he returned, he found that the rice had already begun to mold. Taking this as...

He sat on the ground for a long time; his feet became soaked by the cold and dampness so that he could not rise. Someone carried him to the back mountain, where he began to recover after regulating his breath.
One day, while sitting on a wooden platform, he heard the sound of a firecracker and attained great awakening. From that point on, throughout all times, everything was transparently clear.
He went to visit Guangfu, who asked, "When a person who has undergone the 'great death' returns to life, what is it like? The Master [replied].

[The student] said: "The eyebrows are horizontal above the eyes; the nostrils are large and hang down. [The student] asked: "What is the meaning of the word 'Mu'? The Master said: "The wind blows and the grass bows; the water reaches and the channel is formed. [The student] said:

"When the great earth sinks away and empty space is shattered to pieces, where will you find a place to settle your body and establish your life? The Master said: "When the clouds vanish, the mountains and peaks are revealed;

when the sun rises, the heavens and seas are clear. — Ming Yingzong (Enlightened Emperor) (Note: This passage records a dialogue between a Chan master and a student. The final phrase "Ming Yingzong" indicates that this text was compiled or endorsed by the Ming Emperor Yingzong.)
In the *dingchou* year of the Tiānshùn era, he returned to Mount Qingliáng. The Prince of Dai invited him into the inner palace to inquire about the Way and honored him with great respect.
By imperial decree, a temple was established in Huáyán Gully, named Pǔjì, and the Master was appointed as its abbot. The Master once composed a verse on mountain dwelling that says:
"Within the world, only Wutai is permitted to be high; The person of no rank keeps company with the silent solitude. Let the winds from all quarters blow as they will."
Vast and expansive, with eyes ever empty, he gazes upon the clouds and the sky; Content in poverty beneath the forest trees, his thoughts are far-reaching and serene.
Upon a bamboo couch, he sleeps soundly with a stone for a pillow; His life beyond the ordinary is sufficient in every respect, for there is not the slightest seeking in his breast.
He dwells by himself beside the red cliffs and green waters, Completely free from honor or disgrace, from leisure or haste. This old monk does not understand the principle of returning to the source.
Letting the green mountains turn green and then yellow at will, Deeply hidden in mountain clefts, years are not counted. The tether of fame and the shackles of profit cannot drag him away.
A seven-pound robe, patched together again and again, Baked by the sun and blown by the wind, grows ever more fresh.
In the rustling spring breeze, accompanied by the lament of birds, Pure sounds reach right to the edge of his ears. As incense of cypress wood burns in the brazier, he sits upright, facing the moon.
The remaining sūtras were further unfolded, and later he passed away while seated at his home mountain.
The Dharma-transmission verse of Chan Master Ning of Yifeng at Danggan in Jiangning says: "From patriarch to patriarch, there is no dharma to transmit;
Each person possesses it inherently from the beginning. In the realization of the sands [of the Ganges], there is no bestowed dharma; There is neither before nor after."
Chan Master Lintian Fuzhan of Pongxi in Tongchuan Prefecture entered the Way through diligent austerity and received a prediction from Yuexi.

When he opened his hall to propagate the Dharma, he became a great refuge for those studying Chan in the regions of Chu and Shu. At the age of seventy-seven, at the time of his passing, he left behind these words:
"Riding an iron horse backward, howling in the western wind; the bright moon and the clear breeze are one and the same. This was his verse of departure.
This is a verse from the world [of common parlance]. There was a work titled *Tianyuan lu* (Record of Heaven and Abyss) in two fascicles, which has now been completely lost and forgotten.
Chan Master Wugu Wenquan of Huguo Temple on Mount Cha in Fengyang Prefecture, a successor of Chan Master Guanshan Tan, was the son of the Liu family of Shanghe in Jinan.
At the age of nineteen, he went to Lingyan to shave his head. He first met Yuetian, who bestowed upon him the essential points of the Dharma.
Subsequently, he studied under Biexuan and attained a realization. Biexuan asked, "The void is shattered and the great earth sinks flat; where do you dwell and establish your life?
The Master replied, "Last night the clay ox swallowed the bright moon; this morning the wooden horse breathes forth the pure wind. Biexuan said:
"Where does this 'one' return? the Master asked. The teacher replied, "The white ox has returned to the snowy peaks;
until now, its tracks have not been seen. Chuan nodded in approval. He then went to Mount Jinshan to visit Wuji, who instructed him to see Baoyuetan.
Baoyuetan asked, "Do you have money for sandals? The teacher replied, "The green mountains do not reveal their peaks. Baoyuetan asked, "What is it to manifest form in response to things?"
The Master said, "The solitary light of the bright moon shines across the heavens; the myriad phenomena of the universe are fully manifested.
One day, while sitting in the hall, Guishan Tan called out, "Cold! Cold! The Master immediately moved the brazier forward. Tan asked, "What is the matter by the brazier?
The Master struck the brazier three times. Tan smiled and left. Upon entering the room, Tan took up his staff.
The staff-bearer said, "This is my staff. Now tell me, where is the master? The Master snatched the staff away, threw it to the ground, and stood with his hands folded.
Tanzhu said, "Look at this fellow; he has struck down the staff! The Master shook out his sleeves and departed.
Later, he received formal certification and went forth to Mount Chasha. There, he ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises only by relying on conditions."
The Way is fundamentally wordless; it is through words that the Way is revealed. Now, as dragons and elephants mingle and the various mountains dwell together, this is no small occasion.
It is moved by the Emperor’s great grace and the protection of worthy scholars and officials that we have established this period for meditation, assisting in this sacred transformation.
We have charged this mountain monk to glorify the Eye of the School, so that those in the final age may plant seeds in the field of merit. Nevertheless, although it is thus...
"That is so. Yet it is still not the matter beneath the patched robe. Tell me, what is the matter beneath the patched robe?
A monk asked, "I do not ask about the Three Vehicles; as for the matter of direct pointing, how is it? The Master said, "On the summit of Double Peak, cranes perch in the trees;

at the foot of Nine-Dragon Mountain, birds sing among the flowers. The monk said, "The meaning of the Ancestor’s coming from the West has been pointed out by you, Master. How is it transmitted here in the Eastern Land?"
"What is the matter? The Master said: "The green pines atop the ridge are elegant for a thousand ages; the flowing water by the ravine is evergreen throughout ten thousand years.
He asked, "What is the realm of Baishui? The Master said: "A single expanse of fallow fields stretches across the four wilds;

three thatched huts stand grand amidst all the mountains. He asked, "Who is the person within the realm? The Master said: "At the head of the White Tiger is the Temple of the Son of Heaven; at the side of the Black..."
At Longtan, Emperor Wang Ji asked, "When both person and environment are forgotten, what then? The Master said, "Su Wu did not understand the will of the green ram;
the Seventh Prince always lamented the white crow’s return. The monk bowed. The Master struck the desk once.
Ascending the hall, he raised an ancient saying: "The fan leaps and bounds up to the thirty-third heaven, striking the nostrils of Śakra."
"A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow of the staff; the rain pours down like an overturned basin. Now tell me, what is the meaning? The assembly was speechless.
The Master said, "It is because they do not recognize the true face of Mount Kuang-lu that they remain within the mountains."
Chan Master Dahuì Juéhuā of Chóngfú Temple in Jāngníng was the son of the Liu family of Wéiyáng. Initially, he had an awakening upon meeting Hǎizhōu;
he later studied under Bǎoyuè at Fánchāng and subsequently received certification from him. After taking up residence [at Chóngfú], he ascended the hall and, raising his whisk, said:
Beyond the limit of majestic sound, it is simply this very thing. Right now, before your eyes, it is also simply this very thing.
If you call it a whisk, you blind the eyes of gods and men; if you do not call it a whisk, you blind the eyes of gods and men.
O Great Assembly, what ultimately would you call it? If you can see it directly right here and now, then you will know why Kāśyapa smiled. II.
The Patriarch sought the mind but could not find it at all. He succeeded the Tathāgata’s transmission of the lamp and continued the orthodox lineage of the patriarchs.
After a long silence, he said, "Not even a thousand sages can recognize it," and struck the incense table once with his whisk.
Chan Master De Shan of Cui Feng on Mount Fu Niu in Henan was a native of Xia in Guan-Shan. From childhood, he was simple and unadorned.
At the age of thirty, he first entered the monastic life as a disciple of Hai of Niu Shou in Yun Nan. After Hai passed away, the Master began his travels to study under various teachers;
however, the "obstructing object" within him remained stubbornly unresolved. Following the guidance of Gu Feng, he went to attend upon Bao Yue Tan. Tan said, "I am waiting for you."

His mind was indeed far-reaching, yet he lacked one final, bone-piercing breakthrough. Only after passing through this and coming back to life from the midst of death did his speaking and breathing toward others finally find their proper footing;

otherwise, there would have been no connection at all. Upon hearing this, the Master entered Mount Funiu and practiced with a diligent heart for six years, until he finally attained great enlightenment.
When he appeared in the world, he offered the incense of his realization specifically for Master Tan. How extraordinary!

While he was at the capital, all was auspicious; however, because the assembly had become so vast, public opinion among the officials and laypeople arose. The Master consequently relinquished the assembly and retired to Mount Funiu.
There, the congregation grew even more numerous. He preached the Dharma for thirty years in total. One day, he said to the assembly, "Return! Return!"

"I am a northerner returning to the north; it is my wish to return to my ancestral home. He subsequently returned to Jingzhou to spend his final years. Not long after, he passed away at the age of eighty-one.
His disciples enshrined his entire body and buried it behind the common burial ground of the monastery. There is a eulogy for the Master’s portrait which says:
"With wind there is clarity; with moonlight there is brightness. How magnificent is Cui Feng! Like jade, he vibrates; like metal, he rings."
Chan Master Wuliang Cang of Baiyun in Chuzhou, a successor of Chan Master Zhengan Zhen, addressed the assembly: "Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, follow the *huatou* in your practice."
Abide with the *huatou*, sit with the *huatou*, and lie down with the *huatou*.
Let the mind be like a chestnut burr, so that it cannot be swallowed by any personhood, egoism, ignorance, the five desires, or the three poisons.
Whether acting or remaining still, the entire body is a single mass of doubt. Doubting and doubting, one remains dully and steadfastly throughout the day, even when hearing sounds.
Upon seeing a form, one must surely seize it with a single "kiai! Although this is so, take care not to mistake a bell for a jar. (He lets out a shout.)
Chan Master Yonggang Zongruan of Fagua Fahai at Fenghua, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Zhong of He’an, addressed the assembly:

“In general, when practicing the work of cultivation, one must simply give rise to a great state of doubt (*mahā-vicikitsā*) and not lose right mindfulness. A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt. As soon as there is an interval...”
To sever it is to fall into emptiness. I see that you practitioners have not yet spent half a month or a month bringing [your practice] to a state of "one piece.
How could you avoid falling into error? If genuine doubt manifests before you and remains unshakable, you will naturally not fear confusion.
Furthermore, you must not give rise to even a single thought of joy; as soon as there is the slightest divergent thought, it is immediately shattered.
With two stakes, simply maintain a state of fierce and courageous intensity; all day long, be like a dead man.
When you reach such a state, you need not fear a turtle escaping from its jar.
Chan Master Baowen Hongyin of Tangcheng was a dharma heir of Chan Master Rui of Xichan.
He was the son of the Zhang family of Tangcheng in Guyu. He had paid respects to Chan Master Rui of Xichan for many years;

following Rui’s passing, he traveled far to seek out Chan Master Qi of Chushan. It happened that the Prince of Ding was observing the end of his mourning period and invited Qi to ascend the seat. The Master [was present].
The questioner asked: "The thunderous voice shakes the earth; the field for selecting Buddhas has opened. This single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly as if it had not yet dispersed.
I wonder, how may one repay the Imperial Grace and the Buddha’s Grace? Qī replied: "Vast is the wind of Yao, purifying the six directions;
bright is the sun of the Buddha, illuminating the three thousand worlds. The Master said: "I have heard your words of praise. But what is the meaning of the picking of the flower and the smile?"

Qī said, "In the presence of such a pivot, words find no place for the tongue; only the head-dhūta’s single smile is permitted to be transmitted. The Master said, "The jade plum pierces through the snow;

the crimson leaves wither in the frost. This is precisely the occasion when the imperial house removes the mourning for the Emperor, and the very day the celestial carriage departed on its immortal journey."
"I do not know where he is now. Qī raised his whisk and said, "He is upon the tip of this mountain monk’s whisk.
He has attained perfect enlightenment, emits great radiance, and turns the wheel of Dharma together with the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. Do you see him? The Master said:
"If it is thus, then the entire realm is free from concealment. Qi said, "Even so, there are still eyes that cannot see.

The Master said, "In this very place where one cannot see, not even a hair's breadth is separated [from reality]. Qi said, "That is not yet the subtle wonder. The Master said, "I do not know what, then, constitutes the subtle wonder?
Qi said, "When both extremes are wiped away, only then does one see the person prior to the kalpas. The Master said, "I am indebted to the Master for pointing this out."
He manifested the Vajra Eye and said, "Death and rebirth—no further doubt. Qiji said, "Excellent, you monk! A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net;
your words manifest the school’s essence. You do not disgrace the lineage of Xichan, yet you must continue to maintain this realization.
Do not deceive yourself. The master said, "The devas and humans bear witness. I thank the Master for his seal of approval."
The Chan Master Wujie Wen once composed the "Song of Manifesting the School" (*Xianzong ge*), which says: "This school is realized as being without past or present;

It shatters empty space and then mends it of its own accord. Within the mass of sounds and forms lies the field of wondrous enlightenment; Sending forth and gathering back proceeds without obstruction."
Subtlety within the essence: at midnight, a wooden man gazes into a mirror; on the southern bank of Persia, one chews cold ice;
in the northern borderlands, infants clamor in the marketplace. Subtlety within function: atop a verdant tree, a stone woman blows the flute;

a gourd hangs from the eastern wall in Zhaozhou’s house; in the village, the old Wang burns paper money at night. Essence within essence, subtlety within subtlety: within the jeweled net, they vie for brilliance.
A pearl must have a single aperture pierced through it in the darkness. The Ocean-Tide Sound speaks with blazing intensity; the lute of lion-sinew plays the "White Snow.
The green mountains on both banks smile and nod their heads; the ancient melody of a hundred years is turned anew.

Chan Master Bao Feng Zhi Xuan of Jinling Yishan, a descendant of the twenty-eighth generation under Nanyue and a dharma heir of Chan Master Yishan Cishi, was the son of the Fan family of Wujiang. By profession, he had been a carpenter. Because...
Hai-zhou Ci was building a pagoda courtyard when he lost his axe and injured his foot. In great pain, he asked for wine.

Ci said, "Fan, having your head cut off would be easier to endure than this injury to your foot. Even if there were a thousand *shí* of wine to give you to drink upon having your head chopped off, would you be able to drink it?
The Master attained realization and immediately requested ordination. Ci gave him the tonsure, saying, "Today your head has fallen. The Master replied, "My head..."
Although he had fallen [from his previous status], those who were fond of drinking did not fall [with him]. He was appointed as the head of the kitchen staff.

One day, while carrying firewood, Nanyue Zhi said to him, "Why are you carrying thorns and brambles? The Master replied, "This is firewood. Zhi laughed loudly and said, "Hehe! This is firewood; take it away and burn it.
The Master was perplexed. Zhi said, "This is firewood; take it away and burn it. The Master, intending to ask further, thought, "What principle does the Master ultimately have that he asks me this?"
That evening, I applied myself with focused intent to investigate the matter. Unaware, I was singed on the eyebrows by a fire, and my face felt as if it were being cut by a blade.
When I looked at myself in a mirror, I suddenly attained great enlightenment. I presented this verse: "The Master carrying firewood calls it 'thorns';

The flames burn the brows, and the skin of the face is in haste. The wondrous purport of the Patriarch is clear within the mirror; A single reflection allows one to attain the fundamental essence. Ciming then struck him. The Master [said]: "I have attained it."
[Zhaozhou] snatched away the staff and said, "This six-foot staff has not been used for many years; today it must be taken up once more. Cizhao laughed loudly.
The Master then presented a verse, saying: "Wherever the staff strikes, bloodstains appear; Look closely at the blade hidden within the smile.
Were it not for a truly heroic man, A dead person would dance and chatter while being struck by the staff. Cizhao said, "Regarding this very verse..."
[The Master] said, "You may succeed to my school. He then bestowed upon him a verse, saying: "Delusion and enlightenment are like clouds in the sky;
The azure heavens are clear and bright, pure and without trace. The world is manifest within them, appearing as dew; Whether killing or giving life, whatever is brought forth is already perfected.
From this time on, his fame spread far and wide, and disciples flocked to him like a river. He took up residence at Gaofeng in Jinling, and subsequently moved to Yishan. [His successor was] Tianqi.
Master Rui asked, "Where have you come from? Rui said, "From Beijing. The Master said, "Are you still in Beijing, or do you have another destination?
Rui said, "I am carefree wherever I am. The Master said, "Have you ever been to Sichuan? Rui said, "I have."
The Master asked, "How is the realm of Western Sichuan compared to this place? Rui replied, "Though the mountains and rivers differ, the clouds and moon are the same.
The Master raised his fist and said, "Is there such a thing as this in Sichuan? Rui replied, "No. The Master asked, "Why is it that there is none?
Rui replied, "It is not my realm. The Master asked, "What, then, is your realm? Rui replied, "The Buddhas."

He could not identify it. [The Master asked: "Who would dare to force a name upon it? Dongshan said, "Are you not, then, one who clings to emptiness? Xuefeng said, "I will never make my livelihood within a ghost cave.

The Master said, "Among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in India, you are the foremost. Xuefeng shook his sleeves and departed. The Master was pleased, for he saw in him a true successor capable of upholding the Way.
He then composed a verse: "Xuefeng is like a wild fox; His mind is as clear as a bright mirror. If you wish to know the Buddha, Look at Xuefeng."

The Epitaph states: "Jishan’s staff and shout were like a light touch; from then on, the hands and eyes of killing and enlivening became intimate. Holy understanding and ordinary sentiment were both cut off at once;

yet a fresh branch of the *dharma-puṣpa* still blooms anew. The Master passed away on the ninth day of the twelfth month of the Renchen year of the Chenghua era during the reign of Emperor Xianzong of the Ming.
His stupa was erected to the left of Yishan Temple.

Chan Master Zhiying of Bifeng on Yunxi at Mount Lu was illiterate as a youth and had never studied books. In her later years, she composed verses spontaneously, which were frequently praised by others.
She entrusted her disciple Zhisu with a verse, saying: "Having thoroughly seen the true face of one's mother’s birth, from now on I shall preserve this innate truth.
When my claws and fangs have been fully developed in the days to come, I shall let out a single roar."
The hundred beasts were startled.
The Dharma successor of Chan Master Ning of Yifeng, Chan Master Jin Baofang of Tianmu in Hangzhou, spoke this verse of transmission: "True nature is originally without nature; true dharma..."
"The nature of non-dharmas is fundamentally non-existent; if one thoroughly understands this nature of non-dharmas, where would there be anything not fully realized?

When the Master was nearing death, he called to his disciples and asked, "Is there water? An attendant brought him hot broth, but the Master rebuked him, saying, "Water is used for purification; why use something warm?"
"You all may come easily; the water for the attendants has arrived. The Master rinsed his mouth and, making the sound of a *fanbai* chant, said:
"Life is like turbid water; death is like clear water. Clarity and turbidity have no fixed state—this is just so. He let out a great shout and passed away into stillness.
The Venerable Jūfū Shōshō of Shōbuku, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Zen Master Kūfū Tsū, had long relied upon Daikan. One day, he suddenly attained realization and presented this verse:
“The Dharma-nature is empty and unimpeded; In its equality, it is Avalokiteśvara. Severing the dualistic mechanisms of mind— This is called transcending the three.”
The Master of the Dharma Realm,
Chan Master Xueguang of Sishan Zhengfa, whose clan name was Zhao, traveled extensively throughout various regions before arriving at Lingfeng to spend the summer retreat.
Upon hearing the public case concerning Venerable Yan-yang’s question to Master Zhaozhou, he attained a realization.

He related this to Jizhao, who said, "In the state of non-effort, you must apply effort; do not mistake a mere fragment of light and shadow, lest it mislead your entire life. He then spent the winter retreat at Jingde Temple.

One day, while in meditative concentration, the sound of a mountain waterfall triggered his awakening. He silently invoked the pivotal spiritual mechanisms (*ji*) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity.
Having thoroughly penetrated each and every condition, he went to visit Jie Kong. After recounting everything from the beginning, Kong said, "Have you not heard it said:
'Do not say that being mindless is the Way; even mindlessness still leaves one separated by a further barrier. Having finished speaking, he entered his quarters."

From that time on, the Master was utterly devoid of mental composure; harboring doubts, he could not reach a decision. One day, upon seeing the line from a poem by Hanshan, "My mind is like the autumn moon," his lingering stagnation was suddenly dispelled.
Later, he lived in a hermitage on an ancient mountain, where he passed away after writing a verse at the moment of death.

Chan Master Tiancai Ying of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Tianning Xuan, addressed the assembly: "The Elder Master Mo Tang surges up waves upon level ground and hammers out wooden wedges within empty space.
When the toxic breath returns to strike people, he bluntly says, 'I have personally seen the Treasure.'"
"Month! You do not know how many people's eyes you have blinded. Silence! It would have been better had you remained silent.
The Chan Master Tiantong Xian of Bifeng Temple in Nanjing, a successor of the Eastern Mountain [Dongshan] Chan Master, asked Yuzhi Ju: "Is there such a thing as 'within Bifeng Temple'?"

[The monk] approached and asked, "Could it be that you are the Master? The Master said, "Does the Senior Monk see [me]? He replied, "Even if one were to see you, it would be like gold dust falling into the eyes.
The Master said, "This fellow has been dead for so long; why have you come to beg for his life? He then returned to the abbot’s quarters.
The next day, ascending the hall, he cited an ancient worthy who said: "Break open the Great Tang Empire and find someone who does not understand."

"There is no one who understands the Buddha-dharma," he said. Again he said, "I have traveled all the way to the south, yet I have never encountered anyone on the tip of my staff who understands the Buddha-dharma.
These two statements are highly enigmatic; try to provide a response for them.
Juzhuo said, "In front there is no meeting at the village; behind there is no succession at the inn. The Master said, "That is not it yet; say it again.
Juzhuo said, "If one does not meet a connoisseur, it is a vain labor to speak of the cold of winter. The Master asked again, "You have traveled south to seek instruction;

what words or phrases did you encounter? Try to tell me. Juzhuo recited his verse of awakening to the Way: "The lake's light leaning on my staff—three thousand acres; the mountain colors opening the gate—five..."

Six Peaks: "What meets the eye is originally a manifest reality; the meditation cushion does not now refine empty vacuity. With the fullness of scenery before one’s eyes, one’s daily life is sufficient;
who would distinguish between kin and stranger on level ground? Even if Bodhidharma had transmitted the secret of the mind, were you questioned about it, you still would not recognize him.
The Master said, "Not so, not so" (Feifei). Juzhu asked, "Why 'not so, not so'? The Master said, "If you did not say 'not so, not so,' [I would have no reason to speak]."
Such people are utterly deluded. Emperor Wu of Liang and Bodhidharma both failed to perceive the opportune moment; why bother with breaking reeds and then dispatching someone to pursue him?
Whether ancient or modern, they have fallen into the trap of others. [A monk] asked, "How can one avoid falling into the trap of others?

The Master gave him a slap and said, "Is this falling? Or is it not falling? The assembly prostrated themselves in worship, and what they had long harbored within them was completely dissolved, like ice melting away.
The Master was traveling at Nanping Zongjing Hall when he ascended the Dharma seat and said, "This place is perfectly suited for preaching the Dharma.

As soon as he spoke, Juyi called out from the side, "The preaching of the Dharma is already finished. The Master then descended from the seat and looked back, asking, "Which of these is the place where I preached the Dharma?
Juyi replied, "The sword has long since been lost. The Master nodded in approval.
Chan Master Dongzong Weiqing of Mount Song in Fuwu, Henan, was a successor of Chan Master Longyando. He was the son of the Zhang family from Donglu.

At the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Master Xingtian at Mita Temple in Xiangyang. Having served as his attendant for three years, he was able to pursue the great matter of birth and death.

Failing to achieve any breakthrough, he took leave of his teacher and traveled extensively to visit renowned masters. One master showed him the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one," which immediately gave rise to a profound state of doubt.
He made a vow to remain in strict retreat within Huangshi Mountain for many years of intensive investigation.
One night, while drawing water from a pond, he happened to gaze at the moon reflected in the water and attained a realization. He then went to Jinling to consult with Master Longyan Dao. Dao—

[The Master] asked, "Since you have come from afar, what is it that you seek? The Teacher said, "I seek only the Way. The Master said, "In this place of mine, there is not a single dharma remaining. What is there to seek?
The Teacher said, "If there is no dharma to be sought, then the mind is also without self. Its very substance is vast and empty; thereafter, there is no dwelling.
The Master nodded his head in approval and conferred upon him the seal of certification. He was subsequently invited by various provinces of the Zhou and Jin regions to reside at Fushan.
At Niushōzan, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West, where did the wondrous meaning originally reside?
The Master said, "Every morning the golden crow rises over the Eastern Sea; every night the jade hare flies across the Western Min Mountains."
[The student] asked, "After you have left this world, what will your intent be? The Master said, "In autumn, chrysanthemums bloom by the hedge; in winter, plum blossoms open on the ridges.
[The student] said, "If that is so, then the Way’s transformation is without birth or death, yet the spring breeze undergoes change.
The Master raised his whisk and said, "Once more he raises it to manifest divine function; the myriad phenomena all return to the realm of the Buddha. He then said, "Lay down the wutong flowers."
The non-Buddhists have a wedge driven into their crown; it strikes the bamboo of Xiao and Xiang. Xiangyan opens his eyes within his ears;
Yunmen’s staff leaps and bounds. It touches the nostrils of Śakra; the blade of the Great Sword flies from Fengxue.
It splits open the eyes of Sāgara and terrifies the Ancient Lamp King, who flees into the cavity of a gnat. Old Bodhidharma goes straight to the crown of Vairocana.

[The Master] ascended [the hall]. At this juncture, is there anyone who transcends the school and surpasses the standard? After a long silence, he said: "In the profound ocean, the earthen ox bellows;
in the empty crags, the stone tiger roars while sleeping amidst the clouds. This was the small *chan* (meditation) discourse for the Dragon Boat Festival on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Rice balls wrapped in reeds are offered as a memorial to the heroic spirit. Mugwort leaves are fragrant; pomegranate flowers are pure. This scene year after year possesses a distinct flavor.
The waters of Canglang are clear; Qu Yuan’s one dream has ended. While the world is drunk in turbidity, Qu Yuan alone remains sober.
Through the ages, his loyalty and integrity have been fully realized. Everyone should present this supreme pivot, and the five aggregates and their mixed poisons will all be extinguished. *A shout.*

The lay practitioner Gu Zhiwang of Jinling, dharma heir of Chan Master Yongci (Shanhaizhou) of the twenty-eighth generation under Nanyue (Xiangyan Guxi Cheng).
The preface to the *Xuegu ji* states: "The practitioner’s style was Zuting; in his youth, he was renowned for his filial piety."
In his village, he steadfastly observed the five precepts and dwelt alone in a single-story building for three years practicing *zazen*.
Through diligent application of the upward path, he broke through the silver mountains and iron walls; the flower of his mind suddenly blossomed and his wisdom-eye opened wide.
He received formal certification from the Great Monk Dongshan Haizhou, continuing the lamp of the seventh generation of Chan Master Gaofeng Miao under the Linji lineage. Twenty...
He was the fourth-generation descendant [of the founding master]. When Cishi was about to pass away, he called out three times to the ancestral temple, and Shisan responded.
Their words and intentions were in perfect accord, so Cishi bestowed upon him the great robe and the fly-whisk.

After receiving the Dharma, he wrote the two characters "Xuegu" (Snow Valley) in large script and hung them high above his dwelling, intending to manifest that the Second Patriarch had sought the Dharma in the snow until it reached his waist, never forgetting his origins.

(Appended: The Song of Dongshan’s Final Testament, presented by Guchixing Cheng. It says: "In Jinling there was a remarkable man, Who built his home from bare hands and established the guiding principles. Had he not met a virtuous friend to call him back, He would have nearly been lost amidst the dust of the mortal world. )

Sighing that this floating life is but such as this, he sought direct pointing from an enlightened master. Upon hearing it said that the *Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* was available, the superior man’s spirit rose up to the heavens, and he stirred himself with vigor. Contemplating Amitābha as his own self, he pressed on until the cold ice was transformed into water.

Let others be neither Buddha nor mind; one must strive to reach the very bottom of the river of Chan. Day by day, night by night, the iron ox remains unmoving—apply the whip with vigor. When its horns and head emerge in full majesty, it lets out a lion’s roar, startling the golden sun from the seabed as it flies up into the sky.

Seeking certification and testing karmic conditions, you have several times personally arrived before Mount Dongshan. Circling the meditation seat to present your understanding, I let out a thunderous shout to transmit it to you. One may be called a "great recluse" while dwelling in the marketplace; now you are fit to be a lotus blooming amidst the flames.

You are accustomed to riding a wooden horse among the stars of the Big Dipper, yet you come here to the waters of Dongshan to steer an iron boat. Letting go at the edge of a precipice, you know where you will land; though the thousand-fold net of desire cannot hold you back, the blue-eyed barbarian monk [Shakyamuni]...

There is nothing that can be done. Entrusting the *kāṣāya* as a token of faith—Zhaozhou’s authentic Chan is rarely encountered; who would be willing to search for the cypress tree in front of the courtyard? He cuts off the old entanglements of the Southern Mountains; the unperforated iron hammer receives another stroke of the saw.

Greatly letting go, then gathering back together—the green waters and blue mountains are all wondrous realms. Treading with one's feet upon the uppermost pass, the bright moon does not follow the flowing water away.
The Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, Volume Sixty.
