Proofread by the Imperial Subject Monk Chao Kui, Abbot of Gu Huayan Temple, Capital City. Submitted for Imperial Review.
Presented to the twenty-ninth generation below Nanyue in the Linji school.
Chan Master Tianqi Benrui of Jingling and Jingmen was a dharma successor of Chan Master Baofeng Xuan. He was a native of Zhongling in Nanchang. His father was Jiangtang and his mother was Lady Xu.
At the age of twenty, he suddenly realized that the physical body is impermanent; he abandoned his home to travel afar and entered the service of Wushuo Neng at Jingmen.
After his tonsure, [Zhaozhou] was instructed to investigate the saying, "The myriad dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return? Later, he met Chan Master Quan at Gaoyou and traveled with him to Xiangyang. On the road, they happened to hear a woman calling for her pig.
Quan said, "Mother, she is calling 'na-na' from inside the wall. Do you monks on the road understand? Break through this very pivot! "Niang-niang! (Mother! [Zhaozhou cried out.]
"It is still just the old lady. The Master was startled and broke into a cold sweat. One day, he fell gravely ill.

A Chan practitioner named Hui urged him, saying, "During this illness, you must by no means let your practice lapse. In the past, when Dahui was at Jingshan, he suffered from a back abscess and cried out day and night.
Someone asked him, 'Does the Master have anything that does not hurt? Dahui replied, 'I do. [The questioner] asked, 'What is it?'"
"What is it that does not ache? Huì replied, "It aches to death! It aches to death! At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Furthermore, one day, hearing a wild deer crying out, he realized that within the activities of daily life, there was nothing that was not the Way.
He then went to Shu to visit Chushan. He asked, "When I looked into this during my leisure time, it was perfectly clear and evident;
yet when it comes to the critical moment, why am I so utterly bewildered? Chushan said, "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds apart.
Later, while traveling through Jinling, he suddenly felt as if awakening from a dream; everything he had previously attained seemed like a total failure. He then went to study under Baofeng.
At Gaofeng, Xu found his needle and mustard seed in perfect accord; he subsequently received certification [from him] (the dialogue is contained within the Chapter on Baofeng).
One day, the Master addressed Puzhao Taichu, saying: "Regardless of the three matters of the 'upward' direction, one must resolve the final point. Taichu said:
"What is the final stroke? The Master said, "The wind blows through the willows by the wall; the sun drenches the elms by the stream.
Zhao said, "When the green mountains appear low, one sees the vastness of the sky; when the red lotuses bloom, one smells the fragrance of the water. He then made a retching sound.
This is precisely playing with words. The Master said, "What do you say? Chū replied, "It is like a person climbing a wall with no way out.

The Master made a belching sound, stood up, and returned to his place. Addressing the assembly, he cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the passage on "extinguishing and delivering all sentient beings.
The Master said, "The former sages and worthies all required that they die once and then be revived again. I am not like this. Why? Because the pine—"
The roots of the cypress are verdant; the roots of the cypress are azure. Last year they weighed half a catty; this year they weigh eight taels. Now tell me: is there still death and revival?
If you can understand this, only then will you not have deceived the Emperor. If you do not understand, do not act rashly. Addressing the assembly:
When the Patriarch came from the West, he did not establish written words; he pointed directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha.

There is no other dharma besides this. If, within this very place, you know where it falls, then you have a share in concentration (*samādhi*), a share in wisdom (*prajñā*), a share in the school (*zong*), and a share in the teaching (*jiao*).
There is nothing acceptable or unacceptable regarding either the Buddha-dharma or worldly dharmas;

it is like girding oneself with a hundred thousand strings of cash and riding a crane up to Yangzhou. If it were otherwise, then it would not be concentration, nor would it be wisdom, nor would it be the school.
It is not so. Nor is it the teaching. This is because you do not recognize your own original mind; this is what is called "reckless arrogance. As the Sūtra says:
"The empty, false, and floating mind abounds in various clever views, and thus cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment.

The Buddhas and the Patriarchs have transmitted only the One Mind and have not transmitted any other dharma. You all fail to penetrate your original mind and instead seek outwardly within a deluded mind.

To give rise to false effort is like attempting to pluck flowers from the sky or desire to produce fruit from the void; even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would still be called merely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
You must know that seeing one's nature to attain Buddhahood means that this nature is not the nature of another, and that this Buddha is not a Buddha achieved by another.
It is definitively your own original nature, identical to the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
The realm [of reality] is not obscure even by a hair’s breadth. It is inherently possessed by every person; it is lacking in none.

However, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and in all places, turn the light back upon yourself and reflect: "Look—what is this? Do not fixate on it as being located in only one specific place.
You must give rise to great doubt regarding it in all places. Lowering what is high and following what is mistaken, do not let even a single thread or a hair’s breadth of doubt remain.
Do not let it slip away. When walking, observe who it is that walks; when standing, observe who it is that stands;
when sitting, observe who it is that sits; when lying down, observe who it is that lies down.
When seeing a form, look immediately: who is it that sees? When hearing a sound, look immediately: who is it that hears?
When experiencing a touch, look immediately: who is it that experiences? When cognizing a phenomenon, look immediately: who is it that cognizes?
This applies even to speaking and remaining silent, moving and being still, turning the head and shifting the gaze, defecating and urinating, dressing and eating.
Welcoming guests and attending to visitors, moving back and forth in every interaction—examine each one thoroughly, day and night, without weariness.
Should you forget for even a single thought-moment, look into who it is that has forgotten. When a delusive thought arises, look into who it is that gives rise to the delusive thought.
If you say you do not understand, then who is it that does not understand? As for your current doubts, [look into who it is that doubts].
Who is it that doubts while looking? Looking and looking in this manner, there is no hindrance; every point is uniquely revealed, and every phenomenon is fully manifest.
Ten thousand objects cannot invade it; myriad conditions cannot enter it. Gain and loss, right and wrong—there are no seams or gaps whatsoever.
Brightness and darkness, form and emptiness—there is ultimately no distinction between self and other. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, the moon, and the stars—all are [thus].
The Sage exhausts the ordinary; in the end, it is all just this single word "who. There is no other thought. Above and below there is no path; advancing or retreating there is no door.
Mountains end and waters reach their limit; emotion vanishes and views are severed. Suddenly, with a loud "pop," one finally knows that this is not something sought from another.
If one does not undergo this once-and-for-all freezing to the bone, how can one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose? [Addressing the assembly.]
There is no dharma in the world; there is no dharma beyond the world. One who penetrates these two "no-dharmas" returns home to sit in peace.
When the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he once met the Senior Seat-holder Long, who said to him, "The verdant green bamboos are all True Suchness (*tathatā*);
the lush yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā. The Master pointed to the cypress tree in front of the courtyard and said, "When people see this..."

The pine trees were planted. It was as if it were a dream. After his passing, in the year Guihai of the Hongzhi era, his disciples erected a stupa at Wazi Po on Dayu Mountain in Wanping County, Shuntian Prefecture.
Chan Master Zhisu of the Linyin Jing’an Hermitage at Tianchi on Mount Kuang in Jiuyang was a dharma successor of Chan Master Yunxi Ying. He was the son of the Zhao family of Donglai.
In his youth, both his parents passed away. At the age of fifteen, he received the tonsure from Dayong at Tiantong Chengtian Monastery on Mount Wutai and went to visit Master Yun.

Xiyang received the imperial decree and later resided at Tianchi. He ascended the hall and said: "The essence is exposed; the golden wind shines with brilliant purity. A single color, luminous and unceasing.
When the wild sheep hangs its horns, no trace can be found; the toad at the bottom of the sea swallows the moon.
At the request of the Prince of Jing, he went to reside at Dongsan. He ascended the hall and said: "In heaven, heaven is high; on earth, earth is thick. Upon the tip of a single hair—"
"May you receive blessings at this auspicious moment. This is still a matter of "this side. But tell me, what is the matter of "that side"?
Striking the desk, he said, "Śākyamuni sleeps deeply; Maitreya rises late. He then descended from his seat.
Chan Master Wuyue Xiao of Dongta in Jiaxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Baofeng Jin. When Master Kong (Wuqu) presented his insights, the Master consistently refused to acknowledge them.
One day, the Master said to Kong, "I have a word I must say to you. Kong pricked up his ears to listen.
The Master merely smiled and did not speak. Xingkong repeatedly and earnestly entreated him. The Master smiled again. Only then did Xingkong assume the full ritual decorum and prostrate himself;
kneeling, he pleaded with grief. The Master then said: "The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha."
The essential point lies in investigating directly beneath you. If you can truly believe this, you may set aside all external conditions and investigate:
"Where does the One return? Empty yourself of all concerns and examine this *huatou* with a resolute mind. After three years, one day upon hearing the crowing of a cock, he attained realization.

He went to the Master to seek verification. The Master questioned him repeatedly and exhaustively; subsequently, he bestowed upon him the robe and whisk. Furthermore, the Master presented him with a verse, which said: "Non-dharma..."
It is neither non-dharma nor dharma; it is neither nature nor non-nature; it is neither mind nor non-mind. I have now fully entrusted to you the Dharma of the mind.

Master Fazu of Jigan was a successor of the Dharma lineage of Master Fashou Daoji of Tiantong Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture. He was a son of the Zhang family from Suxian Village in that commandery. At the age of...
Idle flowers are at their finest, yet they provoke sorrow. One might think there is a precious jewel within one’s garment; only when the garment is torn does one believe the jewel is absent.
Last year, there was still talk of the absence of the jewel; today, even the talk of its absence is gone. Within, one does not reflect; without, one does not seek.
The trichiliocosm of sand-grain worlds is gathered within a single hair; every dust mote and every land is the Lotus Treasury. To recognize it as such is still to remain outside.
The mind of every person is fundamentally the Ancient Amitābha. Among those in the age of the Dharma’s decline, many do not believe;
moment after moment they seek the Buddha elsewhere, unaware that every thought-moment is Amitābha himself. Later, he moved to Mount Bian; in his later years, he retired once more to Tianmushan.

Ning passed away in the autumn of the Gengshen year. He was seventy-four years of age and had fifty-two years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*). After his body was cremated, he was interred in a stupa at the Chan-yue Hall.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Tian-tong Xian.
Chan Master Faju of Tianchi Yuezhan Yuzhi Monastery in Huzhou was the son of the Fu family of Jiahe.
From childhood, he would often sit cross-legged upon the ground and fold grass to recite the Buddha’s name. His mother said, "This child will surely become a disciple of the Buddha in the future.

As he grew older, he became thoroughly versed in the classics and histories. At the age of fourteen, he followed Master Jian of Zisheng Monastery to receive instruction; having shaved his head and received full ordination, he resolved his will upon the Dharma.
He studied the Dharma with untiring diligence day and night. One day, while reading the *Platform Sutra*, he attained a realization.
He went to visit Jigan Zuo, but there was no accord. He then saw Fazhou Ji, from whom he received much inspiration. By chance, he encountered Wang Yangming amidst a crowd of scholars.
Wang took a key from his sleeve and asked the Master, "Do you see it? The Master replied, "I see it. Wang then put the key back into his sleeve and said, "Do you see it? The Master—
[The Master] said, "Seeing. The King said, "Not yet. The Master remained in doubt and could not resolve it. One day, he heard a monk cite a question asked of Dadian:
"What is the nature of seeing? Dadian replied, "Seeing is itself the nature. At this, [the Master] suddenly smiled with realization. He composed a verse, saying:

"The lake’s light rests upon my staff—three thousand acres; The mountain colors open before my gate—five or six peaks. Before my eyes, all things are spontaneously manifest; This very place is the Buddha-land."
"I shall no longer refine my 'stubborn emptiness' upon the meditation cushion. Not long after, he entered the formal retreat at Yunfeng in Louze.
Suddenly, he recalled Xueyan’s question to Gaofeng: "When one is fast asleep, with no dreams and no thoughts, no seeing and no hearing—where is the true host?
At that moment, he realized that life and death are of one essence, and waking and sleeping are as one. One day, he heard a friend reciting:
A heavenly being appeared in a dream to Tianzhu with the phrase, "There is a Tathāgata within Bifeng Monastery. He subsequently went to Bifeng; later, he returned to live in seclusion at Tianchi.

Disciples arrived daily, and it eventually became a great monastic center. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Ultimate Way is non-action (*wuwei*). Without purposeful cultivation, one cannot penetrate its depth.
To transcend study and reach non-action, one must rely on diligent learning to attain its ultimate limit. It is like a jade [requiring polishing]."

A gem within its raw matrix, or a pearl in the deep abyss—without cutting, boring, probing, and seeking, one can never obtain them. Thus, [the Buddha] practiced austerities at Mount Snow for six years;
[Huineng] sat facing a wall at Shaolin for nine years; until [Huike] severed his arm to seek the Dharma; [Nanyue Huairang] wore a stone belt to carry out the work of pounding grain;
Zhaozhou did not allow his mind to be distracted for thirty years; and Xianglin only after forty years became a single piece of unified realization. With such diligent and tireless effort...

Those who have worked tirelessly, forsaking sleep and forgetting their meals, solely desiring to investigate and clarify the Great Matter, serve as the models for those who study the Way through Chan meditation.
Alas, now that the autumn of the Chan groves has arrived, the Dharma-path lies in desolation. People pursue delusions and follow heterodoxy, no longer striving to uplift themselves;

they know only the ready-made offerings of gruel and rice, feeling no shame in vainly consuming the faithful alms. Some even allow their minds to wander into heterodox studies, indulging their wills in cleverness and sophistry.
Some dig through circumstantial conditions and race about seeking intellectual understanding; these are all ways of squandering one’s time and needlessly increasing the consciousness of karma.

They are like a destitute son who has lost his father, drifting without support—how lamentable this is! If you are a man of true spirit, you must exert your utmost vigor at the very brink of birth and death.
With a single thought of pure sincerity, not even a speck of dust shall stand; it should be as if encountering a mortal enemy.
Entering directly with a single blade, disregarding danger or death, as if falling into a deep well, every thought is focused on nothing else but seeking an exit.
If one can possess such a profound mind, one may rest assured that the day of reaching home is near.

[Ascending the hall, he cited the case of Zhaozhou’s examination of the two hermitage masters and spoke in verse: Passing through the marketplace is always the same; Who would have known that dead goods could be alive?
A person picks it up. Going east, it is sold at a high price; going west, it is cheap. Only upon seeing through it does one know it is not worth a penny.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When Śākyamuni Buddha was born in the Lumbinī Garden, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, took seven steps, and looked around in the four directions, saying:
'In heaven above and on earth below, I alone am the Honored One. This has already been a leakage."
Few indeed. At the end, he held up a flower and showed it to the assembly, saying: "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana;
I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. This proclamation was revealed once more. Yet the descendants of the Final Dharma age do no better than mad dogs chasing after clods of earth;
to simply let it rest at that would still be somewhat better. To further broadcast the family's disgrace and leave future generations deaf and blind—how could I bear such a thing?
How I wish it were so! As for you, my fellow practitioners: those who have long been refined through training will understand immediately upon hearing this;
how could they possibly require adding a point to an arrowhead? But as for beginners and those of late entry, we cannot help but provide expedient means.

Is there anyone who would like to ask a question? A monk asked: "When the Golden Body first descended, nine dragons spat forth water. Now that the birthday celebration is once again encountered, I wonder what auspicious signs there are?"
Shuì said, “The golden phoenix carries flowers, displaying auspicious colors; the brocade oriole turns its song, playing over the new bamboo.
He asked, “You have shown the true mechanism by pointing and looking about; how do you reveal the message today? The Master picked up his staff and said, “O staff!”
Above, it penetrates the Heaven of the Thirty-three, striking the nostrils of Śakra; below, it penetrates the eighteen layers of hell, smashing open the crown of King Yama’s head.
Looking down, it responds to the myriad capacities of beings, as the ten thousand phenomena and the host of stars all bow their heads;
proclaiming Prajñā, the great earth, mountains, and rivers listen with bated breath. It is said: "If this is so, then the Vulture Peak of old is today's Heavenly Pond."
The Master said, “A single path of divine radiance illuminates the universe; do not compare the distant and the near in terms of past and present.
He then descended from his seat. Layman Lu Wutai asked, “Where are the seventeen hundred virtuous teachers of this land now?
The Master pointed to a cicada chirping in a tree in the courtyard and said, “There is one here. The layman said, “As for that sound...”
"Is that so? the Master said. "To call it 'sound' is already to miss the mark.
The layman then pointed to a rock and asked, "Regarding 'insentient things preaching the Dharma,' how can this very thing preach? The Master replied, "Layman, what do you call this thing?"

The scholar said, "Stonehead. The Master said, "And you say it cannot be spoken. On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the Gui-chou year of the Jiajing era of Emperor Ming Shizong, the Master entered nirvana.
His worldly age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority was fifty-eight. Two volumes of his recorded sayings were circulated in the world.
Chan Master Gu-yin Jing-qin of Dou-feng in Jian-ning Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shou-tang Song. He was the son of the Cai family of Jian-yang in his native region.
From childhood, he was outstanding and unconstrained by convention. He often sighed, saying: "In this world, all that is sought brings suffering; it would be better to seek early on a way out."
At the age of twenty-five, he shaved his head on the Eastern Peak. Initially, he saw Master Dachen, but received no inspiration. Next, he visited Master Xingkong, the abbot of Guanzhuang.
There he encountered the veteran monk Jinghuang sitting beside him. One day, Huang was reading the *Recorded Sayings of Ancient Mei*.
In it, there was an account of a monk who went to the abbot’s quarters and said, "I have a point of entry. Mei struck him out. The monk stepped forward again.
The abbot struck him again with his staff. Huáng laughed and said, "This monk truly has a place of awakening; it is simply that he has not yet clarified the Great Dharma.
Upon hearing Huáng’s words, the Master rose from his seat, prostrated himself, and requested instruction on the essential points for entering the Way.

Huáng said, "Although the Buddha-nature is inherently present in every person, if one does not cultivate and transform it through wisdom, one remains merely an ordinary being. Now, if you wish to achieve..."
To accomplish this matter, you must completely sweep away all the entanglements and branches. Take up only a single phrase of "tasteless" *huatou*;

doubt it yourself, question it yourself, and press upon it with self-exertion. Do not seek for others to explain it to you, and do not rely on intellectual interpretations to force a construction of meaning.
The life-root must be decisively severed; one must personally realize and personally awaken.

Thus, three times during the day and three times at night, one presses on with urgency until, after many years and months, suddenly the flower of the mind blooms with illumination, like the sun appearing when the clouds part.

One then thoroughly penetrates every ancient kōan, finally realizing that there is no Zen to be studied and no Buddha to be made; everything is understood in every instance, and all things are seen as they are.

"Penetrating! It is like a person who has arrived home and no longer asks for directions. Having received this instruction from the Master, I immediately applied myself to deathless study, contemplating the phrase:
"The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Later, I traveled south to Yunnan to visit Shoutang. Upon reaching Jiumingtan, I suddenly attained great enlightenment.
When I finally met Shoutang, we were like a needle meeting its eye; he immediately conferred upon me the seal of transmission. I then returned to live in seclusion at Mount Doufeng. Ming.

In the *Ren-shen* year of the Wuzong Zhengde era (1512), [Master] Ruiyan moved to his new residence and addressed the assembly: "Those who study the Way must sever all external conditions and stifle miscellaneous thoughts.

They should single-mindedly maintain the *huatou* of their primary inquiry throughout all activities—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—and amidst all circumstances, whether of suffering or joy, adversity or favor, never allowing it to be lost.
Furthermore, whatever wholesome or unwholesome objects or conditions one perceives in stillness all arise from a lack of rectitude."
Contemplation: Simply close your eyes and sit in stillness. If the mind lacks vigor and the consciousness drifts with external conditions, you will be half-asleep and half-awake.
Or, by craving a state of quietude, you may perceive various visionary realms. If you are a practitioner of the right cause working on your cultivation, when it is time to sleep, you should sleep;
upon waking, you should wake up immediately. Upon rising, shake off your lethargy, rub your eyes, and clench your teeth firmly.
Shut it off. Clench your fists tight. With single-minded focus and right mindfulness, press on with earnest diligence.

As you move back and forth within doubt, until you reach the point where the mountain ends and the water runs dry, suddenly the mass of doubt will shatter, and you will instantly perceive your own original ground and its natural radiance.

It is not obtained from without; arriving at this very moment is what is called "entering the gate and attaining the ground. Yet, one must further seek a master of clear vision to provide definitive discernment;
one must not stop there. If even a single dharma is not understood, it must be thoroughly clarified; if a single principle is not penetrated, it must be mastered.
You must penetrate through directly. Even if you have attained awakening, if you cannot reach the gate of transformative teaching, the ancients called this "sitting atop a hundred-foot pole.
You must be able to let go over the precipice and reach the ocean of all-knowledge; only by personally accepting this responsibility can you truly take it up.
Having died and returned to life once more, one cannot deceive the Sovereign. Take care.
This is the dharma successor of Chan Master Tianqi Ruchi, the thirtieth generation descendant of Nanyue.
Chan Master Wumen Zhengcong of Longquan Temple on Guanziling in Suizhou was the son of the Xi family of Shaowu.
His mother was surnamed Wu. He left home at the age of seventeen and received full ordination at twenty. He studied the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

One day, while an elderly monk was cross-examining him, the Master answered strictly according to the literal texts. The elder monk rebuked and scolded him; from that moment, the Master’s state of doubt suddenly arose, and he remained absorbed in it whether sitting or lying down.
He remained unsettled for six years. One day, hearing the neighing of a horse, he attained great enlightenment. He then went to see Tianqi.
Tianqi asked, "What is it like to forget the world while remaining in the world? The Master replied, "To realize that things are not things.

Tianqi asked, "What is it like to forget thoughts while remaining in thought? The Master replied, "To have no mind within the mind. Tianqi asked, "What is it like when both mind and things are forgotten? The Master replied, "Huashan."
Towering and abrupt, the peaks of Mount Taihang are majestic. Qiji said, "In the future, the one who will corrupt people will be you alone.

He sealed this with a verse. Later, while residing at Guanziling, he ascended the hall and, citing a monk’s question to Yunmen—“What is the teaching for an entire era?”—Yunmen replied, “I speak to each person.
Longquan, however, was not like this. If someone were to ask him, “What is...”
"This is the teaching for this entire lifetime. He then struck him across the back with a staff and said, "Shut that dog’s mouth!
A monk asked, "What is one's original face? The Master said, "The Stone Incense Pavilion. The monk asked, "What is it like when one goes forth in this very way? The Master said, "..."
"It has been lost. [The monk] asked: "Today is the eighth day of the fourth month;

the monasteries throughout the world all celebrate the Buddha’s birthday. I wonder, from where did the Tathāgata descend to be born? The Master drew a circle on the desk and showed it to him. The monk was speechless.

(Xiaoyan Bao, acting for the monk, performed a prostration and said: "The entire realm gazes upon it everywhere. Xiaoyan came to attend [the Master]. He presented the realization he had previously attained. The Master followed along...
He immediately sealed [the matter]. The next day, when [Yuan] entered the room to pay his respects, the Master said, "Upādhyāya, where did all those complications last night go?
As Yuan was about to respond, the Master laughed and said, "The hawk has already flown beyond the kingdom of Silla.
Yuan then asked, "The Ten Sages and Three Worthies have fully realized sacred wisdom; why do you say they do not understand this principle? The Master spoke in a stern voice:
[The Master] said, "You already know of the Ten Sages and Three Worthies; what is the meaning of this principle? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!

Yan repeatedly offered more than ten turns of phrase, but the Master refused them all. Yan requested that the Master provide a substitute for him. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Only by investigating with earnest sincerity can you succeed.
One day, as Yan was returning from washing vegetables, the Master saw him and asked, "What is this? Yan replied, "A basket of vegetables. The Master asked, "Why..."
He did not offer a single word in response. Yanguan requested that the Master ask another question; thereupon, as each question was posed, he answered, and the Master acknowledged each one.

Yanguan, wishing to travel to study under various masters, took his leave of the Master. The Master raised his whisk and said, "If you can utter a phrase here that transcends the ordinary, you may go.
Yanguan was speechless. The Master said, "As you depart now, refine your resolve with single-minded devotion; do not..."

"Apply your mind with focused diligence; remember my words, for in the future there will be a time when they prove of great benefit. Later, after Yǎn had traveled extensively to study under various masters, he returned to visit the Master.
The Master ordered him to tend the furnace and said, "Every person has their own original parents. Where are your parents?"
Yan said, "A single fire will burn them all. The Master said, "In that case, do you have no parents? Yan said, "I have them;
it is simply that even the Buddha-eye cannot see them. The Master said, "Do you see them? Yan said, "I do not see them either."
The Master said, "Why do you not see them either? Yankou replied, "If one sees them, they are not the true parents. He then immediately presented a verse:
"The original true parents have never been separated throughout kalpas. In rising and sitting we rely on their power; in cold and warmth we share their knowledge.
Meeting yet not seeing, seeing yet not recognizing— I ask where they are now; let me describe them clearly."
The Master said, "By this single verse alone, you are worthy to succeed to my school. He spoke again: "Your mind is my mind; my mind is fundamentally no-mind.
No-mind is identical to the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind is not my mind. He further said: "The Buddha is like a Wheel-Turning King."

The Buddha-dharma is like the royal law. The Son of the Buddha erects the banner of the Dharma and is able to transform the deviant into the correct. He charged them, saying: "Receive and uphold this with earnest attention.
When the conditions for those who encounter it ripen, both the wise and the foolish shall all be saved. To continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom, one must wait for such a person.

One day, the Master suddenly vanished, and no one knew where he had gone. After two years had passed, he returned to the mountain. On the evening of the first day of the seventh month, he said to the assembly:

Having brought both body and mind to their ultimate end, he was well-suited for wandering. The mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue stretch out into the vast distance; with a single staff, he carries the sun and moon.
At Longquan Temple, his discourse was especially long. Having finished this verse, he cast his staff to the ground, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the right of the temple.
Chan Master Da-xiu Shi of Fu-niu Ji-an was the son of the Li family of Xinzheng. In his youth, he entered the monastic order under Baizhu.
At the age of twenty, he visited the veteran master Guxin, who assigned him the koan: “All dharmas return to One; where does the One return?

He subsequently entered the meditation hall for three years of intensive practice and attained realization. He composed a verse, saying: “The Dharma-body is originally without form; The characteristics of dharmas are originally...”
Coming into emptiness, those who grasp this message manifest their family style everywhere. Later, he went to visit Tianqi.
On the way, he encountered two Chan guests, Tianzhen and Yueyin, and they traveled together to Guanzilizheng. Tianqi asked, "Did you two come along the same path?
The Master replied, "Although we came by the same path, our points of origin are different. Tianqi asked, "What is your original face? The Master—
He gave a shout. Xueqiu asked, "Before your parents were born, what was there to shout? The Master said, "Take care," and departed.
Thereafter, he presented several more maneuvers, but Xueqiu did not approve of them. One day, while attending Xueqiu at Chengtian, Xueqiu asked, "'Where one hides the body, there are no traces;
where there are no traces, do not hide the body. How do you understand this? The Master replied, "In the hall itself..."
Taking his seat upright, he responds to the pivotal mechanisms at both ends. A marvel to bring joy! Rising to the high seat, Mount Sumeru performs a dance and the ocean waters surge with waves.
Dragons and elephants mingle; humans and devas gather together. The great earth, mountains, and rivers all proclaim the wondrous verses in unison.
The three worthies and ten sages together realize Bodhi. A jeweled sword emerges from his brow, casting a cold light;
a golden mallet is hidden in his sleeve as he issues the true command. Manifesting the full potential of killing and giving life, he raises his whisk and says:
"Is there any clear-eyed monk who, disregarding peril and ruin, can step forward and take this burden upon one shoulder? He then descends from the seat. Xiaoyan came forward to inquire: "How is it?"
"This is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. The Master held up his whisk. Xuyan asked, "Is there anything further to point out beyond this?
The Master threw down the whisk, and Xuyan immediately prostrated himself. They then discussed the story of their encounter at Guanziling. The Master said:

"Strange," said the Master, "to think that you have come here in person to see a true master. Yanguan then gave a shout. After a short while, the Master asked again, "It has been forty years since we last met.
I do not know how your nostrils have fared lately. Yanguan replied, "They are just like the Venerable One’s nostrils.
The Master said, "Do you see my nostrils, Upāsaka? Yanguan said, "I see them. The Master asked, "Where do you see them?"
Yan said, "It is between the two eyes and above the mouth. The Master said, "There is a secret phrase; have you ever spoken it to the Senior Monk?
Yan said, "I have spoken it. The Master said, "Try to bring it forth. Yan said, "Shut that stinking mouth! The Master picked up his whisk, and Yan immediately swept his sleeves and departed.
Chan Master Daju Yuan of Xiangyang Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tiantai Susu.
He was a native of Hanchuan. His appearance was robust and his voice resonated like a great bell.

Having studied under Jing’an, he attained silent realization; Jing’an bestowed upon him a verse which said: "A single branch of the True Dharma Eye has been transmitted successively by the patriarchs."

"Come. Entrust this to you; wait for the time to arrive, and its fragrant scent shall pervade the nine realms. The Master received the entrustment. Later, he lived in seclusion at Xixiaoyan in Xiangyang.

Shuang'an came to pay his respects and requested to serve him as an attendant. The Master said, "The Senior Monk has made a mistake. This old fool has spent his life content with mere warmth and fullness; I have no other special talent.
Shuang'an said, "For us, the matter of birth and death is of great importance. Before he had finished speaking, the Master beckoned him.
The Master laughed and said, "I, an old fool, also have birth and death; why should you alone be the one to have them?

Shuang said, "I regret that, having entered the path late, I lack a constant resolve. How could a monk like you reject me? The Master replied, "For those who have left the household life, there is fundamentally nothing to do.

Why do you create trouble where there is no trouble? After a short while, he added, "Only when you prepare your own rice gruel and meals will it be acceptable. The Master’s skillful means were unfathomable; he most detested [artificiality].
The timing was not pure. One day, in the hall, he raised the case of the outsider who asked the Buddha: "I do not ask about words, nor do I ask about wordlessness.

After the World-Honored One remained silent for a long while, the outsider attained great enlightenment. The Master said, "Since the question did not involve existence or non-existence, even that 'long silence' is but a passing name.
At such a moment, what did the outsider actually realize? As Yan was about to offer a word in response, the Master suddenly—
He covered [Yanguan’s] mouth with his hand and said, “It still hangs between your lips and teeth.

Yanguan was then relieved and said, “One can truly say that the patch-robed monks of the Eastern Land do not equal the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) of the Western Heaven. He then composed a verse: “I laugh at myself for constantly drawing patterns with my own hand;

Several times it has turned red, several times it has turned black. Now, thanking my old master, I return to my hometown; Who cares whether I have attained anything in my life? The Master [said]: “...”
He was highly praised for this. Later, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-three, having completed fifty-three years of monastic ordination (*saṃgha-vaṣa*).
Master Wenyang Xiao was a successor of Chan Master Wuqu Ruokong of Jiaxing Prefecture;
he was the son of the Shi family from Xiushui in the same prefecture, born during the Xiaozong era of the Ming dynasty.

On the eighteenth day of the tenth month of the Xinhai year of the Hongzhi era, I, Zong, who from my youth admired the vehicle of the patriarchs and devoted myself to investigating its essence, traveled for several years with Fazhou Ji to visit various masters.
Later, upon meeting Yeweng, I penetrated the very source of the Dharma. Opening the Barrier to Address the Assembly:
I have bound the mysterious barrier myself; I am my own living grave. It is I who close it, and I who open it. With a single blow, I have shattered the primordial aperture.

Releasing the former servant Han to come forth—this was the instruction for the assembly on the Lantern Festival. If you can realize it amidst the sound of the painted horns, even Avalokiteśvara is not yet a master.
If you point back within the shadows of the colored lanterns, Śrīmati merely boasts of her skillful hands.

To announce this to all of you in such a manner would surely cause the void to split its mouth with laughter. If you have still not had a sudden flash of insight, look once more at the peak of Mount Ao.
Walking backward. Small Assembly Instruction. The assembly stood in formation. The Master gave a shout and said, "Calamity arises from within one's own house," and then returned to his quarters.
Addressing the assembly, he cited the Sūtra teachings, saying:

"To attempt to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment with a conceptualizing mind is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly. The Master said, "I shall now ask you all: like..."
Coming into the realm of experience, since it is something that cannot be fathomed by measurement, how ultimately should one bring it to a decisive end?

He let out a shout and said, "Do you see the meaning of the teaching? Then he descended from his seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "If you can realize it before words, you are already at the edge of the world;
If you take it up after the phrase, the path grows ever more remote. With a single blow, the Iron Ring Mountains shatter like dust; The ocean is vast and empty, the geese fly in a slanting line."
New Year’s Eve Small Lecture: When time is exhausted, how can it be compared to when the days are exhausted? If the months are exhausted, the same will be true for the year.
Having passed through thirty-six cycles of ten days, Old Wang of the Eastern Village burns paper money at night. This old fellow possesses not a single thing;
he merely responds to the conditions of this particular season. Holding up his staff, he said: "There is only this, which is infinite and inexhaustible, enduring through kalpas and years."
"I am sending this off tonight at once, so as not to allow it to entangle and drag on. [The Master] threw down his staff and said: 'That which was acquired over kalpas is now brought to an end.
Clapping his empty hands together, he continued: 'Welcoming the New Year. He addressed the assembly: "The Buddha is one who has settled all matters within the house of sentient beings;
sentient beings are those who have not yet settled their affairs within the house of the Buddha. If you wish for them to be identical, simply [regard] the Buddha and..."
“Sentient beings—let them all go at once! Then there is neither realization nor non-realization. He stood his staff upright and said:

“If you penetrate the mundane through the mundane, seeing forms and hearing sounds will not leave you deaf. On the Dragon Boat Festival, he addressed the assembly: “This auspicious festival of the Dragon Boat—when was it ever scheduled?
On the fifth day of the fifth month, it strikes every year. The wind shakes the green, serrated *pújiàn* (gladiolus), and the sun shines upon...”
The *liu* flowers are a brilliant red. The Way exists within the conditions of the seasons; how could one distinguish between the Age of True Dharma and the Age of Decline?
Hitherto, you have pursued it with deliberate intent, yet your entire body was nothing but weeds. Today, as you pick it up at random, there is nothing that is not medicine.
Holding up his whisk, he said: "Tell me, assembly, what illness does this medicine cure? He struck the whisk and said: "Not only did the Elder Vimalakīrti [not know]."
"Even the Medicine King and Medicine Superior take a dose of this. Addressing the assembly: "The eye at the crown of the head is wide open, illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
Having become the sovereign of the Dharma, one attains mastery over all phenomena. One night, as the Master was walking by moonlight along a lake, he encountered a monk.
The Master said: "The bright moon and the clear breeze, the water and the sky are of one color. Every person dwells within this."
[The monk] said, "I simply cannot get out. The Master asked, "Why do you 'strike the grass to startle the snake'? The monk asked, "And what about you, Upasaka? [The Master] said, "Watch your step!
The Master laughed loudly and said, "I thought the beard was red; it turns out there is a red-bearded fellow after all.

In the second month of winter in the Jia-mao year of the Wanli era of Emperor Shenzong, the Master said to his disciple Xingchong: "Next year, on the Mid-Autumn Festival, [the day will be] five or six..."
"In the meantime, I shall depart; you should know this. On the sixteenth day of the eighth month of the Gengchen year, Chong arrived as previously scheduled.
The Master gathered the assembly and spoke a verse, saying: "Birth and death are like flowers in the void; Death and birth are but a single dream.
This skin-sack is entrusted to the Lord of Fire (Cing-ding-kung); White bones cross the broken bridge with the multitude. A-he-he! Under bright moon and clear breeze, I chant."
He played with his staff. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. His worldly age was ninety.

Chan Master Da Xiu Zonglong of Seven Peaks in Suizhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Wujin Hai. He was the son of the Jia family of Yidu in Qingzhou. He relied upon [the monastery] in the prefecture...
Shifo shaved his head and later resided at Beisi in Chengdu as the *karmadāna*. One day, while out on the street carrying water, he forgot his destination;
suddenly, his head struck a wall, and he attained realization. Spontaneously, he uttered this verse: "The nature and essence of the great earth, mountains, and rivers are empty."
That portion of movement traverses east and west; by chance, one encounters the phrase of selflessness. Ten thousand rivers and a thousand mountains are all one and the same.
Thus, within the "Inexhaustible Chamber" at Henan Qianming Temple, I present what I have attained.

Inexhaustible then sealed it with this verse: "The Way is lofty, requiring no cultivation; Virtue is weighty, encompassing both principle and phenomena. This single branch of the True Dharma Eye Is entrusted to Long."
After attaining great rest, Dahuizhu spoke three "gate-words" to instruct his students. The first says:
"A precious 'blowing-hair' sword has been taken away by a stone person and hung atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak; the four walls are impassable. How can it be recovered? The second says:
There is a wish-fulfilling jewel that was carried by a wooden man and cast into the waves of the great ocean. Without relying on a boat or ship, how can it be found?
The third [question] says: "The entire earth is a pit of fire; everything has been burned away, except for a single tuft of eyebrows.
I wonder who is able to see this? While in the vegetable garden, a monk asked: "How is it?"
“This is the meaning of the West,” the Master said. [The monk] replied, “Cucumbers and eggplants. The monk did not attain realization. Descending the mountain, he met an elder.
The elder asked, “Where have you come from? The monk replied, “From Seven-Pointed Peak. The elder asked, “What words were spoken regarding Great Rest?
The monk recounted the previous conversation. The elder joined his palms and said, “Truly great compassion! (Recorded in the *Renzong* era, the *Ren-yin* year of the Jiajing reign).
On the eighth day of the eleventh month, he gathered the assembly and composed a verse, saying: "Holding the three periods of time as a staff, The ten directions are originally one's old cassock.
The clay ox and stone tiger know the news; Treading through empty space, one arrives home.
He set down his brush, sat upright, and passed away.
Chan Master Yungu Fahui of Mount Xu in Jiaxing Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Tianning Ji.
He was the son of the Huai family of Huaisian in that same prefecture. He received the tonsure at Dayun Temple.
At that time, Fazhou was secluding himself in a room at Tianning; the Master went there to seek instruction, and [Fazhou] instructed him to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

"Whose words were these? One day, during a meal, his eating vessel fell to the ground, and he attained sudden awakening. Thereupon, he entered Tianjie Monastery and remained in seclusion for three years.
He then returned to a hermitage at the foot of Qianfo Ridge in Xiqia, later moving to Tiankai Cliff, where he dwelt alone as before.
Whenever a guest arrived, regardless of their rank, he would inquire after their daily affairs; after briefly exchanging greetings of warmth, he would invariably [proceed to] unfold [the Dharma].

He had them sit upon meditation cushions and practice *pratyāvekṣaṇā* (introspective observation). Throughout the day, they were not permitted to engage in idle conversation. At other times, he would invariably exhort them, saying, "Human life is impermanent; do not let your days pass in vain.
When they met again, he would inevitably ask how they had applied themselves in their practice since their last meeting. For this reason, those who turned toward his teaching increased daily.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Where there is water, it all contains the moon."
"There is no mountain that does not carry clouds. [The student] asked, "Is there perhaps some other extraordinary place? The Master said, "One must by all means avoid calling a tortoise a turtle.
[The student] asked, "How should I directly apply my mind? The Master said, "If you do not look back when the staff is raised, you will immediately err."
He pondered what kalpa it would take to attain awakening. The Master lived his life without ever providing bedding;

he sat upright day and night for over forty years, remaining as composed on one day as on another. On the fifth day of the first month of the *wànhé* year of the Yǎnshén Emperor’s reign (1615), he passed away.
He was seventy-five years of age and fifty-six years since his ordination. His stupa was erected behind Dàyuán Temple.
Chan Master Fangze of Jingyan Dongxi in Jiaxing Prefecture was the son of the Ren family of Jiashan in the prefecture. He first visited Fazhou at Tianning Temple.

One day, during a private interview, the Master brought up the koan of Longtan seeing the Heavenly King. Upon reaching the line, "Where would he not point out the essential heart of the mind? Fangze attained realization.
Later, he received formal certification and, at the conclusion of the retreat, took up the whisk to preside over the assembly. His Dharma...
Although it pervades all worlds, there has never been so much as a hair’s breadth of leakage; how can it be tied?
Although there has never been so much as a hair’s breadth of leakage, there has likewise never been so much as a hair’s breadth of concealment; how can it be untied?

Chan Master Shun Tianqingshou Shengmo Guang first studied under Bao of Zhengzhou and later under Wangshan Ti.

Having received the Dharma, he emerged from seclusion to open a hall for teaching. He once said to the assembly: "To transmit the Dharma, one should be like Chuanzi; to seek the Dharma, one should be like Ke."
The Patriarch said: "If it were not so, how could one possibly uphold the Great Dharma of the Tathāgata? Ascending the hall, he said:
"In my school, there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. Deshan’s teeth do not meet when the wind blows; he has exhausted all his failures.

If you wish to recognize the fundamental principle (gangzong), you must first recognize the phrase. Yantou saw the jaw behind the head; do not engage in coming and going with him. Altogether, this is excellent."
Thirty blows of the staff—does anyone here still feel dissatisfied? If not, do not take offense at being pressed from the noble into the lowly.
Addressing the assembly, [the Master] raised the story of Jiufeng’s refusal to acknowledge the Head Seat, and offered this verse: The Head Seat’s efforts were in vain for a single stick of incense;
Jiufeng was not suppressing a man of high talent. If one takes a single color as the true succession, One fails the former master and neglects the conditions of non-borrowing.
Addressing the assembly, he cited the story of Magu shaking his staff. The Master said: "Right is not to be found in what is right; non-right is not to be found in what is non-right.

Right and non-right have no master; all myriad virtues return to the same source. The owl and the cock, day and night, merely cause themselves fragmentation. I lack the three inches [of tongue], yet the turtle can call out to the tortoise.

Chan Master Daquan of Daming in Cizhou was a successor of Chan Master Renshan Heng;
having received the essential meaning from Renshan, his disposition was refined and elegant, and he delighted in engaging in humorous banter.
[The Master] laughed. Renshan had once instructed Attendant Ding to keep him in check. The Master said, "Human life is but a single dream. To spend one’s life in joy is a good dream;
to spend one’s life in self-restraint is a bad dream. I would rather have a good dream. People considered these to be excellent words.

Chan Master Xixi Hongxiang of Dajue Monastery in Kaifeng was a dharma heir of Chan Master Qingshou Heng.
He was the son of the Wang family of Yishui. Having initially left home, he served Master Zu Zhao, through whom he mastered the sutras and attained the monastic robes.
For ten years, he read extensively both Buddhist and secular texts. Thereafter, he abandoned these studies to go into retreat under Master Heng of Xuming.
Ten years later, during the Qingshou era, he finally received his official seal of appointment.

He emerged into the world and resided at Dajue Monastery in Zhengzhou, Shaolin on Mount Song, Puzhao in Yizhou, and finally at Qingliang. Yuan Yishan Hao-wen once traveled with the Master to Lanre Peak;
while on the road, they happened to discuss the matter of evading bandits. At that time, the Master remarked that for anyone who goes out...
One faces the world with the body; only by being able to transcend birth and death can one then establish oneself.

Although birth and death are indeed a great matter, if viewed as merely turning over one's hand, then whether halting in a pit or flowing along a stream, there is nothing that cannot be done. This must arise from the practice of stillness;

if one does not set aside this state in every thought-moment, it will naturally mature of its own accord. At that time, on a snowy path where the stones were slippery, the Master slipped and fell. His companions...
No one could save him from falling; he dropped straight down several dozen feet before being stopped only by a large tree.
Yishan asked him in alarm, but the Master remained composed in appearance and demeanor, saying slowly, "I have studied Chan for forty years, yet my heels have now been scrutinized by Shitou."

Those who heard this laughed and were convinced; they sighed in admiration at his words regarding the "maturity of the realm," for they indeed corresponded to the activities of daily life, being pure and without delusion.
At the age of sixty-four, he manifested his passing. His *yulu* (recorded sayings) and collected writings are still in circulation today.
Chan Master Wansong Xingxiu of Baen Temple in Yanjing was the dharma heir of Chan Master Xueyan Man of the twenty-second generation under Qingyuan.
He was the son of the Cai family of Xieliang in Henei. His physical bearing and spirit were—

He was extraordinary, possessing a transcendent aspiration for the world beyond. His parents found this difficult to accept, yet they knew that in the end, worldly appearances could not divert his resolve.

Consequently, they escorted him to Jingtu Temple in Xingzhou, where he paid his respects to Master Yunkyun and received the tonsure. After receiving full ordination, he applied himself with determination to investigation and study.

Carrying his bundle, he traveled toward Yanjing, passing through Tanzhe and Qingshou Temples, where he met Master Shengmo Guang and was instructed to contemplate the "Turning" [of the staff] by Changsha.
He took up the koan "The Mountains, Rivers, and Great Earth Are Oneself. For half a year he made no progress.

He reported this to Master Guangbai, who said, "I only wish for you to understand it late. One day, he attained a realization. However, he still harbored doubts regarding Xuefeng’s words, "Xuansha has not yet reached the ultimate.
He requested instruction from Xueyan Zuqin at Daming in Magu. After only twenty-seven days, he suddenly awakened upon hearing a word and exclaimed, "How near it was! All my former skills..."
The two were reduced to ashes in a single fire. Only then did he realize the true character of Shengmo. He stayed with Xueyan for two years, fully mastering his profound teachings.
Xueyan bestowed upon him the robe and a verse, exhorting him to propagate the Great Dharma. He subsequently returned to Jingtu, where he built the Wansong Studio to find personal solace.
When the senior monks of the temple earnestly requested that he open a dharma hall, he complied. He later resided at Wanshou Monastery in Zhongdu. *Jin* (金) [is the author's signature].

In the *jiachou* year of Mingchang during the reign of Emperor Zhangzong (which corresponds to the fourth year of the Shaoxi era of Emperor Guangzong of the Southern Song), the Emperor issued an edict for the Master to ascend the seat within the imperial palace.

The Emperor personally received him with ceremonial rites; upon hearing the Dharma, he was moved to realization. He personally presented the Master with a great *saṃghāṭī* robe made of brocade and silk. The ladies of the inner palace and the nobility prostrated themselves in rows and knelt in reverence, each offering precious gifts.
A Great Universal Deliverance Assembly (*pudu hui*) was established, and the offerings were extraordinary. In the *dingsi* year of Cheng'an, the Emperor again issued an edict for the Master.
He resided in seclusion at Mount Angyang in the capital. Subsequently, he moved his staff to Baegun Hongji Temple.

In the Gengyin year of the Yuan Taizong era, he again received an imperial edict to preside over Mansu Temple. In his later years, he retired to Chongyong Hermitage. Having successively occupied several great monasteries, he greatly revitalized the tradition of the Dongyang school.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Lotus Palace is specially fashioned as a Brahma-palace; The sacred realm must surely be visited by a sage sovereign."

Today, the first day of the intercalary fourth month, at the end of the *chen* hour and the beginning of the *si* hour, suddenly someone came forward who was said to be thoroughly astute and clever, knowing the proper time and observing the seasonal rhythms;
yet, fundamentally, he lacked even a whiff of the "fragrance of the Way. The mountain monk covered his nose with his hand and said, "Keep back!
Keep back! What are you doing? You smell far too much of the 'fragrance of the Way'! —In praise of Layman Zhànrán.
Zhen said: "The Great Compassionate One with a thousand arms; Zhizhi with a single finger. You have mistakenly identified the serene *zhànrán* as the whisk in my hand.
Xiazhuan asked: "For over thirty years, I have been unable to settle this deluded mind. I beg the Master for a skillful means. The Master said:
"How long has this deluded mind of yours existed? I wonder, did a deluded mind exist from the very beginning? Consider this:"
"How do you sever deluded mind? "It is precisely this deluded mind that, when severed, is itself [enlightenment]; when not severed, it is itself [delusion]. True hearing is vast and open.
Having said this, he prostrated and departed. The Master asked a monk: "Dongshan said: 'A dragon roars in a withered tree; its extraordinary resonance is difficult to hear.'"
"What is an extraordinary sound? He replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "You well understand the dragon's cry. Question:
"Enlightenment and ignorance are non-dual in their nature. What is this non-dual nature? The Master said, "At dawn, nothing is revealed.

Question: "The Buddhas do not appear in the world; why then were they born in royal palaces? The Master said, "The green mountains constantly lift their feet. [The questioner] said, "There is also none."
"There is nirvana. Why, then, did he pass into extinction at the Twin Trees? The Master said: "The sun does not shift its course. "Question:
For those who have cast off their hands [attained liberation] on that side, why do they not abide in the position of correctness? The Master said: "Great achievement is without a presiding agent."
[A monk] asked, "Why do those who turn their heads toward this side not fall into heterodox paths? The Master said, "The ultimate transformation is non-action; when asked, I tell you: 'Do not go.
[The monk asked,] "If one returns, they turn their back on their father. How can one avoid turning their back on their father? The Master said, "Above all, do not turn your head.
[Another] asked, "It is difficult to let go of mind after mind. Who is the person who lets go? The Master said, "Carrying."
Taking it away. [The Master] asked: "In this place there is no Maitreya; there is no gate and no Sudhana. Why is it said, 'On the lapis lazuli palace there is no one to recognize me'?
The Master said: "Once the palace is demolished, we shall meet. Addressing the assembly: "Where the wheel of the pivot turns, even the eye of wisdom is still deluded.
When the precious mirror opens, not a speck of dust can pass. Opening the fist, it does not fall to the ground; responding to things, one knows well."
At that time, when two blades meet edge-to-edge, how can one evade them? To the assembly: "If you go, I will stay; if you stay, I will send you away.
Neither going nor staying—He has no territory; where could one encounter Him? Everywhere, in every place—tell me, what kind of thing is so extraordinary?
To the assembly: "If you move, you bury yourself ten thousand fathoms deep; if you do not move, then..."

The sprouts will grow in their proper place; you must simply scatter [the seed] at both ends and let it fall in the middle. Only then can you buy straw sandals and travel the path. Addressing the assembly:
To kick over the vast ocean, the dust of the great earth flies up; to shout away the white clouds, empty space shatters to pieces.
Yet even the strict establishment of commands is but a partial manifestation. When the Great Function is fully revealed, how is it to be enacted? Addressing the assembly:
The single function that points upward is like a crane soaring through the clouds and mists; the path facing forward is like a hawk flying over Silla.
Even if one’s eyes were as swift as shooting stars, one could not avoid having a mouth as flat as a carrying pole. Tell me, what is the fundamental principle?

The Master was thoroughly versed in the studies of Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the hundred schools of thought. He had read the Tripitaka three times and constantly practiced the Avatamsaka Sūtra. He once selected and excerpted [passages from these works].
Hongzhi’s *Hundred Verses* is titled the *Congrong An Lu*. He also authored the *Qingyi Lu*, which follows in the footsteps of the *Biyan Lu*;
the *Zudeng Lu*; the *Shishi Xinwen*; the *Mingdao Ji*; the *Bianzong Shuo Xinying*; the *Fengming Chan Yue Fa Xi Ji*;
and his *Sihui Yulu*, all of which have been circulated in the world. The Master [passed away] on the fourth month of the year Bingwu, the first year of the Yuanding era.
On the fourth day, he manifested illness. On the seventh day, he wrote a verse which said: "Eighty-one years; these are but these few words. Cherish them, all you people;
do not at all misrepresent them. Thereupon he passed away. His secular age was eighty-one, and his monastic seniority was sixty. He was cremated, and the relics were innumerable.
His various disciples divided them and enshrined them in stupas.
Chan Master Juchuan Hai of Zhulin composed a verse on wind bells that says: "Copper lips and iron tongues, too sharp and new;
Hung from the pavilion, they have not known spring. The hundreds and thousands of *samādhi* dharmas beyond words— Through the wind, they are spoken to those who truly understand.
The scholar Chen Yuxiu once asked Wansong: "Why does Maitreya Bodhisattva not practice *dhyāna*?"
"Samādhi does not mean the severing of afflictions. He further asked Xiangshan Da-run. Run said, "The mind of Chan is already settled;

there is no need for further cultivation. Afflictions are exhausted; there is no need to sever them. Later, he took this up to ask his teacher. The teacher said, "Fundamentally, there is neither Chan-samādhi nor afflictions.
The master said, "Only this is what brings true joy."
Chan Master Xueting Fuyu of Shaoshi in the Western Capital was a dharma heir of Chan Master Ba’en Xiu of the twenty-third generation under Qingyuan.
He was the son of the Zhang family of Wenshui in Taiyuan. While his mother was pregnant with him...

The mother frequently experienced extraordinary dreams. At the time of his birth, auspicious omens appeared one after another within the family. By the age of five, he understood speech and could recite a thousand words daily.
At nine, he entered school; by the time he reached ten, he could read ten columns at a single glance. The local community bestowed upon him the title of "the Holy Child.

Not long thereafter, he encountered the upheavals of the times and lost his siblings. Left all alone and without support, he met an elderly bhikṣu on the road, who exhorted him to study the Buddha-dharma.
The monk said, "If you can recite one fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, then the affairs of this lifetime will be concluded.
The Master asked, "Does the Buddha-dharma end here? Is there no further message beyond this? The bhikṣu marveled at this.
They then went together to pay their respects to the Ancient Buddha Xiulin at Xianyan, saying, "This youth is of the lineage of the dragon-elephants; he shall serve as your attendant."
[The Master] said, "In the future, he will surely become a great vessel. The Ancient Buddha (Wansong) joyfully accepted him, whereupon he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He studied under Guang of Shuangxi for seven years. At that time, Wansong was residing at Ba'en Temple in Yanjing; the Master did not require an introduction to reach him.
He immediately went off alone, shaking his sleeves. As soon as Panshan saw him, he granted him entry into the inner quarters and asked, "From where did you get this news?
Why have you come in such a manner? The Master replied, "Old man, old man! You are losing ground to the hands of a student. Panshan asked, "Where does the fault of this old monk lie?
The Master said, "When I prostrated myself, I merely sought to cover for you, Elder. Panshan was struck with wonder.
He attended him closely for ten years from that point on. From then on, the Master’s Way flourished further, his reputation grew more prominent, and his disciples increased daily.
During the upheavals of the *Renchen* (1252) era, his ancestral monastery fell into ruin. Subsequently, he was invited by Wansong and Haiyun; he then received the command to go to Shaolin.
While the Yuan Emperor Shizu was still in his private residence, he ordered the Master to preside over a Great Precept Assembly (*Dazijie Hui*). In the *Wushen* year of Emperor Dingsong’s reign...
By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Xingguo Monastery in Helin. Before even a month had passed, he was summoned by Emperor Xiaozong to the temporary capital at Beiting.
His discourse on the Way pleased the Emperor. On the day of Gengshen, when Emperor Shizu ascended the throne, he was commissioned to serve as the General Overseer of Buddhist Teachings.

He restored the monastic community of monks and nuns, reclaiming two hundred and thirty-six abandoned temple sites. Consequently, he debated the spurious scriptures and dispatched couriers to burn those texts. Furthermore—

The Emperor bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Zhengbian of the Imperial House of Light (Guangzong). He was commanded to establish a monastery in his native village called Ba’en, and was granted land for the sustenance of the monks;
the imperial favors were most extensive. At that time, the seat at Wanshou Monastery was vacant, and the assembly requested the Master to preside over it.

Subsequently, he established branch monasteries in Helin, Yanji, Chang’an, Taiyuan, and Luoyang. In the spring of the Xunwei year of the Zhiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm.
The disciples of Śākyamuni gathered in the capital, and the Master’s assembly accounted for one-third of them; their dignified presence was truly impressive, which delighted the Emperor.
The Master possessed keen insight and could recite the entire Tripiṭaka after reading it only three times. He exhorted and guided his junior students without ever showing a trace of weariness.

He was well-versed in various secular classics and excelled in calligraphy and poetry. His formal sermons and general discourses amounted to nearly one hundred thousand words, which have been widely disseminated throughout the monastic community.
The disciples requested that he have his teachings carved into woodblocks. The Master rebuked them, saying, "These were merely expressions made during a moment of play.
How can they be treated as mere physical traces? He ultimately refused their request. Later, having grown weary of receiving visitors, he retired to live in seclusion at Mount Songyang.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Wait until Milk Peak nods its head, and I shall tell you. [Another] asked.

"What is the one path of supreme nobility that transcends all? The Master said: "The fisherman’s song startles the herons from the sandbars; they fly out through the reeds, leaving no trace. "Question:
What was it like when he sat facing the wall for nine years? The Master said: "Not even a needle can pass."
A monk asked, "What is it like at the time of 'one flower and five petals'? The Master said, "Private carriages and horses pass through.
The monk said, "In that case, the 'One Song of Xinfeng' was brought forth because of you, Master. The Master said, "Who would buy gold to cast a statue of Ziqi?
The Master asked a monk, "The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not distant. Tell me, where is it? As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout.
On the twentieth day of the seventh month of autumn in the year of Yi Hai, he manifested slight illness and wrote a verse to announce his passing.
His secular age was seventy-three, and his monastic seniority (lǎ) was fifty-two. He was interred in a stupa at the western corner of the temple.
Later, when Emperor Renzong ascended the throne, he initially bestowed a posthumous title and a noble fief, and commanded a scholar-official to compose a text to be inscribed upon his stupa.
Chan Master Conglun of Linquan at Yanjing Ba’en studied under Wansong.
Upon hearing the account of how Aniruddha attained the divine eye, he had a realization and awakened to the "eye above. He presented this to Wansong, who asked, "What is the eye above?
The Master said, "Blind. Wansong said, "Truly blind? The Master said, "Blind, blind. Wansong nodded his approval. Later, he emerged from seclusion to reside at Wan...

Master Shou ascends the hall: Zen, Zen—neither orthodox nor biased; there is no path of intention, yet there is the primordial abyss. It transcends the present and surpasses antiquity, outshining what came before and illuminating what follows.
If one can simply forget traces and footprints, why need one cling to the trap and the lure? Pointing directly at the human mind to see one's nature.
One must rely on the Patriarch’s intent to penetrate the source. The true message of nine years of facing the wall lies therein; there is indeed a distinct transmission within it.

In the *Ren-shen* year of the *Zhiyuan* era of Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty, the Master was summoned to the inner palace to discourse on the Way with the Imperial Preceptor (*Imperial Preceptor*).

The Emperor further commanded the Master to expound the great principles of Chan Buddhism. The Master then cited Guifeng Zongmi’s *Chan-yuan chuan-xi*: "In Sanskrit, it is called *dhyāna*; here [in Chinese]..."
What is called "cultivation through reflection" is also termed "dhyāna" (meditative concentration); both are general designations for samādhi and prajñā.

Because it is the source of all virtues, it is named "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena). Furthermore, because it is the source of sentient beings' delusion and awakening, it is named the "tathāgatagarbha" (womb of the Tathāgata).

Moreover, because it is the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas, it is named "buddhadhātu" (Buddha-nature). Now, as for dhyāna, there are shallow and deep levels, with distinct stages and grades. That is to say:

To practice while harboring heterodox views and feeling joy for the higher realms while loathing the lower is the meditation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). To practice with right faith in cause and effect, likewise through joy and loathing, is the meditation of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
To practice having realized the principle of the partial truth of the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) is the meditation of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
To practice having realized the true reality revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is the meditation of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). If...

To realize that one's own mind is originally pure and fundamentally free from afflictions, and that the nature of impartial wisdom is inherently complete—cultivating practice based upon this is the meditation of the Supreme Vehicle, also called the Tathāgata’s Pure Meditation. Since the time of Bodhidharma, [this has been the tradition].
"That which has been transmitted from generation to generation is the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna. The Emperor said, "Previously, whenever there were questions, everyone said there was nothing to say.
Why is it that you now, however, have something to say? The Master said, "In principle, there is fundamentally nothing to say; for now, I shall speak by way of phenomena.
The Emperor asked, "For what reason is there no verbal expression in principle? The Master said, "Principle is realized through the spirit. It is like a person eating honey."
It is sweet both inside and out. If one asks about the appearance of the honey, it may be described as purple-white;
yet if one discusses the description of its taste, it is truly difficult to express. The Emperor said to the Imperial Preceptor, "Is this statement correct or not?

The Preceptor replied, "This is no different at all from the profound Prajñāpāramitā found within the scriptures. The Emperor further asked about the *gong'an* (public cases) of the Patriarchs. The Master cited six...

Regarding the incident of the Patriarch’s wind and banner: it was not the wind or the banner that moved; rather, it was the mind of the worthy one that moved. The Imperial Preceptor said, "In truth, it was the wind and the banner that moved.

Why do you say it was the mind that moved? The Master said, "All things are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Is this not the mind moving? After they had debated until evening, he departed.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Northern Dipper resembles a ladle; the Southern Dipper resembles a gourd. Let him [the wise] measure and pour as he pleases."
Warm sun and cool breezes; the winter solstice and the hundred-and-fifth day of Cold Food Festival—know that the seasonal rhythms do not yield to one another.
At this point, is there anyone who can swallow and spit out [these conditions]? A monk asked: "Fayan said, 'For twenty years, I have only understood them as objective conditions.'"
"If you do not understand it through the objective realm, how then do you understand it? The Master said: "The ape carries its young back into the green peaks;
the birds sing and flowers fall before the emerald cliffs. Addressing the assembly, he said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a vermilion phoenix soaring into the heavens, leaving no trace.
This arises because the nature is empty and vast, and the sun of wisdom is brilliant and clear. It illuminates that the five aggregates are all empty, causing the myriad..."

When conditions and objects both vanish, one directly attains a state where stars cluster in the azure void and the moon bathes the vermilion steps; emerald curtains hang down as candle fragrance lingers and all is silent.
At such a moment, how could there be room for a breath? How could one permit even a peep? The secret chamber allows no breeze;
the primal gate offers no foothold. Even so, a single point of numinous clarity pervades the universe—how could it be confined by the land of Western India?

At Caoxi, on the twentieth day of the tenth month of the Xinsi year of the Zhizhen era, by imperial decree, the spurious scriptures of the Daoist Canon were gathered at Minzhong Temple in the Capital.
With the exception of the *Daode Jing*, they were all to be burned; the Master was commanded to light the fire.
Receiving this order, the Master struck a circular shape with his torch and said: "O virtuous ones, as for the numinous texts of the Three Caverns, have they ever been verified?"
"This is the Samādhi of the Fire-Flame; there is no such thing as the *Beidou Jing* (Northern Dipper Sutra).

If one has realized this, then the possession of that sutra is merely a false teaching that causes people's minds to remain restless. If this is not yet the case, then after these ashes fly and the smoke is extinguished, let him go anywhere to seek the Celestial Honored One;
look closely! He then cast away the torch, and the counterfeit scripture was consumed by the flames.
When Chan Master Congkuan of Wushan was about to pass away, he asked his second elder brother, "The Buddhas, the Patriarchs, and my parents—I have now shot them all dead with a single arrow.
What do you think of this? He then adjusted his robes and passed away.
Chan Master Chuan Yi-zi Wen of the Huayan Temple in the Capital was the son of the Hao family of Xingzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing ordinary children.
At the age of six, he met Jizhao, whose responses were skillful. Jizhao asked, "Will you become a monk? The Master inwardly consented.
It happened that Jizhao was fleeing the chaos and had gone into long seclusion in Liaoxi; the Master then followed Jizhao’s chief disciple, Bian’an Ne, to receive the tonsure. He heard—
Wuhan Fu opened the Dharma at Wanshou Monastery; his supervision of the assembly was extremely strict. The Master went there with ten monks to assist him. He visited Wansong Xiu a second time;
he possessed a vast memory and extensive learning, and his discursive debate was unimpeded. Xiu appointed him to oversee the attendants' office. Whatever Xiu instructed—

Upon hearing [the teachings] once, he immediately attained full realization. Xiu once had him respond to inquiries on his behalf; his sharp spiritual acumen was unassailable, and he subsequently received the seal of transmission (*kṣānti*).

The Grand Protector Liu Wenzheng, recognizing that the Master possessed the talent to govern the world, recommended him several times to the Emperor. When Emperor Sejong of the Yuan dynasty summoned him for an audience and conversed with him, he was greatly pleased.
He remained in the inner court for three years, providing much support and assistance to the royal transformation of the people. The Emperor granted him official rank.
The Master declined, saying, "The circulation of the Buddha-Dharma throughout the world is the true aspiration of a monk;

anything else is not what I hope for. The Emperor praised him and saw him off with full ceremonial honors. He was bestowed the title "Great Chan Master Puguang of the Buddha-Land" (Foguo Puan Dacishan).
