In the fifth month of the Dingmao year of the Zhizhi era, he manifested illness and passed away lying on his right side. A wondrous fragrance lingered for three days. When cremated, his heart, tongue, teeth, and bones remained unburnt. His remains were enshrined...
He benefited countless beings. His worldly lifespan was fifty-one years, and his monastic seniority was forty.
Chan Master Yuanzhao of Shaolin in Henan, a descendant of the Li clan of Shangdang, was exceptionally intelligent from childhood and abstained from meat and pungent roots.
At the age of eleven, he left the household life at Ciyun Temple on Mount Zituán; at sixteen, he received full ordination and subsequently traveled abroad.
He studied the teachings of the Śāstras with great precision. Later, he relied upon Wansong for many years and attained a thorough understanding of the principles of Chan.
He emerged into the world at Dajian Temple in Dezhou; subsequently, he moved to Puzhao in Qihé, Chongxiao in Que’li, Fawang in Dengfeng, and Wanshou in the capital.
Afterward, he returned once more to reside at Puzhao. On the sixth day of the third month in the Guiwei year of the Yuan Zhiyuan era, he passed away at the age of... (The text ends here).
Seventy-eight [years old]; with sixty-two years of seniority in the Sangha. He was interred at his home mountain. At the time of his burial, several hundred cranes circled above him.
The Chancellor Yila Zhenqing was a layman named Chucái. His original surname was Ye-lü. When the Jin dynasty extinguished the Liao, he submitted to the Jin and changed his surname to Yila.
Initially, while he resided in the capital, there were many masters of Chan; however, only Cheng of Sheng’an held him in high esteem.
Cheng frequently sought him out to inquire about the Way of the Patriarchs, repeatedly testing him with passages he had encountered in the recorded sayings of ancient patriarchs.
"Venerable An, at times you granted me permission, and I personally considered myself to have attained it.

However, since encountering these misfortunes and afflictions, I have grown indifferent to fame and achievement, and my resolve to seek the Way has become even more earnest. I have therefore come once again to consult you regarding my former matters. Daorong then completely overturned his previous position.
"It is not as you perceive it. The official was greatly perplexed and asked for the reason. Fo Tucheng then spoke to him calmly, saying:

"In the past, you occupied a position of great power, which makes one prone to anger and joy. Furthermore, many Confucian scholars lack sincere faith; they merely pick out fragments from recorded sayings to serve as material for conversation.
For this reason, I did not immediately apply the heavy hammer of rigorous discipline. Now, judging by your heart, it is indeed for the sake of the fundamental [truth]."
When you asked me about these matters, how could I dare to fail you again? Thus, I have not been sparing in my bitter words.

However, I am old; there is one known as the Elder Wansong, who is fully equipped in both Confucianism and Buddhism, is thoroughly versed in both the Chan school and the scriptural teachings, and possesses unimpeded eloquence.
"If you can see this, it will naturally resolve your great matter. The scholar responded with "Yes, yes," and went to visit Wansong at Baen Temple.

There, they were deeply in accord. Consequently, he cut off all human contact and set aside his domestic affairs. Whether in bitter cold or humid heat, there was not a day that he did not attend to his practice.
He burned oil lamps to continue through the night, neglecting sleep and forgetting to eat for nearly three years, until he finally attained certification. His title was...
The Layman Zhanran once wrote a preface to *Wansong’s Evaluations of the Ancients*, which states in brief: "The Buddhas, patriarchs, and various masters have their roots buried a thousand feet deep;
yet the hundred cases of karmic conditions sprout shoots in this world. Tiantong was unfit to pull up the branches, and Wansong could not bear to lead out the vines.
Zhanran, upon these very branches and vines, further adds thorny ropes, piercing through the nostrils of those who merely follow fragrances and pursue scents."
To trip up the original essence of walking is to miss the subtle point of the heels.
If you wish to have your heels touch the ground and your nostrils reach toward heaven, you must first pass through this tangle of complications.

Previously, when Emperor Shizu was about to set out on his western campaign, the officials reported that there were monks at Mount Wutai and other locations who possessed incantatory arts and military tactics, as well as great physical strength.
He was serving as a military officer escorting the army on a western expedition. A soldier reported this to the Emperor, saying:

"The high practitioners of the Śākya school must observe the precept against killing and uphold the practices of compassion and patience. Thus, there were those who would rather risk their own lives than take the 'goose-gem,' and those who would rather die than pull up a living blade of grass.
They reverently follow the laws of the Dharma King; even at the cost of death, they do not transgress them. To employ such men as soldiers—"

"How could this be appropriate? Those who do not follow the laws and regulations must surely lack noble intent and conduct. Since they have already violated the Buddha’s will there, how could they be loyal to the King’s affairs here?
Therefore, none of them may follow the Imperial Preceptor. The Emperor followed his advice and consequently withdrew the petition.
In the sixteenth year of Taizong’s reign, the Master passed away at the age of fifty-five (which was the *guimao* year of the Chunyu era of Emperor Lizong of the Southern Song).
The lay practitioner Li Chunfu of Bingshan initially relied upon his literary reputation and took pleasure in disparaging Buddhism and Daoism.

He happened to meet Wansong Xiu at Xingtai, and under a single word from him, he attained realization. Thereupon, he thoroughly perused the Buddhist scriptures and extensively investigated the Chan school.

He annotated such scriptures as the *Vajraśekhara* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and composed treatises such as the *Preface to the Origin of the Teaching* (*Xù fǎjiào yuánjiào lùn*) and the *Treatise on the Origin of the Teaching* (*Yuánjiào lùn*).

He once wrote the "Record of the Face-to-the-Wall Hermitage at Shaoshi," which states in brief: "When Master Bodhidharma came from the West, he uniquely proclaimed the principle of the 'Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings.
How could there be anything further transmitted outside our Buddhist teachings? It is simply that he did not cling to names and forms. As for the true transmission of the teaching, it is not..."
This is a separate transmission. Since the Master’s arrival, his descendants have spread throughout the world, gradually reaching from the śramaṇas of the scholastic schools to the scholar-officials.

Those who secretly corresponded and held a profound spiritual affinity with him are beyond counting. Among those whose teachings were recorded in written form, Qingliang obtained it and used it to comment on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*;
Guifeng obtained it and used it to draft a sub-commentary on the *Bodhisaṃbhāra-parivarta*; and Wujin obtained it to...
He understood the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Yingbin obtained it and used it to explain the *Laozi*; Ji Fu obtained it and used it to discourse on the *Zhouyi*;
the brothers of Yichuan obtained it and used it to instruct on the *Shijing* and *Shujing*; Donglai obtained it and used it to discuss the *Zuozhuan*;

and Wugou obtained it and used it to expound upon the *Yuyan* and *Zhongyong*. Thus, he ensured that the Way of the Sage would not fall into the abyss of extinction nor perish within the void of non-being.
He was not bound by physical form; his inner realization and outward appearance were as consistent as a tally and its seal.
Even a madman or a simple woman could attain sudden enlightenment in the space of a single turn or a glance, like dividing a remaining lamp to illuminate a dark room—how joyful this is!
This master’s writings are numerous, opening the way for later students and performing great service for the Dharma vehicle. At the time of his death, he met it without illness.
Sitting in the full lotus posture with palms joined, he passed away facing west.
Chan Master Hongming Xuzhao of Tianning Monastery in Shunde, a successor of Chan Master De of Xianyan, was the son of the Shen family of Liaozhou. He paid his respects at Wushan in Taiyuan.
Jizu left home to become a monk in the Great Sangha. Not long after, Jizu was instructed to travel extensively to seek instruction; he thus visited Xianyan.

Later, upon hearing the sound of a wooden board, he attained sudden enlightenment and subsequently received formal recognition. He later resided at Guiyi in Yan during the Jichou year of Emperor Yuan’s reign.
His fellow disciple Yuanfu Wuhuanchao requested that the Master expound upon the Dharma of the Pure Land.
On the eighth day of the fifth month of the Renzi year of Emperor Xianzong (1292), he bathed, changed his robes, and addressed the assembly, saying: "The four elements are impermanent."
"You all must cherish yourselves well. He then took up his brush and wrote a verse: "Abbot of two monasteries, there is no dharma to be preached;
Breaking through empty space, here is a single bright moon. Having cast aside his brush, he passed away. His cremation yielded over a hundred *śarīra* relics, brilliant in five colors.
His disciples Ziran and Zihong enshrined them in a stupa at Funan. The following year, the Great Ancestor (Shizu) moved the relics to...
Tianning. He was fifty-seven years old [in secular age] and thirty-eight years in the monastic order.
He was the twenty-fourth generation descendant of Qingyuan and the Dharma heir of Chan Master Shaoshi Yu.
Chan Master Wentai of Lingyin on Shaoshi Mountain in the Western Capital was the son of the Wei clan of Yangcheng in Fenzhou, Taiyuan.

His intelligence and insight surpassed those of his peers, and he possessed a profound affinity for the *zong* (the Dharma-lineage). He subsequently traveled to Shaoshi, where he soon realized the essential point of the mind.
Consequently, he was then renowned as one of the "Two Tais and One Su," and was considered one of the eminent disciples of Xueting. [The following is the section on] Monks’ Visits.

Dongshan spread out his sitting cloth, intending to prostrate. The Master said, "The heavenly net is vast and wide; it is sparse, yet nothing slips through. Dongshan said, "I originally intended to prostrate, but you, Reverend, have held me back.
What is the use of this when I cannot complete my bow? The Master said, "I am merely propping up your rice-bag. Even if you were to strip it down to the bone, what would be the point?
Dongshan said, "Even so, one must take the wrong for the right; I shall go and prostrate. The Master said, "When you do so..."
"What bowl? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "A fellow with a head but no tail. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The events of kalpas as numerous as dust motes are contained within this very moment. The wondrous virtues as vast as the sands of the Ganges are all present at the source of the mind.

Try having him present them face-to-face; yet he does not know how to bring them forth in the wind. Tell me, where does the fault lie? (He struck his staff. It is simply because of [his] discrimination."
"Excessive clarity causes what is attained to be delayed. In the *Jiuzhou* year (1289), during the Zhiyuan era of Emperor Shizu, Yuan, he manifested a slight illness and said to his disciples:
"That the ancients could depart while seated or transform while standing is not impossible; however, from the perspective of a monk, these are all merely secondary matters."
The mountain monk, however, was not so. Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes and lay on his right side; thus he passed away in auspicious tranquility.
This occurred on the final day of the first month. His remains were cremated, and his sacred relics were divided and enshrined in stupas at both Shaoshi and Baoying.
Chan Master Zhitaí of Zhōnglín at Bào’ēn Temple in Tàiyuán Prefecture was the son of the Wén family of Yúchéng in Fényáng.
He shaved his head under Huáyán and specialized in the study of the Sūtras and Vinaya. One day, he sighed deeply and said, “A man of great character should investigate the Great Matter;
how can I confine myself to these trivial matters? At that time, Xuètíng Yù was the abbot of Wànshòu Temple, and the Master went there to rely upon him for several years.
Zai was profoundly awakened to a state of transcendence. The imperial court took note of the Master’s reputation and issued an edict for him to reside at Ba’en Monastery.

A monk asked, "What is the place where there is not a single inch of grass for ten thousand miles? The Master said, "This is not within your realm. The monk asked, "What is 'stepping out the door and it is already grass'?
The Master said, "As soon as you intend to move, you have already gone astray. The monk asked, "What is 'not stepping out the door and it is still grass'? The Master said, "It is right here."
"Vast and boundless," [the student] said. The Master said, "To dwell upon it is an error. [The student] asked, "How can one avoid being involved with movement and stillness?

The Master said, "The entire world is devoid of even a speck of dust; the whole body is without shadow or form. He manifested illness and gathered the assembly, saying, "My karmic conditions shall end on this day.
You must each well protect and maintain yourselves. You should cherish every moment and not let it pass in vain. Those who heard this were all moved.
He wept with emotion and then wrote a verse, saying: "The Master Chonggi has built a seamless stupa; He has toppled his own formless body.
Formless body, formless body— Within this formless body, not a speck of dust remains. Having set down his brush, he passed away with a serene expression.
Chan Master Jingxu of Zu’an at Lingyan in Taian Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of Yongping in Baoding.
He took the vows at Xiangshan Shousheng Temple and made it his teacher. For over twenty years, he devoted himself to the study of the mind and visited more than ten generations of patriarchs.
Finally, he studied under Xueting at Wanshou Temple; after many years of refinement, he attained entry into the master’s room and initially succeeded him on the abbot’s seat.
Longevity! Next, the Master ascends the hall at Lingyan on Mount Shaoshi. The white dew stretches across the river; yellow chrysanthemums fill the garden.
The sound of the washing block strikes through the night moon; the crickets’ cries weep in the autumn wind. Cicadas buzz upon the trees by the bank;

leaves part from the branches beyond the railing. In every form, the Samādhi of the Ocean Seal manifests; in every particle of dust, the fundamental Dharma-wheel turns. If you all can understand this—
"It is attained. It is like a mirror facing a face: the eyebrows and eyes are distinct and clear. Yet, one can only call such a person 'half a monk';
the vulgar air has not yet been entirely removed. When you reach this point, if you can smash the mirror, only then will it be fitting for me to meet you.
But after meeting once the mirror has been smashed—what then? After a long silence, he said, "Wait until I give you thirty blows."
At another time, he later retired to Mount Xiangshan. One day, he gathered the assembly to take his leave and passed away while lying on his right side.

Zhonglin Tai composed an inscription for him, which said: "The nostrils that pierce the heavens; the heels that touch the earth. His mind was clear and his eyes were upright; his conduct followed the ancients and his countenance was warm.
As his deeds grew ever greater, his resolve became ever more steadfast. Elders from all quarters came specifically to knock at his door. He received the transmission from Xueting.

His successor was Wansong. His wheel of *prajñā* turned with lightning speed, like a flash of lightning or the roll of thunder. He raised high the banner of the Bodhi-tree and firmly consolidated its numinous roots.
His lamp of wisdom shone brightly, melting away the manifold darkness. With his total capacity and great function, he shook the very heavens and earth;
he overturned the Bohai Sea and kicked over Mount Kunlun. He swallowed all Buddhas of the three ages in a single gulp; unimpeded by the two extremes, he remained serene in the Middle Way.
Treatise: Third, he resided in great monasteries, where the fourfold assembly all held him in high esteem. His coming and going left no trace; his movement and stillness were without a mark.

Even if empty space were to crumble away, this Way would remain forever. Although the Master’s collected records of his life were destroyed by the fires of war, by reading this inscription by Master Tai, one can discern ten parts of the subtlety of his Dharma-giving and the mastery with which he wielded the "fang and claws" to kill or give life.
First: Chan Master Jueyin of the Northern Temple in Helin ascended the hall. After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? If you say I have something to say, you must cut off my tongue.
If you say I have nothing to say, you must give me back my tongue. He then pushed over a *vajra* staff with one hand.
A mound of mud. Treading upon a scale-weight is not iron. Tell me, is this with words? Is it without words? After a long silence, he said:
"Carelessly losing the oar in one’s hand, all because of greedily gazing at the moon in the sky. A monk visited. The Master asked, "Have you ever seen my teacher, Old Man Xueting?
The monk replied, "I have never seen him. The Master said, "Blind fellow, why are you wandering about so recklessly? The monk said—
"I know that the Master possesses this one pivot. The Master said, "Picking up horse dung to eat as rice—what kind of stomach do you have?
Get out! Zhongqing Chan Master of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Monastery ascended the hall. After a long silence, he said, "Eating salt only increases thirst," and then he descended.
[The Master] was seated. A monk asked, "What is it like when eating salt increases one's thirst? The Master said, "A dog barking at a shadow has no excrement to eat.
Chan Master Shou Rang of Anping, Zhending, addressed the assembly: "The sword that kills and the blade that gives life—this is the style of antiquity.
In my place, there is no need for polishing; it is used exactly as it should be. Now tell me, from where does this handle come?"
"From where does it come? A thousand-fathom snow on Mount Song; a single wheel of moon over Bear’s Ear. He then let out a shout.

After Master Chan Shi Jushan (Longtan Chongxin), the Crown Prince of Taiyuan, took up residence, he ascended the hall for the formal discourse. He cited a monk who asked Dalong: "The physical body decays;
what is the indestructible Dharma-body? Dalong replied: "Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; the mountain stream is as clear as indigo."
The Master said: "Dalong speaks thus, but I, this mountain monk, am not so. If someone were to ask, 'When the physical body perishes, what is the firm Dharma-body?
I would tell him: 'I am blinding your eyes; the stream water is poisoning your ears.
A crane does not cling to its secluded nest; a dragon does not hide in dead water.'"
Chan Master Shuntian Changqing Dedao ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose ancestral style does he succeed?

The Master said, "Riding an ox while wearing a bamboo hat, arriving unexpectedly at Luoyang. The monk said, "If that is so, then the direct lineage of Lufeng flows upstream against the waters of Dong.
The Master said, "When the herdsman’s flute is blown, heaven and earth are still; before the gate of the rustic elder..."
No nameplate was set up.
One day, Zen Master Huiyuan of Pingshui said to his disciples: "In my youth, I was called by others a 'rice-wine dregs eater.
I was so indignant at this injustice that I vowed to travel until I wore out several pairs of straw sandals, yet I could not find a point of entry."
Later, he asked Wanshou, "What is Chan? Wanshou said, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind its head.
If you do not understand this, it is like throwing a fierce fire onto a frying pan of oil. At these words, he finally attained a sense of joy and liberation.
From this, one knows that people must be provoked by others; nevertheless, you must have blood beneath your skin for it to be effective. Thereupon, the monk asked:
"A person may be scolded, but how is it when the words do not pierce to the bone? The Master said, "You are a ruffian; you have no skin, so what 'bone' could there be to speak of?
Chan Master Jueyin of Huayan in Jingzhao ascended the hall and said: "The ancients all claimed, 'I am a descendant of Bodhidharma.'"
Yet it is said: "Shenguang stood in his place; this was attaining the marrow. This very thing is like making a stinking leather shoe sole—it cannot even be called dust or grime.
Why? Because those who encounter [the truth] while lost are few, while those who betray its grace are many.
Cen Master Guangyan Faxing of Gongchang was visited by his fellow practitioner, Yinzhu. The Master said, "It has been a long time since we last met. How are your eyebrows?
Yinzhu replied, "I thought you had forgotten, elder brother. The Master asked, "Can the joyful Dharma of that place be described to an old acquaintance?
Yinzhu said, "One who is sorrowful should not speak of sorrow to another who is sorrowful. The Master said, "In that case..."
"Is it not then that those of the same lineage do not share the same life-force? Yinzhu said, "This makes even Hanshan laugh to tears.

The Master said, "Thank you for your kind words, elder brother. Chan Master Shunde Miaocheng offered these words: "Master Shitou did not know good from bad; what 'clarity' could he possibly speak of?"
Within this there is darkness. That old fellow from Dongshan was turned by his own verbal flow; what need is there to speak of the "five ranks" of orthodox and deviant?
He has dragged the descendants of later generations into such a tangle, unable to extricate themselves.
A monk asked, "Why does the Master not cut through this tangle and open another path? The Master said, "Ouyang is still tolerable; the most painful is the New [Trend]."

Luó. Chan Master Tóngxīn of Yuèquán at Ānshān in Shùntiān, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Lún Bàoen, whose courtesy name was Zhòngyì, was the son of the Gùo family of Fángshān. He followed Ān...
Shanjian tonsured his hair and was able to perform arduous tasks for the assembly. Suddenly, one day, his wisdom blossomed all at once, and he attained the same realization as Xiu.
The members of the assembly laughed at him in derision. The Master was deeply incensed; he wrote a verse on the wall and departed. The verse said:
"A great man whose spirit pierces the clouds—how could he be confined by ordinary ditches and streams? In hand he holds a three-foot blade that shaves hair, and goes straight..."
He took the pearl from beneath the chin of a black dragon and went to pay his respects to Qing’an Fang. Fang asked, “If you wish to travel a thousand li, the first step is what matters.
What is this very first step? The Master stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there. Fang said, “What can you do when your heels do not touch the ground?
The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Next, he visited Daming Gao; under his staff and whisk, [the Master] gained much...

He exerted himself in his practice until, feeling regret that he had not yet reached the ultimate, he returned to a state of pure peace. After another three years, he suddenly attained a great and sudden enlightenment.
He subsequently visited Linquan, whereupon he received the seal of transmission. Soon after, he was invited to Lingyan Monastery to serve as the *yinzuo* (introducer).

As soon as the Master uttered a single note, the multitude cheered; many were able to grasp the essential meaning beneath his words. Not long thereafter, an imperial decree arrived from Emperor Shizu of the Yuan dynasty.
Later, he was appointed as the abbot of Lingyan Temple, but subsequently retired back to Anshan. One day, while traveling to Jie, he entered the summer retreat at Guanyuan Temple.

Suddenly, he fell ill and spoke this verse: "Coming, there is no place from which one comes; going, there is no destination. He suddenly raised his fist and said, "Tell me, is there still any obstruction in this?
He released his fist and said, "With hands cast loose, moving freely—vast and azure is the sky. Then he closed his eyes and passed away.
He then passed away. His age was sixty-six; his years of ordination were forty-five.
He was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Fa Wang Zhao.
A monk asked Chan Master Bin of Xi'an, "What is the partiality within the absolute center? The Master said, "A wooden man beats [the drum] at midnight."
[The Master] was swinging on a swing. [A monk] asked, "What is 'being correct within partiality'? The Master said, "The various officials fear seeing the mirror of the Qin Terrace.
[The monk] asked, "What is 'coming from within correctness'? The Master said, "The wooden boy and the earthen figurine laugh heartily.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'arriving at the union of both'? The Master said, "The wrathful Nārāyaṇa wields his eight arms. [The monk] asked, "What is 'reaching the ultimate unity'? The Master said, "He leans upon..."
He leaned his staff against himself before the wind.
Zen Master Jinsiang of Shifang was asked by a monk, "What is it like when you encounter a bridge and tear it down? The Master said, "Where would one find such a person?
The monk asked, "What is your own intention, Master? The Master said, "A true master from of old never reveals his name."
A monk asked Chan Master Fawang Hui of Mount Song: "What is the realm of the Dharma King? The Master said: "The snow is deep before Five-Milk Peak.
The monk asked: "Who is the person of the Dharma King? The Master said: "On the summit of Mount Song is a nose that reaches the heavens."
A monk asked, "What is it like when the person and the environment intersect? The Master said, "Look at the time when the command is being carried out.
Chan Master Lingyan Fu of Taian Prefecture addressed the assembly: "Thirty years from now, there will be many who harbor doubts about this.
A monk asked, "What is it like if one harbors doubts right now? The Master said, "On level ground, there is no cause for falling into a pit."
A monk asked Chan Master Huguo Yuan, "How does one protect the nation? The Master said, "The Emperor’s decree within the realm.
The monk asked, "Where is the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Sitting upright while receiving offerings."
Upon seeing the mountain gate, Chan Master Chongxiao Pu burst into a great laugh, "Ha ha!
What a joyous day for my entire life! My slaves and servants are all so diligent."
A monk asked Chan Master Jingtulizi, “What is the pure Buddha-land? The Master said, “Do not create defilement. The monk asked, “What is the defiled Buddha-land?
The Master said, “Vainly engaging in conceptual discrimination. The monk asked, “What is your own intention, Master?
The Master said, “The flowers bloom on iron trees; they do not recognize spring.”

One day, after recovering from an illness, Chan Master Hai of Baoying in汝州 (Ruzhou) was asked by a monk: "Regarding 'The Buddha of the Sun’s Face' and 'The Buddha of the Moon’s Face,' what is their essential meaning?
The Master said: "The mountains grow ever higher and the waters grow ever deeper. The monk asked: "When one cannot find a place where [the mind] arises, what then? The Master said:
"Where the skilled physician folds his hands, the Dharma-body has its own separate source."

Chan Master Zhongfu Ziyen of Tianning in Shunde was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tianning Ming. Born into the Yang family of Ningjin, he received the tonsure under Chan Master Tianning Xuzhao and attained realization through his practice.
His reputation was esteemed by the imperial court; Emperor Sejong of the Yuan dynasty wished to confer honors upon him.
The Master stubbornly refused to comply. He took his staff, the precious book, and opened the hall at his own temple.

When a monk came to pay his respects, the Master stepped back and entered, saying, "There is a thief outside. The monk prostrated three times. The Master looked back and said, "The heart of a thief is always apprehensive.
Go to the hall."
The Layman Liu Bingzhong, styled Zhonghui, was a native of Ruizhou. His original name was Kan, and his dharma name was Zicong.
At the age of seventeen, he served as a clerk in the office of the Regional Commander of Xingtai to support his parents. He was often despondent and unhappy;
one day, casting aside his pen, he sighed and said, "My family has been of scholar-official lineage for generations, yet I am now submerged in the life of a mere scribe."

Having thus departed, he retired to Mount Wu’an and entered the monastic order under Tianning Zhao. Through diligent practice and contemplation, he attained realization. Zhao appointed him as a secretary.
When Emperor Yuan Shizu campaigned against Yunnan, crossing the river to attack Ezhou, [Yuan] repeatedly praised him for making non-killing his virtue.

Whenever cities were captured or enemies seized, countless lives were spared. Although his rank reached that of the highest minister, he still maintained a vegetarian diet and lived in simple seclusion.
He changed his former attire. At that time, he was universally known as "Cōng the Secretary. In the eighth month of the eleventh year of the Zhìyuán era, he took up his brush and wrote this verse:
"I have not failed the world; the world has not failed me. My relation to the world is like the moon reflected in water."
"Like flowers in the sky. The flowers fall and the moon sinks. What is this? With a shout, he threw down his brush, sat in the lotus position, and passed away.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Shaoshi Tai of the twenty-fifth generation under Qingyuan.
Chan Master Huan-yuan Fuyu of Bao-ying Monastery in the Western Capital was a native of the Wang family in Ling-shi, Huo Prefecture.
He received the tonsure at Doushuai Monastery in his home district and traveled extensively among the lecture halls, where his eloquence flowed like a stream.

Later, hearing of Lingyin’s Tai, whose spiritual eye was sharp and clear, he went to him with sincere devotion to seek instruction. Tai once said to the Master, "When I raise my whisk, you immediately go toward the whisk."

"Understanding at the 'upper meeting'—as soon as I have just sat for a long while, you immediately understand it within that state of 'long while. If you understand in such a manner, how can you penetrate the matter of your own fundamental share?
The Master’s face grew hot and he broke into a sweat; he had no reply. One day, hearing Taishan ascend the hall and cite the words, "One must by all means avoid seeking from others;
to do so is to distance oneself from me," the Master attained great enlightenment on the spot. He was immediately granted certification, and thus began his initial teaching.
Fàtiānqìng succeeded [him] as the abbot of Bǎoyīng Monastery. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master replied, "The wind carries the sound of the spring to the pillow; the moon shifts the shadows of the flowers to the window.
He passed away in the tenth month of the Gui-chou year of the Huánqìng era of Emperor Wénzōng (1313). He was sixty-nine years old, with forty-nine years of monastic seniority.
Chan Master Chue Jiangjie of Lingyan in Jinan Prefecture was visited by the monk Cheng Xuexuan. The Master asked, "Where have you come from?
Cheng replied, "From Qingzhou. The Master said, "Did you bring the Qingzhou cloth robe with you? Cheng said, "I have already presented it to the Master."

The Master said, “Thirty blows of the staff—wait for another time. Cheng then shook his sleeves and departed. The Master silently approved of this and had him attend the meditation hall for a long period.
One day, Cheng’s long-standing doubts were suddenly resolved like ice melting; he went straight to the Master’s quarters. The Master said, “The golden lock and the primal barrier have been opened.
Cheng replied, “Within a peach pit a thousand years old, what old kernel do you seek? The Master nodded in agreement.
He entrusted him with these words, saying: "Guard and uphold this well yourself. In the future, the one who will be able to propagate my Way must be you.

Chan Master Yueran Yongda of Baoying Temple in the Western Capital was a dharma successor of Chan Master Lingyan Su. He was a native of the Liu clan from Fenzhou. He shaved his head at Tian... Temple in that same prefecture.
At Ning Temple, he constantly used the great matter of birth and death as a stimulus for practice. He traveled south to seek instruction and engage in inquiry.
Hearing that Master Lingyan Su’s Dharma-thunder was resounding far and wide, he admired his virtue from afar and traveled there on foot. Upon meeting him once, [Lingyan] recognized his potential;

after attending him intimately for a long time, he eventually entered the profound depths of his teaching. He then said, "Realization arises through the teacher, but its practice depends on oneself. Thereupon, he went to Taian Prefecture to close himself in retreat.
Later, as the seat at Baoying Temple remained vacant, the monastics and laypeople earnestly requested him to accept. He accordingly ascended the hall and said: "The old man of Lumeng says:
'The entire great earth is this person’s single scroll of scripture; the entire universe is this person’s single eye.
With such an eye, one views such a scripture, without interruption for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas. Thus spoke the Elder Wansong.
Exhausting all one's strength, one can only say that reading and reciting it is no easy matter. Can you all read and recite it? You must know:
who does not possess this single volume of scripture? Who does not have this single eye fully complete?
If one wishes to lengthen it, it is inexhaustible throughout thousands of millions of billions of kalpas; if one wishes to shorten it, it is finished in a single kṣaṇa. Today, Baoying [does not...]
"Pity those eyebrows! He pointed this out for everyone, then snapped his fingers once and said, "Look! You have finished reading it. Everyone, do not let this slip away.
After a long silence, he struck his whisk and said, "From now on, there is no returning; if one returns, it can be attained. Who would vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?
One day, he manifested illness and passed away peacefully.

Chan Master Pujou of Fenglong Mountain in Zhending Prefecture was the son of the Liu family of Huyang. At fifteen, he paid his respects to Chanmaster Cheng at Fenglong Mountain and entered the monastic order.
At nineteen, he received full ordination and immediately began traveling to visit various masters. He first met Chanmasters Cheng, Chong, Xiao, and An of the Pure Land school;
although he received their recognition and appreciation, he never dared to consider himself satisfied. He visited Lingyan Su again, [receiving instruction on] the fundamental...

He was subjected to further intense refinement through the use of tongs and hammers. Suddenly, he attained a flash of awakening (*tunwu*) and immediately received a prediction of enlightenment (*jibie*).
Later, he took leave of the mountain and lived in seclusion at Baoji for ten years. In the year Gui-si, when Guian resided at Lingyan, he invited the Master to serve as the First Seat.

In the *Renyin* year of the *Dade* era of Emperor Chengzong of the Yuan dynasty (1302), Yue’an Hai retired from his position at his home temple and submitted a formal petition requesting the Master to open the hall for teaching.

In the *Dingwei* year (1307), he was specially bestowed with the title "Great Zen Master Miaoyan Hongfa. Subsequently, he was transferred to Longfeng. This was during the *Guichou* year of the *Huangqing* era (1313).
While residing at the ancestral seat of Shaolin, a monk asked, "What is 'falling into the category'? The Master said, "It is not one who is seen wearing fur and horns.
The monk asked, "What is 'falling into accordance'? The Master said, "It is not one who hears sounds or sees forms. The monk asked, "What is 'falling into nobility'?
The Master said, "It is not one who sits upright upon the throne. The monk said, "If it is thus, how can there be..."
[The monk] mentioned the term "three falls. The Master said, "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water.

[The monk] asked, "An ancient said, 'The three falls are the illness of one who has finished their affairs. Since he is one who has finished his affairs, how can he have an illness? The Master said, "Precisely because he has finished his affairs, the illness arises.
[The monk] asked, "When will this illness be cured? The Master said, "Only when there is no body will this illness finally be cured."

He then presented this verse: "The heavy golden locks have long since been flung wide open; Tranquil and at ease, he comes and goes alone through the three realms. As a wild goose flies across the vast sky, it leaves no trace;
Its reflection sinks into the cold water, leaving others to their conjectures. The Master was simple and dignified, rarely adorned with artifice.

His conduct in advancing and withdrawing was measured and disciplined. Later, he returned to live in seclusion at Lingqi. Not long after, he passed away and was interred in a stupa on the mountain itself. He was seventy years of age.
Seventh: with sixty-two years of monastic seniority (sang-lai),
he was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Bāoyìng Yù of the twenty-sixth generation under Qīngyuán.
Chan Master Xiangyan Chunzhu Wencai of Dengzhou was the son of the Yao family of Linfen in Pingyang. From birth, he possessed extraordinary qualities;

whenever he saw a monk, he would join his palms and prostrate, unlike ordinary children. As he grew older, he requested to study the Buddha-dharma and left the household life under Fuyan Pu of Jizhou.
He once read the *Song of Realizing the Way*, and upon reaching the line, "The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body," [he attained realization].
He joyfully attained realization and went to see Huan Yuan to present his understanding. Yuan interrogated him, saying, "As for the saying, 'The Master does not see,' to whom is this referring?
The Master replied, "Presented directly face-to-face; there is no evasion. Yuan said, "You pit-fall-dweller, you talk like that!
The Master asked, "And how about you, Preceptor? Yuan said, "I would shut your mouth tight."
The Master said, "I have thoroughly scrutinized you. Yuan approved this. He spent three years reading the Tripitaka at Longmen Mountain.
In the year Jiazi of the Taiding era, he presided over Shaoshi and ascended the hall, saying: "Having calculated everything on the board, there is only this one move that is most advantageous."
"I venture to ask the assembly: tell me, what is that one point? He planted his staff upright and said, "Do not attempt to speculate.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Not even a needle or an awl can pass through. The monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "Wagons and horses have their paths.
The monk asked, "Why do you overturn the public cases of the ancients? The Master said, "Set forth the upright and cast aside the crooked."
Seeking out Yinxian, he expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* as well as the *Huayan fajie guan*. A monk asked, "What is the dharma-realm of principle (*li-fajie*)?
The Master said, "When empty space falls to the ground, it shatters into pieces that form no pattern. The monk asked, "What is the dharma-realm of phenomena (*shi-fajie*)?
The Master said, "When you arrive, the house is utterly destroyed; thus one avoids being a fool within the dwelling. The monk asked, "What is the dharma-realm of principle? [The Master replied: "..."

[The Master spoke of] the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena. The Master said: "In the three months of winter, withered trees flourish; in the nine months of summer, snowflakes fly. [A disciple] asked:
"What is the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of all things? The Master said: "The clear breeze accompanies the bright moon; the rustic old man smiles as they draw near.
On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the *Renchen* year of the Zhizheng era of Emperor Yuan of the Yuan dynasty, he bathed, changed his robes, and called to his disciples, Shen...

He gave instructions, saying, "When I die, do not trouble yourselves with useless expenses; it will suffice to raise my ashes once the fire has been extinguished. At dawn the following day, he passed away in peace.
His entire body was interred to the right of the Xueting Pagoda. He was eighty years of age.
Chan Master Kongxiang Gui of Xiong’er in Henan addressed the assembly: "If I shout, you immediately understand it as a shout;
you then go everywhere shouting recklessly at will. If I strike with a staff, you immediately understand it as a staff; you then go everywhere striking recklessly with your hands.
If I were to set aside both staff and shout and instruct him to speak a single phrase from within his own fundamental nature, he would not be one who merely strikes."
He circumambulated [the master] and then performed a woman’s bow. This was not merely the fabrication of two lines of ghostly talk; he was like a mute sheep.
Those of such a sort are all like mad dogs chasing after clods of earth; when have they ever dreamed of seeing the bared fangs and claws of a lion?
Suddenly [the Master] asked: "Is there a lion here? Try to show me your fangs and claws! One monk [stepped forward].
[The monk] went out. The Master struck him, saying, "Chasing clods and seeking incense—this does not make for a good dog.

As the monk prepared to respond, the Master struck him again, saying, "Even if my staff were broken, I would still not let you go. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then Yunyan’s path is cut off. The Master said, "It is because you have no way to ascend to heaven;
how can you blame me for cutting off Yunyan’s path? Thereupon, he drove him out with a continuous succession of blows.
Master Longtan Shen of Mount Song in Henan addressed the assembly:
"In my youth, I attained ultimate nirvana at the point in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* concerning 'inverted dreams.
Later, I realized that all the sages and worthies take this very ultimate nirvana to constitute inverted dreams. When I eventually met the old man Huan-yuan, I questioned him..."
"An ancient tomb does not serve as a home. What is Chan? [The monk] said, "These are dead words. The mountain monk asked, "What are living words?
The old man struck him a blow across the face and said, "How can you be so lethargically dead? The mountain monk was about to respond.
He was struck once more with a palm. At that time, this mountain monk was like one who has found a lamp in the darkness. He then declared: "This time it was no dream;
it was truly Mount Lu. Today, I dare not obscure the source of its origin, and thus I have specifically brought it forth for you."
"You people must also undergo such a shedding once before you can attain it. He then struck the table once and said, "How utterly leaking and clumsy!
Zen Master Longtan Chuan of Songshan was asked by a monk, "What is the Shaolin lineage? The Master replied, "The ninefold abyss."

From the depths arose a divine dragon. [The student] asked, "What is the Cao-Dong school? The Master said, "A hundred kalpas of enemies meeting on a narrow path. [The student] asked, "What is the Linji school?
The Master said, "A person without a mouth swallowing a thorny chestnut. [The student] asked, "What is the Yunmen school?
The Master said, "Holding a short blade in hand, running east and west. [The student] asked, "What is the Guiyang school? The Master—
[The student] asked, "Turtle hair is accustomed to binding the wind at the treetop. [The student] asked, "What is the Dharma-eye school?

The Master said, "Joyfully grasping the golden goblet to urge the tipsy old man. [The student] asked, "What is the school not transmitted by the thousand sages? The Master said, "The bell is already hanging;
why strike it? Where would one smelt copper?"
A monk asked Zen Master Tianqing Jiang of Luoyang, "What is it like when the ancient mirror has not yet been polished? The Master said, "The food and drink of ghosts and spirits.

The monk asked, "What is it like when the ancient mirror has already been polished? The Master said, "The enemies of demons and heretics. The monk asked, "What is it like when snow is served in a silver bowl?
The Master said, "Blindness upon seeing with the eyes. The monk asked, "What is it like when the bright moon hides among the herons? The Master said:
"Movement is the very womb of calamity. [The monk] asked, "If so, what is it like when there is no movement? The Master said, "The one who pushes out is a dead man.
[The monk] asked, "I beg the Master to further grant me a skillful means. How does one turn back? The Master said, "When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it;
carry it home in a bottomless basket."
At Mount Song, Chan Master Yongtai Xiang had the monk Jian serving as the guest prefect. The Master asked, "What guests have come today?
Jian replied, "A constant stream of people, none of whom fail to pass through—nothing but Hu, Zhang, Li, and Hei. The Master said, "Can you distinguish them?
Jian replied, "I simply tell them all to go drink tea. The Master said, "You clumsy fellow! You cannot even tell a slave from a master."
"How can one consume the property of the monastery? He replied, "It is solely at the Master’s command. The Master said, "Go and swallow iron balls!
Jian laughed and said, "The Master does it this way too. The Master struck him and said, "Do you do it this way as well?"
Chan Master Xuexuan Daocheng of Tianjie Monastery in Jinling was a dharma heir of Chan Master Lingyan Jie.
He was a distant descendant of Prince Zhao of Yunzhou; his father moved to Baoding, where they subsequently made their home.
At the age of fifteen, he left the household life at Xingguo Monastery in the prefecture. The Master had a broad forehead and a flat brow.
Magnificent and resolute in his aspirations, after receiving the precepts, he formed a group of three companions and dwelt in an earthen cave in Qingzhou.

For many years, they secretly investigated the meaning of the single transmission. Suddenly, an old man of most extraordinary and ancient appearance appeared and said to them, "You three have forgotten both hardship and sweetness;
you have embraced a life of simplicity to investigate and clarify the great matter of the Ultimate. In days to come, you shall surely become pillars of the Dharma-gate."

The Master rebuked him, saying, "Since you have become a pillar within the cave of the layman," the old man replied, "There has never been one who acts constantly without abiding, nor one who abides constantly without acting. Having said this, he vanished. The Master redoubled his diligent efforts.
Hearing that Qiu Jiangjie was extensively propagating the principles of Caodong at Lingyan in Qi, he went there to pay his respects. (The dialogue is recorded in the *Lingyan [Record]*.)

(Chapter on Jie: Jie Mo was permitted to participate in the Hall. After long years of refining and tempering, he returned to Qingshe. The assembly requested that he reside at Puzhao, and subsequently he resided at Dazeshan in Donglai.
In the *Renxu* year of the Ming Emperor Hongwu, the Master was selected by lot; his realization accorded with that of the Prince, and imperial favor was especially profound.
In the autumn of the *Dingchou* year, the Emperor summoned the Master to the Hall and ordered him to reside at Tianjie. The Master submitted a petition [refusing].)
Having realized the Buddha-dharma, the Emperor composed a poem which was inscribed upon a golden tablet and hung in the Dharma Hall, saying:

"Not answering the words of his arrival, he consented through silence; Returning west on a single sandal, the ancient single transmission. Gongs and bells ring at the new and full moon in the Palace of the Empty King;
The seat is shown as it was many years ago. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "Ten thousand acres of white clouds roll and unfold, revealing the true mechanism beyond kalpas. Red..."
A thousand peaks of foliage shimmer brilliantly, revealing the wondrous principle within; it remains unclouded throughout antiquity and the present, eternally persisting through kalpas of dust.
The bird-path is empty yet penetrating, its movement originating from the primal gate. The lion’s string is dense and subtle; fingers press upon the strings with rhythmic precision.
Ancient tones ring out clearly, until even the stone woman nods her head and the wooden man claps his hands. Grasping the golden needle and jade thread, one passes through.

Before the opportunity arises: cutting off the horns of a hare and the hair of a tortoise that have yet to appear; revealing what lies beyond the ordinary; manifesting the absolute and the relative in their nakedness;
encompassing both the hidden and the revealed in their entirety. Thus, in every object and at every point, in every moment and in every land, there is not even a single thread or speck missing.
Do you all understand? Last night a wooden horse galloped through the clouds, startling the Southern Dipper and Northern Dipper into hiding. [Ascending the Dharma Hall] The Yin... (text breaks off)
The extreme yang returns and transforms as the days grow long; plum blossoms everywhere emit their fragrant scent.

Within this, there is not much of a secret to be told—how could it ever be concealed throughout the entire world? Thus, clarity and inclusion go hand in hand; we meet one another at the tips of the hundred grasses.
Proclaiming it deeply and secretly, it is uniquely revealed within the light of the myriad phenomena. Upon the field of profit and fame, recognize the True Man of No Rank;
amidst the mountains of self and other, manifest your original face. When the shadow merges with the mirror of the school, thoughts arise and all manner of dharmas arise;
the body is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease. The barren woman holds aloft the precious seal; its patterns and colors—

Fully revealed. The wooden man secretly passes through the golden shuttle; not a hair’s breadth is obscured. He pulls the mechanism of the wheel beyond the kalpas, blazing brilliantly within the world.

Through the years and months, he subtly connects the distant and the near, until even withered wood sprouts flowers. He encompasses all interpretations of past and present, causing frozen ice to emit flames.
Clouds shroud the ancient path, where the lingering wild colors remain lost; the moon fills the cold crags, shining bright and clear.

Divine light shines everywhere; the mechanisms of the six gates have stilled. Why need one resort to circuitous detours or lateral references? When the function of the single color is perfected, one must strictly avoid being struck at the head and shattered.
The white ox treading its path has already received the conditions for transformation and edification; the jade horse neighing in the wind is entirely a matter of benefiting sentient beings.
But tell me, what is the matter that transcends this? *Tut!* A rabbit-horn staff picks out the moon from the bottom of the pond.
A whisk of tortoise hair hangs upon the clouds at the mountain peak. Entering the hall: The three yang lines intersect in harmony; all things are renewed.
This reveals the wondrous function of the One True Reality and encompasses the profound source of all transformation. In every atom, one merges with the Way; in every place, the ford is open.

The Dharma assembly is grandly inaugurated, and the Garden of Enlightenment is widely opened. The destiny of the nation rises together with the destiny of the Buddha; the imperial breeze fans alongside the wind of the Patriarchs.
It is simply as it is said: "The old year has passed and the new year has arrived. Yet, I do not know where it goes when it departs, nor from where it comes when it arrives.

To comment in such a manner is increasingly seen as a source of confusion. I dare ask the assembly: within the single stroke beneath the patched robe, is there any addition or subtraction regarding coming and going?
If you can realize this, you will see that at the end of the twelfth month, the sun’s warmth shines upon the shadowless tree.
Spring returns and flowers bloom, yet there is no sprouting on the branches. [Ascending the hall: "In the fifth month, the hibiscus flowers shine brightly before the eyes;

the fragrant breeze and warbling birds pervade the mountain retreats. Before the working of the mechanism, there is not a single stroke of primordial subtlety. One must take care not to mistake this for the recognition of form and sound.

I recall Jia Shan’s way of speaking: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the meaning lies within the present moment. It is not a dharma of the present moment; it is beyond the reach of ears and eyes."
As for what has been reached, Tiantong Jue said: "The old man Jiashan has untied his cloth bag and scattered rare treasures before everyone.
At such a moment as this, what then? When the road has no lost items to be picked up, the gentleman praises it.
O assembly, although there is certainly merit in the insights of these two elders, if one examines them closely, they are both...
This concludes the discourse. Fengshan, however, was not like this. If one views forms or seeks sounds, that is not the family treasure.
When one realizes that not a single dharma exists before one’s eyes, every head and every object is in total accord. Should this not yet be so, listen further to the final phrase:
"When the realm is prosperous, the Son of Heaven does not issue commands; when the times are peaceful, there is no need to sing songs of peace. — Recorded by Cheng in the year of Renwu.
The Patriarch’s successor ascended the precious throne and dispatched an envoy to Japan; the Master went there to proclaim the holy transformation.

In the year *Guiwei*, he returned to report his success, and the Emperor was greatly pleased, bestowing upon him exceptional favor. While Renzong was still in the Spring Palace, someone who envied the Master’s prestige fabricated slanders against him.
Once Renzong ascended the throne, he consequently banished the Master to Hainan. When Xuanzong succeeded to the throne, he summoned the Master first and received him in audience.

In the private palace, he was comforted and rewarded with the utmost courtesy. In the spring of the Dinghai year, the Emperor commanded the Master to preach the Dharma at Mount Zhong; those who listened numbered in the tens of thousands.
In the Dingwei year of the Xuande era, when the Master was seventy-six years old, he submitted a memorial to decline his duties and return to the mountains.

The Emperor, moved by his sincerity, dispatched an inner court official to escort him back south to the Xianan Hermitage at Tianjie Temple to spend his final years in retirement. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the Renzi year, he manifested a slight illness.
He took leave of the assembly and spoke a verse, then sat cross-legged and passed away. The Emperor composed a memorial text and dispatched an official to present the offerings.

His secular age was eighty-one, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇerakāla) was sixty-six. On the day of his cremation, the smoke and flames were five-colored, immortal cranes soared through the sky, and a rare fragrance wafted ethereally.

Over ten thousand people, including officials, nobles, and the fourfold assembly, all marveled at such a rare occurrence. After the fire had subsided, the *śarīra* were collected; those that were round and red...
His number was incalculable. He erected a stupa outside the Andong Gate of Yingtian Gate. By imperial decree, the site of the stupa was granted to him and established as Juefeng Chan Temple.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Baoying Da.
Chan Master Ningguang of Renshan, upon ascending the hall, said: "The venerable elders of all quarters are fond of citing ancient cases to receive and attend to monks.
Today, I shall imitate them and cite one case as an offering to the assembly.
After a long silence, he said, "Do not take my lack of refinement to heart," and then descended from his seat.
Chan Master Bin of Taiyuan ascended the hall and, counting with his fingers, said:

"The seven times four of India and the two times three of this land—calculating them all up to one thousand seven hundred—they all fail to emerge from my fingertips. Alas! Alas! When you can go back, then go back;
do not fall into the counting of others. He then descended from the seat.
Chan Master Xianan Yirang of Tianqing Temple in the Western Capital was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fenglong Jiu. He was the son of the Li family of Zhending.

Having shaved his head at the age of seven, he traveled extensively to consult various masters of the school. Finally, he arrived at Fenglong and sought instruction in the quarters of Guyan Jiu. Upon meeting him, Jiu recognized his potential. One day—

He presented the *Dharma-pi-mei-song* (Verses on the Skin, Flesh, and Marrow of Bodhidharma) and asked: "The skin, face, marrow, and bones of Bodhidharma have all been obtained by his various descendants.
But tell me, what is this that returned to the West with a single shoe? The Master said, "I am glad, Preceptor, that you still remember."
Jiuzhuo said, "That may be so, but I still have some doubts about you. The Master replied, "In that case, the Old Barbarian has someone to rely upon.
Jiuzhuo turned to his attendant and asked, "How are my eyes? In the *Renxu* year of the *Zhizhi* era of Emperor Yuanzong (1322), he began teaching at Tianqing.
Subsequently, he moved to Kongxiang on Mount Xiong'er, Lingyan on Mount Tai, and Songshao in Luoyang.

Question: "In the merit of non-merit, is there still distinction between the biased and the correct? The Master said: "The biased and the correct are clearly manifest. Question: "What is the bias and correctness of non-merit? The Master said:
"The stone ox is accustomed to spitting forth mist for three springs; the numinous bird does not perch in the shadowless forest.
Question: "What is the direct pointing to the human mind? The Master said: "The tongue is in the mouth. Question: "What is [the direct pointing]? The Master said: "The tongue is in the mouth."
"Seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. The Master said, "Though gold dust is precious, if it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'do not seek the standard within words'? The Master said, "How has the fire of the Way ever burned my mouth? [The monk] asked, "What is 'clarifying the source beyond phrases'? The Master then struck him.
In the summer of the Gengchen year of Emperor Shun’s reign, he contracted an illness. He then said to his disciples, "This illness..."
"It may be done. I shall certainly go; you must urgently prepare the stupa. On the twelfth day of the fifth month, the stupa was largely completed.
The Master gathered the assembly and took his leave of this world, writing a verse that said: "Coming, it was originally still; departing, it is likewise perfect and complete.
The void performs a dance, wandering freely as it pleases. He then passed away lying on his right side.

Chan Master Rong of Lingyan on Mount Tai in Taian first attained realization while investigating the koan "All Dharmas Return to One. However, he could not yet resolve his doubts regarding the statement:
"When the lion roars once, both grandfather and grandson are exhausted. One day, he was traveling through the mountains with fellow practitioners.

He ascended Mount Rizhi Peak. By chance, he stumbled and nearly fell to his death; after a long while, he rose and revived. In a stern voice, he cried out, "Is this not the time when both grandfather and father have perished?
The ancients surely did not reach such a state. Thereupon, he went to visit Fenglong Jiu to present what he had realized.
Jiu said, "You must further know that there is a 'gate-latch' above this before you are finished. The Master gave a shout and—
He came out and, meeting with joy, sealed [the matter].
Master Ningxin of the Jin Dynasty once raised his fist and said, "All the patch-robed monks of the world use only this to kill or give life.
Whenever a monk arrived, he would strike him out; none were able to grasp its meaning. Consequently, people called him "Iron Fist."
The Hermitage Master.
Baimeochun (White Thatch Spring) Hermitage Master once associated with Sin Chokkwan (Heart Iron Fist). A monk asked, "What Dharma does the Master employ to receive people?
The Master said, "Just use cold eyes to watch the crab; see how long it will continue its sideways crawl. [The monk] said, "In that case..."
"Then there is the aspect of cold eyes and iron fists; resentment is bound up within the world. The Master said, "These patch-robed monks are all too fond of chewing on dung-worms.
This was the twenty-seventh generation under Qingyuan.
Chan Master Songting Ziyán of Wannan Temple in Nanyang Prefecture was a successor of Chan Master Caishī of Shaoshi. He was the son of the Fán family of the ancient Gōu region in Henan.

As a youth, he suffered frequently from illness; his parents, out of pity for him, permitted him to leave the household life. He paid his respects to Yúnjì at Shaolin, and at the age of eighteen, he received full ordination.

He was endowed with qualities that surpassed others in intelligence and acumen. He was extensively versed in both Buddhist and secular classics; as for poetry and prose, he was capable of them without formal study.
Whether responding in verse or composing spontaneously, his pen moved with immediate fluency. Great masters and eminent scholars all regarded him as a vessel of the Dharma.

Initially, he studied under Jiang Yuezhao, and subsequently under Xianan Rang, from whom he received instructions on the essentials of Chan and experienced a moment of awakening. Later, he studied under Chun...
Zhucai brought up what he had previously attained to test him. Zhucai said, "Do you not hear of the household with the *gǔ* poison, where no one dares to taste the water?
The Master said, "One must be able to swallow it in and spit it out before one can be said to have a good constitution. Zhucai said, "Heaven! Heaven!
This only adds to my grievances and suffering! The Master said, "I thank the Monk for his seal of approval," and he turned over the *Bǎojìng sānmèi* (The Jewel Mirror Samādhi) repeatedly.
Zhengbian, having had his doubts and obstacles completely dispelled, said, "The burdening of the Great Dharma rests entirely upon your person. He then transmitted to him both the robe and the Dharma.
There were verses [of praise] that said: "A lion cub atop the Five Milk Peaks; illuminating the past and shining upon the future, he transcends the multitude.

At that time, the Wan'an Monastery in Nanyang Prefecture was vacant, and they invited the Master to preside over it. After three years, during the Jiyou year of the Hongwu era of Emperor Ming, the Master... [presided].
Shaolin. Tilling the fields to provide for the assembly, he spoke in verse: "Returning home after the chaos, I personally tend the furrows;

Who can discuss this life of toil and hardship? By day, I pick up clods of earth to drive away mountain birds; By night, I sit in my thatched hut to chase off wild pigs. My heart breaks as the autumn wind frequently strikes the watch-tower;
My eyes gaze at the night moon as if my soul were melting away. Only recently have I come to know the bitterness of the farmer; Even a single meal..."
Reflecting on the kindness of the donor. A monk asked, "Dizang plowed the fields to earn his rice; is this the same as or different from the Master?

The Master said, "Though we lean upon the same railing, we view the mountain colors differently. The monk asked, "When Baizhang opened the fields and spoke of the Dharma, he simply extended both hands.
What was the meaning of this? The Master said, "Although there were no words, the sound was like thunder. The monk asked, "Master..."
"Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, "By day he picks up a stone to drive away the mountain birds; by night he sits in his hut to send off the wild boar.
[The student] asked, "Yantou studied under Dongshan but was not accepted by Dongshan; he succeeded Deshan but was not accepted by Deshan either. What excellence did Yantou possess?
The Master said, "If he had been accepted by those two masters, he would have failed them both. [The student] said, "He said, 'Dongshan..."
Shan Hao said, “The Buddha is simply without radiance. [The monk asked,] “But how is this so? The Master said, “It would ruin an entire shipload of people.
A monk asked, “When the Abbot ascends the seat, why does Qin Feng Huai not come to listen to the Dharma? The Master said, “Do you see Qin Feng Huai?
If you, O *dārali*, see him, then you have a share in hearing him preach the Dharma. A monk asked, “When Bodhidharma sat facing the wall...”
"What? the Master said. "Already you are possessed by demons. [The monk] asked, "How can one completely eradicate them? The Master said: "Twist the hemp rope backward to bind the little ghosts.

In the winter of the Gengshen year, Emperor Zhou Wang Jing commanded the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma for the sake of the deceased merits of the late Empress Dowager Cixiao, the mother of the state.
He bestowed upon him a *saṃghāṭī* robe to honor his extraordinary excellence. Later...
Having reached the age of seventy, he retired to live in seclusion and passed away there.
Chan Master Zhenren of Zhuan’an, who had ascended Mount Songshan, was a native of the Wang family of Nanyang in Dengzhou.

He ascended the hall and, citing Fandeng Qin’s opening of the Dharma hall, said: "Fandeng, I originally intended to dwell in mountain caves to hide my talents and pass the time in simplicity; however, due to circumstances..."
"The former master has a kōan that remains unresolved; come forth and let us settle it. A monk suddenly asked, "What is the unresolved kōan of the former master?
Yantong immediately struck him, saying, "If the patriarch fails to resolve it, the calamity reaches his descendants.
The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? Yantong said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity reaches you. Tiantong Jue said: "If this monk..."
"This fellow! As soon as he comes out, I shall overturn his meditation seat.

Not only will he have a way for himself to emerge, but he will also avoid seeing that his ancestors have left a case unresolved, thereby sparing his descendants from the calamity. The Master said, "I am not like this.
If today someone were to ask, 'What is the unresolved case? I would take up my staff and strike them, saying: 'A lion bites.'"
People are like Han’s hound chasing after clods of earth.
Chan Master Foyan Ren ascended the hall and said: "The heroic recognize the heroic; the eminent delight in the eminent.

This mountain monk is neither of these two, and thus it has been difficult to form a friendship in my life. Only this seven-foot rattan cane understands me, cherishing me and finding joy in me. Last night, suddenly—"
They turned against me, intending to break my waist. "Brothers," you ask why he acted thus.
It was because I had disclosed the very marrow of Bodhidharma’s heart to everyone. This morning he again sought repentance;
it was precisely because his love for me was so deep that he mistakenly revealed this secret instruction. Certainly no one else could have discerned it, nor could even this mountain monk.
If you wish to snap it as well, will this not result in two separate pieces? Then, planting his staff upright, he said:
"As before, both are made joyful; let idle disputes be cast aside."
Master Chan of Dengfeng Huayan ascended the hall and said: "To speak it is not as good as to practice it; to practice it is not as good as to forget the framework.
How can one attain the forgetting of the framework? Leaning on his staff, he said: "White clouds arrive unbidden at the green ridges;
the green waters have no mind to play with the blue moon. He then descended from the seat.

In ancient times, Master Cai Yuanchen held a small informal lecture (*xiaochan*). He said, "Tonight, I will not answer questions. A monk stepped forward. The Master said, "For a fellow who goes out seeking a beating, when will it ever end?
The monk asked, "Why do you not simply strike me with the staff? The Master replied, "The thief is the petty person," and he took up his staff.
He then returned to his quarters.
Zen Master Deng of Xianzhou’s Bear Ear Mountain ascended the hall and said: "Dharma’s single sandal is unknown to whom it has been stolen.
Yet this story still circulates widely; do not say there is nothing to rely upon. Alas! If one were to proceed entirely in this manner..."
"Where would you go? Today, I have not the slightest bit of interest in this. He then threw down a shoe and said, "Is this worth even a fraction [of the truth]?
He laughed to himself and said, "I simply want these words to circulate widely. He then descended from his seat.

Zen Master Xingxi Ziding of Xiong’er Mountain in Shan Prefecture was a dharma successor of Chan Master Tianqing Rang. He was the son of Ma of Yan County; at the age of seven, he paid respects to Gurong and received the tonsure.

When Gurong passed away, he went to study under Xianan, where the Master served as the Librarian (Zangshi). While reporting on matters there, [he attained realization] upon hearing the Master’s words.
He attained sudden and great enlightenment. The Master’s interrogations and discernments were as formidable as the frost of autumn or the scorching sun;
his spontaneous responses to circumstances were like a pearl rolling upon a platter. One day, manifesting illness, he said to his disciples:
"My worldly ties have come to an end, and the time for my passing has arrived. You all must not harbor worldly attachments. Listen as I deliver the final word. Having spoken, he passed away.
He then went to his pillow and passed away with serene composure.
Later, Zen Master Shundong of Linggu Monastery in Jinling ascended the hall and said:

"Recently, I was honored by an imperial decree stating that the four characters 'Purify the Mind and Cleanse the Self' constitute the transmission of the Buddha’s mind-seal and are the bright pearl that anchors the sea. I have specifically brought this forth."

It is bestowed universally upon the great assembly. You must know that the mind of Heaven is unfathomable; as the mountains grow ever higher, the ocean grows ever deeper. The words of the Sage are inexhaustible;
as Heaven spreads its vast canopy and Earth provides its vast support. Do you all understand? Is it not that one remains unstained by the dust of the world?
Is it not that you do not crave the flavor of the Dharma? Is it not that you do not drink the wine of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and do not sit upon the bed of nirvāṇa?
If you understand it in this way, it is not that what is wrong is not wrong; rather, what is right is not right. Today, I, this mountain monk, dare not keep [this truth] hidden for long.
"For the sake of all people, I shall now point directly outward. He then took up his staff, struck it once on the ground, and said:

"A wooden man dances out before the Dharma Hall; let the white snow fly through the blazing heavens as it pleases. The Master resided at Xuefeng in Fuzhou during the Renwu year of the Ming Yongle era.
In the Jiachen year of the Hongxi era, he was appointed by imperial decree to reside at Linggu in Jinling. He passed away at the beginning of the Xuande era. [He] possessed...
His recorded sayings (*yulu*), titled *The Samādhi of the Ancient Mirror*, circulates in the world.
Zen Master Kōgyoku Ei was asked by a monk: "What is it like when you suddenly encounter a tiger?

The Master said: "Do you see the Great Void and the Small Void? The monk let out a tiger’s roar. The Master said: "You beast! Why are you leaping about? [The monk asked: "How can one attain [liberation]?"
He did not leap away. The Master said, "Under the gate of Empty Apricot, there are no weak generals.
Chan Master Guangping Shishi was asked by a monk, "Among the nine tribes and eighteen caves, who is it that can transform and guide them?"
The Master said, "The staff. [The monk] said, "It does not understand the local dialect. The Master said, "Only this child is clever.
[The monk] said, "I venture to ask the Master to lend it to me to serve as a guide; how about that? The Master then struck him and said, "How would it ever deign to act as a favor for others?"
Chan Master Taoning Shou of Dadu, successor to Chan Master Kongxiang Gui, ascended the hall and said: "The business of the donkey is not yet finished, and the business of the horse has arrived.
Across this vast, boundless earth, who is there to let go of their heart? A-ha-ha! Return! From the rootless tree, a pure breeze arises—no waiting required."
When spring returns, the flowers bloom of themselves.
Master Taining Cai ascended the hall and said: "In my life, this mountain monk has been plagued by impatience; it brought me illness.
