What are the mandarin ducks? The Master said, "A pair flutters down to the ground, flying all alone like this. The monk asked, "What is the golden needle? The Master said: [He remained silent.]

From the outset, he did not cross over [the river]. He asked, "What is the matter with the story of the Soul Departing from the Corpse? The Master said, "The moon is pale; the flowers shift their shadows.

He asked, "I wonder, is this the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*) or the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*)? The Master said, "The wind stirs; the water forms waves. He asked, "Ultimately, is it one, or is it two?
The Master said, "Form and shadow need not be manifested; thus one escapes the den of the fox. He said, "Escaped!"
"How will it be hereafter? The Master said, "Swiftly, as the ritual command. In the winter of the Dingchou year, he arrived at Mount Ying;

his physical condition was frail and emaciated, and the hearts of the assembly were filled with anxiety. In the midst of this silence, someone asked, "How is the Master's health? The Master snapped his fingers once.
Mì said, "The final word must also be entrusted. The Master asked, "Tell me, am I alive or dead? He then smiled and passed away.
He had sat in meditation for thirty-seven summer retreats and lived to the age of fifty-three. His remains were brought back to Boshan, where a stupa was erected on the western slope of Lotus Peak.

Among his writings are the *Zhideng lu* (Record of Selected Lamps), the *Chuixiang tang shiwen shu* (Poetry, Prose, and Letters from the Incense-Burning Hall), and the *Fuyu lu* (Record of Further Sayings).
A Brief Account. Master Taodu Songru Daomi of Huai’an Prefecture was the son of the Tang family of Sizhou. At the age of fourteen, he entered the monastic order under Master Jinghui.

Initially, he attended lecture halls and studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "Though one may attain great learning, it does not constitute the fruit of sainthood," [he attained realization].

He then abandoned them. He first visited Shouchang, and subsequently visited Boshan Lai. Boshan’s teaching style was solemn and rigorous; the Master regarded him as his "Dead Heart" (a teacher who brings one to the brink of death).
One day, while gathering tea with the assembly, white clouds suddenly rose from the bottom of a mountain stream. Upon seeing this, the Master attained realization.
Huineng returned and presented the verse to Huairang. Huairang said, "Set that aside for a moment.
But when the single breath no longer comes, where will you establish yourself and find your life? The Master replied, "It is not within the realm of what can be communicated to you, O Monk.
Huairang asked, "Is this not precisely where you establish yourself and find your life? The Master said, "Dao Mi would never entertain such a view. Huairang said, "Excellent!"
He was struck with thirty blows of the staff. Following this, he came to receive his name and the precepts, and was further sealed with a verse.

Thereupon, he took his leave and went to Mount Yuzhou, where he lived for several years in a thatched hut. Only then did he begin to propagate the Dharma at Tandu in Huai'an. Subsequently, he resided at Nengren Temple in Andong.
At Yunlong in Xuzhou, as well as at places such as Qingfeng Puti and Faqi, he ascended the hall and said:
"O worthy ones, the Buddhas of the past have already entered nirvana; you should not dwell upon them with longing remembrance. As for the Buddhas of the future..."
"It has not yet appeared in the world. You must not harbor deluded thoughts; it is precisely this very day. Furthermore, what is it like?
A slender shadow reflects alone upon the spring water; you must pity me, and I must pity you. Ascending the hall, he said: "One-nine, two-nine:
when we meet, we do not take our hands out. Three-nine, four-nine: the ice blocks roll along the Yellow River. Frozen, they snap the waist of Mount Yunlong. Kui..."
Atop the mountain pagoda, he stretches his neck, intending to go and see it all together; yet, alas, the weather is cold. Standing for a long time, he ascends the hall.
Master Shouchang’s bottom was a stone block; Master Boshan’s predecessor saw it as a single tree.
Brother Master Yingshan and Brother Master Jingshan—alike they have their mouths hanging over their noses. As for this old monk, he beholds the white clouds.
"Hmm. He looked to his left and right and said, "Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bodhisattva Sūradatta, Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, Bodhisattva Viśiṣṭacāritra, and Bodhisattva Vyūharāja.
He let out a shout and said, "Stop! Stop! What the old monk sees, you do not know;
what you see, the old monk does not know. Suddenly rising from his seat, he said, "The Samādhi of the Wisdom Torch, Pure Light."
"Clarifying Samādhi. [The Master] struck the whisk repeatedly and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Yesterday there was snow; today it has melted.
Look closely with eyes wide open; do not misunderstand this! He nodded repeatedly and said, "Śākyamuni’s mouth is not narrow; Maitreya’s belly is not small.
If you wish to penetrate from top to bottom, you must also have a full stomach. After a long silence, he said, "Call for the bell!"
Making a Jar. Entering the hall, the Master looked around left and right and said, "There are guests from Jiangnan among those seated here;
why must one sing of the *zhègū* [partridge] before the wine? A monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I am not at all ashamed.
The Master struck him with a staff and said, "Seven blows for thirteen. The monk said, "That was unnecessary. The Master said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Once again—
As soon as the monk came out and prostrated, the Master said, "I am afraid you will rot. The monk replied, "Namo Buddha. Namo Dharma. The Master said, "What a pity!
The monk said, "Thank you for your repeated kindness, Preceptor. The Master looked at his attendant monk and said, "The old monk’s three-inch tongue is extremely tight.
[Later,] when he ascended the hall, Linji held up his fist; Deshan performed a dance; Guishan prostrated; and Fayan praised the prostration. Only...
There was the ancient master Dongshan, who spoke repeatedly: "All you brothers, you are all alike—just like those who, having eaten their fill, play with their chopsticks.
These four fellows, even here, simply go back to their respective quarters. Suddenly, he picked up his staff and said:
The host was a man of two-thousand-stone rank. His tent shed consisted of only two or three bays. As he saw him off, he repeatedly gestured with empty, weary movements.
After a long while, Zuo struck his staff once and said, "One must not say that this old monk is the thirty-third generation of the Dongshan lineage. He then ascended the hall for formal instruction.
A monk asked, "Stonehead said, 'The large is large, the small is small; neither can be grasped. When the thirtieth day arrives, how can one ultimately attain liberation?
The Master said, "Three days before, five days after. The monk said, "Singing out an impartial melody in the open, hearing and seeing are clear with nothing hidden.
The Master said, "The mountain remains as it was high; the water remains as it was deep."
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then the Buddha-sun increases in brilliance and the wind of the Way fans far and wide. The Master said, "What are you doing with these few leftovers?
[The monk] said, "Venerable Sir, listen carefully, listen carefully. The Master struck him with a staff and said, "These three hundred and fifty blows were not in vain.
He then said, "Three days before, five days after—the mountain remains as it was high, the water remains as it was deep. What are you looking for in these few [remnants]?"
"What about what remains? He then spoke in a loud voice: "Three hundred, five hundred—not in vain. He looked to his left and right and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The jade countenance is not revealed; its nobility is natural. Before the precious seal is applied, its brilliance is fully manifest.
Upon the ground where yin and yang do not reach, auspicious grasses display their luster. In the mountains where a cry finds no echo, pure sounds pervade the earth. Arriving..."
In this very place, it is indeed a fine occasion. But how can one take it up? Listen! After a long silence, he said:
"The fragrant pouch is smashed to pieces, perfuming the great kingdom; the celestial cavity is cleared away, letting the true wind pass through.

On a spring day, he ascended the hall and said: "The time has come for the withered tree and the cold cliff; the spring breeze blows up the ashes from the ritual tubes. The stone man claps his hands and laughs aloud—do not..."
Recognizing the Spring Ox as a Mound of Earth. Entering the Hall: Look at this land of Zhendan!
Dongshan was brought down by three catties of hemp; Zhaozhou was toppled by a seven-catty robe;
Yunmen was crushed by a dried piece of dung; Lingyun was changed by peach blossoms; and Xuansha was changed by his own toes. Tian...
The dragon-robed one has exchanged his fingers. *Du du!* Dark clouds arise from the bottom of the great ocean; turning the head, the sun first rises over the western mountains.
After a long silence, he performs a woman’s bow and says: *Imperial Decree:* Ascending the hall on New Year’s Eve:

"To speak of it is not as good as to practice it"—rare are those who pierce their ears. "To practice it is not as good as to speak of it"—often seen are those who mark the boat's wake. Practice and speech...
Neither arrives. A post station every ten *li*, where fallen flowers scent the wine shops; a pavilion every five *li*, where wild moonlight, field bridges, and mist mingle.
He picks up his staff and says: "Is this the sound of a carriage? Is it the sound of wind or fire? Is it the sound of water? Or is it the sound of gongs and drums?"
[The Master] made a striking sound with his staff and said, "What place is this?

A monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "If it were not for this night, how could there be anyone who finds even a moment's leisure? The Master said, "That too is just something from the left side of Dongshan."
He then looked to his left and right and said, "The man who pierces his ears; the man who marks the boat. He struck his staff once and said, "How can one find a moment of leisure?
A monk asked, "What is 'the partial within the central'? The Master said, "At midnight, the sun is at its zenith. The monk asked, "What is 'the central within the partial'?
The Master said, "The *nāga* is in meditative absorption amidst the bustling marketplace. The monk asked, "What is 'coming from the central'? The Master said—
[The student] asked: "A wooden horse dances on the spring terrace. [The student] asked: "What is 'arriving within the simultaneous'? The Master said:

"A stone woman wanders through an ancient temple. [The student] asked: "What is 'reaching within the simultaneous'? The Master said: "A footless person can build it. [The student] asked: "Who provides the witness?
The Master said: "A tongueless person. [The student] asked: "What are the words witnessed by the tongueless person? The Master said: "Who dares to speak them?"
Zhuo asked, "Regarding the five ranks of the orthodox and the biased, is there anything further beyond them? The Master replied, "The Daoist wears his crown even at the age of seventy.
During this exchange, both responses were imbued with the intent of parting. He then took the road to Lian-shui and ascended Qingfeng Peak.
The practice for the summer retreat began. Returning to rest at Puti (Bodhi), on the fifth day of the third month in the Wuxu year of the Shunzhi era, he ceased taking food.
He offered repeated and earnest instructions and wrote a verse containing such phrases as "a spark of stone and a flash of lightning" and "thorns in a level field.

On the eleventh day, having bathed and sat upright, he passed away. He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-eight years since his ordination. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Puti Monastery.
To the right [of this entry]:
Chan Master Zongbao Daodu of Changqing in Fuzhou, a native of the Lu clan of Guangzhou. Having left his home region at the age of seven, he went to visit Boshan Yuanlai.
Upon first meeting him, Yuanlai recognized his potential. One day, Daodu presented a verse, saying: "In my haste to reach my destination, I did not realize it was dawn; the more I sought..."

The more it turns, the more remote it becomes; meeting him is not encountering that [usual] person. As soon as one is, one is inverted: ants pull a great millstone, while the stone man claps his hands and laughs.
There is another vital mechanism that does not fall into the musical scales of *gong* and *shang*. Come, and you shall enter deeply into the inner sanctum.
Later, he opened the Dharma at Luofu in Guangzhou, Changqing in Min, and Haitang in Yue.
A monk asked, "All Buddhas emerge from this sutra; what is this sutra? The Master let out a thunderous shout.
Addressing the assembly, he cited the Sixth Patriarch’s dialogue on the wind and the banner, offering this verse: "It is not the wind, nor is it the banner; The mountain pass stands firm."
Traveling on the road is difficult. The fool merely preoccupies himself with the journey ahead; who considers that his entire being is right here?
Addressing the assembly, he raised the story of Gaofeng’s “no dream, no thought” and offered this verse: “No dream, no thought—is the master present?
Even if you follow along, what can you do? Whose gate does not have the bright moon? Yet alas, those traveling at night are even more numerous. Master Tong.
Zhennru entered the Way at the age of sixty and passed away at Haichuang Temple.
Chan Master Doyan of Dufeng and Zhushan in Jinling was a native of Dazhu County in Xichuan. His clan name was Shen.

Having donned the monastic robes since his youth, he traveled south to visit various lecture halls. One day, while traveling to Jingkou, he ascended Lingyun Pavilion; suddenly, body and mind... [the world]... became still.
The entire temple grounds suddenly became empty. He then hurried down to the White City (Bai-xia) to visit Master Bolun Lai at Tianjie Monastery.
He asked, "Master, having left Boshan to come to the White City, what is your purpose for visiting?

Lai said, "Today I have specifically come to offer incense and prayers for my late father. The Master asked, "Is there anything further beyond this? Lai said, "There is. The Master asked, "What is it?"
This was a matter of transcending [the mundane]. Dayu said, "Please sit and drink tea. Thereupon, he appointed him to the second seat.

When he led the assembly into the room, his responses to the immediate situation were perfectly in accord with the fundamental tenets. Dayu was exceedingly pleased and once remarked, "A single branch of Boshan has grown out askance;
its secret lies within you. From then on, he concealed his traces while receiving the Master's grace for four years, until he opened the Jetavana Grove of Pure Land.

Another five years passed while he was at Chushang. He then resided at Dufeng. Upon entering the monastery, he felt as though it were his old home. Thereupon, the Master made plans for his final years.
He once posted three questions to test those who came after him. The first said: "It is not the mind, not the Buddha, and not an object;
what, then, is it ultimately? The second said: "This sutra is profound, solid, and remote; no one is able to..."
"Arrived! Now tell me: what do you call this sutra? He spoke three times: "The path to the solitary peak is perilous; the orders at the frontier post are strict.
Those who wish to arrive, try first to borrow a pass. On the day of his passing, he gathered the assembly to offer his final instructions. At noon, after completing his ritual bath, he passed away.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Longshan, the mountain where he resided.
Chanzhi Master Zhou of Huilong on the ancient waterway in Jianning Prefecture was the son of Zheng from Jinjiang, Quanzhou. He was born in the year Wanyili (1605).
Having lost his father in childhood, he was renowned for his filial piety toward his mother. Upon her passing, he left home and took up residence at Chengtian Temple.
While reading the *Record of Shouchang*, I reached the point where he asked a monk, "When you have died and been cremated, what is your original surname?

At this, I felt doubt and went to visit Boshan. Boshan shaved my head and conferred the full precepts upon me. I sat in meditation without speaking for three months, my eyes never closing in the hall, as my investigation became increasingly earnest.
Just then, Yu Jisheng arrived; our conversation was in accord, and he invited the Master to enter a period of retreat behind closed doors.
Quánlíng washed his face one day and experienced a sudden awakening. He said to himself, "In a place where there was nothing I could do, I have grasped the essential point.
Later, when Bóshān preached the Dharma at Tiānjiè Monastery, the Master went up to the hall and asked, "Before the bell has tolled and before the drum has sounded, is there still any Buddha-dharma?
Bóshān replied, "A wooden man blows into the bottom of a well. The Master said, "A stone woman by the stream..."
Wu said, "Mount San, as for that single phrase 'carrying the origin within speech,' how would you express it? The Master replied, "Midnight is perfectly bright;
at dawn, nothing is revealed. Mount San then descended from his seat. Upon returning to Boshan, Mount San handed him the *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) and said:

"You must be careful not to fail this old monk. The Master then closed his retreat again. The following year, he hurried to the news of Bo Shan’s passing and entered Min Province to preside over the Dharma at Hui Long.
He later went into seclusion at Dai Yun Mountain in his home village. In the year Bingzi, Lin Zongbo Jizhong invited him to establish the retreat season at Cheng Tian.
In Dingchou, he succeeded to the seat at Xue Feng and held the winter retreat at Chang Qing. In Wuyin, he returned to Hui Long. In Jimao—
Residing at Boshan, in the year of Xinsi, he established wooden spirit tablets for his parents at Anjian Temple.

Regarding the location where he stayed, he did not follow the custom of requesting formal opening ceremonies (*kāntáng*), but only gave public instructions (*shìzhòng*). Thus, he had this instruction to give: "This old monk does not ascend the hall because there is no Dharma to preach.
My nature does not conform to human sentiment; I am just like an iron stake, consistently manifesting a state of simple-mindedness, leaving it to others [to judge]."
The Way is decayed and ruined. Although one is called a *zhuchi* (abbot), it is truly a matter of having no tongue in one's mouth;

this is the bare truth. To the assembly: When the flower was held up for the assembly, there were mouths that could not open; when the arm was severed and returned, there was no Dharma to be obtained.

The forty-seven patriarchs did nothing but call out toward the empty sky; the descendants through the generations have all been nothing more than digging in the earth to seek heaven. I, this old monk—
In those days, not knowing good from evil, I mistakenly joined the community of Boshan and was deceived by him with fervor; even now, my grievance remains unredressed.
Although I have received the leadership and reside as abbot, I keep my mouth shut in three ways—not out of a desire to neglect you all, but for fear of bringing disgrace upon the Dharma-gate.
Tell me, Great Assembly: Is staying in this monastery in such a manner for the sake of others, or is it not? No.
Seeing the Path: "Crying until the blood flows is of no use; it is better to keep one's mouth shut and pass through the remainder of spring. Addressing the assembly:
"Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep—this is a true confession of guilt. Morning after morning, one rises together with him—a deathbed admission personally summoned.
Rising and sitting, they are always in each other’s company; even an axe could not cleave them apart. They are like a form and its shadow; they cannot be separated. If you wish to know the Buddha..."
"As for where he went, I do not yet dare grant you an answer. It is simply this sound of his voice; one must by all means avoid mistaking it.
Brothers, do you recognize Great Master Fu? You only know that opening the mouth is easy; you do not consider how long the tongue is. A monk asked, "Zhenjue said:
'When the stone egg has burst and the tamarisk branches have swept the ground, I shall return. Now that you, Master, have succeeded to the seat, is this not his return?"
"Are you coming? The Master said, "To charge another with a crime and then impose that very crime upon them. The monk said, "In that case, the case is closed according to the facts.
The Master said, "I accept the indictment in full. While the Master was ill, a monk asked, "What illness does the Master have? The Master said:
[The student] said, "There are illnesses that acupuncture cannot cure. The Master said, "If that is so, then the divine physician must fold his hands in impotence.
[The student] said, "One must know that there is one who is not ill. [The student] asked, "What is this one who is not ill? The Master took up his *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) and struck him.

This is the Dharma-talk of Prince Huai, a close relative of the King of Jingzhou. In the Gate of the Patriarchs, there are no words or phrases; truly, there is not a single dharma to give to others. It is simply intended for people...
It is simply a matter of self-investigation and self-awakening, self-realization and self-cultivation, to see one’s own original face;
there is no other method. For this original face is not adorned by sages and worthies, nor is it made ugly by the common and the ignorant.
It is the same for kings and dukes as for scholars and commoners; scholars and commoners are equal to all living beings. All who possess sentience share this same fundamental substance.
There is no duality. It is simply that through delusion one fails to participate [in this reality], obscuring the brilliant light of one’s own self; thus one is called a "sentient being.
If one investigates until a single clarity arises—like the sky universally covering all, or like the earth universally supporting all—then one is called a Buddha or a Patriarch.

Buddhas and Patriarchs and sentient beings differ only between delusion and awakening; whether one investigates or does not investigate, there is a distinction as vast as that between heaven and earth. —Bodhidharma.
Coming from the West, he pointed directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one’s nature, one becomes a Buddha. A person of keen intelligence understands upon a single glance;
there are no further complications. Thus, Baozhi said: "If you wish to know the true essence of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, and speech."
In this matter, there is no doubt. To speak of "seeing one's nature" or "attaining Buddhahood" is already superfluous talk.

For those who have not yet realized it, you must rouse your spirit with fierce intensity. Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, look and see: who sees? Who hears? Who is it that perceives and knows?
Who is it that puts on clothes and partakes of meals? Who is it that rises, sits, and moves about? Look until you reach a point where there is nothing left to look at; then, of itself—
He attained great enlightenment, penetrating to the very bottom with complete clarity. The clouds of delusion were dispersed, and the sun of wisdom rose high.

Only then did he realize that all sentient beings in the great earth have always been of one body; that the myriad phenomena of the forest and the heavens share a single thread and are interconnected.

Since there is no distinction between the insentient and the sentient, how could there be any difference between the noble and the base, or the ordinary and the sage? The Master’s nature was formed of upright integrity, and toward his disciples...
He was one of supreme spirit; there were no words of acquiescence or refusal. Thus, he felt no shame before his own towering, precipitous integrity.

In the year Yiwu of the Shunzhi era, he manifested a slight illness, yet he attended to his affairs as usual. On the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month, at the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), he sat cross-legged and passed away.
His lifespan was seventy-one years; his *dharma*-age was thirty-three. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Fengshan in Jianyang.
Chan Master Xuejian Dao of Boshan in Guangxin Prefecture was the son of the Gong family of Jianyang. From his youth, his spiritual faculties were exceptionally sharp and extraordinary.

From childhood, he abstained from meat and pungent roots. At seventeen, he experienced a profound resonance upon hearing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and subsequently went to Zhiti Temple to shave his head and receive the precepts.
At twenty-six, he followed Master Zhang through Fengshan, Luoshan, and Xiansha; after barely two years, he came to realize the matter of his own fundamental self.
He then arrived in Zhejiang. He studied under Zhenji for many years, and subsequently visited Boshan. Boshan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the kiln.
Boshan said, "The heavens cannot cover it and the earth cannot support it; why then are you buried in a kiln? The Master said:
"This morning I am truly glad to have met you, Master," [the student] said. The Master asked, "What have you been doing lately? The student replied, "I have been watching where it all returns.
The Master asked, "Where is that which is watching right now? The student replied, "The reaching hand is already within the withdrawing hand."
Mountan said, "Where did you learn such empty talk? The Master replied, "I truly do not dare to deceive myself.

Later, at Shao-an, upon hearing a rooster flap its wings and crow loudly, he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "The incense of the cypress has burned down until the flames are nearly spent;
Suddenly, the neighbor’s rooster lets out a single cry. In years past, I mistakenly mistook it for a donkey peering into a well; Only today have I come to know."
"Looking down a well at a donkey; running to present it to the mountain; the mountain nods its head. In the *Pingxi* year of the Shunzhi era, he opened the Dharma at Yingshan.
In the *Bingshen* year, he succeeded to the seat at Boshan. Gaquan Puning occasionally invited him to ascend the hall. [The verse says: "On the banks of the water, at the foot of the mountain."
In this place there are peach blossoms; in this place there are cultivated bamboos. The red is red and the green is green;
their common nature emerges spontaneously from the natural world. The straight is straight and the curved is curved; those who claim to have found their way back merely speak of Xulingyun in vain.

Those who skillfully employ [these things] need not boast of their "abundant blessings. To the ultimate extent, the subtle and winding sentiments within them are all like drawing a snake and then adding extra feet. No.
Adding legs. Six times six—who says it is thirty-six? Taking the head for the tail and the tail for the head; when hungry, one eats rice; when weary, one goes to bed.
*Du!* Small Assembly Sermon: Today is the fifth day of the ninth month. The weather is half-sunny and half-rainy.
This is the most excellent of seasonal conditions, witnessed by the ears and seen by the eyes of the entire assembly. But tell me: what is it that sees and hears?
The great beast of the Southern Mountain bites and kills the heavy-fanged tiger; the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms all dance together.
Assembly, let us set aside for a moment the tiger biting the great beast. Why do the myriad phenomena dance? Have you not heard it said:

"The sweet melon is sweet to its very stem; the bitter gourd is bitter to its very root"? In the spring of the Jiyou year of the Kangxi era, I entrusted the affairs of the monastery to the Seat-Holder, Ming...

On the twentieth day of the sixth month of that year, he manifested his passing. As he was approaching death, Huanglong Cen pressed against the Master’s body and asked, "When the roof collapses and cannot shield one from wind and rain, what then?
The Master replied, "When heaven and earth turn upside down, by whom else can it be done?
Huanglong said, "If so, then the entire assembly shall have cause to look up to you. The Master folded his hands and passed away. He was seventy-nine years old; sixty-two years since his ordination.
The reliquary stupa was enshrined on the southern slope of Lotus Peak at the home mountain.
The layman Yu Dacheng, whose courtesy name was Jisheng and who hailed from Tongcheng, came to visit Boshan and stayed within the Dharma Hall.

He raised his head and beheld a couplet. Upon reaching the phrase, "Taking a single step in secret movement," he attained realization. From then on, his conviction was firm and beyond doubt. He sent a letter stating:
"Since meeting you, O Master, I have realized that the various poisons within my breast have been completely washed away by a small portion of *amṛta* (nectar).
Upon returning, I have relegated my brush and inkstone to the dragon of the Yellow Emperor [the books], and my volumes of scripture to my piglets and calves. Thus, in the patriarchal hall—
Externally, not a single thing is carried; alone, one sits and cuts off the ten directions. To secretly shift a single step is to have a rough knowledge of practicing according to the teaching.
Yet, while Chang’an is most bustling, my country is tranquil. When I untied my official ribbons and returned last winter, I embarked upon a frozen boat and made a vow of silence for eighty days.
As it is said, "Even the Buddha has no recourse"—this is truly so, truly so. One day, with him...

Two fellow practitioners were disputing over a public case (kōan), each refusing to yield to the other. One said, "I am most fond of Changqing’s saying: 'Only when one consents for oneself does one become intimate [with the Way].
The other practitioner said, "Only when one does *not* consent does one become intimate. Upon hearing this, the Layman [Liu] spat out his tongue.
Xueguai Yin asked, "What is the purpose of closing the door to live one's life? The Layman replied, "To sell a wheelbarrow drill."
Question: "What is the use of mending a net and setting a wind-catcher? The Master said: "To add another black scoop-net.
Master Xinglang Xiong of Yefu in Lujiang was a native of the Lin family of Longxi in Min. His family lineage had long been distinguished by high official rank.

In his youth, the Master heard the recitation of a verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and resolved to leave the dust of the world. He frequently visited senior masters to seek their instruction on the essential points of Chan practice.

Chan Master Tanzhi of Linggu in Jinling went to visit the Patriarch Xiaoyan Bao. He asked, "The ancients said, 'Break the mirror and we shall meet.
Now that the mirror has been broken, where do we meet? Bao replied, "It would put people to shame."
Upon these words, the Master suddenly attained realization; he forgot to perform his prostrations and departed dancing. He served [his teacher] diligently for several years.

The Treasure was entrusted to him with this verse: "The first opportunity of the smile and the plucking of the flower— The transmission through eight times eight remains unknown as either right or wrong.
Now, I entrust these non-dharmas of the ancestors To you, O worthy one; take up the burden and return."

Chan Master Guangtong of Rui Peak on Mount Wutai attended the Patriarch Xiaoyan Bao for a long time. When their spiritual faculties were in accord within the master’s room, he was entrusted with a verse which said:
"When a single thought does not arise, all calculations cease; When myriad functions are brought to rest, the ten directions are empty.
With realms empty and calculations ceased, the bubble clears upon the sea; All Buddhas and sentient beings appear as reflections therein. Later, he resided at Mount Wutai. [From] Shouchang Jing...
A student asked, "I still have doubts regarding the karmic conditions and teachings of the ancient worthies; I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master said, "Try bringing them forward and see. [The student] cited the Scripture: "Master Linji said, 'The Buddha-dharma is not much; after all, what is it?'"
The Master said: "I told you there was not much to it; what, then, is this? The Sutra says: Xuan Sha remarked that Lingyun had not yet reached full penetration.
Where, then, was his lack of penetration? The Master said: "It seems Xuan Sha himself had not yet reached full penetration. The Sutra says:
Zhaozhou said, "As for the old woman of Mount Tai, I have thoroughly exposed her. I do not know where exactly she was exposed.
The Master said, "In fact, it was the old woman who exposed Zhaozhou. As Jing was about to step forward and ask another question, the Master said, "If you know it is such a matter, then simply stop.
Jing bowed in thanks and withdrew.
Chan Master Tianning Huan’ye Fohui of Jiaxing Prefecture was the son of the Shi family of Kuaiji. His mother dreamed that a monk stayed overnight before she conceived.
From childhood, his aspiration was to leave the household life. At the age of fourteen, he paid respects to Songgu at Tiantai to receive formal ordination.

One day during his morning recitations, when he reached the verse, "The white tuft curls like five Mount Sumerus," his body and mind suddenly fell away, and the boundaries of past and future were severed. He raised [his staff]...

He showed this to Gu (Gu). Gu was instructed to go on a pilgrimage and subsequently traveled to the capital of Yan to pay his respects to the Patriarch Xiaoyan Bao. Having stayed with him for a long time, he received the Master’s seal of approval.
Later, while presiding over the Dharma hall at Tianning Monastery in Yanshan, he ascended the seat and said: "The flute is blown and the phoenix arrives; the zither is played and the crane comes.
The alms bowl is opened and the dragon descends; the staff is carried and the tiger crouches. When causes and conditions meet, the needle and the eye fit together. O worthy ones, right now—"

"Is this waking or dreaming? Is it awakening or delusion? Is there anyone who has attained the Way? After a long silence, he said: "The sound of the bell pierces the dawn as dreams and souls multiply;

the cock crows at dusk for the guest who remains steeped in intoxication. Even if you wish to resolve birth and escape death, it will not suffice. *Oṃ muruḷin svāhā.* Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The Great Meaning of the Westward Journey is a dry piece of dung. How many [have understood it]?"

The practitioner chews on this but cannot penetrate it. At that time, I regretted my belated arrival. Otherwise, had I seized him by the chest and pushed him to the ground with a single shove, I would have ensured he could neither defecate nor urinate.
This would have spared his descendants from their endless horizontal and vertical prattle. *Ei!* A thousand peaks see the sun depart;
Spring returns to the flowers of the great earth. Willow smoke turns green beyond the gate; The traveler has not yet returned home. *Chan* (Investigate!). *Ju* (Dwelling).
For four years he served [his master]. He moved the *udumbara* jewel [to another location]. In his later years, he returned south and resided at Tianning Monastery in Jiahe.

A monk came for an audience, and the Master asked, "Where are the spirits? From which direction do the numinous saints come? The monk replied, "Jin-su (Golden Grain). The Master asked, "What are you doing there?
The monk said, "I serve as the head gardener. The Master asked, "When vegetables are being cut, do they cry out in pain? The monk made a gesture of bearing such pain. The Master—
[The monk] said, "The old monk has not even yet lowered his blade; why do you cry out? [The monk] replied, "Today I have personally seen the Master.
The Master said, "It is like the blind men feeling an elephant, each describing it from a different perspective. As for matters of benefiting others, there was nothing he did not attend to.
He lived a life of frugality and never sought favors or audiences. When he was about to pass away, he ordered his attendant monk to fetch the almanac and look at it, saying: "The second..."
"The day has come for me to depart," he said. A serving monk asked in alarm, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am about to go elsewhere.

The monk knelt and wept, entreating him, "Please remain for a short while for the sake of the assembly. The Master smiled and said, "Three days from now would also be acceptable. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away.
This was the fifth day of the eighth month in the Wuchen year of the Chongzhen era. He was ninety-one years of age. His remains were enshrined in a stupa.
The Master resided at Lanshi Hermitage to the north of the city. His "Lanshi Sayings" were circulated in the world.

Chan Master Guang of Nanming at Mount Jing in Hangzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Chong of Chexi; he was the son of the Han family of Yanguan and entered the monastic order at Xingshan Monastery.
He visited Che-xi Chong, who showed him the "No-Character" (Wu-zi) koan of Zhaozhou. One day, while traveling at Mount Jing, he picked up a scrap of paper from the ground which contained the lines:
"Only by observing can one know where it has gone; that which goes does not arrive at the destination. He was suddenly enlightened upon reading this.

When he went to see Chong and presented his realization, he received formal certification (*inka*). Later, while serving as the head of the assembly at Mount Jing, he addressed the community, saying: "Last year..."
The nostrils lack even half; last year both eyes could not be whole. This year, at thirty, my vital bones are offered to the blue sky.
My Zen has already been spoken; how will you act? Examine! Addressing the assembly: Such a marvel is wondrous and difficult to describe.
In a straight line, Gaoteng leaps up into the heavens; Śakra’s nose-ridge is struck and shattered, and the Persian...
Painfully collapsing before the Sea Gate, he addressed the assembly: "What thing comes in such a manner? The stone man dances his sleeves with smiles filling his cheeks;
the clay ox enters the sea leaving no news; the wooden horse neighs in the wind and does not return.
If it should suddenly return, the iron walls and silver mountains are all cast open. He suddenly took up his staff, drew a line, and said: "Here there is yet another layer."

"O assembly! The setting sun is like a suspended drum. Observe closely before the peaks: the radiance of the clouds intermingles with the great earth; the mountains and rivers are a single expanse of brocade.

If you interpret this as a description of external scenery, you betray your lifelong practice. If you do not interpret it as a description of external scenery, you likewise betray your lifelong practice.
Ultimately, how is it? While the snow was falling, an attendant monk pushed open the window and said, "The entire mountain is covered in snow."
The Master said, "A fellow who follows after sounds and pursues forms. The monk said, "I ask the Master to provide a single phrase apart from sound and form.
The Master said, "All over the mountain is snow. During a communal work session (*pǔqǐng*), the Master took his work tools and led the assembly to the mountain gate.

At that moment, the garden head was washing vegetables and the miller was drying towels. Pointing to the two men, the Master said to the assembly, "In the garden there is a garden head; in the mill there is a miller."
He struck his head. Then, pointing to himself, he asked, "What about the essential point? The assembly remained silent. The Master threw down his sitting mat and returned to his quarters.
On the twenty-seventh day of the second month of winter in the first year of the Taichang era (the Gengshen year), having finished his final instructions, he passed away while sitting upright.
His stupa was enshrined at Mount Jing. He was forty-five years of age and had been a monk for twenty-three years.

Chan Master Yunmen Chuan of the thirty-third generation under Nanyue, the Dharma heir of Chan Master Mingzhou Tiantong Miyun Yuanwu, was the son of the Jiang family of Yixing. His father was Xi and his mother was Pan. He was a child...
At that time, Xi sat upright as if holding something in his memory. Later, upon reading the *Platform Sutra*, he developed deep faith in the matters of the Chan school.
One day, while gathering firewood, he had an awakening upon seeing a pile of wood protruding before him. At twenty-nine, he left home to join Master Chuanzuo at Longchi.
At thirty-three, he received the tonsure. During this period, he perceived that mind and objects existed as two separate entities, and he requested further instruction from [the Master].
Fozu Sanzhuan (The Three Transmissions of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) records: When [Zhaozhou] arrived at the master’s quarters, he threw himself down and lay flat on his back.

Master [Xuefeng] became increasingly bewildered and confused, while Fozhao only continued to scold him. Zhaozhou sat and lay about restlessly; eventually, while passing by Tongguan Mountain, he stumbled and fell, whereupon he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.

He realized that the sentient and the insentient appeared with equal clarity, and not even the slightest trace of fault or affliction could be found. At that time, Fozhao was residing at Puzhao Temple in the capital of Yan.
Zhao went to visit the Master. Baizhang said, "You have been away from me for three years; do you have any new realizations?
Zhao said, "When one person rejoices, the myriad people enjoy their work. Baizhang said, "And what about you? Zhao said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
Baizhang said, "Out of consideration for your journey from afar, I grant you thirty blows. Zhao brushed his sleeves and departed. One day...
While standing in attendance, [Zhaozhou] Chuan said, "Suppose someone were to ask you a question right now; how would you respond? The Master stepped forward and held up his fist.
Chuan also raised his own fist and said, "I, this old monk, do not understand. What is the meaning of this? The Master replied, "Do not say that the Master does not understand;
even the Buddhas of the three periods of time do not understand. One day, Chuan summoned the Master to him.
[The Master] stepped forward, picked up his whisk, and said, "Is there such a thing as this anywhere else? The Master let out a thunderous shout. Xuedou Fanchan said, "A fine shout!
The Master then shouted twice in succession and returned to his place. Fanchan said, "Shout one more time and see. The Master then left the Dharma hall.
The following day, Fanchan ascended the hall and bestowed upon him the robe and whisk. One day, he summoned the Master into his room and said, "Old..."
"Last night I got up and took a walk once; the handle is now entirely in my hand. You all must support the Buddha-dharma for me.
The Master said, "If it comes to my supporting the Buddha-dharma, let him [blank]—I will give him thirty blows all at once.
Do not say that I am being clear about rewards and punishments. Ascending the hall, he said: "If you intend to practice Zen..."
To seek to escape birth and death is already a mistake. To not intend to practice Zen while seeking to escape birth and death is yet another mistake.
I dare ask you, brothers: how can one act so as not to fall into error? *Pah!* It would have been better to stop this imprisonment and let your intelligence grow.
[Ascending the hall: Zen is not found in practice; the Way does not require awakening. To understand directly and thoroughly is to transcend Buddhas and patriarchs. Suddenly—
He held up his staff and said, "Is there anyone here now who transcends the Buddhas and patriarchs?

He struck the ground with the staff and said, "Just right for three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred blows in the evening. He threw down the staff and asked, "Why is it so? Then he clapped his hands and laughed.
To let this matter pass here would be unacceptable. [He] ascends the hall and says: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to all under heaven;

when a single speck of dust arises, the great earth is gathered up. Raising his whisk, he says: "A single speck of dust has arisen. But what is the principle of the great earth being gathered up? He throws down the whisk and says:
"If you know that what falls is not something other, only then will you see that its horizontal and vertical spread is not dust."
Ascending the hall, he held up his whisk and said, "Brothers, do you see?
All the Buddhas of the past, all the Buddhas of the present, and all the Buddhas of the future gather their heads together upon the tip of Wuzu’s whisk to spin webs of conceptualization, saying:
'All that has marks is empty and false. If one sees that all marks are not marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. If you let go..."

[The Master] opened [the assembly]. "Following the teachings merely exhausts the mouth and tires the tongue. If he were to hold it fast, he would strike the meditation seat and say, "Not even a single blow is required.
Then, raising it up, he would ask, "Do you see? He threw down his whisk and descended from the seat. Because of the snow, he ascended the hall. "Yesterday was the green mountain."
This morning there was white snow; good news for all you brothers. Wild deer and travelers leave tracks at every step, yet only the horn-hanging antelope is utterly breathless.
From the beginning, hunting dogs have found it difficult to seek him out. Only by raising your eyes high can you ascend to the Dharma hall.
(He stood, striking the ground with his staff. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like a person using a marker to designate the center."
Looking east, it is west; observing south, it becomes north. Since the manifest form and the essence are thus intermingled, the mind should become confused and disordered.
He raised his staff and called out to the assembly, saying: "Do you know where Old Śākyamuni stands?
Even if you were to know exactly where Old Śākyamuni stands, do not pass beneath the gate of Yumen; a single blow will break your donkey’s waist. Do not say I did not warn you."
[He] said, "The Way. He threw down his staff, gave a shout, and descended from the seat. On the anniversary of the passing of the Patriarch [Changqing Da’an], he held up the incense and said:
"At that time, Baling established the memorial service for Master Yunmen and had three turning words.
Gaofeng, when establishing the memorial service for Venerable Xueyan, had only one word. Today, I, the monk Wu, am establishing the memorial service for the Elder Huanyou; I have not even one word."
"None. Why? He held up an incense burner and said, "Is this one phrase, or is it three phrases? He then inserted the incense and said, "When meeting people, do not mistakenly raise [your hand].
Ascending the hall, he said: "Panshan said, 'The path that leads upward is like the sound of a hot bowl. I, this old monk, say:
'The path that leads upward is to tread through and break one's straw sandals. Ascending the hall, he said: "Even so, it is not permitted. The fire of the Way..."
When has it ever burned the mouth? Not so is also not permitted. Chewing the void until it is crushed, the teeth emerge.
Neither "so" nor "not so" is permitted. The Old Man of Stone has a boneless tongue. He suddenly picks up his staff and says, "So is also permissible.
He sets it down and says, "Not so is also permissible. Again he picks up the staff and throws it down, saying, "Neither 'so' nor..."
"It is all so. You people, do you yet know where the Dragon Gate falls?
[He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall: 'The ten directions have no walls; the four sides have no gates.
Within there is a single treasure, moving freely and unhindered. [He ascended the hall and] gave a shout, saying: 'No!'"

I have stood here for too long; let us enter the hall. The fifth day of the fifth month is the Double Fifth Festival; the ninth day of the ninth month is the Double Ninth Festival. Right now, it is indeed a fine occasion.
You need not deliberate on this separately. Therefore it is said: "The Three Origins and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish;
when one attains the meaning, forgetting the words, the Way becomes easy to approach. A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena—on this Double Ninth, the ninth day."
"Chrysanthemums are fresh. Although this is so, I, the old monk, shall further add footnotes to the footnotes.

"The Three Origins and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; one must know for oneself to be half-way there. When one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach. There is no idle sentimentality here.
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena—why let your eyes grow dim? On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. *Hah!* (A shout).
"Ho! [The Master] ascended the hall. He raised the following case: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
Yunmen said, "On the water above the Eastern Mountain. Fuguo said, "Tianning does not say so. If someone asks, 'What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
I would say: 'A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. The Old Monk also does not say so. If someone asks...

"What is the place from which all Buddhas emerge? [The Master] struck him across the back with his staff. Ascending the hall, he said: "When the sky clears, the sun comes out; when it rains, the ground becomes wet.
This matter is extremely clear, yet whenever questioned, people all attempt to speculate about it. Do not speculate!

Just look at the person on the road holding an umbrella, and the person in the field wearing a bamboo hat. If you still try to speculate, you will have to study for sixty kalpas over three lifetimes. *He gave a shout.*
A shout. Entering the hall: "To speak in silence; to be silent while speaking. The Great Gate of Giving is open, without obstruction.

How can one compare this to Linji’s little lad, who with empty hands fully wields the 'white-thief' ruse? He lets out a shout. Entering the hall: A monk asks, "I, a student, am about to cross the Dragon Gate;
I beg the Master for a single reception. The Master makes a gesture of casting a hook with his whisk. The monk prepares to speak again.
The Master said: "Grasp the meaning at the hook's tip; do not mistake the fixed weight on the scale. He then continued:
"Upon entering the gate, guest and host are clearly distinguished; upon opening one's eyes, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously manifest.

If you seek understanding in the place where guest and host are clearly distinguished, you will inevitably establish names where there are no names and perceive forms where there are no forms. Thus, you will see heaven as heaven, earth as earth, mountains as mountains, and waters as waters."
Water is water; the monastic community is the monastic community; the laity are the laity; men are men; women are women; the Buddha is the Buddha; the patriarchs are the patriarchs.

There are all manner of distinctions. Yet, if one perceives them at the point where the myriad phenomena manifest as a single whole, then heaven is not heaven, earth is not earth, mountains are not mountains, water is not water, the monastic community is not the monastic community, the laity are not the laity, and men are not men.
The man is not the man; the woman is not the woman. The Buddha is not the Buddha; the Patriarch is not the Patriarch.

The guest is not the guest; the host is not the host. All are one path of equality, a vast and great equilibrium. Furthermore, without involving either extreme, there is a single phrase of solitary liberation.
How do you speak of it? Do you understand? "The clouds have the momentum to leave the mountains; the water has no sound as it enters the ravine. [Ascending the hall: There is...
To have a question and an answer is to fall into the realm of verbal expression. To have neither question nor answer is to remain in silent stillness. Silent stillness becomes deception;
being stuck in verbal expression becomes slander. Therefore it is said: it cannot be constructed through speech, nor can it be communicated through silence.
Yet, above both speech and silence, there is a path that penetrates the great way. Furthermore, how is this so? After a long silence, he said: "White."
The sun and blue sky are fully revealed. [Ascending the hall,] a monk asked: "The essence is pure and fundamental; how is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
The Master said: "Why do you see flowers in your eyes? The monk asked: "What is the pure and fundamental essence? The Master said: "Seeing the cheek behind the head. He then said:
"In this one stroke of the present moment, there is no place to open one's mouth. When the true eye is clearly penetrating, there is no place to evade."
Therefore, it is said: There is a thing, bright and vivid, black as lacquer. It reaches up to heaven and down to earth;

it is ever present within movement and function, yet cannot be grasped within movement and function. [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says: "It has already been pierced through! Do you all understand?
If you do understand, then in the midst of daily life—whether turning, walking, bowing, or looking up—everything is none other than this very reality."
The earth, wind, and light—were one not thoroughly acquainted with them, the common people would use them daily without knowing it. (He lets out a shout.
Ascending the hall to open the furnace, a monk asks: "I do not ask about the simultaneous integration of the orthodox and the deviant; what is the 'house style' of Linji? The Master strikes him.
The monk prepared to speak, but the Master struck him again, saying, "A second offense will not be tolerated. He then said: "The flames preach the Dharma for the Buddhas of the three periods.
How many strands of eyebrows do you take care to watch? The Buddhas of the three periods stand upon the ground and listen; it is distinct and clear, starkly awake.
When the dead firewood emits flames from its entire body, only then can one join the radiance and continue the ancestral lamp. He gave a shout.
"Ho! [He] struck the meditation staff. The Goryeo monk Tán-huì requested the Master to ascend the hall. [The Master] raised the example of Dēngshān, who said: "Tonight I shall not answer questions.
Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff. At that time, a monk came forward and bowed. Dēngshān immediately struck him.
The monk said, "I have not even asked a question; why do you strike me? Dēngshān asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied—
[The monk] from Silla said, "Before he has even stepped onto the ship's railing, he deserves thirty blows.
The Master said, "Deshan issues extraordinary commands and maintains a practice beyond the norm; he is indeed a masterful hand. But I, this old monk, would not do so.
As soon as he says, 'A man from Silla,' I would strike him down with a continuous series of blows, making him a truly liberated monk. Would that not be delightful?"
"Alas! Yet he said, 'Before you have even stepped onto the boat's railing, I would give you thirty blows.
This monk could not help but take refuge in the kingdom of Silla before he had even stepped onto the boat's railing; it is very much like having the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake.
If there is anyone among this assembly who can act as a patron for Deshan and come forward to give this old monk his staff..."

[The Master] saw [the monk]. "If there were none, I, this old monk, would have performed a solo performance," he said. He dragged his staff, descended from the seat, and immediately dispersed the assembly.
Returning to the Abbot’s quarters, he ascended the hall for formal discourse. A monk asked, "What is it like when the twelve peaks are shrouded by clouds and mist? The Master said, "Blind!
The monk asked, "What is it like when the waters of the Nine Dragon Pool surge with white waves reaching the heavens? The Master said, "Do not act recklessly. The monk asked, "..."
"Right at the moment when the water is clear and the clouds are pure, what is it like? The Master said, "Go.
The monk bowed and said, "In that case, I am going to the green mountains and blue waters. The Master said, "Wrong. He then said: "On the first day of the sixth month, it is intensely hot;
everyone’s entire body is dripping with sweat. Suddenly a gust of cool wind blows, and everyone is once again dry and parched as before. Now tell me:"
That which is parched and withered is this; that from which sweat flows forth is this. If that from which sweat flows forth were this, then there should be no time when it is parched and withered.
If that which is parched and withered were this, then there should be no time when sweat flows forth.
Fearing that I might mislead or deceive you all, this old monk dares not reveal the secret. You must each awaken for yourselves;
only by seeking a clear understanding can you succeed. Ascending the hall, he said: "This is a ready-made case; there is no need for deliberation. The eight-character eyebrows are already parted."
It is beyond the power of the mind to interfere. Thus, it is not permissible to say "it is so," nor is it permissible to say "it is not so.

It is not permissible to say both "it is so" and "it is not so" together. Otherwise, one cannot avoid merely hiding one's roots within stagnant water. Suppose, however, that even "it is so" is permissible...
"It is also possible not to be thus. It is also possible to be both thus and not thus. Yet this is still making a living within the thicket of entanglements.
Not falling into the mechanism of the two extremes, nor descending into the position of the middle—tell me, how do you make use of this during the twenty-four hours of the day?
Walking alone with one foot atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak. [He lets out a shout and strikes the meditation staff. [Opening the furnace, he ascends the hall for the formal discourse.]
In Mount Taibai there is plenty of firewood; not a single branch is permitted for anyone to carry away.
It is not that this old monk is being overly stingy with it; rather, it is because I wish for everyone to feel the cold to the very bone.

Even so, when it is said that the three realms offer no peace and are like a burning house, where will you all go to take refuge? If you can indeed find such a refuge, then you may truly be called high-minded.
Transcending the three realms, he strides alone across the great square. Should this not yet be so, each of you must first take care of your own eyebrows and whiskers before ascending the hall.
[The Master] cites the Great Master Linji, who said: "A single phrase contains the three gates; a single gate contains the three essentials.
There is the provisional and there is the functional. How do you all understand this? He then descended from his seat and called out, "Great ones!"
"Assembly! As for that question and answer just now, where did it go? If you know its destination, then there is both skillful means and function.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In this place of Tiandong’s, I do not dare to wrong anyone. If you have half a catty, I weigh you at eight taels;
if you have ten feet, I measure you at one zhang. If there were a man among the assembly who, hearing such words, were to give rise to a temper—"
As for this Way: it is entirely, in its totality, a scale without marks. What more could possibly be weighed? I simply tell them: "A single cast and it is caught.
If you understand this, there is merit and you shall be rewarded. If you do not understand, then grasp the meaning at the tip of the hook;
do not fixate on the zero point of the scale. Ascending the hall, he said: "Before you have reached Tiantong, you will naturally be filled with doubt."
Having already reached Tiantong, it is like tiles shattering and ice melting away. Why is this so? Have you not heard it said: "Hearing a name is not as good as seeing the face"?
Now that the face has been seen, what kind of matter has been accomplished within the realm of each person? If there is a single film over the eye, empty flowers fall in confusion.
Question: "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said: "A face covered entirely in dust. Question: "How is this so?"
"This is the guest within the host. The Master said, "This old monk has no companion.

"How is it the host within the host? The Master said, "Under the moon at the third watch, no one recognizes him. "How is it the guest within the host? The Master said, "Sitting before the hall, no one accompanies him. Question:
"What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'? The Master said, "Slaying Yan Liang amidst a million troops."
"What is 'seizing the object but not seizing the person'? The Master said, "Having taken Jingzhou, he let Lu Su go. "What is 'seizing both the person and the object'?
The Master said, "He killed Chen Youliang and annexed dozens of states. "What is 'neither seizing the person nor seizing the object'?
The Master said, "Today the world is at peace; long live the King! [The student] asked: "What is 'discerning' (liao-jian)?"

[The student] said, “I have already received the Master’s instruction; how is it to fully bring forth the matter that transcends [the ordinary]? The Master struck him repeatedly with his staff and said, “Go away!
Go away! [The student] asked, “What is the first primordiality? The Master said, “Though one has a mouth, it cannot proclaim it.
“What is the second primordiality? The Master said, “The feet are square and the head is round. “What is the third primordiality? The Master said, “Just so.”
[The Master] reached for his waist [to strike him]. The student asked, "What is the Three Essentials? The Master opened the seal and said, "The vermilion dot is narrow.
The student struck him. The Master said, "I strike you with one blow. The student said, "Why not strike me twice? The Master said, "You dull-witted monk!

A student asked, "When clear water washes away dust, where do the dust and water go? The Master said, "Into the latrine. The student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Go ask someone else."

Jingtou departs. [A monk] asks, "What is the perfect clarity of the five eyes? The Master says, "This old monk has only two. [The monk] asks, "What are the Three Jewels? The Master says, "One meal of flatbread and two meals of congee. [The monk] says, "I am not asking about those three satiations. The Master says, "This old monk observes them daily. [Another monk] asks, "Why does a great practitioner carry a cangue and wear shackles? The Master says, "Because he has no place to go. The Diamond King’s Precious Sword: sometimes a single shout is like a lion crouching on the ground; sometimes a single shout is like a probe-staff and its shadow-grass;

Likewise, take the four shouts and place them within my one shout; you will not see the name of even the four shouts.

"Preceptor, do not force the noble into the lowly. Nevertheless, such gentlemen-scholars as these are very difficult to find nowadays.
