"Speak," the Master said. Xiu replied, "I have a verse. The Master asked, "What is your verse? Xiu presented his verse: "To whom does 'not associating with the myriad dharmas' refer?
Who is it that, from the very beginning, stands alone in intimacy? If one seeks with intention, one drifts further apart; If one realizes through non-mind, there is no contradiction.
Xiu said, "I am not asking you about 'not associating with the myriad dharmas'; I want you to understand it in a single stroke."

He inhaled [the air] completely. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment; he shook out his sleeves and departed. Whenever Zongxiu subsequently posed questions or inquiries, the Master never yielded on the spot.
Zongxiu deeply approved of him, bestowing upon him the title "The One Who Has Come Again. Later, when Zongxiu moved to Baoen Temple, not long after, the Master passed away.
The Master then ascended the seat. Entering the hall, he held up his staff and said: "This staff of the new Baoen—sometimes its blood splatters against the Brahma Heaven;
sometimes spring returns to the great earth; sometimes it distinguishes dragons from snakes at a glance;
sometimes even a thousand eyes cannot perceive it. But tell me, how do you meet this staff of Baoen? With these words, he whirled the staff like a whirlwind.
[He] dispersed [the assembly] and ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he looked left and right and said, "O Great Assembly!

I now clearly show you: you are originally Buddhas. He struck the ground with his staff and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is it like when the Great Matter has not yet been clarified?
The Master said, "Suffering. The monk asked, "And what about when it has been clarified? The Master said, "Suffering. The monk remarked, "The clouds have cleared; the mountain's luster is moist."
"Spring has returned and the plants and trees are new. The Master said, "Bitter! Then the assembly of monks vied with one another to come forward and pose questions.
The Master said, "Do not say that because the water is cold the fish do not eat; I have now caught them until my boat is full and am returning home. He then descended from his seat.

He ascended the hall again and, holding up his staff, said, "Sagacious Zen practitioners, come forth from the assembly to meet me. Two monks came forward together. The Master struck once with his staff.
He said: "Grasp the meaning at the hook's tip; do not fixate on the zero point of the scale. Opening the furnace, he ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said:
"A single blow and it is accomplished—this is not yet being impatient with nature. Without relying on a single blow, one remains a dull-witted lacquer bucket.
A monk who can enter the ancient furnace and bellows must come forth from the assembly to meet me. A monk stepped forward and bowed. The Master said: "I wish to catch the whale."
He cleared away the vast expanse of water, yet sighed that the frog’s steps were still confined to the mud and sand. One monk hesitated; the Master struck him out. Another monk stepped forward;

the Master let out a thunderous roar and shouted. That monk hesitated; the Master likewise struck him out. Yet another monk stepped forward, and the Master said, "We meet face-to-face on this very stage."
"One must be a true master. The monk shouted. The Master said, "Why this reckless shouting? The monk shouted again, and the Master struck him out.
Then, planting his staff upright, he said: "It is not that I find it difficult to harmonize with others; generally, one must distinguish between the black and the white."

[The Master] threw down his staff and descended from the seat. On the occasion of the opening of the retreat, he ascended the hall and called upon the retired monk Chan Master Chong to lead the assembly.
Holding up his whisk, he said: "Today is the fifteenth day of the fourth month. At Golden Wheel Peak, the brocade stream dances; grasses, trees, earth, and stones all turn over their bodies;
mosquitoes, gnats, and fleas ride upon Buddhas and patriarchs. Yet there is yet another extraordinary matter: two heads within a single enclosure."
The Deer swallows up ten thousand mountains and a hundred thousand tigers. Looking left and right, he says: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya—these are your slaves.
In the morning they trample upon Vairocana; in the evening they embrace Shewen and lie down on Mount Tiantai.

You, Reverend Master, must not let this pass! Addressing the assembly: To break through the final, secure barrier, Yun’an was truly scolding. He thoroughly penetrated the ancestral framework of Bodhidharma.
Even Miaoxi still rebuked them. You all who are heading toward this Dharma-gate must be extremely careful. "The water in the front stream is swift and the fish move with difficulty;

the wind on the rear ridge is high and the birds find it hard to perch. This was the small *chan* (meditation) discourse for the winter retreat. Having served in the master’s room morning and evening and finished burning incense, I now receive [this instruction]:

"At the beginning of the year, I have led the assembly at Mount Ou for the first time. My late teacher had no dharma to permit me to proclaim; after I finished burning incense while attending his quarters day and night, I received [this teaching]."
Small Assembly for Fellow Students Tilling the Field. In the past, Chan Master Qianyan called himself the "Old Man of Ignorance" (Wuming).
This mountain monk is his descendant; every day I let loose the fire of ignorance, and even stubborn copper and dull iron are cast into the furnace until they are completely melted away.
Only those students who come these days have two ears that are obstructed by this and that; they cannot even endure being burned, let alone facing the harmony [of the Way].
Sengbian’s [reckoning of] kalpa-ashes will ultimately be but a chaotic blur. If you do not awaken to this, go and ask Puo-zao-duo of Mount Song.
**Small Assembly (Xiao Can):** "A single leaf falls and the world turns autumn; a single speck of dust rises and the great earth is gathered. Now tell me:
what matter do the ten thousand Bodhisattvas in the Mañjuśrī Hall and the five hundred Arhats beneath the Stone Beam Bridge be discussing as they gather their heads together today? Liang.
[Long pause. A shout! [He lets out a shout. Small Assembly Sermon. Holding up his staff, he said: "At the tips of the hundred grasses, Śākyamuni glares with bared teeth;

in the midst of the bustling marketplace, Maitreya furrows his brow. In a village of three households, Old Man Liao loses his temper and charges headlong through the corner of the lapis lazuli palace in the thirty-third heaven, crushing the thumb of the Persian merchant from the South Sea. Now tell me, who can save him?"
[He] attained it. After a long while, he struck the ground with his staff and said: "Study! **Small Sermon:** In the sixth month, one knocks upon ice; the door is filled with snow.

Since we have not yet studied the "Ping-fen" [scriptures], the evening sermon has ceased. Not only have six people here become great vessels; throughout the hall, fragrant rice is served amidst vast auspicious clouds.
**Small Sermon:** Old windows and dilapidated rooms; a paper curtain and a blue lamp. Is there anyone here who has caught even a hint of its flavor?
The night wind has grown sharp; it is already three parts ready to brew snow. *Evening Assembly.* Last night, a monk asked:
"When there is no dream and no thought, where is the host? Before his voice had even faded, I, the mountain monk, covered his mouth with my hand.
To those who can penetrate this, I offer a substitute word on their behalf so that they may not fail me. After a long silence, I spoke again: "Rainfall."
The mounted official surveyed the mountain and entered the Buddha Hall. *Small-scale Sermon:* Holding up his staff, he said:

"The ancients said, 'A crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt does not fire its trigger for a mere field mouse. Yet another said, 'Whether seizing an elephant or seizing a rabbit, one exerts the full power of one's strength.
Now, regarding a Zen practitioner who is muddled or distracted—if they strike him, it is right; if they do not strike him, it is also right. But if they strike..."
This would be like setting a trap for a field mouse; if one does not strike, one will fail to capture the rabbit with full force.

A monk prostrated, and the Master said, "This monk has blood under his skin. He then threw down his staff. In the evening session, the Master held up a bamboo stick and made the gesture of playing the zither.
A monk came forward and asked, "How can one ensure that all four corners touch the ground? The Master said, "I am about to cast my line."
Jingni said again, "Last night, Master Xiangyan entered the room and informed me, saying:
'In the Dharma Hall, there are many who understand my story about the old monk climbing the tree. Now tell me, which one was it? The assembly remained silent.
The Master struck them repeatedly with a shout, saying, "He performed a somersault in the assembly of Panshan; only now do we know that Puhua was mad. This was the evening instruction.
Looking around at those on his left and right, he said, "This is the evening session. Questions are not permitted. Those who do not ask a question shall receive thirty blows.
As the assembly hesitated, the Master said, "Since the man who stood in the snow returned, several fragments of white clouds have guarded the verdant peaks.
This is the evening session; I, this mountain monk, have a discourse on the Buddha-dharma to deliver, which I have hung upon the Yu-hua Bridge. Everyone, go forth!"
"Look! After a long silence, he said: "Bai Le once came three times; who could have added a thousand pieces of gold? You were offered it, but you did not accept;
the perfect jade rests against a withered vine. For the early winter assembly, he took up his whisk and said: "Yellow leaves pile deep, three feet at the gate;
cold spring water hangs ten thousand fathoms from the teeth. Enduring the bitter cold, one forgets the silence; the plum blossoms do not wait for the mountain ridges."
Early Spring. [The Master] strikes the whisk with his staff and lets out a shout. Evening Sermon: "On the Tian-shan mountains, summer is like autumn;
coolness arises in one's robes early and late. This decrepit mendicant has no dharma to speak; everyone stands beneath the flowers in the stone courtyard.
Evening Sermon under the Tree: "How many people are at the gate? At the crossroads, they miss the way. "Great Assembly, speak!"
"Look at this phrase for entering the gate. A monk stepped forward; the Master immediately shouted. A monk asked, "What is the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma?
The Master said, "Dragging through mud and carrying water. He asked, "What is the Tathāgata’s solid body? The Master said, "Burn it as soon as it is dead.
He asked, "What is the Tathāgata’s impartial Dharma? The Master said, "The Main Peak is high; the Forehead Mountain is low. [He] asked about recitation.
"Who is the Buddha? The Master said, "A dog. The monk asked, "Ultimately, who is it? The Master said, "It is a dog.

The monk asked, "What is it like when the wind is calm and the waves have subsided? The Master said, "The monkey covets the moon. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A dog licking an oil cauldron.
The monk asked, "I do not ask about the great earth, mountains, and rivers; what of the matter upon the tip of a single hair? The Master said, "..."
[The monk] swallowed seven or eight [words], saying, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Vomit out two or three!

[The monk] asked, "Regarding the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable wondrous meanings, what is the primary meaning? The Master said, "Horizontal sevens and vertical eights. [The monk] asked, "What is the great purport of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "The braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs. [The monk] asked, "How is it? The Master said, "The braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs."

[The monk] tried to avoid [answering] by heading toward a place free from cold and heat. The Master said, "You are accustomed to finding such opportunities. [The monk] asked, "What is the state that is free from cold and heat?

The Master said, "When it is cold, it is cold; when it is hot, it is hot. The Master added, "I have emptied my belly and turned over my guts for you. [The monk] asked, "What is the fundamental matter?
The Master said, "He manages the household's smoke, whether it rises in great or small volumes. [The monk] asked, "What is 'investigating' (chán)? The Master said, "Eating porridge, eating rice."
[The Master] ate his meal. [A monk asked: "What is Chan? The Master said, "Carrying pigs, carrying dogs. The Master cited Yunmen, who held up a fan and said:
"[It] leaps up to the thirty-third heaven, striking the nostrils of Śakra. A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow of the staff."

The rain poured down like an overturned basin. The Master asked a monk, "What is the meaning of this? The monk’s answer did not accord with the truth, so the Master struck him out with his staff in succession.
He then commanded the layman Hu Yan-yuan to provide an answer. The layman came forward and knelt, saying in a loud voice, "The Great Lord of the Blue Sky looks on above;
what I testify to is the truth. The Master nodded in approval. The Master then asked Vice-Governor Dai Ting-cheng, "From where does the cloud arise?"
The Vice-Minister said, "It arises from where the Master questioned. The Master replied, "This mountain monk is at fault.

During the reign of Emperor Shizu Zhanghuangdi, the Master was summoned twice to the inner court to discuss the Way. He was bestowed the honorary title of Chan Master Dajue Pujie, along with purple robes and a golden seal.
In the autumn of the Yimao year of the Kangxi era, he traveled to Mount Wutai; while on the way, he stayed at Ciji Temple in Qingjiangpu.
Yun’an manifested a slight illness. He requested a brush and wrote a verse, then passed away on the tenth day of the seventh month.
He was sixty-two years of age and had been a monk for forty-three years.

His disciples escorted his remains back and enshrined them in a stupa at the eastern valley of Tianmu Mountain in Qianyang, where it stands facing the stupas of the two patriarchs, Gaofeng and Zhongfeng.
Chan Master Citzongji of Mount Heng in Hengzhou Prefecture was the son of the Li family of Tongzhou.

His courtesy name was Dunsou. His father possessed hidden virtue and served the Buddha with utmost reverence; his mother observed a vegetarian diet. After she had been pregnant for one full year, the Master was conceived.

When the Master was barely a year old, he was already able to distinguish between meat and vegetarian food. An elder named Jiachuan of Tianning Monastery said to the Master’s parents: "This youngest son, though at an early age..."

"You are a vessel for the Way; why not abandon [your current path] and follow me? He was only at the age of *zhixue* (the age of beginning one's studies) when his parents permitted him to follow Master Jianchuan.
There, he observed the conduct of a *śrāmaṇera*. At the temple, there was Dharma Master Ruomei, who expounded the Dharma through lectures. The Master thus came to study these expositions.
Whenever he heard the words regarding the swift passage of impermanence, he was struck with a sense of alarm. "When a single breath does not return, where will one find rest? he pondered.
He established his life through his physical presence; although he had undergone many years of lecturing, this was not his true intent. Yet, this single thought remained earnest and persistent.

One night, while walking in meditation (caṅkrama), he happened to lose his footing and attained a realization. He resolved to travel to study under various masters. Initially, he visited Tiantong Wu at Jinsu.
He asked, "When guests have dispersed and the hall is empty, what is it like? Wu said, "What kind of time is this? The Master gave a shout. Wu struck him. The Master again—
"Ho! [Yuan] woke up and struck him again. The Master prostrated and said, "From this day forward, I shall serve the Master.

Later, he went to study under Xiu of Qingshan. Upon their first meeting, they reached a mutual accord. One day, while attending to him, Xiu asked, "Just as it was with Baizhang under Mazu’s shout—what did he gain?
The Master replied, "If there were anything gained, that would be to do Mazu a disservice. Xiu said, "He said, 'For three days my ears were deaf.'"

[The monk] said, "Venerable Sir, I must no longer harbor the views of a wild fox; I shall now depart. On another day, Xiu raised the question regarding Yantou’s four "concealing the point" (zangfeng) phrases.
He asked, "What is 'concealing the point' in accordance with principle? The Master said, "In the Hall of Emperor Liang, he said, 'I do not recognize you.
He asked, "What is 'concealing the point' in accordance with phenomena? The Master said, "Today the rain falls, and the steps before us are wet. As [he spoke], Xiu attained realization.
"What is 'concealing the blade in both principle and phenomena'? The Master said, "Walking, one does not leave the door; sitting, one does not occupy the hall.

"What is 'concealing the blade in neither principle nor phenomena'? The Master said, "An eight-cornered millstone rolls through the void. Xiu said, "These four turning words can carry on the lineage of the predecessors.
Nevertheless, they are still a jumble of seven and eight. [He] resided at Dongming and swept the floor for Chan Master Xian.

At the ancestral stupa, he held up the incense and said: "This old fellow has been hiding here for two hundred years; neither humans nor devas have known him, and even Buddhas and patriarchs find it difficult to approach him.
Today, his descendants have arrived at his feet and have personally exposed him. But tell me, by what means is this verified?
He looked left and right, inserted the incense, and addressed the assembly: "An ancient said: 'To do it this way is not permitted; not to do it this way is also not permitted.'"
"Not so" is not permitted. "It is so" and "it is not so"—neither is permitted.
Brothers, in the end, how can it be attained? After a long silence, he said: "The dripping before the eaves has nothing to do with rain; the thunder rushing through the mountain streams is not sound.
To the assembly: "In the late spring, wind and rain have disturbed the night; one should know that the silkworms and wheat will surely not fare well. Before the mountains and behind the mountains..."

Women and men, day and night, are consumed by sorrow and forget both hunger and satiety. Yet when one turns to reflect upon us practitioners of Chan, it seems our application of mind is far inferior to theirs.
We enter and leave monasteries merely to pursue the clamor of the gates; we speak of "investigating Chan" with our mouths, yet our minds have not realized it.
In a frantic bustle, we reach the point where our hair turns gray, yet we remain ignorant of our own fundamental matter. Suddenly, the murderous ghost of impermanence arrives, and all at once—
It is useless to beat one’s breast in vain resentment; you and I dwell together, so you should know this well. Do not treat birth and death with such negligence.

If your practice is as diligent as a silkworm worrying over its cocoon or a farmer watching his wheat, it is certain that before long you shall realize this Way. Our gathering in these remote mountains has but a limited time;
you must cherish every moment and not seek elsewhere. Addressing the assembly: Today in all quarters the hearth is opened, and [monks] rush about in the four directions.
The sea of Chan practitioners—each one aspires to become a Buddha or an Ancestor. Yet, even with true inquiry and ultimate realization, there is still nothing to attain.

How can they compare to those several disciples of Dongming? They keep their mouths shut all day long while sitting in *kaḍa* (lotus) posture. Frosty winds strike their faces; their bowls and alms-pans are pure and empty. With firm resolve, they accomplish what they intend.
They constantly recall the ancients dwelling in tattered huts, where the entire bed was strewn with snow-white pearls. [This concludes] the departure from the assembly due to certain circumstances.
He said: "The Way has grown thin and cannot endure dwelling in the patriarchal hall. It is fitting to follow the clouds and cranes and listen to the murmuring stream.

Let it be taught that another of virtue from among the monks be selected; he may be made to lift the six-foot staff once more. He then departed for the Green Vine Hermitage on Mount Nanyue, where he addressed the assembly:
In this place of mine, the mountain monk does not discuss the primordial, nor the wondrous, nor Zen, nor the Way.
I require only that your mind of birth-and-death be shattered. If that mind of birth-and-death is not shattered, you are right before Old Man Yama.
"One who swallows an iron bar. This is why Master Gengzhao said: "Study must be true study; awakening must be true awakening. King Yama does not fear much talk.
Do not trouble yourselves by standing here long; take care. Addressing the assembly, he raised a case:
A monk asked Chan Master Yunfeng Yue of this mountain, "What is the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground? Yue said, "It is not obtained from others. [The monk] said, "Not from..."

"How is it when a person attains [this]? Yue said, "It is not far from here to Hengyang. The Master said, "Although Yunfeng’s response met the immediate occasion, it still involves traversing a certain distance.
I, the dull old man, am otherwise. What is the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground? It is not attained from another.
When it is not attained from another, how is it? [Yue] replied, "I would simply give him a blow across the back with my staff."
Addressing the Assembly on New Year’s Day: The first day of the year opens a new reign; all things are renewed. Village elders sing songs of joy to celebrate the Great Peace.
With my own eyes, I witness the ancient events of the Patriarchal Garden. The spring breeze blows forth upon the plum blossoms. Addressing the Assembly: It is said that a monk asked Yunmen:
"What is Yunmen’s Single Song? Yunmen said, "The twenty-fifth of the twelfth month. The Master said, "The twenty-fifth of the twelfth month; today I raise it for you.
To understand it with deliberate intent is surely difficult. Shooting a stone tiger at Lantian.
Residing at Nanyuan in Changsha, he addressed the assembly, citing Yangqi: "With meager merit I dwell at Yangqi; my strength has declined in recent years. The cold wind..."
Withered and fallen leaves—yet I still rejoice that an old friend has returned. *Lara-lari*. Placing it upon the head of dead firewood, let us for now dwell within the smokeless flame.
The Master said: "The gate and courtyard are cold and stern; the flow of his words conceals its sharp edge.

This was my distant ancestor Yangqi, who bore the burden of the Dharma path and served as the guiding pillar for the monastic community—a model for all. I, a humble monk, being his descendant, also have a verse. [I am] of meager merit."
Dwelling at Nanyuan, the frosty wind makes the thatched cottage cold. Wrapping myself in my robes, I sit by the brazier;
my withered form resembles Lanchan. My bare bones do not deceive you; I ask you all to sweep away the yellow leaves. When the moon rises over the thousand peaks, we shall boil the ice-balls.

The Master, together with the assembly, was cultivating the fields. He addressed the assembly, saying: "This one plot of land has been entrusted [to us] for a long time from the very beginning. It is simply...
Because their descendants were unworthy, they abandoned their homes and squandered their livelihoods, wandering far away in pursuit of external pleasures.

This has caused the ancestral fields and gardens to be overgrown with thorns for years and weeds to grow daily taller. Today, I, this mountain monk, shall take out the original land deeds and display them before all of you.
It is necessary for everyone to each quickly sharpen their focus and recognize this very plot of land. Cut down the weeds of ignorance and clear away the forest of false views;
only then may you cast and scatter in both directions, plowing deep and sowing shallow.

Donning the raincoat under the moon and wielding the rake amidst the clouds—reaching this point, it is not beyond you to change the stalks of rice into ears of millet, or transform clods of earth into pure gold. All of it!
"It manifests only upon this small patch of ground. Great assembly, at such a time as this, tell me: by whose power of grace does it do so?
Then, striking the earth three times with his mattock, he said: "How many times have I sold it only to buy it back? Out of pity for the pines and bamboos, it draws in the pure wind.
Regarding the Lantern Festival, he said: "Great assembly, today is the fifteenth day of the first month; everywhere there are village songs and community celebrations."
Dance! Only within our Nanyuan Temple do we raise the command to transcend Buddhas and patriarchs.
It is not like Bimao holding up his staff, nor is it like Yunmen saying, "The Way is universal. We strike up the light of infinite lamps to illuminate the Lord of Lords.
Great assembly, tell me: what is the face of the Lord of Lords? Xiajiu said: "Heh! Addressing the assembly: In all quarters there are the "Original" and the "Subtle."
As for Chan: there is the Chan of the nature-path; there is the subtle and refined Chan; there is the Chan of daily progress;
there is the Chan of "resting and ceasing"; there is the Chan of the Great Dharma and the Small Dharma. There is Chan that engages with people and Chan that has them chew it over.
In this place of mine, there are none of these many kinds of Chan; there is only the "dull blade" left behind by our distant ancestor, the Great Wisdom Zen Master Baizhang.
The iron hoehead: every day it requires the use of all people.

When its use becomes thoroughly proficient, if one reaches the point where effort is forgotten by the self and the hand is forgotten by the mind, such that before one’s eyes there is no field to be opened and beneath one’s feet there is no ground to stand upon—suddenly the hoe turns, and the mountains, rivers, and great earth shatter into a hundred fragments, revealing the two eyes of the person themselves.
"Eyes! Great assembly, who now holds the handle? [He] suddenly threw down his staff and said: "Held out in the open light for everyone to see!
Addressing the assembly, he raised an example: "The Inspector-General Wei of Min often saw monks and would say:
'When I have completed my term of office and leave Jiangxi and Hunan, I shall pose a question that will kill the old masters of Jiangxi and Hunan. The monk [responded].
The Master asked, "How does the Military Inspector ask? The Inspector said, "No need for hands or feet. The monk was speechless.
The Master spoke on his behalf, saying, "When the Military Inspector asks in such a manner, it truly makes one laugh the old masters of Jiangxi and Hunan to death.

A monk asked, "What is the place where a student establishes their body and sustains their life? The Master said, "Wait until this mountain monk has a place to establish my body and sustain my life; then I shall tell you."
Question: "What is the phrase of the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*? The Master coughed once and said, "Your view is biased and stunted. How can it become perfect?
The Master said, "This mountain monk’s administrative duties are many. Question:
"At that time, did Xuefeng obtain the power of Deshan or the power of Yantou? The Master said, "He obtained neither from either place. Question: "Ultimately, how was it? The Master then—
"Hai! [The monk] said, "If that is so, then I shall go to prostrate. The Master gave a single sigh. A monk asked, "When the stone tiger on the mountainhead strikes a blow and takes a step, what then?
The Master said, "Take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. A monk asked, "For one who has already attained liberation from birth and death, how should they apply their effort?
The Master remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? The monk bowed, and the Master gave him a kick.

The monk is at a loss. The Master says, "A mere parrot of words! and drives him straight out. Another monk visits.
As soon as he spreads his sitting cloth, the Master strikes him. The monk says, "Thank you for the Master’s compassion. The Master says, "As for this mountain monk now..."
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the Wuma year of the Kangxi era, the nun Rishili asked, "What is the original face of a student? The Master said, "A complete display of shame.
The nun bowed; the Master said, "It is difficult to deceive the eyes of the multitude. On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the Wuma year of the Kangxi era.

After sending letters of thanks to all the donors who had assembled, the Master joined his palms, offered words of farewell, and passed away. He was sixty-four years of age and forty-two years since his ordination.
His stupa was enshrined in his quarters.
The Complete Writings of the Five Lamps, Volume Sixty-Eight;
The Complete Writings of the Five Lamps, Volume Sixty-Nine.
Compiled by the Abbot of Saint-Guan Zen Temple in the Capital, the Monk (Chao Yong).
Verified and presented by the Abbot (Subject Monk) Chaokei of the Ancient Kegon-ji Temple,
Rinzai School.

Chan Master Mingxing Yangzhuo Minyin, the thirty-fifth generation descendant of Nanyue, was the son of the Chang family of Changzhi in Puzhou, Shanxi. At the age of twenty, he took leave of his parents.
He shaved his head at Putuo and went to attend upon the Elder Wulu at Jinsu, where he attained realization under the staff.

Later, he followed Wufeng to study and served as the Superintendent (Jianyuan) of Tongqing Monastery. When Wuxue was about to pass away, he took the whisk from his source and transmitted it to the Master.
The Master ascended the hall and said: "In the past, Xuansha carried a letter to Xuefeng. Xuefeng tore up the letter and saw only white paper."
Three times he spread his sitting cloth. He called to the great assembly, saying, "Observe closely! Observe closely! With a shout, he descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Buddha after Buddha appears in the world for the sake of the one great matter. But tell me, what is this great matter?
He held up his whisk and said, "I have nothing hidden from you. He further cited Zhaozhou, who said: "The clay Buddha does not cross water; the gold Buddha..."
"A clay Buddha does not cross water; a wooden Buddha does not cross fire; the true Buddha sits within.
Today, this mountain monk cannot help but take up this staff to overturn Zhaozhou’s barrier and open another path. [He draws a circle with the staff and says:
"A clay Buddha can cross water without relying on the power of another. [He draws a circle inside a square with the staff and says: "A wooden Buddha..."
"One who can cross the fire. This matter is as clear as the sun. Again, he drew a circle with his staff and said: "A golden Buddha can cross the furnace."
"None of you see it. The True Buddha has no dwelling place. Everyone is right here; look with urgency! Do not hesitate.
He threw down his staff and said, "Do you see it? He then descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall to cremate the sacred remains of Master Wupeng, a monk asked, "The World-Honored One had eighty-four thousand śarīras; I wonder how many the late master had? The Master [responded].
The Master struck his staff once. A monk shouted; the Master then struck him. He then cited the occasion when Xuefeng passed away and Xuansha served as the presiding mourner.
Holding up a tea cup, he asked, "Do you understand? If you can understand, the late master was without fault; if you do not understand—"
The fault lies with the former master. The assembly remained silent. Shanshan then smashed the tea bowl. The Master said, "Mount Huangbo neither raised the bowl nor smashed it;
he simply presented what he had obtained through his own rightful portion to all people. Raising his staff, he said:
"Do you see? Disperse at once! He returned to the Abbot’s quarters. Ascending the hall for a formal discourse, a monk asked, "What is the matter of the 'one step beyond'?
The Master said, "Step back. The monk asked, "And what about the 'one step after that'? The Master said, "Do not engage in false imaginings. He then said:
"Speaking in every speck of dust; speaking in every land. How could one speak beyond the limit of Vīraśabda? [The Master] held his staff horizontally and said:
'The nostrils of all Buddhas of the three periods are pierced at once; when the myriad phenomena hear this, their hearts and livers shatter.
Why is it so? 'The colt tramples the people of the world to death; the treasury of the true Dharma-eye is extinguished by the blind donkey. [Addressing the assembly: "Great men, cease!"
[The Master] was about to deliberate [on the matter]. With a turn of his body, he drew forth his blade-sharp hair. Like a great garuḍa spreading its wings, there is no obstruction;
it passes straight through a thousand layers and ten thousand folds. At midnight, the rector entered the abbot’s quarters and said, “I return the original object to the Master.
The Master asked, “What do you say? The rector struck him immediately. The Master also struck him. The rector said, “Now I am no longer hindered by the old monks of the world.”
[Zhang] Man bowed and departed. The Master said, "Thirty blows are well-deserved for the soles of his heels.
On the following day, the Master himself struck the drum and said, "The mountain monk is going on campaign. Turning around, he entered the hall and said, "Last night, I was ambushed by the Rector."
"Victory or defeat is not distinguished. Today I have come specifically to beat the drum and engage in battle with you all.
No need for 'how' or 'what'; simply request that we enter directly with single blades. Is there anyone? Is there anyone? The Rector then came forth and assumed the posture of a wrestler.
The Master said, "A defeated army and a vanquished general are no match for the enemy. He then returned to his quarters. The Master entered the hall and sat cross-legged on the floor.
As he sat, there was a monk who sat upon the master’s mat. The master rose and bowed to the monk, whereupon the monk fled.
The master sat back down on the ground and said, "I cannot rise. Who among you in the assembly will help this mountain monk up? A monk pushed the master, causing him to fall to the ground again.
The Master rose from his meditation seat. The monk then returned to the Abbot’s quarters.
A monk asked, "What is the living word? The Master said, "Pull out your tongue. The monk asked, "What is the dead word? The Master struck him and said, "Press down on your nostrils."
The monks prostrated. The Master gave a single kick and asked, "Do you understand? In the spring of the Jichou year of the Shunzhi era, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was interred in a stupa at the foot of his mountain (Wufeng was his dharma heir).
Chan Master Fanyi Hongzhi of Sanfeng in Haiyu was the son of the Tao family of Haiyu. In his youth, he received the tonsure under Master Lang of Baoyan.
When Lang wished to travel elsewhere, he took the Master, along with Dingmu Che, and personally entrusted them to Sanfeng Zang, commanding him to serve as his attendant.

He was instructed to investigate the "Cane" koan and was frequently tasked with guarding the mountain gate. At that time, he used stones as a bed and bound together wattle fences for walls. It happened that—
It was the dead of winter; the cold wind pierced to the bone. He went to the storehouse to request paper. When Zang heard of this, he said in anger:

"Do you not realize that the years and months are fleeting and you have already failed to understand the Way? Instead, you are preoccupied with trivialities regarding your bedding and matting—do you take pleasure in such idle comfort?

From then on, whenever he had anything to ask, Zang would merely revile and scold him. One night, while practicing walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), at the fifth watch, he heard the sound of a great pine storm rising.
Suddenly, he had an awakening and composed a verse, saying: "Throughout the morning, I set my mind on seeking from others; My boundless spirit was exhausted for naught.
Last night, I stepped through and broke the heel of my straw sandals; The stone ox was shattered, and fresh blood dripped. Jiangzang still did not grant him approval.
One day, he suddenly asked, "Where are you currently practicing? The Master replied, "I sit firmly upon the stone bed at the stroke of midnight."
"A single cry of a cold wild goose breaks through the clouds. Mazu said, "The Qingzhou robe is here. The Master said, "Seven or eight tiles underfoot.
Mazu said, "I am not asking about that. The Master said, "Vajrapāṇi’s eight-sided staff. Mazu drove him away with his staff.
Later, he was ordered to contemplate the story of Deshan Carrying the Alms Bowl. He then entered the inner sanctum and presented a verse on the essential meaning, which began: "Two..."
Two iron oxen, their twin horns powerful; thunderbolts flash across heaven and earth. Though they share the same lineage, their modes of killing and giving life differ;
they exhaust the great chiliocosm to the very limit of its nature and destiny. Turning back one’s head to gaze upon the layered ridges, a single expanse of level lake is serene with wind and moon.

[The Master] concealed his chin [in silence], granting him entry into the inner chamber. In the *dingmao* year of the *Tianqi* era, he emerged from seclusion to reside at the Qingliang Monastery on Mount Sanfeng.

Addressing the assembly: For a long time I have been busily occupied, not speaking of Chan; wild weeds entangle one another, blocking the edge of my tongue. Today, the spring breeze first makes its acquaintance;
once more I take up the single bamboo whisk. The wind is piercing, the spirit is at ease; with a stroke across the spine, it brandishes the void as a fierce fire blazes.
Having severed both ends and three arms, it overturns the two eyes to wail to the blue heavens. Suddenly he takes it up.
[Brandishing] the bamboo whisk, he struck once and said: "Examine! To the assembly: When the heels have not yet reached their destination, the thread of the mind is severed;

before the corners of the mouth have opened, one's own self is lost. You must act like a flash of lightning overturning the sky, like a thunderclap suddenly striking—the face-gate must be smashed through, every sound like the rain at night.
Only then will you be fit to sleep in the Hall of Diligence, or to turn over upon the Flower-Light Seat."
Body. He brandishes the Vajra King Sword; there is no room for sentimentality. To repay anger with anger, to repay joy with joy.
Like a rushing torrent through a ravine or wind piercing through rain, he lets out a shout and says: "Stop! Stop! Addressing the assembly: "Once you realize the One, all things are finished.
The mountains are verdant and the waters are clear. My heart and marrow are exhausted from saving sentient beings. Where there is one blow, there is a palmful of blood."

Eight thousand times coming and going—how wondrous and subtle is this single phrase! The heavens, the sea, the mist, and the rain are vast and boundless; everywhere in the farmers' fields, the water-lifting levers have come to rest.
Addressing the assembly: Heaven is high and earth is low; the wind moves and the clouds arise. Seeing to the very limit, one finds that the ultimate rite is no rite at all.
All phenomena are thus from the beginning, beyond the reach of mind or speech. To proceed in such a manner already constitutes a failure of understanding. Therefore...
Zhangda said: "When the 'Blow-off-Skin' sword has been used, it must be sharpened immediately. Its cold radiance swallows the world of men.
To the assembly: After long rain, the day finally clears. White clouds bask upon the tips of the pines. The sound of the stone spring suddenly slackens; the shadows of the misty trees begin to part.
I shall discuss this matter to its very core and explain it clearly to you: it is precisely because you have two ears that you do not hear me even when facing me directly.
[The Master] struck [the assembly] and addressed them: "At midnight, autumn insects trample a cow to death; their foul cries spread throughout the Zen lands.
The Buddha of the Sun’s Face is angry with the Buddha of the Moon’s Face; the entire household is filled with sorrow."
The Hundred Houses’ Sorrow. A monk asked, “What is the Buddha? The Master said, “A bottomless cauldron boiling thick gruel. He was asked, “What is the meaning of the West?
The Master said, “Vines and trees intertwine to a height of a hundred fathoms; rising and falling, they curve like dragon-snakes.
A monk requested instruction on the story of the bamboo stick. The Master said, “The pine tree bends in winding curves; the bamboo...”
"Green and straight. If you cannot understand this, go ask the stone at the foot of the steps.

When the monk could not find words to ask, nor could he remain silent, the Master said, "A rat has kicked over the jar of sour pickles. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him, saying, "You have squandered the monastery's property and still do not realize it.
He passed away in the first year of the Chongzhen era. His recorded sayings (*yulu*) were circulated.
Shi (the successor of Han Yuezang):
Chan Master Yimo Hongcheng of Doushuai on Mount Heng in Hangzhou, a native of Qiantang. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with the utmost filial piety.
At twenty-three, he left his family home to undergo tonsure and ordination. He traveled extensively to seek instruction from various lecture halls, including those of Mingzong and Shaojue at Yexi.
Having requested the precepts, he visited Yunqi Zhuhong to practice the six periods of recitation with single-mindedness and without distraction.

Encountering the encouragement of fellow monks to investigate the Way through inquiry, he invited the aged master Hanhui Qi at Xiangfu Temple to establish a retreat session; the Master served as the presiding host.

Just then, Sanfeng Zang passed through Xiangfu, and Qi took the Master along to seek his instruction. Zang said, "If I were to provide an exposition for you, it would only serve to cause you to awaken."
"You have no profound skill or core of realization; you are merely dragging me along with you. The Master then went up to Sanfeng to study, but for seven years he failed to attain awakening.
At that time, his fellow student Tanzu urged him, saying, "This matter has been neglected for many years. If you do not clarify it, how will you ever reach a resolution?
The Master was so overcome with shame and sweat pouring down his back that he could not answer. That night, he sat in meditation until the fourth watch.
Yuan again raised the story of the bamboo whisk to interrogate him. As the Master was about to offer a reply, Yuan suddenly covered the Master’s mouth with his hand.
Thereupon, the Master attained realization and said, “I understand. Yuan said, “Setting aside your understanding for a moment: when birth and death arrive, what then? The Master gave a shout.
Yuan asked, “What is the meaning of that shout? The Master replied, “It cuts off my elder brother’s tongue.”
The Master departed and proceeded straight to the abbot’s quarters to present what he had attained. Xuedou nodded in approval.

One day, while attending Xuedou, the Master saw a monk requesting instruction on the words of the "Three Yuan" (San Yuan). Xuedou took a red paper from atop the desk, turned it over, and showed it to him.
At that moment, the Master suddenly realized the meaning of the phrase: "Two water buffaloes, their horns entangled in a single manger. Xuedou expressed his joy for him, and so...
He was appointed to the first seat. The Master bestowed upon him the robe and whisk as symbols of his lineage and transmission.

He resided at Doushuai Yuan on Mount Xiangshan. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master pointed his staff at the monk's mouth and said, "Swiftly, as the ritual command dictates.
The monk hesitated; the Master struck him three times with the staff. Another monk asked, "What is the upward-moving pivot? The Master—
He said, "A tiger's head grows two horns. [Someone] asked, "What is the final phrase? The Master said, "A pestle ground upon the tail. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"The local deity of Mount Hengshan has meager resources; what it produces is mostly bamboo. Having fashioned bamboo rakes from them, I sell them to various venerable Chan masters.
If you ask for the price, I will strike you right on the mouth with one blow. Shown in the Xinsi year of the Chongzhen era.
Ji was interred at Dengwei. His recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulate in the world. (Sanfeng Zang was his successor.
Chan Master Wenshi Hongcheng of Jiaoshan, Zhenjiang, was the son of Xiong of Jingling. Less than a year after his marriage, he abandoned his wife to shave his head and dye his robes.
He first visited Huangbo, Yunmen, and Jinsu, and later studied under Sanfeng Zang, where he investigated the Way with great diligence for two years.
One day, while standing in attendance, a monk asked Zang, "When there are no walls on the ten directions and no gates on the four sides, what then?

Zang let out a thunderous shout. The Master immediately attained realization and sighed, saying, "The Master’s way of receiving people is exactly like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold.
He then presented a verse, saying: "A single application of the elixir-head; it transforms iron into gold."
"Jin! Even the lamp-stands and pillars would find their souls melting at this. He then presented a verse on the bamboo stick, saying: "To whom shall I tell my innermost heart?
Half is longing for my lord, half is resentment toward him. The moon sets over the clear pool, its night-shadow vanishes; A single cry from a frost-bound wild goose chills the soul in dreams.
Zang Kezhi hid it away. The Master served him diligently for six years. One day, he presented a verse on "having words and having no words," saying:
The two horns support the heavens and enter the earth; their tips curl into a loose, disheveled tail. Who blew this flute atop the high tower?
Plum blossoms fall in confusion as the moon fills the void. Cang nodded his head in approval. Cang raised a question:
"When a monk came to Xuefeng, he propped both hands against the gate of the hermitage and threw his body out. What was the meaning of that? The Master took up his two sandals and kicked them away.
[Zhao] Zang came out. Zang asked again, "When Xuefeng lowered his head and returned to his hut, what was that about?
The Master covered him with his sandals. Zang said, "Is there anything more to it? The Master drew a circle around the sandals. Zang then desisted. (Chongzhen Jisi year).
He entrusted [the teachings] to Zang, who then went to reside at Jiaoshan. King Chu, having heard of the Master’s spiritual transformation, sent letters and gifts to request the Dharma.
In the year Guiyou, he resided at Jiufeng Zhengjue. Ascending the hall, he said: "It covers heaven and earth; it penetrates past and present.

The great void cannot be used as a metaphor for its vastness; a mote of dust cannot be used as a metaphor for its minuteness. When demons and spirits hear this, their hearts shatter with fear. Ghosts... [text breaks off].
The soul of the strange touch vanishes. Now tell me, what is this? A three-headed wooden horse neighs as it departs on the wind;
a one-legged clay ox bellows as it comes under the moon. One day, because a monk requested instruction on the words from the assembly of Sanfeng, the Master said:
"A pile of bricks filtered through the Buddha’s mouth—every character lacks tonal level. Within the staff, a tongue three feet long—every word..."
There was a measuring line. He kicked over the pure flask; Huishan’s nostrils won out, reaching straight up to the heavens.
When a fierce tiger blocks the road, one must stop. Huangbo would have deserved thirty blows. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
In the year Dingchou, Prime Minister He Zhiyue invited the Master to head Tianlong Monastery in the White Gate. Later, due to an invitation from the Prince of Chu, he traveled to Hongshan in Wuchang.

He preached the Dharma. In his later years, he retired to Baiyun on Mount Shen as a means for his leisure in old age. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell, saying:
"If I were to remain long in this world, I fear you all would not give rise to the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find."
"You all should arouse diligent and courageous effort; then you will realize that the principle is appropriate to the occasion and free from obstruction.
Having spoken thus, he composed a verse and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. This was the twentieth day of the eighth month of the year Yiyou of the Shunzhi era.
His disciples erected a stupa on the summit of the mountain behind Baiyun Temple (the successor being Sanfeng Zang).
Chan Master Daśu Zaike Hongzheng of Mount Yu was the son of the Zhu family of Wuxi. From his childhood, he aspired to study Buddhism;
at fourteen, he left the household life. Upon reading the *Cengjin Chan guan* (Exhortations for Progress in the Zen Barrier), he first understood how to apply himself to spiritual practice.
He visited Sanfeng Zang and diligently engaged in intensive inquiry for six years, yet remained entirely without entry. One day, the wall before him stood upright and a white light shone brilliantly.
Suddenly, it was as if his chest and spine were bursting apart. Looking down, he saw the objects behind him on the bed curtains; the entire assembly called him the "Back-Breaking Bhikṣu.
Later, following Master Zang, he went to Huishou on the Lou River. For seven days and nights, his eyes did not blink.

Suddenly, he recalled that the World-Honored One "taught without teaching" and Kāśyapa "heard without hearing," whereupon he attained immediate enlightenment. After four years of study, he received the transmission.
The Robe-Whisk. Continuing the lineage at Sanfeng, he ascended the hall to expound the Dharma. Flowers smile and birds sing; sleep is free from dreams.
Clouds part and the rain clears; there is inspiration for wandering and viewing. As the heavy gates close and the mist withdraws, the Great Being is born with a willow branch whisk.
Now tell me, what dharma-gate is this? Do you understand? He let out a shout and said: "Just realize it in this way!"
Addressing the assembly: Now, one who acts as a patriarchal master must possess the claws and fangs of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and the essential core of the patch-robed monks.
Grasping the handle of the ladle in one’s hand, one must emerge a head above the world. At times, with great capacity and great function, the host yields while testing the guest;

at other times, crouching on the ground or concealing one's form, one acts spontaneously without regard for others. This extends to the arts of killing and giving life, granting and seizing, unfolding and rolling up, suppressing and uplifting—all performed in alternation.

They merely exchange one thing for another, leaving the head while exposing the tail. If one can fully embody the subtlety of all these forms, only then can they emerge into the world as a human being to untangle adhesions and remove fetters.

Reaching the point where one deals with demons before a word is spoken and discerns dragons and snakes beneath the staff—this is originally their ordinary handiwork and their natural fodder; what is there to be extraordinary about? A monk asked: "If..."
"What is the phrase for being human? The Master said: "Green jade encircles the peaks with a thousand bamboos; azure scales fill the ravines with ten thousand pines. "Question:
What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said: "Treading upon the reeds beneath Bodhidharma’s feet.
"Question: Caoshan spoke of three kinds of falling. What is 'falling by category'? The Master said: "A deep, heavy snoring."
[The student] asked, "What is 'falling into accordance'? The Master said, "Going east, going west. [The student] asked, "What is 'falling into nobility'?
The Master said, "Sleeping exposed upon the fragrant grasses. The Master traveled through and resided at famous monasteries. In his later years, he occupied the patriarchal seat at Huazang Monastery.

Following the eras of Mian, Yi’an, and Tudu, the transmission of the Dharma teachings had not been heard; it was until the Master’s time that the Dharma assembly was restored to its former glory, and his spiritual influence spread far and wide.
[He] passed away on the sixteenth day of the ninth month of the Bingxu year of the Shunzhi era. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Sanfeng (the successor of Han Yue Zang).
Chan Master Dingmu Hongche of Riguang Qingliang Temple in Suzhou, a descendant of the Jinling Bai clan, lost his father in childhood and had no opportunity for formal study;
nevertheless, he knew how to serve the Buddha. At the age of twenty-four, he went to Sanfeng Zang to receive the tonsure and served as a rice-gatherer. Zang...
One day he asked, "What is the purpose of leaving the household life? The Master said, "I am here to study the scriptures.
Huizang said, "I have been traveling with you until my hair has turned white; what can be done about birth and death? The Master was startled and asked, "How then may one attain it?

Huizang replied, "I regard you as being like wood or stone. First, uphold this verse to awaken your wisdom. He orally transmitted the verse of Nan-yen for him to hold, and the Master applied his mind to it.
He did not cease his practice. Every time he went down the mountain to collect food, the thirty-li round trip left him as if he were a fool or a pillar;
children would mock him, yet he would sometimes lean against a mountain crag for the whole day, forgetting to move a step. For three years he continued thus without the slightest slackening.

One day, he suddenly perceived that the sound of the wind and the songs of the birds were all reciting this verse. He thought to himself: "Having reached this point, why have I not understood its meaning until now? Thereupon—

Seeking advancement, he spent seven days at the Guanzhong Barrier (Guangzhou) investigating it with all his might. As soon as his foot crossed the threshold, everything before his eyes vanished in a flash, and the great earth sank level beneath him.
He suddenly realized the meaning of the verse and hurried to the abbot’s quarters intending to pose his question. However, Master Zang immediately drove him away.

It was the time of the Upper Yuan Festival, the snow had cleared, and there was an Arhat playing with the snow in the courtyard. Master Zang ordered the assembly to compose a verse on this; the Master was asked to transcribe it, and he presented the following verse: *Vast...*
A lone snow-robed Arhat in the void—where could one find a judge for the end of such contemplation? A single shard of an ice-basin is difficult to point toward or describe;
it arrives precisely on the fifteenth day of the first month. He treasured this and remarked: "Only you, Illusory Void, harbor hidden dragons and coiled serpents;
were you to encounter the spring thunder, mountains would topple and ravines would overflow. One day later, he heard the sound of a bamboo chair falling over and was suddenly enlightened.

He attained great enlightenment. Xuechou Zang expressed his joy and bestowed upon him the name Dingmu (Eye on the Crown). He presented a verse, saying: "One eye is not enough for viewing; two eyes are still insufficient for viewing.

Only by possessing the Eye of the Crown can one simultaneously exercise both granting and withholding. The Master attended him as a disciple for fifteen years, daily attaining the profound depths of the Dharma.
In the Jisi year of the Chongzhen era, Xuechou Zang conferred the seal of transmission upon him. Thereupon, he succeeded to the Dharma seat of Sanfeng. Afterwards...
Moving to Suzhou Rui Guang and ascending the hall at Jinkou Jinshan, he brandished his whisk and said: "The green shade spreads across the ground as spring draws to a close;
beneath the trees, a gentle breeze heralds the arrival of summer. In this fleeting passage of time, you must rouse a fierce resolve;
when the thread at your heels snaps, your roar shall shake the thunder. He then gave a shout and said: "If you can see through to the very top and the very bottom in this one blow..."
Then there will be no barrier that cannot be penetrated and no matter that remains unresolved.
Where else would there be any further effort to be made, or any *huatou* (critical phrase) to investigate? Even if you do not yet attain realization, this very shout itself is the *huatou*.

Simply direct your investigation here—investigating horizontally and vertically, standing as firm as a wall ten thousand fathoms high, and pressing forward with all your might until you reach a place where the path of thought is blocked.

This is precisely the moment for a sudden awakening. When words fail to convey it, you must immediately fix your eyes and gaze upon it—like a cat pouncing on a mouse, its four paws planted firmly on the ground, head and tail in a straight line, all its senses directed forward;
when it intends to strike, there is no miss. When you reach this point, you turn yourself around and attain the Great Function.
If you can move as swiftly as a flash of lightning or a shooting star, I shall overturn the abysses and topple the mountains. Is there anyone who can do so?
"Is there anyone? A monk came forward and bowed. The Master then descended from his seat and gave a small lecture:
"If we discuss the supreme point beyond, the mouths of all Buddhas are too narrow; the patriarchs find it difficult to lift it up, and even this mountain monk’s tongue is knotted.

Having no choice, I shall take the great void as my mouth and Mount Sumeru as my tongue, stirring them through the ten directions to speak for the sake of the assembly. The green bamboo shakes its staff..."
Pine trees wave their brooms; birds sing and monkeys howl. Orioles call as flowers fall; strange rocks tower with jagged peaks; flowing springs murmur; wind arises and the sea surges;

vapors rise to form towers and pavilions. This is precisely what is meant by "the teaching of the land," "the teaching of sentient beings," and "the teaching of all things throughout the three periods of time."
He spoke with fervor without ceasing. "The great assembly, tell me: what was it that he said? After a long silence, he said: "Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ. Small-scale Sermon:
"If you can penetrate through, I shall give you a slap. If you cannot penetrate, my palm shall bleed. Ultimately, how would one explain this?
The waves of the Nine Peaks and Three Lakes overflow the heavens; the vast earth stretches on, yet people do not recognize it. The Lion..."
A single roar from amidst the clouds; the great earth, mountains, and rivers become one expanse of snow. *Tuḥ!* Ascending the hall: Today is the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
The bright moon hangs in the sky, pure and radiant. Perfectly full, without flaw and without excess, its tenfold brilliance is entirely revealed.
Suddenly, the bronze mirror is turned over; the great earth, mountains, and rivers all turn pitch black. At this moment—
The essential point lies in the definitive conclusion. If it is definitive, it is like a pure lapis lazuli vessel containing a precious moon;
if it is not definitive, the hundred-jeweled pearls all lose their luster. Truly thorough! *Du-du-du!* Deep in the night, let us together gaze upon the snow on a thousand crags.

The Layman Huang Hai-an, the Judicial Commissioner, came to pay his respects. He arrived just as the Master was ascending the hall. The layman stepped forward and asked: "When you block off the vital ford—"
"What? the Master asked. "Where did you get this news? The Layman clapped his hands once and said, "The assembly, look!
The Master said, "You are merely pretending to be the host. The Layman gave a shout, and the Master struck him. In his later years, he retired at Qionglung Nianhua Temple in Suzhou.
In the *Xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era, the Imperial Relative, Minister of Works Tian Hongyu, was granted gold by imperial decree [to support the temple].

Wearing a robe with a pleated lower garment (*lanjiasha*), the fourfold assembly repeatedly urged the Master to leave the mountains to guide and transform others. The Master firmly declined, refusing their request.
On the eighth day of the ninth month of the Wuzi year of the Shunzhi era, he passed away. He left behind a verse which says: "At the age of sixty-one, I have finished entrusting both my hands."

Sitting alone, he made no distinction between high and low; amidst the leisurely white clouds, his presence was never absent. At the call of a servant to burn incense, he passed away in serene stillness.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the Zhenzong Hall to the right of the temple. Zhang Sīnóng Yǒuyù composed the inscription for it.
His disciples Jìsēn and Chóngxū compiled his *Yùlù* (Recorded Sayings) in four fascicles, which circulated in the world. (Han Yue Zàng was his successor.)
Chan Master Hanyu Hongyuan of Xianing Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhu family of Gusu. He was of robust and imposing stature, earning him the epithet "Jade Maitreya.
At the age of ten, he left home to become a monk at Shengxiang Temple in Taicang. At fifteen, he dreamed of wandering through hell, which led him to awaken to the illusory nature of the human world;
from then on, his resolve to seek the Way became most earnest. At nineteen, he went to attend upon Yunqi and asked:

"What is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Xiqi smiled and did not answer. The Master was perplexed by this. Later, he visited Sanfeng Zang and investigated the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one.
He attained a slight degree of awakening, yet he had not yet achieved complete clarity. Consequently, while traveling with Lingyin Li, they were detained by snow at Chang'an Town.
There, he repeatedly received encouragement and exhortation, and suddenly attained a realization. He remained in close attendance upon Sanfeng for twenty years, [deeply...]
Having entered the profound depths of the Dharma, he finally received the entrustment. He went forth to reside at Xianning on Gaoting Mountain.

A monk asked, “What is the matter within the Gate of the School? The Master raised his whisk and showed it to him, saying, “That is merely the business of the outer gate.
The monk asked, “How do you proclaim it? The Master struck once with the whisk and said, “Speak! Speak! The monk asked, “As for the matter within the inner sanctum, how is it ultimately?
The Master drew a circle and added three dots inside it. The monk bowed and said, “I thank the Master for this instruction. The Master [said], “Go away!”
