Two verses [were spoken]. He passed away while sitting upright in meditation on the eleventh day of the eleventh month of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era. He was sixty-three years old.
His final instruction was to cremate his body; his remains were collected and a stupa was erected at the mountain’s base (the successor being Sanfeng Zang).
Chan Master Poushi Hongbi of Suzhou Dengwu was the son of the Zheng family of Wuxi. Having lost his father at the age of nine, he became aware of the great matter of birth and death.
At twelve, he sought to leave the household life; at seventeen, he received the tonsure and dyed his robes.

He devoted himself to the study of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for five years. At twenty-two, he visited Sanfeng Zang to inquire about the essential instructions for practicing Chan meditation. After two seasons of winter and summer had passed, every day...

In the evening, he did not slacken his efforts. Later, he entered the Hall of Diligent Practice (*Saddhā-vīrya-śālā*) and set a deadline to realize the realization. On the third day, he suddenly raised a fan and struck his own face;
he then attained sudden enlightenment regarding the words and phrases of the Patriarchs. He composed a verse on the Qingzhou monk’s robe, which says: "The Qingzhou cotton robe weighs seven catties."
A biting, vicious dog crouches at the gate; having eaten his fill of rice balls, he is exhausted all day long. Turning over, he tramples the broken sand-pot to pieces.
Zangyin said, "Your realization is just like mine was in the beginning.

He then received full ordination and traveled everywhere to visit various masters, including the venerable elders of Boshan, Huangbo, and Mount Kuanglu. He subsequently journeyed through the two Zhejiang provinces to pay his respects at Jinsu.

Ultimately, he remained in doubt because the Great Dharma had not been fully penetrated. Consequently, he returned once more to the forge of Sanfeng, where he was subjected to rigorous pressure and intense scrutiny.

On the first day of the New Year in the Dingmao year of the Tianqi era, while prostrating before an elderly master, he attained sudden enlightenment regarding the fundamental principles of the school.
When Master Zang heard of this, he immediately beat the drum and ascended the seat to interrogate him. When the Master came forward, his words were in perfect accord with the truth.
Zang looked at the assembly and sighed, saying, "A true lion cub; he truly roars the lion's roar. After eight years had passed, Zang personally wrote out the lineage of Linji and entrusted it to him.

Thereupon, [Zhaozhou] succeeded him as the abbot of Sheng'en. He ascended the hall and said: "Buddha after Buddha hands it down, using emptiness to seal emptiness; patriarch after patriarch transmits it..."

The mind is like water merging with water. Therefore, from the time of the ancient patriarchs, in their reception of beings and benefitting of life, they sometimes used words and phrases, sometimes employed the staff or the shout, sometimes presented critical situations, sometimes drew circular diagrams, sometimes displayed physical gestures, and sometimes gave instruction through silence—all of these were direct pointers to the fundamental great matter right before one's own eyes.
Alas, how is it that people are unable to realize this directly?
Indeed. Thus one fails the various sages and buries one's own spirit. Today, Mount Deng has no choice but to provide a provisional indication.
He then set down his staff and said: "A true lion leaps with skill; a wild jackal guards its den.
When the antelope hangs from its horns, all traces are lost. Entering the hall, he said: "The eye for the moment is peerless throughout the ages. Or..."
Whether yielding or seizing, there is a beginning and an end; lightning cannot catch up, and sparks from flint cannot penetrate.

If you hesitate to deliberate, white clouds stretch ten thousand miles. Entering the hall: lifting tea and washing the bowl are nothing other than one’s fundamental livelihood; clearing the throat and stretching the limbs—
All of this is the wondrous functioning of spiritual powers. Wherever the eye touches, it is Mañjuśrī’s samādhi; wherever the ear hears, it is Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration.
Everywhere is the Dharma-gate of Maitreya; every step is the realm of Samantabhadra. But tell me, where is Vairocana?
"Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; stream water is as clear as indigo. The Master would often pose this question in his room, saying:
"To bring forth one as function is most manifest. How do you understand this? He further said: "One can speak it but cannot act it out;
one can act it out but cannot speak it. Such a person sees only one side. Right now, how do you speak it? How do you act it out?"
He further said: "To have a head but no tail is not permissible; to have a tail but no head is not permissible. What is the phrase for both head and tail?

Among those who had traveled extensively to study under various masters, there were few who could penetrate his essential point. In his daily life, the Master sat peacefully upon a single mat, remaining silent all day long.
For thirty years, he did not set foot in a city or town. As his Dharma path gradually became renowned, he began to manifest his spiritual power and forge disciples.

In his training, he did not rely on mere words or facial expressions; if there was even the slightest lack of accord, he would immediately rebuke them with a stern countenance. When preaching the Dharma, he absolutely refused to allow anything to be recorded.
His disciples privately compiled his teachings and requested permission to publish them in woodblocks, but the Master did not grant it.

On the second day before the New Year’s Eve of the Jiyou year of the Kangxi era (1709), as the Master was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he took leave of his old friends, distributed his robes and alms bowl, toured the various quarters of the monastery, and gave them a final, earnest instruction.
Hei. At deep night, he returned to his quarters, gathered his saṃghāṭī robe, took a few steps, and passed away. He was seventy-two years old.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the Huayan Altar at his home mountain (the lineage of Sanfeng Zang).
Chan Master Yupo Honghong of the Huayan lineage in Wujiang was the son of the Jiang family of Pilin. By nature, he was extremely intelligent.
Having lost his mother at a young age, his father took him to Mount Sanfeng to seek ordination, entrusting him to serve as an attendant. After a long time, he attained realization.
One day, when Master Zang was ascending the hall, the Master (Xuefeng) came forward and prostrated. Zang struck him immediately. The Master said, "I already know your divine spirit;
please do not strike me first. Zang made a loud sound. The Master said, "Facing you directly as an opponent, I request the Master to advance for battle.
Zang struck him again with his staff three times. The Master said, "Today I have personally seen the Master," and then he prostrated. Zang nodded in approval. Wén.
After long study, he finally obtained the seal of realization. He went forth to reside at Huayan Monastery on Wujiang. A monk asked, "The Master An-yin composed writings to save the five schools;
when you, Reverend, appear in the world, which school do you save? The Master struck him and said, "For now, I shall save this one school.
The monk asked, "As for Tiantong, who frequently used the staff to respond to stimuli, why do you say he did not regard the host and guest? The Master said:
"First receive the message from the staff of Tiantong; then I will discuss guest and host with you at leisure. When a monk hesitated, the Master shouted him away.
He once said to the assembly: "There are depths and shallows in the realization of the Way, but there is no distinction in the preaching of the Dharma."
Therefore it is said: Within a single phrase, there are contained the fundamental and the essential, the guest and the host, the provisional and the real, and illumination and function.
Those who have not yet penetrated the guiding principles do not know this. If one penetrates the guiding principles thoroughly, the Great Dharma originally contains no such manifold matters;

what "Great Dharma" or "Small Dharma," what "extraordinary" or "subtle mystery," could there be to provide you with a conceptual understanding? It is further said: Nowadays, the eye of the Way is not clear.
Those who have transcended the world are many. Yet, upon the high seat before the great assembly, they brandish their staffs and strike recklessly;
they raise their fly-whisks and deceive or slander others, coveting honor and material gain, acting as if they were deaf and blind.
"Is this not enough to drive one to distraction? You say: 'Muzhou always kept his door shut; Luzu spent his whole life facing the wall.

Is this acting for the sake of others, or is it not? In the Jīmō year of the Chongzhen era, the Master fell ill. A monk requested instruction, asking: "When birth and death arrive, what is to be done?
The Master said: "Lacking even a single moment of birth; having even a single extra moment of non-death. He then passed away.

He entered *parinirvāṇa*. Furthermore, a monk asked, "I request that you entrust me with the affairs for after your passing. The Master said, "When a person faces old age, sickness, and death, that is the end of it.
Why bother with square tombs or round mounds?

However, after my death, I shall undergo cremation, and my remains shall be placed within the *pútóng* (universal) stupa, to signify that life and death are never apart from the great assembly. After his passing, his disciples followed his final instructions and respectfully...
[He was] unbroken [in his lineage]. He was enshrined to the left of the Patriarchal Stupa at the Ten-Thousand Peaks (the Three Peaks [lineage] was transmitted by Zang).
Chan Master Juede Hongli of Lingyin, Hangzhou, was the son of the Zhang family of Kuaiji.

In his youth he was devoted to the study of the *Yuan* (Metaphysics), and as he grew older he took a liking to the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). He went to Putuo to receive the tonsure and subsequently attended lecture halls. There he heard that Sanfeng Zang was opening a Dharma assembly at An’yun Temple.
He hurried to see him. At first, he investigated the "original face" koan. One day, while looking into a mirror, he had a sudden realization. Yunmen did not grant him approval.
Later, while serving as the latrine attendant, as he was carrying excrement down the mountain, the pole shifted on his shoulder and the yoke snapped; at that moment, he attained sudden enlightenment.

His spiritual capacity manifested with sudden brilliance; he was known throughout the monastic communities as "Iron [Bundle]. Subsequently, he traveled extensively to visit various masters before returning to reside under Master Zang at Dengwu.

There, he secretly realized the profound essence of the ultimate teaching. Master Zang appointed him as the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable of the Hall), where he managed the entire assembly. Not long after, however, he took his leave once more.
Upon hearing that Master Zang had entered the "dead-monk's gate" (*si guan*), the Master hurried back to pay his respects and receive his final instructions. Therein it says:
The verse says: Dwelling in the mountains, I have nurtured until the conditions were ripe; I sought extensively for those with true, authentic iron-bone Chan.

Do not fail the old monk’s earnest entrustment; ruthlessly eliminate demons and outsiders to establish the true transmission. In the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era, while residing at Guangxiao Temple in Yunmen.
Tilling with the blade and sowing by fire—this bears the style of the ancient worthies. Monks all vie to rely upon him. Entering the hall for the discourse:
"The spring breeze sweeps vast; the spring air is harmonious. The countenances of the successive patriarchs are manifest; the original mind of the infant is still present.

The Master of the School acts as their guide into the Way; virtuous friends act as their companions. With such a mind and such a resolve, one enters the forest without disturbing the grass. Entering...
The water does not stir its waves; there is not a single blade of grass that does not manifest the golden body, nor a single drop of water that does not circulate the benefit of the Dharma.

Nevertheless, if you wish to recognize the meaning of Buddha-nature, you must observe the conditions of time and season. When the time and season arrive, manifest true diligence and true Dharma-offerings.
(He lets out a shout. [He descends from his seat. Ascending the hall: Nature arises from conditions; the people of Shuangjing come from Heaven.

Above, we have discussed practicing in accordance with the Dharma. Those from Vulture Peak have returned to the Double Path (Shuangjing). Nevertheless, the guest remains a guest from beginning to end, and the host remains a host from beginning to end.
One must not travel at night without holding a torch; one must directly face the people on the path for a small discourse (*xiaocan*).
"Good snow covers the head and blankets the feet. The old hermit in his mountain cottage stirs the ashes and plays with the fire.
Monks from the Five Lakes tread through the snow to seek out plum blossoms; they stir the ashes and play with fire. This is the realm of Mañjuśrī.
Treading through the snow to seek plum blossoms is the very face of Samantabhadra. A blue lion transforms into a white lion; the old blue lion becomes an old white lion.
Fortunately, Old Xiangxiang is of one flavor, the true color and the true portion. But tell me, what is this matter of the true color and the true portion?
After a long silence, he said: "Washing rice and washing vegetables; carrying water and moving firewood; welcoming guests and seeing them off; following the custom to pass through the hall.
Speaking of Chan or speaking of the Way need not wait for the formal assembly; clenching the fist without seams when gathering it up, opening the palm when letting it go."

Without partiality, neither constrained nor relaxed; Mount Sumeru stands towering, the ocean waters surge, the great earth quakes, and the sun’s orb blazes—truly there is such a work that startles the multitudes.
The dragon yields its palace to the dragon; the tiger yields its lair to the tiger; the Buddha yields his land to the Buddha.
In the Buddha-land, he attains equal and perfect enlightenment; in the dragon-palace, he attains equal and perfect enlightenment.
In the tiger’s den; in the tiger’s den, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment. In all places, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment.
Thereafter, this essential mystery is sealed shut: the dragon knows it not, the tiger understands it not, and even the Buddha does not recognize it.

Spontaneously, Mount Sumeru becomes still and tranquil, the waves of the ocean subside, the great earth is at peace, and the sun’s orb shines in full radiance. Thus it is with me here at Jingshan, together with my disciples.
As for this point: how so? Each returns to the hall to drink tea. Entering the hall: where one lets go of body and life, the woodcutter’s axe-handle reaches the heavens;
where the mind is level and ever-true, the fisherman’s line emerges from the sea. Three inches away from the hook, he has caught every *kūṇ* and *jīng*;
sitting serenely on the Five Peaks, he directs the dragons and elephants. How much more so when the fragrant breeze blows from the south—the patch-robed monks spread their mats!
The lapel. Alone he obtains sweet rain filling the sky; the old farmer sows his seed. Simultaneously amidst the dust, recognize the patriarch.
Among the hundred grasses, he rouses his descendants. Where the student exerts effort, not even a breath can pass.
Seizing it, he uses it immediately. "The person of yesterday was Zishao; today it is this man. Clapping their hands together, he strikes the whisk and says: "Still there is a little difference. Up!

The Master stood in the hall, held up his whisk, and said, "Look! Look! The mountains, rivers, and the great earth flow forth from within this. The four sages and the six classes of beings flow forth from within this.
He struck the whisk and shouted, "Cutting off all streams, the mountains and rivers cast no shadows; the sages and common folk leave no tracks."

Although this is so, phenomena do not follow a single direction; principle values universal accessibility. The Buddha is the shadow-grass of sentient beings, and sentient beings are the shadow-grass of the Buddha.
Each shadow-grass is the very face of Linji; this very face is the Buddha, the place where the entire body of the Venerable Elder manifests.
If we speak of the functioning of the whole body, meeting a Buddha, one strikes the Buddha; meeting a Patriarch, one strikes the Patriarch. Ultimately...
"How can one ensure that practice is not in vain? [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "A true Zen guest turns at a single push.

To leave such a master frustrated is like trying to pierce with a needle where there is no opening. Even if you all were to shout from the east and shout from the west, would that have anything to do with this matter?
You simply do not realize that sometimes this mountain monk’s single shout is like deploying an army on the back of a river; sometimes..."
One shout: adding to the hearth while withdrawing the troops. Sometimes one shout: reducing the hearth to lure the enemy.
Sometimes one shout: a hidden crossbow at a wooden gate. Do you all still understand the advantage and the peril? One day the Master picked up a grain of rice and showed it to the assembly, saying:
"Do you see this single grain? It is most supreme and most noble, beyond comparison and peerless. If you look to the left, you will achieve the center."
Looking at it from the right, it is "partial yet central. Looking at it from the center, it is "central yet coming forward.

Looking at it from below, it is "comprehensive yet arrived. Looking at it from above, it is "comprehensive yet reached. If you look at it as a whole, he throws down some rice, makes a thunderous sound, and shouts:
"There is no place for you to fix your eyes! He addresses the assembly: "Since childhood, I have raised a tawny-tailed tiger; its life depends on meat. Because..."
He did not eat his own food at all. Standing with his staff propped upright, he said, "Tianning does not know how to avoid forbidden foods. A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return? The Master said, "A rat bites a cat. A monk asked, "What is the true person of no station? The Master said, "A rat bites a cat."
The Master said, "A flash of joy, a flash of anger. Question: "What is the 'arrow-point' pivot? The Master said, "Neither yields to the other.
Question: "Tsk! Tsk! Having a basis, what do you rely upon? The Master said, "An infant riding a white elephant.

The Master presided over ten monasteries in succession, yet he remained at Lingyin alone for the longest time. Although it suffered the calamity of fire, he renovated the old and established the new; his Dharma seat flourished.

His reputation grew even more flourishing, and his assembly of students reached tens of thousands. Later, he retired to Mount Shuangjing; not long after, Tianning Temple in Yangzhou invited him again, and the Master joyfully accepted.
Upon his arrival, monastics gathered like clouds. As he preached the Dharma in response to their needs, it was twice as frequent as usual.

Only seven days had passed when he ordered the preparation of an offering for the entire mountain. That evening, they engaged in intense discussion until past midnight before he finally retired to rest. When he awoke...
On the nineteenth day of the tenth month of the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era, he rose at dawn, changed his clothes and shoes, and hurriedly called for his attendant.
He stamped his foot once and said, "Quickly follow me to the upper realm. The attendant monk arrived in haste, but the Master had already passed away.
His age was sixty-eight; his years since ordination were forty-seven. Three days later, his disciples sealed the coffin within the earthen niche.

He was welcomed back to Lingyin Monastery, where a stupa was erected for him at Huiri Xuan. His *yulu* (recorded sayings) in thirty volumes circulated throughout the world. (Han Yue Zang was his successor.
Chan Master Tuweng Hongchu of Lingyan in Suzhou was the son of the Li family from Tongzhou in Jiangsu. While his mother Gao was dreaming of a monk offering her a golden ring, she gave birth to him.
At the age of seven, he observed the fasts and already knew how to serve the Buddha. As he grew older, he applied himself with diligent effort.
With the two characters for "birth and death" (saṃsāra) across his chest, he traveled to visit various Dharma masters and eminent elders throughout the Fakan Valley and other regions.
Having resolved to leave the household life, his parents did not grant their permission. At the age of twenty-five, due to the guidance of Master Hengshan Cheng, he [proceeded].

Upon meeting Sanfeng Zang, he was immediately granted the tonsure and full ordination. Over the following year, while serving Zang at the An-yin Monastery in Hangzhou, he vowed to realize the Way within seven days.
On the sixth day, sitting upright like a cast statue, the hall opened for the period of quietude;
seeing two rows of monks facing one another in greeting, his body suddenly collapsed with a loud crash. That which had remained obscure through accumulated kalpas manifested completely before him.
He hurried straight to the Abbot’s quarters. When Master Zang saw him from afar, he immediately said, “Behold the arrow! The Master threw himself down.
At that moment, Hóng of Huáyán called out from the side, “Brother, why do you not prostrate? The Master then went down.

That evening, during the informal discourse (*xiǎocān*), as the Master was about to prostrate, Master Zang asked, “The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? The Master replied, “Precisely this very day, the winter solstice.”
On the third day of the month, Xuedou said, "Is it the same as Zhaozhou’s robe, or is it different? The Master replied, "A drop of water, a drop of frost.
Xuedou asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? At that moment, the bell tolled in the main hall. The Master said, "The sound of the bell bites through my seven-strip robe.
During the midday meal, Xuedou cited Zhaozhou, who said, "For thirty years, I have not used a distracted mind, except for the two times [of eating]."

"Congee and rice are objects that involve the mixed application of the mind. He then pointed to the inside and outside of his alms bowl and said, "This rice involves the mixed application of the mind; these bamboo shoots involve the mixed application of the mind.

The Master pointed to his chest and said, "It is this [chest] that involves the mixed application of the mind. Xuanzang said, "I have committed a transgression. The Master performed a prostration and said:
From this day forward, Hongchu did not dare to answer a word again. A monk asked his fellow student Xue-sheng, "When the red sun rises, what will you do?
Xue-sheng requested the Master to speak on his behalf. The Master said, "How could a mountain stream ever hold it back?"

"In the end, they all return to the great ocean to become waves and tides. Just as he was completing his period of service with propriety within the city, Xue Shengli came forward and asked about the rites.
The questions and answers were no different from before. When Zang heard this, he said, "These two sons shall cause my lineage to flourish. The Master again served him diligently for three years.
He further attained the ultimate profundity. The Tripitaka was thus the source of his scriptural lineage, entrusted to him by his master.

Initially, he resided at Xiangfu Temple on Mount Fupeo in Changzhou, where he displayed the essential tenets of the Five Schools in the Dharma Hall and manifested twelve kinds of sun-rotating *samādhi* within his quarters to verify the capacities of those yet to come.

Later, he withdrew to Mount Tiantai, remaining in seclusion for three years without descending the mountain. Upon being invited by the local magistrate Wen Keji to reside at the National [Temple], he accepted.
Cheng ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said, "The heart-essence of Bodhidharma has been transmitted down to this day; were it even slightly off-kilter, it would already be tomorrow.
He struck the floor once with the staff and said, "What further day do you wait for? He then ascended the hall. "The weather is cold and the days are short."
Three pieces of firewood burned in the shape of the Chinese character "Pin" (品). Without needing to poke or stir them, the flames blazed forth as they preached the Dharma.
The walls have ears; they heard it most intimately. Since there was no sevenfold confusion or eightfold disorder, nor did one fall into duality or triad.
Directly revealing the true teaching, it is truly capable of shattering [delusion]. If a person can penetrate this, they will be able to emerge from the realms of the five aggregates.

[The Master] lets out a shout and says: "Do not say that this old monk does not treat people with urgency! Ascending the hall, he said: "One who speaks well of words—those words are like thunderous fire.
One who traces well the tracks—those tracks are like the light of the moon. To call this 'the single pivot of the ultimate' is still merely within the realm of the disciples."
This matter requires that, within the gate of the Patriarchs, one extend a single hand;

it must be entirely transcendent yet grounded in reality, exhausting all subtleties until even the spirits of all sages are brought down simultaneously. Its natural bearing is such that who could possibly grasp it? (He strikes the meditation staff.)

The assembly descends from their seats; the Master ascends the hall. This old monk has not opened the hall for a long time due to illness. Without cause, he has been pushed into the ancestral temple by others.
Since I am now a descendant in his lineage, how could I bear to shrink from the blade or avoid the arrow? To abandon my own field and weed another’s—this would be unacceptable.
Therefore, I shall borrow your clappers and mallets to assist me, performing the play as the occasion demands, while devas and humans gather around.
Amidst the gathering, one must see through the ancestral lineages and schools. Before nobility and meanness have taken form, recognize your original face.
Only then will you believe that by the platform of Master Sheng, the wind and moon have always been present; and before the shrine of Duandubu, the forests and peaks remain as they were.

If you ask further about the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma, how could it be anything other than adding a handle to the alms bowl? Ascending the hall, he let out a shout and said: "A slumbering tiger has turned over!"
It is the body itself. It truly causes wind to arise in the great ravines and its majesty to command the long forests. Foxes and hares hide their tracks; mountain sprites and demons vanish from view.
If one intends to manifest one's true face and deploy one's claws and fangs right here, it is a pity that such a worthy opponent is rarely encountered.
Then, picking up his staff, he said: "Look, look! Today this mountain monk enters the tiger’s den to seek out the tiger cub. There was [a sound].
"Those who are bold enough to disregard peril and ruin—can you follow step for step and stride for stride? After a long silence, he threw down his staff and said:
"If you wish to startle the multitude and rival the victors, you must straightaway transform into a dragon throughout the night. He ascended the hall.
Whenever a monk stepped forward, the Master would strike him and drive him away in the same manner. He then took his seat, picked up his staff, and said: "Since the seven Buddhas of the past..."
With such methods and such a forge, he smelts this troop of dragons and elephants, forging them into this protective community.
He severs all life-roots and blocks every path of escape; he allows them neither to crouch nor to sit.

He would rather have them point to a deer as a horse than tolerate their wasting away on salt and vinegar, like the common run of people in recent times who carry [their ignorance] in carts and measure it in pecks.
This measure has been proclaimed everywhere. Five hundred years ago, the venerable Master Long also personally broke it open:
"The first stroke is true practice; the second medicine is wondrous awakening. Today, this unworthy grandson takes up his broom and sweeps it all away at once.
He strikes the meditation staff once and says: "If you wish to keep the fire in the brazier ever-renewed and unceasing, everyone, pull it out!"
He stood upon a stone among dry trees that had no roots. A monk came and paid his respects, saying, “I beg the Master for instruction.
The Master extended both hands. The monk said, “I do not understand, Disciple. The Master said, “Carrying firewood and drawing water are entirely dependent on the power of others.
One day, while walking in the mountains, a monk asked, “Where is the Master going? The Master raised one foot and said, “To here.”
"Go! The monk hesitated. The Master struck him with his palm and said, "You do not even know where to go.

One day, the Master saw a layman looking into a mirror and asked, "What is a man of the Way taking care of? The layman was speechless. The Master said, "Why do you not say, 'I seek only to see through him'?
He successively resided at Xinghua, Lingshi, Tianting Ruiyan, and Lingyin in Suzhou.
At the monasteries of Fuhou at Mount Yu, Longhua at Huaiyang, Jinsu at Xiuzhou, and Fuyan at Mount Nanyue, crowds gathered like clouds and rain wherever he went.
Yet the Master had no lingering attachment; he took sole delight in the majestic elevation of Lingyan Mountain, which rises above the seventy-two peaks like surging billows.
He resided there alone for a long time, establishing the six accomplishments and the eight essential gates. By means of these six...

There is no fixed rule or prohibition that can contain this. He ascended the hall and said: "My waist is stiff and my back is sore; it is difficult to stand for long. As soon as I approach the meditation seat, sleepiness comes upon me.
Before me is a magnificent mountain; beneath my feet are spirited monks, all crowding together like creditors pressing for payment.
I shake out the fragments within my belly, yet in the end, I cannot gather them up. Though I try again and again, there is no remedy to be applied."
I have briefly deliberated with you all on these points: first, one must not sever the stream of birth and death; second, one must not occupy the seat of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
third, one must not arbitrarily distinguish between guest and host; fourth, one must not engage in the frantic pursuit of question and answer; fifth, one must not pander to the whims of the occasion;
sixth, one must not settle for a state of ordinary, mundane reality. Have you not heard? That even the absence of the slightest speck of dust is still a form of contention.
Dharma. He took up his staff, struck once, and said: "Though the House of Han had its Three Codes of Law, how could they compare to Lingyan’s 'Six Non-acceptances'?

In the ninth month of the Renzi year of the Kangxi era, the Master fell ill. He first composed his own funerary inscription for the stupa, and further inscribed the seal for the enshrinement of his remains, saying:
"What need is there for a tower piercing the clouds built of river stones? It would save the fragrant casket from being buried in the ground. White bones..."
Like a mound of earth covered in frost, the Cold Peak of the Wondrous Summit admits no artifice. On the twenty-seventh day, as he was about to pass away, he wrote these words of instruction:
"There are further urgent matters to be spoken; you must provide them. The Way values truth.
I was born on the eighth day of the second month in the year of Yisi (1605) of the Ming Wanli era at the time of sunrise. Sixty-seven years have passed. Remember this. He signed it: Ge.

Fujibakushi’s "Toppling the Sun" is a total prohibition against scattering flowers upon withered wood. How could the brilliant masters of former generations have ever fixed their gaze upon the very tips of branches?
To see gods and ghosts—this is the tradition of various schools in recent times;

every master claims to know when the time has come, and everyone sits and dies or stands and passes away. This is truly laughable. If my descendants were to live in such times, they would still surpass them.
Regarding the carving of my body for posterity, I shall do it myself; I must not seek out famous calligraphers to falsely embellish my life, thereby increasing my karmic burden.
Nor shall I permit the performance of the seven-day rites, the offering of vegetarian feasts, or entry into secular society.
Furthermore, neither eminent masters nor their disciples shall be allowed to seal the coffin or light the funeral pyre—engaging in such useless matters. Having finished writing, he said: "Old man..."
The Master felt that his practice of the Way had not been sufficiently diligent and that he was ashamed before his late teacher at Sanfeng. He then requested a bath and changed his robes;
after drinking a single cup of tea, he sat upright in the full lotus posture and passed away. His disciples followed his final instructions and kept the coffin for twenty-one days.

During the cremation, extraordinary light was emitted and a sound like thunder shook the air. After the fire subsided, śarīra were recovered, along with a crystalline image. His crown and teeth remained uncorrupted.

His stupa was erected at the summit of Yao Peak and named the "Great Luminous Treasury" (Dà Guānmíng zàng). His recorded sayings from various assemblies comprise over one hundred fascicles and circulate in the world.
(Sānfēng Zàng was his successor.)
Chan Master Hongxian Shuangji Huirun of Huzhou was the son of the Liu family of Wujin, Changzhou.

He studied under Chan Master Zang of Sanfeng at Dengwu, where he investigated the "Cloud Gate’s Broken Leg" koan. One day, after Chan Master Zang had finished presenting the koan during the evening assembly, a monk was just about to step forward when Zang rose and immediately left the Dharma Hall.
At that moment, the Master suddenly attained realization and composed a verse, saying: "Just as he came, he seized me..."

The two gates are the barrier; within them, the power is so great it shatters a thousand mountains. If one asks about the meaning of the broken leg from those years ago, even now the blood-stains are visible upon the pillar.
One day, while Master Zang was ascending the hall, as soon as the Master (Xuedou) stepped out, Zang said, "I do not permit a question regarding the first phrase;
there is no need for a question regarding the second phrase. As soon as these words were spoken, the Master let out a shout and said, "Tell me, which one is this?"

[The Master] said, "One phrase. This was the second phrase. Zang then struck him. The Master prostrated and departed. Thereafter, he attended to [Zhang] by carrying his handkerchief and water pitcher, and day by day he attained the profound depths of the ultimate mystery.
He subsequently received the seal of approval. Initially, he resided at the Jingming Monastery on Mount Wukang. [He then] ascended the hall and addressed the assembly.
The Master’s body is ink-black, yet his mind wears it upon his head. With poison mixed and smeared, who would dare to destroy it? A hundred flowers cluster together;
spring remains forever. Clear light shines upon people; how could it not be unimpeded? A stone hut, though only as large as a peck-measure, covers the heavens.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Within this realm, one is lively and active. 'Put it down'—what thing is there? Clearly, nothing at all can be brought forth. Serpents and tigers appear.
"How can it always be by one's side? Thieves, thieves! When the pure wind pervades the earth, what limit can there be? He ascended the hall. "The fan leaps and bounds."
He struck immediately upon opening his mouth. Seizing him and pulling him away, there was no seam or gap at all. If you understand, you will find that meaning transcends words;
if you do not understand, you will fall over a precipice. Holding up his staff, he asked, "What is this? The assembly hesitated, and the Master struck them and drove them out of the hall.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The sound of the poisonous drum cuts off the life-root at every stroke. Who can discern this source? The carp..."
Eating the staff like a torrential rain, he slashes through the old face of Vairocana.
Entering the earth and ascending to heaven, both rising and both falling, he transcends directly before the Ancient Sovereign;
the cold light flashes, the edges of the sword fly. Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "What is the Patriarch’s Heart-Seal? The Master said: "Seven."
The eight curves and eight bends of the dragon-and-serpent script—dot by dot, stroke by stroke, not a single deviation. [A monk] asked, "What is the mechanism of the iron ox?

The Master said, "Pushing crosswise and charging straight ahead, there is no obstruction; the level fields on all four sides open up above and below. [The monk] said, "Ei! and immediately withdrew his body back into the assembly.
The Master said, "The thief is a petty person, yet his cunning surpasses that of a gentleman. He then said, "The stars in the heavens, the earth..."
He lowers the wooden block. "The human carriage has eighteen linchpins; they cross, slant, and wind about beyond measure. Dense and distinct, they are unrestrained.
Looking left and right, he says, "Carefully observe that single axle in the middle. Again, he points with his staff and says, "Alone! He ascends the hall.
"The white ox and the wildcat—two heads, three faces, their horns locked and intertwined. The whole body emerges."
Manifested. The double locks of the Iron Gate—intentions layered upon intentions. In the blink of an eye, they cannot be seen. Do not seek to meet them.
Deep within the myriad flowers, lightning and thunder are hidden. Ascending the hall, he said: "Drill into it, look up at it; heaven is high and earth is deep—this requires profound reflection.
Before and behind, the sun rises and the moon sets—they roar with a single voice. Exhausting all one's talent and sentiment, there is no way out; the pool is deep and the water vast."
Cold and unable to open one's mouth—Confucius and Yan Hui face each other like a pair of iron hammers; for a thousand ages, neither can find a place to strike.
*Tu!* The Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists; the black dog and white ox, however, do know it exists. Ascending the hall, he applied both function and utility simultaneously.
Waves surge and clouds billow; killing and giving life are fully wielded. Mountains shake and peaks tremble; not a single point arrives. The whole body is a lacquer bucket.

To overturn it and return to the spearhead, one changes the battle formation. A master of the Way vainly bears a thousand-jin courage. Pointing with his staff, he said: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

Upon arriving at court for the morning audience, he returned directly to the abbot’s quarters. He subsequently resided at Shuangji on Gaofeng Peak in Lake District, and later at Xiangfu Temple on Fujiao Mountain in Pilin.
On the twenty-second day of the seventh month in the Jichou year of the Shunzhi era, he passed away. His stupa was enshrined at Xiangfu.
His various *yulu* (recorded sayings) are in circulation. (Han Yue Zang was his successor.)
Chan Master Ji Hongren of An-yin Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Zheng family from Zichuan in Shu. In his youth, he possessed great talent and strategic acumen.
At the age of twenty, he left the household life. Regretting that he lacked a true teacher or a worthy friend, he became immersed in the study of literary compositions for fifteen years.
Whenever he encountered scenic mountains and waters with friends and companions, or when his mind was at ease amidst poetry and prose, he would invariably feel shame and reproach himself.
He said, "I have left the household life; how could I do such a thing? Thereupon, his aspiration for the Way surged forth. This occurred dozens or hundreds of times.
In the *Xinwei* year of the Chongzhen era, he set out on a southern pilgrimage. Upon reaching the region of Wu, he encountered his fellow countryman, the *xiaolian* Liu Changqian.

Seeing the *Recorded Sayings of Sanfeng*, his hair stood on end involuntarily. He then entered the mountains with him to seek instruction. Whenever Zang scolded or reviled him, [Changqian] remained steadfast.
Not satisfied, the Master felt that his purpose had failed; he took his leave abruptly and went to visit Tiandong, yet there too he found no resonance.
Later, while lying ill in Wulin, he happened to read the records of Huanglong seeing Ciming and suddenly exclaimed, "The laughter and anger of the ancients were all skillful means.
He immediately returned to see Chang at Dengwei, carrying his illness with him as he sought admission into the Hall of Diligence (Jingzindang). The assembly considered this impossible.

Baizhang said, "To die while practicing Chan—is this not better than suffering from other illnesses? Because of this encouragement, the Master’s spirit grew even more robust and his resolve even firmer.
Whenever others advised him to cease formal practice and instead cultivate self-restraint, he would avoid them and refuse to hear such words.

Since Baizhang perceived that the Master’s wisdom had penetrated deeply and feared he might suddenly become exhausted, he instructed him to investigate the karmic conditions concerning Yunmen’s broken leg, yet he ultimately did not offer him a single word of explanation.

He said, "Shi Hu’s bulging eyes are truly extraordinary; in his dreams he turns the marrow inside out along with the skin.

This time the moon emerges from the root of the spring, illuminating the lame master Yunmen. Cáng then raised the koan concerning Miaoshan’s “sentence of existence and non-existence” to interrogate him, but the Master could not answer.
After investigating it for a long time, he suddenly heard the sound of a wooden fish during a brief nap and attained realization.
Gao Feng’s intention was like a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail; he said, "When the head of Mount Wei is straight, the tail is straight.

Today I have again met one who understands. From this point on, his realization reached the ultimate profundity. Once, when Master Zang was ascending the hall, as soon as the Master stepped forward, Zang gave a shout.
The Master also shouted. Zang shouted again. The Master shouted once more. Zang said, "You have missed it. The Master then draped his sitting cloth over his shoulder.
He then departed. On another day, he asked Zang, “Having passed straight through ten thousand layers of barriers and not dwelling atop the azure heavens, I wonder where you reside?
Zang said, “A fireball bursts forth from Mount Sumeru. The Master said, “What about when the old nest has been overturned?
Zang said, “An iron boot without a bottom pierces the great ocean. The Master said, “The Master, however, has been caught by me.”
He deceived him face-to-face. Xiangzang said, "Thief! You are caught; the iron chain was on your neck all along. The Master then prostrated himself.

In the year Yihai of the Chongzhen era, as Xiangzang was about to pass away, he entrusted the Master with the essential tenets of the Linji school. The following year, the Master went to reside at An-yin Temple.
Entering the hall for the formal discourse, he held up his staff, struck it once, and called out to the assembly: "The crown of the thousand Buddhas and the patriarchs..."
For all people, a single blow brings total clarity. Even for those who "lift up their skirts and go," thirty blows are well-deserved beneath their feet.
The Master resided there for three years. One day, as he was about to leave the monastery, he manifested a slight illness. He composed a verse to bid farewell to his Dharma brothers.
On the day before he displayed his illness, he sent a letter to the Elder Meigen, in which he said: "I..."
The illness will certainly not abate; it will likely end this very night. Struggling against my ailment, I have written this as my final exhortation.
My only hope is that you will exert yourselves with diligence and inspire your fellow practitioners—this is what I look for from you. Thereupon, at midnight, he entered *nirvāṇa*.

"When letting go at the edge of a precipice, what then? The Master made a gesture of listening. The monk repeated his previous question. The Master said: "..."

"Three lives, sixty kalpas. When the Master was asked by the presiding lecturer about the ninety-seven circular diagrams of the Shitou-Yangshan school, the Master drew a diagram with his whisk to show him.
The lecturer rubbed it out. The Master drew it again; the lecturer rubbed it out once more. The Master said, "I will not draw."
"What do you say to this? The master was at a loss. The Teacher said, "You salt-smuggler! One day, the Teacher cited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"The ultimate reality is firm and solid. He then smashed a tea bowl and tested the assembly, saying:
"Tell me, is it firm or is it not firm? If you say it is firm, I have already smashed it. If you say it is not firm, then what about the ancients?"
"Why is it so? asked Mingmiao Chen Daopo. She had been studying the "Cane" koan for many years. One day, while at a place where carts were being turned, she suddenly attained realization.
Later, when she entered the mountains to provide a meal for the monks, she asked, "I have heard that you, Master, smashed the tea bowl."

He tested the matter for its solidity, asking, "Is it so? The Master said, "It is. He asked, "How do you understand this? Ba said, "Even if the vast ocean were to change, I would never speak for you, Master.

She then turned around, bowed, and departed. Five years later, she passed away, leaving behind a verse that says: The body is like a bubble, the breath like dew; When life is exhausted, one returns to the dust. I have already paid my respects to the Buddha; Now I go forth to be reborn in the Pure Land.
"Who comes? Who goes? With both legs stretched out long—just so, just so. When the Master heard this, he granted him permission.
The Master’s preaching of the Dharma possessed the style of the ancient worthies. On the day he opened the hall, a layman requested that he write the characters for the plaque of the Cloud Hall.
The Master said: "In the place where one sweeps away the Buddha," he gestured left and right with his sleeves and said, "The mountains and rivers are it; the grasses and trees are it.

Regarding such various arrangements as the questions and answers concerning the four dhyānas and the four eyes, how could one achieve this without having reached profound depths and traversed a long path?
The Master revered the Way and cherished virtue; he did not hanker after profit nor seek the glory of fame. Through heat and cold he wore but a single robe, and his diet was simple.
A single bowl. Thus, among all those who have entered the gate of this master, none have failed to conduct themselves with integrity and purity.
The elders of Shu often said, "The descendants of the Buddhas and Patriarchs such as our Elder Wolong may truly be said not to disgrace their lineage.

During the years of the Jia-shen cycle under the Ming Yi-mi era, amidst the agony of slaughter and the horror of burning, where not a square inch of land remained clean, the Master, accompanied by five or seven others, sought refuge.

He took refuge in Fangcheng; he took refuge among the Nine Dragons; he took refuge among the Ten Thousand Peaks. Within less than seven months, the two prefectures and thirty counties were devoid of both people and goods.
The Master was at Guangfu in Xinning when it fell under the control of the military encampment.

Fortunately, the Master’s reputation for virtue had long been widely disseminated, such that even those bearing arms knew of him. They vied with one another to come and pay their respects, offering [him protection].
He offered pure food and requested that the Master repent for his transgressions. The Master then fully explained to him the matters of sin and merit, loyalty and filial piety;

consequently, he spared those who had been executed. The following year, the military camp was moved to Liangshan. The Master observed this environment and felt it was not a place where a śramaṇa could find peace.

On the twenty-seventh day of the second month, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Since I became a monk, I have never accepted clothing or food obtained through unrighteous means; how much less so [in such a place]..."
"Amidst spears and halberds, how could this be my pleasure? From this day forward, do not offer me food or drink. On the first day of the next month, I shall depart from the camp.
Let the fools of the camp fear losing me upon hearing the Master’s words; let the Master guard them all until the first day of the month. Thus he spoke.
He summoned his attendant and ordered the lamps to be lit, saying, "Exhort him to strive diligently on the Path; I shall part from you at this very moment.
When the attendant requested a verse, the Master wrote several for him. He added, "The Dharma Protector Xu held me in singular esteem; shall I not leave him even a single face?
Furthermore, passing away while seated is one way to assist others in their transformation. Because of these words, he was entreated to remain until noon.
Xu led his assembly to him to request the Dharma. The Master joyfully ascended the hall. At times he called out in a loud voice; at other times he cried out in a low voice.
He said, "It is bitter, it is bitter. Why does he share this with others? He said, "It is not bitter, it is not bitter. There are thorns in the soft mud.
Looking to his left and right, he said, “Do you understand? This old monk has, for no reason, fallen into the hell of war.
Who is like him who lay on his right side within the twin groves three thousand years ago? He let out a shout and passed away while sitting upright.

This was indeed the first day of the third month of the year Wuyou. He remained for five days, and his cremation took place within the military camp. Those who admired the Master all brought silk and brocade...

Incense such as agarwood was vied for and cast into the funeral pyre to express their reverence. When the remains were collected, five-colored *śarīra* (relics) were obtained, which everyone scrambled to pick up.
A stupa was erected at Wansong An of the Hu family, behind Jincheng on the west side of Liangshan.
His secular age was forty-one, and his monastic seniority (*varṣa*) was twenty-eight. Regarding his *yulu* (recorded sayings), the first edition carved at Qiling consists of eight fascicles; next...
Those carved at Mount Yao amount to eight fascicles; those collected and carved at Mount Wo-long total twenty fascicles.
What is now carved here exists only within the satchel of Attendant Bi and is not the complete set of the Master’s works (by Poshan Ming).
Chan Master Shengyuan Bolang Haizhou of Jiangxi went to visit Wanfeng Ming. He served as the *karmadāna* (Vina). Ming bestowed upon him a verse of dharma-transmission, saying:
"Enmity has its source; debt has its owner. Who can be a companion for this inner message?

Only after treading the straw sandals everywhere will you know it. Go wherever you please and beat your mouth-drum. He ascended the hall and said: "In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; in turning, moving, bowing, and stooping..."
Looking up: A three-legged donkey trots on its hooves; it tramples through heaven and earth until no trace remains. He lets out a shout and says:
"Master Zhigong was no idle monk" (Pōshān Míng’s successor).
Chan Master Lizhifang of Baoning Caotang was the son of the Chen family of Bishan. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Today is the fifteenth.

There are three or five layers of old buildings, and hundreds of thousands of idle clouds. In vain do I lean upon my broken staff."
Ankle-irons. Brandishing the axe that shattered the rotten tree trunk, he cooks coarse grain for his hunger; his robes are patched with lotus leaves. There is no need to study the Buddha-dharma;

Chan Master Tizong Daoning of Kaisheng Temple in Luzhou relied upon Wanfeng Ming. After a long time, Ming entrusted him with a verse, saying:
"For six years you served in labor, assisting the monastic community; In a single day, through your earnest devotion, you have fulfilled this mind.

Chan Master Nizuru Lan of Longshan in northern Shu ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is it like when meeting on a narrow path?
The Master said, "I have never deceived you. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and said, "In the blow of the staff, there is no patience with birth."
"When you do not yield at the critical moment, which 'turning point' (*ji*) is this one blow? The Master struck again, saying, "Which turning point are you yielding to?
The monk gave a shout and returned to his place, saying: "The Tathāgata’s true decree has long been proclaimed;

beneath the blow, there is no birth—how truly earnest! When the waves warm, the dragon leaps from the Gate; let thorns fill the mountain forests as they please. He then cast down his staff and descended.
(Zuo [Pōshān Míngsì]).

Fighting for profit in the marketplace, one’s blunders are soon discovered by others; the old barbarian has gone back to the West (Pōshān Míng was his successor).
Dharma Master Lín’ān Shīzǐ Rèn Wēiyìn addressed the assembly from the high seat. A monk asked: "What is the primary meaning?"
The Master said, "The sun shines across the vast sky. A monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "The moon illuminates the great earth.
He then added, "When the bell tolls and the drum resounds, before a single question or answer, the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*) has already been proclaimed to all of you.
What more would you have the old monk say? After a long silence, he said, 'There are no superfluous words,' and then descended from his seat."
(From the lineage of Poshan Ming).

Dipping the hammer into the vinegar—neither of these counts. Furthermore, how is it? Suddenly he seized his staff and said:

On the Day of立秋 (the Beginning of Autumn), Chan Master Minshu Ruxiang of Ciyun in Wan County ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said, "Do you see, great assembly?

"When the turbid waters have run dry, the cold pond is clear; when the misty light congeals, the evening mountains turn purple.

With a shout, he ascended the hall. The staff has not been used in the hall for a long time; leaning against the wall, one relies on the barrier and there is no room for deliberation. Today, by chance...
Picking it up with his hand, he looked at it and gave a laugh in the face of the *kalyāṇamitra*. "Tell me, Great Assembly," he said, "what was the old monk laughing at?
He laughed because the Buddhas of the three periods of time, upon reaching this point, have their mouths hanging on the wall;

the ancestral masters of successive generations, upon reaching this point, conceal their sharpness and tie their tongues; and the old monks of the world, upon reaching this point, have no choice but to withdraw."
The Master has thus made this announcement. I do not know if there is any monk among the assembly who feels indignant at the side;
come forth and speak! After a long silence, he said: "If there is none, I, the old monk, shall have to speak for myself. "Who can comprehend that which supports the earth and props up the heavens?
Beating the wind and shouting at the rain until the year of the donkey! He struck his staff and descended from the seat. (Póshān Míng, successor).
Chan Master Xingmi of Dazui Tanzhu in Sichuan ascended the hall and said: "On a clear spring day, amidst the fragrance of a hundred flowers, there is the singing of orioles.
Seen with the eyes, heard with the ears—the Great Canon and the Lesser Canon, the nostrils and the lips. He suddenly struck the meditation staff and said:
"When inspiration strikes, I take up my staff and stroll about at leisure; I do not strike the broken drum hanging in the hall. (Successor: Poshan Ming)
Chan Master Dēshēn of Yānjū on Mount Shī in Qīngzhōu ascended the hall and said: "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it be sought externally?
The Dharma transcends seeing and hearing; no verbal explanation can reach it. Even Śākyamuni Buddha was helpless; so too were the patriarchs of successive generations."
There is no calculation from which to emerge. Today, I shall briefly convey a message. [The Master] threw down his staff and said, "Does the assembly understand?
When a guest arrives, there is no tea or refreshment; mugwort soup serves as the ritual offering. (Póshān Míng’s Succession)

Later, he studied under Wanfeng Ming and resided at Dongta in Huzhou, where he secretly received the formal transmission of the lineage.
