The Master said, "Three Sages planned from within the tent, withdrawing himself to let others have their place. This monk stepped forward to face the white blade, yet beneath his skin there was nothing."

Blood! Baoshou acted according to the command; it was like a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail. Although the three men’s acts of giving and taking were worth observing, they could not avoid having their gains and losses.
Today, when I open the hall, if someone were to push forward a monk, I would likewise strike him across the back with my staff.
If he were to say, "To act for others in such a way will blind the eyes of the people of Xichu," I would strike until the staff breaks.
He had not yet let go. Why? Because he wished to save the eyes of all people in the world.

While taking refuge from the war at the Dàyǒu Chan Monastery in Yòuyáng, on the full moon day of the seventh month in the year of Xīnmǎo, he manifested a slight illness and spoke this verse: "Coming, there is no place from which it comes."
In departing, there is nowhere to which he goes; in coming and going, there is fundamentally no trace. There is neither "is" nor "is not. He cast down his brush and entered into stillness.
His worldly age was fifty-three, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was thirty-one. (Póshān Míng was his successor.)
Chan Master Xue-men Han-pu-can was a native of Qiu-lin. In his youth, he attended lecture halls; in his maturity, he practiced seated meditation. He was profoundly silent and composed.

Upon first encountering the teachings of Wan-feng, what he had internalized became liberated and unimpeded. Later, he resided at the Fu-zǐ-yuàn in Zhāng-fāng, where he changed the name of the establishment to Xue-men.
Ascending the hall, he said: "I do not ask about the place where a patch-robed monk walks and practices; rather, [what about] sleep and dreams?"

At that time, [the monk] asked, "How does one act as the master? The Master said, "At midnight, the window is bright; there is a fire in the neighbor's house. [The monk] asked, "What kind of news is this?
The Master said, "It applies whether you open your eyes or close them. He then said, "Every person is bare and clear;
by parting the clouds and mist, they behold the blue sky. Each individual is perfectly round; though wearing a soiled robe, they ascend to the pure ground. It being thus—

At this time, dragons and snakes are in turmoil, and ordinary beings and sages intermingle. [A loud shout] Ascending the hall: Treading upon the stone beam bridge, one returns home to the place of cool clarity.
The autumn waters bathe the golden goose; the flower of awakening blooms upon the iron tree.

Within the ancient Celestial Gate amidst the nine-fold mountain forges, how many are truly alert, and how many have attained realization? Addressing the assembly: There is a thing whose head touches the heavens and whose feet tread the earth.
Without feet, one excels in walking; without eyes, one excels in seeing; without hands, one excels in grasping; without a tongue, one excels in discussing the Dharma.
The Way flies far without wings; its nature is eternally firm without roots. If you can realize this, there is no hindrance to forming a bond of fellow-study with others.
He let out a shout, signaling that the end of the kalpa was approaching; he manifested a slight ailment and passed away. He was enshrined in a stupa at Jiulianping (the successor of Poshan Ming).
Chan Master Danxia Daci Wulei Han was the son of the An family of Xinpan. Initially, he studied under Zang at Dengwei. Not...
Qie later saw Ming, who struck him through to the core. Qie presented a verse, saying: "Nine years of tempering have forged this blade;
The martial art is fully wielded without further practice. Drawn from its scabbard, it alone can pacify the universe; Only one who does not yield on the field may be called a hero.
While staying at Danya, he ascended the hall. The layman Shixi approached and offered incense, saying: "I burn this within the burner to become clouds of radiant light, pervading everywhere..."

"Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, he makes offerings to my Head Elder. Here, amidst these clouds, upon this purple cypress seat, he parts his face-portal and reveals his crown-mark for all people to behold.
The Master said, "An adept. The monk asked again, "What is it like when presented face-to-face?
The Master said, "Clouds emerge from the mouth of the cave. As the monk was about to open his mouth to ask further, the Master said, "Water flows toward the rock."
[The Master] came from the borderlands and said: "The rain falls fine and the mist spreads vast; gust after gust of northern wind pierces the heart with cold.

It is only because you all have not yet reached the ultimate depth of cold that you have traveled so far, patrons, to cross the Peng Pass. Ascending the hall, he said: "This matter has never had a place to settle since of old;
how could it admit thought, like a flash of lightning or a spark on stone? Without trace and with severed news, the Persian cries out in pain while the stone man stands silent."
Weeping, he suddenly manifested a slight ailment; sitting upright, he passed away. His stupa was enshrined to the right of Jinsang Temple (by Poshan Ming).
Chan Master Shengjing Sheng’en Xuebi Luan was a native of Wuchang. He took the tonsure at Huanglong Temple and studied under Tiantong, serving as the *xunzhao* (inspector of the monastic community).
Suddenly, upon hearing the sound of a bell, he attained realization. In the autumn of the *Xinsi* year, he entered Sichuan to study under Wanfeng Ming.

Amidst the smoke of war and the fires of ruin, he lay upon wooden chips and tasted gall, placing himself at the forefront. Attending the Ming Emperor through seven hardships, the Master showed no sign of distress;
perhaps hoping to take their suffering upon himself, he relied on him for more than twenty years. He once praised his staff, saying:
"The entire body is black, yet the entire body is knotted. To manifest great function and unleash great potential—only then does one believe that one can lift one's head and support the universe."
Even the Buddhas and Patriarchs knit their brows at this teaching. In the summer of the Gengzi year, as the turmoil in Shu gradually subsided, he brushed off his robes and traveled north.
He resided at Tanyuan Puzhao Monastery in Daming Prefecture. Ascending the hall, he said: "The true Buddha has no form; the true Way has no substance; the true Dharma has no marks.
Within this, if you can realize them, the three are one; if you do not realize it, the one is three. He then suddenly picked up his staff and struck it down.
He struck the meditation desk once and said, "Does the assembly understand? He struck it again and said, "The three sections are not the same; they are gathered back into the preceding category.

Later, he moved to the Patriarchal Stupa Monastery at Hutuo in Cizhou. Entering the hall, he said: "Before the stupa of the Second Patriarch there is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth;
it has no boundaries or exterior, nor does it stand in the center. You cannot encounter it by grasping for it, yet you cannot leave it by abandoning it."
Face it and they are not intimate; turn your back on it and there is a bond. The Buddhas of the three periods of time have realized enlightenment through this;
the patriarchs of successive generations have attained awakening through this. In heaven, it is called wind, clouds, rain, and thunder; on earth, it is called birds, beasts, grasses, and trees.

Among the Five Constants, it is called benevolence, righteousness, ritual, wisdom, and trustworthiness; among the Five Elements, it is called metal, wood, water, fire, and earth. Whether wise or foolish, if one is a monk...
Whether among the mundane world, the various classes of creatures that fly, crawl, wriggle, or move—whom do they not produce through this?
[The Master] held up his whisk and called to the assembly, saying: "Does anyone here still recognize even a single thing? After a long silence, he gave a flick of the whisk and said: "Depart, depart!

On the road to the West, the journey extends for a hundred thousand leagues. Later, he spent nine years reading the Tripitaka at three different locations and passed away from a slight illness (succeeded by Poshan Ming).
Master Chuzen Jōshaku of Chengdu’s Shōkaku-ji was the son of the Li family from Zhongchuan. His temperament was profound and steady, and his spirit was serene and unassuming.

Initially, he studied under Wanfeng Ming; upon being unable to pull on his shoes, he attained a realization. He subsequently traveled to Tiantong, where he achieved great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of the wooden clapper.
Later, he returned to Wanfeng, who saw him and granted him formal certification. He then went on to propagate the Dharma at Niusan, Yumen, and Hanzhong.

At Caotang of Jingming Baoning, he rectified the collapsing discipline. Amidst swirling smoke and flames, he fully exerted his true command; [the teachings] spread like dawn light and gathered like clouds.

Ascending the hall, he said: "After long rain, the sun has suddenly cleared; the world and its people are in turmoil. As the golden crow (the sun) casts its shadow over the eastern ridge, dew drips and a grass bridge spans the way.
Within the station of a patch-robed monk, what aspect of the matter do you clarify? If you can discern it, even so—"
The Turtle Breaks Through the Wall. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises by relying on conditions.
Since conditions do not exist, from where could Dharma be established? Raising his whisk, he said: "This is the condition. What is the Dharma? Throwing it down, he said:
"From now on, I cast it onto a heap of refuse, where rain falls upon it and the wind blows it away. Entering the hall for the memorial service, [the Master] said: "Every morning, sleep until..."
"The sun is red in the east. [The Master] did not strike the wooden bell before the assembly.
Instead, he struck the incense table with his staff and said, "Heaven and hell have been shattered into seven pieces and eight fragments by this mountain monk's single blow!
Only the Venerable Maudgalyāyana raised his voice and cried out, "What joy! What joy! The assembly, tell me: from what source of majestic spiritual power does this old man derive his joy?
Is it obtained from the mountain monk’s staff? Try to discern and distinguish this for me. If you can discern it, then the six expeditions to Mount Qi were not the deeds of a true warrior;
only the seven captures of Meng Huo may truly be called heroic. Ascending the hall, the Master asked:

"Is there anyone here who is accustomed to charging through the enemy lines? A monk stepped forward. The Master struck the monk and said: "If that is so, then the mud ox has swallowed the Great Void."

[The monk] departed empty-handed. The Master said, "If the general at the head is not fierce, he brings misfortune upon his three armies. The monk made a gesture of brandishing a spear. The Master said, "Excellent! Excellent!
The monk hesitated, and the Master said, "The bandit has been utterly defeated. When the winds of calamity had somewhat subsided, he reopened Zhaojue. At that time, he was seventy-six years old.
Sweeping away the ashes of the disaster, he recovered fragments from various quarters and stitched them together as the "Brocade River" (Jinjiang).

*Chandelu* (The Lamp of Chan). In the autumn of the Guiyou year of the Kangxi era, he commanded his disciple Chesheng to carry the manuscript to Jiahe to have it carved for circulation (the successor of Poshan Ming).
Chan Master Kuai Xue Guo, the founder of Sichuan, was the son of the Wang family of Dangqu.
He entered the lineage of Shuanggui and later resided at Dongchan Temple in Nanlong. Upon ascending the hall, he was asked: "What is the scenery within the mountains? The Master replied:
"The green waters flow surging through the mouth of the cave; yellow leaves flutter and fly from the treetops. He then said: "Since my coming of age, I have split open this..."
The gateways: though I clutch them, they do not rise; though I support them, they cannot be sustained. Amidst deep mountains and vast wildernesses, there is no one on either side to rely upon.
I struggle to sustain myself alone; tilling with the blade is my livelihood. I harvest three or five pecks of grain, and my clothing is quite sufficient.
Day and night, my mind never rests; my backbone is cast from forged iron. I rouse my aged spirit and nurture it within.
The Mind-Tree: For several years I did not leave the mountains; there was neither honor nor disgrace. Having encountered a heartless fellow, he forcibly drove me out.
I do not yet know the Way of Chan, nor am I proficient in human affairs. As a mountain man, I am ashamed of my own lack of ability;
all day long I remain as if dazed, like one who is utterly motionless. (By Pu Shan Ming)
Shouchan Master Longyou of Puyang was the son of the Yao family from Jialing. He first entered the "Drunkard's Room" at Yumen, where he attended and followed [his master] for a very long time.
He subsequently went to Shuanggui, where he received formal certification (*inka*). He resided at Puyang You, where his single mat was desolate and devoid of any superfluous possessions;
he possessed the style of returning to Shitou. A monk asked: "Before you, Reverend, had seen the Old Man Po, what was it like?"

"What? the Master asked. [The monk] said, "The light of my eyes pierces through the four worlds. The Master asked, "What is it like after seeing? He replied, "Blind. The Master said, "It is not so for you, student.
The student said, "When I had not yet seen you, Master, I was blind; after seeing you, the light of my eyes pierces through the four worlds.
The Master held up his whisk and asked, "Do you see? He replied, "I see. The Master then struck him. [End of Excerpt]
The Hall: Longyou has no way to speak. Transverse and vertical, lively and agile. He picks up the tortoise-nosed snake; he reveals the soaring crane.

Letting it go, it traverses the universe; gathering it back, it follows its natural fit. Not lingering in the mechanism of existence or non-existence, how could one distinguish between the great and small moons?
In essence, everything is thus. Who can transcend this? (By Poshan Ming, successor).
Master Huanchan of Luzhou Yunqing was the son of the Yang family in Jiazhou. From birth, he was exceptionally intelligent.

At the age of seven, he went to Mount Emei to shave his head. He studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, and by the age of nineteen, he ascended the Dharma seat to lecture on the sutras, surrounded by a retinue of more than ten thousand people.
Later, he traveled extensively throughout various regions before returning to Sichuan, where he again visited Shuanggui and subsequently received the transmission of the seal of approval.
Thus it was. The officials and commoners of his home province requested that he open the Dharma at Yunqing. He ascended the hall;
as the drum was struck and he took his place, he planted "tortoise-hair" within the fire and rolled up the mats from amidst the assembly. He turned a millstone through the air.
Such is not permitted, nor is the alternative permitted, nor is both such and otherwise permitted. Why? Because where there is no wound, do not inflict one.
...as well. Zunyi Songqiu Liangsheng was the son of the Ding family of Yongchuan in Shu. Both his parents dreamed that a monk who had truly come from afar was making offerings to them;
that very night, a son was born in their chamber. Therefore, both the old and the young [regarded him as such].

Zhēn called out to him from afar, whereupon he was given the name Liǎngshēng (Two Lives). From childhood, he abstained from alcohol and meat. At the age of seven, he followed his paternal uncle into the monastic life;

he was seen to be extraordinary compared to ordinary children. He studied the lectures on the scriptures in his youth and later received the seal of approval (*yìnkě*) from Shīnguì Míng. Subsequently, he accepted an invitation to serve at Héngzhāo Temple.
Ascending the hall: Today is the first day of the tenth month; everywhere the work of plowing and harrowing is finished.
Only here in Mount Hengze is there yet another precedent. But tell me, what precedent is this? A new herd of calves has emerged, and only today have their noses been pierced.
When the time comes, each one shall turn over the great earth. —Defense Commissioner
Please ascend the hall. This morning is the fifth day of the first lunar month; the Star of Longevity shines brightly, presiding over the prefecture.

The subordinate officials pass by like smoke; where does the man of the forest dwell? The assembly has gathered in the Dharma Hall in great numbers, yet they still desire the mountain monk to beat the drum of the mouth.
I ask you all, do you understand? (He strikes the floor once with his staff and says: "Pick up the whisk!"
The *Jia* (holy flute) in eighteen sections; its melodic harmony of *gong* and *shang* shall endure for a thousand ages. He reached seventy-two years of age and passed away without ailment.
His entire body was interred to the right of Songqiu (by the monk Poshan Ming).
Chan Master Zhuyi of Mount Yunjing in Western Shu was the son of the Hu family of Dazhu. He left home at the age of twenty and entered the mountains to gather firewood.
While breaking off a pine branch, it made a sound that triggered an awakening. He went to study under Master Ming of Shuanggui, who certified his realization. Later, he resided at Mount Yunjing.
Ascending the hall, he went before the seat, drew a circle with his staff, and kicked it away.

He called out to the assembly, "The Buddhas of the three periods have been trampled to death by this mountain man. Is there anyone among you who can save them? If so, please come forward. After a long silence, he said, "If there is none, I shall save myself.
He then ascended the seat and said, "To transcend the ordinary and surpass the holy, one must be such a person. Break through the void!"
"Empty! It does not hinder the skillful hand. In the coming and going of a patch-robed monk, there is no room for running about;
even the slightest false movement will wound one's own life. (A shout—Póshān Míng, the successor.)
Chan Master Mìxíng Rěn of Kāifēng in Hénghzhōu ascended the hall and said: "In the worlds of the ten directions, there is not even space enough to insert a needle;
yet upon a single blade of grass, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel to benefit sentient beings and receive all things.
Looking to his left and right, he asked: 'Do you understand? Looking up, it is heaven; looking down, it is earth. Looking east, it is west; looking south, it becomes north. He let out a shout. (End)
In the Hall, [a monk] asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world and before the Patriarch came from the West? The Master said, "Having eyes, one is like the blind;
having a mouth, one is like the mute. The monk was at a loss. The Master struck him and said, "The blows were like falling raindrops; the shouts were like thunderclaps.
To find realization within this is precisely to be a madman running outside. But tell me, where does the fault lie? He raised his staff.
He said, "On the battlefield, do not blink; seize the true soul from all eight directions. He then descended from his seat, dispersing [the assembly] like a whirlwind.

Calling out again, he said, "Great Assembly! The assembly turned their heads. The Master let forth a thunderous shout and returned to his quarters. Ascending the hall for a discourse, he cited the case of a general who had returned from battle.
The Emperor comforted him, asking, "When you were brandishing your blade on the front lines yesterday, did you encounter anyone old there?"
"Do you know anyone? The General replied, "At such a time as this, I do not even possess a self; who else could I possibly know?
The Master said, "Students of the present day must have such an experience once before they can succeed. A lay practitioner came to visit.

The Master asked him, "Have you come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, or have you come out of human sentiment? The practitioner replied, "I have come for the sake of the Buddha-dharma. The Master looked to his left and right.
Pointing and looking about, he said: "Look here! Which of these is the Buddha-dharma? When the scholar hesitated, the Master shouted at him to leave.
Regarding the verse on the Plucking of Flowers and the Smile, he said: "In the end, it invites laughter; the full edge has already been blunted.

What need is there for the Eye of the True Dharma? It shall wait until the blind donkey is extinguished. Regarding the verse on Deshan Carrying the Alms Bowl, he said: "Deshan carrying the bowl passed through the hall, causing..."
This has given rise to a calamity. Who says that a father should conceal for his son? [Yet here,] it is clearly proven that the father stole the sheep (Pó Shānmíng sì).
Master Wúsī Yuán of Jiǔlóng on Mount Éméi was a native of Jiāyáng; he traveled together with Shèngkě Yù and had been wandering as a mendicant for the longest time.
Having received the Dharma from Shuanggui, he traveled extensively throughout all regions.

After spending many years at Jiulong on Mount Emei, in the spring of the Jiazi year of the Kangxi era, he purchased a boat and sailed eastward until he arrived at Huayan. Having exchanged greetings with Yuhan, he said, "I shall die here upon my return;
I hope you will cremate me. Huayan jokingly said to a nearby monk, "Beat the drum! The monk asked, "For what purpose?"
Mo’an said, "We are escorting Master Wushan for cremation. The Master said, "One day too many is not permitted; one day too few is not permitted.
When the next morning arrived, he requested the administrative officers to divide the robes and bowls. Having finished, he said, "Heaven covers all without partiality;
Earth bears all without partiality; Man exists without partiality. Today, the name of 'impartiality' is entirely relinquished. Hereafter, you should simply address me by my given name."
"The realms are subtle indeed. Having finished speaking, he became silent (Pōshān Míngsì).
On the occasion of the Dharma Hall discourse by Chan Master Shāolǎng Zhāolǎng of Dāngyáng: "Today is the fifteenth day of the seventh month; everywhere the gongs are struck and the drums are beaten.
This mountain monk, leaning on his staff, ascends the hall. My practice is entirely one of plain, honest simplicity and rustic ignorance. I do not know how to perform the lion’s turnabout; I only—"
Understanding this, one strikes the drum of the mouth; it speaks of retreating from the demonic armies of birth and death. It thoroughly awakens the *lilu* (the cat) and the *baigu* (the white ox).
Small Assembly: Before the fifteenth day, the front does not reach the village; after the fifteenth day, the back does not overlap the shop.
On the very fifteenth day itself, the prior limit is not continuous, the subsequent limit is not born, and the middle way is not settled. How is this so? It is not.
"Night travel is permitted; you must arrive by dawn. A monk asked, "What is the Seal of Vairocana? The Master said, "Wearing straw sandals, treading through the snow.
The monk stamped his foot and said, "Is it not this? The Master said, "Do not mistake it. A monk asked, "I do not ask about picking leaves or seeking branches;
what is the matter of the direct root? The Master said, "To speak of it would be like being mute. [The monk] said, "It is extreme!"
"How is it when one abides [in this state]? The Master said, "Listen as if you were deaf. He asked, "What is the matter before it has even arisen?
The Master said, "Wait until Mount Wushi nods its head, and then I will tell you. [He] asked, "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know that there is [something]."
"The wildcat and the white ox, however, do know it exists. But what is it that they know? The Master said, "I have always been earnest about this.
As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Just go over to that side! (Póshān Míng was his successor).

Chan Master Cheng of Lianyun Guyuan in Chuzhou was the son of the Wang family of Changle, Fuzhou. From childhood, he was precocious and distinguished; his gaze was piercing and intense.
Having lost his father early, he was orphaned at a young age. His mother pressured him into marriage, but he would not accept it.

At the age of twenty-two, after recovering from a severe illness, he changed his clothes and fled by night. He went to Pizhi Cliff to seek refuge with Xuzhou [Xuzhou] and received the tonsure and precepts. He was taught...
Because he had no point of entry through the *huatou*, he heard that Huangbo Qi’s monastic style was solitary and austere, so he went to rely upon him.

He applied himself with vigor, practicing with diligence day and night for nearly two years. Qi tested him according to his capacity, and through their mutual exchanges and invigorating dialogues, there was much to admire.
Before long, he took his leave and went to study under Jinsu Rong. When Rong tested him with the Three Barriers of Huanglong, the Master responded.
The answer was like a flowing stream, concise and without stagnation. Having accommodated his own mind-consciousness, he served as the "grass for the family" (a successor).

First, he received the *vimalakīrti* (the succession) from Weimo; next, he received the *abhiṣeka* (transmission) from Xitang. He went forth to reside at Fagong and Guangfu in Yongjia, and later at Tianmu Zhaoming.

At the end of the Ming dynasty, he responded to the call of Lianyun in Kuocang. Ascending the hall, he said: "The ancestral intent from the West is utterly beyond calculation. The neck of the wild duck [is naturally long]..."
The short-necked crane makes its own neck long; what it sips when sour is vinegar, and what it bites when pungent is ginger. If you understand it thus, you are carving sores in good flesh;
if you do not understand it thus, you are utterly flustered. The golden-winged garuḍa soars through the wind; the wild sheep hangs from the cliff’s edge.

If you further pursue the traces and seek their scent, know that you are merely laboring in vain for a flurry of busyness. Ascending the hall, he was asked: "How is it at the peak of the high mountain?"

"Step by step, treading upon the cloud-ladder. I pray you, Master, bring forth the meaning of the Patriarchs. Do not fail the intent of my journey from afar. [The student] asked: "I do not ask about the meaning of the Patriarchs;
what is the host within the guest? The Master said: "Firmly plant your feet. [The student] asked: "What is the guest within the host? The Master said: "Specially seeking out people.
[The student] asked: "What is the guest within the guest? The Master said: "Blinding the eyes. [The student] asked: "What is the host..."
Zhongzhu asked, "Master, please cut off my tongue. The Master said, "Guest and host have already been pointed out by me;
is there anything further beyond this? Zhongzhu said, "Look with eyes raised high! The Master then said, "Makakashyapa’s true decree is like adding frost to snow."
The mechanical contrivances of Shaoshi Mountain are like pouring oil to extinguish a fire; to be mired in names and attached to forms is to betray one’s entire life.

To refine one's conduct and extinguish the mind is merely to labor in vain. How much better it is to manifest benevolence and conceal utility, to harmonize with light and blend with the dust—to attain the wondrous by following the current and preserve the authentic through effortless spontaneity.
With monkeys and deer as companions and springs and rocks as kin, who would care whether the Qin dynasty fell or the Han was hegemonic?
Li defeated Zhang Cheng; my family remains in a state of total simplicity. We do not concern ourselves with whether we lie high and deep within the clouds of the mountain forests.
Therefore it is said: "To make offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is not as good as making offerings to a single mindless man of the Way.
What is a mindless man of the Way? "Last night the bedding was warm; one sleep reached until dawn. The Head Officers and Administrative Executives ascend the hall. Desiring—

To increase the spirit of the monastic groves, one must be a man of iron will and fierce resolve. One must cast aside conventional strategies to reach the heavens; the depths of one’s mind must be utterly boundless.
Do not shrink from standing on the edge of an abyss or treading upon thin ice; do not fear the tiger’s den or the palace of demons.

You must certainly abide by the laws and regulations, and it is essential that the roles of host and guest be freely exchanged. When all join their hands in unison, the Way of the Patriarchs shall be newly manifested in brilliant splendor—this is what is truly precious.
Ah! Never changing one’s original resolve, the beginning and end are naturally a single thread. On the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, he ascends the hall:
“The Zen of the Tathāgata is as brittle as iron; the Zen of the Patriarchs is as soft as cotton. Not bound by nirvana, not released from the entanglements of birth and death.

Spreading out ancient brocade with its floral patterns is merely a waste of arm strength. To celebrate the meal, a swift arrow is shot toward the heavens; with an empty mouth wide open, one eats to one’s full satisfaction.”
Deeply asleep! How could he know that this morning is the time after his parents have already given birth, yet before he has even been born?

If you were to ask him, he would strike you with a fist right between the chest and face, letting him wallow in the mud and enter the weeds, shrouded in fur and wearing horns, merely to settle the debt for his meal. Nevertheless.
Before you have penetrated to the point where there is not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction, do not let these reckless students speak. Entering the hall, he said:
"To give rise to thoughts and stir the mind is the very root of birth-and-death delusion. To stifle deliberation and forget conditions is yet another fetter, the shackles of the Two Vehicles.
Even if one cultivates causes and refines practices, what can be done about the toil of the journey? And even if, at all times, one does not give rise to delusive thoughts—"

All deluded minds likewise do not cease; they dwell within the realm of false conceptions without applying clear understanding. Lacking such understanding, they fail to discern reality, remaining instead caught in their ordinary routines.

Even if one were to take Great Perfect Enlightenment as one’s monastery, dwelling peacefully in body and mind with the wisdom of equality, one would still not be a true monk of the original color. Ultimately, how can one attain this mark?

The Master held up one finger. Yong said, "I have seen through you. The Master let out a shout. Yong then struck him.
At that moment, the Master suddenly attained realization (Feiyin Yong was his successor).
Chan Master Kongyan Tan was the son of Fang of the Cishui clan. He studied under Fuyan Rong, who asked him, "What is this broken sand-pot?
Rong replied, "It swallows up heaven and earth. The Master then presented a verse, saying: "A seven-holed, eight-pierced old-time wares."
Scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind until this very day. After being lightly tossed aside by a beggar, it deceives people with its chaotic and profuse depictions.

Chan Master Chenzhen of Chengjiang in Changzhou was the son of the Xu family of that prefecture. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

He traveled extensively among the lecture halls and became proficient in both the Nature (Xing) and Characteristics (Xiang) schools of Buddhism. Shortly thereafter, he abandoned these studies and went first to attend upon Master Cheng at Jinsu Temple, where he was instructed to contemplate the koan:
"The state before one's parents were born. He attained a realization. Later, while reciting the Heart Sūtra, he reached the passage: "Where there is no wisdom, there is also nothing to be attained."

Suddenly, a trigger was set off; whatever doubts or obstructions he had were all at once thoroughly penetrated. When the Celestial Youth came to visit Master Wuzhu, as soon as he saw him, he clapped his hands three times.
Wuzhu paid him no heed. The Master then let out a shout. Wuzhu said, "After three or four shouts, what then?"
The Master turned and went out. He then presented another verse. Baizhang (Wu) received it and immediately threw it to the ground.

The Master picked it up and went out. Baizhang called him back; once he had finished reading it, Baizhang asked, "Lingyun said, 'Since the first time I saw the peach blossoms, until now I have had no more doubts.
What is there not to doubt? The Master spread his two hands. Baizhang said, "You have only spoken half of it. The Master—

Yunrong then struck him out. One day, the Master asked, "How is it with the matter of casting down the hook?"
Yunrong took up his staff and made a gesture as if fishing, saying, "Watch closely! The Master said, "To startle the multitude, one must be a man of extraordinary spirit;
to overcome the victor, one must be a lion’s cub. Yunrong asked, "Who is that person? The Master gave a shout. Yunrong said, "Do not show off so much. The Master shouted again. Yunrong struck him.
From this point on, their master-disciple relationship was established, and he finally transmitted the robe and whisk to him. Thereupon, he withdrew into seclusion.
In a village by the Clear River (Chengjiang), he spent his days discussing the Way with the layman Huang Jiezǐ.
Contented in his simple and tranquil life, in the autumn of the *shunzhi* year *yǐyou* (1645), he composed a verse on departing this world, saying: "For over twenty years I have not traveled in vain;
This morning, leaning on my staff, I am through with all worldly style. Let no one else pass on news of me; I leave it as a koan for my patrons. One day he said:
The attendant said, "I have no desire to speak. You all may withdraw. He closed his room and lay there for three days before passing away.
His disciple Ju Bo-heng enshrined his remains in a stupa on Zhongfeng Peak in Wukang (the successor of Feiyin Rong).

Chan Master Taoming Zong of Longhua in Songjiang was the son of the Dong family of Yanguan. From his early childhood, he abstained from meat and was devoted to the Buddha, repeatedly requesting to receive the tonsure and ordination;
however, his mother found this difficult to accept. At the age of fifteen, he fell so ill that he nearly passed away.

In a state of trance, he beheld the sublime form of a Bodhisattva and suddenly felt a sense of lightness and peace. Thereupon, his original resolve grew even more fervent. Realizing that his will could not be changed, his mother finally...
He granted his request. Having recently left his bedding, he immediately went to Qinxi to receive the tonsure from Fachao. One day, filled with resolute determination, he went to see Wuzu.

On several occasions, he was struck by severe blows of the staff. Later, while pouring tea, he dropped the cup by accident; his entire body felt as if it had fallen away, and only then did he truly attain the ground of realization.

He visited Jin-su Rong again and subsequently became a true disciple who had entered the inner chamber; Rong entrusted him with his robe and whisk. That same year, he received the invitation of the Lohan Monastery in Luocheng.
Thereafter, the monastics and laypeople of Yunjian requested him to take charge of the ancient temple of Longhua on the banks of the Hu River.

Before long, the monastery was filled with beehive-like quarters and grand halls, lush with golden and green splendors worthy of admiration. Within a decade or so, followers gathered like clouds returning to their home and waters flowing to the sea, as elephants assembled in great numbers.
Longben may be said to have rendered service to this land, and his illustrious reputation has spread far and wide. Entering the hall [he said]: "An octagonal millstone rolls through the void;
a three-legged donkey trots on its hooves. A frog at the bottom of the well swallows the moon; white hair grows upon the back of empty space.
Those who understand this are like a dragon finding water or a tiger relying on a mountain; those who do not understand— [The text ends here.]
"Speaking with the mouth is like being mute; seeing with the eyes is like being blind. When neither understanding nor non-understanding is present—how is it then?
He suddenly brandished his staff and said, "A single piece of *zhuli* wood, as hard as iron, swallows up the three thousand worlds and the great chiliocosm.
He then cited the case where Layman Pang asked Master Mazu: "The person of original nature is not obscure; I ask the Master to open your eyes wide. Master Mazu...

The Master looked straight up at him. The Layman said, "This is a single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it wondrously. Mazu Daishi looked straight down at him, whereupon the Layman prostrated himself.
The Master then returned to his quarters. The Layman followed after him and said, "Just now, my cleverness turned into clumsiness.
The Master said, "One man offered a price reaching the heavens; the other returned the money from the ground. What a pity—this shall be remembered for a thousand ages."
[The Master] said: "Below this [level], there is no one to bear witness. Today, I, this mountain monk, wish to settle the matter for him with absolute clarity.
He propped his staff against his shoulder and said: "Gold has its own price; it is never sold to others mixed with sand. [He then ascended the hall.]
The wind is gentle and the waves warm as I glide my small boat; at every streamside, I cast a single hook. Alas, the jeweled fish do not bite at all;
the fishing line flows empty against the current. (He makes a gesture of casting with his staff and says: "Is there any whale or sea monster here?
A monk brushes him once with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*). The Master says: "Lowering the line upon the river to catch a fierce dragon—hidden in the weeds..."

The frogs emerge in a chaotic scramble. The monk remained silent. The Master said: "The red-tailed one does not know where he has gone; with a single raincoat against the wind and rain, he returns to his boat.

Ascending the hall for discourse, he said: "Leaves fall from the treetops, revealing them; the clouds part, showing the azure face of heaven. The pivot of the Patriarchs' gate is clear and distinct in every detail.
Last night the winds and waves were great at the Yellow River; drifting along, they have reached Luyou."
The city—no one knows who here is a true connoisseur. Standing alone at the head of the stream, he glares with eyes wide in rage.

Longhua intends to take a single broken length of rope, pass it through his nose, and beat him three thousand times in the morning and eight hundred times in the evening. Yet he fears that if the law is applied to its full extent, there will be no people left.

Again, he raises the case of the Great Being Mañjuśrī: having given rise to views of the Buddha and views of the Dharma, he was seized by the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual power and cast away.
"Between the Iron Ring Mountains, throughout the entire earth, it would be difficult even to find a single person to save you.
Today, as this mountain monk makes such a proclamation, I too shall surely fall victim to the plow that furrows the tongue. Is there anyone among the assembly who can save me?"
If there is nothing, you can only receive the consequences of your own actions. [The Master] took up his staff, descended from the seat, and gave this informal discourse (*xiaocan*):
"Spring on the head of a shadowless tree; the moon upon a branch that never sprouts. Pointing it out, it is most clear;

at every turn, it is lightly revealed. Lightly revealed! Where the partridge cries, the sound penetrates everywhere. To understand this is none other than the Gate of Non-duality. Splendid blossoms fill the eyes."

Engaging in dialogue with the assembly: The fullness of spring splendor before one’s eyes is indeed not absent. Yet tell me, regarding the station of a patch-robed monk—how do you express the phrase "adding flowers upon brocade"?
"The nightingale cries out the blood of a thousand mountains; the spring light across the four fields is a brilliant crimson.
Addressing the assembly: Practice apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness; study that cuts off the paths of sage and ordinary. The strainer is with outflows; the sieve is without outflows.
The wooden ladle is perfectly manifest; why must one grope for it? If you grope for it, you are plucking feathers from a tortoise’s back or cutting off the horns from a horse’s head.
If you do not grope for it, you cannot avoid wild guessing and reckless conjecture.
Tell me, after all, what is it? After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said: "Heaven! Heaven! Secret Demon dances empty-handed with his prong; Puhua merely shakes his rattle."
Duo: One night there was a monk standing in the darkness. The Master seized him and said, "Are you committing a robbery here?
The monk then shouted. The Master said, "Caught red-handed with the loot. The monk attempted to flee, and the Master struck him with a palm.
One night the Master sat with the assembly. Suddenly hearing the sound of a mouse, the Master said, "The Buddha Vairocana has appeared!"
A monk let out a thunderous shout. The Master said, "As expected. The monk was speechless. The Master said, "So, you were unable to take it on. Question:
"What is the phrase that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? The Master said, "Rain falls before the steps and wets them.
[The monk] said, "In that case, I shall follow him. The Master said, "As expected. Question: "Why do you wish to die yet refuse to die?"
The Master spread his two hands and said, "What business is that of mine? The monk asked, "How does one find life within death? The Master said, "I will tell you once you have come back to life.
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "You are already dead. The monk let out a shout.

The Master said, "That too is just staring with eyes wide open inside a coffin. A layman asked, "In the heavens the moon is full; in the human world it is half-moon. What about in the Master’s house?"
“Wind! I ask the Master to judge this. The Master said, “I have never suffered from blurred vision since I was a mountain monk.

Later, in accordance with Yunrong’s final instructions, he succeeded him on the seat at Fuyan. For three years he made no changes, thereby bringing his unfinished kōans to completion and offering sufficient consolation to the eternal, tranquil spiritual light.
Foreknowing that his life span was nearing its end, he returned to Longhua to bid farewell to the assembly. He sat in the lotus posture and passed away. (Kangxi Bing...)
The twenty-fourth day of the first month in the fifth year of the Wǔ reign period. His secular age was fifty-six; his years of monastic seniority were forty-one.
His remains were interred in the northwest corner of this very temple. The Grand Historian Shì Dàchéng composed the inscription for the stupa (the successor of Fèiyǐn Róng).
Master Guang of Tianshui, Zisheng Temple of Xujang, served as the First Seat under Master Jin-gul.

One evening, Guang addressed the assembly, saying, "The wind is somewhat stiff tonight; each of you should return to your hall. When the Rector Jianmei struck him, Guang said, "Chasing the wind and following the waves.
Jianmei shouted, and Guang said, "He has already set out. He added further, "If you go, you will follow the current."
"Chasing the waves. "If you do not go, you are a man dead on the spot. The Master stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Spare your eyebrows;
I shall accept your chin" (Feyin Rong, successor).

Chan Master Lingji Guanzhi of Zifu Temple in Huzhou was the son of the Zhou family of Longxi in Min. From childhood, he abstained from meat. Upon reaching the age of seven, he happened upon the realm of impermanence;
his sorrow and lamentation increased daily. Resolving his mind, he paid respects to Jiuyun Huitan and shaved his hair to enter the monastic order.
Seeing that the Master’s aspirations were extraordinary, Huitan immediately packed their belongings and departed with him across the mountain ridges. Along the way, Huitan fell ill and passed away.
The Master wiped away his tears and escorted him on his way. He first visited Wuzu at Tiantong, where he suffered several severe blows; his investigation became even more earnest.
Next, he went to see Yong at Jinsu, where he hung up his mat in the meditation hall and did not sleep throughout the night, constantly standing and practicing bitter inquiry.
One evening, as thunder and rain suddenly broke out and lightning flashed, his *huatou* (meditation topic) unexpectedly fell away. Overjoyed and leaping for joy, he returned to the hall immediately.
While he was lying down, a neighbor-monk asked, "Brother, have you woken up? Why are you so negligent? The Master said, "Wait for me to take one more nap;
then I shall speak to you. The entire assembly was struck with alarm. The Master then hurried into the abbot’s quarters; the Abbot examined him and questioned him until no doubts remained.

Furthermore, he presented the verse on Mazu’s second visit to Baizhang. After the Abbot had finished reading it, he asked again, "As for the verse, let it be your verse; but tell me, what about 'three days'?"
“Lung, what is your meaning? As the Master was about to answer, Rong let out a thunderous shout.
At that moment, the Master’s sweat poured forth as he realized the total function of the Great Use. Rong asked, “When the World-Honored One held up the flower, what did you do?
The Master suddenly raised his fist. Rong said, “You must not call this a fist; how would you respond then? The Master then gave him a punch. Rong also struck him, saying, “Now tell me—”
"This is reward; this is punishment. The Master said, "Do not show off so much. He granted his consent, and the monk subsequently received the transmission of the Dharma.

Not long after, he accepted an invitation from Yangfen Zifu in Huzhou. When he first took up residence there, he cleared away the weeds and reclaimed the wilderness, cutting rushes to bind together huts.

With jackals and tigers as neighbors, the Master dwelt there with serene composure. He was most strict in disciplining himself; even a single fruit or a single vegetable he would never keep for himself, but shared with the community. Thus...
The disciples did not shrink from toil or hardship; with united effort they managed the affairs until a great monastic center was established.
Holding aloft the ultimate teaching, they examined those who came from afar. Monks from all quarters arrived, drawn by his reputation, fearing only that they might be left behind;

those gathered around him never numbered fewer than ten thousand. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Patriarch’s coming from the West originally possessed nothing extraordinary. A single thought that turns back toward the source—"
Attaining the same root is simply not fitting; it is like losing an arm by intercepting divine light, or losing one’s own shoe.
Where is that one shoe? Where is the other? Neither in this land of China nor in the Western Heaven can they be found. A-he-he!
If one is a monk with clear eyes, one will never be deluded by him. Entering the hall [the Master said]: "Had you not yet crossed the Yangfen Ferry, you would have cast off your hands and returned;
there certainly would have been no business as it is today. Now that you have come over and he has tied the mouth of his cloth bag, even if you possess all manner of tactical skill,"
In the end, it is of no use. Furthermore, what is the matter of today? Do you all know?
If you do know, drawing lines on the ground to make a prison is ultimately not the final goal; binding oneself with no rope—how could one be content to simply stop there?
You must be vital and lively, like a swift hawk soaring toward the heavens; you must be bright and unadorned, like a splendid fish leaping through the waves. If this is not yet so, I urge you all:
People, do not be fussy. Arranging it is not the Buddha; twisting and manipulating it is not Chan either. A man of refined elegance is not drunk even after a thousand cups;
he has swallowed the entire Western River without spending a single coin. Ascending the hall after leaving the monastery, [the Master] suddenly raised his staff and said:
"The entire great earth is the face of the former master. It relies entirely upon this very thing to circulate throughout the dust motes of all lands; this is the practice of this mountain monk."

"Conduct. There is absolutely nothing to dwell upon, nothing to pursue or grasp. Nevertheless, if you wish to see this mountain monk’s conduct, you must recognize the countenance of the former master.
Once you have recognized the former master’s countenance, tell me: where is this mountain monk’s conduct to be found right now?
"Thank you for the rain upon the Quannong Bridge; it most earnestly saw me out through the pine pass. Dragging my staff, I went straight to morning practice (*zōsan*).
Standing in the snow with waist-deep piles, severing one’s arm to find peace of mind—these are still outward pursuits. "I shall take this mind and set it at ease for you.
Yet, when seeking the mind, it cannot be found. This, too, only saves half the matter. But tell me: what of that other half? How is it?
I shall not refuse to speak to you. I only fear you will scold your father. Morning Consultation: There is an old public case from before one’s parents were born;
though Buddhas and Patriarchs have raised it up, they have never reached a final verdict. With my grandmotherly heart, I, Zifu, shall judge it anew for you. But how shall it be judged?
(He whirled his staff like a whirlwind and struck them all down. Kangxi Xinsi...
In the autumn of the year Hai, he again presided over Fuyan for three years. He passed away on the twenty-ninth day of the ninth month of the Xinyou year.

His secular age was sixty-six, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vaṣa) was forty-nine. By his final testament, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Longshan at this very temple.
Two volumes of his recorded sayings (yulu) have been circulated in the world.
Gaoting Zhizhi Lingyue Gu Chan Master attended Jin-su Rong as a member of the attendants' office.
One day, Rong suddenly reached out his hand and asked, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? The Master replied, "Do not show off so much. Rong then extended his foot and said:
"Are my feet like a donkey's? the Master asked. Yunrong replied, "The more I see, the more I find it unbearable. The Master said, "Everyone has their own 'birth-condition' (*jìngyuán*).
Where is yours? Yunrong said, "Face-to-face, I do not recognize it. The Master said, "Having passed through the three barriers, what then?
Yunrong gave a shout. The Master said, "A good thirty blows for you. Yunrong said, "The Master, too, cannot escape [this]."
"There is no fault. You may go and rest," the Master said. One night, he dictated a verse to Yongrong, saying:
"Eat stalks of rootless vegetables; Investigate this flavorless Zen. Three meals a day by day; One sleep at night.
Yongrong asked, "What if the King of Yama comes to demand your meal money? The Master replied, "It will be either my fist or my palm. Yongrong said, "..."
"Where does the fault lie? The Master said, "It was improper to disturb the men and women of a household. Yong nodded in agreement (Yong was the successor of Feiyin).
When Chan Master Hong of Qiyuan Zhengfa was serving as the West Hall attendant at Jinsu, he remarked that [Master] Yan was fond of traveling abroad. Yong said:
The ancients said, "Every day is a good day. How do you understand this? The Master snapped his fingers. Yunrong said, "To understand it in such a way is wearisome.
The Master said, "Venerable sir, you are exhausting yourself. Yunrong said, "The nostrils hang down with a large head.
One day Yunrong said to the Master, "At that time, the Patriarch Huian said: 'If you wish to gamble at guessing the number of beans, everyone must put out a hand. And so he spoke.
Daoce asked, "What is this 'what'? The Master suddenly raised a fist. Daoce said, "Not it, not it. Why do you not ask me?
The Master then asked him the same question. Daoce also raised his fist. The Master said, "Indeed, indeed. Daoce said, "You have needlessly added a footnote.
After the Master passed away, Huizhi Zongbai had the *Qiyuan Sui Lu* (Record of Following the Garden) carved into woodblocks for publication.
(Fei Yin Rong, the Dharma Heir).
Chan Master Liyan Fa of Chaoguo in Songjiang was originally from the Gong family. His ancestors had lived by the seashore for generations.

When he was fifteen years old, he encountered a tidal wave that swept away his home. The Master resolved to leave the household life and went to visit Tiantong Wuzhuo, immediately asking: "It is not the wind..."
The banner moved. [The Master] asked, "How is it that the mind moves? Wuzhuo shook his fan and said, "It moves like this. The Master then bowed.
While the Master was performing manual labor, Wuzhuo picked up a stone and made a gesture as if to throw it. The Master split open his chest with his hands, making a gesture as if to receive it.

Wuzhuo smiled and desisted. Because the Master was ill, he applied himself to the practice of death. He sealed the door for a seven-day meditation retreat (*qijiu*). On the fifth day, he heard someone knocking at the door.
The sound was like the sun suddenly rising in the dead of night, making it as bright as broad daylight. Overwhelmed with immeasurable joy, he spoke a verse of self-conviction, saying:

"Long I have fought on the battlefields without deciding the outcome; Today, with joy, I have secured the River East. Only now do I believe in the wondrous truth not transmitted by Buddhas and Patriarchs:

Reaching out the hand was originally within the hand that draws it back. After this realization, Huigu entered *parinirvāṇa*. He then went to attend upon Yuanrong of Jinsu. Yuanrong asked him: "As you approach death..."
"Who knows that my treasury of the true Dharma eye has been extinguished within a blind donkey?
Is it extinguished or not? The Master said, "Please, Reverend, speak. Huairang said, "Extinguished, extinguished. The Master said, "I suspect there is no connection. Huairang nodded his head.
Later, ascending the hall, the Master cited Nanquan, who said, "At eighteen, I already understood how to make a living. Zhaozhou said, "I [understood at] ten..."

"Eight Superior. He then proceeded to dismantle the house and scatter the estate. The Master said, "As for boasting about the sutras and peddling the records, there are indeed those two venerable elders who do so;
however, if you wish to establish my school, you must first attain enlightenment. Here at Chaoguo, there is no house to be dismantled."
There is no livelihood to be pursued. During the day, one eats coarse vegetables and plain rice; at night, one bends the arms and rests upon a high pillow.
One simply watches the flowers bloom and fall; who cares for the passing of years? Tell me, is there still any principle of the Buddha-dharma here?
The Master Shufo said: "If one only succeeds in not losing the sheep, what need is there to weep at the forked road?

In the second month of the Gui-mao year of the Kangxi era, the Master fell ill. On the twenty-fourth day, he requested a brush and wrote this verse: "Form and name are entrusted to the world, yet they lack solidity;
Since dwelling is thus, so too must departure be. Earth, water, fire, and wind are now in flux; For now, I simply let go and depart."

He returned home. Furthermore, having finished writing the words for the reliquary casket and the verse for the cremation, he went to his pillow and passed away. During the cremation, five-colored auspicious lights appeared;
his cranial bone, teeth, and jaw remained unburnt, and the śarīra relics were as brilliant as pearls. Monastics and laypeople alike vied with one another to obtain them for worship.
His recorded sayings (*yulu*) comprise thirty volumes and circulate in the world. He built a stupa at Husheng Hermitage in the prefecture (the successor of Feiyin Rong).
Chan Master Qianfeng Li of Juewang Temple in Haining went to visit Jin-sul Rong, who appointed him as the Second Seat.
Rong posed a question, saying: "Is there anyone here to add charcoal to the brazier? Come forth and meet me. The Master asked: "In the past, the Master..."

Weng Dao said: "The great earth is clearly a single furnace; look at it, and it is entirely nothing but fire-tips. When the old monk casually picks and prods with his hand, one can immediately turn over and flow, shaking the very ground.

Setting aside for a moment this 'shaking the ground,' if the great earth is indeed a furnace, where would you, O Monk, turn to avoid it? Rong said, "Even the life of a *jialie* (junior brother) is not spared.

The Master said: [Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a Zen dialogue. The final line "The Master said" indicates that the preceding dialogue likely concluded there, though the specific response of the Master is not included in the source text.]
“This old fellow has fallen into a trap,” said Xuefeng. Yunrong said, “The words of a parent come from the mouth of the parent. The Master then shouted. Yunrong withdrew.

Yunrong asked, “What is the price of rice in Luling? What is the meaning of this? The Master said, “It blocks the throats of all people under heaven. Yunrong said, “Why did you answer me back? The Master then shouted.
Yunrong said, “What can be done about this public case? The Master— [shouted].* *Note: The original text ends abruptly with "師" (the Master), implying another shout or action by the Master.*
Feyin Rong said, "I do not even recognize the *huatou* (critical phrase). He also gave a shout. The Master said, "That was eight *ke* (two hours) too late" (Feyin Rong succeeded him).
Chan Master Taibai Xue of Yuyang ascended the hall, gave a shout, and said: "This Dharma is not reached through thought, deliberation, or discrimination.
To advance is to strike one's head and forehead against the wall; this meaning is not produced by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. To retreat—"
Then one falls into ditches and pits; whether advancing or retreating, one sees nothing but the ordinary affairs of daily life, which are naturally vast and open.
If there were anyone among you who could hide the sun and moon within their breast, please come forth and leap about here!
If there is no such person, let us all simply groom our two eyebrows. Ascending the hall: Affairs are myriad and diverse, yet a pure breeze fills the assembly. The Dharma has no divergent teachings.
The wild scenery is clear and bright; scattered and sparse, broken and intermittent. On the trees, the yellow orioles sing, attaining pure clarity free from a single speck.
The flow pours forth as the eternal truth; its principle exhausts the three periods of time. Like piled peaks and heaped mountains—do not attempt to deliberate, do not attempt to accept.
No trace; nothing to deliberate upon. Waves within a cauldron; a thunderclap in the void. Truly, whose household’s smoke and fire, whose tea and rice? He lets out a shout and says:
"If you have not cast off the dust of emotion, having eyes is like being blind. Ascending the hall, he said: "The entire great earth is gathered up and made as small as a grain of millet.
Why, then, do you go from door to door twice a day picking up the spittle of others? Even if you were to..."
The Dharma is not to be found outside the gate. One must meet the two elders Deshan and Linji, where blows fall like raindrops and shouts roar like thunder.

On this day, as he ascended the hall, the Master said: "An ancient said that when officials and lay devotees enter the mountains to seek instruction, they speak three or four sentences of plain talk to manifest their support from without. Today, in this broad assembly, there are three matters. The first is..."
The Lantern Festival has not yet ended; drums are beaten and gongs struck, while firecrackers spray toward the heavens.

This awakens the earless tiger, which lets out a series of roars that shake the mountains and rattle the earth. Second: The donor rides backward upon a donkey, dancing his sleeves in the spring breeze;
the clouds and mist part to reveal heaven and earth, yet their original form and face remain unmanifest. Third: Firewood is scarce and rice is expensive; he gazes with his eyes.
The Milky Way. A staff-wielder from Tiantai strikes Mount Wutai; touching it, he knows gratitude and repays that kindness. The mountain peaks are steep and precipitous;
advancing one layer after another, the waters flow secretly and circulate; returning once more, then again. Last night, the Stone Beam Bridge transformed into a dragon and departed;
its head and horns are fierce and majestic, its eyes protrude, its scales glisten, and its fangs and claws are distinct. And so—
The Way. Where is the pearl? One day when thunder and lightning arise, see the time the command is executed.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Three unbroken lines of Qian—by this all things grow and flourish. Six broken lines of Kun—the sun and moon rely on this to produce their light.
But tell me, before the lines were drawn, where were the nostrils and the eyes? The Sanskrit language of the Western Heaven; the Tang language of this Eastern Land."
Ascending the hall: To discuss the subtle and the primal is like grasping at the moon in water; to employ the staff and the shout is to labor in vain. It requires no more than a snap of the fingers.
When the gates of the pavilions open, there is no need to stir a foot; one reaches all hundred cities, deploying dynamic mastery as the occasion demands.
Gallop and run without missing the proper measure; overturning Mount Sumeru, one may know the vastness of the universe;

trampling over the great ocean, one then perceives the depth of the blue sea. Amidst a cluster of a hundred flowers, there is a single state of empty stillness; even in wine shops and brothels, [this remains].

All return to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The whole body is the eye. Facing one another, seizing the opportune moment; killing and giving life proceed together. How can one find a place to settle?
It reaches the point where sound resonates through the ten thousand phenomena and majesty shakes the eight directions.

One might suppose this is the realm of such a person. The Sleeping Dragon rises to dance; the Vermilion Phoenix soars aloft. Ascending the hall [he said]: "The bean is for making tofu; the rice is for boiling into porridge. On one's body, one wears..."

Clothing only wards off the cold; speaking of food with the mouth never satisfies. This has been heard throughout antiquity and the present—why must one force another to bare their heart and expose their gallbladder?
It is like digging the earth to seek the heavens. Green plums are like a snap of the fingers; the new moon resembles a silver hook. (Feyin Rong, the successor).
Master Jian’an Qian of Shijiao ascended the hall and said: "In old age, I let things take their course as I pass these declining years; all day long, I am dazed and do nothing but sleep.
Yet, I am needlessly hurried along until my *kāṣāya* falls in disarray before others. These seven items that accompany me are but idle furnishings;
what need is there to speak of the 'sovereign,' 'minister,' or the positions of 'correct' and 'deviant'? At the single-word barrier, I have lightly broken through it—casually."
Crushing the "roundness" within appearances, he struck the ground once with his staff and said: "In whose hearth is there fire without smoke?
He ascended the lion’s seat without donning his upper robe. The wind and rain have raged incessantly for days; everyone’s very bones are chilled through.
Even if one possessed the Buddha-dharma, one could not speak it while freezing so cold. You all, each possess a pair of eyes.
The eyes—dark and glistening—are right here. What is the use of looking east and looking west? [The Master] struck them at irregular intervals with his staff to disperse them.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the fifteenth day, do not raise it again; after the fifteenth day, do not attempt to measure it. Right now, on the fifteenth, the moon is perfectly full.
With my staff, I shall pick it up and show it to you all. A single divine light presses against your faces like ice."

"Who would suddenly feel a chill at the crown of their head? [This is] a small-scale sermon (xiao can). Come forth, one who has a question to ask. A monk came forward and bowed. Chan Master Ding of Chao’an at Qianming Temple in Gaoyou was the son of the Chen family of Xinghua. Upon exiting his seclusion, he ascended the seat and said:

Jiemò. You must know that in the past it was closed—closed all over heaven and earth at once. Today it is opened—opened all over heaven and earth at once.
When it was closed, there was never any attachment; when it is opened, there is likewise no separation. There is no difference between now and then.
Consistent from beginning to end, it does not hinder shortening hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas into a single moment without diminishing by even a hair’s breadth;
nor does it hinder extending a single moment into hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas without increasing by even a hair’s breadth.

This very state of neither diminishing nor increasing is like the sky universally covering, like the earth universally supporting, like the sun universally shining, and like the wind universally cooling. There is no principle that does not pervade it, and no matter...
Nothing is incomplete; there is no dharma that is not perfected. There is no capacity that is not reached.

Entering and exiting with ease, gathering and releasing with mastery—this is still merely a provisional arrangement at the gateway of constructed transformation. It has never touched upon the path that goes beyond. Therefore it is said:

[The Master] was present. [A monk] said, "Old man, old man! You are making such talk. The Master then struck him. Question: "How is it when the ancient sail has not yet been raised?

The monk hesitated; the Master struck him immediately (Wanru Wei was his successor).
Chan Master Foke Shi of Ciyun in Quan’an, a native of the Chen clan of Liyang, was asked by a monk: "A honeybee gathers flowers."
"Why do you not pick out the flower from the lamp? The Master said, "I have no other place to lodge; the monastery has caught fire.

The monk asked, "Since you are a Dharma-protecting deity, why can you not even protect yourself? The Master said, "I exert my utmost strength for the sake of the assembly; calamity arises from one's private door.

The Master wrote: "I have no words to give you; I have no dharma to transmit. If you wish to know my meaning, Look at the mountain flowers and valley streams."
