A true lion cub does not hesitate upon arrival. You people of the assembly, how will you find a place to settle? (Hongjue Man, successor).
Chan Master Chang of Yuyan at Dizang Monastery in Shucheng composed a verse on the World-Honored One holding up a flower:

"Thoroughly overturning it all to speak to people— No sentiment surpasses the truth of this moment. He yields to the heavenly eyes of hundreds of thousands of men; He has deceived the dhūta’s unfinished mind.
He composed a verse on "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere": "The stream flows from the eastern ravine to the western ravine."
Water. Clouds rise from the southern mountain and clouds from the northern mountain; one does not know that their ultimate activity returns to the King’s transformation.
When spring arrives at the cold cliff, the strange grasses turn green. The verse on Zhaozhou visiting two hermits reads: In both places, he presented his single case;
throughout his life, he laid bare his liver and gall toward others. His mechanisms of killing and enlivening were like lightning; even iron eyes and copper pupils could not let him pass.
In the verse on Bao-shou’s opening of the hall, the Three Sages push up the mountain. One monk says: “A golden mallet split across the face, swift as lightning;
To receive it costs no effort from the bowl’s rim. Cast it all together into the blue waves— Nowhere in heaven or earth can it be found.
(Hong-jue Man was his successor.)

On New Year’s Day, Chan Master Dailei Qing of Baofeng in Jiangxi ascended the seat. The iron flute is blown across the universe, pure and clear; throughout the myriad nations, joyful sounds drift on the wind.
With mouths full and bellies drumming, the mulberry trees and wheat flourish; the seas do not toss their waves, and dogs do not bark in alarm.
This is the intention of protecting the Dharma, serving the sovereign, benefiting the people, praying for bountiful harvests, and seeking long life. But as for us who dwell beneath the forest trees—
"How can one praise a person? Then he rose and said: 'The August Heaven has no second path; the Sage has no dual mind. He ascended the hall;
as soon as he entered the gate, he let out a shout. Indeed, the Buddha-dharma is not many. He struck him across the spine and pulled him up. What need is there for worldly exertion?
Therefore, to arrange flowers and cluster brocade is but to vainly obstruct the abyss of the Great Way. To loathe death and rejoice in life is still not to be liberated."

Beyond the realm of conscious intellect. Therefore, in the family of patch-robed monks, their eye-sight pierces through the four heavens; from the pores of their skin they horizontally swallow the great earth.

They cast aside the teachings of the Tripitaka and revile all the "little children. Having emerged from their mother’s womb, they immediately let out a lion’s roar—yet even this is not yet the work of a man of impetuous nature.
Will you still consent to it being so? Throwing down his whisk, he said: "The mountain house does not understand."

Admonishing on Winter and Summer: "The rocks crumble and the pines wither—this is one year. Addressing the Assembly: Moss and creepers overgrow the thickets, their weeds and brambles obscuring the heavens.
An earthen cauldron is used for cooking porridge; a bed is propped against the roots of a pine tree. One dwells there, wearing a bamboo hat and eating while reclining on the grass.

Deer, pigs, chickens, and sparrows are one's companions. The moon reflects in the pool, its light mingling with jade; snow cascades down the waterfall like scattering pearls. Tigers roar and monkeys cry; dragons coil and phoenixes soar. For a moment, they withdraw.

Recite: "The gate of the pavilion opens; the pivot of the mind turns directly downward. From the tip of a hair, worlds surge forth; the palaces of the Tathāgata are boundless. The Self-Awakened One dwells within them.
If one does not behold the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha), how can one recognize the voice of Śākyamuni? At the opening assembly of the retreat, the Master ascends the hall.

The picking up of the flower and the smile were a profound and secret resonance between the divine mechanism and the Sage’s heart. Crossing the desert to seek the worthy, the Great Function resounded like thunder.

Resounding throughout Zhendan, the five leaves spread their fragrance while two branches stand out in solitary beauty. Towering above ten thousand followers, he was the first to open the "Selection of Buddhas" at Falin Monastery;
his model shall endure for a thousand autumns as he continues the pure regulations at Shengshou Monastery.

Under his feet are all but his descendants; within this excavation there are none but lions. The Dharma assembly on Vulture Peak is as if present; the statutes and edicts of the patriarchs remain manifest.
Now, once again, the selection of Buddhas is reopened and the great furnace is fully ignited. What is the meaning of repaying one’s sovereign and parents?
It is when the seas are calm and the rivers are clear; it is the moment of passing the state examination with an empty mind. (Hongjue Man, successor)
The Late Evening Assembly of Chan Master Shengyìng of Wanshoushen Mountain in Huzhou: The rain has not ceased for a long time. Yunmen pierced through it; it fell scattering into the blue sky.

This breach is difficult to mend. Even if one were to refine the five-colored stones and snap the legs of the six giant turtles, possessing the heroic majesty to repair the heavens and bathe the sun, it would still be nothing more than weary toil.
If one looks from the vantage point of those who have emerged beyond the heavens, it is not worth a penny.
A single spittle brings both calamity and fortune; it nearly killed Pòzào Duò of Mount Sōng. Tonight’s late assembly for opening the furnace:
everywhere else today they open their great furnaces and smelting hearths to forge Buddhas and patriarchs. Dàofēng has neither firewood nor charcoal;
from within the cold ashes, he stirs deeply until a single spark flares up. If you can press down upon this spark beneath your own feet, I guarantee that winter will be warm and summer cool.
The treatise says that even through kalpas of enjoyment it would not be exhausted; a wooden Buddha need not be burned, and an ancient mirror likewise need not be compared [to the real].

If you belong to the ranks of the truly gifted, you will understand it directly and immediately. Early Assembly on the Winter Solstice: When all the yin has been stripped away, the sky remains as it was.
The return of the first yang occurs before the trigger is pulled. Sprouts emerge from the stone pillar, tender when cooked. Flames burst forth from cold ashes; guest and host are complete. Suddenly—!
Pointing with his staff, he said: "If you have doubts, go study elsewhere. On the verse for the Woman Emerging from Samādhi, he said:

"Exerting effort does not win the coin; winning the coin does not require effort. The woman and Gautama—neither were they white-handed thieves. On the verse for the Old Woman Burning the Hermitage, he said:
"The great general who has ceased hostilities is no longer called a hero. He passes in secret while practicing openly on a narrow path. It is exactly so."
At that time, he kills or gives life at will; his banner and spear turn independently, manifesting the Cold Family’s style (Hongjue Mian succeeded him).
Chan Master Xiangshan Qi ascended the hall at Shuntian Fangshengchi: "The secret intent of Vulture Peak; the true doctrine of Shaoshi."

Successive generations have continued this lineage, revealing it throughout the world. Auspicious clouds gather around his seat, and fragrant rains of flowers fall thickly. Multitudes of humans and devas assemble here to follow these lofty footsteps.
Ten thousand layers of misty trees encircle the landscape from west to east; amidst the red dust and purple thoroughfares lie willow groves and fragrant clusters.
At sunset, the short flute sounds; entering its resonance, one finds it inexhaustible. Meeting the occasion, he performs his play; with staff and wood, he follows along.

Responding as circumstances arise, he guides the ignorant masses toward benefit. Having realized the Supreme Vehicle, he has attained the "Pass" with a mind empty of self. It is just like this today, before all the dukes and ministers of the realm.
Never forgetting the entrustment, he respectfully requests the opening of the hall to extend the Emperor’s divine longevity and repay the Imperial grace.

How shall one unfold this? Thereupon, he suddenly rises and bows, saying: "May Your Majesty’s sagacious calculations match the North Pole; may the imperial reign flourish as grandly as the Southern Mountain.
The Small Assembly for the Mid-Autumn Festival: The floating clouds have vanished and the azure sky is vast; the bright moon shines directly overhead.
Ten thousand mountains. When the tower overlooks the water, all eyes turn toward it; at night deep, one leans exhaustively against the jade balustrade.

[The Master] strikes the circle sign with his whisk and asks, "Do you all see? After a long silence, he throws it down and says: "The fragrance of the osmanthus grows cold, and the autumnal countenance fades."
Wild geese fly through the frost; chrysanthemums by the fence are crimson. In praise of Nanquan’s Beheading of the Cat, he said: Longquan is raised up before the pivot of action;
Killing or enlivening as the moment demands, blood splashes the heavens. Who dares meet the blade to vie for victory or defeat? To mobilize troops behind the battle lines is all in vain.
In praise of the Woman Emerging from Samādhi, he said: Deep and secluded flower paths, sealed by azure clouds; Three or two form a flock.
The display of skill is exhausted; with a single cry from a bird, the mountain colors break into dawn.

Having sung the "Spring" to its conclusion within the painted pavilion (the successor of Hongjue Myn), on the first day of the new year at Longshu, Chan Master Gengchuojie held a small assembly. Distant mountains are drenched in ink-black, wild waters drag trailing sapphire;

crows caw and magpies chatter—every word is upright, every utterance correct. To understand this is the *tathatā* Buddha-nature; not to understand it is to remain muddled and vague. As for this mountain monk:
To announce it in such a manner is very much like following after sounds and chasing after forms. Is there anyone among the assembly who does not fall into sound and form?
If you can be clear and precise right here, only then will you be able to travel the same path and follow the same tracks as the two venerable masters Xiangyan and Lingyun.
I wonder, do you all truly understand? After a long silence, he let out a shout and said: "Rarely do we encounter a guest with pierced ears."
I often see those who mark the boat [to find what was lost in the water]. Tonight’s small *chan* discourse: the year is spent and the age exhausted; winter passes and spring returns.
Whether rich or poor, noble or base, suffering or joyful, sorrowful or happy—the joyful find joy and their spirits soar; the suffering find suffering and their brows knit in frowns.
Yet they fall short of us monks beneath these forest trees, who do not follow such shifting turns. We exhaust them until it reaches the very marrow of our bones, right until there is no ground left.
"Without a needle—this is precisely where one lets go of body and life; only then can one be in harmony with the Way. Suddenly, amidst cold ashes, a bean pops;
its enjoyment through kalpas remains undiminished. Is there anyone among you who is like this? Guangxiao shall provide testimony for you."
After a long silence, he said: "This mountain monk is utterly exhausted; who would have known that the ground is so vast and people so few?

On the occasion of the opening of the retreat, the formal procedure was followed on the fifteenth day of the tenth month. The officials struck the bell and beat the drum, thereby opening the great forge and the red furnace.

It is precisely here that Buddhas are cooked and patriarchs are refined. Whether they be dull iron or stubborn copper, all without exception must enter within this space. Take care not to scorch your own forehead!
"Scorched head. One must strictly avoid carelessness and negligence. Once the dust is cleared and the light arises, you will naturally transcend both the present and the past.
If you continue to procrastinate and remain indifferent in your progress, when—like the donkey-year—will you ever attain clarity? Friends, tell me: where does the point of benefit or harm lie?
"The sweet melon is sweet from stem to tip; the bitter gourd is bitter from root to fruit. Thus asked the Elder Dajue Xiu.
"When the skull is smashed to pieces, what then? The Master said, "Fill the ditches and block the ravines. Xiu then withdrew. A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return? The Master said, "The tongue does not leave the mouth. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm.
He composed a verse on the World-Honored One’s ascent of the seat: "Gautama was too frugal; Mañjuśrī was extravagant. [It is] before the eyes of all people."
Scattering sand. This draws forth those who merely echo empty sounds, their deliberations vast and numerous as hemp seeds.
The Verse on the Old Woman Throwing Her Child says: "Meeting an adversary, the war drums are struck; It is not like the wondrous array of golden sands.
Delighting in a single decisive cut—how truly swift! Who knows this divine mechanism through a thousand years? (By Shiweng Min, successor).
Chan Master Guzhuo Zhe of Lishang was from a prominent family in Henan.

After attending upon Tiantong Muan and receiving his formal entrustment (*śāsana*), he tied up thatched grass to dwell in the Fiquan Hermitage. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma within the bustling marketplace? The Master said:
[The assembly] could not push their way through. [A monk] asked, "How can this be seen? The Master said, "At the pork butcher's stall; in the tea and salt shop.
(Shanweng Mien was his successor).
Chan Master Jingjie Langpingli of Luzhou ascended the hall and said: "To speak in such a way is too exposed; not to speak in such a way is too superficial.
One must by all means avoid seeking it from others; only upon returning home does one reach the ultimate. Be careful not to wander outside, for there you will still find freedom.
The mountain monk has thus proclaimed this; is there anyone among the assembly who can take it up? After a long silence, he said: "Also..."
This is pitying one’s child without realizing the shame (from the lineage of Master Mí Shānwēng).
Chan Master Chōng Xī’ān of Pǔmíng in Jiāxìng ascended the hall and said: “The Dharma has no fixed form; it accords with conditions as its principle.

The Way does not travel in vain; it acts as the master wherever it is. You must know that even in a place where the wall stands ten thousand fathoms high, there is no hindrance to mixing water with mud.”
Sometimes, when mixing water with mud, it remains standing upright as before, towering thousands of fathoms high.
Even so, [the Master] drew a line on the ground with his staff and said, "This too is adding legs to a snake. Today, since Upāsaka Chong has arrived here, [I must speak].
Furthermore, how does one act as a person? Opening a new shop where the old one stood, bustling about with every step, yet the heart bears no grudge against others and the face shows no shame.
Regarding the verse on Linji’s story of the two head monks of the two halls shouting at the same time, it says: "Why need one further lead troops when already so formidable?
The dragon roars and the tiger shouts, moving freely in all directions. True wind naturally returns to the royal transformation; A single sword, frosty and bright."

The cold pervades the ten thousand lands; the pure mind is not the Buddha, and wisdom is not the Way. It is said: "Reflecting back, I enter the village lanes; when sorrow comes, with whom can I speak?
On the ancient road there are no travelers; the autumn wind stirs the grain. (By the Elder Myn, successor to [Master] Shan).
The Complete Works of the Five Lamps, Volume Seventy-Five.
Compiled by the monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital;
reviewed by the monk (Chao Kui), Abbot of Gu Huayan Temple in the Capital. Presented for Imperial Review.
A Record of the Succession of the Thirty-Fifth Generation under Mount Heng in the Linji School, Presented for Inspection.
Chan Master Tianning Shiguo Jiefan of Ningbo was the son of the Zhu family of Huating. At the age of thirty-five, he cast aside his Confucian cap and underwent tonsure.
He first studied under Wanfeng Bi, contemplating the koan "The Water Walking on East Mountain," but did not attain realization.
Later, he took up the "Bamboo Stick" koan, neglecting both sleep and food. For one period, he did not recognize the faces of those in his quarters. While he was walking in meditation, he heard—
A monk beside him said, "You must not interpret this as a substantial dharma. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying:
"The bamboo stick, when taken up, makes touch and avoidance difficult; Cast out in the open light, it chills the people to the bone.

From now on, having realized the true message, I shall overturn the old banner-pole before the gate. Yuanbi approved of this. Later, he went to Jinsu, where he relied upon Master Ming, and subsequently received the Dharma at Pingyang.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Damei says 'this very mind is Buddha'; Mazu says 'neither mind nor Buddha.
If one does not perform a great somersault upon the earth, even the void will be made to burst asunder. Tianning, however, is not like this:

casting aside mind and discarding Buddha, he holds aloft his black-lacquered staff and beats people until their heads split and brains shatter. Is this blind punishment and blind flogging? Or is it the compassionate heart of an old woman?"
[The Master] said: "Everyone! There are those who can analyze and discern things down to the finest detail; I grant you that your eyes do not harbor a speck of dust.

Today is the fifteenth day of the seventh month as we conclude the summer retreat. Each one of you has sandals like tigers at your feet, with satchels and carrying poles slung across your shoulders, intending to roam through various monasteries.
Yet, because the prohibitions are so strict and the regulations so severe, all six gates are locked fast; indeed, they are so tightly sealed that not even a breath of air can pass."
Even with wings attached, it would be difficult to fly across. It is best to stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high;

beneath one’s feet, one must tread with steady steps. When the time and conditions meet, the eight directions are all mine. With a single blow, I shatter the vast void; the True Person of No Rank has nowhere to hide.
(Master Mǎn Shānwēng, successor to the lineage.)
Chan Master Boreyan Benhuang of Baoyan on Mount Yu was styled Gouqiu. He was the son of the Xu family of Changshu.

His father dreamed that an elderly monastic from Tiantai came to stay with them before he was born. Initially, he studied the Tiantai school under the senior scholar Guansan. Later, he associated with Jin-su Rong and Gu-nan Men;
consequently, he focused single-mindedly on the "Upward" (transcendent) teaching and vowed to don the black robes [of a monk]. His mother’s surname was Tao.
Because his master had previously received a betrothal gift, he was urgently ordered to complete the marriage. For four seasons, winter and summer alike, he did not remove his belt from his robes.

His mother, realizing that his resolve could not be forced, finally permitted him to leave the household life. (Sun Xuewu composed a poem for him, containing the lines: "The golden *dhūta* accomplishes secret practice; the flower-scattering goddesses do not wet his robes.

At the age of twenty, he requested Master Rong of Mount Jing to preside over the Vimalakīrti assembly. He presented his realization, and Master Rong gave his approval, personally inscribing a verse as a gift.
There was a man of penetrating insight who had reached the root of heaven; he transcended the mundane and met with the wondrous words of the source.
The following year, the Master packed his bag and went to Tiantong to seek Ming’s tonsure. Ming presented him with the koan of the World-Honored One’s first birth.

At these words, the Master’s doubts were suddenly resolved, and he spontaneously offered this verse: "Eyes horizontal, nose vertical—the face as born of one's mother; The myriad sages have always been but one."

Mian said, "I am rather suspicious of Tian Tong’s single staff; it seems he has taken fresh mugwort to cauterize a healed scar. Mian nodded in agreement and appointed him as the head of the secretariat.
After Mian had recorded his formal certification (*jibie*), the monk traveled to various regions for several years.

Later, when the Imperial Preceptor Qian Mozhai invited him to reside at Baoyan Monastery, he visited the temple on the occasion of Gu Nan’s birthday to avoid guests. There, he engaged in a spirited conversation with the Master for two nights until after midnight.

San Gu composed the *Gujie* (Ancient Explanations), consisting of over seven hundred words, in which he expressed his hope that the Master would serve as a pillar for the Dharma during the final age (*mofa*).
Later, he appeared in the world and resided at Wanshou Monastery in Guangling, Huqiu in Wumen, and Anchan in Kunshan, traveling among various monasteries to propagate the teachings.
There exists a collection of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) that circulates in the world (he was a successor of Shanweng Min).
Chan Master Jinghui Xiangguang Benji of Yangzhou was the son of the Shang family of Puzhou in Shanxi.

From the moment he left infancy, he knew how to serve the Buddha. Upon reaching adulthood, he went to Jinghui to receive the tonsure and subsequently followed the Vinaya master Samit Guang to receive the full precepts.

Having received the full precepts, he felt that his own fundamental matter remained unclarified; consequently, he neglected both sleep and food. He first visited Wengu Yin of Zhexi, who instructed him on the essentials of the Buddha-remembrance practice (*nianfo*).
Next, he visited Tianyin Xiu, but no realization was awakened within him. He then went to rely upon Master Wumen of Tiantong.

One day, the Master approached with indignation and requested instruction on the koan regarding the state before one’s parents were born. Wumen struck him across the face with a resounding slap. The Master—
He stood watching. It happened that the Head Seat Rong was standing nearby. Rong scolded him, saying, "Head Seat, why do you not pay your respects?
As soon as the Master rose from his prostration, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Just as he was about to offer words of response, Rong again raised his staff to strike him.

The Master caught the staff and said, "Please, Old Monk, show me respect. He then shook out his sleeves and departed. Thus, it was under Tiantong that the Master stayed for the longest period of time.
In the *guisi* year of the Shunzhi era (1653), Daofeng Hongjue Muan retired from his monastic duties to return to Mount Kuanglu.

As his boat passed through Wiyang, the Master [Zhixu] presented his petition for purification to the authorities, urging them with increasing earnestness to detain him. Muan granted his request; consequently, the regulations of the monastic community were gradually restored and promoted.
The Master further exerted all his strength in this endeavor without the slightest laxity. On another day, he entered the presence [of the authorities] bearing incense.
Baizhang reported what he had attained to Baoming; Baoming laughed loudly and, glaring at him with anger, scolded him, saying, "Not yet!
Baizhang was startled, his sweat pouring down, and he could not answer. He then engaged in intensive investigation for over an hour, whereupon he suddenly saw the true nature of Baoming’s person.
Later, when Baoming went to Faying in Qingzhou, he entrusted the construction of the Kumu Hall (Dried Tree Hall) that he had previously initiated—its work being unfinished—to Master Baizhang.
The Master further exerted his utmost efforts in its management, never finding rest even for a moment; thus, he was able to complete the work.

He also constructed the Great Hero Treasure Hall (*Mahāvīra-vihāra*), with pavilions, towers, halls, and quarters arranged in order on all sides—left, right, front, and back—which may truly be called the height of prosperity for that era.
In the year Gengxu, when Ming traveled through the Jianghuai region and arrived at Guangling, the Master again welcomed him back to his own quarters, serving him with ever greater diligence.
Before long, he ordered his attendants to call the Master to him and asked, "When Mazu’s single shout left Baizhang deaf for three days, what was the underlying meaning?
The Master replied, "It was a case of thoroughgoing elegance. Ming then called to an attendant, "Bring the staff! The Master said, "Draw the bow after the thief has fled. Ming nodded in approval.
He then slowly handed over his robe and whisk to the Master, along with the lineage seal (yuanliu), and spoke this verse: Yellow... [the rest of the verse is omitted in the source text]
At midnight, the plum blossoms do not allow a breeze to pass; this brings shame upon the descendants for three days of deafness. When emerging from the weeds, do not disdain re-entering them;
distinguish the fish from the dragons amidst the waves of the Hutuo River. He then commanded the Master to succeed him as abbot and addressed the assembly: "O students of the Way!"
Simply attain the root and do not worry about the branches; once the root is attained, the branches will come of themselves. You practitioners of Chan—what, after all, do you call the root?
This monk has throughout his life established himself by means of this, engaged with the world by means of this, and tested people by means of this.
"You all, do not let your time pass in vain, content to be among the common crowd of this age. [The Master] addressed the assembly:
"Lately, groups have gathered in various quarters, numbering three hundred or five hundred at a time, engaging in a vast clamor of 'Chan.

Now, one who acts as a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) must possess a heart of genuine sincerity toward the Buddhas and Patriarchs before they may be permitted to speak of Chan or the Way, or to employ the striking of staffs and the shouting of *he*."
Not so. Even if one’s spiritual capacity were like a flash of lightning and one’s eloquence like a cascading river, I would simply say to such a person:
"It is not yet. You all, tell me: how can you possess the true heart-mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Simply wait until the snow melts away.
"Spontaneously spring arrives. His instruction to people was as earnest and direct as this.

In the winter solstice of the year Jiwu (1279), he personally wrote the "Verse on Sweeping Away Dust" and showed it to the assembly, saying: "On the final day of every year, sweep away the dust of the entire year."

"Dust returns after a hundred years; one does not see the person who sweeps it away. When the assembly saw this verse, they all privately suspected that the Master harbored a desire for world-weariness.
In the spring of the following year, he happened to manifest a slight illness and consequently ceased eating grain.
On the twenty-fifth day of the second month, his disciples were all struck with alarm and wept as they knelt in a circle around him, entreating him with verses. The Master said:
"Throughout my life, I have taught people with nothing but the unadulterated essence of my true nature. I have never used idle talk or superfluous words to defile the ears and eyes of the world.
Today, you wish for this old monk to do so? The assembly pressed their request firmly. The Master rose from his seat and said, 'In my years, I am approaching seventy.
Today, it shall not be improper for me to manifest the form of a great man for all of you to behold and take to heart.'"
He rose from his seat and, stretching out both hands, looked at the assembly and asked, "Do you understand? After a long pause, he struck his knee once with his hand and passed away peacefully.
His secular age was sixty-nine, and his monastic seniority was forty-nine (he was the successor of Shanweng Min).
Chan Master Fozhi Benxiao of Tiger Hill in Gusu was the son of the Hu family of Changzhou. From his very conception, he possessed a divine nature.
At the age of nine, he went to the Ice Valley on Mount Baotang to receive the tonsure and the full precepts. He studied under Cangxue Che.
One day, he met Fuyan Rong, who asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Suzhou. Rong asked, "What are you doing here? The Master said:
He came specifically to beg for a severe beating. Xue Rong said, "I will not strike you, you dead man.
The Master said, "Where is your compassion? Rong said, "I let you go; have some tea first. Later, while serving Mǎng at Píngyáng, they heard thunder.
Mǎng said to the Master, "Thunder awakens the hibernating insects; why does it roar on New Year's Day? The Master said, "I am executing the *Vimalakīrti* command in reverse. Alone.

Lü said, "It is the dawn of spring. Mǐn said, "Suppose there is a person who studies in the morning and recites in the evening, never departing from Chan and the teachings. Suddenly, they encounter a thunderbolt—what then?
The Master said, "To experience this throughout one's entire body is a kindness too great to repay. Mǐn approved (Mǐn was a successor of Shānwēng).
Master Benjian Chan of Yanfu Suoyan held a ceremony for opening the furnace and ascended the hall to speak. "There is one phrase that pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
there is one phrase that cannot be lifted by a spoon; and there is one phrase that I shall tell you only when Mount Ziwai nods its head.
You all, if you can see clearly within these three phrases, you will penetrate the three kinds of illnesses of the Dharmakāya."
What difficulty is there in this "Planting Light"? If you have not yet realized it, then among these three phrases, there is one phrase that is your very own flesh-and-bone shirt and fat-smeared cap.
For now, return to the hall and examine it closely. In a small-scale sermon (*xiao can*):
When Maitreya Buddha appears in the world to preach the Dharma for the sake of others, he possesses nothing more than a single cloth bag. Within that cloth bag, he wraps and carries everything.
Goods are spread out on the street for everyone to see; they are nothing more than rice, flour, fish, meat, straw sandals, wooden clogs, sand, gravel, and shards of tile.
Seeing that people do not understand, he again draws up the mouth of his cloth bag and carries it elsewhere.
What this mountain monk speaks to you brothers tonight is, for the most part, simply each of you...
The things wrapped within this human skin bag are nothing other than ignorance and afflictions (*avidyā-kleśa*).
Bodhi and nirvana, true thusness (*tathatā*) and buddha-nature, as well as the twenty-five realms of existence within the triple world—these too can be laid out for all you brothers to see.
Then, taking up his whisk, he drew a circle (○) and said: "Ignorance and afflictions; bodhi and nirvana; true..."
"Is the Buddha-nature such that the twenty-five states of existence within the triple world are all this very thing?
He then drew a circle (○) and said, "Is rice, flour, fish, meat, sand, stones, tiles, rubble, straw sandals, and wooden clogs also this very thing?
"Brothers, if you understand, then all of these are this very thing. He threw down his whisk and said, "Pick up the whisk and go. "If you do not understand..."
Reaching out his hand, he said: "I beg for a single coin. In the evening sermon, he took up his staff, struck it once on the left side, and said:
"This is principle (li). He struck it once on the right side and said: "This is phenomenon (shi). Principle has its own path of understanding."
Regarding matters, there is a path for resolving them. For instance, before I even raised my staff, how would you have resolved it?
[He] lowered his staff and said: "Three thousand blows at dawn; eight hundred blows at dusk. Addressing the assembly on the Mid-Autumn Festival:

"The light upon the head is brilliantly clear; what lies before the eyes is pure and white. If you say this is the clarity of the eye, the moon is shining in the midst of the sky. If you say this is..."
The moon is bright. What is before one’s eyes at dawn? At this moment, you all should quickly press forward.
If you fully realize the moon of tonight, you will not be deluded for ten thousand kalpas. If you do not realize the moon of tonight, you will be needlessly disturbed by worldly toil.
Each person is fundamentally perfected; every individual lacks nothing. He gives a shout and says: “If you miss it by the side of the tea bowl, where is the clear light?”
When Master Taoshu arrived at Shuanggui, as soon as he entered the hall, the Rector asked: "The National Teacher gave ninety-six circular diagrams to Danyuan;
what was the meaning of this? The Master took his incense-ruler and placed it crosswise across the burner.
The Rector said: "Danyuan advanced three steps and performed a woman’s bow—what about that? The Master turned the incense-ruler upside down. The Rector said: "This is learning."

"Bottom. "This is the bottom of awakening. The Master then struck him. On another occasion, the Master took a bamboo staff and drew a circle on the ground, standing in its midst and saying, "Who can enter here?
A monk leaped into it. The Master immediately stepped out and pointed at the circle.
The Master said, "I am referring to the Sangha. You, monk, try coming out and looking! The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "You foolish madman!
Who has bound you? (Shanweng Min, successor).
Chan Master Xuedian Chi was the son of the Chen family in Tongzhou. At the age of fourteen, he went to Daoyin Chengji at the capital to receive the tonsure and full ordination.
One day, when a guest raised the koan regarding one’s "original face," the Master was unable to answer.
He then traveled extensively to visit various monastic centers and sought an audience with Xuyun Men at Tiantong. There, he experienced a sudden awakening.

He subsequently followed Men through Wulei, Longchi, and Jinsu, where he refined his studies for a long time until finally receiving formal certification (*yinke*). When he ascended the hall to preach, his wisdom-light shone forth clearly and penetratingly, without any sense of direction or bias.
With a single phrase held forth in the open, he cut off all manifold distinctions. Thus, as he fully wielded the correct command, the paths of sages and ordinary beings were blocked.
Severed! The arrowheads meet point-to-point; illumination and function are simultaneous. Yet, even though this is so, you must still bite through the iron sorrel cake, which contains every flavor.
Just as when, two thousand years ago, Kāśyapa was born and pointed at heaven and earth, Yunmen said:
"If I had seen him then, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to a dog, so as to bring peace to the world."
Now tell me: what kind of eyes did the old fellow Yunmen possess? After a long silence, he said: "Do not let us discuss this further face-to-face;
the Vinaya was originally the old Jeta Grove. (Master Mön, successor to Shansheng).
Chan Master Guzhan Cizong Benming of Zhenzhou was the son of the Wang family of Fuliang. At the age of fifteen, he received the tonsure and initially followed Guxue Zhe.
He applied himself diligently to the koan of Nanquan’s “Beating the Cat” and attained a realization. Later, he studied under Shanweng Min, who posed this question to him:
"The mind-moon is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. The light does not illuminate a mirror, nor does the mirror exist [as a separate entity]. The light..."
When both mirrors are forgotten, what thing is there? The Master said: "Splitting Mount Hua in two paths; the waters of Wan’an flow on, unaware of spring.
Mǐn said: "Not yet—speak further. The Master said: "I know not where the human face has gone;
the peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze. Mǐn nodded in approval. Addressing the assembly, he raised the case of Shānwēng Mǐn and posed the question: "There is a person..."
"Attending court in the morning and reciting in the evening, never departing from Chan and the teachings—what is it like when one suddenly encounters a bolt of lightning?

He answered on his own behalf: "The peach pit is smashed to pieces; the original kernel is revealed. The Master composed a verse: North and south are not distinguished, yet one still falls into views;

The paths of sage and ordinary are severed, yet dust still remains. With a single blow to the back of the head, all are turned over at once; Body and mind stripped bare, without reliance, naturally peerless.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Go thus. The monk asked, "Is this not it?
The Master said, "Falling into pits and falling into ditches" (Shanweng Myn, successor).
Chan Master Lin-yuan Ying of Liu-an was a native of the Zhang family in Kunming, Yunnan. His household had long served the Buddha, and from his youth he took delight in Buddhist scriptures.

Upon reaching adulthood, he followed Master Lang at Shui-mu to receive formal training. While reading the *Zhimen Jingxun* (Admonitions for the Monastic Gate), he closed the volume and sighed, saying, "This is a bridge and a ferry for saving the world.
To clarify the Great Dharma, one must seek the meaning of the 'separate transmission outside the teachings.'"
Having taken his leave, he headed for Sichuan to receive full instructions from Chan Master Mingbin of Shuanggui. Not long after, Mingbin passed away.

While reading the *Record of Gaofeng* with fellow practitioners, he encountered the four lines beginning with "The mud ox at the bottom of the sea" and could not shake the doubt they provoked from his mind. He subsequently resolved to leave the mountain ranges.
He went directly to Pingyang in Yuezhou to visit Mian. After half a year, he repeatedly received the teacher’s instruction that acted as a medicinal cure.

Thereupon, the obstruction that had weighed upon his chest throughout his life suddenly melted away like ice. One day, while recounting his insights, Mian praised him with admiration. After a long time, Mian appointed him as the guest master, and subsequently promoted him to the position of attendant.
He was then granted a formal transmission of the Dharma. Thus, for ten years by Mian’s side, he never shied from labor. Mian—
He returned to seclusion. Upon moving to the Dabe Temple in Liu'an Prefecture, he ascended the hall for the opening of the meditation furnace.
He declared: "I shall take ninety days as the furnace and forge; I shall take the painful staff and the hot shouts as the tongs and hammer;

I shall take the three hundred and sixty joints of the body and the eighty-four thousand pores as a single ball of doubt. You all, during the twelve periods of the day—whether walking, sitting, or lying down—should simply [apply this] there."
When putting on clothes or eating a meal, exert your full brilliance and strike with a single blow until everything is pulverized. Then, sparks will naturally fly forth;
the nature-ground will open up, illuminating heaven and earth and penetrating the past and present through and through. Looking left and right, he said:
"Is there anyone among you who, disregarding danger and ruin, plunges in with their whole being? If there is, this mountain monk’s staff will serve as witness for you."
He then took up his staff and struck it once. Military Officer Dong arrived with a square bamboo staff as a gift. The Master ascended the hall and, holding up the staff, said:
"It was not brought from Mount Tiantai, nor did it originate from Mount Nanyue. Its appearance is exceptionally unique; its form seems poised to soar into the clouds.
Its firm nodes are serene and elegant, transcending the crowd and rising above the rest. At times, I call it a 'hare's horn staff'; at other times..."

They call it a crane-knee staff; sometimes it kills or gives life, bestowing or taking away, fully manifesting its wondrous function. Sometimes it is held crosswise or set upside down, briefly revealing its style and character.
Even if Linji were to arrive, he would have no choice but to look on from the sidelines; even if Deshan were to emerge, he would be left with nothing but a sigh.
There is no door for bearing this burden. Even so, as for my own role as a military officer (*canyun*), how shall I proceed?
To bring peace and stability to the state depends entirely upon this; when the wind blows, the grass bends—how could this be left to human effort?
(He strikes the meditation seat once. Evening Sermon: An ancient said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. Even to speak thus is already to miss the point. You all...
"Throughout the twelve periods of the day, how must a person ultimately conduct their life in order to be in accord with this? Try to say something. The assembly stood waiting expectantly.
The Master took up his staff and struck them all at once, dispersing them. Evening Sermon. A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master?
The Master said, "Two bowls of gruel and one meal. The monk asked, "Is there anything extraordinary within this? The Master—
He said, "Having eaten, the belly is not hungry. Then he remarked, "This monk’s question was extraordinary, yet my answer was commonplace.
I shall now bring forth our house style for all to deliberate upon. Even if you were to deliberate it to the very end, it would still be like adding frost to snow.
In the evening *can*, he looked to his left and right and said, "In this place of mine, even a sword cannot cleave it; even a needle cannot pierce it."
They did not enter. Bodhidharma could only gaze at the cliff; Linji retreated a thousand miles. How will you all ultimately manage?
Even if you can approach the mountain monk’s gate and enter the mountain monk’s room—though you may indeed approach and enter—you must by all means avoid dozing with your eyes open.
(He gives a shout. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When Prince Siddhārtha was born from his mother’s right side, he pointed with his hand..."

The Heavenly Being points to the earth and takes seven steps, walking all around; it is quite like creating a demonic apparition or a grotesque specter, bringing trouble upon his descendants for generations to come.
Today, Great Compassion sees injustice on the road and cannot help but draw his sword to assist; he pours cold water right upon their heads for all to see clearly. Evening Assembly. Question:
"When Deshan holds the evening assembly, he does not answer questions. He says that anyone who asks a question receives thirty blows."
"I do not know, Great Wisdom, whether you permit students here to engage in dialogue. The Master said, "Does your skin still have blood?
As the monk prepared to respond, the Master struck him and said, "In other quarters they say: 'It is walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
it is putting on clothes and eating food; it is carrying firewood and drawing water. But when one arrives at the gate of大悲 (Dabei), I tell them:"
It is certainly not so. But tell me, what excellence does Great Compassion possess? After a long silence, he said: "The water rises and the boat floats higher. Evening Sermon:
He then slung his staff over his shoulder and said: "I look toward the woodcutter to emerge; at dusk, I return with the white clouds.
Treading upon the path from whence I came, do not speak of the 'highest-grade faculty. When Great Compassion speaks thus, do you approve? If you approve, you have not yet escaped the net."
Roots and objects. Refusing to give rise to them, one avoids falling into hell. Evening Assembly. The Patriarch came from the West; he did not establish written words.
He pointed directly at the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha. I dare ask you all: how do you see this Buddha-nature?
Even before your tongue has moved, thirty blows are well-deserved! And another thirty! Master Bodhidharma shall take these for himself; it does not concern others.
Everyone, tell me: where does the mountain monk’s intention lie? "In vain one harbors the intent not yet returned, speaking it to those on the path of desire.
Evening Session: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; to what place does the One return? The lantern loses its nose; the pillar's cold hair stands on end.
What basis is there for the seven-pound robe? [He] strikes the whisk and says: "Zhaozhou was reckless; few people recognize it."
I know. I urge you not to travel the path of the mind. Opening the furnace, I ascend the hall. Throughout the various quarters, they discourse on the wondrous and discuss the ultimate;
yet here at the Great Compassion Hall, we do not rely on words and speech. Since we do not rely on words and speech, what is it that is being spoken upon this seat right now?
And what is it that is being heard by those seated below? If you are one who can "mention one and clarify three," then [you will understand].
Yet it cannot be confined within a cage, nor can it be summoned back by calling. Killing and giving life are applied according to the moment; moving forward and retreating with sovereign ease.
If this is not yet so, then fierce flames will not allow even a mosquito to alight, and refined gold must be tested in the fire. [Evening Sermon:
If one discusses this matter, both ordinary and sage are forgotten, and delusion and enlightenment are both cast aside. To enter into my Dharma and have even a slight resonance with it—if, however...
"Not so. Dwelling among the ordinary and the holy, one is obstructed by the ordinary and the holy; entering into delusion and awakening, one is obstructed by delusion and awakening.

He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Does this mountain monk’s staff have any place where it is obstructed? He struck the ground once with it and said, "The spirit of a man of purpose rivals the Ox and Dipper constellations;
it is no ordinary curved branch. A monk asked, "What is the realm of great compassion? The Master said:
A bridge spans both banks; water winds around one side. [The monk] asked, "What is it like to be a person within this realm?
The Master said, "For many years he has not stepped outside his door, yet his footprints cover every street and alley. [The monk] asked, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
why then does the dog lack it? The Master said, "How can you be so stubborn and perverse? [The monk] asked, "What is the Linji school? The Master—
He said, "A 'white-handed' thief is not yet a true robber. [The student] asked, "What is the direct path back to the source?
The Master said, "It is not far from here to the West Gate. [The student] said, "Is this very place it? The Master said, "It is more than one hundred thousand miles away" (Shanweng Man, successor).
A monk from Wuchang Yuan Tong went to visit Master Yingtuorei. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan.
The Master said, "Have you been to Mount Nanyue? He replied, "I have never climbed the mountain. The Master said, "Where have you been wandering? He replied, "Today I arrived directly at Yuan Tong.
The Master said, "I knew you had come from afar; you have spent a great deal on the price of your straw sandals. (This was the lineage of Shanweng Min).
Chan Master Lingfu Xian ascended the hall and said: "A constellation appears in the heavens; Beneath the earth, one has already become a Buddha.
Turn your head and observe closely: Nailing a wooden peg into empty space. All sentient beings throughout the great earth— Having verified the turtle, they all become turtles. (Shanweng Wensi)
The lay practitioner Du Zilian, courtesy name Chuan, was a native of Qingzhou in Shandong. In the Dinghai year of the Shunzhi era, he served in various provincial and regional magistracies.
Having received the Dharma from Tiantong Muan, he traveled freely through all quarters of the land. One day, he visited Tiezhou Hai at Mount Jinshan.
The layman asked, "Today there is a grand performance of the Water and Land rites; can all sentient beings truly be delivered? Hai—
[Daokai] asked, "What do you call a sentient being? The Master said, "Once one tastes the flavor of the Dharma, one becomes a Buddha on the spot.
Daokai said, "That is his own inherent nature; it has nothing to do with me. The Master said, "A double win, a single match. The Master then traveled to Tianting in Mingzhou.
When Shao Gujie met with him, the scholar asked, "What kind of people have lived on this mountain in the past? Jie replied, "Da Hui of the Song dynasty and Zu Chan of the Ming dynasty;

three hundred years have passed since then, and now the Wheel of the Dharma has turned once more. The scholar pointed to a monk standing nearby and said, "The Wheel of the Dharma has turned again after three hundred years.
Today, Master, do not let it slip right before your eyes! Tell me, what does 'slipping it' mean?"
"What is it? Jie said, "Blue sky and bright day; do not speak of dreams. The Master said, "I have found a true insider of our household.
Jie then withdrew. Later, the Master visited Shi Chao Ning at Tianjie Temple.

Seeing a seal impression on the wall that resembled a *mandala* (the circular mark), he asked, "Is this one with the *mandala* of the Miao-yang school, or are they two different things? Ning replied, "What is this?"

The Master asked, "Where is it located? Yunmen said, "I say it is Tianjie Temple. Fengxue said, "How regrettable! The Master asked, "Are the Three Principles and Five Ranks the same as or different from this?
Yunmen snapped his fingers. The Master also snapped his fingers. Yunmen said, "Is this the same or different? The Master said, [It is neither.]
"In the same pit there is no different soil. [The Master] asked, "Regarding Lingyun seeing peach blossoms—what is the meaning?
The Master said, "The head remains as it was, covered in dust. [The Master] asked, "And what about 'The Chezhong monk’s robe weighs seven catties'?
The Master said, "It crushes the fellow carrying a wooden board" (Shanweng Min, successor).
Chan Master Chang of Zhan’an at Jingxing Temple on Tiantai was the son of the Wu family of Gushan in Ningbo.

At the age of twenty-seven, he received the tonsure at Jinsu Temple and attended upon Old Man Wu. His witty exchanges were swift and incisive, and his reputation grew weighty within the monastic community.

Later, he received the transmission and seal of approval from Shiqi Yun. Ascending the hall, he said: "A jackal occupies the lion’s den; a mountain fowl roosts in the phoenix’s nest. Their feathers and plumage..."
Their substance is difficult to equalize; yet the wondrous mind is present in all. What distinction can there be between the ordinary and the sage? The Great Way knows no intervals;

it is only in terms of awakening and delusion that we speak of them. Thus it is said: "The Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs is like the mechanism of an iron ox—it admits of no deliberation and requires no thought.
He struck the meditation staff and said: "If one can take up this burden here, one is like a lion king crouching on the ground, while the hundred beasts hide away."
Trace. The vermilion phoenix soars aloft; all other birds gather together. How could they be like those that merely cling to grass or lean upon wood, attempting a mere semblance?
Is there anyone here who can truly shoulder this burden? He then joined his palms and said: "I dare not slight you; you shall all become Buddhas.
Ascending the hall, he said: "When the sky is clear, the sun shines; when it rains, the ground becomes wet. We face one another directly—what need is there for further words?"
"Thus, matters do not have a single direction. Holding up his staff, he said, "This too is washing clods of earth in the mud. He then descended from his seat.
At the commencement of the retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "The ox-hide drum covers the pillar; the pillar chirps and squeaks. The pillar hangs the lantern."
The lantern laughs "he-he. The lantern radiates light from its entire body; the pillar is completely without any openings.
Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind on this long ago, yet until now he has not attained the wondrous. A monk visited for an audience.
As soon as the monk made his salutation, the Master stepped out to bow to him. The monk bowed in return. The Master said, "I bow once, you return one bow. Why do you return my bow?"
The monk said, “One bow for one bow. The Master said, “It is because of me that you bow; what then? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him out.
A verse on "All Dharmas Return to One" says: On the west side of the painted bridge is my home;
If you, young sir, have leisure, come to drink tea. With yellow earth for walls and thatched roofs of reed, Before the courtyard stands a tree of purple *zhijing* flowers.
The Master resided successively at Yukxi and Huangyan Bao’en in Tiantai, Tonggang Fengming, Xianju Shizi, Fangshan Jingfeng, and various locations including Loujiang Nan’guang;
he has recorded sayings for each of these places that circulate in the world. On the full moon of the intercalary sixth month in the Jiachen year of the Kangxi era, the Master fell ill.
He composed a "Song of Recluse Freedom" (Xiaoyao ge) in the manner of the Elder Xueqiao. This continued until the twenty-seventh day.
He took up his brush and wrote a verse, saying: "In my life within this world, I have been utterly bare; Upon death, I shall likewise require the fire.
Take heed, my sons, there is nothing else to say: At my final moment, I beg only for a single stalk of thatch.
His stupa was erected on the left ridge of the Fangshan summit (Shiqi Yunsi).
Chan Master Fatcheng of Daming in Ningbo was surnamed Lin by birth and was a native of Ruian in Dong’ou. His original name was Zengzhi.
Having passed the local examination, he studied at Xingshan Temple in Yongjia, where he immediately developed faith in the supramundane Dharma and observed the precept against killing.

All his activities consisted of releasing captive animals and burying the remains of the dead. Recently, I observed that the lay practitioner Masengma had gained a deepening faith through my guidance.
One day, while sitting in a bamboo grove, a leaf happened to fly down. The layman picked it up and asked, "What news is this?
The Master said, "The nature of the leaf is fundamentally empty. The layman asked, "How then can there be this leaf? The Master lowered his head and remained silent.
[The Master] spoke. For seven days and nights he did not allow for formal visits [to his room]. One day, the Master took up the line from the *Song of Realizing the Way*:
"Grasping the moon in the water," and posed it as a verbal pivot (*chuyǔ*), saying: "Only when you grasp it is it the Chan of the Patriarchs. The Master immediately presented a verse, saying:
"When deluded, one mistakenly recognizes the moon in the stream; Upon awakening, one knows the stream is within the moon. A single expanse of radiance—take it in your cupped hands."
"There is no need to stretch out your arm; you have already attained realization. Linzi was granted this permission, and it was said that he had attained Zen.

He subsequently resided at Mijin Temple on Mount Doutu, which was the site of the Tang dynasty master Yisuojue’s practice hall. Seeing that the temple was ancient and on the verge of collapse, he immediately formed a vow to restore this ancestral monastery.
In the spring of the Wuchen year of the Chongzhen era, he dreamed of a giant holding a tall lantern, upon which was written:

In the Wuchen (5th year of the cycle) examination, he later recorded his vow not to kill or commit adultery. When the list of successful candidates was posted, he indeed ranked first in his own category.

Upon his first appointment, he served as the Magistrate of Puyi in Chu; he maintained integrity and tranquility while eliminating administrative burdens, exercised extreme caution regarding criminal justice, and showed compassion for widowers and widows.

He strictly prohibited hunting and fishing and restored what had fallen into ruin. He moved the heavens so that the sweet dew descended repeatedly upon the mountains. One day, while conversing with a practitioner of Chan, they discussed the kōan of Zhang Zishao’s "Slaying the Elephant. Using Li Guang and Shi Hu as analogies, the monk Mo immediately questioned the Master on his own insight. The Master said, "One cut, and all are severed. The scholar remarked, "This is the Buddha-dharma of Dahui. The Master replied, "It has not yet reached my level. The scholar asked, "How so? The Master said, "He only knew how to slay the elephant; he did not know how to slay himself. The scholar was greatly enlightened by these words. Subsequently, the Master composed a verse to commemorate the event: "One cut, and all are severed; The elephant is slain, and the self is also slain. If you do not understand this principle, You will surely fall into the pit of views. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he summoned the scholar and said, "I have bestowed the Dharma upon you; you must propagate it widely. The scholar wept and said, "I am unworthy. The Master said, "Do not speak such words. You are the one who will uphold the lineage. The scholar then bowed and departed. The Master passed away on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the first year of the Jiading era (1208). His remains were enshrined in the pagoda at Mount Yunju. He was seventy-one years old. He was posthumously titled Great Master Xianji. His dharma heirs included the scholar Yang Jie, the monk Shouze, and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over three hundred. Among them, the monk Shouze was the most prominent. Shouze later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the second year of the Jiading era (1209) at the age of sixty-nine. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Zhenjie and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over two hundred. Among them, the monk Zhenjie was the most prominent. Zhenjie later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the third year of the Jiading era (1210) at the age of seventy-one. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Daoyuan and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over one hundred. Among them, the monk Daoyuan was the most prominent. Daoyuan later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the fourth year of the Jiading era (1211) at the age of seventy-three. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Fashen and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over eighty. Among them, the monk Fashen was the most prominent. Fashen later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the fifth year of the Jiading era (1212) at the age of seventy-five. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Mingzhao and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over sixty. Among them, the monk Mingzhao was the most prominent. Mingzhao later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the sixth year of the Jiading era (1213) at the age of seventy-seven. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Wenzhao and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over fifty. Among them, the monk Wenzhao was the most prominent. Wenzhao later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the seventh year of the Jiading era (1214) at the age of seventy-nine. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Xingzhi and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over forty. Among them, the monk Xingzhi was the most prominent. Xingzhi later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the eighth year of the Jiading era (1215) at the age of eighty-one. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Changqing and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over thirty. Among them, the monk Changqing was the most prominent. Changqing later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the ninth year of the Jiading era (1216) at the age of eighty-three. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Lingyuan and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over twenty. Among them, the monk Lingyuan was the most prominent. Lingyuan later resided at Mount Yunju, where he propagated the teachings extensively. His reputation spread throughout the realm. He passed away in the tenth year of the Jiading era (1217) at the age of eighty-five. His remains were enshrined in the same pagoda as the Master. His dharma heirs included the monk Miaozhuangyan and others. His recorded sayings and verses are extant. The Emperor conferred upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Xianji. His stupa was named "Donglin. The Emperor also bestowed upon him the purple robe and the honorific title of "Great Master Xianji. His disciples numbered over ten. Chan Master Tianxi Qian of Fucha Monastery in Pinghu, a successor in the thirty-fifth generation of the Nanyue lineage, was a native of the Chen family of Shangyu in Yue. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
From birth, he was exceptionally gifted. In his early twenties, he encountered a fellow practitioner of Chan who showed him the way of transcending the world;

he subsequently went forth under a certain master and received full ordination at Baoguo Monastery in Wumen. He first visited Master Wuzhun Shifan of Tiantong, and after that master passed away, the teacher lived in seclusion at Fu’an in Pinghu.
Later, he visited Master Nanquan Men, with whom he shared a profound spiritual affinity; the master appointed him to a position where he did not handle administrative affairs.

He served in these capacities and later held the position of Hall Master (*tangzhu*), presiding over the assembly. On the day the summer retreat concluded, the Master bestowed upon him a *ruyi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) staff and entrusted him with a verse, saying:
"To uphold our school, one must value maturity; to maintain practice without weariness accords with the Way of Heaven.

Do not discriminate between a thousand mountains or a single stream; sit upright and open the eyes for all people. Having received this entrustment, he returned home, and his followers among both the monastic and lay communities gradually increased in number. Furthermore...

The hermitage was thus transformed into a Buddhist monastery. For forty years, his feet did not cross the threshold. The Master alone esteemed frugality and simplicity; he regarded fame, reputation, and material gain as if they were floating clouds.
Although he did not ascend the high seat to lead a vast assembly, his conduct in guiding others and regulating himself was so upright that he stood far above the world.

The Master once said: "Those who merely receive the words lose the meaning; those who linger in phrases are deluded. Therefore, whenever there was an inquiry or an examination of the student's capacity, [he would respond accordingly].

Regarding the verses spoken to the assembly, it was not permitted for any attendants to record them. However, my disciples happened to remember a verse concerning the World-Honored One’s birth, which says:
"The wind blows through the iron horses, making a tinkling sound; Rain falls into the drainage ditches, filling them with flowing water.
How many travelers worry about the slippery roads? Yet the village farmers rejoice in the bountiful harvest. [There is also] a verse on High Peak’s pillow falling to the ground.

It is said: "The phrase 'dragging a corpse' is a delusion for those who harbor doubts; when the nostrils are clearly evident, whom else can one ask? The sound of the pillow falling was transmitted beyond the kalpa of emptiness;
you should know that not a single step has ever been moved. Suddenly, in the sixth month of the Bingchen year of the Kangxi era, he manifested a slight illness.
He sat upright morning and evening without a trace of weariness. He then instructed his disciples on his final affairs. On the seventeenth day, he issued a notice stating:

"At noon tomorrow, I shall take my long leave of the assembly. He commanded his disciples to convey his farewell to the patrons and strictly enjoined them not to send funeral announcements or wear sackcloth, as such practices imitate worldly customs.
"If you follow these final instructions of mine, I shall have no regrets," he said. This was recorded by his fellow disciple, Xiuan-an.
The Master met with a certain monk who was investigating his physiognomy; the Master immediately joined his palms in greeting and took his leave.
At noon, he requested a bath, sat upright, and passed away with a serene expression. His secular age was seventy-two, and his years as a monk were fifty-two.

Eight years later, in the spring of the Jiazi year, his remains were enshrined in a stūpa built at the foot of Mount Yu at Xingfu Temple. This was commissioned by Cao Zhi, a jinshi degree holder from Danghu.

Zen Master Seongui Bong of Longyan in Zhangde ascends the hall and says: "How far away is the Way? It is true in every encounter.
Crimson mists and purple clouds; green mountains and white clouds. How distant is the Sage? Embody it and you are divine. From the heavens above to the earth below..."
From antiquity to the present day, Master Shuzi said: "Dharma Master Zhao’s nostrils have been pierced through by this mountain monk’s whisk.
Do you all know this? If you know it, you are turned by what is known; if you do not know it, you are turned by what is not known. Cast away knowing and eliminate turning.

The Hall. A frosty wind blows cold upon the face; the great earth is entirely a winter scene. A chill hue flows for ten thousand miles; a thousand peaks stand in rows of frozen shadows.
The leaves of the trees have all abandoned their branches, fluttering down into the stone well. The monk from Mount Xiong’er is quite courageous and fierce in his study of the Way.
Suddenly he grasps his staff and brandishes it, saying: "This is no venomous snake or turtle-nosed serpent; let everyone understand it as they will."

He then threw down his staff and composed a verse on Devadatta’s slander of the Buddha: “The World-Honored One sells his charm with his whole body; Devadatta lets loose his stupidity with his entire being.
How laughable is the attendant Ānanda, Coming and going, delivering messages and transmitting words. He then composed a verse on the character “Bei” (北) at the beginning of the scripture:
“Dōu, tōu, tōu, dōu—these are the rhymes for the tongue; Shū, shū, shin, shin—these are the sounds for the upper teeth. The six meanings and the four [tones]...”
Sound has no place to rest; why do patch-robed monks toil so hard in their pursuit? A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?
The Master lifted one foot and said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. The Master said, "These straw sandals were bought for seven-tael silver.
The monk said, "Are you pointing this out? The Master said, "If it is, then take them off and go! The monk bowed.
The student bowed. The Master struck him. The Master asked a monk, "What is that sound outside? The monk replied, "The sound of the cuckoo.
The Master said, "Crying until its blood flows is of no use; it is better to keep one's mouth shut and pass through the remainder of spring. (Muyun Men’s lineage)
When Chan Master Jiqle Qianru Tai was performing communal labor to mow grass, he addressed the assembly: "This mountain monk knows himself to be of meager virtue and lacking in karmic affinity.
With thatch upon my head, my face covered in dust and ash, I have nothing but the mattock for my companion.
Whether it be tilling the soil and digging the earth, or planting, watering, and weeding, I have no leisure time to speak of Chan or discuss the Way with others. Nevertheless—"
Suddenly, someone asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? How should he have answered him?
He called out loudly, "Today we are all being pressed into service to mow grass; there is no room for a single person to shirk their duty! Thereupon, he put on his straw hat and went straight out.
At that time, a monk said, "Master, you must not hide your roots here. The Master seized him and said, "What kind of place is this?
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him with his palm. Small Assembly (Xiaocan): Power returns to the Red Emperor;
the scorching sun blazes with heat. Travelers hurry along, sweat dripping profusely. Beneath the tea stall, those who are cool sit at ease while others drink their fill.
The heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot be fully revealed. Now, what more could this mountain monk say?

If one merely follows old precedents, it would be nothing short of falling seven or eight steps short of the mark. But how is it, after all? "The night is short and sleep is insufficient; the day is long and hunger remains. Small Assembly Sermon:
The autumn wind whistles, the autumn waters stretch vast and wide. Autumn leaves upon the branches are like brocade. Autumn...
Beside the flower hedge, it is like gold. The meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings are exceedingly clear.
The night has grown increasingly cold; it makes one longingly think of a paper quilt. Question: "What is the form-body (*rūpakāya*)? The Master points to his own body and says:
"Keep your eyes wide open. Question: "What is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)? The Master again points to his own body and says: "Keep your eyes wide open. Question: "This old man..."
