The Master was born within his official residence; even as an infant, whenever he saw a Buddha image or a monk, he would immediately feel a sense of profound reverence.

Yue lost his mother on nine occasions. As the times were fraught with many hardships, Fang sighed and said, "If a great man cannot bring stability to chaos, it is better to enter the Gate of Emptiness and pursue the Buddha Vehicle.
He then resigned from office and followed Huayan to receive the tonsure. The Master likewise followed Fang to have his head shaved and received the precepts at Lingyin Temple.
There, he took up the koan of the bamboo whisk for investigation. Once, while traveling to Beifeng Peak, he raised [his head]...

Upon opening his eyes, he saw the moon; his mind and its objects became vast and clear, and his mass of doubts was suddenly dispelled. He traveled extensively throughout all quarters before finally entering the room of Jinming.
Jinming asked, "The lion’s den is sealed with clouds; there is no door from which to face it or turn away. By what means did you enter?
The Master replied, "One who enters through the gate does not possess the family treasure. Jinming said, "You are a wandering monk; why are you inside the womb of a donkey or a horse?"
[Zhaozhou] was performing his daily chores. The Master [Baizhang] said, "Today I have seen the Abbot in person. Zhaozhou stepped forward and said, "Look at the old monk's eyebrows;
how many hairs have fallen out? The Master said, "They are growing. Zhaozhou then struck him. The Master said, "If one does not enter the great waves, how can one see the tide-surfing man?
Zhaozhou said, "What principle do you perceive that leads you to speak thus? The Master shook his sleeves and went out. Thereupon, he appointed [Zhaozhou] as the *weina*.

Next, he was transferred to the position of Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) and received the transmission of the Dharma-seal. He went forth to reside at the Great Compassion Monastery in Linqing, the Jiaxing Pagoda, and the Upper Hall;
there he raised the banner-pole, reopened the ancient shop, opened the treasure-store, and brought forth the family jewels to scatter before everyone, leaving them free to take as much as they need.
If you understand it in this way, you are still somewhat off the mark; if you do not understand it in this way, you are even further astray.

The staff provides another path for growth. Striking it once with his hand, he said: "To shatter the lair of Pāpīyān and manifest the ancestral reputation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one must rely on this very thing.
To grasp the Vajra King’s sword and suspend the numinous talisman behind the elbow requires, after all, the right person."

I, this mountain monk, today have received the command of the various donors; in principle, I cannot decline. I shall cut through the brambles and clear away the undergrowth to reveal the faces of both the living and the Buddha;
I shall till the soil and dig into the rocks to expose the natural radiance of the original ground. Instantly, I shall cause cold ashes to burst into flame and withered trees to sprout in spring.
The stone lion roars, startling the peaks of the green mountains into a sudden awakening; the wooden horse neighs in the wind, trampling the path until it is severed.
"The waters of the Yellow River flow backward. Is there anyone who can cast a single eye into this? After a long silence, he planted his staff on the ground and said:
"Holding a golden whip in hand, he asks the returning traveler: 'In the deep night, who will walk with him through the imperial stables? Ascending the hall, he brandished his whisk and said:
"Lowering the hook across the four seas, he catches only the leviathans. Taking his seat and donning his robe, he does so for the sake of seeking true knowledge. Suddenly—
Brandishing his whisk, he said: "The past has already passed; the future has not yet arrived. Today, it is precisely when this mountain monk preaches the Dharma.

You must take Great Perfect Enlightenment as your monastery and dwell securely in the preaching of the Dharma of equality and suchness, so that those present—both monastics and laypeople—may likewise attain understanding according to the Dharma.
Only then will voices of like kind respond to one another and breaths of like nature harmonize, causing all to..."
Demons and heretics have vanished; Buddhas and sentient beings are universally encompassed. Entering a single mote of dust, he manifests infinite bodily forms;

sitting within the tip of a hair, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—the sentient and the insentient—all emerge and submerge within this very place.
(He lets out a shout. Waving his whisk, he descends from the seat. Question: What is the Venerable One of Immovability?
The Master said: "Born in the hour of the Rabbit; born in the month of the Dog. [The student] asked: "What are the three types of transformation bodies?
The Master said: "Novice, have you ever killed anyone? [The student] said: "In the royal treasury of my sovereign, there is no such blade.

The Master struck him and said: "You are not of my kind. What is the stage of non-retrogression? The Master said: "Public affairs rely on official documents; private matters rely on contracts. [The student] asked.
“I do not ask about the physical body’s decay; what is the indestructible Dharma-body? The Master said, “The eight-armed Nāṭa strikes the Imperial Bell.
[The student] said, “I beg the Master to clarify this further. The Master said, “A stone man topples the five Sumeru mountains. (Ji’ān Jìn sì)
Chan Master Tie Yuan of Youkeshan in Jianning ascended the hall. For over thirty years he has lived alone in a cave;
the steps are cold and cannot withstand the grass that entangles his skirt. His Chan mind has become like the snow of midwinter; let others be born as horses or donkeys as they please.

Why is this so? Because sitting for too long causes back pain. [He] ascended the hall; as soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master descended from the seat. The administrative official seized him.
A monk asked, "Why did the Master not utter a single word before descending from the seat? The Master said, "This morning I ate two bowls of cold congee;
my stomach feels somewhat unsettled. Wait a moment until I have gone to the latrine, and then I will speak for you.
The assembly was at a loss. The Master then returned to his quarters. Ascending the hall, he said: "Half the window is a painting of plum blossoms and the moon; do not treat it as such."
Observe quietly: "A pillow of waves and the wind through the pine trees. Do not listen in a muddled or distracted manner. You all, if you wish to know this matter, it is far too obvious!
Ascending the hall, the mountain monk said: "Yesterday I attended a village feast and bit into a black, shiny grain of sand.
It has continued until this morning that my toothache has not ceased, so I am unable to speak of this or that with you, my brothers."
He then descended from his seat, and the monk took his leave. The Master asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "If I have a place to stay, I will come and inform the Master.
The Master said, "You are a man who upholds the precepts; why do you not observe the monastic regulations? He replied, "Master, please do not treat me as a sinner.
The Master said, "I shall not treat you as a sinner. An ancient said, 'After eating gruel, wash the bowl and depart.'"
"What do you think? [The monk] said, "Last night in a dream, someone asked me this question. Just as it happened, I was so overcome by sleep that I did not answer him.
The Master then dismissed him. (Jiegan Jin)
Chan Master Yuzu Jue of Jiangning was the son of the Zhang family of Yangzhou.

He received the tonsure under Qingliang and traveled extensively to visit various masters before finally meeting Jinming, from whom he received the seal of certification. He subsequently went forth to reside at Ganlu.
On New Year’s Day, General He-shuo Efu Shi invited him to ascend the hall. The Master planted his staff on the ground and said: "When mercury falls to the ground, every drop is perfectly round."
An ancient mirror facing the hall: in every speck of dust, radiance shines forth. As soon as the spring breeze passes, all things are renewed.

One person has cause for celebration, and the myriad people rely upon it. The General Who Attains Buddhahood on the Spot is one who kills without blinking an eye; the General Who Kills Without Blinking Attains Buddhahood on the Spot.
Like a pearl rolling across a tray, and a tray rolling across a pearl. He suddenly held up his staff and said, "Heaven-born."

Once while visiting a Buddhist monastery, his mind took delight in transcending the mundane world. He received the tonsure under Yunmen and subsequently traveled extensively throughout various regions. Finally...

Climbing mountains and wading through waters, I never rested. Now the whip and reins are hung high; Wagging its tail and holding its head high, its nature is tamed. Only...
This is merely taking a little bit according to one's capacity; the mountains are vast and the waters are vast.

This crew of old "iron-wizards" stirs up waves where there is no wind and spreads the family’s disgrace. They are not men of true character themselves. Here in Muyuan, I hold it fast.

The borders are already set; there is no need to further draw snakes or add feet. You lot have eyebrows growing above your eyes and ears reaching your cheeks, yet you come here seeking what kind of bowl?
[The Master] struck his staff and said, "Each of you, please return to the hall for tea. In the first month of spring in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, the Master fell ill.
On the twelfth day of the fourth month, his disciple Yuanjing led the assembly to visit him at Fang... [text ends].
"Venerable sir, I beg you for an instruction. The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, have from the outset never been involved with delusion or enlightenment.

For three months I suffered from dysentery until my entire body was reduced to skin and bone. If anyone can understand it in this way, they will surely transcend both Buddhas and patriarchs. He then addressed the assembly, saying:
The ancients said: "When the Dharma-body is ill, the form-body is the Dharma-body; when the form-body is ill, the Dharma-body is the form-body.

Now, having been asked by the great assembly about the source of my illness, I, this mountain monk, have searched throughout the entire Dharma-realm to find the place where the root of the illness arises.
He was utterly ungraspable. Thus it was said: "The illness has reached the vital organs; even the divine physician folds his hands.
He further spoke a verse, let out a great shout, and then passed away in peace. His worldly age was sixty-two, and his years of monastic seniority were forty-one. (Ji'an Jin-si).
Chan Master Zheng of Hou’an at Zhushan in Xinghua addressed the assembly. He cited a monk’s question to Shoushan: “What is the point of intimacy for a student?
Shoushan replied, “The five nines end, and the day meets spring again. The monk asked, “Ultimately, what is the matter? Shoushan said, “Winter arrives;
it is the one hundred and fifth day until Cold Food Festival. The Master offered this verse: Spring warmth fills the level plains, the oriole’s song is clear; the lutes and songs...

From this point on, those who delight in the Way look back with derision upon those who spur their horses while shrouded in the cold; they have betrayed the profound intent of the Eastern Lord (the Sun).
Master Jue of Qinglian at Pinghu Lake, a native of the Fan clan of Jiaxing, received the tonsure at Jinming Temple. He served as the head of...

The Secretary [of the assembly] had been there for many years. Later, while residing at Qinglian, he addressed the assembly. Having finished citing the story of Mañjuśrī spending the summer retreats in three places, the Master said:
"Mañjuśrī spent the summer retreats in three places, disturbing the pure regulations. Kāśyapa struck the gavel, intending to expel him, thereby startling the multitude and agitating the assembly.
The World-Honored One’s questioning was merely perfunctory, causing people to engage in mutual strife. Had the true command been put into practice, the three of them would have been punished."
The staff has its own divisions. Why is this? Under the gate of Qinglian (Ji’gan Jin succeeded him):
Chan Master Ni Lianhua Kedu of Xiuzhou was the daughter of the Tian family of Huai’an. Her father died while serving as a military commander (*zhishi*) due to a crime.

When the Master was seven years old, she saw her father’s corpse and was moved with deep sighs; she immediately conceived the aspiration to transcend the mundane world, yet she was not yet free to do so.
At forty, he went to visit Fanzhou Shouyu and subsequently paid his respects to Jinming Jin, seeking to have his hair shaved.

Jin did not grant permission. The Master, overcome with grief and indignation, vomited blood that filled a basin. Jin, moved by his sincerity, then shaved him and ordained him, instructing him to contemplate the koan:
"All phenomena return to One. He forgot both sleep and food; before a year had passed, his vital energy was nearly exhausted. One day he saw Jin, who asked: "Where does the One return?"
"Where [is it]? The Master related the reason for his distress. Jìn said, "It has been spontaneously perfected from the very beginning; why exert so much effort?
The Master felt his mind settle into tranquility and offered this verse: "The entire being is elegant and refined—do not seek its limit. Majestic and manifest, the Lord of the House stands alone.
In the morning, changing the water and burning incense for my recitations, All is found within the ordinary activities of daily life. Jìn approved him (Jiè'ān Jìn became his successor).
Chan Master Foyin Nimingxin of Zhulin was the son of the Ye family from Puzhen. Having lost his mother at a young age, he invited a monk to recite sutras;
upon seeing painted images of the hells, his heart was immediately moved, and he abstained from meat and vowed to leave the household life. His father, however, arranged a marriage for him.
He vowed never to comply with this, and subsequently went to a master to shave his head. He practiced asceticism for several years and received full ordination at Jinming Temple.

His master commanded him to contemplate the koan of "the state before one's parents were born. After investigating it intently for a long time, one day while ascending a tower, he had an awakening upon the creaking sound of a floorboard.

He presented his realization to the master, who further refined and tempered him. Eventually, he attained the realization: "From now on, I recognize my mother’s original face. From that point forward...
Regarding the phrase "A peerless man among the multitude," one day the Master was mending felt at the home of Layman Luo Guangwen.

Luo asked, "What is the phrase that provides strength in daily life? The Master made a gesture with his needle as if piercing something. It being the end of the year, Luo asked, "With what will you pass the year?
The Master held up his fist. Luo said, "Is there anything else besides this? The Master replied, "Tomorrow morning, I shall come to visit you, Layman."
The Way. On the day after the full moon of the ninth month in the Jia-yin year of the Kangxi era, he bathed, sat upright, recited a verse, and passed away (Ji’an Jin-si).

The layman Luo Kailin of Zhuili, whose style name was Kongzhu, was a native of Zhulin. From his youth, he studied the classics and was able to polish and refine his understanding of the ultimate realization of Confucius and Yan Hui.
One day, he accompanied his father, Duke Hengyang, to visit Jin-gu on Mount Jingwei. Upon arriving at the upper reaches, he...
He did not yet have deep faith and still treated it with neglect. Subsequently, his parents passed away one after another, and he underwent every kind of hardship.
His elder brother, Shi Yuokan, constantly inspired him, leading him first to visit Dongta Qi and then to study under Fuyan Rong. When Rong held out both hands and asked, "Do you understand?
the Master was utterly bewildered. Rong said, "You have missed it right before your own face. At this point, the Master gained entry through faith. He then went on to study further.
Jinming Jin advanced to his quarters to attend to the well and mortar. One evening, he entered the hall and raised his incense board, commanding the assembly to offer a statement.
A monk stepped forward, seized the incense board, and said, "The master’s handle is already in the hands of this disciple. Jin looked at the assembly and said:
In this period, he obtained nothing more than the status of a common man. Master Shi threw down his incense board and gave him approval.

Master Shi’s works include commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a manual for visualizing the Buddha in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and collections of *capping-words* and verses from the Chan school, totaling several volumes, which have been circulated in the world (Ji’ān Jìn was his successor).

The Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Kiku (Chou) Reibeika, whose lay name was Kyōken and who styled himself Sōan, was a seventh-generation descendant of the Duke Gyōgi and the son of the Great Golden-Water Official (Daikinku) Shunkyo.
Before his retirement from office, he visited Baso and Ra Jishō, both of whom engaged him in dialogues containing kōans.
Upon resigning from his post, he formed the closest bonds of affinity with Konan Mon and Tenkai Sei. Later, he went to pay his respects to Jin at Kinmyō, because...
The conditions were most harmonious. He then presented a verse, saying: "Upon hearing a mere mention, one immediately accepts it; A fine piece of flesh is needlessly scarred with a sore.

If you fix your eyes before the pivot of the occasion, you will understand the clear intent: The red sun at the crown of the head shines through the Fusang tree. He then conferred the seal of approval (*inka*).
The Master once cited the koan of the Bridgekeeper of Mount Yū falling while crossing the bridge, saying: "Brothers, look at the sky with one eye, and [stand] with both feet..."
Stepping on the ground. Now tell me, where is the bright pearl? After a long silence, he said: "Spring is upon the tips of the grass;
how many young nobles know it? There is a *Jiuxin lu* (Record of Investigating the Mind) circulating in the world (by Jieguan Jin).
The lay practitioner Lu Xing of Shuixian lost both his parents while still young. He delighted in visiting monastic assemblies and engaging in discourse with spiritual friends.

He went to visit Master Jin at Jinming Temple, who assigned him the koan: "All phenomena return to One. After three years had passed, he happened to read the story of the "Three Blows of the Staff" and felt as if a poor man had suddenly found a treasure.
He composed a verse and presented it to Master Jin, who said: "This is merely the work of the conscious mind; it still remains within..."
"Halfway there is not yet the news of having arrived home. The scholar took this to heart and came again for further instruction later on. Xuefeng pointed to an ancient vase upon the seat;
the scholar composed a verse that was perfectly suited to Xuefeng’s intention. One day, a monk asked for money, and the scholar sealed it up according to the requested amount, saying:
"If you can speak it, I shall give it to you. The monk said, "I am old. The layman said, "The four great elements age; how could this [the mind] possibly age?
The monk pointed to his chest with his hand. The layman said, "Try to bring it forth and show me. The monk stepped forward, and the layman struck him with his palm (Jiegan Jin succeeded him).

The layman Lu Tao, a scholar and practitioner whose courtesy name was Xuandu, was by nature serene and detached. He had once perused the Buddhist scriptures (Zhudian) as if he had practiced them since his youth.

He subsequently visited various venerable masters, including Putong, Tiantong, Pingyang, and Xilin; their exchanges of "critical words" (jiyu) were later carved and recorded in his *Xinglu* (Record of Practice).
In the year Renchen, he went to consult Jin Mingjin. Jin asked, "Have you ever met a true teacher? The layman replied, "Six or seven. Jin asked, "Which ones?"
A certain scholar said with satisfaction, "If one has attained the Way, then one does not come here. Dahui Zonggao laughed and said, "Do not deceive this old monk.
The scholar requested instruction. Zonggao said, "This matter is not obtained from without; you must clarify the mind-ground. To do so, you must contemplate the *huatou* (the critical phrase)."
The scholar responded with "Yes, yes" and withdrew. One day, while walking, he broke his leg and suddenly realized its essential meaning. He spoke in verse: "At the crossroads, I struck it directly;
In one moment, the white sweat broke through the crown of my head. The stone man raises me up and laughs aloud; Stretching out my legs was all along within the drawing in.
He presented this. Jinshen (Jiegan Jin) gave his approval. (Jin succeeded Jiegan.)

The layman Zhu Yixian, whose courtesy name was Qincheng, was a scholar of letters. Due to the upheaval of the dynastic transition, he harbored the aspiration to transcend the world but had not yet realized it.
Around the year Xinnmo, he suffered from a blood ailment and consequently visited Jin Mingjin to seek instruction and investigate the essential points of the Dharma.
Mingjin said, "Layman, look back to the time before a single thought has arisen: from where does this root of illness originate? He spoke thus repeatedly.

Do not look outward; do not disdain the noisy for the sake of seeking the quiet; do not loathe the mundane for the sake of seeking the sacred. This was no more than what Su Shi and Huang Tingjian attained in their mastery.
Following these instructions, the scholar’s illness was indeed cured. One night, as he raised his head, he saw the moonlight shining with brilliant clarity.
Thereupon, he attained awakening and composed several verses in succession. Their gist was as follows: "The five-colored clouds part, and the ten thousand phenomena are clear;

the single wheel of the mind-moon penetrates to the bright heavens. When empty space falls to the ground, there is no news; why labor over a single speck of dust in the world? He then presented these to his teacher.
Jin said: "Your bone and spirit are fierce and sharp; your will and nature are resolute and daring. You may be named Zhenyi (True Resolve). (Ji'gan Jin was his successor.
The layman Li Qian of Jiaomen, who had mastered the Confucian classics, was fond of the Buddhist teachings and had frequently perused the inner scriptures. He was twenty-two years old at the time.
He encountered a monk who showed him the koan: "When you have not thought of good and have not thought of evil, what is that which is your original face?
He visited the masters Yingning and Sishui, for whom he underwent rigorous training. Once, while conversing with Kongzhuo and Luozu, he went to Jinming to inquire about progress.
Just then, the bell rang. Jin asked, "Is it the sound of the bell, or is it the ringing in my ears? The Master said, "A single string has threaded them all together. Jin [attained realization].
Heng said, "Can you still pass through this? The Master bowed and said, "The kindness is too great to repay.
During tea, Heng asked, "How do you understand Baizhang’s story of the wild fox? The Master then turned the teacup upside down.
Heng asked, "But as for 'neither falling nor being oblivious,' how would you explain that? The Master stood with the teacup held upright. Heng said, "Set it aside."
"Such trifling skills—try and say a single phrase. The Master (Shishuang) then gave a shout. Xuefeng said, "Why shout so recklessly?
The Master said, "Preceptor, do not act strangely. Xuefeng then struck him. The Master bowed. One day, while attending him, Xuefeng asked, "How did Zhaozhou discern the old woman of Mount Tai?
The Master said, "Old Zhao’s tongue has no bone. Xuefeng nodded in approval and immediately recounted this.
The verse says: Zhaozhou bit his tongue and ran with haste; the old woman reduced her hearths while adding soldiers. When the day of Great Peace is settled, victory or defeat is decided;
meritorious deeds are recorded everywhere in the annals of history. Let go of the hand at Chang’an—there is no need to ask the way. (Ji’ān Jìnsì)
The layman Xu Zhen-sheng, whose courtesy name was Wusheng, had been fond of texts such as the Śūraṃgama Sūtra, the Zhuangzi, and the Laozi since childhood.

Upon hearing of Master Jinming’s reputation for advancing the Way, he immediately placed his faith in him and received his instructions. He applied himself with diligence to investigate the essence of the teachings. One day, he entered the inner quarters to seek further guidance.

Jin raised his fan and gave it a single tap. The scholar was suddenly enlightened and offered a verse of realization. Jin approved it and instructed him on his conduct, emphasizing that he should strive for substance rather than mere formality.
In the first month of winter in the year of Xinyou during the Kangxi era, he contracted a slight illness. At the time of his passing, he spoke this verse:
"My name is Zhensheng (Vibrant Sound). From where does this sound come? The Dharma is named Zhenxin (True Fragrance). Where has this fragrance gone now?

People say I am one among the followers of the Buddha-Dharma; this is truly a grievous injustice. I have read but a few lines of the books of Confucius and Mencius, yet I rejoice that I did not enter their ranks.
Ha ha ha! At midday, the sky was clear and the moon bright; thus, I departed in tranquility. (Ji’gan Jinsi)
Chan Master Kaichen of Baoben Chongmo in Xiushui was a native of Huguang. He went to attend upon Yongzheng Yuan, who asked, "Where have you come from?
The Master replied, "Xin City. Yuan said, "Before you even set foot here, I should give you a beating! The Master made a sweeping gesture with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*), whereupon Yuan struck him.
After a short while, the Master presented a verse; Yuan accepted it but demanded more. The Master said, "I thought the Master..."

There is another [case]. Yuanshen Ken addressed the assembly, citing the story of Shishuang’s study under Fenyang, based on the karmic connection of Linji’s realization that his Way transcended ordinary circumstances.
The Master offered this verse: He emptied his belly and poured out his guts to show it to others, yet they failed to realize it; how could such a grievance be set straight?
One day he was caught in the act—a matter no light one—his eyes covering heaven and earth, his spirit and bearing fresh. (The first part by Yuansi)
Chan Master Duanyuzhi of Dongxi presented this to the assembly. He cited the karmic occasion of Xiangyan ascending a tree and offered this verse:
“One grade, fully manifesting the upward-moving function; The man with no land to call his own acts with wondrous skill.

Unafraid of the onlookers in the midst of the fray, He possesses a distinct majesty that stirs the four quarters. In the year Kāngxī Yimao (1675), he resided at Yongzheng. In the late autumn of Dingyi (1677)...
On the twentieth day of autumn, he ordered the drum to be beaten to assemble the congregation. The Master held up his fist and said, "The matter of birth and death is great;
impermanence is swift. Each of you must exert yourselves; do not treat this as a triviality. He spoke again: "Throughout my life I have been too lazy to speak;

upon parting from the assembly, I have no other words. Sit upright and close both eyes; when meeting people, do not speak erroneously. Then he asked, "Tell me, what is it ultimately like? He let out a shout.
He subsequently passed away, and his stupa was enshrined in the abbot’s quarters (the first successor of Yuansu).
Geng Weizhen, the Zen Master Cang, went to visit Yong Zhengyuan. Yuan asked, "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens;
after they appeared in the world, why is there no further news? The Master replied, "I have cut off the tongues of all under heaven."
Yuan said, "Not yet. The Master then presented this verse: Before the sound of the poisoned arrow, it was not yet heard; Within the sleeves where the point is concealed, how could one contend?
Suddenly emerging in the open, there is no handle to grasp; It strikes away the very eye of Maheśvara. Yuan looked at it.
At evening, he entered the hall for instruction. He took up the Master’s verse and asked, "This one has a 'handle' (a point of mastery);
what is the meaning of having no handle? The Master then shouted. Yuan said, "Is there anything else besides this? The Master said, "There is indeed, but it is not fit to be brought forth.
Yuan asked, "Why is it not fit to be brought forth? The Master said, "For fear of scaring the people of the world to death. Yuan then took up his whisk.
The Master struck him. The teacher bowed. Yuan struck him again (the first instance is from Yuan’s succession).
Zen Master Faxuyu Xinghong visited Yongzheng Yuan. Yuan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Shimen.
Yuan said, "Whom did you personally attend? The Master replied, "Tiantong, Baoen, and Foyan. Yuan said, "Have you seen anyone else besides them?"
The Master said, "Two eyes facing two eyes. Yuan immediately raised his fist and said, "Speak a phrase here! The Master said, "If you speak it through, it will be no good.
Yuan then struck him. Later, he went to visit him again. Yuan asked, "The wind and rain are pouring down; it was no easy matter to travel such a long distance."
"Has the area beneath your heels ever been soaked? The Master let out a thunderous shout. Yuan said, "It still carries mud and water.
The Master replied, "It is precisely because the Master’s compassionate heart is so earnest. Yuan then struck him. The Master prostrated, and Yuan approved him (Yuan became his successor).
Chan Master Yuyong visited Yongzheng Yuan and remained in his service for several years. One day, Yuan asked, "How have you been practicing while staying here all this time?
The Master replied, "I put on my clothes and eat my meals. Yuan said, "Is there anything more besides that? The Master said, "If there were, I would be failing the Master.
Yuan said, "If you say there is nothing, you would likewise be failing me, old monk. The Master said, "I take my leave with deep respect."
He performed three prostrations. Yuan immediately struck him (the first instance of Yuan’s succession).

Later, when the senior monk Yongzheng Tongji visited Yuan for a second audience, Yuan raised his whisk and said, "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world and before the Patriarchs came from the West—was there already this very message?
The Master (Yuan) then shouted. Yuan said, "As for the Buddhas appearing..."
"Worldly one! When the Patriarch came from the West, what was that about? The Master said, "When all sentient beings have been saved. Yuan said, "That is the understanding of a lecturer.
The Master asked, "And how about you, Preceptor? Yuan then gave a shout. The Master suddenly attained enlightenment and said, "I thank you for your compassion.
Yuan then struck him. (Yuan was the first successor.)
Gaoru went to receive further instruction from Chan Master Zheng’an Yuanzheng. Yuanzheng asked, "Where have you been hiding yourself until now?
The Master replied, "I have never concealed anything. Yuanzheng asked, "How is it that you do not conceal anything? The Master said, "The mountains are green and the waters are blue."
The magpies chattered and the crows cawed. Yuan said, "Is this not your original face? The Master said, "Though the streams and mountains differ, the clouds and moon are the same.
Yuan said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master then gave a shout. Yuan struck him with a *ruyi* (ritual scepter), and the Master bowed.
Yuanran (the first, Yuansu).
Chan Master Celiu Puren, at Peak □□, addressed the assembly: "If you raise one, you must not raise two; to let pass one step is to fall into the second cause.
The Master commented: "Those two great elders were like children from Mount Kunlun bumping into one another."
He was wearing a Persian cap when he rolled into the great ocean.
Swallowing and spitting out, emerging and submerging, his hands and feet entangled, he produced most extraordinary and strange phenomena. Is there anyone who can discern this?
If you cannot discern it, you are merely a blind turtle with a lame tortoise. Again, he cited how one day Yaoshan asked the head cook: "How long have you been here?"
Touzi said, "Three years. Yaoshan said, "I do not recognize you at all. The monk departed in a fit of indignation. [The Master] commented:
"This monk practiced austerities for three years, toiling without merit. Yaoshan’s compassion for a single occasion, however, resulted in nothing but trouble."
Nevertheless, his heart never betrayed others, and his countenance was never devoid of a sense of shame (as recorded in the *Ruo'an Wensi*).

Chan Master Jinhua Mingbie Chuanhua of Jiaxing was the son of a butcher from that same prefecture. At the age of nineteen, he relied upon Chan Master Jinming for ordination and received full precepts.

While investigating the koan "The Three Are Not," he attained realization. Jinming subsequently appointed him to oversee the record office (*jishi*), and later bestowed upon him the seal of transmission (*jibie*).

Chushi appeared at Qinxi. By nature, the Master was serene and detached; whenever he ascended the hall to instruct the assembly, he would guide them according to their individual capacities, never permitting anyone to record his words (Ji’gan later succeeded him).
The Complete Collection of the Five Lamps, Volume Eighty-Two.
Compiled by the Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital, the Monk (Chao Yong);
reviewed by the Abbot of Gu Huayan Temple in the Capital, the Monk (Chao Kui). Presented for Imperial Review.
A Record of the Succession of the Thirty-Sixth Generation under Mount Heng in the Linji School, Presented for Inspection.
Chan Master Daopei Huishan of Tanzhou was the son of the Lin family of Shanghang, Fujian. At the age of fifteen, he accompanied his father on a business trip to Henan.
Having exhausted his resources on the road, he sought lodging at a hermitage, where a monk urged him to leave the household life; thereupon, he resolved to take ordination.
At twenty-one, he arrived at Hanyang and received the tonsure at Jijang-am. He went to Tonggyeong to attend upon Mijin Myeong.
When asked, "What have you come here for? the Master replied, "To practice Chan. Myeong said, "In this place of mine, there is no Chan to be practiced.
The Master was at a loss. Myeong asked again, "Why did you leave the household life? The Master replied, "I wish to bring an end to birth and death. Myeong said, "Birth and death..."
"How is it brought to an end? The Master had no reply. Ming struck him, saying, "Since even birth and death cannot be found, what do you mean by 'bringing it to an end'? He then drove him out.
The Master was filled with doubt and thought to himself, "What is the meaning behind the Master speaking in this way? Thereupon, he applied himself to the investigation with bitter resolve.
One day, while carrying water, he lost his footing and fell, injuring his foot; the blood from his toe stained his straw sandals, yet he did not even realize it.
Upon awakening, as soon as he reached the gate outside Mount Ming’s monastery, he saw him and said, “The cord on your sandals has snapped, *ācārya*.
The Master replied, “Today I have caught you out, O Monk. Ming laughed heartily; the Master clapped his hands and entered.

The Master attended Ming for fifteen years before taking his leave to go to Mount Nanyue, where he built a thatched hut at Bilu Cave. When Ming was about to pass away, he left behind a handwritten letter and—
*Saṃghāṭī*. [The Master] commanded the assembly to welcome him back to succeed to the seat. He addressed the assembly, citing the room of Ciming of Shishuang:

"He always kept a sword stuck upright in the center, with a basin of water placed to one side and a pair of straw sandals. Whenever he saw a monk enter for an interview, he would suddenly say, 'Look at the sword!
If the monk hesitated even slightly, he would immediately shout and drive him out. The Master said, "The Elder Ciming’s arrangement was much like this..."
[They] create a web of deception to ensnare ordinary people. At Daowei, it is not so. When a monk enters the gate, [Daowei] immediately calls out in a loud voice, "Be careful!
If the monk's eyes flicker, he strikes him with his staff and drives him out.
The Elder Hongjue Man of Tiantong sent a Dharma robe to the mountain. He ascended the hall and said, citing the case where Mahākāśyapa was asked by Ānanda: "World-Honored One..."
"Beyond transmitting the golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*, what else was transmitted separately? Nanquan called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded.
Nanquan said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate. The Master said: "Like water poured into water, like gold traded for gold—the two elders were not without merit.
Yet, if one examines it closely, they expended no small amount of effort. If it were I, Daowei, seeing such a question, I would have struck him across the spine with my staff."
[The Master] struck him with his staff. "Why is that? he asked. "You ungrateful fellow! [This was] Yang Zhuo's successor Ming.
Chan Master Binghuai Neng of Bailong in Cixi was the son of the Zhu family of Shanyin. Initially, he was in the Golden Grain Hall (Jinsu Tang).
While contemplating the koan of the "dry dung pellet," he repeatedly received severe blows from Old Man Wuzhuo, yet he remained painfully unable to find an entry point.

Later, while staying with Han Yue at Beichan, he suddenly saw the window shutters of the refectory wide open; in that instant, he attained realization. When Han Yue entered the hall, he asked him, "Speak!
Speak what you have realized! The Master stamped his foot on the ground. Han Yue said, "This one kick of yours is like that of a horse..."
When National Teacher Nanyue Huairang kicked down Master Shuilao, were they the same or different? The Master said, "In neither case is there any connection.
Zang held up a bamboo stick and said, "To call it is to offend; not to call it is to turn one's back. What then? The Master said, "The mass of pain flows into the waters of the Chang Jiang.
Zang said, "Now is exactly the time for you to apply yourself to practice," whereupon the Master took his leave and went into deep seclusion on Mount Kuanglu.
In his later years, Sanfeng invited the Master to join him, and together they vigorously debated the public cases (gong'an) of the ancestral masters.

One day, seeing peach blossoms in full bloom, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "In years past, I fell into the tangle of vines; Only today have I finally emerged from them.
From now on, I shall sit until the moon over a thousand peaks is worn away, And exchange the eyes and brows of the world. Thereupon, he concealed his traces.
Yunmen. The fourfold assembly welcomed Master Bailong. Ascending the hall: Lake light meets the azure sky; Bodhidharma turns upon the water.
He bumps into Old Man Wang San, who strikes him until his very bones shiver with cold. *Du!* Ascending the hall: This staff does not preach the Dharma.

The whisk is raised to proclaim it: two barriers are threaded through as one; the sound of the stream makes the tongue even longer. Leaning on his staff, he descended from the seat and resided at Haihui in Ningbo.
He held a small *can* (informal sermon): "In days past, I dwelt coiled upon Flower Island by the lakeshore, where I cleared the land and hewed the stones."
The official will not allow even a needle to pass. Today, it has fallen upon the crossroads. To raise a whisk or strike with a mallet is to secretly allow the passage of carriages and horses.
If there is such a person who can take this up and bear it upon their own person, I shall entrust the staff to them with both hands.
If this is not yet the case, I, Xinhui, shall further communicate the news. [He draws a line with his staff and says: "The dragon lies hidden in the ancient cave, shrouded by clouds."
A long time had passed. As soon as he emerged from his retreat, his bearing was fresh and new. Master [Hui]xing revived the Daoxingshan Monastery on Mount Bishan in Hailing;

monastics from both north and south vied to seek him out. Later, he retired to Xiangfu Monastery. On the nineteenth day of the first month of the year Kāngxī Yǐsī (1685), having returned from a mountain excursion, he suddenly manifested a slight illness.
On the twenty-second day, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His stupa was enshrined at Bailong. Among his writings:
There is a work titled *The Collection of the Tiger’s Horn* (*Jiaohuji*), which contains various records of his sermons and has been circulated in the world (compiled by Fan Yizhi).
Chan Master Hetang Yan of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou was the son of the Guo family of the Hangzhou Guard Commandery. His mother, Lady Wang, raised him;
at the age of seven, upon hearing a neighbor singing the line, "How long can the tongue remain fat? he vowed never again to consume meat. At the age of ten, his father...

He left Lingyin Monastery to enter the monastic life at the age of fifteen. He traveled to Mount Tiantai to pay his respects to Wujingdeng, and subsequently visited various venerable masters such as Hanshan Deqing, Daoguan, and Yinyue Ke.
On every occasion, he gave rise to doubt regarding that which is beyond the reach of conceptual thought and the limits of verbal expression;
he investigated with all his might until he forgot to sleep and neglected his meals. Later, he visited Sanfeng Zang at Jingci Monastery, where Zang rebuked him, saying: "All of these..."
To rely on consciousness for understanding and speculation is precisely the root of birth and death. To seek Chan in this way is like heading north while driving a southward-facing carriage.
The Master (Zhaozhou) was suddenly startled and requested further instruction. Guishan Zang snapped his fingers once and said, "In my place, there is no Chan that progresses day by day.
The Master then took up the story of the bamboo stick and contemplated it for seven days and nights until he was utterly exhausted.
As he was about to lie down, he suddenly heard the sound of the wooden board signaling the end of the session. Fearing that it had struck and fallen, he immediately presented this verse:

"On level ground, no wind stirs the waves; Without cause, they surge from all four sides to the heavens. The 'Turtle-Nose' of the Southern Mountain emerges, And with a single breath, dries up everything before him.
Master Lingyin, who was then the Abbot, invited the Master to preside over the Head Quarters (Vihāra). The Master first championed the school's tradition and strove to propagate it.
The powerful and arrogant were subdued, and he returned Feilai Peak to the temple. At that time, the grass before the Dharma Hall was one zhang deep;

thereupon, he composed the *Pòtáng jí* (Collection from the Ruined Hall) to express his own views. He first received the transmission of the Tripitaka at Hengshan, where he alone maintained a noble character, standing apart from the crowd.

For a long time he kept the "pearl in his robe" hidden, until in his later years he began to feel despondent, sighing over his precarious situation like a thread suspended from above. Just then, the monk Sùrú attended him.

A bystander said, "Hottang Am has often remarked that after Sanpung’s passing, there is no true master in the world. Thinking to repay his teacher’s kindness, he is burning with a sense of urgency for the sake of the Dharma;
if you are willing to humble yourself and take up the burden, go at once and inform the Master, saying that Sanpung’s lineage lacks a successor."
The Master watched with forbearance as [the lineage] was on the verge of being severed. Before he had finished speaking, the Master’s countenance moved with compassion;
he then went to Mount Heng and requested to ascend the hall. There, he presented the public case concerning the transmission from Kāśyapa to Ānanda, proclaiming it to all humans and devas:

"To treat a son as a grandson, and to serve an elder brother as a father"—such a marvel of transmission has a resonance that transcends a thousand ages. Lingyin Li then invited the Master to succeed him.

Seated at the manifest serenity of Gaotings, he ascends the hall: "The numinous light is never obscured; it bestows itself impartially upon all things. This single path of true permanence is without interval between past and present.

If you can be like an arrow fixed to the bowstring, leaving no room for the tiger-stone [obstacles], then the thousand monkeys will cease their howling, and you may rest high on your pillow, forgetting all worries.
If you recognize this person of non-action who is perfectly complete, it is the very public case before you."
"Is there any evidence? He leaned on his staff and said: "In stillness, the universe is vast; in leisure, the days and months are long.
On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, he ascended the hall. At that time, there are past and present, yet the stars do not change through the Zhou, Qin, Han, or Wei dynasties.

People undergo succession and change, yet the seasons remain as they are, regardless of spring, summer, autumn, or winter. If awakening is thus, how could delusion be otherwise? If the sages are so, how could ordinary beings be different?
At such a time as this, truth cannot be established; from where could delusion possibly come? The Dharma is fundamentally perfected; what gain or loss can there be in the Way?
Nevertheless, if you simply remain thus, the realm of the Great Man becomes a prison drawn upon the ground.

If you do not remain thus, you will gouge out sores and make holes upon the bare flesh. How does this compare to the white ox that, with its heels, tramples through the canopy of Vairocana? The dark-skinned slave...
The face is prominent, with the eyes of Maheśvara; let them shine forth as they naturally can. Merit is high yet not dwelt upon; its governance is subtle and difficult to fathom.
Even if one does not neglect the royal army, it will likewise not harm the foundation of the state. Let them shine as they please;
since one does not prize omens of auspiciousness, nor fall into the poison of complacent ease, though civil culture flourishes, military preparedness remains ever vigilant. Only...

Just as people existed two thousand years after the World-Honored One, so too do they exist today; the stars of antiquity are the stars of today, and the visions of antiquity are the visions of today.
It is said that the Single Qi (One Breath) speaks not, yet it contains all forms within it. I do not know how the myriad spirits can express their gratitude for this impartiality.
Pointing his finger at the sky, he asked, "Do you see? The assembly looked intently. He then let out a shout and said, "The sword has long since departed."
You are merely marking the boat while showing it to the assembly. Grinding wheat in the evening and drawing water in the morning—how could this be nothing more than a mouth full of chatter?
The matter beneath the patched robe is perfectly clear; why seek filth pointlessly from the outside?

If you simply persist in such toil and hardship, it is still better than lying dead in the street in complacent ease. Frowning in anger, gnashing teeth in resentment—if you wish to recognize what is intimate and direct before your eyes, look here!
The Essential Meaning: A single blow from the azure sky pours down a basin of rain; a golden-scaled carp leaps forth from the mountain peak;
the stone woman and wooden man clap their hands together, singing in unison: "Shengping lila li! Addressing the assembly: In the forest, winter is warm and many bamboo shoots sprout;

by the river, the wind is clear and the plum blossoms open early. The sun and moon revolve in cycles, urging the jade wheel forward; the stars and constellations follow their courses, like a string of pearls turning back.
Forming the *mudrā* (circle) with the *yathā-vat* (as one wishes), he said: "Within this, maintain total integrity and secrecy, allowing the vital mechanism to circulate alternately.

It is utterly transcendent and beyond the subtle; it is never obscured from beginning to end. Those who have not yet attained verification—please inquire of this circle of wise ones. A questioner asked: "What is 'taking away the person but not taking away the environment'?
The Master said: "The mind is a den of transgressions. [The questioner asked: "What is 'taking away the environment but not taking away the person'?"
"Seizing the person. The Master said, "The mouth is the gate of calamity. [The monk] asked, "What is meant by 'seizing both the person and the environment'?

The Master said, "Cutting the grass and eradicating the roots. [The monk] asked, "What is meant by 'neither seizing the person nor seizing the environment'? The Master said, "Pressing down the ox while it grazes. A monk arrived for an audience.
He asked, "Since this is the pure Dharma-body, why is there such a dripping of pus? Before he had finished speaking, the Master pulled him.
The Master took his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters. The attendant followed him in and asked, "Why did the Master hide from that monk?
The Master asked, "Is that monk still here? The attendant replied, "He has gone. The Master threw down his staff and said, "How nearly he would have defiled my staff!
While the Master was conversing with a monk, another monk nearby suddenly prostrated himself. The Master asked, "What did you see that you act in such a manner? The monk hesitated.
The Master hurriedly propped his staff against the monk’s mouth and, looking back at the monks before him, said, "When the city gate catches fire, the calamity reaches the fish in the pond;

you cannot sit idly by and watch. He asked, "If you touch it, you cannot grasp it. As the monk reached out, the Master struck him. He said, "If you turn your back, you cannot grasp it either. The Master struck him again.
As the monk attempted to offer an excuse for himself, the Master drove him straight down. He asked, "When Lingyun saw the peach blossoms, what did he realize?"
The Master said, "A thief enters an empty house. A monk asked, "Is Xuan Sha also a master? The Master said, "He has not yet reached the ultimate. The monk gave a shout, and the Master struck him.

In the fifth month of the summer of the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, the Master suddenly resigned from his administrative duties at the monastery and appointed his dharma heir, Zongheng, to lead the assembly.
Shortly thereafter, he was caught in an unjust situation. On the day he was brought for interrogation, the fourfold assembly blocked the road, wailing and crying out, begging that he be spared.

The Governor consoled him, telling him not to worry. During the intense heat of midsummer, they carried him to the military headquarters. There, he composed a verse, saying: "Reflecting on myself, I possess no talent to serve at the command tent;
For whom has the gate of the chariot-entrance been opened today? How many heroic and sagacious men are there within these walls?

Yet they have allowed me to be carried upon a sedan chair into the government office. Upon his arrival in Jiangning, the authorities took up the case for re-examination. Because the Master was elderly, they exempted him from shackles. The Master remained resolute.
He could not say, "The royal law surely makes no distinction between old and young. A disciple saw this and wept;

the Master sighed and said, "Wujingyi, the offering of a necklace of the seven treasures to Pumen is not as sincere as this. He remained composed while in prison, preaching the Dharma according to the capacity of his listeners.
Even the prisoners and the fierce guards were all moved by his influence. In the winter of the following year, his innocence was cleared, and he was released.
While the Master was at Huanyuan Temple, he traveled from Jinling to Wuling and then returned to Jingci. Incense banners and jeweled canopies gathered like clouds from a thousand li away.
On that day, the Master did not enter his quarters; he immediately took leave of the assembly and withdrew to live in seclusion at the Puning Village Temple.

When Minister Feng Yizhai of Yidu wished to invite the Master to the capital residence, the Master replied, "A monk ought to dwell only among the mountains and valleys. The Emperor [acknowledged] this.

The phrase "the gentleman’s mat within [the hall] was most unsuitable" was rejected. In the summer of the gengxu year, I passed through Wumen to visit Lingyan and Xuanmu, where I paid my respects at the stupa of Wanfeng Bi.
Intending to travel across the San'ao Lakes to seek the traces of Chuansizi, I learned that Master Heng had recently passed away.
The fourfold assembly requested the Master to return to the mountain. He would not enter the abbot’s quarters, saying, "Before long, I too shall depart this world.
Why must you carry me on your shoulders again at Nanping? He requested a calendar and selected the hour of noon on the twentieth day of the seventh month for his passing.
The great assembly was astonished; because he had not previously manifested illness, none had dared to believe it.

On the nineteenth day, he gathered the assembly for his final entrustment, writing several hundred words by hand to bestow predictions upon his disciples. He left instructions that they must not wear mourning garments or white silk.
Rising at dawn, he bathed and changed his robes, ordering that offerings be set out in every hall. He then wrote letters to bid farewell to the various patrons and protectors of the Way.
Furthermore, he wrote a verse on departing this world: "When born, one lies down and does not sit; when dead, one sits and does not lie down.
Right now, clouds rise and winds blow; flowers fly and leaves fall. The attendant asked, "At such a time as this, can you still pick up a single blade of grass?
The Master raised his brush and said, "Do you see it? The attendant bowed. The Master said, "One guest need not trouble two hosts," and then he wrote "Closing the Coffin."
The verse says: "The final phrase—dare anyone speak it? The secure barrier is held fast; even the Patriarchs find it difficult to reach.
Now tell me, where does this old monk serve others? He drew a circle with his brush and said: "From of old, I have never borrowed the power of the spring breeze."
"The birds can speak for themselves, and the flowers are fragrant by nature. Thereupon, he cast aside his brush and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.

His disciples erected a stupa containing his entire remains on Mount Huiri. Feng Pu, the Minister of the Left, composed an inscription for his tomb, and Gong Dingzi, the Grand Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, erected a stele commemorating his spiritual conduct (Yimo Cheng succeeded him).
Master Ruru of Gong’an Baoci was once staying at Mount He-ye. Entering the hall for the formal discourse, he cited Changqing, who said:
“When everything has been swept clean and put away, you step forward and seek me out. I shall strike you across the back with a blow of my staff.
If there is a blow that reaches you, you must feel shame; if no blow reaches you, where will you go to understand?”
Mingjue said: "When you have cleaned and tidied yourself up, you will finally be fit to approach.
I shall strike you once across the back. If a blow reaches you, you will be wronged; if no blow reaches you, it is granted to you equally. If Baoci were here, it would not be so:
when you have cleaned and tidied yourself up, you will finally be fit to step forward. I shall strike you across the back."
"A single blow. There is a single blow that reaches you; you must not understand it as a blow. There is no single blow that reaches you;
you must not understand it by lingering in silence for a long time. But how, then, do you understand it? He struck the meditation staff and said:
"The moon in the empty expanse over the azure depths of ten thousand ages—only after repeated scooping and searching can one finally know it. (Asked by Seokseung Si).

Chan Master Li of the Ancient Rock at Donglin, Xishan, was the son of the Cheng family of Xin'an. While still a layman, he encountered doubts while reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* and resolved to investigate them through practice.
He paid respects to Dashi Zheng to receive a meditation topic (*huatou*) and established a retreat center within his own home, where he practiced with great diligence until he attained realization.
Later, he renounced his household and went to Fupiao, where he relied upon Lingyan Chu to receive the tonsure and ordination, continuing to study under him.

Sanfeng cited the *Linji* kōan. At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and immediately presented this verse: “The earthworm before the courtyard transforms into a dragon; Pointing to the wutong tree, he calls it a pine. At the mountain peak, the surging waves are perilous; The boat sinks straight down, overturning the old fisherman. A monk came for an audience. As soon as he entered the room, the Master said, “It is not so. The monk replied, “I am just a student. The Master said, “Speak! The monk said, “My speech... The Master struck him. The monk bowed. The Master said, “This fellow has some eyes. The monk then left. The Master called out to him. The monk turned his head. The Master said, “What a pity! What a pity! The monk bowed. The Master said, “He has eyes, but he does not see. The monk then departed. The Master said, “He has ears, but he does not hear. The monk then departed.
