"To open a great forge and smelt the sages while cooking the common folk is merely a provisional arrangement of the gate. It is setting up a net that covers the heavens to ensnare dragons and strike down phoenixes."
"It is nothing more than ordinary hands and feet; I do not yet know the extraordinary mechanism—how should it be proclaimed?
The Master said, "Rice is made from grain. [The student] said, "Is that so? Is that so? The Master said, "Would you say that vegetables are not boiled with water?

[The student] said, "Today may truly be called surpassing the past and excelling the future, something rarely heard in all antiquity. The Master said, "A pity to add salt and vinegar on top of that. Thereupon...
It is said: Vast and empty, with walls and partitions entirely absent; towering and precipitous, with steps and ladders utterly cut off.
To say "untying the glue and removing the bonds" is already to stumble on level ground; how much more so to add the word "knot"? Yet, one has always been proceeding in this manner.
The Patriarch at the head of the hundred grasses is often missed; countless ordinary people sink into obscurity—how regrettable!
The former sages bestowed their compassion through manifold skillful means: within a state utterly devoid of walls, they conjured walls;
where stairways were entirely absent, they reclaimed stairways. They drew the barrier of the single character, blocking the paths of many forks, in order to teach him.
What comes from outside cannot enter; what goes out from within cannot leak through. At such a time, can you perceive it with your intellect?

Can you manifest it through supernatural powers? In that very moment of urgency, if you suddenly stumble and step upon your own ground—*kiai!*—you will find that beneath each and every one’s shoes there is a square brick. As soon as it is thus...
It is not like that. One must trample this very brick to pieces along with everything else.

Only then—when the clouds of the southern mountain and the rain of the northern mountain, the seven stars of the Southern Dipper and the eight stars of the Northern Dipper, have all been thrown into chaos, and one has emerged above the heavens—is there finally a share of true freedom.
Yet, even so, if you wish to see that monk, you are still far from it. After all, what long-standing excellence does a monk possess? [He] throws it down.

[The Master] leaned his staff against [the wall] and said: "Enter! [I] address the assembly. The years since the time of the Universal [Era] are remote; the ancestral origins are blurred and indistinct.
Before the Dharma Hall, the weeds have already grown a full ten feet deep. What wonder that the fields and gardens are overgrown? The old monk has no skill left to employ;
he can do nothing but gather up these yellow leaves to try and stop the crying of the child. Yet, alas, they continue to scorch and fry one another—how can this be stopped?"

"It cannot be obtained. Fortunately, Layman Menggan was of the same stream; he opened the storehouse wide and brought out the *bi-die* (steamed buns) and *zhui-zi* (dumplings), letting everyone freely swallow them horizontally or chew them vertically.
Even when one tries to calculate it, it does not reach the mark. Biting into one mouthful, one finds that there is no sauce inside the *hu-bing* (sweet cake).
It is truly laughable! Addressing the assembly: "As soon as there is right and wrong, confusion ensues and [the truth] is lost."
The mind—its defilement or purity before one’s eyes—is neither right nor wrong; its transgressions or observances upon the body are neither right nor wrong;
its inclinations or aversions within the intellect are neither right nor wrong. Since you are thus, I am also thus. Where does this "mind that never loses" reside? Has it not been said:
"If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of land in the great earth"? How could the Wine Immortal (Jiuxian) or the Clam Master (Lianzi) have spoken otherwise?
This misses the point. If it were not so, then even killing mosquitoes in one’s sleep would not be called *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
To the assembly: the spring days are pleasant, but the spring winds are fearsome. A true student of Zen must be skilled in discerning the shifting opportunities;

if you intend to head toward one side or another, yet remain one who cannot be summoned back, you will seek refuge from the heat within the boiling cauldrons and glowing embers, or dwell amidst the snow and ice in the frozen pits.
"Bathing in a river—what is so extraordinary about that? [The Master] suddenly struck the table once and said, "I too enter from within this.
To the assembly: When donors give wealth, everyone says they are providing a vegetarian feast; yet can there truly be rice in their bowls?
When monks hold their alms-bowls, everyone says they are receiving offerings; yet can there truly be monks in the hall? As long as one has not emptied the bowl, it is not yet the true meal.
"Within the hall, one is not yet a monk. How can there be giving? And how can there be receiving? Holding up his whisk, he said:
"If you can utter a phrase of self-expression right here, then even practicing giving is supreme, and maintaining the precepts is also supreme."

To spend ten thousand taels of gold a day would not be considered excessive; yet if you were to hesitate and reflect further, you would not only be rebuked by Vimalakīrti, but even drinking water one must guard against choking.
Addressing the assembly: For over two thousand years, this old monk has never failed in reverence, nor has he ever been indolent.
Today, there is a single ladle of water—upon whose head shall I pour it? Truly.
Jiur said: "I should have known it was like this sooner. I regret not having been like this. Addressing the assembly, he said: "One person transmits a rumor; a thousand people transmit a reality.
Everyone says that the World-Honored One attained great enlightenment upon beholding the morning star. But what, after all, did he awaken to?

All sentient beings present here behold the morning star every night—do they also awaken? Setting aside the sentient beings for a moment, consider the morning star of ten thousand ages throughout the night."

Seeing all sentient beings at night—do they still awaken? To say that "the sentient and the insentient together realize perfect enlightenment" is, as before, to remain within the domain of the World-Honored One.
[The Master] suddenly lets out a shout and says: "The night crow flies; the morning hare runs."
Willingly coming forward to guard beneath the stump, he addressed the assembly: "Master Neng, as an incarnate Bodhisattva, received the full precepts;
the novice Gao knew that such matters were simply to be let go of; and the wine-sobered sage Mingjue appeared among those of different species."
They walk upon unwholesome paths. As for these three Chinese men—who is holy and who is ordinary? Who is bound and who is liberated?
To place them together in one spot is like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits (*akṣaphala*).
To grasp one is to fall; to look at one is to go blind; to smell one is to split the nose. What is the path for a patch-robed monk to emerge? *Hūṃ!*
With a single shout, he said: "The bright pearl is in the palm; the spiritual blade is in the grasp. If there is reward, all are rewarded; if there is punishment, all are punished.
However, no one shall interfere in the path or seize the market. (Retu Weng Chusi)
Chan Master Shaoyuan Ju of Wumuchan Temple in Piling was a native of Tongxiang. He cited Dongshan’s saying: "The entire Tripitaka is this character 'Zhi' (the letter Z).
The Master offered this verse: Wiping away the empty sky, one peers into the curling incense smoke; Turtle hair and deer antlers are planted before one's eyes.
Who says this single character "Zhi" encompasses the Dragon Canon? It is merely a plagiarism of Xuansha’s "white paper. He also cited a monk’s question to Dongshan... [text continues]
Shan [Guishan] said: "There is the 'Gate for Testing People' and the 'Phrase for Reviving People. What is the Gate for Testing People? Shan opened his mouth wide and said, "Please.
[The monk asked: "What is the Phrase for Reviving People? Shan stuck out his tongue to show him. The monk bowed and said, "Thank you, Master, for answering my question."
Mount [Shishuang] said, "In the future, do not mistakenly resent this mountain monk. The Master offered this verse:
"The barrier for testing men and the phrase that gives life— Have you understood it yet, with tongue protruding and fangs bared? Look at the man walking on water atop Eastern Mountain;
He seizes the vital ford and follows him wherever he goes. (Retung Chu)
Chan Master Sheng of Yuenuo-an in Wujiang composed a poem on dwelling in the mountains: The monk living in the hermitage grows old and fears his robes are thin;
With not a single thread remaining, he struggles to act with feigned innocence. He fears even more that in the future he will have to don a crane-feather cloak;

Let him be—having few servants, he feels shame within himself. Seven pounds of rags are all worn out and patched upon his bed; How shameful this makes the Venerable Zhaozhou of old! Pressed to the limit until the fifth watch of the night...
The frosty moon at dawn; even needles and awls find no purchase, let alone a hook. This mother-born pair of trousers has seen its time of use;
already mended with many scars, they can no longer be supported. Though worn out in my old age, they still will not come off; they have truly deceived the child by the roadside until his death.
(By Tuweng Chusì)

Chan Master Xingre Cui of Lingyun in Taixing was a native of Taixing. When he ascended the hall to recite the precepts, he opened the gate of expedient means—scarifying healthy flesh—and revealed the mark of reality—placing grit in one’s eye.
How could it be endured that, at the mountain gate, one joins the palms while bearing a cangue and facing indictment;
or that, within the Buddha Hall, one burns incense while clutching one’s hair and heading for the yamen? To further speak of "Abbot" and "Kalyāṇamitra"—is this not [a case of]...?
They were putting on airs and making a display. Xuanfeng then scattered them with his staff, saying: "How strange this crew of yours is!
You who are like figures carved from clay or wood, yet you still remain so stubborn. **Ascending the Hall for the Buddha’s Birthday:** On this day every year, there is no respite.
It seems to be summoned by the karma of one's past life. How few descendants are able to undergo transformation? I shall not pour foul water over your heads.
Evening *Zanchan* after the snow has cleared: Deep within the snow of the village beyond, Suddenly, a single branch blooms.
Is it a plum? Is it a pear? After a long silence, he roared: "The flower must bloom through the night; Do not wait for the morning breeze to urge it on. (Teweng Chusi)
Wujin Taiping asked about Master Songyuan, a native of the Zhang family from Jiangling whom the world calls the Venerable Baoshu.
He addressed the assembly: "Within the station of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, there is nowhere to be contained; across the level fields and shallow grasses, one may roam freely as one pleases.

Speaking of the journey through the years, one never leaves home; sitting alone by the brazier, the dialogue transcends guest and host. At the thatched inn when the cock crows, it is truly a scene of bustling activity."
A single orb of bright moon; human tracks on a wooden bridge; desolation everywhere with frost upon the ground.
If you say there is something else to be discussed, it is no more than trying to quench thirst with salt. (Tuiweng Chusi)
Chan Master Xixing of Ba’an in Wuxi was the son of the Xu family of Suzhou.
While residing at Ba’an in Wuxi, he ascended the hall and gave a shout, saying: "If one can open this mouth, what harm is there in being above heaven and below heaven?
But if one is hesitant and evasive, looking back and forward, this person’s light does not penetrate through; there is something obstructing them within their breast."
When I, this mountain monk, resided at Xiangfu, whenever a patch-robed practitioner arrived, I would first give them a bowl of lake water to drink.
Once their internal organs were washed clean, their speech naturally became straightforward. When speech is straightforward, the Wheel of the Dharma can be turned.

When the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is likewise pure. When one turns the Great Dharma Wheel toward a pure Buddha-field, then all sounds are the voice of the Buddha, and all forms are the form of the Buddha.
One may see me through form, and seek me through sound.
Within this trichiliocosm, there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed that is not where you have attained perfect enlightenment.
As for this place, tell me: in attaining perfect enlightenment, what is so extraordinary about it? It is simply that one may go when it is time to go, and stay when it is time to stay;
there is no preference and no aversion, no weighing of pros and cons. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, suppose a man were to step forward from the assembly and say, "Recognize that which goes;
recognize that which stays. Before his voice has even faded, I would strike him across the back with my staff.
It is said: "Do not wait for right and wrong to enter your ears; those who have known you from before will turn into enemies. (Attributed to Tuweng Chusì).
Chan Master Shengyan Heng of Shousheng Monastery in Suzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Eastern Zhejiang.

He relied upon Chusì of Lingyan Monastery and attained realization while contemplating Huangbo’s three blows of the staff. Chusì raised his bamboo stick and said: "If you can speak, you get thirty blows; if you cannot speak, you get thirty blows."
"Thirty blows! If you cannot speak the Way, let it be; why then do you receive thirty blows when you can? The Master said, "What is familiar is difficult to forget.
Cuchu asked, "When one who has undergone the Great Death returns to life, what is it like? The Master said, "By day one sees the sun; by night one sees the stars.
Cuchu said, "Indeed, what is familiar is difficult to forget. (Tuiweng Cuchu was his successor.)
Chan Master Shaozhong of Suzhou Yuezhang ascended the hall and said: "The rushing torrent beneath the shout—why such haste?
The swift flames from the staff—right here they are. Possessing the function of 'the water reaching the channel,' it naturally surges with waves upon level ground;
endowed with the mechanism of 'the wind blowing and the grass bending,' why need one draw lightning from the void? Although...
Yet illumination and function proceed in tandem; at the very least, person and environment must not obstruct one another.
If you wish to uphold Linji’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, it is like a mosquito trying to shake Mount Sumeru or pulling a great elephant with a lotus fiber.
You must proceed slowly. He let out a shout and said, "What is this? Then he added, "Having a mouth, do not leave it idle. Entering the hall, he bound empty space into a bundle.
Strike! A thief who plunders by stealth finds no place to set his hand; he grinds the great earth into dust. Yet for the limping master, there is no path for him to set foot upon.
Beneath the heels of every person, there is the orthodox eye that pierces through the heavens.

Whether ascending the eastern corridor or descending the western corridor, whether on the winding or straight steps, or in the shallow or deep quarters—nowhere can one deceive him by even a single point. Before the hall of the ancient Buddha, there is a fragment...
"I once stayed at Fangzhuan. You all come in the morning and leave in the evening; why do you not reflect upon this?
He raised his staff and said, "Right now, I am pointing it out directly for you. Those who have eyes with pupils, each of you should examine it for yourselves!
He struck the floor once with the staff. Ascending the hall, he said: "Prajñā is like a great mass of fire. The entire earth is a mass of fire. Old Deshan—"
Han: He adds flames to already burning firewood. Linji Daoshi: He tears open his bag and fans the wind. The Buddhas of the Three Ages: Their nostrils are thoroughly permeated.
The Patriarchs of the Six Generations: Their eyebrows are scorched away.

You hair-path ordinary folk, if you wish for ignorance to be extinguished and your minds to become cool and refreshing—after a long silence, he said: "Do not engage in false conceptualization! Ascending the hall, [he spoke of] flowers.
The laughing oriole sings on the morning of the fourth month; where the patch-robed monks see, all is heroic and bold.
With eyes opened beneath the blue sky of the bright day, how could there ever have been so much as a hair’s breadth of birth-and-death? *A shout!* He ascended the hall and said:
"All forms are the Buddha’s form; all sounds are the Buddha’s sound. Earthworms pierce through the ear canals; frogs leap into the eyes. Whether high or low..."

[The Master] descended from his seat. Suddenly joyful, suddenly angry, he let out a shout and said: "One blow splits Mount Hua into two paths; the waters flow for ten thousand years, unaware of spring.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Eyes with sinews, a tongue without bone.
Zhaozhou drinks tea all day long; Zihu catches thieves at midnight. Having caught the thief, who can discern him?"
"Look! We have played until dawn; every one has brows arched and a nose straight. Holding up his staff, he said, "Thief! Thief! He ascended the hall and said:
"Sentient beings are fundamentally not deluded; how could the Buddhas ever have attained enlightenment? Neither enlightenment nor delusion—everywhere, everything is manifest.
It is lamentable that those with eyes open see all this yet pay it no heed. He suddenly looked left and right and said, "The assembly, listen!"
"Seven holes here, eight holes there—is he looking or not? Across and down beneath his heels—is he looking or not?
He gave a shout and said: "If you wish to see the Yellow River clear, it happens but once every three thousand years. (Tuweng Chusì)
Chan Master Yushao Fen of Baotong Monastery on Mount Hong in Wuchang was the son of the Wu family of Jingling.

His father was a local scholar, and his mother, the Lady Xu, had become a widow at an early age; she devoted herself to Buddhism and recited the sutras. Whenever the Master attended her side, he listened to her teachings and was moved to inspiration, vowing to become a monk.
His mother nodded in approval. At the age of twenty, he went to the Dharma Master Xuancui of Liantai Monastery in Yingzhou to undergo the tonsure and receive the precepts. Following [Xuancui]...

The Vinaya Master Samadhi received full ordination and lived in seclusion at Yùquán in Jīngnán. One day, while reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, he encountered a point of doubt and questioned an elder. The elder rebuked him, saying:

"Though you are extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka, you still remain caught within the snares and traps of words. As long as the sacred mind remains unpenetrated, it is difficult to escape birth and death.

Your spirit and intellect are profound and far-reaching, and your natural endowment is pure and refined. The Chan school is flourishing greatly in the south; why do you begrudge yourself the opportunity to seek it?"

"A single pair of straw sandals—will they suffice for this great matter? The Master then resolved to travel south in search of instruction. Upon passing through his hometown, he encountered his mother’s illness at its terminal stage;
he remained to attend to her with medicinal decoctions and completed her final affairs. Arriving in Wulin, he first visited Master Lingyi Li, but there was no accord.
Next, he visited Master Lingyan Chu at Tiantai, where he was granted access to the Chou chamber. Whenever he posed questions, Chu would treat him with arrogance, saying:
"In my place here, there is not a single word to hang upon one's lips. Why must you painfully seek it from another's mouth? You lacquer tub! Get out at once!

He never showed even the slightest concession in his words or expression. Because the Master had not yet clarified his own matter, he was further subjected to such insults and abuse; he was deeply resentful and unhappy.
On the first day of the first month of the Xinmao year, he gathered eight or nine fellow practitioners to initiate a seven-day session of *samādhi* (vigor). The Master also...
He joined them. In the afternoon, he encountered Master Chu as he descended from the hall. The Master approached and prostrated; Chu immediately struck him.
As the Master was about to pose a question, Chu struck him again, saying, "Do you intend to interpret this as the Buddha-dharma? At these words, the Master grasped the essential meaning.
He then composed a verse on an ancient precedent as a song of realization, saying: "Leaving the White Emperor Palace amidst colorful clouds, I returned to Jiangling in a thousand li in a single day."
"The cries of the monkeys on both banks do not cease; my small boat has already passed ten thousand layers of mountains. Chuxiao said, "I assist you in your joy;

you have now reached your native land. From this point on, his spiritual acumen became sharp and penetrating, earning him the reputation of being one who "bites through the arrowhead" (a term for swift and decisive realization).
He went forth to reside at Qianming in Lushan, Huan at Tiantai, Guangxian in Jiayu, Tongquan in Jingshan, and Zizhi in Jingling.
Bian Xiaozhi was likewise [invited]. The Integrity Commissioner of Jiangnan ordered him to establish Dongyan Jingshe and invite the Master.

Zhang Chaoshen, the Governor of Chu, and Xu Xing, the Provincial Governor, requested the Master to restore Hongshan Baotong Temple. [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "Last night, snow was followed by frost;

this morning, the Buddha’s face has increased its hundredfold ugliness. For Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, the road is difficult to travel. He struck the gong. *Liliang*. (A sound indicating the end of the discourse.)
The slave and the white ox, however, know there is something more. Hanshan’s head is covered in ashes from the burning fire;
Shide picks up his broom in the wind. After a long silence, he looks at the assembly and says: "You lot, you freezing cold bunch—what kind of bowl are you looking for here?
Ascending the hall, he said: "A good rain knows its season; in spring, there are no three days of clear weather. At Mount Gui, there were five hundred heads of cattle. True.
"What a pitiful creature! Whether east or west of the stream, let him be dragged about as he pleases. But tell me, to whom does this patch of ground belong from beginning to end?
A monk stepped forward and said, "How can you, Master, question anyone else? The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk hesitated;
the Master struck him with his palm and said, "I thank you for not being thorough. [He] ascended the hall and held up [an object].
Holding up his staff, he said: "Strike once, tap twice—there are hands and feet. Let go of two, cast away three—there is no front or back. Those with clear eyes cannot see it;
yet those who can see it, I truly entrust this to you. He struck the staff once and said: "Be careful not to falsely accept it. He ascended the hall and said:
"After long rains, the plum season is ripe; firewood grows and smoke fills the hearth. Between the trees, the mud is slippery."
"Smooth. At that time, he called out from the edge of the roof. "In the copper cauldron, oil is filled to the brim; along the road, it flows well without a single drop being lost.

Where could one see any leakage coming? You ask about the ordinary and answer with the ordinary; you ask about the sacred and answer with the sacred. Why do you merely follow the turning of his tongue?
After a long silence, he said: "The mud beneath one's feet is deep. He ascended the hall and said: "The myriad dharmas return to the One."
Where can one find refuge? The waters of the sea cannot be measured with a peck; empty space cannot be gauged with a ruler;
pure ground cannot be strewn with sand; and soft mud cannot support a foot. The "Seven-Pound Qingzhou Shirt"—that which seems thin is actually thick.
A single brick in the middle of a crossroads. That which is thick becomes thin; it is as vexing as a lacquered bucket. Do not bring it up any further.
Your worn-out straw sandals must be cast off. Striking them all at once with his staff, he said: "A thousand mistakes, ten thousand mistakes!"
"This is not wrong. He addressed the assembly from the high seat, picked up his staff, and said: "Seize upon one pivotal moment, and every thought will be liberated.
Striking it down once, he said: 'Let fall a single phrase, and every word shall flow freely. It adorns the myriad phenomena within the immediate presence, radiating celestial brilliance;

it merges the thousand differences into a single wisdom, casting a golden sound as it strikes the earth. Thus, one transcends the patriarchs and surpasses the masters, following the Way in accordance with nature."
When things are equalized within oneself—at such a moment, the fact exists like a container and its lid, and the principle corresponds like the tips of two arrows meeting.
It should only be unfolded with you; it is not something to be deliberated upon in the world. Furthermore, who is able to go out from within the body? Thereupon, he threw down [the whisk] and said:
Entrusting the Dharma to the Head Seat Rui this morning, he ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he struck it once and said, "The mind is not the Buddha;
both the Buddha and the mind are negated. He struck it again and said, "Wisdom is not the Way; both the Way and wisdom are discarded."
The stone pillar outside the mountain gate—washed by rain and blown by wind, it turns green and then yellow. Suddenly, one cannot find its nose-tip.
Now, as for the almsbowl with its mouth turned toward the sky and the exposure-pillar with its feet planted on the ground, they have never changed from the beginning.
Tell me, what kind of matter does this constitute? (He lets out a shout. Question: "Tranquil and silent beside the River of Bliss... [The text continues: "...the golden [lotus]..."
The coffin specifically displayed his two feet [in the lotus position]. At such a moment, is this not the Buddha? The Master said, "At midnight, Mount Sumeru puts on its nostrils.
[The monk] said, "Fortunately, we have met the Master to bear witness. The Master said, "This will leave all people under heaven in a state of doubt.
The Master called to a monk. The monk responded, "Yes? The Master said, "It is not far from here to Hanyang. A monk came for an audience. The Master immediately shouted. The monk also...
"Ho! The Master shouted again. The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Henceforth, you must not imitate this old monk.

Wuchang was a major metropolitan center at that time, and the imperial court was then launching a punitive expedition against Hunan. Troops were streaming in incessantly, yet the Master alone remained composed and free from worldly concerns.

From the high officials who governed the various provinces above, down to the commoners, servants, and soldiers below, all who saw the Master’s compassionate guidance of sentient beings cast aside their weapons, prostrated themselves, and departed.
On the fifth day of the first month of the Gengshen year, he manifested a slight illness and said to those around him:
The old monk knows; you fellows do not. Riding in a sedan chair, he took his leave of all his patrons.

On the eighth day of the second month, he burned incense for the anniversary of his own birth, making offerings simultaneously to the successive patriarchs of his lineage. Moving to a separate room, he took up his brush and wrote this verse:
"In this world, hatred and love struggle over the fragrant blossoms; How have these matters ever truly accorded with the opportune moment? If you wish to know the true [nature] of Hongshan..."
His intent was this: as he prepared to depart, he simply listened to the falling snowflakes. On the thirteenth day, he passed away peacefully.

Indeed, outside his door, the snow was three feet deep; those near and far were struck with wonder at this marvel. The Master’s worldly age was fifty-nine, and his years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*) were thirty-eight.
His disciples, including Sang-rye, enshrined his entire body in a stupa in the southeastern corner of Tongch’on, Gyeong-san (the successor of Toe-ung).
Chan Master Yūqīngāo (Rainy Green Ointment) of Tiānfēng in Tàizhōu was the son of the Fēng family of Hǎimén, Tōngzhōu.
He left home to become a monk at Bìfēng Temple in his youth, and later received full ordination under Sìruì. Initially, he studied under Xián of Bào’ēn, and subsequently relied upon Chǔ of Língyán.
[Chǔ] ascended the hall and said: "The golden scissors cannot cut it through—ten thousand miles of blue sky. The colored brush cannot paint it—this one river of bright moon. Long...
Tranquil upon the road above, coming and going without abiding; within the Han-yuan Hall, the noble deity dwells.

If one were to deliberate on this according to the Buddha-dharma, everyone would incur immeasurable transgression. Ascending the hall, as soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master spread his two hands and said, "What is missing?
He then descended from the seat. In the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era, the Master passed away at Changqing in Wujiang (the successor being Tuweng Chu).
Chan Master Wuren Nengren of Tiantai, a native of Wuxing, gave a small-scale sermon on New Year’s Eve:

"Look, look! As the twelfth lunar month draws to a close, the spring breeze has already arrived. Poor as I am, I do not even possess a needle; how could there be anything else? I brew mugwort decoction for tea and sit by the brazier at my leisure.
I do not seek to display my own excellence; I have only the ambition to compete with those who are inferior. [He then] recited the verse: "Leading the ox, I draw the public..."
"Wrong! Burning paper money increases the power of ghosts; running headlong into Śākyamuni is also a thorn in the eye. Where there is a Buddha, run away quickly;
where there is no Buddha, do not stay. Ultimately, where is his dwelling place? When you have pursued this until tomorrow morning, I will annotate it for you from the beginning.
The Master took up residence at Bodhi Temple. Every day he sat upright, with nothing to do, maintaining his practice.
He continued his practice until old age without ceasing; people called him an "Ancient Buddha" (Tuiweng Chusi).
Chan Master Zhidu Fanzunsheng of Changsha was a native of Taizhou. Regarding the karmic occasion of Nanquan spitting out "Suchness," he composed this verse:
"The golden rooster crows, shattering the lapis lazuli shell; The jade hare pushes open the heart of the azure sea. Within the single chamber, nothing is known."
Heaven knows the early and the late; from the beginning, the power has resided with the descendants (referring to Tuiweng’s heir).
Chan Master Xutang Qi, the abbot of Sangehua Hermitage at Zhixing, was by secular surname Han. Having passed the jinshi examinations, he served as a Hanlin Academician.
Upon the dynastic change, he donned the monastic robes and studied under Juelang Cheng. He daily investigated Wan-song’s *Pingchang*, yet remained stuck on a point of internal obstruction.
He was not yet liberated. Later, he went up to Lingyan. One day, the Master asked him about the dialogue concerning De Yun’s meeting with Biéfēng.

[The Master] said, "I share the same surname as you. The scholar said, "And yet you say I do not have the surname Ye.

The Master said, "Those who do not have the surname Ye—do they possess the ability to turn words and respond with wit? Or do they also possess conduct? The Master then pinched his tongue with his hand and said, "Tell me."
"How many footprints are there upon my tongue? The monk bowed. The monk asked, "When one leaves the gate, it is all grass. Why has the Master come to this place?
The Master said, "White clouds block the mouth of the valley. The monk said, "If that is so, then the moon reflects in a thousand rivers, and the sea embraces all streams.
The Master said, "The traveler, however, loses his tracks. The monk said, "This too is 'seven flowers and eight petals' (disorderly)."
[The monk] cleft [his staff]. The Master then shouted; the monk also shouted. The Master stopped. (Tan Ji-ren succeeded him.
Chan Master Longya Junming Ti of Ruizhou ascended the hall and, citing the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, said:

"You need only abandon birth-and-extinction and maintain true permanence. When the light of permanence manifests before you, the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will all vanish away. He then suddenly picked up [the staff].
[The Master] held up his staff, struck once, and said, "You rice-bag! You go right off like that.
Seeing this as unjust, Longya [Daoxian] acted as a guide for all future generations, casting down the staff and saying, "Do not harbor deluded thoughts! This was the evening instruction.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, this is a single-edged sword; it can kill people, and it can also bring people to life.
But tell me, in whose hands does the hilt lie? Suddenly, he picks up a bamboo staff and says: "Those who dare to risk their lives, come forward!
I shall press you down all at once. (Shuoji Shengsi).
Chan Master Yunfu Zhi of Xifeng on Feng Mountain in Yiyang, Tanzhou, was the son of the Li family from Qushan in Shu.
In his youth, he entered the monastic order under [Master] Liudu. Initially, he frequented lecture halls; upon hearing the *Lotus Sūtra*, he attained a sudden and profound realization.
He then went to visit Xiangya Ting, who asked him as soon as he entered the gate: "I do not ask about descending from heaven; what is it like to turn one's body upon the ground?"
He asked, "What? Hei Ting replied, "Right under the heels—thirty blows are well-deserved! At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.

While residing at Dazú, he ascended the hall and raised the example of the Elder Tiantong Wù, who said: "The first move at the head cuts off the vital ford; as soon as one tilts the ear, the family treasure is lost.
From the beginning, the Buddha-dharma has never conformed to human sentiment. The Master remarked, "That old fellow Tiantong..."
This seems much like praising the noble while disparaging the humble; yet one does not realize that he has already conformed to human sentiment.
At that time, a monk came forward and gave a shout. The Master said, "This shout of yours—is it for Tiantong, or is it for this mountain monk? The monk hesitated.

The Master struck out directly and gave a small discourse (*xiao can*): "Spring has arrived and the flowers bloom, all leaking the secret. Neither green, nor yellow, nor red, nor white. Cherish this, O *kalyāṇamitra*, and observe it carefully;
do not follow after the eyes to engage in false discrimination. False discrimination! There is a tangle of vines for which there is no one to speak. He let out a shout.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month in the Gui-chou year of the Kangxi era, the Master announced [the end of the period].
Ji (Xiangya Ting) took up his brush and left a verse, saying: "A thatched hut consumed by a single torch; Ashes fly as the earth becomes free of dust.
The mechanism of the Iron Ox is revealed; Responding to things, it moves wherever it will. (Xiangya Ting succeeded [to him]).
Chan Master Huiyue Jiliang of Luopu, whose courtesy name was Shuizhuo, once related:

"In years past, while I was at Tiantong, I asked Old Man Ming about the meaning of 'the one step above, which not even a thousand sages can transmit. I received several severe blows of the staff for this, yet to this day I have not awakened to it.
I beg the Master to provide me with instruction. Shuizhuo said, "A light boat floats upon the surface of the water. At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
Upon sudden enlightenment, he prostrated and said, "I am delighted to have had my doubts resolved today.
(The character for "water" [水] appears here; this refers to Master Suozhué). Guangfu Dayi Guansui Chan Master went to visit Master Suozhué at Zhimue.

Suozhué asked, "Your nostrils hang downward, and your eyebrows are divided across two sections. How do you understand this? The Master rose from his prostration and said, "I do not dare [to speak further]."
He offended his *upādhyāya*. (His style name was Shuizhué; he succeeded [to the lineage]).
Chan Master Sīchāngyì of Bǎilù in Tánzhōu ascended the hall and said: "If you can realize it directly before your eyes, you will be taught to transcend antiquity and surpass the present.

Only when you know where to return beyond the formal teachings can you truly believe in the total functioning of the great utility. If you merely seek words and pursue phrases, you are indeed plundering [the Dharma]."
"Spitting out mucus and spittle! Hanlu, relying on consciousness and halting thought, is much like a dead man standing still.
Is there anyone among you who has transcended the limits of emotion? If so, join me in raising a single hand. Otherwise, I shall pick it up and play with it myself.
After a long silence, he brandished his whisk and said: "How many times have you weathered frost and snow? How many times have you encountered the cold?"
How many times has spring come? In the past, there was the coughing of ten thousand peaks; this morning, the cough is for all to see.
Tut, tut, tut! (Yue Zhuzhou Si)
Dharma Master Tingsue of Dongchuan Xinning went into the presence of the nun Zu Lan. He encountered her as she was ascending the hall for formal instruction.

She raised the question: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? [The Master] replied: "The cypress tree in the courtyard. "If you understand it in this way," she said, "it is already not so.

"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? she asked again. "The cypress tree in the courtyard"—only when you understand it in this way will you finally get it. Before the sound had even ceased—
The Master came out and clapped his hands, saying, "Not so, not so. Lan then asked, "What then is it?
The Master said, "Fortunately, there is this very thing. Lan asked, "And what is this? The Master again clapped his hands and said, "Not so, not so."
Lan nodded his head (Nizu Huan succeeded him).
Chan Master Shengyi of Deshan in Dingzhou was a native of Bayu in Shu. He ascended the hall and said: "Does the assembly recognize this karmic occasion?
In years past, when I was in three places in Qian, I did not distinguish between good and evil; I simply took up a white whisk..."
A blow! Whether it be a Buddha who comes or a Mara who comes, he strikes them both. Those who see him or hear him retreat in awe, as if looking down from a precipice.

Thereupon, he dispersed his followers and vanished from public view. Later, at the command of Master Zhufan, he resided in this monastery; there, he clenched his teeth with determination and spoke not a single word of Dharma.

If habitual tendencies are not eliminated, the questioner will receive a severe blow—this is called "the staff. To enter hell like an arrow by engaging in intellectual reasoning and deliberation is the same as entering hell like an arrow.
If you can realize this, the Great Matter is finished. If you are still unable to do so, [you must continue to practice].

"You must exert yourself with all your might. When the Master arrived at Tiantong, he swept the pagoda of the Patriarch Wuzu. Yuan'an Fangyuan invited the Master to occupy half the seat and preach the Dharma.
One day, he suddenly informed the assembly of his departure. He spoke a verse and passed away while sitting upright. Fangyuan composed a verse for the closing of the coffin, which said:
"From three thousand li away, he came alone with a single staff; Amidst ten thousand fingers, he pushed through the crowd and returned home. The seas and mountains are all at once somber and dim."
The Dharma-gate shines eternally through the ages (Xuebi Luan Si).
Chan Master Yingxiu Wuzhu of Longshan in Chenzhou was the son of Huang of Changshou in Bayu. He ascended the hall and said: "The ultimate principle is wordless;

those with clear eyes discern it. The true mechanism is uniquely revealed; those who have attained penetration know it. If you try to understand it through Zen, you are creating something out of nothing."
It is unconventional; it is not to be understood through the assembly of Chan. To miss it face-to-face is to stumble.
If you can realize it here and now, you will see that the Great Way is broad and level—like the wind passing through, the grass bows down (Minshu succeeded him).

The thirty-sixth generation successor under Nanyue, Chan Master Tiantyi Chao of Longtan, ascended the hall and gave this discourse. He let out a shout and said: "How long has this true mantra been transmitted?
It is simply because of the passage of many years that it has become unclear; errors have been passed down as truths, until now there is nothing left."
This is efficacious. Now, because a donor has made an invitation, I have specifically struck the bells and beaten the drums to come forth and serve as a witness for you all.
He gave two shouts and said: "Henceforth, you must not forget. Ascending the hall, he said: "The seventy-two peaks of Mount Yuefeng respond with standard measure;
the thirty thousand acres of the Xiang River swallow and spit out without partiality. From where have you all come?"
Amidst a mass of turbulent clouds, he treads upon the uneven ground of seven hollows and eight protrusions.

Having traversed every hoofprint of donkey and horse, he still leans upon the doorways and walls of others, yet is called a "lord" by the people of the world. Unable to sit idly by and watch, this mountain monk flings open both doors for you;
though they were born of your mother, they shall never be cast away in vain. With a shout, he says: "If you can enter here—"
"Let him walk alone through the Great Way. Entering the hall, [the Master] said: "Longtan today is thus; tomorrow he will be thus.
Even until the final five hundred years, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall speak with one voice in the same way.
He struck the meditation staff and said: "Such a Dharma—listen closely, listen closely! (Tuiweng)
[The Successor].
Master Yunzong of Huayao gave a small-scale sermon (xiaocan): "Exerting one's utmost strength to proclaim it, the tongue has never moved.
Quietly, suddenly turning over, the black lacquer bucket is smashed. Five fives and three threes—upside down, panic arises. In a state of alarm...
Busily picking it up—this is "not included in the six. Yet he goes before the gate of the Master to question Kong Qiu. Groundlessly, he uses this "one not established" to compete with him;
Xiang Yu and Fan Kuai have faces as black as lacquer. Suddenly looking to his left and right, he says: "Do you understand?

One could compose a thousand poems on rustic interests, yet they would not exhaust the idle days in the Sangha hall. On the eve of late spring, ascending the hall, he says: "The Great Way is divided..."
Clear! Who can understand? Green waters and blue mountains are even more beautiful in the depths of spring. A hundred kinds of bird songs fill the forest; their calls and cries must be heeded early.
The cuckoo cries until its blood flows as spring departs; the partridge’s bitter lament turns the very core of one's heart upside down.
"Bring the pitcher, bring the pitcher!"—its beak is naturally loud. "Lord of the Field, Lord of the Field!"—I clearly inform you, sir. Caw, caw, the crow!

The magpie calls, "Magpie! Morning and evening it cries out before the courtyard to startle one awake. [The Master] pats the meditation seat and says: "This mountain monk has a mouth, yet it is not as good as his.
**Small Sermon:** Amidst flowing waters and white clouds, the secluded bird utters several calls. To exhaust the heart of the Patriarch—do not say there are few expedient means.
**Ascending the Seat:** There is a great expedient means, which accords with the manifestation of the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata manifests.
"Relying on unimpeded wisdom to clearly understand the Dharma—let us speak of it. Upon what does this unimpeded wisdom rely to clearly understand the Dharma?
After a long silence, he said: "Pang’s rake; Qingping’s wooden ladle. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Huangmei plum falls to the ground;

it is just like a young gentleman dropping his golden pellets. Spring grass spreads across the steps; it is as if a beautiful lady has spread out her emerald felt rug. Now tell me: is this the environment?"
"Ya-ren-ya. One must by no means say this. "Diao-dao" cannot be distinguished; "yu-lu" are inconsistent. Question:
"What is the true countenance of the Great Sage of Sizhou? The Master said: "A single note of a fisherman’s flute in the Canglang River. [The questioner] said:
"I nearly fell into a heap of sounds and forms! The Master said: "A stone tiger in the bustling marketplace—though it does not startle people, it strikes fear into them."
A monk asked, "I ask the Master to point out the path that leads upward. The Master said, "The Stele of Lord Yang stands at Xian Mountain Pavilion.
The monk asked, "How should one comprehend this? The Master said, "Those who read it frown. Later, while a monk was attending to him, the Master said, "Why do you feel so wronged?"
[The monk] asked, "In what way am I at fault? The Master said, "I see even less reason for it. [The monk] said, "It is a grievance, a grievance!

The Master struck him, saying, "Even though you have confessed, thirty blows are not to be avoided. While the Master was residing at Nengren, a monk asked, "Why has the Master not been preaching the Dharma lately?
The Master said, "Beyond the painted streams and mountains, the bamboo-cock cries. The monk paid his respects.

Next, the Master spat directly in the monk’s face. The monk was speechless. The Master spread out his hands and said, “Give me back my spit! The monk again remained speechless. The Master then struck him out.
A monk asked, “Why do the Buddhas of the three periods not know that they exist? The Master replied, “Their noses are deep and their eyes are large.
The monk asked, “Why do the ‘wildcat’ and the ‘white ox’ (the spirits) instead know that they exist? The Master replied, “Their bones are thin, but their will is long. (Teweng)
[The Record of] Master Hui of Shigu, Yunsi Leishui, a native of the Jiang family of Hezhou. Having opened the Dharma at Yunsi Leishui, he ascended the hall and said:

"The lamp of wisdom illuminates the earth; the flames of the Dharma-texts light up the heavens. Rain and color intermingle in radiance, their light pervading beyond the kalpas. Let me ask you: [what is it?]"
Do you all understand? If you can understand, then your nostrils hang down like twin tassels and your eyebrows form the character "八" (eight). At the moment of planting [the seed], extend one hand;

upon a bottomless boat, take up the oar and grasp the rudder to roam through the waves of the bitter sea. Having delivered all sentient beings, in the end there is not a single sentient being who can be delivered.
One must simply join hands with this old fellow of the great belly and laugh "he-he," only then to realize that there is something else.
He lived in prosperity for a time. Later, while residing at Songhe Yuan in Chengdu, on the first day of the fourth month of the Gengzi year, he manifested a slight ailment.
He spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly: "A decrepit, solitary, and stubborn stone man, I have returned to this Sahā world a million times over.
Coming is like the spring breeze upon withered wood; Departing is like a flash of lightning in the autumn moon. At times, I dwell within the pores of all Buddhas."
Sleeping. At times he appeared upon a mountain of sword-trees and blade-edges. "A shout from ten thousand miles of clouds and mists—this is not like ordinary rolling or piercing.
Having finished speaking, he passed away (Xiangya Ting was his successor).
Chan Master Yushan Rui of Dongshan, Qujing, was a native of Guang’an. He was a Dharma heir of Xiangya Ting. Once, he ascended the hall and said: “A dry dung pellet!
From out of thin air, he hurls forth a lump of iron. It shatters the hot skin on everyone’s faces, leaving one with nothing but a mouth unable to explain it.
A barefoot Persian enters the Great Tang; the carp of the Eastern Sea has already leaked the secret. Within the purple silk curtain...”
Scattering pearls inside—this would make the Indian monk laugh until his teeth fell out. Looking left and right, he said: "Where is the True Person of No Rank? Ascending the hall, he said:
"A thousand hands and a thousand eyes is the Great Compassionate One; he shines through all that is right and wrong among men.
Fully wielding the pivot of the earth, he transcends the ten thousand phenomena; the resonance of the lion’s lute penetrates Mount Sumeru. Is there anyone among the assembly who can..."
"What is this 'spiritual capacity'? He looked left and right, struck his staff once, and descended from the seat.

In the summer of the Guihai year, while residing at Dongshan Temple in Qujing Prefecture, Yunnan, he passed away. His age was seventy-four; his stupa was erected at the mountain temple (he was the successor of Xiangyue Ting).

Chan Master Zizhi Cang of Zhulin Temple in Baxian was the son of the Zhang family of Baxian. He received the tonsure at Mount Dae and attended upon Master Lingfa Chang for many years, serving as his attendant.
After receiving formal certification (*inka*), he opened the Dharma at Zhulin Temple. In ascending the hall, he said: "He cuts off the tongues of all people under heaven;
solitary, perilous, and steeply precipitous. He opens the precious treasury of the *Cintāmaṇicakra*; object and wisdom are clearly manifest."
The single mind is the immeasurable mind. To show that one dharma is all dharmas is to cause every person, at once, not to remain in ignorance:
that originally, every dharma is already fully present. A thousand-year-old cypress tree remains ever fresh; ten million years of flowing gold are reflected therein.
Although it is thus, such a realization is rarely met with by those who truly understand. Who, then, is the one who understands? After Xiatang has passed away...
"Unconditioned Consciousness. Who would have thought that Master Yuan would come today? He ascended the hall and, holding up his whisk, said:
"High above, there is nothing beyond; deep below, there is no limit. It is the root of humans and devas, the source-flow of the patriarchs and Buddhas.
From insects and plants to birds, beasts, dragons, and fish—none do not receive this majestic radiance and each perceive their own original face. Only the Bamboo Grove stands alone and detached."
The Path: Transcending all streams, it manifests speech in the realm of wordlessness; it gives rise to function within the useless.
It can cause the Demon King to fold his hands in submission and cause the wandering monks to turn their hearts in devotion. At every step, it clarifies the original mechanism;
at every point, it reveals extraordinary matters. To see what these extraordinary matters are—study! (Lingra Changsi).
Chan Master Tiantuanyuanri Dudai of Nanpu was the son of Xu of Changshou. He was unacquainted with mundane affairs and remained aloof from the world;
the old man Po constantly called him "Baguaizi" (Sack Man). He received the Dharma lineage from Minsu Xiang. Entering the hall, he said: "The great sun overflows the eyes;
ten thousand miles are not hung with a single cloud. The autumn waters are clear and limpid; a single abyss can contain all waters. The dragon..."
Mists rise as they chant; tigers roar and winds arise. Gazing at the well, gazing at the donkey; the face of the sun, the face of the moon.
The thorny chestnut; the diamond circle; the dried dung pellet; three pounds of flax—put all of these aside for a moment and go straight onto the Buddha’s head and shit upon him.
"Who is it that unties the bell beneath the lion's chin? It is ever tranquil, never departing from its place;

if you seek it, you will find it cannot be seen. Ascending the hall, he said: "The three great collections of the Buddha’s teachings—Gautama exhausted every stratagem therein. Laozi’s five thousand words—he used every skillful artifice there.
Yet when brought forth, they are of no use; why labor so hard to contemplate them? If one turns toward the time before Eon-Voice..."

Previously, when I took up the task, it was much like a silver mountain or an iron wall; with a single blow, I smashed it to pieces and cast it into the vast ocean, leaving not even a grain of dust behind.
Because of the conditions for appearing in the world, I established the roles of guest and host according to circumstances, avoiding the trap of "sleeper Zen" and nurturing a horned tiger.
Be careful with your steps; do not be reckless along the way. When I, this mountain monk, speak thus, it is out of love for my child that I am unaware of my own faults.
"Ugly! Is there anyone here who understands the opportune moment and possesses the true eye? After a long silence, he let out a shout (Minshu Xiang succeeded him).
Chan Master Jichu Shang of Kaiyuan Temple in Qizhou Prefecture was the son of the Chen family from Yidu, Huguang. At the age of twenty...
Liying received the tonsure and entered Fenghuang Mountain to practice in seclusion. He made a vow, saying: "If I do not achieve enlightenment, I shall never descend from the mountain.

Subsisting on wild fruits and drinking from mountain streams, he remained there for nearly five years. One day, while sitting upright in weariness, he suddenly felt as if a mountain were collapsing at midnight;
startled by the sound, his entire body broke into a sweat, and he attained a state of unimpeded clarity. Thereupon, he descended the mountain and went to visit Shuanggui.

He was well-versed in the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and had received full ordination. Later, he fashioned an image of the Bodhi tree and received formal authorization (*abhyanujñā*). Residing at Kaiyuan Temple, he ascended the hall and said:
"The clouds follow the dragon; the wind follows the tiger. A single beam of cold light pervades heaven and earth. The sunflower inclines toward the sun; the willow catkins dance with the wind.
Now that the new Elder has arrived, he must respond to the timing of the moment. He can only steer the rudder with the wind and release the hawk upon seeing the hare."
Sometimes it is so; in the human realm and the heavens. Sometimes it is not so; not even a drop of water can pass through.
Suddenly grasping his staff, he said: "Tell me, how would you express the phrase that cuts off the vital ford? He gave a shout and said: "The official seal does not admit a needle;
yet in private, carriages and horses may pass. (Minshu succeeded him.)
Chan Master Wanshou Xiaoyuan was the son of the Liu family of Longchang. Upon reading the *Record of Dazhu*, he reached the passage:

"When the eyes resemble the eyebrows, the Way begins to settle. Thereupon, he resolved to leave the household life. He first visited Shuanggui Ming, with whom he attained realization of the essential meaning. Later, he received the seal of approval from Danzhu Mi.
He subsequently opened a dharma seat at Wanshou. Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Before King Vairocana (Viyūnaprabha), there were some..."
This news: the thousand hands of Great Compassion cannot reach it. Since the time of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, there has been no such news.
All the people of the great earth stumble and cannot rise. At this very moment, I gouge out the eyes of Maheśvara and pierce through the nostrils of you all.
But how can one speak of it clearly? After a long silence, he said: "The mountain monk commits a transgression. (Danzhu)
Mimi (the Dharma successor).
Chan Master Houdeng of Jinguan Caotang was the son of the Wang family of Rongchang. He received the Dharma from Danzhu Mi and resided at Jinguan Caotang Temple.
Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Spring returns once more, and all is renewed; let us not vainly discourse upon our private possessions."
To the people: the eyes have sinews that can see forms; where within the ears is the place from which sound is heard?

Fish swim without disturbing the water; birds fly without clinging to the clouds. Striking the drum of Heyishan, he raises up the broken sand-basin. Making a gesture of support with his hand, he says:
"Look! Look! Ascending the hall: Waves lash the heavens in the Jianshui Pool; clusters of fishing lamps dot the night.
A boat. From the tip of the pole, a fine line with a tiny bait dangles. Where can the golden-scaled fish hide as it breaks through the waves?
Holding his staff in the manner of casting a hook, he said: "Is there anyone? Is there anyone? (Danzhu Mi succeeded him.)

Chan Master Kuyu Yin of Cishou Monastery in Xindu was the son of the Ding family of Yuzhou. Having left the secular world from childhood, his spiritual capacity accorded with that of Dashi Mi of Daisui, who subsequently granted him certification.
He resided at Cishou in Xindu and at Caotang in Chengdu. Ascending the hall at Caotang, he said: "Shouldering the *zhuli* staff, I enter Caotang;
dragons gallop and tigers stride in the midst of spring’s warmth. Yet, lacking the virtue of coolness, I cannot illuminate my ancestors. (He then led [the assembly] out.)
Watering the Vegetables Awaiting the Later Master (Danzhu Mi’s Successor).
Xinggu Xi Chan Master of Baoguang Temple in Xindu was a native of Anfu. In his youth, he was immersed in the midst of warhorses; though he drifted through life, he possessed great ambition.
He visited Danzhu Mi and received the Dharma succession from him. While presiding over Baoguang Temple in Xindu, he ascended the hall and said: "Right now, it is exactly like this..."
At that moment, all traces of dust are severed. Who can recognize the person of former times? Standing tall, face-to-face, there is no obstruction;
if you hesitate or deliberate, ten thousand miles of clouds. (Danzhu Mi’s succession.)
Chan Master Xingyuan of Yumen Creek in Suíyáng was a native of Píngshān. His family had served as hereditary military commanders for the Liao Zhongcheng.
Because he did not understand why the Chén-kòu invaders had invaded Shǔ, he first shaved his head and donned the dyed robes of a monk, retiring to live among the mountains of Suíyáng.

Not long after, he went to the hermitage of Chángxuě Zuì to study, where he received full ordination. After several years of serving in general administrative affairs at the monastery, he was entrusted with the lineage and began to propagate the Dharma. Above...
The Hall. Regarding the matters transmitted from of old: sitting does not occupy the hall; throughout successive dynasties, compassion was aroused without ever leaving one’s door.
Having no other choice, one must dig into the void and open wide the gate of the second meaning, wielding the mallet and raising the whisk, with staff and shout hurrying back and forth.
Sometimes sweeping the ground at the roots of pine trees; sometimes waiting for people on the street;
even drawing his bow, brandishing his pitchfork, whetting his blade, or rolling a ball—though this mountain monk is but "grass grown in another's field," he ultimately does not hide his body here.
(He let out a shout. Later, he moved to Pingwu and passed away. His remains were collected and enshrined in a shrine to the left of the ancestral stupa at Zhaojue. (Zhaixue Zu succeeded him.)

Chan Master Wanchan Lingsongduanbi was a native of the Guo clan from Neijiang. While listening to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he harbored doubts regarding the "ever-abiding true mind" (*nitya-citta*) and repeatedly sought clarification, yet failed to attain realization.
He ascended Baiyun Cave, where at night he dreamed of a strange monk with hair and beard as white as silver.
The monk clapped his hands three times and said, "Hurriedly recite the Buddha’s name. Upon waking, he composed a verse: *In a dream, I was moved by a strange monk...*

Clapping his hands, he came; Amitābha was vividly cast upon the platform of his mind. Looking back, the path of affection and worldly dust was merely the haphazard carving of axes that destroy one's nature.
He subsequently went to Jiang’an Panlong to study under Shuanggui Ming, where he repeatedly inquired into the essential points of the heart-mind.
Later, while attending the ordination ceremony at Bai niu Mountain under Zhangxue Zhu, he passed through Yumen and read the records of the Patriarch Miyun of Tiantong.
There was a phrase concerning "advancing and retreating" that had obstructed his chest for three years. One day, it all became as if he were suddenly awakened from a dream;

there was no longer any lingering obstruction. He composed a verse, saying: "Between advancing and retreating lie two heavy gates; How many heroes have been trapped within them! Clearly there is a path leading to the Milky Way;
It is neither the 'three before' nor the 'three after. He immediately received certification [of his realization], and the prophecy was fulfilled at Changsong.

At Lingfeng, the assembly requested that he ascend the seat [to preach], but he firmly declined, refusing to consent. He took pleasure in traveling and sightseeing; whenever he encountered a scene or circumstance, he would spontaneously compose verses.

A brief excerpt reads: The solitary peak presides over the night, the realm vast and still. Entering the chamber, the cold wind has no time to flee. Dwelling in wealth, one clings to it and loathes its lack;
Living in poverty, one maintains simplicity and delights in its nobility. How can exquisite delicacies compare to the nourishment of yellow rhizomes?
Magnificent robes are no match for a hundred-knot robe; universally responding to myriad affairs, he sings the "Snow" melody.
Heaven and sea are one color—how joyful for us! (By Changxue Zuishi)

Chan Master Lansheng Sheng of Jinchuan Gaofeng was the son of the Jian family of Rongchang. He studied under Yumen Zui, whose words and his own met with mutual resonance, whereby he received the seal of transmission.
While presiding at Jinchuan Gaofeng, he ascended the hall and said: "Hitherto I have embraced simplicity and lived in poverty;
today, however, I can no longer conceal it. Although I thus expose my myriad shortcomings, I insist that you all take heed. Now, take heed!"
"What is this? He gave a sweep with his whisk and said, "The old fellow at the head of the mountain forcibly pushes me forward;

I run before people without a second thought. I laugh to death the Patriarch of the Wall-Facing Era. To the very end, utter poverty leaves only a mouth full of froth. With a shout, on the eighth day of the first month of the Bingchou year of the Kangxi era, he manifested a slight ailment.
Sitting upright, he passed away. Upon cremation, the *sāra-garbha* (the adamantine core) was collected. As follows: [The remainder of the text follows the description of the relics.]
Shuboshi (Zhushishi), who resembled millet in appearance, had several [disciples]. His dharma-heir, Zhuyou Jiefu Ji, returned to Gaofeng in Luoyuan and erected a stūpa for him.
He was seventy-four years old and had fifty-two years of ordination seniority (the successor of Zhangxue Zui).
Chan Master Da Hanwo of Kunming Xiangguo was the son of the He family from southern Sichuan. He inherited the Dharma from Zuifu of Yumen.
On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall and said: "Since I bound my tongue at Longjiu, my appearance has remained truly peerless in all the world.
Originally, when Huming first descended, it was as if Śacī departed from the Golden Palace. Even when seen by those in the Jade Towers, one finds him full of elegance; yet—"
Leaning on a crimson silk fan to shield the moon—this is not because a man lacks a black heart; it is because a man fears his heart lacks blood.
Even if one were to wash away the flesh until the bones are revealed, how could the marrow ever be thoroughly exposed? (By Chángxuè Zuìsì)
Chan Master Hanyue Wen of Hongshan in Yiling was the son of the Huang family of Taizhou. He received the Dharma lineage from Zui of Zhaojue.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The poison-drum is struck before the dais; A single tune is blown on a holeless flute.

When the multitudes of humans and devas assemble from all quarters, The ten directions are cut off, yet clarity remains vivid. This rattan staff is not like Dongshan’s hemp; It pierces through Shanzhou."
The iron ox’s nose; the Great Elephant of Jiazhou harbors deep grievance. The primordial mechanism is shattered, leaving no room for intellect.

Insects, grasses, and trees are pressed toward the return of spring. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are brought back to the armory. The eight characters of the mountain gate open like the heavens.

When ordinary and holy beings intersect, who can walk alone? Ascending the hall at the beginning of the summer retreat: Three months of *an-gu* (sitting in seclusion), ninety days of restraining the feet. This was the ancient way.
Nowadays, leaning against gates and by doors, with spears and halberds leveled on level ground—what harm is there in Sun Bin practicing divination?

With drums beaten and bells rung, I invite this mountain monk to wield the mallet and raise the whisk; though all say it is the formal opening of the retreat and the ascent to the hall, one cannot deceive the eyes and ears of humanity. (Zhengxue Zu)
Chan Master Foyuan Gang of Chengdu’s Zhaojue Monastery was the son of the Li family of Neijiang. At the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Master Zuohui at Yumen.

He served as the attendant for twenty years and traveled between the regions of Wu and Yue. He received full ordination under Master Rong at Yao Feng and returned to Jingming, where he first received formal certification.
He was subsequently appointed to preside over Zhaojue. Ascending the hall, he said: "The superior man of universal penetration perceives before the movement of the occasion; his spirit is awakened."
A secret operation; the mind transcends all measure. The star is held in the land of Han; the moon sets over the realm of Chu.

Thus, the news before one’s eyes cannot be transmitted by mouth or ear. Observe how the sages of antiquity employed a thousand metaphors and myriad words—exhausting every turn of the wheel of skillful means, yet all was in vain.
If you wish to stand at the bottom of the deepest sea, you must directly shatter the gate above.
"Tell me, what skillful means are employed? After a long silence, he said: "Pushing down Mount Sumeru like rolling a mustard seed; investigating it, there is no obstruction within a single kṣaṇa.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The abbot has been in residence for one year; having encountered winter twice during the retreats, opening my mouth reveals the celestial mechanism, and raising my eyes exposes true wisdom.
I do not chant the promptings prior to words, nor do I discuss the meaning subsequent to phrases. In the midst of casualness, I strike upon it."
The tip of the nostril—iron eyes and copper pupils cannot perceive it. [The Master] then held up his staff and said, "With the sword that settles chaos, the four seas are tranquil and clear.
He then lowered the staff and said, "Without the Bai Ze map, the myriad demons withdraw their traces. "As for this one phrase of Baoen," he asked, "how would you speak of it?
Majestic and towering throughout the universe, it hangs suspended against the wind; ten thousand li of rivers and mountains fortify the imperial domain.
(Changxue Zuisi). Chan Master Xiang of Kaishua, Yunnan, was a native of Nanlong. At the age of twenty, he received the tonsure at Gigu Temple.

Having heard that Zhang Xue had attained the Dharma while intoxicated at Fayuan Temple, he personally went to pay his respects and investigate the Way. He attended him for many years and was subsequently granted the transmission.
While presiding over Kaishua in Beisheng Prefecture, Yunnan, he ascended the hall and said: "The staff strikes the head of the stone man; Yellow and black paint cover his face in shame."
With wide-open, crystalline eyes, he startles the flowing heavens; He swathes the thousand-fathom moon and personally ascends the White Jade Tower.
Where clouds and mists drift and vanish, the mountains and waters flow on together. Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If you try to hold him back, the secure barrier is firmly closed."
The Buddhas and Patriarchs are difficult to fathom. When they let go, the Big Dipper hides its body and the true wind pervades the world.

To unfold it or to roll it up—to gather the entire earth together—it is as small as a grain of millet. To gaze upon it or to look up to it—there is nowhere that is not the heart-essence of all Buddhas.
[End of] Small Assembly for Inquiry. Riding a raft, one mistakenly enters the bridge of the Ox and the Cow; It crushes empty space without the need for oars. Precious!
The heavy winds and clouds exerted their power together; the latchless iron chain shook at both ends. On the Buddha’s Birthday in the year Bingchen, he passed away peacefully.
Upon cremation, fifty or so grains of five-colored śarīra were obtained and enshrined in a stupa to the right of Qingmen Temple (the successor of Zhuixue).

Chan Master Nuyun Shi of Caotang in Langzhong was the son of the Yang family of that locality. He studied under Master Zui of Zhangxue at the Diantang, where he attained realization and received certification.
He was subsequently appointed to succeed him on the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout; Shigong drawing his bow."
Daowu dances with his ritual tablet; Xuefeng’s ball and Puhua’s bell startle Yangqi’s three-legged donkey, who tramples the Three Mountains and the Five Peaks.
Hehehe! What a fine brother! This is also like spitting directly in one’s face before the eyes. Ascending the hall for the conclusion of the retreat:
Today is the fifteenth day of the first month. The attendants strike the bells and beat the drums, and the mountain gate is commanded to open wide.
He unleashed the fierce tiger of Xuansha, its paws and fangs bared in a crouch, its breath stirring a spirit that would swallow Buddhas and patriarchs whole.
Then, shaking his authority, he let out a single roar, saying: "Only a cat knows how to catch mice" (Master Zuisi).
Chan Master Ban-yue Han of Yumen Temple in Zunyi Prefecture was a native of Linshui. At the age of twenty, he shaved his head under Master Chuang-xue.

Later, he studied under Shuanggui, where he underwent a "great death," suddenly awakening from his dream as if from sleep. He subsequently returned to Zhaojue for certification and was invited by Yumen to succeed him on the abbot’s seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"A single utterance of the wondrous mechanism values nothing more than a true知音 (zhinyin—'one who knows the sound'). The ancestral seal is held high."
Circulate the True Eye and expound the True Vehicle of Non-arising; magnify and manifest that which is inherently present, and plant the crimson banner of Kāśyapa.
Reveal it to those of the present age: studying the Way is like climbing a mountain—one must reach the summit; studying the Way is like rowing a boat—one must reach the abyss.
Only upon reaching the summit does one know the vastness of the universe; only upon reaching the abyss does one perceive the depth of the lakes and seas.

What is called "investigation must be true investigation; awakening must be real awakening. If a student does not cease their thieving mind, they will wander about outside the gate and instead blame the path of Chan for lacking efficacy.

Only when one abandons both sleep and food and lets go of the thieving mind—suddenly snapping like a twig and bursting like a firecracker—is the root of birth and death from immeasurable kalpas shattered by a single flash of insight. Thus, O Good Knowledge, [it is realized].
What can be done? It would have been best to receive a blow from the staff in the hands of Chan Master Yuhan. Why?
Unless one’s bones are thoroughly chilled by a single frost, how could one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose? (Recorded by Changxue Zu)

The Record Secretary of Zhaojue asked Chan Master Chaoyu: "You were born into the Li clan of Fengling. You left home to become a monk at the age of seven and traveled to study under various masters throughout the land.
Finally, you met Changxue Zhenke while he was intoxicated at Hesheng; you served as his record secretary for over thirty years and received the seal of transmission from Zhaojue."

On New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall to hold the whisk and address the assembly: “One person rejoices, and the eight directions are at peace. Cold and warmth intermingle; the light and deep hues exude their verdancy.
In this atmosphere of harmonious prosperity, the staff is raised in unison; within the vast expanse of heaven and earth, they cultivate their studies amidst the dew and rain.

Since the seasons are thus, all things and beings are entirely in spring. Not subject to the transformations of yin and yang, what need is there for the labor of molding and forging? The myriad wilds...”
Without relying on the power of the Eastern Sovereign, how could one attain such composure as to emit this extraordinary fragrance? [The Master] held up his staff and said:

"Since it does not belong to the creative transformations of yin and yang, nor does it follow the seasonal shifts of the new and the old, after all, how should one proceed? He let out a shout and said:

Do you still know? Throughout the four seas, eyebrows are raised to sing of the sun of Emperor Shun; ten thousand spirits bow their heads to celebrate the sky of Emperor Yao (Venerable Xuezui’s *Zuisi*).
Zen Master Dingyuan of Fenglin Bamboo Waves in Qingcheng was the son of the Wang family.

At the age of twenty, he received the tonsure under Master Youyu and completed his full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) under the guidance of Master Tizongning at Yunfeng. Later, he returned to Zhaojue and inherited the Dharma.

He subsequently entered Qingcheng Fenglin and studied the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) of the Zhou dynasty. In the *Xinyou* year of the Kangxi era, he was summoned while intoxicated to succeed [his predecessor] at Zhaojue Temple.

He ascended the hall for the opening of the retreat, saying: "The light penetrates the three thousand worlds; brightness and darkness cannot encompass it. Wisdom transcends the sentiments of sages and ordinary beings; form and name are altogether unestablished.
One does not fall into the stages of existence or non-existence, nor does one descend into the realm of numerical categories. [He] ascended the hall. Peak...
Layered peaks are draped in emerald green; bamboo and trees manifest auspicious signs. Azure streams give rise to clouds; hoarfrost flowers vie for beauty.
This is, in truth, a ready-made koan—why labor to dig through the earth to seek out heaven? If you are one who dwells within this realm, you must perform the deeds of this realm;
if you perform the deeds of this realm, you must be one who dwells within this realm. (He plants his staff upright and says: "All of you, realize it right here! The Beginning of Spring.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring day is bright; the spring breeze is clear; the spring mountains are exquisite; the spring waters are level. Birds warble their songs; frozen clouds gather thickly.
Transformation and growth flow forth without the need for artifice. Those with eyes see this together; those with ears hear it together. He called to the assembly, saying:
"Great assembly, since such a state is seen and heard by all, why is it that out of ten people, five do not understand?"

"Twofold. To reach this point is to miss it face-to-face. As the Master was walking along the corridor, a monk asked, "When there is no dreaming and no thought, where is the host? The Master slapped him with his hand and said, "Do you understand? The monk did not grasp it. After the Master had walked two or three steps, he called to the monk. When the monk turned his head, the Master said, "What is this? While the Master was weeding grass with the assembly, [a monk] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West? The Master pulled out a blade of grass and held it up. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If you can understand this, you will understand the Patriarch’s coming from the West. A Zen practitioner asked, "Where does the road to Fenglin lead? The Master lowered his hoe and said, "This patch of ground has not been plowed thoroughly;
that is why there is so much grass. The guest asked again, "Where does the road to Fenglin lead? The Master lowered his hoe twice more and said, "In other places they burn the dead;
here, we bury them alive. Recorded in the Guiyou year of the Kangxi era (1693) by Fengzhang He.

I further command that these be carved once more as the *Jiamu* (Transcript) and the *Jinjiang Chan Deng* (Lamp of Chan from the Jin River), both recorded in their entirety and appended to the *Lengyan Zangshi* (Lankavatara Sutra Repository) for wide circulation.
(By Zhu Xuezui, the Dharma heir).

Chan Master Yuejing of Suyang Wuya was the son of the Lei family of Jiangling. At the age of sixteen, after both his parents had passed away, he took refuge with Master Shiyen and received the tonsure.
Hearing that the Chan school of Zhaojue was flourishing greatly, he went in person to visit him, whereupon his spiritual potential was awakened and he received certification.
He resided at Wuya in Suyang. Entering the hall, he said: "The Great Way has no front or back; the ultimate principle transcends words and explanations. It stands far apart...
Transcending the Three Worthies and soaring far above the Ten Grounds, even if Śākyamuni and Maitreya were to arrive, they would not dare to accept it;
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra would have no room for deliberation. An ancient worthy said:

"To take the entire universe and the great earth and compress them into the size of a single grain of rice—this is still not the ultimate talk. But tell me: how is the single phrase that fully upholds the true command? Liang.
Jiurui said: "Walking until the water's end, sitting to watch the clouds arise. On this occasion of the Buddha-Bathing Ceremony, his physical radiance blazes intensely;
who would dare to stir so much as a single hair? His wondrous marks are perfectly luminous; one must strictly avoid offending him head-on.
Now, this unworthy descendant can only respond to the season: using the true water of the nature-emptiness, sometimes its waves and ripples are vast and boundless.
At times, it is completely clarified. I ask the assembly: Is it bathing that is it? Or is it not bathing that is it?
