Chan Master Ying of Ruiyun Mountain in Yongchun, Quanzhou Prefecture, was the son of the Lin family of Zhangzhou. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
At the age of twenty-two, he went to Nanshan Miyu at Guangyan Temple to receive the tonsure. Later, he received the seal of approval from Jin-su Yuan. He ascended the hall and said:
"To ask about the Buddha or the Dharma is like putting sand in one’s eyes; to speak of mind or nature is like putting [gravel] in one’s ears."
Water cannot enter. There are those with the Eye of the Path who can place Mount Sumeru inside their eyes and fit the waters of the great ocean into their ears.
For such people—those who merely echo empty sounds—it is precisely right to give them three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred blows in the evening.
Why? In a world of peace and clarity, one must strictly avoid false speech. Ascending the hall: Yesterday was the eighth day of the twelfth month; today is the ninth. The Stone Bridge.
Behold the plum blossoms. In the cold weather, they do not show their hands. This brings to mind Zhaozhou’s “drinking tea” and Caoshan’s “drunkenness.
Accepting whatever comes one’s way, it reaches the point where one’s entire body is nothing but mouth. Since one’s entire body is mouth, why then do you come to drag out these idle complications?
He then looked around left and right and said, “I only wish for those who know the time and recognize the season.”

"Why must you place a head upon a head? The Master, during the third circumambulation, offered incense and said: "Three circumambulations and three turning words—how could these suffice to repay his kindness?
A single blow leaves a scar; this is ultimately intended to clear a grievance. This wandering son has not even a single tile above him."
There is not even space for a single awl below; one must simply go to the crossroads, rummaging here and there until a single fragment is found.
It is neither confrontational nor averse; it is burned within the brazier. Now tell me: is this for repaying kindness, or is it for clearing a grievance?

[He] beats his breast with his hand and says: "The Persian who discerns rare treasures has encountered [it]; Longing for it, how could he not weep to the blue heavens? This is a verse on the World-Honored One.
Holding up a flower, he said: "The fair lady rises at dawn to stroll through spring; The young gentleman, on a clear day, treads upon the grass.
Though they are enemies meeting head-on, Their union is naturally and perfectly suited. How many bystanders along the road Fail to recognize the springtime beauty, And suffer in vain frustration!
In praise of "The Woman Emerging from Samādhi," he said: "The Celestial Gate is severed and the River of Chu opens; Clear waters flow eastward to the sea."
Northward, the distant peaks: green mountains emerge facing each other on both banks; a solitary sail comes from the direction of the sun.
In praise of Zhaozhou’s story of washing the alms bowl, it is said: The Lake Dongting is vast and the autumn moon is fine; when taking advantage of the current, one must set sail early.
Do not wait until the empty waves toss up the "Shiyou" rocks; neither this side nor that side will suffice. In praise of the Old Lady of Mount Tai, it is said: Transverse and vertical.
The crossroads are vast and level; going out ten thousand ways or coming in a thousand, one acts as one pleases. Without cause, one asks others whether it is acceptable;
beyond the forest, the cries of monkeys sound like heart-rending wails. The official warrant and the true eye are clearly distinct;
this troop of patrols has all been laid low. Naturally returning home, the body is light. A verse on Mañjuśrī’s three summer retreats says: "Transversely across the sea of right and wrong."

Entering the body, he wanders freely amidst packs of jackals and tigers. To truly know the elegant domain of Mañjuśrī, one must have only two or three hairs of the gallbladder covering him (Bai-chi Yuan-si).
Master Mingfa of Yuantang in Songjiang ascended the hall on the nineteenth day of the sixth month and said: "Before the nineteenth day of the sixth month, one must not dwell where there is no Buddha.
After the nineteenth day of the sixth month, one must hurry past even where there is a Buddha.

On this very nineteenth day of the sixth month, the Gate of Universal Pervasion stands open and ten thousand trees form a deep shade. Those who have come here find rest for their shoulders; those who dwell here let their minds find peace. Why is this?"
Therefore: "The warbling of the yellow orioles outside the cage is mature; clearly, face-to-face, it is Guanyin" (Bachi Yuansi).

On the following morning, Chan Master Shengmo Pu ascended the hall and said: "I have traveled extensively through the cities and towns of the realm, and I have passed through every wealthy village and hamlet.
Yet, when the bowl has not even been brought to the mouth, the wildcats and white oxen roar all day long. You people of virtue," he continued.
Do not clamor so. Sit upon your meditation cushions and cease your discursive thoughts. We await your inquiry regarding the second hexagram of Junping.
Small Assembly: In the Hall of the Rising Sun, it is vast and tranquil. For what reason do you all remain stubborn at your feet?

It is because from the past you have merely taken a wrong step, which has caused you to this day remain unable to pass through the barrier. To the east and west are walls; to the south and north are mountains. In between flows a single stream.
The waters flow with a gurgling murmur. Turning his body and shifting his steps, he ascends the perilous peaks and treacherous crags at will. Ascending the hall:

On the fifth day of the fifth month in the year of Jiayin, what need is there for peach-wood talismans or mugwort tigers? This year the Wood Tiger stands in the sun; let no demons or monsters act with reckless insolence.
It is only within the lineage of the Patriarchs that demons and heretics dare not even glance upon it. In short, this is the domain of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
He enters. He wishes to follow the rules and regulations. Why is this so? Thus it is said: "The guest remains a guest from beginning to end;
the host remains a host from beginning to end. Ascending the hall: The minds of all Buddhas are for the sake of sentient beings; there are none who do not compassionately manifest skillful means.
Sentient beings, in every thought-moment, oppose all Buddhas; there is none who does not commit perverse and rebellious acts.

Last night, the "True Person of No Rank" struck off half the nostrils of the "Faceless Man. Letting out a great cry, he so startled the bell tower that it began to dance and the Buddha Hall rode over the mountain gate.
He specifically issued this judgment, bringing upon himself the blame of the Great Being Maitreya. Ha ha! Great laughter! O Assembly!
Tell me, what was he laughing at? Countless people come and go; how many among them are truly seeking the Way? To the assembly:
Today is the fifteenth day of the seventh month. Everywhere, they have untied the bags and released the golden lions and jade phoenixes, the mad dogs and wild oxen.
These are not merely those who trample the crops or fall for the fisherman’s hook; here, there is but one flavor.
Acting according to conditions. There is no drawing or untying of the "cloth bag" knot. When there is business, everyone works together; when there is no business, everyone rests together.
There are golden lions and jade phoenixes, as well as mad dogs and wild oxen, yet none are ever suppressed; let them go or stay as they please.

If they are the weeds of my own house, they shall certainly neither sink nor float. Ascending the hall: Monasteries everywhere are desolate; let the wandering clouds and drifting waters go as they will.
He remained there. Autumn arrived and green grass filled the steps. "In the Buddha-dharma, there is not a single word. What can be directed with 'tortoise hair' and 'hare's horns'?
How could the luster of silver tubes and wheat be disseminated? Holding his staff as if making the gesture of a fisherman, he said: "In my leisure, I have been practicing like a fishing old man;
at the close of day, the scarlet-scaled fish has still not been caught. Resting the staff upon his shoulder, he said: "The line and net are gathered; I shall compose a verse."
Return! The bright moon and clear wind fill the roads. Entering the hall: The autumn light before one’s eyes is magnificent;
there is no need to seek it elsewhere. The fragrance at the tip of the nose is rich and sweet; beneath the hedge, all is golden. Brothers, do not groan in distress.
After Yuanming has departed, the flowers remain. Why must you knit your brows, brooding over past and present? (By Bachi Yuansi)
Chan Master Tian’ang Ya of Huguo Renwang Temple in Wulin was the son of the Hu family of Putian. He first studied under Huangbo Qi and long served as an attendant at Zifu.
Later, he received the transmission and prediction from Mingfa Yuan. Upon succeeding him and appearing in the world at Huguo, he ascended the hall and said:
"Nirvana has no divergent paths; there are many gates of skillful means. [The Master] drew a line with his staff and said, "The path to Nirvana is cut off all at once.
He struck the ground once and said, "The gate of skillful means is opened through and through.

Look! How will you all proceed? He gave a shout and said, "The sword has long since been lost; you are merely marking the boat. This was the Small Lecture for the Mid-Autumn Festival at Lingquan Monastery.
Mount Shide points to the moon; Caoqi speaks of the moon; Master Ma contemplates the moon. Huguo, however, does not do so at all. Why?
Because in every person’s mind, the moon of the heart is solitary and full; in every individual’s nature, the sky of character is bright and radiant. Have you not seen Hanshan say:
"My mind is like the autumn moon, clear and pristine within the blue pool. Nothing can be compared to it; how am I to describe it? Thus speaks this mountain monk.
"I have also finished speaking. What, then, is the true moon? Holding up his whisk, he drew a circle (○) and said, "Above all, avoid letting your eyes grow dim.
Small Assembly (Xiaocan): "For a long time in these mountains it has been cold and desolate. Today we prepare a modest offering to reward you all.
He then extended his left hand and said, "First, take the *yunmen* cake. He then extended his right hand and said, "Next, serve the *zhaozhou* tea. You must—
Chew thoroughly; do not eat hastily. Although this is so, what would you do if Yunmen or Zhaozhou were to suddenly demand the price for tea and cakes?
The assembly remained silent. After a long while, he said: "The night is still bearable when deep, but after midday, it troubles people more.
He ascended the hall and said: "After snow comes rain; after rain comes snow. Falling in profusion, when will they ever cease? [He continued: "The affairs of the neighborhood and the marketplace..."

He cried out to the azure heavens: "The mud-ox at the bottom of the sea has its horns snapped off in the cold! You patch-robed monks, who receive the lingering shade of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, must not stay within your own courtyards;
you must also know something of the bitter and the pungent before you can succeed. Looking left and right, he said: "Do not say I have not spoken! Addressing the assembly, he said:
"Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma. He struck the meditation staff firmly and said: "Right here is the Buddha-land!"
"What is the Dharma of the One Vehicle? After a long silence, he said: "The yellow birds sing by the willow embankment as the warm sun shines;
after the rain, the frogs drum noisily across the mulberry fields. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The seawater is salty and the river water is fresh—everyone knows this.
Yellow gall is bitter and licorice is sweet—who does not understand? Why then, when asked about the matter within one's own house, do ten out of ten fail to arrive?"

There are five pairs. When the eyes are covered with rheum, it is because the moisture of emotional consciousness has not yet dried; thus, one meets obstacles wherever one goes, resulting in a lack of freedom.
Today, this mountain monk shall reveal the secret for you. He then spread his two hands and said: "When meeting people, do not fail to speak it.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "In this world there are two kinds of people. One person sits at the bottom of the water and is burned by fire."
"Kill! One person was sitting in fire; he was drowned and killed by water. Try asking this: what offense did these two commit?

After a long silence, he said: "To err by a hair's breadth is to lose by a thousand li. Addressing the assembly: "The crown jewel of Buddhas and Patriarchs, the eyes of humans and devas—if one is not a man of exceptional talent, one’s efforts at interpretation will be in vain.
Even if you were to penetrate through with such interpretation, you would still be caught by the clear-eyed master of our school."
If the Master were to apply a single pressure to the back of one’s heels, one would still inevitably engage in wild guessing and confused conjecture.

You must know that for refined gold from a great furnace, there can be no change in its color; how could lead, mercury, or common stones ever find a place to settle within it? Addressing the assembly:
At the gate of Huguo, we do not trade black beans for people’s eyes, nor do we stuff people’s nostrils with dung-balls. Each person must see the scene for themselves and give rise to realization.
Feeling a sneeze coming on, he looked at his attendant and said, "That one was speaking behind my back to the assembly.

The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet it is difficult to see while looking right at it. If you wish to recognize the true substance of the Great Way, it is not separate from sound, form, and speech.
Today, this mountain monk’s tongue aches; I cannot break it open for you all. He then returned to his quarters.

Master [Zhaozhou] addressed the assembly: "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable wondrous meanings—without moving the faculty of the tongue—I expect you to have a sudden flash of realization.
If there is a mountain where one may dwell, and things with which to trade for profit, one should know the opportune moment in a single flavor, without resorting to avoidance or taboos.
But tell me, what is it that you avoid? Have you not heard it said: 'As soon as Shuilao stepped into Mazu’s gate, he gave him a kick, and Mazu laughed heartily?'"
Having finished, he addressed the assembly: "Uphold the *huatou* with fierce resolve. With one blow, you must see a handful of blood; at the third watch, the red sun shall burst forth.
How could a turtle ever escape from within a jar? He addressed the assembly again: "Today is the fifteenth. The bells are struck and the drums beaten;
I hold this up face-to-face. Do not be reckless! Do not be reckless! A sweet melon is sweet to the core; a bitter melon is bitter to the core."
The bitter melon is bitter from root to tip. [A monk] asked, "What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said, "All day long he wanders the streets, his feet never resting.
[Another monk] asked, "What is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth? The Master said, "Ten thousand li east and west; eight thousand li south and north.
[He] asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said, "The Stone General atop Mulan Reservoir. [He] asked again.
"What is the phrase of following the waves and riding the currents? The Master said, "A wild ferry-crossing stretches across the head of Qili Tan.
"Question: What is the phrase of penetrating the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Performing somersaults within the eye of the golden needle.
"Question: What is spiritual penetration and transformation? The Master struck him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! (Baichi Yuan’s lineage).
Chan Master Nanguang Bing of Yanjing ascended the hall and raised the case of Chu-shih Qi, who said:
"If one relies on the entire Great Canon, there is not even a single word to be spoken; if one relies on the gate of the Patriarchs, there is not even a single word too many.
At the point where there is neither too little nor too much, bring forth a single phrase! A monk hesitated, and Qi struck him out. Xian Jinsu said:
"If one speaks according to the Great Canon of the Teachings, not a single word is lacking. If one speaks according to the Gate of the Patriarchs, not a single word is in excess.

He swept the pagoda and ascended the hall. "In the spring forest, there are naturally no withered trees; in the great ocean, how could there be separate tides?

Brothers, have you not seen? Breathing out from the nostrils, he thus beats the drum at Siming, yet preaches the Dharma within the Nine Palaces;

he walks in meditation by the waters of Yue, yet ascends the seat at Tiantong. Throughout the heavens and across the earth, from antiquity to the present, there has never been so much as a hair’s breadth of separation.
Suppose there were one who does not borrow another's nostrils—tell me, from where would they breathe?
Vapor. Clouds enshroud ten thousand mountains as they stand side by side in homage; the moon divides into two mirrors, flying together in radiance. A questioner asked, "What is one's original face?

"What is the meaning? the monk asked. The Master said, "To open one's mouth is already an error. The monk asked, "And what about not opening one's mouth?
The Master said, "Error, error. The monk asked, "How can one avoid being in error? The Master said, "For now, please return to your quarters and sit in meditation.

Another monk asked, "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The Master said, "What you have asked is exactly right. The monk said, "No..."

The Master said, "For now, please return to your quarters and sit in meditation. The two monks simultaneously grabbed the Master and said, "What, after all, is the essential meaning?

(Taomin’s Successor). Chan Master Yuancang of Guangfu Monastery in Yuezhou ascended the hall and said: "The great furnace for smelting Buddhas and Patriarchs has its flames reaching to the heavens;

Seven hundred [pounds]—all are cast and refined away here. Even if one considers the sentient and the insentient, all living beings without exception shed their skin and change their bones here;

the white clouds returning to their cave are fundamentally without mind. Therefore, amidst the flower-lined streets and willow-lined lanes, one’s original face is uniquely revealed."

yet when one looks closely, the eyebrows remain as they were. Do you understand? Though the ritual protocols of the Seven Buddhas have been leaked, they return home with the moon’s brightness filling their empty boat. (Liyen’s Dharma heir.)

A snake with a three-foot sword; casually, the stone tiger’s teeth and fur grow long. With a roar, he ascends the hall: "Today is the fifteenth of the eleventh month.

"Boo! Boo! Truly this is a fine performance. Yet, how does it compare to here at Huayan, where sound and light respond universally, and every beat and clap is perfectly timed?

Chan Master Zheng of Sōngān at Yangfén Zífú in Húzhou was a native of the Chen family of Qiānzhōu. He ascended the seat for a small-scale discourse (*xìcān*):
Wind and rain howl through the day; the traveler’s heart is desolate. The guest beneath the forest trees opens his breast—never has a single hair been stirred.

If you can personally realize this within yourself, then sentient beings and all Buddhas are fundamentally of the same root. If this is not yet so, then for now, behold the solitary crane crying out in the biting frost;
a single hook of the waning moon hangs from the tips of the plum branches. To the assembly: Last night the rain fell in torrents.
The weather is hot this morning; everyone knows this well. If one asks what season it is, after a long silence he says: "Three catties of hemp; a dried piece of excrement.
The True Dharma Eye has been extinguished by a blind donkey. (He lets out a shout. Winter of the Bingyin year of the Kangxi era.
He manifested a slight illness. On the fifth day of the first month of the following year, he requested a bath and changed his robes; sitting cross-legged, he passed away.
He was fifty-eight years of age and twenty-six years since his ordination. His stupa was enshrined at Wulu on Qianling (the successor was Lingji Guan).
Chan Master Zifuli Xiangfeng of Huzhou, a native of the Cheng clan from Wumen, addressed the assembly:

"Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is nothing that is not the radiant light of the original ground. Eating and dressing are entirely the wondrous functioning of spiritual power.
In the eyes, Manjushri manifests; in the ears, Avalokitesvara’s essence is revealed. Everywhere is the gate of Maitreya; every step taken is universal liberation."
Virtuous ones, tell me: where is the Heart-Seal of Vairocana? The universe floats upon the palm of the hand; the sun and moon revolve like ants on a millstone.
Evening Assembly: Last night it rained, today it is clear. These two states are like stains upon a mirror. When the stains and grime are completely gone, the light is finally seen:
in the evening, the slanting sun sets behind the green of the distant mountains. Those who understand this return home to sit in peace. Do not—
A man of realization who had drifted through the winds and dust of the mundane world. A monk asked, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return?
The Master replied, "Beneath the three rafters, before the seven-foot mat. On the ninth day of the winter month in the *jisi* year of the Kangxi era, the Master manifested a slight illness.
On the night of the thirteenth, he gathered his disciples, finished his final instructions, and passed away while sitting upright. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa.
To the right of Fengshan, his worldly age was sixty-one and his monastic seniority forty (his spiritual successor was Lingji Guan).
Chan Master Xiangfeng Dazhan Yi of Huzhou was a native of Jiahe. Having studied early on, thirty days were counted as a "great month" and twenty-nine as a "small month.
As days passed and months came, in an instant his hair turned white; he urgently needed to break through Zhaozhou’s barrier. Everyone—!
Looking south, one sees the Northern Dipper. What is Zhaozhou’s Barrier? [He] struck his staff and said: "Study! Addressing the assembly:
Studying Chan and learning the Way is beyond all deliberation. In daily life, principle and phenomena manifest at every turn. One must completely cut off both form and sound, sitting them both still.
"Generally speaking, all names and holy titles are merely empty fabrications. (He lets out a shout. A monk asked, "What is one's original face before one's parents were born?
The Master said, "Striking the void to extract the marrow. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Digging into the earth to seek the heavens.
The monk asked, "What is 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'? The Master said, "Yesterday the cold plum blossomed. The monk asked, "Where does the One return?"
At the dwelling, the Master said: "This morning auspicious snow is falling" (Lingji Guan’s Successor).

The lay practitioner Weiwei of Longxi, Zangzhou, Fujian, whose courtesy name was Daweng, entered military service at the age of twenty. He was granted the rank of Second Class Vice Commander for his merit.
Although the imperial court bestowed generous favors upon him, the scholar did not consider this an honor; his ambition was to aspire to the Lineage of the Patriarchs. He went to consult Yang...

Fen Guan instructed him to contemplate the character "wu" (no). After a long time, he made no progress. By chance, he encountered his dharma-brother Xitang, who cited the verse: "The Great Peace was originally settled by the General; it begins with a word.

At these words, he captured Zhaozhou’s defeat and attained sudden, unimpeded realization. He presented a verse, saying: "In studying the Way, there is no other principle; when the mind is absent, it is immediately vast and open.
Lofty and great is this sovereign freedom—apart from this, there is no other Chan. Fen Guan said: [Note: The text provided ends abruptly after Fen Guan's name, suggesting the narrative may continue.]
"A single phrase encompasses the eighty thousand gates of Dharma. Do you understand? The Layman said, "I have no mind at all;
what use have I for any dharmas? Guanyou said, "Is a drop of water the great ocean? The Layman said, "I can swallow it all in one gulp.

Guanyou asked, "Do you still recognize Master Pang? The Layman bowed. Guanyou smiled. When Guanyou was about to pass away, the Layman went into the mountains to inquire after his health. Guanyou seized him and held him fast.

[Zhaozhou] said, "Tell me, where is the mountain monk? The layman replied, "Covering heaven and covering earth. Guanzhi presented him with a white prayer bead and said, "In the past you were Layman Lu;
today you are Layman Wei. The layman said, "You have come again to defile me. Guanzhi said, "Keep this clearly in mind.
The layman composed the *Xuedao pian* (Chapter on Studying the Way), which contains a verse on dull faculties: "Realize the unmoving wisdom of non-arising, and rest."
He boasted that his verbal arrows were sharp, yet he allowed others to laugh at him for being of dull faculties.
He said, "My Way is the clear and manifest primary principle" (Lingji Guan’s successor).
This Dharma companion, Xitang, was a man from Min who attended Guan for thirty years without wavering in thought; he thoroughly penetrated to the very bottom of the source of the Dharma.

The Mind-Seal was transmitted. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'three pounds of hemp'? The Master said, "Grasp the meaning at the tip of the hook; do not mistake it for the fixed mark on the scale.

He offered this verse on the saying "The Mind-Moon is solitary and full": "The light does not illuminate the object, nor does the object exist; When both light and object are forgotten, all traces are severed.
When the rain has passed and one lifts their head from the thatched hall, The distant mountains remain as ever, layer upon layer of blue. (Lingji)
[The Record of] Chan Master Lintu Juyi of Shizilin in Hengtang, Hangzhou (Successor of Guanzhi). He was the son of the Liu family of Renhe. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Shigong drawing his bow merely wastes the strength of his wrists; Heshan beating the drum needlessly tires his arms until they ache. Snow—
Feng rolling the ball ruins the children of others' families; Daowu dancing with his ritual tablet—truly, habitual tendencies are difficult to eliminate.
Suddenly, if there were a brilliant monk who came forth and asked, "What about Shilin? one should simply say to him: [The lion's roar].
Having moved the pitcher away to buy village wine, he put on his robes and acted as the host. He gave a shout. A monk asked, "The myriad dharmas return to the One;
where does the One return? The Master said, "A lantern hangs upon the wall. The monk said, "I do not understand.
The Master struck him and said, "Who says you do not understand? (Lingyue was an ancient successor).
Chan Master Duiyao Jian of Chongqing, of the Zhao clan of Renhe, succeeded to the seat at Wulin Zhizhi. Ascending the hall, he said:
"If you wish to inquire about Direct Pointing Chan, there is nothing to do but sleep late in the day. Without venturing out into the city markets, one avoids being resented by the world.

I neither cite the present nor discuss the past, nor do I employ the mutual application of staff and shout. When idle, with sufficient rice and sufficient congee, one simply lets thirst run its course."

"Drinking when hungry and eating when famished; only when one knows where to land does one realize that all flavors are complete. After a long silence, he looked left and right and said: "Investigate! Ascending the hall, the Master raised up the words of Chan Master Xu:

"A golden cast iron K'un-lun; pushed out before people, fearing to be seen or heard. The four sevens and two threes gasp in shock; they bury their heads and flee eastward, running westward. The Master said: [The Master then continued: "When one drinks hunger and eats starvation, only then does one know where to find rest; only then does one realize that the hundred flavors are all present. After a long while, he looked to his left and right and said:

'Investigate! [He then ascended the hall and cited Chan Master Xu’s verse: "A golden cast iron K'un-lun; pushed out before people, fearing to be seen or heard. The four sevens and two threes gasp in shock; they bury their heads and flee eastward, running westward. The Master said:
The Old Man of Suiryak did not begrudge his family treasures; he scattered them like a wolf in the wind. I, this mountain monk, am not so:
when the stone tiger gives birth to a jade Qilin, it flees before the wind beyond all sight or hearing. Neither the Four Sages nor the Six Realms can fathom it;
one may wander freely through both heaven and hell. (Lingyue Gu-si)
Mida Duobai Lin Chan Master was the son of the Lu family of Shangyang in Yunjian. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Red and white peach and plum paths;
green and yellow vegetable and wheat fields. With a single cup, let us drink together for a while—this would put even Jin’s Tao Qian to shame.
But tell me, when Minister Bi and Scholar Li arrive, what then? Even if there is nothing that can be said, one cannot help but let saliva flow from the mouth."
Addressing the assembly, he brought up the story of the "Chezhou Cloth Coat" and offered this verse: The yellow warbler’s shuttle weaves the brocade of the Green Emperor;
The Mother of Transformation relies on the swallow to cut the pattern. Willow threads and pine needles are sewn so tightly, That Zhaozhou has stitched his way out through the inner chamber.
He then raised the karmic connection of Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms and offered this verse: Wandering the rivers and lakes for several decades, I am ashamed of my own [lack of realization].

Seeking a fief with one’s own hands; returning to the forest, one laments the affairs of spring. Grasping the sword, one vainly strikes it, grieving for one’s white hair (Lingyue was an ancient successor).
Chan Master Ouyang Hui of Zhiguo in Hangzhou was the son of the Xu family of Shanyin. Before he had even reached the age of nine, he attained realization of the Three Vehicles.
He petitioned his parents to seek ordination and subsequently entered the monastic life under Master Lingtai of Zhiguo. His parents, too—
He immediately made his own home a place for ascetic cultivation. Among the Brahmans today, there is one named Jiqing’an (Caiqing Hermitage), which was the master’s birthplace.

At twenty-one years of age, he went to the Elder Jin-su Mi to receive the precepts. Later, he studied under Chongqing Gu; through a single word, they reached a secret accord, and he was granted formal certification.
The master further said, "The station of Zhilu in the Eastern Sea awaits you to propagate the practice. Subsequently, [the master] took pity on those who had strayed into peripheral currents.

He was unconventional. He did not concern himself with the gateways of worldly affairs, nor water or fire; he did not lead a community, nor did he ascend the hall, nor appoint administrative officials.
With staff and traveling hat, he wandered freely among mountains and rivers. In the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, he restored Zhiguo Temple and completed the construction of a Buddha statue.
Not long after, he manifested a slight illness. When his disciples came forward to offer medicine, the Master declined them, saying, "The retribution body is not ill; what need is there for this?"

"How much more so now that the temple’s construction is complete? I shall not remain. On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of the Jiyou year of the Kangxi era, he requested a brush and wrote this verse:
"The face of the sun, the face of the moon; The void, a flash of lightning. For sixty-six years, this has been my discourse;
Go ask the lanterns and the Buddha hall! Thereupon, he passed into stillness. His stupa was enshrined to the west of Zhiguo (at Lingyue Gusi).
Chan Master Xuechan of Qingu Valley at Mount Nanyue ascended the hall and said: "The ancient mirror is suspended on high, illuminating the earth and shining upon heaven.
The Mohe sword is held crosswise; there is no place for anything to settle. Ten thousand phenomena are realized before one's eyes; all worldly mechanisms are cut off in this very moment.
A single phrase is all-pervasive, completely transcending the Dharma-realm. Within the field of original enlightenment, there is nothing remaining. How extraordinary! Deshan was right here."
Ji. The staff and shouts fly back and forth; swift as a blazing flame passing through the wind, ten thousand miles of white clouds. (Lingyue Gu-si) strikes his staff once.
Chan Master Xue Weitao of Fubao Monastery in Chuzhou, a descendant of the Yu clan, ascended the seat. "Danxia burned the wooden Buddha; Cuiwei made offerings to the Arhats.
The wealthy display their wealth; the poor calculate their poverty. Fundamentally, this is one and the same way of holding up the Dharma."
For what reason does he manifest these two aspects? If one reaches the gate of Fubǔ, not even a single pinch is required.

Why? When the golden needle is raised, there is no turning back; it embroiders the fine plumage of the mandarin ducks. In the autumn of the Renxu year of the Kangxi era, he manifested a slight illness.
He ordered craftsmen to construct his coffin and gave instructions for his funeral affairs. He wrote the verse for sealing the coffin, which begins: "The four quarters of space are one..."
A flake of snow: it falls as drenching rain and drizzling sleet without ceasing. Yet now, the entire great earth beholds nothing at all. I dare ask you all: have you penetrated this or not?
*Ei!* It is precisely this that pierces through empty space. This day is the Mid-Autumn Festival. It reached midnight.
Sitting upright, he passed away (Lingyue Gu-si).
Chan Master Wozhan Caru of Gaoyang addressed the assembly: "Flowers cluster thickly, the grass grows lush; The nature of phenomena has never undergone change.
Today I shall once again annotate and break through this for you: In the pond’s springtime, the willows hold the mist. (Lingyue Gu-si)
When Master Nanchuan Hai of Xiangyuan Tongna, a descendant of the Chen clan of Qingpu, ascended the hall, he said: "Before signs have yet manifested, the full brilliance is already revealed.
Heaven and earth are cut off; not even a hair's breadth is established. There is no front or back throughout past and present;
it has never been hidden anywhere in the world. At such a time as this, tell me: where is the 'True Person of No Station'? He then looked toward his left.

The Master said: "A west wind blows against my face; my eyebrows both stand erect. Ascending the seat, he said: "After the rain, the mountain colors are emerald; with gentle winds, the birds' nature grows wild.
Heaven and Earth allow you to be idle, yet fame and profit drive them to be busy. Even this very mind is not yet it."
Without a Buddha, do not vainly assume the burden. Directly beneath, there is no turning away or evasion; whether moving vertically or horizontally, nothing is concealed.

If you thoroughly understand this, the seas will be calm and the rivers clear, the state settled and the nation at peace. Should it not yet be so, do not take offense at this mountain monk for lancing a sore on healthy flesh.
(With his staff, he drove them all away at once. [This was the successor of Liyan.]
Chan Master Wuyi of Zixiao, Xinghua, Fujian, ascended the hall and said: "The treasury of the true Dharma eye is a broken sand bowl;
spoken from the mouth as it comes, it darkens the seas and mountains. Truly, at this one moment, sweat breaks out from one's own skin; why need one deliberately stir up wind and clouds?"
[The Master] struck his staff and descended from the seat (Qianfeng established the succession).
Compiled by the monk (Chao Yong),
Abbot of Shenggan Chan Temple in the Capital, for the *Wudeng Quanshu*, Volume Ninety-Two.
Verified and presented for the Rinzai School by the Abbot (Subject Monk) Chōkai of Kyoto’s Kokegwan-ji Temple.
The Record of the Thirty-sixth Generation of Nanyue:
Chan Master Jue of Qiantang Jiedai. Master Jue ascended the hall and said:

"From the time I crossed the Wulong Bridge on a single oar from Bantang, I picked up along the way thirty-six thousand *qǐng* of land and a large silver basin. There were seven... [text fragment ends].

Twelve blue lotuses were within; today, they are presented on the platter. I bring them forth for the assembly, feeling ashamed that I lack local offerings, yet borrowing these as a token of my personal courtesy.
It does not matter that I am disposing of Suzhou’s滞货 (stale goods) in Hangzhou.

Setting down his hands, he said: "Do not take offense at my meager hospitality. I pray you all, take care of yourselves. Among the assembly, if there is anyone who asks, "How can the Master [do this]?"
Using official temple property as a personal gift—when the new abbot spoke thus to him, the other replied, "Yes, yes. It cannot be used as a gift for you; it can only serve to delight oneself.
Ascending the hall for the opening of the furnace: In years past, when I was at another monastery, monks who admired the Way came from afar, drawn by my reputation.
Once they had entered the great forge of my furnace and been melted down, there was no distinction made between gold, silver, copper, iron, or tin. [The resulting vessels were] jars...
Belt buckles, bracelets, and hairpins each form their own distinct vessels.

Today, as we open the furnace here at Hushu, those who come from Suzhou, Songjiang, Changzhou, or Zhenjiang have not yet passed through the Beixin Pass; how could they know the customs of our reception?
Those who come from Jinhua, Quanzhou, Yanzhou, or Shaoxing cannot see our monastery flagpole across the river; how then could they know the realm of our wondrous practice? Do not—
I wonder why crows fly and flies swarm from all directions; it is solely because this local Prajñā is like a great mass of fire.
To approach it is to have one’s face scorched by its flames. Thus it is said: "The *jiaoming* insect can alight anywhere, yet alone it cannot alight upon the crest of a flame.
Nevertheless, this mountain monk takes the entire earth as a single furnace and the myriad phenomena of the universe as...

Using firewood for charcoal, using the wind as a bellows, using the sun as fire, and using the two characters "birth" and "death" as the tongs and hammer for smelting—whether the world is one foot wide and the furnace is one foot wide, or the world is ten feet wide and the furnace is ten feet wide—I ask you:
where will you seek refuge? He let out a shout and said: "It is all right here!"

While the Master was entering the room for his next session, it was the turn of Cangya. Cangya instructed a young attendant to enter the abbot’s quarters carrying a sword and present it to the Master, saying, "Cangya has arrived.
The attendant did exactly as he was told. The Master called out, "Attendant Shen! (or "Stretch!").
He pointed at the table. The boy immediately extended his finger. The Master raised his knife and cut it off. The boy cried out and fled.
Later, when the Master entered the hall, he struck his knife against his staff to make a sound and said to the assembly, "This is the Elder Old Cangya."
[The Master] sent Da Cheng to enter the room [of the abbot]. He said, "How will you all explain this? To speak it is one blow of the blade;
not to speak it is also one blow of the blade. Yaya stepped forward from the assembly. The Master raised his blade and said, "You have come! Yaya made a gesture of fear and returned to his place.
The Master said, "Cangyaya is afraid of death and has shrunk away. Is there anyone who is not afraid of death? Come forth!"
"Ma! The assembly was speechless. Shanyue addressed the assembly, saying, "Though a sharp blade is fast, it does not slay the innocent.
The Master then threw down the knife and called out to Cangya, "Come, come! Old in years and at ease in heart, with no external affairs;
even a seat of hempen grass will accommodate one's body. Why do you still wish to travel on foot to sell this blade? Cangya replied, "I also want the Master [to buy it]."
"Recognized," the Master said. "I have recognized your dull-witted goods. He then returned to his quarters. On the day before the eve of the year’s end, he addressed the assembly:
"If we speak of each family's gate and each household's door, one should not concern oneself with idle affairs, nor should one speak of the faults of others.
Why is this? Lately, monks from all quarters have been diligent in their studies, practicing day and night, three times by day and three times by night."

After a year of toil and hardship, three days of leave are granted. Yet the old man of the hall feigns deafness and dumbness, allowing everyone to display their myriad follies and clumsy antics at will:
some sing, some dance; some practice boxing, some wield short clubs;
some paint their faces with theatrical makeup to perform plays, while others dress as Arhats subduing demons. Thus it goes, until they have grown truly old and decrepit.
This is the trickery of children. Like the blind leading the blind, they occupy the four corners and strike their eyes until they become stubbornly sightless.
They imagine that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated since beginningless time can never be shaken off or suppressed;
thus, they want to utterly extinguish them once and for all and confess everything with total abandon. Only then do they claim to be pure. Little do they realize that this is merely one more...
Seize upon it with a fresh turn of mind. Reflect upon it once, and it becomes matured once more; within the *ālayavijñāna*, it will never be forgotten for kalpas on end.
It is better to let go and set it down; naturally, one will be at peace and settled. Here, where I receive guests, I am in the midst of a village settlement.
No leave shall be granted. Tomorrow is the eve of the year’s end. We request that Head Seat Wei preside over the small discourse (*xiaocan*).

Following the discourse, during tea, we permit you all to "take up the root and continue the branches. If you fail to maintain this continuity, everyone will laugh; yet even such laughter is already a form of negligence.
Therefore, the ancients used the matter of life and death as a metaphor for the "thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month," when all corners and patterns are finally resolved.
Day. For those who have not yet reached home, white clouds stretch for ten thousand *li*; where is one's native land? Time does not wait for the moon; what joy can there be? It is said:
"Gazing west toward the Jade Gate, my heart is nearly broken; how much more so when tomorrow is the New Year. The Master descended from the hall.
Seeing a wooden basin placed upon a meditation seat to catch the dripping water, he called to the assembly, saying: "You all..."
People in general do not equal this Wooden Seat (Muzang). Sitting upon his meditation mat, he is settled as soon as he lets go.

He does not contemplate the *huatou*, nor does he wander in idle thoughts, nor does he engage in discursive thinking; he is neither dull nor distracted. Thus, I need not trouble myself to patrol the incense with effort.
[The Master] then struck the wooden basin once with the incense board and said: "This lacquer bucket! You have still not spoken."
[The Master] finished speaking and then dozed off. The entire assembly remained solemn as he ascended the hall. He raised the following case: Xuefeng Zhan said, "All dharmas are without distinction.
Yunmen’s 'moldy bread,' Zhaozhou’s 'tea,' the jade flute blown atop the Yellow Crane Tower—'In the fifth month, plum blossoms fall over the river city.
I am ashamed before Elder Fu of Taiyuan: at the fifth watch, the drums and horns sound; at daybreak, the lute is played."
Xuejiao said: "All dharmas are without difference. The magpie faces the crow; at the birth-platform they scramble for food, striking out in a chaotic tangle like hemp fibers.
An appointment was made but he did not come until past midnight; idly tapping the chess pieces, the lamp-flower fell. How shameful!
The Baoshu Pagoda by West Lake, where the six bridges see the evening sun slant through the mist and rain. The Master said: "All dharmas are without difference. Spinning..."
"Spinning silk and weaving ramie, shaking cotton; children who do not yet understand the toil of plowing and weaving, yet by the shade of the mulberry trees they learn to plant melons.
How shameful, Old Wang the Elder of the Eastern Village! When the peach blossoms bloom and the spring waters rise, she gathers fish and shrimp from beneath the hearth. She patted her knee and said:
The more one sings, the higher the pitch; the fewer those who can join in harmony (a successor of the "Great White Snow").
Chan Master Xue of Stone Buddha Bridge at Linji ascended the hall, held up his whisk, and said: "Within this, it is just so."
Accept it directly; there is but a slight difference. If you wish to hesitate further, the sword has long since departed.
Whenever I see those who come to inquire about the Buddha-dharma, they fail to realize that the stone Buddha has never been bound by the Buddha-dharma to anyone.
This is true not only for the stone Buddha, but even for the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods of time—it is likewise so. Why? Because as soon as there is speech, it is all...
No Real Meaning. Ascending the hall, he struck his staff and said: "Do you understand? This mountain monk beats the drum;

there is no other dharma to deliberate upon, yet one thing must be announced to the assembly gathered here: the commencement of the retreat for universal salvation. All of you, practice walking meditation."
Where shall one set foot? At my monastery, Pudu Changzhu, there is a small patch of pure white ground that no one may tread upon.
Should anyone tread upon this small patch of pure white ground, they commit a fundamental *pārājika* offense.
He lowered his staff and descended from the seat to enter the hall. After the Rector had finished striking the gavel, the Master called to the assembly, saying:
"As for the primary principle, the Rector has already explained it to you all. He then descended from the seat. (Tai Bai Xueci)
Chan Master Xianshuai of Ruinding ascends the hall: "In an old monastery, a new elder: Night after night he trims the dying lamp;
Day after day he clears away the wild weeds. Do not disdain the stubbornness of the stone; With diligence, sweep and sprinkle it often. Sip the plain soup of wood-apple with quietude."
Guarding the treasure within one’s robes, yet too lazy to practice the Buddha-Dharma; when human affairs are just to one’s liking, one immediately attends to the old monasteries.
The bells and drums resound loudly at dawn and dusk. Striking the empty air with his staff, he calls to the assembly, saying:
"Tell me, amidst this loud resonance of the morning and evening bells and drums, what do you hear? He plants his staff in the ground and says: "Speak! Speak! Speak!"
Take care. Descend from the seat. Small-scale Sermon. A monk asked, "Having laid down the butcher's knife, who is counted among the thousand Buddhas?
The Master said, "Lay down the butcher's knife and then ask. The monk said, "In that case, one has transcended both Buddha and Patriarch.
The Master said, "I only fear it is not jade. The monk gave a shout. The Master also shouted. The monk was speechless. The Master said, "How pitiful! He then said, "The great earth..."
The fire pit: majestic and bare, revealed alone. Take a single step and you tread upon the path beyond birth and death. It is simply that one has lost one’s head and refuses to walk;
cast down the butcher’s blade and you are numbered among the thousand Buddhas. Looking left and right, he said: "Behold it! Look up to it! To worship emptiness is to fall into subject and object.
If you cling to even a hair’s breadth, you will have failed. In a single thought-moment is ten thousand years; one transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs. Planting millet does not produce beans;
a sweet melon is sweet from stem to tip, and a bitter gourd is bitter from root to blossom. How pitiful!
A clay figure wearing tattered diamond armor—cut directly to the source, with no room for evasion. Yunmen’s “Universal” and Xuansha’s “Tiger”—do not imitate Heshan’s drum-beating.
The drum was broken. [The Master] threw down his staff and descended from the seat. At the place where a monk was selecting vegetables, the Master said, "Do not take the good ones.
The monk threw a single stalk before the Master. The Master said, "Why do you not say, 'That one stalk is not the good one'?

While the Master was traveling at Yanzi Ji, a monk asked, "Where have you come from, Master? The Master raised his foot to show him. The monk asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going there."
The Master strode up the steps. While the Master and a monk were lifting a wooden beam, the Master asked, "Which end is lighter?

This end or that end? The monk replied, "That end is lighter. The Master set it down and said, "This end is lighter. That end is lighter. The monk said, "Master, you have set it down; why speak of lightness and heaviness?
The Master asked, "Are you trying to imitate me by setting it down as well? Just as the monk was about to set it down, the Master struck him.
Lifting it up, he said: "It cannot be put down; I shall carry it away for you" (Jianmen Qiansi).
Chan Master Chishan Song of Qingliang in Jinling, whose secular surname was Jin of Dantu, was moistened by the Dharma.

On the hundredth day after the passing of Qian of Qingliang, while holding incense, he said: "This master displayed his nature within the Hall of Transcendence; he exhausted his potential beneath the solitary mulberry drum."
The source benefits the Mara-lord and acts as an enemy to the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it takes the unsurpassed vehicle of the Dharma and tosses it about, overturning and upending it.
It has rendered the Great Meaning of the West a chaotic mess, peerless and incomparable. This "Stone City Manifesto" has been in circulation for twenty-two years.
Throughout the entire realm, clouds move and rain falls; at a single moment, a thousand streams bury their heads. Within the borders of the nation, the grass withers and people die.

Ascending the hall, he took up his staff, struck the ground once, and said: "Among these, there is a man; yet there is nothing new."
It is neither ancient nor new; it does not wither with the four seasons, nor does it shift with the cold and heat. It governs all living beings and encompasses the myriad existences.
When the harmonious breath pervades the times, villages sing and communities dance. Does the great assembly recognize this person?
Amidst the accumulated kitchens and heaps of things, there is much spirit and vigor; blending light with the world, he delights in non-action (Duguang Jingsi).
Chan Master Fiyulin of Ezhou ascended the hall: "The doors and windows are flung wide open; ten thousand miles of space are not hung with a single cloud. The pagoda-pole is raised up;
fragrance wafts through the world upon the chrysanthemum blossoms. With a single fist, the Yellow Crane Tower is toppled; a thousand mechanisms are severed at once."
Kicking over Parrot Island—eight-sided and translucent. Letting loose the iron ox of Shanzhou, he bites to death the great elephant of Jiazhou.
To sing such a song is still to fall into the present age. How can one speak a phrase that transcends the ordinary? (He lets out a shout. Entering the hall:
Untying the bell from the neck of a fierce tiger requires a master hand; seizing the pearl from beneath the brow of a blue dragon must...
"This is a remarkable person. Truly there is such a person as this. One who acts and takes up such matters—does such a one actually exist among the assembly?
After a long silence, he said: "Since the lamp was divided from Shaoshi, until the present day, news has been rare. Ascending the hall, he said:
"If you were to rely on the true command, it would cause all Buddhas and patriarchs to [be reduced to] nothingness. If you wish to speak of true reality, do not look for it here."
[Blank] struck his knee with his hand and said: "To cry until one's blood flows is of no use;
it is better to seal one's mouth and pass through the remainder of spring" (Duguang, Jingsi).

Liusi Wen Shi Chanshi was the son of the Chen family of Cixi. While passing through the Guanxiang Lane in Hangzhou, he was moved by the sight of a woman being subjected to the punishment of slow slicing. He went to Liusi to seek tonsure and ordination, where he investigated the koan: "When one breath does not come back. Later, while traveling by boat at Qianqing, he fell into the water and attained realization. When Liusi asked him, "I heard you had an awakening when you fell into the water," he replied: [He then spoke a verse: "Ten thousand miles away, I have come; The boat has already reached the shore. If you ask me about the meaning, I have no words to speak. Liusi said, "This is indeed the meaning of 'one breath not coming back. He then bestowed upon him the dharma name Wen Shi. Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Tiantong, where he served as the head monk under Master Daoyuan.

One day, Daoyuan asked him, "What is the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West? Wen Shi replied, "A dog has no Buddha-nature. Daoyuan struck him and said, "This is merely the meaning of 'a dog has no Buddha-nature'; what is the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West? Wen Shi remained silent. Daoyuan struck him again and said, "You are like a wooden man reciting a sutra. Wen Shi bowed and withdrew. Daoyuan then praised him, saying, "This fellow has finally arrived. He subsequently became the abbot of the Lingfeng Monastery in Wuzhou. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away at the age of seventy-four. His remains were interred on Mount Tiantong. He was posthumously titled Chanshi Xingwu. His dharma heirs included the Chan masters Zhenxie Qingliao, Foyan Qingyuan, and others. His recorded sayings circulated widely throughout the world. His stupa was named "Jingzhuang. The stele inscription was written by the Grand Councilor of State, Zhang Shangying. The epitaph was composed by the Vice Director of the Imperial Library, Huang Tingjian.

The calligraphy was executed by the Vice Director of the Imperial Library, Li Gang. The temple was named "Xingwu Chan Temple. It is located within the Lingfeng Monastery in Wuzhou. It is said that when Wen Shi first visited Liusi, he had already been practicing for twenty years. He was a man of great virtue who deeply loved the Way. Whenever he encountered a person of superior character, he would treat them with utmost respect. He never sought fame or profit, and his conduct was always upright and pure. He was truly a rare and extraordinary person. His disciples numbered over a thousand. His teachings were vast and profound, and his influence extended far and wide. He was truly a great master of the Chan lineage. His legacy continues to inspire practitioners to this day.
"If one's single breath does not return, where will one find a place to settle and establish one's life?

The Master said, "With a hundred thousand strings of cash girding one’s waist, riding a crane up to Yangzhou. Xuefeng said, "There is still this remaining. The Master said, "But you, Monk, are doubting me.
Xuefeng nodded his head. Xuefeng asked, "Now, tell me right now: what is the 'right-now' phrase? What is the 'right-now' phrase?"
The Master said: "Lotus leaves join the sky in emerald green; willow branches brush the earth in azure. [The student] said: "Master, do not point to external objects for people. The Master said:
"This mountain monk has a gap between his front teeth; my words do not concern the wind. A Verse on the "Three Nots":
"Not mind, not Buddha, not things. The heavens are high and the earth is thick. Crows are black and cranes are white. Zhang San does not recognize bamboo."
"Strainer. (This makes East Village Old Man Li laugh; *Lú Zhōu shěng sì*).
Chan Master Xuédìng Yù of Bǎojiè on Yáng Hú in Wèngjiā was the son of the Yè family of the district.

Initially, he visited Dàméi Chì, with whom he attained a profound resonance like a needle meeting its eye. Later, he went to see Liusì Shěng at Hǒushān. Shěng asked: "A three-legged donkey is playing..."
[The Master] walked on tiptoe. "How would you say it? The Master performed a dance and went out; [the monk] was suddenly enlightened.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Chuitai. The Master said, "Do you hear Prince Jin blowing the sheng? He replied, "I do. The Master said, "..."
"What tune is this? [The monk] replied, "It is not *Manjianghong*; it must be *Xinglunan*. The Master cocked his ear as if listening.
The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "Once again, it has been blown by the wind into another tune" (Lu Zhou sheng si).
Chan Master Nan’an Ke-xue Can was a native of Nan’an in Jiangxi. He went to study under Foyan Rong, who said to him, “Since you have come from so far away, I grant you thirty blows.
From that time on, the Master’s state of doubt (yiqing) flared up intensely. After some time, he attained realization upon hearing the sound of the wooden board.
Just as Foyan was passing by the hall, the Master went forward to greet him with a bow and said, “I received the Master’s gift of the blows; now I know their sting. [The Master] made a sound.
Before he had finished speaking, Yunrong struck him. The Master said, "In that case, you are adding an awl to a sore spot. Yunrong asked, "Who is it that knows pain and itch?
The Master bowed and said, "Your kindness is too great to be repaid. Yunrong praised him highly. The following year, he remained there with his staff while Yunrong went to visit Zhoushan.
He presented a verse on the Woman Emerging from Samādhi, saying: "You call it marvelous; I say it is strange. Striking the head of a stone man with a staff—"
*Pō pō lùn shí shì* (Lú Zhōu Shěngsì).
*Wǔ dēng quán shū*, Volume 92; Supplement to Volume 92.
Recorded by the thirty-sixth generation descendant of the Linji lineage under Mount Nanyue, Chan Master Xiangyan Gui of Puming Temple in Jiaxing, upon ascending the hall:
"In the heavens, the moon is perfectly full; in the human world, the lamp is perfectly bright."
Excellent! The lamp and the moon shine together; the four crossroads are bustling and vast. In my house is a single lamp of the Patriarchs;
its radiance pervades the world and endures for long. Not only does it unfold its fragrance on the first night of the New Year, but one must see that it is present at all times.
Lying on the official streets, drinking the official wine—one who understands this knows that three threes are originally nine. Unbinding the cloth bag, one moves freely in all directions. Flowers...
The willows by the streets and the paths reveal the family’s shame; thus he addresses the assembly. He cites the conclusion of Mañjuśrī’s three summer retreats. The Master said:

"If one looks from the perspective of principle (*li*), Kāśyapa is like one who plucks at fixed strings while playing the lute. If one looks from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), Mañjuśrī has no sense of restraint whatsoever.
Had Puming been present at that time, he would have employed a transformative skillful means to harmonize both phenomenon and principle, even if it were Śākyamuni himself..."
"Ka-lao-tzu (Kālacitta), you too shall be cast beyond the great trichiliocosm. Addressing the assembly, after concluding the discourse on Xinghua’s beating of the *karmadāna*, the Master said:
"Kebin was much like Su Wu, who upheld his integrity and remained unbowed.

Having endured one instance of neglect and coldness, he has left behind a fragrance that endures for a thousand years. Addressing the assembly, after concluding the discourse on Lingyun’s seeing the peach blossoms, the Master said:
Lingyun clearly built the plank road; Xuansha secretly crossed at Chen’ang. Although their actions were distinct, their nostrils were exactly the same.
Yuanwu said: "One who possesses the eye that penetrates the barrier can discern where another has not yet reached the end—it is like sucking soup from inside a fried cake.
Addressing the assembly, after concluding the story of Zhaozhou visiting two hermits, the Master said: "The hermit..."
Two fists, as massive as Mount Taihang and Mount Wangwu, towering majestically for a thousand ages—this is Zhaozhou’s function.

Like the Yellow River pouring backward, it adapts to the moment, whether slow or swift. Yuanwu said: "If you can grasp the supreme纲 (gāngzōng) [the fundamental principle], then you will be like the two hermits;
you can thereby distinguish dragons from snakes and separate the monastic from the lay. Do you wish to know where Zhaozhou’s function lies? Old..."
With a heart of profound compassion, he laughed heartily, leaving it to others to speak of his merits or faults (Shiguang Ling Si).
Master Chanyue Zhongming Qianling, a native of the Wang family of Danghu, had known of the matters beyond the mundane since his youth.
He went to Fuan Qian to receive the tonsure and was instructed to engage in *chan* (meditation). Weeping in secret, he said: "The Great Matter has not yet been clarified; with a single breath..."
Thinking, "If I do not come, what can be done? he investigated day and night without untying his sash. He went to visit Longhua Zongji and subsequently paid respects to Zhe Lu Jie.
While reading the records of Wuzu Fayan, he came across the passage: "As for this matter, it is like a thief who, when teaching his son, leads him into a cupboard so that they may escape.
His doubts were suddenly dispelled; he immediately entered the abbot’s quarters and cried out for justice. Jie struck him repeatedly with his staff.
He went out and presented a verse, saying: "For sixteen years I have sought the horse-riders; each time we met, I was filled with doubt. Today I have seen through the thief’s lair;
mountain flowers bloom everywhere along the stream. Xuedou laughed and nodded his head. The Master covered his ears and departed.
He then went to study under Jin-su Sheng. One day, Sheng asked the assembly: "Heaven and earth share the same root; the myriad things are one..."
[The Master] said, "Body. The mountain monk [Dongshan] replied, "Last night my ribs ached; why do you people not ache? The Master said, "Do not add a handle to a bowl that does not need one.
[Sheng] raised his staff. The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Finally, he went to the quarters of Ling of Puming.

Upon entering the room, Ling asked, "Regarding the saying, 'A phrase with no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree,' what is its meaning? The Master gave a shout. Ling said, "The tree has fallen."
The wisteria is withered; where does the verse return? The Master spreads his two hands. Again he asked: "The World-Honored One did not speak what is spoken; Kāśyapa did not hear what is heard.
Tell me, was there still any Buddha-dharma in between? The Master said: "The pillar testifies. Thereupon, he presented this verse:
"The mechanism is revealed before the tongue has moved; Kāśyapa’s lack of hearing has already exposed the thief. If you can understand this point..."
Regarding the meaning of the message: "The plum branches have put forth blossoms, some short and some long. Ling said, "I grant you thirty blows. The Master then departed.
Having served him for a long time, he finally received his seal of approval (*inka*). Thereafter, he lived in deep seclusion, wishing no longer to involve himself in the world of men;
it is said that twenty years passed as if they were a single day (Shiguan Ling was his successor).
Chan Master Jianning Chong’an Wuyi Shouzong was the son of the Lu family of Zhangpu. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
When he was over twenty years old, he paid his respects to Xinyi Miyu at Nanshan to receive the tonsure. He traveled extensively to study under the great masters of Jing Shan and Gunan.
Later, he received the seal of certification from Yuanzhi of Jingu. He served his mother with the utmost filial piety. When the world fell into chaos, he built a thatched hut at Wuyi.
Yiyang raised his mother and did not step outside the mountain for over thirty years. A monk asked him, "One who has attained great penetration is fundamentally liberated from birth and death;
why then is your life-root (*mìnggēn*) not severed? The Master said, "Snowflakes fly upon the flames of a red furnace.
The monk asked, "The public cases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs all share a single principle; why then is there clarity and lack of clarity? The Master said, "The heavens are high."
The eastern land slopes toward the northwest. [A monk] said, "One who practices great cultivation should follow the conduct of the Buddha. For what reason, then, do you not observe the *vinaya*?

The Master said, "If one does not enter the startling waves, it is difficult to encounter a fish that suits one's heart. [The monk] said, "When the bright sun is in the sky, there is nowhere it does not illuminate."
"Why is it that it is obscured by a single cloud? The Master said, "Even the clear blue sky must receive a blow of the staff.
[The monk] said, "Every person has a shadow that never leaves them for a single step; why is it that they cannot realize it? The Master said, "It is precisely because it is too close.
[The monk] said, "The entire earth is a pit of fire; what samādhi can one attain so as not to be burned? The Master said, "I, this mountain monk, dwell here in Wuyi."
It has already been nearly thirty autumns (according to Bai Chi Yuan’s successor).
Dharma Master Fagong of Yongjia was the son of Wang of Gutian. In his youth, he followed his father in farming and wood-gathering.

After his father passed away, he witnessed the cremation and felt a profound sense of spiritual resonance upon seeing the white bones. He then entered the monastic order at Jile Temple. Later, when Lianyun Cheng returned to Min, Fagong saw him for the first time.

He took refuge in the mind and applied himself with diligence to investigation. Later, hearing that Yuanzai of Jinsu was opening the Dharma hall at Baishan, he went there and served as the fire attendant.
While tending the fire, he suddenly heard Yuanzai’s thunderous voice say, "You are the fire attendant! At that moment, it was as if he had been awakened from a dream;
he immediately realized the point where the "clouds and mists" staff fell. Subsequently, he became the abbot and propagated the Dharma. This is the Master.

He visited [Fuzheng] again for an audience. Throughout Yuan’s travels among famous monasteries, the Master never parted from him, carrying his bowl and staff. Although he repeatedly suffered beatings and lashes, his faith and acceptance grew ever firmer.
At that time, Fuyan Yong was residing at Mount Shuangjing; Cheng took the Master with him to pay his respects. When Cheng took his leave to return home, Yong kept the Master behind.

He served as the temple steward (*zhai sui*) for three years, during which they attained a profound mutual resonance through their spiritual interactions. Observing that the worldly conditions of his life were nearing their end, Cheng urged the Master to go south.
He returned and took charge of the storehouse. That winter, Cheng encountered a disaster. After his cremation, [the Master] took what was left behind and went to Fuyan to present it to Rong.
Rong nodded in approval. He subsequently remained as the *zhisui* (yearly steward), and later remained as the storekeeper.

Having spent six summer retreats there, he took leave to return home and was appointed to lead Lianyun, followed by a succession of residences at Fatong. He again served at several monasteries, including Miyin and Fuchang. Entering the hall, he said: "Jade..."
Gold is naturally yellow; the mandarin duck is naturally short; the crane is naturally long. These are matters that have been perfected from the very beginning;
why use further deliberation? The Tower of Blowing does not lie beyond the green mountains; the Ou Sea has never left the Zhejiang River. —The Hall Discourse for the Opening of the Retreat.

Ever abiding in profound stillness and detachment, the patch-robed monks are scattered and sparse. Although the host persistently requests that I ascend the hall, this mountain monk finds it difficult to decline.
Setting aside broom and dustpan, I grasp the hair of a tortoise and the horns of a hare;
I shall not speak of "this," "that," "who," or "what," but simply hold up the single point beyond the ordinary. While the furnace is red-hot, everyone must exert themselves with diligence.
If you should hesitate for even a single thought, you will not escape having your eyebrows singed away. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:
"Beneath Mount Touduo, before the Hall of Mimi, there is no Way to study and no Dharma to transmit. When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps.
Not relying on written words, how could one fall into the trap of verbal explanations? There is only this one point of intimacy: as the great gong resounds, everyone scrambles for it."
The former master once wrote a verse that said: "This mountain monk is sixty-five; there is nothing in his person to worry about.
I shall simply wait for the one of Silent Radiance (*jigō*), and then I will depart for Silent Radiance. He kept this among the pages of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* he was reading.

The following morning, he suddenly said to his attendant Dōshi, "The corner of the hall is about to collapse. Dōshi replied, "Wait until this winter to repair it. The Master said, "It will not last until then."

That evening, a monk from Jiguang Temple requested that the Master perform the cremation rites. The Master smiled and said, "I shall come. When asked who he would take with him, the Master replied, "I shall go alone.
The assembly did not understand his meaning. After his bath, he entered the abbot’s quarters and lay down in the lotus position as usual.
By dawn, he had already passed away while seated. On that same day, the *chīwén* (gargoyle) on the roof ridge of the hall suddenly tilted. The Master was born... [text fragment ends].
He was born in the Renxu year of the Tianqi era and passed away in the Bingyin year of the Kangxi era. His secular age was sixty-five, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was forty-nine.
After the cremation, his teeth, robes, and hairpins remained unburnt; dozens of five-colored, solid relics were recovered.
His disciples built a stupa at the foot of Chuitai Mountain to enshrine them. (Guyan Chengsi)
Master Dongyuan Ji of Mengze Jiyuan Monastery ascended the hall for formal instruction. He cited the teaching of Guoqing: "Yuantong does not open a pharmacy of life-giving medicines;
he sells nothing but dead cat heads. Who knows which one, being free from calculation, will have cold sweat flow over their entire body upon tasting it?
The Master said: "Guoqing wishes to sell his wares with flair; he hurls out a dead cat head, yet it only stirs up trouble."
Mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and gnats pursue the stench and seek out the foul; when will there ever be an end to this? Looking at the assembly, he said: "Tell me, what about Jetavana?
"The pharmacy is open, yet there is nothing else for sale; it sells only a single dose of castor oil pills.
It makes them purge all filth and impurity, so that once the illness has left the entire body, the mind is naturally at peace. Ascending the hall, he said: "Clearly held up before you, yet..."
One must doubt. Directly overturning it, he displays his great capacity; though he speaks to all people, they still do not understand.
How pitiable—that both rows of eyebrows are wasted! Ascending the hall, he said: "A thousand people pushing against a door is not as good as one person pulling the bolt. One person pulling the bolt—"

"A thousand people together attain peace and happiness. Does the great assembly still recognize this person? After a long pause, he gave a shout and descended from his seat for a small discourse (*xiaozan*).
"At the head of Dayu Ridge, he did not catch up; Daoming did not know his original face.
Before the cliff of Shaoshi, he did not stand in the snow; how could the Second Patriarch have attained peace of mind? Therefore it is said: 'If you have not yet found a point of entry...'"

To dwell [in this state], one must encounter the right person; if one does not encounter such a person, it is like the dragon painted by Wu Daozi that has not yet had its eyes opened—it cannot fly or soar.
Is there anyone here now who wishes to have their eyes opened? (Taking up his staff, he struck everyone at once, dispersing them, and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
(From the Ancient Succession of Lingyue)

With earnest devotion, he beats the Heshan drum; clouds follow the dragon, and wind follows the tiger.
What man among us would not be a true hero? His ears are not deaf and his eyes are not blind. Why must he rush about seeking Buddhas and patriarchs? Look!

I see many commoners who mistake the thief for their son and take the servant for their lord, regarding this as the essential point of the mind. This is truly an error.
Meeting. Whether in a word or in silence, there is no engagement. Neither in speech nor in silence, there is likewise no engagement.

[The guest] was at a loss. The Master struck him. A guest came to inquire about the Way. The Master said, "Please be seated. The guest said, "The Dao cannot be left for even a moment;
that which leaves it is not the Dao. At that time, the sound of a donkey braying was heard. The Master said, "This is leaving; this is not leaving. The guest was at a loss.
The Master said, "The root of your affliction lies right here. (Xingkong Zhen’s lineage).
Chan Master Xueqiaolin of the Vairocana [Temple] in Guangling, a native of the Shi clan from Shanyang, addressed the assembly.
He brought up the story of Xiangyan ascending the tree and offered this verse: "Lord Zhou raises arms and banners upon level ground; Goblin faces and godly heads abound in great number.
Suddenly encountering Zhuge Liang looking on with a single glance, A hundred thousand wiles and skills are all consumed. He again addressed the assembly, citing Nanquan’s mowing of the thatch.
The Verse says: Meeting face-to-face, he brandishes a sickle; For you, he points out where it is clear. Disregarding even the official road, He walks only through the weeds.
Addressing the assembly, he cited the story of National Teacher An of Yanguan calling his attendant to bring him the rhinoceros-horn fan.
The Verse says: The waters fill the clear stream, flowers cover the hills; An old fisherman, following his inspiration, drifts in a small boat.
Leaning over the riverbank, he repeatedly casts his bait; Yet he laments that the roaming fish do not take the hook. (Shi’an Fusi)
Chan Master Lue Luo Yuetan Yuan of Jinling asked, "What is the phrase that penetrates to the very bone and marrow?
The Master replied, "Yesterday it snowed; today the weather is cold. A verse on the occasion of a difficult childbirth:
Yangju commits a blunder; the World-Honored One leaks the secret once more. It was indeed the heart of an old woman, yet her cleverness turned out to be clumsy. A verse on Baizhang:
The wild fox said: "Neither obscured nor falling, not clinging to either side—though there is a principle, it is difficult to extend;
who can recognize what is good and what is bad? (Bai Songjun, successor).
Chan Master Zhengzong Huairi ascended the hall and said: "The earthen ox battles into the sea; the iron horse neighs in the wind by day.

The stone woman lifts her eyes; the wooden cock crows to the moon. This causes the dragons and serpents to tremble in the waves of the vast ocean, and the nursing tiger to take on the wings of Mount Sumeru.
You worthy ones, this matter is ever present within daily life. Do you understand it thoroughly? (After a long silence.)"
Zhuo leaned on his staff and said: "Wind and clouds swirl; thunder startles the hibernating insects. Clapping hands in the crimson heavens, it is spring beyond kalpas.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Dharma banner is newly erected; the Way of the Dharma is raised once more. The sound of the Dharma is manifest and profound;

the flavor of the Dharma is fragrant and sweet. Yesterday was sunny, today it rains. The patch-robed monks have eaten their fill. Look clearly at this: when it is cold, it is cold; when it is hot, it is hot. But tell me—what of the cold?"
From where does it arise? From where does this heat come? If you can find a place of rest for both the black and the white here, you will clearly realize the Vajra-seed Wisdom.
If this is not yet so, you will only know that affairs pass before your eyes, unaware that old age is coming upon you from above.
(Tianze Chen succeeded [to his master]).
Chan Master Shifan Jian of Cihang at Fengxi in Suzhou was the son of the Zhu family of Dinghai.
He ascended the hall and, having finished citing the story of Yaoshan’s long absence from the seat, the Master said: “The bone-chilling plum flower surpasses all other fragrances;
Revealed in the courtyard, it reflects the brilliant light. Alas, it meets no hand to pluck its blossoms; How much fragrance remains scattered upon the branches! He struck the meditation seat.

Descending from the seat, [the Master] enters the New Hall of Offerings at Eishōin. Ascending the seat: "The collapsing framework is re-established; we receive the high-flowing waters of travelers from afar.
