Epitaph for Master Fāng Róng (Rúxǐ), Dharma Heir of Jīngāng Shèng, of the Hóngjì Monastery in Jānhīng, Compiled by Xué Lífúyuán Kuān (Dharma Successor of Jué Làng Shèng).
Master Fāng Róng, whose secular surname was Rén and who hailed from Xīnyáng in Shǎnxī, ascended the hall [to preach].

His countenance was ancient and his form spare, yet his spirit was majestic. At ease in the bustling marketplace, he played with the golden-haired lion. With one thunderous roar, all people were struck with awe.
"Beasts and birds flee at the mere sight of his shadow. Is there anyone who can emerge from beneath the point of the arrow?

After a long silence, he said: "On the day of the Winter Solstice, I ascend the hall. The winter solstice is short; the summer solstice is long. Spring equinox brings warmth; autumn equinox brings coolness.
The movement of the four seasons over all things is like the turning of a wheel; the eight nodes of time urge people on as if by the haste of an arrow. Only this mountain monk..."
The staff does not belong to the realm of creation nor to yin and yang. It eats when hungry and drinks when thirsty; it defies the snow and overcomes the frost.
This one piece of true wind exists beyond the empty kalpa; it never departs from daily life, yet it transcends the ordinary. On the Mid-Autumn Festival, Hongji ascended the hall and said:
"Upon the river, the clear breeze sweeps softly; in the mountains, the bright moon is full. Hearing and seeing are fundamentally of one essence; sound and light each..."
Since the tradition has been transmitted, this mountain monk has used this fine setting to bring forth this matter for everyone.
He then held up a finger and said, "Look! Look! To fixate on this old monk’s finger is to lose your own eyes.

A monk asked, "Regarding the saying, 'The phrase with and the phrase without are like a vine leaning against a tree,' what is the meaning? The Master said, "One pull and the root is severed. The monk asked, "Ultimately..."
"Where do these phrases ultimately return? The Master said, "The wild fire cannot burn them; when the spring wind blows, they grow once more.
A monk asked, "What is the white ox on the open ground? The Master said, "What do you have that covers it? The monk asked, "And what of one who has attained it? The Master said:
Do not tread on living grass (Juelang Cheng’s succession).
When Chan Master Simuyu Dawen of Tianmu first visited Baoshou at Dongta, he remained there for a long time without attaining any realization.
Later, when Baoshou moved to Furi, the Master exerted his resolve and entered the hall. After two weeks, becoming exhausted and falling into a daze, he suddenly—
He entered into realization. He hurried away to see Fang. Fang asked, "What are you doing here at such a late hour?
The Master said, "I have a matter. Fang asked, "What matter? The Master said, "A night mouse has bitten a sacred cat. Fang said, "There is no need for sharp wit or turning phrases.
An ancient said, 'To enter through conditions is to never again fall back. What have you realized? The Master said, "I, this humble one..."
Having woken from his drowsiness, Fang asked, "What is it that has awakened? The Master said, "When it is cold, it is cold to the very bone. Fang rebuked him sharply.
The Master was reduced to such a state of embarrassment that he asked, "How about you, Master? Fang replied, "Then you must go elsewhere to seek clarity."
The Master prostrated and departed. From then on, he traveled extensively throughout various regions. Later, he visited Tienjie Cheng at Changshu.
Upon meeting him, Cheng ordered him to serve as the Hall Superintendent. One day, Cheng asked, "How are matters in the hall going these days? The Master replied:
The night-bright curtains were not rolled up; golden halls rested in the morning clouds.

[This was] Chan Master Tianran (Xiao Feng) of Qingyuan in Jizhou, whose secular surname was Sheng (Juelang Sheng, his successor). He was a descendant of Ni Wenzhuan, the Duke of Wenjie of the Song dynasty.
From childhood, he delighted in study without weariness. In the *Renxu* year of the Ming Tianqi era, he passed the jinshi examination and joined the ranks of the elite scholars.
I, Gong, was his fellow official. The Master and Gong both studied the "Mu" (No) kōan together. One day, while leaning on a staff, he suddenly entered a state of meditative absorption;
unconsciously, the thought of "Mu" escaped his lips, whereby he attained the severance of past and future. He nearly left secular life to complete this one matter, but did not succeed.

It was not until the year of Yiyou that he finally resigned from office. In the following spring, he submitted his formal request to Zhuan-yu Heng. In the year of Dinghai, he went to study under Tianjie.
Sheng entered the room to inquire about the matter of whether a dog has Buddha-nature or not. The Master said, "What do you mean by 'having' or 'not having'?
Sheng replied, "You still understand this through intellectual reasoning. The Master urged him, "Speak quickly! The Master repeated his words with increasing urgency: "You cannot say it!"
Dongcheng said, "How can you even say you have attained it? The Master replied, "I understand. Dongcheng struck him and said, "What do you understand?
As the Master was about to respond, Dongcheng struck him again, saying, "I want you to see Zhaozhou intimately right here. The Master bowed respectfully and departed.
The next morning, he saw him again and immediately asked, "Yesterday I had doubts regarding that koan of yours. As the Master was again about to respond, Dongcheng then—
He laughed heartily. The Master suddenly attained awakening. Just as he was about to prostrate in thanks, Sheng asked, "Did you just now understand my laugh?
The Master replied, "The whale swallows the sea until it is empty, revealing the coral branches. Sheng approved of this.

In the year Xinmao, Sheng presided over Taiping Wanshou Temple and certified the Master with a verse. In the year Renchen, he commanded him to succeed him at Qixia. In the year Dingyou, he took up residence there.
Qingyuan Yuanduan ascended the hall. Striking the *ruyi* (monk’s staff), he said: "The rooster calls to the sun; the dog barks for the year.
The one cries, the other barks—do not let these sounds disturb the neighbors, for they interfere with this mountain monk’s spring nap.
Today, having woken from sleep when the sun is high, I suddenly stepped upon the Huangmei pestle. At midnight, I took my robes and crossed the ridge."
Qingyuan and Nanyue face each other from afar; the horse’s hoof tramples men, making their very bones and marrow cold. At Shitou’s slippery ledge, one’s heart and gall are shattered.
Do you know? Do you understand? Or do you not? To gain one year is to lose one year. What, then, is the meaning of the West’s coming?
Carelessly picking it up, one is utterly intoxicated. Setting this matter aside for a moment: as the ancients said, “The First Day of the New Year begins...”
"Fortune! All things are renewed. What do you think of this? After a long silence, he said: 'The thorn-tree has already sprouted after a thousand years;
before the courtyard, twin blossoms of the cassia tree have opened. With a shout, the Master ascended the hall on his birthday and said: 'This mountain monk is seventy years old this year.
My birth sign is the year of the Ox (Jichou). Calculating it, I am indeed a man of the Ox. Wherever I go, I pull the plow and drag the harrow.'"
He runs! Plowing the stony fields, he brings forth iron caltrops; they cannot be swallowed or spat out, making one vomit. Driving the plow is the very act of a laborer;

giving him food turns him into a hand that robs the meal. On the South Mountain there are some, on the North Mountain there are some—why need there be the music of flutes and bells to sing of the *gao* and *niu* trees?
Suzhou has them, Changzhou has them—they have long since hidden their bodies within the Northern Dipper, yet they are caught by the rope of Qingyuan.
Suo Qian, you who once swept the floor in the Patriarch’s ancestral land, ask me about the price of rice in Lin’ang:
to this very day, who has ever taken a mouthful? Let this matter rest for now; as for this mountain monk’s place of birth, was it indeed the year of Jichou, or not?
When the iron ox sheds its golden horns, the golden-haired one transforms again into a silver-hoofed dog. An octagonal millstone—empty.
[The Master] ran inside. "Tell me, where did he run to? He struck [the ground] with his *ruci* (willow-leaf whisk) in the shape of two zeros (00), saying:

"Within a single atom, the twin wheels turn; the mind-ground is ground away, yet it moves not, neither before nor after. He let out a shout and descended from his seat. On the Lantern Festival, a monk asked:
"What is 'bias within the center' (*zhengzhongpian*)? The Master said: "When it is round, the pointed form remains. The monk asked: "What is..."

"Entering correctness from partiality. The Master said, "When it is pointed, the circular mark is hidden. [The student] asked, "What is 'coming from the center of correctness'? The Master said, "Today it is perfectly round.
[The student] asked, "What is 'arriving through the integration of both'? The Master said, "Clouds and moon gather together.

[The student] asked, "What is 'reaching through the integration of both'? The Master said, "The clouds disperse and the moonlight shines bright. [The student] asked, "What is the Sovereign? The Master said, "..."
"Among the stars, the moon is most honored. [The student] asked, "What is the minister? The Master said, "Under the sun, the red clouds are struck.

[The student] asked, "What is the minister serving the sovereign? The Master said, "All the stars bow toward the North Star. [The student] asked, "What is the sovereign regarding the minister? The Master said:
"There is no water that does not flow eastward. [The monk] asked, "What is the convergence of the Way between ruler and subject? The Master said, "Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger.
[The monk] asked, "What is the house style of the Master? The Master said, "Under the Azure Screen Cliff, the waters murmur. [The monk] asked, "What is the realm of Qingyuan?
The Master said, "Beside the Moon-Waiting Bridge, the wind whistles. [The monk] asked, "What is..."
Regarding the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, the Master said: "A rainbow stretches across the empty courtyard. [The student] asked:

"As for the supreme vehicle of the ancestral school, do you permit this student to pass through its message? The Master said: "A broken stele lies prostrate like a dragon or snake. (Juelang Cheng was his successor.)
Chan Master Jiehong Da’i of Pucheng Haoshan was the son of Huang of Danxia in Min. He received the precepts from Xue of Bianshan.
When Xue asked him, “Who dragged your dead corpse here? the Master was suddenly struck by a surge of doubt and remained unsettled for ten days.
At the fifth watch of one night, he had an awakening upon hearing the sound of a bell. He entered the abbot’s quarters, and Xue said, "Who is it that drags this corpse here?
The Master replied, "The fragrant plum blossoms of early winter. Xue asked again, "Which of these is your true self?
The Master replied, "Facing each other, we do not recognize one another. Xue asked, "Where did you learn that? The Master gave a shout and departed. Xue then asked, "The insentient..."
"What is the intent behind preaching the Dharma? The Master said, "The mountain is naturally high, and the water is naturally deep" (Juelang Cheng, successor).
Chan Master Qingyuan Yemiao Daquan of Jizhou was a native of the Wu clan of Guangchang.
He left home to become a monk at age nine at Dajue Temple in his home district and received full ordination at Quanshan. Later, while reading the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, he exclaimed: "This is not you!"
The Master’s mind finally found its entry point. He returned to visit Master Tianjie Cheng; upon entering the room and bowing, as he rose, Cheng grabbed him and said, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! The Master then let out a shout. Cheng struck him out of the room. The Master entered again and shouted repeatedly. Cheng asked, "Who is that?
The Master also grabbed him and said, "Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Cheng leaned against the meditation seat and called for his attendant to save him. The Master slapped the attendant.
The monk said, "This palm should be struck by the old fellow himself," and he immediately left. Upon the conclusion of the retreat, he ascended the hall and said:

"The rain falls upon the mountain peak; The pine branches grow ever greener. Following the pines, one passes through the sacred realm; A single path leads out to the vermilion pavilion. When coming, it comes thus:

Even this very body does not exist—how much less can anything external to the body be spoken of? View it with the correct eye."
"Come! What a laughingstock this has been. Now that the Sage Ruler has issued his decree to convert monasteries into Shenshao Palaces, it is like placing a crown upon the Buddha’s head.
Calculating it, what could be wrong with that? Today, I, this mountain monk, cannot help but carry my staff across my shoulders."
Suspend your alms-bag high and dwell within the seamless stupa; establish your life beneath the rootless tree, chanting with the wind and calling to the moon.
Leave it to the cloud-riding immortals and the crane-mounted transcendents to come here to chant incantations over water, write talismans, and perform rites by clacking their teeth.
When you attain the Way in years to come and ascend on a white day, you will be able to repay the unrepayable debt of gratitude and assist in the realm of non-action.
"Regarding this transformation, I fear it may not be jade; yet if it is jade, how extraordinary! Nevertheless, tell me:
what is the monk’s turning-about phrase? How would you say it? Do you understand? Having cast down his whisk, he passed away.
The Prefect submitted a memorial regarding these matters. By imperial decree, the name of the temple was changed to "True Body" (Zhen-shen).
On the day when Master Ming of Tian-ning in Ru-zhou was ordained as a *de-shi*, the Master ascended the seat; after finishing his expression of gratitude for the imperial favor, he said:
"The wooden tally is grasped at hand; the sitting mat is laid down in the moment. Clouds disperse and waters flow away; all is silent, heaven and earth."
"Emptiness. He then closed his eyes and passed away.
Later, a monk asked Zen Master Renwang Qin of Shu, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Hearing the name is not as good as seeing the face.
The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "A monkey performing in a bustling marketplace. The monk asked, "If..."
"What is the Way? The Master said, "A tiger looks at a water mill.
A monk who was the abbot of Tiesuo Mountain in Jinling asked, "I have long heard of Tiesuo; I wonder what its face and form are like?
The Master struck the pillar and said, "Thank you for showing me. The abbot asked, "On what basis do you speak thus? The monk then struck him.
The pillar was exposed. The Master said, "Tell me, where does the search lie? The monk made a gesture of measuring the space. The Master said, "Today I have met a fellow practitioner.
As for Master Louzi, it is unknown where he was from; his name and lineage have not been handed down. One day, while wandering through the streets...
While passing by a wine shop, as he was adjusting his socks and sash, he heard someone on the upper floor singing a song that said:
"Since you have no heart, I shall also desist. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment; for this reason, he was called Louzi (The Tower Man).

The Dharma Master Shenzhao Benru once requested further instruction on the essential meaning of the sutras from the Venerable Siming. The Venerable called out in a thunderous voice, "Your name is Benru!
At that, the Master attained immediate realization and composed this verse: "Everywhere one encounters the path back home;
At every turn, one reaches one's native land. This matter has been perfected from the very beginning— Why wait for deliberation?"
The Dharma Master Yuanzhi Zhengwu of Shangzhu Monastery in Lin’an was the son of the Lin family of Taizhou.
He relied upon Bailian Xian and inquired about the Way of "Possessing Transformation. Bailian pointed to a lamp and said, "A lamp such as this is devoid of self-nature and transcends all attributes;

it is fundamentally empty and still. In principle, it is 'complete' (ju). Yet, the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of sages perceive it differently; thus, 'transformation' (bian) resides therein. The Master did not attain realization.

Later, while sweeping the floor and reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he reached the passage: "Know that all phenomena are eternally without self-nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions.
At this point, he first grasped the essential meaning and informed Lian. Lian agreed with him.

Since the Master had led his disciples, he had long lamented that scholars of his own school were confined by names and forms and bound by literal records, even treating the transmission of Tiantai as a mere study of texts—a view held in contempt by the Southern School.
He then went to visit Huogu Ciana Yuan. During their conversation at night, the Master recited the verse by Dongpo on staying at Donglin and said, "It is not easy to reach such a state.
Yuan said, "You have not yet even seen the path; how can you speak of reaching it? The Master said, "As for what he said:
'The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; the color of the mountains—is this not the pure body? If..."
"One who has not reached this stage—how could they have such news? Yuan said, "He is merely a man from outside the gate.
The Master said, "If the Master is not stingy, please explain it for me. Yuan said, "Rather, you must simply exert your utmost energy right here."
"Observe and catch it. If you can observe and catch its breaking apart, then you will also know where your own *benming yuanchen* (original life-source) resides.
The Master did not sleep all night. When the dawn bell rang, he removed his secret concealment and spoke another verse:
"Slope-Dweller, the Layman, is far too talkative; He wishes to pass through the barrier of sound and form. If the stream were sound and the mountain were form, There would be no mountain..."
"Having no water is a cause for sorrow for a man. He took this and informed Yuan. Yuan said, "I told you before that you were a man from outside the gate. The Master prostrated himself in thanks.
Not long after, there was one who went to transform the roof tiles at Mazu’s temple and requested words to promote [the teaching]. The Master wrote: "Send word to the old adept of Jiangxi:
let him be scorched by the sun and fanned by the wind as he pleases. His descendants are not without means of care; they simply wish to see..."
When the ice melted and the structure crumbled, Yuánjiàn laughed and said, "It must be this very *śramaṇa* who can achieve it.
Chan Master Shǒumì of Jìngjiè in Hézhou was asked by a monk, "What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "Prostrations! Prostrations!"
The monk asked, "Does a student have a share [of the Dharma] or not? The Master said, "Prostrate yourself! Prostrate yourself! The monk performed a dance and departed.
The Master said, "It resembles it, indeed it resembles it; yet it is not yet it."
Master Ben-sung, at the request of Layman Yang Jie (Wuwei), was asked about the essential nature of the *vinaya* as taught by Master Xuan.
The Master replied with this verse: "How could emotion and wisdom ever be different? The dog barks while the snake moves on its own.
The true meaning of Zhongnan— At midday, it strikes the third watch."
Once there was an elderly master who did not engage in conversation with his disciples for an entire summer retreat. A monk sighed and said, "I have spent this whole summer in vain;
I did not dare hope that you, Master, would preach the Buddha-dharma, but even to hear two characters of the True Cause (zhengyin) would have been enough.
Upon hearing this, the master said, "Dharmācārya, do not speak so hastily. As for the True Cause, there is not even a single character of it. He then spoke:
Yaoliao struck his teeth together and said, "Just now, without cause, it was improper for me to speak in such a manner.
An elderly practitioner living in an adjacent wall heard this and remarked, "What a fine pot of soup that has been defiled by a single mouse dropping!"
Once there was a monk who stayed within the sutra hall but did not read the scriptures, sitting in meditation every day.
The Librarian asked, "Why do you not read the scriptures? The monk replied, "I am illiterate. The Librarian said, "Why do you not ask others?
The monk stepped forward, joined his palms, and bowed, asking, "What kind of character is this? The Librarian was speechless.

Long ago, there was an elderly master who lived in a hermitage. He wrote the character for "mind" (心) above the door, he wrote the character for "mind" on the window, and he wrote the character for "mind" on the wall.

Formerly, there were two masters of a hermitage living together in a hut. For ten days they did not see one another. Suddenly, they met; the master from the upper room asked the master from the lower room:
The Upper Hermit said, "It has been a long time since we last met. Where have you been? The Lower Hermit replied, "I have been in the hut building a seamless stupa.
The Upper Hermit said, "I wish to build one as well. May I borrow the model for the stupa from you?
The Lower Hermit said, "Why did you not say so sooner? It has just now been borrowed by someone else."
Once there was a hut-dweller who, seeing a monk approach, held up a fire-tube and asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not.
The master said, "This is something that has been used for thirty years without being exhausted. The monk then asked, "What did you use before those thirty years?
The master had no reply.
Once there was an elder who, when questioned by the Prince of the State of Jiangnan, replied: "I have a water buffalo that has traveled ten thousand *li* without a single blade of grass.
I do not know where to let it graze. The elder remained speechless.
Once there was an elderly master who asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "I have come from paying my respects to the Patriarch at Oxhead Mountain.
The master asked, "Did you see the Patriarch? The monk was speechless.
Long ago, there was an elder who spoke in verse: "A single void atop the mountain of the five aggregates; Though we pass through the same gate, we do not meet.
For immeasurable kalpas we have lived in rented rooms; Yet to the end, we fail to recognize the true Master."
A monk asked an old master, "What is it like to be one within the secret chamber? The old master said, "When there is a guest, I do not answer questions.
Long ago, there was an old master to whom a monk asked: "The soul returns, come back; eat the mulberries of my home garden.
"What are the mulberries of the home garden? he asked.
Behind him, an elder said: "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years to seek the sound of wisdom.
If you understand it in such a way, the day will come when you shall receive an iron staff. Another elder said: "The Patriarch sat facing the wall for nine years;
how can you not feel ashamed? If you understand it in such a way, you must buy more straw sandals and travel as a pilgrim for thirty more years."
Once there was an elder monk. When a monk asked him, "A lion uses its full strength when seizing a rabbit, and it uses its full strength when seizing an elephant;
I wonder, what kind of full strength is this? The elder said, "The strength of non-deception."
Long ago, there was an elder who said: "This plot of land has been entrusted to you for a long time;
I shall stand here and wait for you to grasp its meaning.
Long ago, there was another elder who kept a novice boy who knew nothing of the rules of conduct. Once, a wandering monk arrived. Thereupon—
He was teaching a young novice the rules of propriety. In the evening, seeing an elder returning from outside, he went to pay his respects.
The elder was surprised and asked the novice, "Who taught you this? The novice replied, "A certain senior monk in the hall.
The elder summoned that monk and asked, "Senior monk, you have been traveling among lay families; what kind of practice is this? This child has been raised for two..."
It has been three years. Fortunately, he is a pitiable fellow. Who taught this Elder? He has ruined that quick-witted one. Packing his bags, he sets off;
at twilight, drenched by the rain, he is driven out.

Long ago, there was a monk who arrived at Caoxi. At that time, the monk in charge of the robes and bowl held up the robe and said, "This is what could not be carried further than the summit of Mount Dayu.
The visiting monk asked, "Why is it now in the hands of the Senior Monk? The monk in charge had no reply.
In the past, there was a monk who, while studying the *Lotus Sūtra*, reached the passage: "All dharmas, from their very origin, are by nature eternally in a state of quiescent extinction.
Suddenly, he was struck by doubt that he could not resolve. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he constantly investigated this for himself, yet attained nothing at all.

One spring day, hearing the song of a warbler, he suddenly attained awakening. He then continued the preceding verse, saying: "All dharmas, from their very origin, Are by nature eternally in a state of quiescent extinction."
When spring arrives, the hundred flowers bloom; the yellow oriole sings atop the willows.

Long ago, there was an elder who asked a presiding abbot, "Regarding the commentaries and sub-commentaries that explain the meaning [of the scriptures], how do they differ in their breadth and brevity?
The abbot replied, "The commentaries explain the sub-commentaries; the sub-commentaries explain the scriptures. The elder asked, "What do the scriptures explain? The abbot was speechless.
Formerly, when people from the kingdom of Goryeo came to Qiantang to carve a sacred image of Avalokiteśvara, they were unable to move it once it was placed upon their ship.
Consequently, they invited it into Kaiyuan Temple in Mingzhou to offer worship. Later, someone raised this question:
"If there is no land where he does not manifest his body, why did the sacred image not go to the kingdom of Goryeo?"
Before the pagoda at Sizhou, a monk was prostrating. Someone asked him, "Venerable sir, you prostrate every day; do you actually see the Great Sage?
The attendant at the Sizhou pagoda would lock the door at the appointed time. Someone asked, "Since he is the Great Master of the Three Realms, why..."
"What is it that has been locked by the disciple? The attendant had no reply.
"The image of the Holy Monk is being dripped upon by leaks from the roof. Someone asked a monk, "Since he is the Holy Monk, why does he have leaks?"
The monk had no reply.
Someone asked the monk, "What kind of lamp do you light? The monk said, "A perpetually burning lamp. [The person] asked, "When was it lit?
[The monk] said, "It was lit last year. [The person] asked, "Where is the perpetual light? The monk was speechless.
There was a presiding master (zuozhu) who, while reciting the name of Amitābha, was called by a junior monk. When the master turned his head, the junior monk did not respond.
This happened three or four times. The master scolded him, saying, "I have called you three or four times; what is the matter?
The junior monk replied, "Master, it has been many years since you last called him, yet when I call him just now, he immediately gives rise to karmic activity."
There was a monk who, having finished reciting the scriptures with a young boy, instructed him to place the scriptures inside a case. The boy asked, "Where shall I put what I have recited?
Another monk was composing a commentary on the *Daode jing*.
When someone asked, "I have long heard that the Great Virtuous One is composing a commentary on the *Daode jing*," the monk replied, "No."
[The Master] dared to ask: "What about Emperor Minghuang? Fadelu replied: "He was my disciple.

There was a monk who entered the underworld and saw Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva asked him: "What practice did you cultivate throughout your life? The monk replied: "I recited the Lotus Sūtra.
[The Bodhisattva] said: "'Cease, cease! Do not speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. Was this spoken or unspoken?"
The monk had no response.
At the assembly of Yanguan, there was a presiding administrative monk who suddenly saw a ghost messenger come to pursue him.

The monk said to him, "I am currently serving as an administrator and have not yet had the leisure to practice; I beg you to grant me seven days. Is this possible? The messenger said, "Wait, I shall report it."
"O King, if you grant permission, I shall come back in seven days; otherwise, I will arrive in an instant. Having spoken, he vanished.
When the seven days had passed, he returned again and sought the monk, but he could not be found at all. Later, someone asked another monk:
"If you were to be sought out and found, how would you deal with him?"
A monk from Liutong Monastery in Taizhou was about to board a boat when someone asked him, "Since you possess the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), why do you rely on a boat?
The monk was unable to respond.
One day, the Prefect of Hongzhou, Lord Song, requested a monk from Dajian Temple to open the hall for the second seat.
The Lord asked, "Why do you not request the first seat? The assembly was speechless.

The Chancellor of Jiangnan, Feng Yanshi, was traveling with several monks to Mount Zhong. Upon reaching the "One-Man Spring," he asked, "How can so many people find it sufficient at a spring for one person?
A monk replied, "It does not allow anyone to lack. Feng Yanshi did not accept this answer, so he offered another: "Who is it that lacks?"
The official asked the monk, "What is your name? He replied, "No selection. The official said, "If someone were suddenly to give you a bowl of sand, what then?
He replied, "I thank the official for his offering."
In Guangnan there was a monk living in a hermitage. When the ruler of the state went out hunting, his attendants informed the master of the hermitage, "The Great King is coming; please rise.
The master said, "Not only would I not rise for the Great King, I would not rise even if the Buddha were to come. The king asked, "Is the Buddha not your teacher?"
The Master said, "Yes. The King asked, "Seeing the Master, why do you not rise?
There was a monk on Hongtang Bridge in Fuzhou; when an official sat in a row with him and asked, "Is there a Buddha here?
the monk had no reply.

Long ago, there was an official who entered the Tianwang Monastery in Zhenzhou and beheld a divine image. He asked the monastery’s custodian, "What meritorious work is this? The custodian replied, "It is the Guardian King of the State. The official asked, "Does he protect only this country, or does he protect all other countries as well? The custodian replied, "When he is in Qin, he protects Qin; when he is in Chu, he protects Chu. The official said, "On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month, you shall break down the city walls of Zhenzhou! The deity said, "So be it. That very night, the city walls were indeed shattered. The official was struck with awe and immediately prostrated himself before the image. This is why the verse says: "In Qin he is for Qin; in Chu he is for Chu. It is like a mirror reflecting forms—there is no fixed location. How could there be any fixed location? Therefore, the verse concludes: "The heavens have broken the city of Zhenzhou. The meaning is that the heavens have manifested their power to break the city of Zhenzhou. This is called the "Transformation of the Heavenly King. It is not that the Heavenly King has transformed; rather, it is the person who has been transformed. Why? Because the Heavenly King is originally suchness. Since he is originally suchness, how could he be transformed? It is simply that the person has been transformed. For this reason, it is said: "The heavens have broken the city of Zhenzhou. "Where has the King gone? The Master had no reply.
Long ago, there was an official who composed a treatise denying the existence of ghosts. One night, while he was wielding his brush, he suddenly saw a ghost appear and say:
"You claim there are none; what about me?"
Once there was a practitioner of the Way who sat with his back turned toward the Buddha in front of the Buddha Hall. A monk said, "Daoist, do not sit with your back to the Buddha.
The practitioner of the Way replied, "In the fundamental teaching of the Great Virtuous One, it is said that the Buddha-body fills the entire Dharma-realm.
Where, then, could one possibly sit? The monk was speechless.
There was a practitioner who followed a Dharma Master into the Buddha hall. The practitioner spat toward the Buddha. The Master said, "The practitioner lacks propriety;
why do you spit at the Buddha? The practitioner replied, "I have come from a place where there is no Buddha, so I spit here for my own sake. The Master had no response.
A dead fish was floating on the surface of the water. Someone asked a monk, "Is it not the case that fish take water as their life?
The monk replied, "Yes. The man asked, "Why then have they died in the water? The monk had no reply.
A hawk pursued a pigeon, which flew onto the railing of the Buddha Hall and trembled.
Someone asked a monk, "All sentient beings dwell in constant peace and joy within the shadow of the Buddha. Why, then, does this pigeon tremble upon seeing the Buddha? The monk was unable to answer.
Once there was a monk traveling toward Fushan who encountered an old salt peddler on the road.
The monk asked, "Which way leads to Fushan? The old man remained silent for a long while. When the monk asked again, the old man said, "Are you deaf?
The monk replied, "What did you say to me? The old man said, "I told you which way leads to Fushan. The monk asked, "Do you understand Zen? The old man said, [silently].
"Do not say you understand Zen; you must understand the Buddha-dharma completely as well. The monk said, "Try to explain it to me.
The old man lifted up his salt basket. The monk said, "That is difficult. The old man asked, "What do you call this? The monk said, "Salt.
The old man said, "What connection does that have [to the Buddha-dharma]? The monk asked, "And what do you call it? The old man said, "I cannot tell you again that it is salt."
In the past, there was an old woman who supported a hermit for twenty years. She constantly sent a young girl of eighteen to serve him with meals.
One day, she ordered the girl to hold the hermit firmly and asked, "At this very moment, what is it? The hermit replied:
"A withered tree leaning against a cold cliff; for three winters there has been no warmth.
When the woman reported this to the old woman, the old woman said, "For twenty years I have provided offerings only to a worldly fellow. She then sent her away and burned down the hut.
Once there was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered an old woman living in a hermitage.
The monk asked, "Do you have any kinsmen? She replied, "I do. The monk asked, "Where are they? She said, "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth;
whether grass or trees, all are my kinsmen. The monk said, "Are you not perhaps a nun? She replied, "What do you see in me? The monk said—
The laywoman said, "You cannot be a monk. The monk said, "Old woman, do not cause confusion and disorder within the Buddha-dharma.

The laywoman said, "I am not causing confusion and disorder within the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "If you act as you do, is that not causing confusion and disorder within the Buddha-dharma? The laywoman said:
"You are a man; I am a woman. How could we ever be confused?
When the nun Pang entered Lukmen Temple to offer a vegetarian feast, the rector requested her instructions.
The nun took up a comb, stuck it behind her hair-knot, and said, "The dedication of merit has been made. She then departed.

The nun Chen Dao-po of Wenzhou once traveled extensively to consult renowned masters throughout the various regions. Later, she attained enlightenment under the guidance of Master Jing at Changlao Mountain.
She composed a verse which says: Upon the level summit of the high hill, There are but woodcutters everywhere.
Everyone harbors the intent of axe and hatchet, Yet they do not see the mountain flowers reflecting red in the water.
In the past, there was a female patron who entered a monastery to distribute "money according to seniority" (nien-ch'ien) to the assembly of monks.
A monk said, "Place one portion before the Holy Monks (ārya-saṃgha). The woman asked, "How old are the Holy Monks? The monk had no reply.
Chan Master Fojue of Qingzhou (doubtfully of the Yunmen lineage) composed a verse on Master Yaoshan’s Lion: "A single color, nothing surpasses its pointing out to people;
Within a world of white silver, he lets out a groan. Transcendently, he knocks one down and then raises one up; How can this compare to the spring breeze, ever-new as it shines upon the sun?"
When National Teacher Yuantong Shan (who was likely a successor of the Yunmen lineage under Fojue) traveled from Jiangyou to Yanjing, he stayed at Dashing'an Temple.
One night, while conversing with Fojue and Huitang, the Master was twelve years old and standing in attendance to their right.
Yunju said, "I have come from the south, and I have never once struck upon a single person who understands the Buddha-dharma with my staff.
The Master stepped forward with his hands joined and said, "This is simply because your staff is too short, Reverend.
Yunju was greatly startled and said, "I beg you, take this man to continue the lineage of our Linji school. The Master replied, "How could there be two schools—Yunmen and Linji? Yunju praised him.
The Emperor’s praise was unending. Emperor Jin Shizong visited the Shrine of the Auspicious Image at Sheng’an Temple and asked the Master, “Is it right to pay homage?

Or is it not right to pay homage? The Master replied, “To pay homage is to show mutual respect and honor; not to pay homage is for each person to claim their own supremacy. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Later, while residing at Yansheng Temple, he addressed the assembly, citing Dongshan: “In the late summer and early autumn, brothers may go east...”
"Go west, go west! You must go directly to a place ten thousand miles away where there is not even an inch of grass.
He asked again, "Even if it were a place ten thousand miles away with not an inch of grass, how would you go? Shishuang said, "As soon as you step out the door, it is all grass.
Dayang said, "Even if you do not step out the door, it is still a sea of spreading grass. The Master said, "Now tell me, right at the base of your feet this very moment—"
How would you express this? If you say, "Ten thousand miles without a blade of grass," I grant that you have seen Dongshan.
If you say, "Stepping out the door is already grass," I grant that you have seen Shishuang.
If you say, "Even not stepping out the door is a vast expanse of grass," I grant that you have seen Dayang. If you cannot say any of these, I grant that you have seen Yansheng. How so?

Therefore, there is only a fine breeze coming upon the mats, and no idle talk falling among the people. Addressing the assembly, he raised the story of Master Yunmen regarding the "Guanyin glutinous rice cake.
The Master said, "The old man of Shaoyang may indeed be said to have a song that rises ever higher while those who join in the harmony grow ever fewer.
Now, however, he has entered the Samādhi of Fangguang upon the tip of the whisk at Yansheng Monastery, entering from the east."
Entering samādhi from the west and emerging from it in a male body, or entering samādhi in a female body and emerging from it in a male body—do you understand?
The wild landscape is no longer interrupted by mountains; the moonlight connects directly with the water.

The Chan Master Yuwu Yujing of Qingshou Monastery in Yanjing (doubtfully of the Yunmen lineage; successor of Yuan Tong) was questioned by the Jin Emperor Xianzong, who sent an imperial messenger carrying a sheet of paper on which the two characters "Heart-Buddha" (心佛) were written.
The Emperor asked the Master, "What kind of characters are these? The Master replied, "They are not 'heart'."
"It is not a Buddha. This pleased the Emperor's mind. On the following day, the Emperor bestowed upon him a long-short verse (ci'ou-tz'u), which said:

"If one can only achieve purity, what need is there to inquire about the causes and conditions of the myriad dharmas? In daily life, act without effort; throughout the twelve hours of the day, do not harbor further doubt.

One must always remain autonomous; recognize that from the beginning there has been no obstruction. Buddha after Buddha, mind after mind—if the mind relies upon the Buddha, it too is but a defilement. The Master replied: "There is none."

To act without action—recognizing action as the unconditioned is still bondage. Illumination and function are simultaneous; even "swift as a flash of lightning or a shooting star" is already too late.
That which is neither mind nor Buddha—calling it "not mind" is still a thing. When both person and environment are empty, the myriad phenomena are reflected within a single mirror.
The lay practitioner Zhao Wenyu of Huangshan (likely of the Yunmen lineage; successor of Yuantong) once composed a verse: "Deluded thoughts are originally and fundamentally true;
To try to eliminate them is to raise another layer of dust. In speech, thought, movement, and stillness—who provides the power?
If you look closely, there are no two people."
When Chanding (Ding Chan) of Gaoyou State first visited Yuanwu, [the master] raised the following case in his room:
A monk asked Yuansha, "What is the pure Dharma-body? Yuansha replied, "It is dripping pus. At this, the Master attained realization.
Later, when a monk asked him, "What does the golden fish that has passed through the net eat? the Master replied, "A dry piece of excrement."
Chan Master Yun’an Qing of Jingshan, Hangzhou, was a native of Jianyang. When a monk asked Yangqi, “What is the Buddha?
Yangqi replied, “A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves. The monk asked, “Is this it?
Yangqi said, “The Elder of Hunan. The verse says: Yangqi’s one donkey, Its eyes flashing like lightning, Tramples everyone underfoot.
It speaks of the three-legged foot.
Zen Master Juchuan Hai of Zhulin composed a verse on wind bells: Copper lips and iron tongues, so sharp and new;
Hung from the corner of the tower, they forget the passing spring. The hundreds of thousands of *samādhi* dharmas beyond words— Through the wind, they speak them to those who truly understand.
Chan Master Wuyi of Yunfeng Qiaoyin was the son of the Nie family of Huai’an. During the Huangqing and Taiding eras, he was granted the title “Buddha-Wisdom” (Fozhi).
By imperial decree, he resided at Xuefeng three times, restoring all that had fallen into ruin; this was a great flourishing event for the Dharma gate.
He once wrote a preface to the *Xuefeng Lu*, stating: "After Old Zhenjue’s bottom fell out beneath Deshan’s single blow, he attained such a state that even the shopkeeper at the Dragon Gate..."
The moon is cold; the snow has cleared from Elephant Peak. In a single ladle, he grasps the *amṛta*; with three balls, he manifests the Great Function.
It is like the crashing of ten billion peals of thunder beneath the four heavens—through hundreds of generations, the true sound grows ever more majestic.
All that is shown forth flows from his breast, covering heaven and earth. It is like a single performance on the slender strings at Guangling; the vulgar melodies of Xialing can no longer be heard.
He passed away in the second year of the Yuansheng era (1334). His stupa was erected at his home mountain.

Master Yangbei had extensively studied the classics and histories; his speech was concise and profound. He wore his hair in a disheveled topknot and kept his face soiled, remaining unconstrained in both his movements and stillness.
He once inscribed a poem that said: "Ten thousand purples and thousands of reds are all spring; What need is there to use flowery words to ask the Lord of the East?
When a mute person has a dream, to whom can they tell it? Raising an empty fist, he points toward the white clouds. He also said: "Neither leaning nor biased, standing in the center;
Not clinging to the west, not clinging to the east. Transcending the realms of east, west, south, and north, One casts the hook upon the tip of a single hair."
Canglong once said to his assembly, "My transformation of grace is coming to an end. You all must exert yourselves. As soon as he had finished speaking, he cast off his body.
Later, Zen Master Lai of Jia Mountain in Zhenzhou asked, "Where is the stupa of Iron Ox? The Master pointed toward it with his finger.
At that moment, Lai attained sudden awakening. He then presented this verse: "Iron Ox, Iron Ox! Do not seek anything else. If someone asks..."

I raised my finger. Chan Master Taichu of Mount Gui, whose courtesy name was Zifu, was a native of Wenling. His family had been Confucian scholars for generations. He was a man of noble character with great ambitions;
he could recite from memory anything he read upon a single glance. He extensively mastered both Buddhist and secular classics and achieved many insights into them. As for his poetry and prose—

He was in every way extraordinary, and many officials and scholars looked up to him with high regard. One day, he abandoned his former life and entered Zunseng Monastery to "select the Buddha" (seek enlightenment), disciplining himself according to the Vinaya and completely casting off his habits of aristocratic extravagance.
He traveled beyond the ridges to visit various masters, gaining renown throughout the monastic communities. After a long time, he ceased his travels and returned to Min.
At that time, Nanjian Ba’en Monastery had its seat vacant; the Prefectural Governor, Chen Fu, having heard of the Master’s reputation, appointed him to preside over it.

Not long after, Zhen Dexiu, the Layman of West Mountain (Xishan Jushi), invited the Master to preside over Da Miao. For over twenty years, he restored all that was neglected, and his daily congregation numbered ten thousand.
The Master’s exposition of the Dharma was versatile and vast; his forging of scholars was such that his style did not fall short of that of the ancient patriarchs.

Once the Layman of West Mountain had retired from official service, he frequently visited the Master, and as they conversed at ease on the Way, there were none who did not become intoxicated with admiration. Great...
Master Di received people with straightforward sincerity, and thus the various scholars esteemed him.

Iron-Leg Yuan of Wutai Mountain, the Great Master Huirong, while reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, reached the passage: "When one person gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions all vanishes.
Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and subsequently traveled to Hesuo to see Chan Master Wen.
The Master recounted his realization, and Wenyin certified it. At the time of his passing, he spoke a verse, saying: "Sixty years of springtime, plus eight more;
The floating clouds have cleared away, revealing the blue sky. As I depart, I kick over Mount Sumeru; In the night that follows, the moon atop the mountain is perfectly full.
He changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away.
Chan Master Hui-kong Yuan-mo of Mount Jiangshan in Jianning Prefecture was the son of the Su family of Gutian.

In the year of Gengzi during the Dade era, while traveling in meditation to the Yuanjiang Monastery on Mount Jiangshan, he encountered an old man who came forward to greet him and said, "I have guarded this mountain for five hundred years.
Having finished speaking, the man transformed into a black dragon and departed. Upon awakening, the Master said, "I shall select this place [as my dwelling]."
[He was] Shanyue. He then went to establish a hermitage. One day he said to the assembly, "In the past, at the place of the Buddha, I was known as Bodhisattva Huikong.
Now that my conditions for transformation are exhausted, I shall enter nirvana. He then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the assembly and further spoke a verse, saying:
"For more than forty years I have dwelt amidst the secular dust; today I reveal the Honored One within this very midst. On one night at Yantou..."
The wind arises; it blows the flowers open, filling the trees with spring. An iron boat has neither rudder nor sail, yet it is steered into the ocean of the nature of the golden lotus.
This final pivot of the mechanism is now revealed: white clouds have never been separate from the vast sky. Throughout the mountains and rivers of the great earth, not a trace can be found.
When empty space is struck through, the ultimate reality is seen. Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head, one’s original nature remains.
"Perfect clarity shall never be lost. He spoke again: "In the Western Heaven, the third patriarch, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, dwelt in seclusion at Mount Gajaśṛṅga;
there he manifested the *nāga-vikrīḍita-samādhi* to preach the Dharma and subdue all non-Buddhists, after which he transformed himself into fire and consumed his own body.
Now, before this Elephant Trunk Rock, I too shall do likewise. Having finished speaking, clouds and mist rose up on all sides, and thunder and rain broke forth.
He performed the act of self-immolation by fire. His stupa was erected to the west of the hermitage.
Chan Master Foguang Daowu of Puzhao Temple in Zhengzhou was a native of Guanzhi in Lintao and Lanzhou.
While staying overnight at Wanzi Inn, he heard the neighing of a horse and attained sudden, great enlightenment. Upon returning home, he told his mother: "On the road, I have picked up..."
"One thing. His mother asked, "What thing? The Master said, "That which has not been seen through since beginningless time. His mother struck him with her palm and said, "What joy is there in this?
He then took his leave of his mother to travel to various regions for study. His mother asked, "Where will you go? The Master replied, "Water flowing must reach the sea;
a crane emerges from atop the white clouds. He subsequently went to visit Baiyun Hai and received his seal of certification. This was the twenty-fourth year of the Taiding era.
The Master Chuzhu was universally radiant. He wore a white shirt, rode a yellow calf, and played a short flute as he wandered through Luoyang. He once said:
"If you say I am an ordinary person, I have come from the rank of the sages. If you say I am a sage, I am going back to the rank of the ordinary."
He asked, "Do you consider me neither ordinary nor holy? He then turned toward the crown of Vairocana’s head, where there is a separate place of practice.
In the fifth year of Taihe, he entered nirvana.
In the fifth year of Jiayou, Chan Master Pujue Chunpeng of Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou was ordered by imperial decree to restore the Nine Li [Monastery].
At Mount Jiqing, occupying the path, he ascended the hall and said: "A single expanse of idle land before the mountain; for vast kalpas it has had no boundaries.
Today, having been reclaimed, it returns once more; I sit, cutting off both head and tail. East is so, West is so;
north, south, vertical, and horizontal—all are not otherwise. Ultimately, how does one repay this debt of gratitude? Ten li of lotus flowers, nine..."
Lisong. A single incense stick before the Hall of Direct Pointing.
Chan Master Chang of Xuedou in Mingzhou was a high-ranking disciple of Hengshan. He was not versed in literary texts but specialized exclusively in the practice of dhyāna-concentration;
his peers called him "Chang-Dharma. The gāthās and verses he composed were characterized by the perfect integration of principle and phenomena, with their rhythms and tones perfectly harmonized.
Chang’s verse on the Iron Ox says: Rolled out from within the hundred-fold smelting furnace, Its horns are towering and its body is free of dust.
It cannot be struck, nor can it be pulled; This time, it truly shall not enter a womb. Haimen’s verse says:
The karmic winds blow up waves like mountains; How many fishermen find it difficult to set foot [upon them]? Only by risking one's life and casting away the body Can one force one's way through.

"I know the jade doors have never been closed. The verse on the bitter bamboo shoots says: "The purple robes are stripped away until white as silver; Within the hundred-boiling cauldron, one turns the body.
Those who have undergone such bitter toil will not believe this; But when casually chewed, the flavor is entirely true. Xichan’s verse says:
"At the top of a hundred-foot pole, cease asking for the way; On a solitary peak, at the highest summit, nourish a leisurely life. Although it is a dilapidated hut..."
Without hindrance, it is difficult to explain one’s private inner experience to others.
Lady Ding of Haotou in Huangyan, Taizhou, whose name was Juezhen and whose style name was Zhuxin, first had an awakening upon meeting Juetian Gengzi at Weiyushan;
she subsequently left her family home and built a dwelling for herself. She later went on to study under Yongquan Gu.
Yuyuan said, "Fool! Fool! Why do you, a daughter of a good family, run hither and thither? Zhaozhen said, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master.
Yuyuan said, "There is no room for you here. Zhaozhen then clapped his hands once and said, "That which you have used for thirty years has been caught out today!
Yuyuan then desisted. Zhaozhen then went to Yanshan Chunyuan Hermitage to visit Wuji.
No sooner had he entered the gate than [Zheng] said, "The spring rain is like rich cream; travelers loathe its mud. Jì said, "Not so, not so.
Just as [Zheng] was about to offer further words, he was shouted out by Jì. In his later years, [Zheng] established a reception hall beside Mingyin Temple in the county seat.
One day, a monk carrying a bundle and a hat went straight into his quarters. Zheng asked, "What is that? The monk replied, "A wandering monk."
Zhen suddenly pointed to his feet and said, "The laces on my straw sandals have broken; why do you not notice? The monk had no reply.

Zhen then threw out his pack and rain-cloak, saying, "There is no place here for you to set foot. One day, Mingyin Kui went to visit Zhen and asked, "I have heard it said that you, Elder, fathered a son last night—is this true?
Kui asked, "Tell me, is it a boy? or "Is it a girl? [Note: The text provided ends at "且道是男", which translates to "Tell me, is it a boy?"].
This woman, Zhen, said: "A rooster runs off with a lamp-stand; a turtle bites a fishing rod.
Mingzhou Yuyang Mian was the cousin of Attendant Kongshe. In his youth he possessed great ambition, yet unfortunately died young.
He once composed a verse to send a fellow monk traveling to Mount Tiantai and Mount Yan, which began: "The bird’s nest blew its cloth-hair; the attendant..."

Upon hearing this, he immediately attained awakening. Although it did not involve verbal explanations, it had already become a public proclamation: "The clouds atop Mount Tiantai; the trees within Mount Yandang.
From here on, one should deliberate well; do not touch upon the taboo that stands before you. His verse at the time of death says: "Birth is fundamentally not birth;
death likewise is not death. Bimiya holding up a fork; Jueyi pointing upward with a finger."

The barber Zhang, whose name was De, was a native of Xiashui in Ningbo. For generations his family had served as attendants at the Daci Monastery, where he followed the assembly to hear the Dharma until he attained a realization.
One day, during a heavy snowfall, a novice monk rolled snow into the shape of a Buddha statue, and everyone in the assembly composed verses in praise of it.
Birth also follows in succession. The divination verse says: A single flower holds forth a Tathāgata; Six petals unfold in a round, smiling countenance.
If one recognizes that the skull is originally water, One will not enter the womb in Māyā’s palace.
Chan Master Chenggu of Jianfu in Ruzhou was of lofty and pure conduct and possessed a nature that was open and luminous.
Upon visiting Chan Master Jingxuan of Daguang, he remarked, "He is merely a fellow from within the weeds. He then visited Venerable Yaya of Fuyan, who likewise said:
He was simply a liberated monk. Consequently, he remained silent all day long, deeply investigating the grand regulations of the former masters.
One day, while perusing the words of Yunmen, he suddenly attained awakening. From then on, he concealed his brilliance and sought no fame.
He settled at the site of the stupa of Chan Master Hongjue of Yunju, where students from the four quarters flocked to him; thus, he became known as "The Ancient Stupa Master. Jing...

In the fourth year of the Yuanshou era, Lord Fan Zhongyan was appointed as the governor of Poyang. Having heard of the Master’s virtue and realization, he invited him to reside at Jianfu Temple to propagate the ancestral teachings.
A monk asked, "Great Teacher of Virtue, with what do you instruct people? The Master said, "Do not. The monk said, "If that is so, then there is questioning and answering.
The Master said, "Do not. The monk asked, "The green bamboo stalks are all True Suchness; the lush..."
"Yellow flowers are nothing other than *prajñā*. What is *prajñā*? The Master said, "In the Yellow Springs, there is neither old nor young.

[The monk] said, "When spring comes, the grass turns green of itself. The Master said, "One's reputation is imperishable. [The monk] said, "If that is so, even the blue-eyed barbarian monk would frown.
The Master said, "Step back three paces. The monk said, "It is painful. The Master then uttered, "Hūṃ, hūṃ. [A monk] asked about Linji raising his whisk. The student—
A monk raised his fist. "Is this the same or different? The Master said, "False words confuse the multitude. The monk said, "If that is so, then I shall act according to your command.

The Master said, "To the ends of the earth and the corners of the sea. The monk asked, "Regarding 'A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function operate simultaneously'—what is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "Dry firewood and damp reeds. The monk then shouted. The Master said, "Blazing red flames reaching to the heavens. He ascended the hall for formal instruction.
Now, those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the unconditioned dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit.

Lately, those who have left the household life have become greedily attached to blessings and wisdom, which is entirely contrary to the Way. If you seek blessings and wisdom, you must first clarify the mind;
yet if you wish to realize the Way, there is no place for you to apply the mind. Therefore, I constantly advise people: do not study the Buddha-dharma; simply [be yourself].
Rest the mind. Those of sharp faculties attain liberation at the moment of hearing; those of dull faculties may take three or five years, but not more than ten.
If you do not awaken, old monk will send you to the Hell of the Plucked Tongue. *Chan*.

Verified and presented for imperial inspection by the Abbot of Kyoto’s Kōkegonji, the monk (Shin) Sō Chōkai;
the lineage of his Dharma heirs remains undetermined.
The Head Seat Lingjiang Hao of Yongfu relied upon Gulin at Yongfu in Ruzhou. While serving as the First Seat, he held the whisk during the summer retreat.
A monk asked, "What is it like when one takes a step forward? The Seat replied, "One crashes through walls and bumps into barriers.

The monk asked, "What is it like when one takes a step back? The Seat replied, "One falls into pits and drops into ravines. The monk asked, "What is it like when one neither advances nor retreats? The Seat replied:
Lidishi Han. The late Senior Seat Su-shou had throughout his life maintained a profound and hidden barrier, such that few recognized it.

During the Tianli era, a monk obtained three hand-copied verses on "Expressing My Feelings While Dwelling in the Mountains" and went to Zituo to request that Master Zhu Yuan provide a commentary (*zhuyu*).
Zhu Yuan said: "People everywhere regret that he did not appear in this world and did not preach the Dharma.

Now, having read these three verses, it is as if a great golden bell or a large bronze gong has been struck once, causing all other sounds to cease. Can one say that he did not preach the Dharma? The verses say:
'Having finished reading the *Lamp Transmission*, my hair is already white; My achievements still compete for a few more *lakṣas*. Rising from my midday nap, the dust..."
The table is full; half the eaves are bathed in the slanting setting sun as flowers fall upon the courtyard. This pointed-roof hut is not built low; above it are tall forests, below it lies a pond.
Through the long night, startled winds sweep across yellow leaves, just like when rain falls beneath a thicket of reeds. The light of this floating world is naturally short;
I have composed these verses merely to respond to the passing years. Today I stand with my back turned beneath a great pine tree.
The west wind stirs several crows.
At Luohan Temple on Mount Yan, the Head Seat Zen Master Zheng was blind in both eyes; yet his realization of the Way was clear and bright.
Every morning, he personally swept the grounds. Someone asked him, "Have you swept this patch of ground clean? The Head Seat held up his broom and showed it to him. Furthermore—
Question: "In the realm of true purity, there has never been a single speck of dust. What is there to sweep? The Master then held up his broom to show him.
He once composed a verse on Mount Jiuniu, which says: "For four or five years they have lived in herds; Spring comes and autumn goes, satiated by wind and smoke.
The clear stream has water, yet why have they never drunk? The green fields are unplowed, yet they sleep forever. Each and every one of them—[their] heels...
All points toward the earth; every head and nostril reaches up to the heavens. Usually abiding atop a thousand peaks, how can one lead the people of the great earth?
Yuan’an Huì, the Librarian of Jingci Monastery, was a native of Lin’an. He studied under Huījī at Jingci and resided in the Móngtáng Hall. Because—
He constructed a hall for attaining nirvana. There is a verse that says: "The single path to nirvana has been completely overturned; The effort required at every turn is not difficult to see.
While washing one's face, one suddenly touches the nose; A needle for embroidery can hide a mountain within its eye. Huiji praised this highly.
The Abbot of Kuai-an on Mount Tianmu in Hangzhou was a native of Suzhou. By nature he was quick-witted and proficient in both Buddhist and secular classics.

He was a close friend of Pingshi Di and dwelt among the crags and valleys, keeping himself aloof from the world. Only the descendants of the Hong family from the foot of the mountain would come and go to deliver offerings.
One night, a woman of the Hong family dreamed that the abbot arrived at her house riding in a palanquin.

Upon awakening, he had fathered a son. The following day, he climbed the mountain to await him; indeed, the child had already passed away. He thus named the boy Yingkui (應魁) and gave him the style name Shiyuan (士元).

As a youth, he studied books and was admitted to the local school. He married and fathered a son. At the age of thirty, one day he suddenly attained a profound realization and abandoned his household.
Having built a thatched hut on the summit of the Eastern Peak, he practiced the Way with diligent devotion day and night. One day, [he entered] emptiness...
Master Shi, while fleeing from bandits, passed by his hermitage at Mount Jing.
Observing that the Master’s deportment was serene and elegant and his responses were composed and unhurried, he inquired into the reason for this and learned that he was the reincarnation of Yishan.
He then said to him, "In your previous life, you and Elder Pingshi were inseparable friends. This year the Elder is nearly ninety years old, yet his hearing and sight remain keen."
Ming: "Why do you not send a message? It is as if one sees two awakenings within a single dream; yet are dream and awakening not one and the same?
The Master joyfully took up his brush and composed a verse to send him, saying: "Words sent to the old man of Tiantong, Pingshi: A single thought is neither now nor then.
If you wish to hear the midnight bell of Hanshan, The Wu River remains as ever, merging with the azure sky."

Chan Master Juezhao Hui of Shouchang in Wenzhou once spent the summer retreat at the East Latrine Quarters of Jingci Monastery. On the wall there was a water-ink image of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Avalokiteśvara).

The Master prostrated before it morning and evening, praying with great earnestness. One day, he suddenly saw the water from the pure pitcher surge forth from the wall; his entire being was filled with joy and clarity. From then on, his wisdom-mirror became increasingly bright. He once composed a verse, which says: The wall is not a wall; The image is not an image. If you can see through this, Then the Bodhisattva is right here before you.

The water flows freely from the wall; The light shines clearly within the heart. When the myriad phenomena are all empty, The true person stands alone. The moon reflects in the thousand rivers; The wind blows across the ten directions. If you wish to know the Great Sage, Look directly at the tip of your nose.
"Before one has reached the ground of perfect mastery, how many times have I leaned upon the railing alone in sorrow? Today is the third day, tomorrow the fourth;
snow and frost easily settle upon the heads of men. Upon hearing this, those with resolve will surely be stirred to action.
Such is the power of his utmost sincerity to move others.
Chan Master Seng’an Si of Lingyun in Wenzhou was upright and principled by nature. A native of Ninghai in Taizhou, he was the eldest of four brothers.
They all simultaneously resolved to leave the household life; they distributed their ancestral inheritance entirely among their relatives.

He traveled extensively to visit various masters before eventually taking up residence at Lingyun, later moving to Lingyan. On the occasion of the Summer Retreat, he ascended the hall and spoke of the Great Perfect Circle.

"Awakening! Cow horns and horse horns serve as my monastery; melon baskets and vegetable baskets [are my furnishings]. Ascending the hall, he raised the koan of Zhaozhou’s "The dog has no Buddha-nature" and offered this verse:
"The dog has no Buddha-nature," "The dog has Buddha-nature. "The monkey worries, clutching its head; "The dog runs, shaking its mouth.

In his later years, he retired to the front mountain of Lingyun. (Jiading) Jia... *Note: The final characters "至正甲" (Zhizheng Jia... appear to be a fragment indicating the date of composition or transcription, likely referring to the Jia year of the Zhizheng era.*

Shen, along with several monks including Kongshi, went to pay their respects. At that time, the Master was over ninety years old; with long, bushy eyebrows and white hair, he stood tall and dignified.
He stepped out dragging his sandals and, as he walked, asked, "Where have you come from? Kongshi replied, "From the heart of the river."

The Master said, "How many fathoms deep is it? The monk replied, "You cannot deceive the Old Monk. The Master said, "Sit for a moment and drink some tea," and then slowly examined the inscriptions on the wall.
There was a poem deriding monks, its style much like that of Hanshan; the verse read:
"The Five Pestilences do not strike him, yet his head is shaven of itself; Yellow cloth covers his body, and he is a monk indeed. He understands neither the Buddha-dharma nor the worldly dharma."
He was as capable as one who eats pigs and dogs; in an empty room, he took his leave in an instant, not daring to encounter his sharp edge again.
The layman Huang Qian, courtesy name Jinjing, was a native of Yiwu in Wuzhou.

At the beginning of the Tianli era, an imperial decree summoned all monks and scholars skilled in calligraphy to assemble at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou to gild the characters for the Great Canon of the Honored Sutras. The layman also...

He anticipated this; whenever he ate, he invariably stayed together with the assembly of monks. If separate utensils were provided for him, he was displeased, even to the point of reviling them and departing without eating.

He once inscribed a poem on a hanging cliff depicting ink-plum blossoms, which said: "Fluttering, the spring breeze blows equally upon all; Why do you perch upon such a high place? Let others harbor their own inverted thoughts;

I wish to see you cast yourself from the precipice."* *The final line is a pun: "sàxiá" (撒崖) means "to scatter from the cliff," but it is homophonous with "shāxiá" (殺崖), meaning "to kill at the cliff," referring to the act of committing suicide.*
Hand Shi also inscribed a eulogy for the portrait of Dongpo, saying: "The Fifth Patriarch, a man beyond the mundane world, Long ago severed the causes of birth in Saṃsāra.
Who could possibly capture with a brush The hand that reaches into empty space, To seek his body beyond bodies in years to come?
He inscribed the portrait of Huang Valley (Shangu), saying: "Laughing to death was Old Huaitang back then; Upon meeting, he insisted the osmanthus was fragrant. [He] opened the scroll...
His countenance remains entirely as it was before; how could his nostrils ever have been longer or shorter?

This scholar has attained fame through his writings and flourished as a preeminent master of Confucianism in his generation. Because his realization had reached the subtlest depths, he unconsciously accorded with the intent of the Sages.
Moreover, living among our own kind, he did not deign to distinguish himself from us—this too is truly admirable.
The verse sent by Chief Seat Xuan’an Shi of Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou to the Hermitage Master Woyun says: Horses gallop together within the golden garden;

A mere inch often triggers the suspicion of one clutching his sword. When the moon shines upon a thousand trees of plum blossoms like snow, It is the moment one returns from a dream upon the pillow of the cloud-reclining hermitage.
The verse composed by Huàn’ān Zhù, the Head Seat at Tiāntóng in Míngzhōu, upon paying respects at the ancestral pagoda of Yìng’ān, says:

A slumbering tiger, glaring with eyes that pierce through a keyhole; He took Zhōngfēng as his mountain of refuge. Had he not possessed even a single broken sand-pot, It would have been difficult for his descendants to survive.
The Venerable Xichang Yong of Tiantong in Mingzhou composed a verse on silkworms that says: "The mulberry trees are bare and the *zhè* trees are exhausted;

only then does the heart find rest. The laborious work of weaving is gathered into a single cocoon. Having dared to enter the furnace coals and the boiling cauldrons, for the sake of others, it depends upon a single thread."
The verse "Listening to the Rain" by Chan Master Keshang of Fulong in Yixing says: "Drops dripping from the eaves are perfectly clear;
Sentient beings, deluded of themselves, call them 'sounds. I too have spent many years chasing after external things; On this spring night, one pillow makes sleep difficult to achieve."
The verse of Chan Master Shou, Head Seat of Jiufeng in Ruizhou, at the time of his death, says: "Seventy-two years, this side and that side;
Eating the food of the ten directions, practicing the Zen of Bodhidharma. This morning, with one cast, I turn my body and depart; Laughing until the bystander’s eye is split in half."
Chan Master Wujin Zu-deng of Yunfeng on Mount Tiantai was the son of the Wang family of Siming. Initially, he met Rixi Yong at Tianning Temple;
he subsequently studied under Fangshan and various other great masters. Eventually, he planted his staff atop Yunfeng Peak and remained there for fifty years, never venturing beyond the mountain.
On the eighth day of the second month in the Jiyou year of the Hongwu era, he manifested a slight illness. Toward night...
Halfway through, he looked to his left and right and said, "Is the sky beginning to brighten? They replied, "Not yet. Someone asked, "At such a moment as this, what would you do, Master?
The Master broke into a smile and said, "In the past, when Deshan was sitting ill, a monk asked him, 'Is there anyone who does not fall ill?'"

Deshan said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is it that is not ill? Deshan said, "A-ye, a-ye. [The monk asked,] "Can one call such a thing 'ill'? The assembly was speechless. The Master said, "The physical body is impermanent; seek realization while there is still time. When the moment comes, I shall depart. An attendant held up paper and requested a verse. The Master said, "It is not as if I have no verse; would you rather I did not die? The attendant said, "Please grant me one. The Master wrote: The body is like a tree in the autumn wind; The mind is like the moon reflected in water. When the tree falls and the moon sets, How can there be any more sorrow? Having finished the verse, he passed away. The attendant asked, "Why did you say earlier that you would not die without a verse? The Master replied, "I was merely testing you. The attendant said, "If you had not granted me the verse, I would have died with you. The Master said, "You are truly a man of the Way. He then had the attendant burn the verse and cremate his remains. The ashes were placed in a stupa at Mount Lu. At that time, the Master was seventy-two years old. The Master’s dharma heirs included Xuefeng Yicun, Yunju Daoying, Dongshan Liangjie, and others. His lineage flourished greatly. Later, the Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty bestowed upon him the posthumous title "National Teacher Dajian. His stupa was named "Jingshan. His teachings are recorded in the *Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Dajian*. This concludes the biography of National Teacher Dajian. It is said that the Master’s teaching style was simple and direct, and he was particularly skilled at guiding students through sudden encounters. He often used everyday activities—whether eating, sleeping, or working—as opportunities for awakening.
