The man’s request became even more insistent. [The Master] then wrote: "Arising and ceasing, coming and going—these are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
Having toppled the five Sumeru mountains, all is vast and open, without front or back. He threw down his brush, sat upright, and passed away.

Chan Master Xueting of Xianlin Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Gui family of Renhe. Having lost his father at the age of seven, he suffered from smallpox and wind-related ailments, which left both his eyes with impaired vision.
He sought to leave the household life several times and eventually visited Xiuxiu at Xianlin Temple; upon their first meeting, they reached a state of mutual accord.
While reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he encountered the passage, "Upon the tip of a single hair, a jeweled king-realm appears," and harbored doubts. Later, he traveled to Qianming Temple in Jiangyin.
At the temple, he beheld the Wanfo Ge (Ten Thousand Buddhas Pavilion) with its golden and azure splendor towering before his eyes. Suddenly, he attained a realization.
On New Year’s Eve of the first year of the Hongzhi era, hearing the sound of the bells, his years of practice and conduct dissolved of their own accord like a crumbling wall.

He composed a verse: “The perfect resonance is not heard by the mind; The great chiliocosm is illuminated as one. Having brushed past the ultimate barrier, There remains nothing more of primordial subtlety. Yimao [1495]. Xiuxiu.

He accepted the invitation of Yingjing Ci and again attended upon him as a disciple, whereupon he received his seal of approval. The Master styled himself Huanjì (Illusory Dweller). He once said: "Illusion is the trace of dwelling;
dwelling is the mark of illusion. When illusion arises, dwelling perishes; when dwelling is fully realized, it is entirely illusion. When illusion pursues dwelling, it is entirely dwelling.
When cataracts in the eye produce flowers, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth appear; when the cataracts do not produce flowers, there is only true emptiness."
The ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is entrusted to illusion; truly, it is like a child’s play.
When the Chan Master Yongning Guyuanqing of Jinling heard the crowing of a cock, he attained realization. He composed a verse, saying: "Cock-a-doodle-doo!
The golden cock announces the dawn; Were it not for its cry, how could one know? The three thousand worlds are entirely like snow— At the bottom of the well..."
The mud snake dances the *zhazhi*.
The Venerable Huainyou had long served in various monastic assemblies and was held in high esteem by his peers.

While staying at Tianwang Temple in Dingzhou, he cultivated himself through the Way, remaining beyond the reach of intimacy or estrangement with others. After some time, he said to the assembly, "I am departing. Some...
This was his playful jest. Urged to compose a verse, he immediately took up brush and paper and wrote in large characters:
"Coming, he does not enter the gate; going, he does not leave the door. He shatters empty space, with no room for evasion. Clapping hands and laughing 'he-he,' he returns home;

the white clouds have dispersed, and the green mountains are revealed. Thereupon, he sat cross-legged and passed away suddenly. The monastic officials hurriedly called out and shook him, whereupon the Master opened his eyes once more.
Mumu raised his hand in thanks and said, "I have not brought trouble upon you; please take good care of yourself. At that time, the Prefect, Lord Su, also went to pay his respects.
Touching the master's remains, he remarked, "He was truly a monk who had settled all matters."
Chan Master Yiweng Keguān of Shèngshòu Monastery in Jiāxīng left the household life at Nánpíng. He attained realization under Chēxī.
At the beginning of the Jiànyán era, he presided over Shèngshòu; subsequently, he moved to Dècáng in Dāng hú and retired to Zhúān.

He often expressed his own contentment, saying, "The wind through the pines, the mountain moon—these are my inexhaustible robes and bowl. In the *Xīnmǎo* year of the Qiándào era, Chancellor Wèi Jì invited him to preside over [Wú].
At the North Chan Monastery, he entered the hall just on the Double Ninth festival. Pointing to the seat, he said: "An inch of ash within my breast has long since grown cold;
a thousand strands of snow upon my head have not yet melted. My aged steps are fit only for level ground; I know not for what reason I have climbed this high again."
Chan Master Baiyun Mingxing of Mount Wugong in Jizhou was the son of the Zhang family from Changting in Min. He entered the monastic community at Longgui Tong and received the full precepts.
Devoting himself exclusively to the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), he suddenly sighed, saying: "A man of great purpose must not leave his path of cultivation incomplete."

"What does it matter if one undergoes birth and death? he asked. He then traveled everywhere, seeking out renowned masters; whenever a karmic connection was established, the Master would not readily accept them as his teachers.
Upon meeting Panyang, his lingering doubts were suddenly resolved. Panyang bestowed upon him his dharma robe and whisk. He lived in seclusion at Mount Xiaofeng for over twenty years.

When Governor Wang urged him to emerge from retreat and take up a monastic seat, the Master again moved to a remote thatched hut. Disciples flocked to him, and the community gradually grew into a refined assembly.
Lan took his leave of the assembly one day, saying, "I am going. When the assembly asked where he was going, the Master presented this verse:
"The bright moon falls into the heart of the waves; white clouds span across the ridge. If you wish to recognize the original mechanism, it is like an iron ox swallowing a great elephant.
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at his home mountain. He was eighty-four years of age at the time of his death.

Chan Master Fomi was a native of Kunming. He left the household life at Tianhua Temple. In the *guihai* year of the Hongwu era, he traveled to the capital, where he was granted a robe, alms bowl, and mendicant’s staff.
He subsequently journeyed through the two provinces of Zhejiang. On the twelfth month of the *jiyou* year of the Xuande era, he bathed, changed his robes, and wrote this verse:
"Last year I was seventy-nine; this year I have reached eighty. I have traveled ten thousand *li* in search of the Way; now my worldly ties are severed."
Having finished [his work], he threw down his brush, sat upright, and passed away.
Chan Master Jingfeng Ying of Mount Jing was the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*) of Mount Jing; he returned to Ningbo. Chushi Qi composed a verse to see him off, which says:
"The first seat atop Mount Lingxiao, who has thoroughly clarified and shattered all Mahāyāna dharmas; the hundred negations and the four propositions are all..."
Already free from [duality]. "Who dares to harmonize with the white snow and springtime? Entering the hall, he said: "The conduct of a patch-robed monk is no ordinary matter.

Drawing the blade from its scabbard, it leaves nothing hidden. Seizing the food and driving the plow, the true command is fully realized; east and west, there is no longer any plunder for ghosts to divide."
Chan Master Jing’an Zhuang of Mount Jing was a native of Taizhou. From childhood, he loathed the impurities of meat and wine and held the worldly dust of secular life in low esteem.

His parents allowed him to renounce the household life, and he traveled extensively to study under various masters until he thoroughly realized the source of the Zen lineage. He subsequently went to rely upon Quan Shi at Tianjie Monastery, where Quan appointed him to two seats of authority.
Before long, he was promoted to preside over Mount Jing, where his spiritual influence flourished and prospered. In the twelfth year of the Yongle era, he received an imperial decree.

He entered the capital to assist in the compilation of the Great Canon. While residing at Tianjie Monastery, the Junior Mentor, Lord Yao, and others submitted successive memorials recommending him to serve as abbot;
he firmly declined and would not accept. He returned to Mount Jing and passed away there. His stupa was erected on the small pond at Shuiling.
The lay practitioner Shen Shirong was a native of Jian’an. During the Hongwu era, he served as a *dai-zhao* (waiting-call scribe) at the Hanlin Academy.
He once composed fourteen treatises titled *Xù Yuánjiào Lùnbiàn Jiè* (Continuation of the Treatise on the Original Teaching: Debates and Explanations). A summary of his arguments states:
"Because the categories of human beings differ, the teachings of the Sage are not uniform; this is why the traces of these teachings vary. Nevertheless, in practicing goodness..."
They are the same. They all converge upon order. When one exhausts their ultimate subtlety, it does not go beyond the single mind. This is why the principle of these teachings is the same.
This mind and this principle have never differed throughout the world. Although their outward manifestations differ, if one traces them back to their limit, they must necessarily result in the same.
It is further said: "If one attains the root and forgets the branches, one will not be constrained by their manifestations."

If one investigates the source of the nature of the mind and proceeds directly toward the ground of ultimate goodness, then diverse paths will converge at the same destination, with no distinction between self and other.
It is further said: "This mind transforms yet remains unmoved; it dies yet is not extinguished.
This principle is as clear as the bright sun; how could it possibly be obscured by oneself? If a person recognizes this mind and awakens to it...

This principle: in the Confucian tradition, one who embodies it is a true Confucian; in the monastic tradition, one who embodies it is a sage-monk. When the mind is clouded and the principle is lost, one knows not where to turn.
Since the foundation itself has been forfeited, what benefit is there in further polemical debate?

Furthermore, it is said that the Confucians are intent on excluding Buddhism, and thus they propound the doctrine of annihilation upon death in order to refute the theory of the cycle of birth and death; yet they do not realize that they, in turn, contradict the teachings of the Duke of Zhou.
The intent of the Sage Confucius was profound; yet [this doctrine] goes so far as to deny cause and effect and abolish the principles of Heaven, attributing the creation of all things to ignorance.

It claims that both good and evil carry no retribution: the most benevolent suffer premature death while the violent live out their full span; the reverent and cautious meet with calamity, while the licentious and dissolute obtain blessings.
The petty man prospers by mere chance, while the gentleman suffers though innocent. Failing to clarify prior causes, it offers convoluted explanations that are logically untenable.
It obstructs correct knowledge and vision; its delusions are likewise profound. Furthermore, it is said: "Since the Han dynasty, successive scriptures have arrived.
Examining their ultimate aim, they truly exhaust the source of mind-nature and enter the realm of supreme goodness.

Moreover, they are not merely words and letters. Even such things as the sun, moon, clouds, and mists; the flying and the hidden, the moving and the stationary; and forms, sounds, scents, and tastes—"
All arrive at the wondrous principle; this is the essence (*tattva*) of this teaching.

Gain and loss, opposition and compliance, birth and death, suffering and joy, and the flux of phenomena—all within which the eternally abiding true nature remains; this is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of this teaching.

Writing and sound, speech and silence, eating and acting, movement and rest, and the codes of deportment and ritual regulations—all universally responding according to conditions; this is the function (*vṛtti*) of this teaching. Possessing these three, its Way is great.
Go forth! Who could possibly refute and destroy this, or reject and sever it? The wise person embodies the principles of our Buddha and contemplates the Way of the Sage Confucius;
thus, their study of the nature and principles of things becomes even more detailed, while the texts that exhort toward good and warn against evil—

This is especially urgent and of great benefit to the teachings of name and instruction (mingjiao). How could one allow oneself to create such contradiction and obscure the innate knowing (liangzhi) of one’s own mind?
His *Brief Explanation on Contemplating the Mind* (*Guansin jie*) states: "The mind encompasses all phenomena, and phenomena penetrate the source of the mind.

The ultimate principle is difficult to know; by contemplating the mind, it is attained. Therefore, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he sighed, saying: 'How marvelous!'"
He universally perceives that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, due to deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize them.

Generally, because people are deluded regarding the essence of this mind and do not know how to seek it within themselves, they are externally distracted by the six sense-objects and internally afflicted by the two maladies of dullness and agitation.
Consequently, they remain cramped and ignorant, harboring biased and heterodox views. Only the Buddha...
The Tathāgata looked back upon this mind and suddenly awakened to its fundamental nature, thereby attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.

Consequently, regarding the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of mundane dharmas and the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of supramundane dharmas, there is none that he does not penetrate with clarity and without obstruction; there is none that he does not comprehend with vast penetration and without contradiction.
Therefore, he is titled the Great Teacher of the Three Realms and the Compassionate Father of the Ten Directions. Yet even today, the Confucian scholars still do not recognize this.
The fundamental mind—how could it possibly use the mind to observe objects? It is further said: "If one does not recognize one's own mind, then its very foundation is lost;
how then can one observe things and clarify principles? It is also said: "The *Book of Yu* states: 'The human mind is perilous; the Dao-mind is subtle.
Only through refinement and singleness may one truly grasp the Mean. This is the source of the study of the mind. The human mind consists of deluded thoughts..."
Furthermore, one is endangered by attachment to perversions. The mind of the Way is the principle of Heaven; it is subtle because it is beyond the reach of discursive thought.
"Refined" means not being obscured; "one" means not being mixed. Because there is no thinking, it is not obscured; because there is no conditioning, it is not mixed.
Only thus can one exhaustively fulfill ultimate sincerity and firmly maintain this Middle Way. This "Middle" is precisely the "Middle" of the *Zhongyong* (Doctrine of the Mean).

It resides in the mind and not in external things; it resides within and not without. This is precisely what Mencius referred to as the state where "joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been manifested.
Later Confucian scholars simply equated this "Centrality" (*zhong*) with the meaning of the state before emotional consciousness has moved;
this is close to our Buddha’s principle of the "non-arising of a single thought-moment," lacking only the element of awakening. The Confucians explain Centrality as being "neither biased nor..."

To say that "leaning" (yi) refers to being neither excessive nor deficient, and thus constitutes the harmony of the emotions already manifested in their due measure, would contradict the intention of Zisi.
For when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been manifested, there are no visible forms or appearances;
how, then, could there be matters of partiality, excess, or deficiency? Furthermore, he said: "Since they do not know the subtlety of observing the mind, they merely wish to..."
To calculate with a deluded mind and observe objects to exhaustively seek principle is like trying to use a dusty mirror that has not been polished or water in which a whirlpool has not ceased;
it is impossible for them to reflect objects. Failing to realize this principle within oneself, one strives only to seek it externally;

thus, while scholarly understanding increases, one moves ever further from the Way. It is also said: "If one day you observe the mind and realize the principle, then all the myriad things under heaven—"

The principles of all things and all affairs are thoroughly permeated by this. The Master also said: "If for a single day one can overcome the self and return to the ritual propriety (*li*), the whole world will acknowledge his benevolence.
This, too, seeks that which resides within. A brief discussion on the distinction between the Inner Teaching and the Outer Teaching states:
Because there are differences between the Inner and Outer teachings, there is a disparity in the depth of their realization of principle. One seeks it within the mind.
The nature is this very thing; to seek it externally is merely intellectual understanding. Therefore, when the mind is penetrating, the myriad dharmas are all harmoniously integrated;
when one clings to appearances, one is naturally obscured even before one's own eyes. Alas! The error of seeking externally is most extreme.

Today, the decline of Confucian learning is such that those who are superficial and flowery certainly take literary composition as their task, while even those who are sincere and substantial do no more than focus on textual meaning.
As for our school, when it comes to the study of the mind, we are all utterly bewildered. The great Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty deeply understood this malady;

they also knew that the work upon the mind is what constitutes the fundamental root. It would have been appropriate for them to emphasize the root and suppress the branches, thereby refuting the errors of mere words and texts.
Why, then, do you contradict yourself? Furthermore, you say: "In the past, the sages all [focused] on the internal..."

Learning is fundamental, yet its application is extended outward. Later generations of literary scholars focused exclusively on external matters and consequently failed to recognize the source of learning in the mind;

they instead took intellectual understanding as their primary task. Only with the school of Henan in the Song dynasty did there first emerge discourse on human nature and principle (*xingli*), accompanied by traces of practical cultivation.
Nevertheless, they understood only the function of the mind without investigating the substance of the mind, and thus remained ignorant [of its true nature].
They nourish the "centrality" that has not yet been manifested, yet remain obscure regarding the principle of the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*).

Prior to the differentiation of the two polarities (*liǎng yí*), they sometimes mistake physical principles for the principle of human nature (*xìng lǐ*); consequently, the relationship between the fundamental and the derivative, as well as essence and function, remains unclarified, and the Way of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius becomes obscured.
Furthermore, it is said: "To awaken is called 'internal,' while to understand is called 'external'"; this refers to the internal teaching and the external [teaching].

This is why their teachings differ. Confucians apply their efforts exclusively to the external; regarding all that lies beyond the reach of intellectual understanding, they no longer pursue investigation.
Consequently, they do not know the Way of "upright adherence to the Mean," nor the place where the Heavenly Principle flows.

All these occur when thought does not arise and the desires for material things have been completely purified; yet, though one may practice with single-minded devotion, one will ultimately fail to enter the realm of the Sage.
Regarding the phrase "its functioning is its nature," a brief explanation says: The Great Awakening is without thought, yet it universally knows the Dharma-realm.
When consciousness and emotion possess attachments, they vainly give rise to the toils of the mundane world. Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally one.
The essence is one, yet due to delusion and awakening, there appear divergent paths. Buddha-nature resides precisely within the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue;

its wondrous function is never separate from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. It is simply this: not receiving a single speck of dust, yet not abandoning a single dharma—this is called "directly reaching the site of enlightenment" and "suddenly beholding one's original face.
Furthermore, it is said: The Sutra states, "If I press my finger... [The text continues: "...the ocean [of consciousness]..."

Yin Fangguang, as soon as you raise your mind, the dust of affliction arises first. If you can realize this through non-mind, then the myriad phenomena of the universe will be reflected clearly in a single mirror.
This is what is meant by "the finger pointing, light is emitted," which refers to the manifestation of the entire body when not a single thought arises.

If one speaks of this "nature," it is merely to cling to a shadow. Should even a hair’s breadth of thought remain attached, or a fleeting emotion arise, the signs of karma will be manifest once more, and one remains as before in delusion and inversion.
This is what is meant by "the dust of the mind arises": as soon as the six sense organs move, they are obscured by clouds.
Reaching this point, there is no way to apply effort. It is also said: "In the eras prior to the Three Dynasties, there was no name for 'Buddha'; only..."
The Sage Emperor, succeeding Heaven and establishing the ultimate standard, traced the origin back to Heaven. He spoke of how humans obtain this principle of luminous awareness from Heaven;
therefore, he said, "That which Heaven mandates is called nature (*xing*). Nature refers to the fact that all people take this luminous awareness as their essence.
To act in accordance with this awakened nature so as to remain constantly unobscured is called the Way (*dao*). Cultivation (*xiu*) means nourishing one's joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure.

It is the state of equilibrium before any movement has arisen. This "equilibrium" refers to the time when private desires have not yet emerged; it is that which is purely the principle of Heaven (*tianli*).
When private desires have not yet arisen, there is neither thought nor action; it is tranquil and unmoving. This tranquility is sincerity (*cheng*). Ultimate sincerity is without ceasing.
Therefore it is said: "The Way cannot be departed from for even a moment. This is followed by the injunctions to be "cautious and apprehensive" (*ji-jin kong-ju*).

At the juncture where there is neither seeing nor hearing, one must not allow the hidden and subtle [mind] to be stirred. All of this is to nourish this "centrality" (*zhong*) prior to its manifestation;

because one is constantly aware and never deluded, what is manifested becomes the harmony of being "moderate in accordance with the seasons" (*zhong-jie zhi he*). Thus, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom will hit the mark without the need for deliberation. This—
This is the purpose of the teaching. A later chapter states: "The sincere is quiescence; the enlightened is awakening.
Quiescence within awakening is called the Way of Heaven; awakening within quiescence is called the Way of Humanity. Both are principles for the cultivation of the Path. It further says:

"The Sage, having attained this principle, established the laws of worldly governance and instruction. Our Buddha, having attained this principle, established the worldly [teachings] that transcend [the world]."
Regarding the Dharma of liberation in the world: the Confucian school clarifies only the Way of Heaven and Man;
our Buddha, however, clarifies the Way of the Four Sages and the Six Realms of Beings. If one exhaustively masters the Way of Heaven and Man, one can then advance toward the Buddhist Way.
If one lacks clarity regarding the principles of nature (*xingli*), then the principles of Heaven and Man will remain obscure; how then could one possibly fathom the principles of the Buddha?
Ah! This scholar possessed far-reaching insight and complete talent; he profoundly mastered the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
His discourse was versatile and unimpeded, excising hidden obscurities and directly clarifying the essence of the mind. Moreover, his phrasing and purport were skillful and exquisite.
To say that he "Continued the Original Teaching" may truly be called one who was able to carry on the legacy of Tiantan.
The Great Master Yunqi Lianchi Zhu Hong was a native of the Shen clan of Renhe County in Hangzhou. At the age of seventeen, he enrolled in the local district school (*xiangxiang*).

He would regularly inscribe the four characters "the matter of birth and death" (*shengsi shi da*) upon his desk. One day, while handling a tea bowl, he dropped it and it shattered; at that moment, he attained a profound realization.

He recorded this experience as "seven strokes of the tally" (*qibigou*) to manifest his resolve. He then went to Mount Xishan to receive the tonsure under Master Xingtian and subsequently traveled north to visit various masters.
Yong again visited Xiaoyan at Liuxiang to seek instruction. Xiaoyan said, "You have come from three thousand li away to ask for my instruction;
what instruction do I have for you? The Master was suddenly enlightened and took his leave to return home. While passing through the road of Dongchang, he...
Hearing the sound of the drum at the watchtower, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "The events of thirty years ago are suspicious;
What marvel was this meeting three thousand *li* away? To burn incense and cast aside the halberd is but a trivial matter; Demons and Buddhas vainly contend over right and wrong.
Later, while residing at Yunqi, when the Court Gentleman Wang Zongmu asked him about the meaning of the mice scurrying about last night, he replied: "They have recounted it all."

Regarding a section of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Master asked, "When the cat suddenly bolts out, what then? Wang was speechless. The Master provided an answer on his behalf, saying, "The Dharma Master has run off;
only the lecture desk remains. He then offered this verse: "The mouse squeaks; the *Avataṃsaka* is clearly manifest.
How extraordinary, Minister Wang! You have been deluded by a beast. The cat suddenly bolts before the painted hall; At the head of the couch, he preaches the Dharma."
No news. No news. *The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya*, Chapter One: "The Sublime Array of Worldly Rulers.

At a time when famine was rampant and pestilence spread widely, with people dying of hunger by the roadside, the government opened its granaries to provide relief and ordered physicians to offer medical aid.
Master [Hui]ru was appointed to oversee these matters. The Minister of Personnel, Lord Yu Chunchi, requested that Huirui ordain five hundred individuals.
Regarding the circumstances of the sick monk, the Master said: "Huiri willingly accepted the status of a destitute son and abandoned himself to follow others;

Xiuyuan humiliated an ordinary citizen and led him from life toward death. It is a pity that five hundred monks only knew how to nod their heads in agreement and depart, yet not one remained lying high and did not rise.
This caused Huiri to manifest eccentricities and delude the masses, bringing calamity upon his descendants. The Lord of the Prefecture [is deeply concerned]..."
I deeply feel the maladies of the people. This mountain monk hurriedly rushed forward in a time of difficulty; in the midst of such urgency, I lost my bamboo staff.
Having no other recourse, I could not help but strike the abscess upon the layman’s body with my empty fist. I dare guarantee that his chronic ailment has been broken open and dispersed.
The poisonous blood flows freely; the ten thousand channels circulate; the hundred bones relax and stretch. Although it is thus, how can one person cause sentient beings not to see the Way?
When a single leaf returns with the turning of the Yang, spring fills the thousand forests. Let this matter rest for now.
As for holding a bamboo staff all day long, pointing east and waving west—this is not as good as remaining constantly upon the wooden block, morning and night.
Hold fast to the evening watch. As you guard and re-guard, suddenly the withered tree will bloom again. This is nothing other than the dead person coming back to life.
What need is there to speak of bamboo and wood? Take it for granted that all the grasses, trees, and forests throughout the entire world shall all attain Buddhahood.
Why is this? The empty essence beyond the green things is itself the Tathāgata’s solid and true mind. Question: Regarding the practice of Zen meditation (chán).
"Can the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha be harmonized [with other teachings]? The Master said: "If they were two separate things, how could they be harmonized? Question:

"When the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) said, 'You have cleared away my clouds of delusion. When Subhūti sat in meditation without speaking, Śakra declared, 'You have well explained Prajñāpāramitā.
What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "In that state of long silence, one desires to have one's delusions cleared away, yet the five aggregates [remain]."
The haze stretches for ten thousand *li*. Sitting in quiet contemplation at the border, one intends to hear the *Prajñāpāramitā*;

yet after much time has passed since the teaching was finished, even so, those who "catch the meaning on the tip of the whip" or see "flowers flying in the void"—what exactly have they seen? To those gathering ferns, he said: "The heart-essence—how can I explain it to you?
You have missed the fine season before the mountain. Fern, fern! He then raised his fist toward them.
On the first day of the New Year, the Master addressed the assembly: "Today we celebrate the New Year; the seasons have changed once more. But what was it like yesterday?
[This was spoken on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month. He once praised himself, saying: "Nine out of ten drawings fail to capture my likeness;
they vex the artist to no end. Perhaps this one comes close enough; for now, let it remain as an offering. If you say this is the true one, it remains just as it is.
"Two things? Not two things? Thirty blows! At the time of his death, he informed the assembly half a month in advance, saying, "I am about to depart for another realm.
No one could fathom this. When the appointed day arrived, he manifested a slight illness; facing west, he sat upright and passed away.
Zibo Daguan Zhenke was the son of Shen of Jiqu. By nature, he was generous-spirited and fierce;
as a youth, he did not enjoy playing games and had no fondness for seeing women. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and began traveling to study under various masters.

Upon hearing the recitation of Zhang Zhuo’s verse—which states that severing deluded thoughts increases one's afflictions and that even seeking True Suchness is a form of deviation—he became deeply perplexed by it. One day, during a midday meal, he...
Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and said, "Had I been under the seat of Linji or Deshan, a single slap would have awakened me; why use such talk of 'how' and 'what'?
He traveled north to the capital to visit Bianrong. In the autumn of the *wuli* *guimao* year, the "Seditious Book" (*yaoshu*) incident suddenly broke out.
The Master met with misfortune. Previously, Emperor Shenzong had personally transcribed the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; by chance, a drop of perspiration fell and soaked the paper.

Suspecting that the scroll should be placed in a new case, he sent a close attendant to consult the Master. The Master presented this verse in response: "A single drop of imperial perspiration shall serve as a bridge and raft for ten thousand generations."
The inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma radiates light from this source; [the Emperor] was greatly delighted and thus bestowed his attention upon it.
Upon seeing the memorial, he felt deep compassion for him. Since one cannot escape the Dharma, when the imperial decree finally arrived, he merely composed the "Shen" (Examination).

During the interrogation, the Master remained composed in countenance and maintained his principles with great rectitude. With his aged and infirm body, he fully endured the lashes and beatings. When he was brought before the throne...
He did not yield even unto death. On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he was cast into prison. When the judicial authorities were about to execute him, the Master spoke a verse, saying:
"A single laugh has its own cause; Who would have known that the Great Mass does not tolerate a speck of dust? From this moment, I gather up my mortal feet;
The flower upon the iron stake shall bloom without waiting for spring. He further said: "Since worldly affairs are thus, what is the use of remaining here for long? And so...
After finishing his bath, he instructed his attendant, saying, "I am departing now. Please convey my thanks to all the Dharma protectors of Jiangnan.
He then spoke a verse: "When circumstances arise, one finally beholds the heroic bone; The meeting between Master Da and Mr. Wu was surely a karmic affinity from past lives.

I shall return to the West while you remain in the North; Our conversations over many lifetimes shall be even more clear and resonant. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. At that time, it was the [Xth] year of the Wanli era of Emperor Shenzong of the Ming dynasty.
The date was the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the Gui-mao year. He was sixty-one years of age and forty-one years since his ordination (*lajia*).
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa to the left of the Mañjuśrī Terrace at Mount Jing. His works, the *Zibai ji* (Collected Works of Zi-bai), were circulated in the world.
Chan Master Wunian Shendao of Huangbo in Ruizhou was the son of the Xiong family of Macheng in Huangzhou.
While wandering at Mount Dangshan, he encountered a long-resident monk who said to him, "A single grain of rice from the ten directions is as heavy as Mount Sumeru;

if you do not realize the Way, you shall return wearing fur and horns. The Master was struck with awe. Later, he heard a monk cite a question asked of Dayu: "How is it? [Dayu replied: "Like a man carrying a bowl of rice on his head, walking through the marketplace. The Master was deeply moved.

"This is the meaning of the Westward Journey. Xiu replied, "Yellow gourd, eggplant. The Master was greatly perplexed. He subsequently traveled to Mount Wutai and Mount Funiu, visiting and questioning various spiritual teachers everywhere.
One night, he heard the sounds of laughter and weeping mingling together and attained a realization. On another day, he accidentally struck his head with the lid of a chest;
sweat poured from his entire body, and he clapped his hands, laughing and saying, "The whole earth is this very state of non-thought—what is there to doubt?"
Having visited Longhu, he went together with the lay practitioner Li Zhuowu to Sima Mountain. There, a lecture master arrived.
The layman asked the master, "The essence is originally pure; why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

After the master had finished his lecture according to the text, the layman looked at the Master [Zhaozhou] and said, "Try to explain this for me. As the Master was about to open his mouth, the layman placed his hand upon the Master's knee.
Tou said, "What about this? At these words, the Master suddenly attained great enlightenment. He spoke a verse, saying: "For over forty years I did not rest my efforts;
I pursued it and pursued it until no trace remained. Now that I have pursued it to the point of having nothing to rely upon, Only then do I regret the efforts I previously applied.
Later, a monk asked, "Is the Way truly existent, or is it non-existent? The Master replied, "To speak of existence or non-existence—both are [dualistic extremes]."
[The student] fell into contradiction. He asked, "How can one attain it immediately? The Master said, "Seeking nothing, one attains it. He asked, "What is the essence of the Way?
The Master said, "My mouth is full; I cannot speak of it. He asked, "What is it like when the four elements disperse? The Master held up his fist and said, "It is this."
"This does not belong to the four great elements. Question: "The ancients said, 'Expel it from the throat and lips.
Speak one phrase! How would you speak this one phrase? The Master said: "I do not expel it from my throat and lips.
You, first, try to speak a phrase! The monk had no reply. The Master said: "You have your mouth stuffed by sounds. Question: "Seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha."
“Is it so? The Master said, “It is. [The monk] asked, “Nature is formless; how can it be seen? The Master said, “Nature has form; it is simply that you do not see it.
[The monk] said, “I beg the Master to point it out for me to see. The Master said, “I say that you do not see it.
[The monk] asked, “How does one transcend birth and death? The Master called to the monk. The monk responded. The Master said, “From this very place...”
[The monk] came out and said, "I do not understand the words spoken by the Master. The Master said, "If you wait until you understand them, what will you be fit for?
He further wrote in a letter to a friend: "Sitting motionless in the mountains, I hear no news of worldly affairs.

To study the Way, one must seize the sharp intensity of the initial resolve; one must seek a clear understanding immediately. Only when one can achieve liberation amidst the conditions and objects encountered in daily life will it be so."
Otherwise, as days turn into months and years deepen, one gradually forgets their diligence and continues to drift along with worldly sentiments.
These days, practitioners of the Way merely seek eloquence and cleverness; they forget their own fundamental life-source (the *benming yuanchen*) until illness and suffering descend upon them.
When their hands and feet fall into a frantic scramble, not even a single bit of that cleverness is of any use, yet they still harbor no resentment toward themselves.
Your mindfulness is not earnest; your resolve is mistaken. To say, on the contrary, that even the ancient sages and Buddhas were merely like this is to slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
You have not yet awakened from your dream; do not misunderstand.

A single word or half-sentence of the ancient sages is like a hair-piercing sword, rice with iron nails, soup made of wood chips, or a drum smeared with poison—there is no place for you to lean your ear. There is none.
At the place where you bring forth your words, there is no place for your intentional effort; there is no place for your proximity. Meeting on a narrow path, one misses it in the blink of an eye.
Reaching this point, emotions wither and thoughts are severed; reflection is exhausted and the spirit is spent. Cold and heat are both forgotten, and sleep and food are alike abandoned.
In this state where nothing can be grasped, one suddenly awakens in a flash of insight. The mind that runs in pursuit ceases all at once, and there is a sense of profound joy and liberation.
Throughout his life, he no longer pursued sounds or forms; his intellectual perceptions were entirely dissolved, and the traces of right and wrong vanished.
Having reached this state, all clever understanding and the supernatural powers of subject and object were surrendered to others.

Day after day, he appeared as if dull-witted and mute, with an empty belly and a leisurely mind. No one in the world could recognize him, and even ghosts and spirits could not see him. What could Old Yan do?
To settle the mind in its proper place is itself true mastery.
Chan Master Fangtan Yifeng of Baima Temple in Kuizhou was the son of the Luo family from Dazhou.

He studied under Yun’an at Jinfoshan, who instructed him to contemplate: "What is this mechanism that ghosts and spirits cannot perceive? After three years, he attained realization. He then left the gorges.
He visited various spiritual friends and settled in a thatched hut by the Double Creek (Shuangxi). One day at noon while cooking rice, he heard a sound from within the steamer;
suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "The Three Essentials and the Three Principles have no origin; Exhausting all mental ingenuity, there is nowhere to seek them.
Suddenly, a single sound—what could it be? White clouds and blue peaks nod their heads in unison. He once traveled through Zhejiang and resided in a hermitage in Qingliang, Hangzhou.
Píngzhēnjìyìn once relied upon him. One day, the Master brought up the story of Qingfeng’s "The Boy Bǐngdīng Comes to Seek Fire" and questioned him, saying:
"Qingfeng spoke thus, and Fayan also spoke thus; why is it that some attained awakening while others did not? Yìn replied:
"At first, he attempted to settle his mind through conceptual cognition, and for that reason he did not awaken. Later, he directly took it up as his own."
Thus, he was able to achieve a great awakening. The Master suddenly raised his fist, struck the desk once, and said in a stern voice, "If that is so, have you now attained great awakening?
Dayin hesitated; the Master then scolded him harshly and drove him out. Dayin was left with sweat pouring down his back.

From that point on, he applied himself to practice with resolute determination. In the Renchen year of the Wanli era, the Master returned to Baima. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?"
Yi. The Master said, "Fire burns at both ends, yet smoke issues from only one. The Master constantly held a small hand-drum (*tiao-gu*) in his hands;

on one face was inscribed the character "Chù" (矗), and on the other, the character "Bēn" (犇). Whenever he responded to an occasion, he would frequently raise and shake it. He passed away peacefully, and his stupa was enshrined at Longshen Mountain.
Chan Master Xian of Yang’an at Ehu in Guangxin Prefecture was the son of the Zhu family from Shangrao in the prefecture.

While visiting relatives, he happened upon a practitioner of the Way who was discussing the meaning of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). Upon hearing these words, the Master thoroughly realized the great principle that all things and the self are equal.
He went to Taiting in Luoyang to shave his head, then returned south to Jiaoshan to observe the winter retreat. There, while on the river, he heard the sound of a boat being pushed through the water.
Having attained realization, he composed a verse, saying: "The night is still and the river is vast; I push my boat with a heavy thud. I know not where it goes."
"The load is light on one side. He visited Huashan and heard the master’s teaching on the kōan "A lifetime's livelihood, neither six nor seven.
He harbored doubts and applied himself with fierce intensity for seven days, until his body and mind were suddenly liberated. He subsequently returned to his hometown and resided at Lingshan.
He once painted a great circle (*mahāmaṇḍala*) upon the wall and wrote: "Inside, do not let it be stained black; outside, do not let it be marred by words. When someone approached him...
Whether within the circle or outside the circle, those who can provide a definitive commentary are permitted to study the Way without doubt; otherwise, it is all merely a state of despondency.
Later, he moved to Ehu, where for ten years no seat-holder (abbot) was established. When Wuxi came to attend upon him, they reached mutual accord through the "Mu" (No) koan of Zhaozhou.
He was invited to occupy that office, and [the Master] presented him with a verse, saying: "Ten years at Ehu, the seat remained vacant; one..."
In the morning, for what reason is the "Youth" established? Two eyebrows with eight strands. You must know that Buddhas and Patriarchs do not allow anything to pass before them;
they have also placed him within a room locked with a gateless lock to test those who come later. A verse says: "The lock handed down from ancient times."
Rely on the key of wisdom to open it. If you lack the method for unlocking it, there is no need to come to meet me.
On the final day of the second month in the Dingsu year of the Wanli era, he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, prepared a vegetarian feast to bid farewell, and further presented this verse:
Within the illusory dream of over eighty years, An iron ox has plowed through the great void. At the moment of departure, I entrust to you this one phrase: The golden [rooster] at midnight...
The sun was red as it set behind the mountains when he sat upright and passed away.
The Great Master Hanshan Deqing of Caoxi in Shaoguo was the son of the Cai family of Quanpiao. In his youth, he studied the Confucian classics;
at the age of twelve, he took refuge with Master Lin of Ba’en as his teacher. At nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination, becoming a friend to Miaofeng. Once, by chance—
While reading Sengzhao’s *Treatises*, he reached the passage where a Brahmin who had left home returns white-haired;
a neighbor sees him and says, "Is that still the same man? The Brahmin replies, "I am the same man as before, yet I am not the man of before.
Suddenly, he attained realization and said, "Only today do I know that my nostrils point downward. Miaofeng asked, "What have you attained? The Master replied, "Last night, two earthen oxen met."
Dòu entered the water and departed; to this day, no news has been heard of him. Fēng laughed and said, "I am glad you have the capital for living on the mountain.
He then went to the capital city of Yān to visit the Patriarch Xiàoyán Bǎo. Bǎo asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the South. Bǎo said:
"Do you remember the way you came? The Master replied, "Once passed, it is simply over. Baoshou said, "You, however, have a clear understanding of where you have come from.
The Master then prostrated himself. Later, he was falsely accused by a Daoist priest for privately founding a temple and was sentenced to military exile in Leizhou.
Upon arriving at Shaoyang, he offered this verse of homage to the Patriarch: "A drop of water from Caoxi is itself the numinous source; it flows into the vast ocean where waves strike the heavens.
How many fish and dragons vie to undergo transformation, yet that single stream at the source remains refreshingly cool. Eleven years passed.

He was exempted from military service and remained at Caoxi for another nine years. Only then did he return to his monastic robes and go back to Mount Kuanglu, where he built a hermitage on Wuer Peak to plan for his retirement as a recluse.
The Master once visited Deshan to pay respects at the ancestral stupa, composing this verse:

"In the hall, idly holding the alms bowl, The lion playfully tames its cubs. In the moment of direct confrontation where turning back is difficult, At the time of silence with bowed head— I have not yet clarified the final word."
This verse leaves me in doubt to this day. I ask: regarding the events of those three years, how was it that you were able to know them so early?
A Verse on Dwelling in the Mountains says: Throughout my life, my traces have wandered east and west; Now in my old age, how could I choose where to perch among the trees?
Though my backbone may be as hard as iron, Alas, my leg bones are as soft as mud. Leisurely, I watch clouds rise from the precipitous ravines; Sitting, I face the solitary peak.
Listen to the birdsong; there is no need to further pick at words beyond the literal. The sounds and forms present before you are the total transmission, returning once more to Caoxi.
Not long after, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying: "My karmic conditions conflict with the times; where shall my transformation be entrusted? My work for this one period is finished."

"I shall now return," he said. He sought a bath, changed his robes, and sat upright until he passed away. This was on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the Guihai year of the Tianqi era of Emperor Ming Xizong.
He was seventy-eight years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination. His entire body was enshrined in the ancestral hall of Nanhua.
His work, the *Mengyou ji* (Dream Excursions Collection) in forty fascicles, has been circulated in the world.
Chan Master Wengu Guangyin of Zhenji Temple in Hangzhou was the son of Zhou [family] from Jiaśan.

His mother dreamed that the God of the Northern Dipper (Yuanshu Wu) brandished a sword and led various armored soldiers to protect her door before he was born. At the age of seven, he would often sit upright with his eyes closed.
His parents sent him to Kaiyuan Temple in Hangzhou for ordination. After his tonsure, the Master returned to visit his kin. His mother admonished him, saying: "The three..."

"Welcome, new bride! You are a Chan practitioner for a lifetime; you must exert yourself in this. The Master would often recount these two lines, finding them inexhaustible in their utility throughout his life.
One day, seeing a diagram of the Dharma-realm on the wall, he asked his teacher, "The ten realms arise from the mind."
"From where does the mind arise? His teacher was unable to answer. At that time, Master Yifeng was living in a thatched hut at Qingping; the Master went there to consult him.
Yifeng said, "If you wish to understand, you must attain a wondrous awakening. The Master asked, "How can one attain awakening?

Yifeng then instructed him to contemplate the character "Lu" (Exposure) from Yunmen’s teaching. Upon hearing this, the Master immediately gained faith and applied himself to it with direct intensity, to the point of forgetting both sleep and food.

He then traveled to Mount Shuangjing and built a thatched hut at the foot of White Cloud Peak. While contemplating the karmic conditions of Master Liang’s encounter with Mazu, his doubts remained unresolved.
One day, upon seeing yellow fragrant rhododendron flowers, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and said: "It is indeed empty space that can preach the sutras;
even common bricks and rubble are fit to listen. All along, I have been twisting my mother-born nose and mistaking a gourd for a melon."
[He carried] a pure water flask. Thereupon, he went to Yunqi and fully obtained the benefit of Master Lianchi’s teachings.
Next, he visited Master Chuan of Longchi. At that time, Master Chuan was basking in the sun beneath the steps. The Master asked, "Where is the Abbot? Chuan replied, "By chance, he is not here.
The Master immediately performed prostrations. Once the formal greetings were concluded, Chuan showed him the verse he had composed on "Deshan Carrying the Alms Bowl."
The Master said, "For now, try composing a verse on it. The Master then composed a verse, saying: "Is there or is there not the final word?
Deshan and his father are too much of a muddle. Born of the same lineage, yet they die of different lineages; Having lived for three years, my regrets grow ever more numerous.
Chuanxi was greatly pleased and said to the Master, "Why do you not take up this matter and join us in chanting and responding? The Master did not consent. Chuanxi...

He constructed bridges and repaired Buddhist monasteries; his meritorious deeds were so numerous they could not all be recorded. Emperor Shen宗 dreamed of the Master’s image and summoned him to court.

He was summoned to the capital, where he was granted purple robes and a monastic title. Upon his passing, he was interred at Mount Tai. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "True Son of the Buddha.
(The name of the master does not appear after the inscription on the Great Thousand-Stone Stele; this is omitted due to uncertainty and is appended here for future reference.)
When Chan Master Nankang Yunju Zhuan Yu Guanheng was traveling on pilgrimage, he once passed through Yunnan. He went to visit Chen Meigong, sending his calling card three times;
however, as the Master was occupied with affairs and had not yet been able to receive him, the Master left a verse and departed.

The verse says: "The inkstone pool has the beauty of the Three Lakes; The brush-stand peaks rise high as nine summits. The scholar reading his books within the hall— A pure breeze blows upon his cloth robe.
When the Official saw this verse, he hurriedly called for a boat to pursue him. By the time he reached Suzhou, the Master had already closed his door and would not see him.

[The Master] composed one hundred verses on "Perfect Penetration" (*yuantong*), the first of which says: "Stretching out my legs, I sleep long beneath the white moon; Its radiance does not yield to [the sun]."
The Crystal Palace: sleeping deeply, one does not dream of Universal Penetration (Samantabhadra). Buddhas and patriarchs are all but passing winds over the ears.

One says: Vast and universal is the Gate of Entry, deep within the deep; ninefold is its remote stillness, even more profound and silent. At the jade steps, the green locks cut off the traveler’s path.
All day long the curtains hang down and not a bird calls. One says: "Whose young lord is so accustomed to gallantry?
In light robes and shallow sandals he roams the brocade market. Drunk at the spring terrace, he loses his way; he does not know his own body is upon Yueyang Tower. Another says:
"The music of flutes and pipes in one's sight can never be fully heard; the crimson characters by one's ear remain discordant. Flying blades and rain-like arrows fall in profusion from the sky."
This is precisely the time of perfect penetration and sovereign freedom.
Dáchéng Shòuzhāo Chánshī was a native of Tōngzhōu; he did not disclose his surname or clan. He once attended upon Tiāntóng Wù and served as a Xītáng (Western Hall Attendant).

Not long after, he suddenly abandoned his position, and no one could fathom his intention. At times he would walk upon ice during the bitter cold; at other times he would ascend [mountains] in the deep of night.

His hair was matted like mountain peaks; sometimes he dressed in the garb of a layman, sometimes in that of a commoner. He would speak to himself alone, exclaiming "Duo duo" incessantly, or discuss matters of ghosts and illusions, causing those who heard him to be filled with doubt and alarm.
When encountered by crowds who bowed around him, he regarded them as mere passersby and would suddenly scold them, saying, "I do not know you."
Or he would bow in return. When the master Qiliu resided in a separate room at Tiantong, his courtesy and reverence were extremely profound.
After a short while, all the beds and seats were suddenly smashed and thrown down the steps. The assembly was stunned, not knowing what it meant.

As they rearranged the furnishings once more, the Master immediately closed the door and remained silent. When the porridge and rice were brought in through the window, the disciples called out their names one by one from outside the door.
Whenever he went to pay his respects, the Master would not admit him. One day, he suddenly departed and was never heard from again. The fourfold assembly grieved and longed for him.
Muchun Men erected a stupa for the Master's spiritual conduct.
Qinglin Rujian (青林如鑑) was a senior monk from the Lin clan of Hou'an. At the age of eighteen, he resolved his will upon the Way.
He left the mountains to pay homage to Yunqi Zhuhong and later studied under Xiansheng Zhencheng. While contemplating the "Mu" (無字) koan, he attained a realization and presented it in verse, saying:
"Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; I have stripped off my trousers to cover my face. But the face has not been fully covered— Half of the body remains exposed."
His outward appearance was loathsome. Cheng stroked him and sealed him with his approval. The Master did not consider himself worthy of this. Later, he returned to Min to visit his parents;
upon shaving his head, he again crossed the mountain pass to attend upon Cheng. After a long time, he returned to Gushan and resided in the Eastern Hermitage.

When Master Wuyi of Boshan began teaching the Dharma on this mountain, [Foyin] harbored a profound devotion toward him from the start and served him with all his heart. He subsequently claimed to have attained the essential meaning of the teachings. From that time forward, he remained deeply reclusive.
Toujiao practiced in secret and refined his cultivation in solitude until the age of eighty-seven, when he manifested his passing at his former hermitage in Shilin.
For seven days, a golden-colored light shone forth and a fragrant aroma wafted through the air. The wooden rosary he had carried throughout his life remained intact.
Chan Master □□□ was a native of Huguang. His clan name was Ning. At the age of nineteen, he went to Zhuan-yu Heng to receive the tonsure.
Later, he visited Tian-tong Wu and attended him for a long time. One day, seeing the Master lifting a stone, Wu suddenly shouted, "Turn that stone over!
At these words, the Master attained realization. Wu deeply approved of this. The following day, the Master took his leave and retired to a secluded place to build a thatched hut.
Yin later resided in Jingjiang Prefecture. Disciples gathered daily, yet the Master never accepted them; he muttered incessantly, his chanting of Buddhist hymns (*brahman*) never ceasing.
Whenever anyone requested instruction, he would rebuke them, saying, "Go away and practice! On the first day of the fifth month of the Renzi year of the Kangxi era, he manifested slight illness.
On the eighth day, he summoned his disciples into his room and asked them, "Do you still know Old [Shen]?"
"Is this where the monks go? En the attendant said, "The bright moon clearly illuminates the traveler at night.
The Master said, "That is a cliché. En asked, "What is your own intention, Master? The Master said, "Not born in the year of Renyin; not dying in the year of Renzi. "Speak again," he said.
[The monk] said, "I was born in the year of Renyin, yet I died in the year of Renzi. The Master raised his voice and shouted, "How can you defile an old monk like this?
[The monk] asked, "Ultimately, what is it? The Master showed him a verse: "Cloudy paths but a few inches away, yet spanning ninety provinces."
